title: ‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in? | Movies | The Guardian
description: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?
Content: Radical transparency? … Elizabeth Holmes with Nathan Fielder in the background in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24View image in fullscreenRadical transparency? … Elizabeth Holmes with Nathan Fielder in the background in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24Movies‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in?With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?Henry RobertsWed 21 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInYou Can See Everything, convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invites film-makers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into her home in a supposed act of “radical transparency”. Holmes is filmed, along with her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children, in the weeks before starting a prison sentence for defrauding Theranos investors. “The best way for people to see who she is,” Evans says, “is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”. It may also be the best way to market “Theranos 2.0”, which the couple are working on during filming. But the documentary questions whether Holmes is presenting her authentic self or a manufactured persona. Fielder speaks for the audience when he asks Holmes in a tense exchange whether she’s “being real” with him. “I’m always being real,” she says.That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew?You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreSome people, like Holmes, think a documentary will help rebuild their reputation after public disgrace. When Anthony Weiner, who resigned from Congress after tweeting a photo of his bulging groin, tried to stage a professional comeback with a New York mayoral bid, he allowed cameras to film the journey. Only, he had more to hide: when further sex scandals emerged, his campaign went from a story of public redemption to innuendo-laden humiliation. And all the while, the cameras kept rolling.Weineris a prime example of a subject losing control of the narrative.View image in fullscreenHumiliation … Launching a New York mayoral bid, Anthony Weiner, with wife Huma Abedin, 23 July 2013.Photograph: Kathy Willens/APWeiner may have wanted a sympathetic portrayal, but he should have known that film-makers always have their own agendas. In the book The Journalist and the Murderer,Janet Malcolmreflects on the relationship between journalists and their subjects: “The subject becomes a kind of child of the writer, regarding him as a permissive, all-accepting, all-forgiving mother, and expecting the book to be written by her. Of course, the book is written by the strict, all-noticing, unforgiving father.” The same is surely true of the documentarian.When Jackie and David Siegel allowed Lauren Greenfield to film their attempt to build a modern-day Versailles in Florida, the director wasn’t giving them free PR. Rather, withThe Queen of Versailles, Greenfield was interested in the corrosive effects of extreme wealth. The Siegels agreed to be filmed because they were proud of their success. When their dream collapsed following the 2008 financial crash, The Queen of Versailles turned from a story of Xanadu-like grandeur to one of hubristic overreach. David later sued Lauren – unsuccessfully – for defamation, but he should have known from the beginning: it may have been his story, but it was never his film.A few years after Versailles, Greenfield madeThe Kingmaker, about former first lady of the Philippines Imelda Marcos and her attempt to return the family to power. From the beginning of the film,Greenfield said, there was a power struggle over who was telling the story. Marcos, known for her lavish lifestyle during her husband’s brutal rule, understood the power of optics. In a children’s cancer ward, she hands out money to children in a public display of compassion. “Perception is real,” Marcos says in the film, “and the truth is not.”Some people agree to projects believing they will have editorial control. Idi Amin gave Barbet Schroeder unprecedented access after the director essentially promised that they would make the film together. But Amin was unhappy with General Idi Amin Dada: A Self Portrait and demanded some footage be cut, rounding up more than 100 French residents in Uganda and holding them hostage until his demands were met. Schroeder agreed. It helps to be as ruthless as Amin if you want final cut.Documentaries are often about the past, but some of cinema’s most memorable moments show people acting violently in the present, fully aware that they are being filmed.Frederick Wiseman’s austere filmsshow abuse in psychiatric institutions (Titicut Follies) and horrific police violence (Law and Order). Why did people do unspeakable things in front of a camera? “People basically go about their business,”Wiseman told an interviewer, “and the presence of the camera doesn’t have much, if any effect on their behaviour.”View image in fullscreenMorally complex … a scene from The Act Of Killing, 2012.Photograph: Real/Novaya Ze/Rex/ShutterstockBut cameras did have an effect on the subjects ofJoshua Oppenheimer’s The Act of Killing, probably the most morally complex example of the film-maker-subject relationship in cinema history. Perpetrators of Indonesia’s mass killings gleefully re-enact their crimes, restaging their violent memories in the style of Hollywood movies. They do not profess their innocence. Rather, they agree to be filmed because they are proud of what they did. They really do want us to see everything.UK cinemas report ‘bonkers’ demand for documentary You Can See EverythingRead morePerhaps the most interesting case of someone willingly putting themselves under scrutiny is Lance Armstrong.Alex Gibney’s documentary on Armstrongwas expected to be a puff piece. When the full extent of Armstrong’s doping was revealed, however, Gibney’s film changed direction, becoming a documentary not on a cyclist’s triumph but on a master manipulator who lied to everyone, including the film-maker. In The Armstrong Lie, Armstrong admits that he “was prepared to say anything” to keep his lie going.Some people are simply arrogant enough to think they can get away with their lies. But others become so invested in their skewed version of reality that to refuse a documentary crew would be like admitting their deception. So they welcome the cameras, often doing more damage than if they had simply retreated from public view. But unlike Armstrong, Holmes still insists she has done nothing wrong. As she says in You Can See Everything: “I have nothing to hide.”Explore more on these topicsFilmYou Can See EverythingElizabeth HolmesNathan FielderLance ArmstrongTheranosAnthony WeinerfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Don’t sweat the small stuff’: hospice workers share 12 lessons about life and death | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Hospice and end-of-life workers discuss what they’ve learned from their work and patients in their last moments
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: Hospice and end-of-life workers discuss what they’ve learned from their work and patients in their last moments
Content: ‘The best way to have a good death experience for all involved is to be able to have conversations about it with your loved ones.’Illustration: Ibrahim Rayintakath/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The best way to have a good death experience for all involved is to be able to have conversations about it with your loved ones.’Illustration: Ibrahim Rayintakath/The GuardianMemento mori: a series about deathWell actually‘Don’t sweat the small stuff’: hospice workers share 12 lessons about life and deathHospice and end-of-life workers discuss what they’ve learned from their work and patients in their last momentsMadeleine AggelerWed 21 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTShare“Hospice” can be a loaded term. Some see it as synonymous with death and “giving up”, as Courtney, a full-time hospice nurse practitioner in Missouri, puts it. But Courtney, who asked that her last name be withheld for privacy reasons, doesn’t see it that way.“Hospice is giving someone a gift,” she says of her patients, who have typically received a terminal diagnosis with a timeline of six months or less. “It is giving them the gift of being able to stay at home and eat or not eat whatever they want. It is the gift of comfort.”Courtney first started working with dying patients when she was an oncology nurse. Patients would come to her from the intensive care unit (ICU) or other areas of the hospital when they had a limited time to live and were on comfort measures only – a medical term for care that focuses on relieving pain and distress rather than prolonging life.“I fell in love with it,” says Courtney. She loved getting the rooms ready, dimming the lights, and creating a gentle, pleasant atmosphere for the patient and their families to say their goodbyes.After a brief stint working in the ICU, Courtney began working in hospice care full-time. She says her job has reshaped how she approaches her life both personally and professionally. We spoke to her and other hospice and end-of-life workers about what they’ve learned from their work and their patients.Have open conversations about death“The best way to have a good death experience for all involved is to be able to have conversations about it with your loved ones,” says Penny Smith, a recently retired hospice nurse of 20 years who lives in Washington state.People are often reluctant to discuss death, experts say, either because they are worried about upsetting their loved ones or because of superstition.‘We live in grief-phobic societies’: experts on how to get more comfortable with deathRead more“People think that talking about [death] is going to make it happen faster,” says Dr Luyi Kathy Zhang, director of the palliative care serenity unit at Bellevue hospital in New York City. “It seems silly when you say it out loud, but it is a real fear people have because the topic is so uncomfortable.”But open dialogue “ensures that your end of life wishes are met”, says Smith, whether it’s what music you’d like to listen to when you’re dying, or whom you would like to be in the room.Death can be beautifulDeath often brings up painful feelings like fear, loss and discomfort. But Courtney says it can be a beautiful experience as well.“That’s something we get to see with hospice. Someone dying at home, surrounded by loved ones, listening to music and sharing stories,” she says.“Death can be sad,” agrees Zhang. “But there’s so much beauty in being able to witness the amount of love and devotion between people which gets magnified at the end of life.”Don’t wait to check off items on your‘bucket list’Too often, we put off our goals and dreams indefinitely, figuring we’ll get to them when we have more time, more money, more energy. But our time is not infinite, hospice workers emphasize.“So many of my patients waited to take the vacation of their lifetime and were never able to,” says Smith.Zhang hears lots of patients talk about how they regret not following their dreams or pursuing what they wanted because of fear of judgment, risk and the unknown.“We all think that we’re going to live to 80, 90 or 100, but that’s not the case for everyone,” she says. “Just go for things.”Know what you can controlWorking with death highlights how little of life is in our control, says Courtney.“I cannot control what is happening in somebody’s body,” she says. “I can’t control cancer, I can’t control COPD [chronic obstructive pulmonary disease], I can’t control any of those things.”‘Death is not a mystery’: what happens to your body when you’re dying?Read moreBut knowing what is outside our control can make more clear what is in our control.“By the time someone gets to be my patient, I can’t control those other things they have going on, but what I can control is making sure that they have their wishes honored, that their loved ones are cared for,” Courtney says. “I can ensure they have dignity, and that their death is a phenomenal, beautiful thing.”Nurture relationships“A lot of people are alone at the end of life for one reason or another,” says Zhang.Many of Zhang’s patients tell her about people they miss or friends they regret losing touch with.Seeing this, she says, has made her more intentional about cultivating the relationships in her life. She tells herself: “‘I am going to be the one to reach out and try to have a meetup. And if people aren’t reaching out to me, I’ll be the one to do it, because it’s important to me.”Keep things in perspectivePut differently: “Don’t sweat the small stuff,” says Courtney.Working with death day in and day out has made this easier for her, she says, because it “puts into perspective what is worth reacting to and what’s not”.When she’s stuck in traffic or dealing with minor inconveniences, Courtney says she tells herself: “If I’m fortunate enough to live to be 80 years old or I’m on my deathbed, I’m not going to be thinking about this.”Be presentZhang says the greatest lesson she has taken from her work in end-of-life care is “being present, and taking advantage of and being grateful for the life I have”.Before joining this field, Zhang says she was always wondering about the next thing she had to do or achieve. This isn’t necessarily a bad idea, she says, but it led her to neglect where she was at that moment.“I’m so much more grateful for the little things – even waking up and being able to enjoy coffee,” she says.Everyone is someone’s favorite personThis reminder from a colleague years ago changed the way Courtney worked.“We are so used to compartmentalizing death,” she says. “But when we step into that room, that isn’t just Mr Johnson – it’s also Sara’s dad.”This can help you remember that other people are human, and make you feel more patient and generous, even if someone is cutting you off in traffic.A job is just a jobCourtney considers hospice work her passion. But even so, her patients remind her all the time that a job is just a job, and that there is more to life.Tell us: are you a single woman? We want to know about your relationship to sexRead more“Even though it’s meaningful, we have to be able to leave that at the door sometimes,” Courtney says.People want to know their life matteredWhen trying to comfort someone in their last moments, loved ones will often tell them that it is “OK to go”. But in Smith’s experience, what people really want to hear at the end of their days is that “their life had meaning and purpose”.‘You laugh a little, you leak a little’A patient said this to Courtney once, and it has stayed with her. “It was just so funny,” she says: a reminder that life is delightful and messy, often at the same time.Gone but not forgottenThis doesn’t just apply to those we love the most, but also so many others, Courtney says. “There are little interactions with patients that I remember from years and years ago,” she says.“I think that’s beautiful, because at the end of the day we don’t get to leave much on this earth except the impact we had and what we’re remembered for,” she adds.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyMemento mori: a series about deathHospicesBereavementDeath and dyingShare

title: Can UK pop cut immigration and stop the boats? I suppose we’ll find out with GB News Music Radio | John Harris | The Guardian
description: An ‘all British, all day’ station is a nativist dream come true – but good luck with the playlist. And anyway: how many artists will want to be on Farage FM? asks Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: An ‘all British, all day’ station is a nativist dream come true – but good luck with the playlist. And anyway: how many artists will want to be on Farage FM? asks Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: ‘What will happen in the case of, say, the Gallagher brothers, who self-identify as Irish?’ Noel Gallagher on stage with Oasis at Maine Road, Manchester, April 1996.Photograph: Ilpo Musto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘What will happen in the case of, say, the Gallagher brothers, who self-identify as Irish?’ Noel Gallagher on stage with Oasis at Maine Road, Manchester, April 1996.Photograph: Ilpo Musto/ShutterstockOpinionGB NewsCan UK pop cut immigration and stop the boats? I suppose we’ll find out with GB News Music RadioJohn HarrisAn ‘all British, all day’ station is a nativist dream come true – but good luck with the playlist. And anyway: how many artists will want to be on Farage FM?Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTShareIf you want a quintessential “It wouldn’t happen now” story, try this. Two months before Margaret Thatcher became prime minister in May 1979, a national Militant Entertainment Tour wasorganised byRock Against Racism.On 20 March 1979, itcame to the West Runton Pavilionnear Cromer, the (very) small town on the coastal edge of East Anglia. The bill mixed the black and white musicians in three bands then at their artistic peak – the post-punk maestros Gang of Four, the punk-reggae hybridists The Ruts, and Misty in Roots, the renowned reggae collective from Southall in west London – and thereby made a stark symbolic point: that the multiracial nature of large swathes of the UK was not to be decried or attacked, but actively celebrated.The UK was then – and some of this may sound familiar – in a bitter, polarised state, seemingly locked into deep economic problems, amid rising fear about the neo-fascist National Front. The previous year,Thatcher had said– and this may feel familiar, too – that British people “were really rather afraid that this country might be rather swamped by people with a different culture.” Amid such a grim political atmosphere, RAR and the musicians who supported it felt duty-bound to try pulling their audiences away from such toxicity, and point out that what we now call diversity was something to be celebrated.Nearly half a century on, the lack of any comparable cultural response to this country’s equally unsettling current state seems quite remarkable. There is, then, a vacant cultural-political space – and look what has now come along to fill it. GB News, that bracingly rightwing TV channel whose regular faces include Nigel Farage, the Reform MP Lee Anderson and the party’s failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin, is about tolaunch a music radio station.According to its promotional blurb, it will be “dedicated exclusively to artists from Great Britain and Northern Ireland”, with tagline “all British, all day”. By way of further explanation, one of its presenters, the blackGB Newshost Nana Akua, says that “It’s easy to forget how this country has shaped the global music landscape” – a strange point instantly disproved by a mention of any number of artists (such as those four fairly successful fellas from Liverpool). But here, perhaps, is the strangest thing of all: according to GB Media, every track on the station’s playlist will be an “artist from Great Britain or Northern Ireland, or where the main proportion of the band is British.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yet | Polly ToynbeeRead moreThis sparks no end of questions. Does anyone in the ordinary world actually perceive music like this? Will someone frantically be employed to sift through Wikipedia, finding out whether this or that band fits the “main proportion” criterion? What will happen in the case of, say, the Gallagher brothers,who self-identify as Irish– and should, therefore, be excluded for the same reasons as U2, CMAT and Fontaines DC? Should the Jimi Hendrix Experience be ruled in or out, given that the two supporting members of the trio were respectively from Ealing and Folkestone? And to get into the real nitty-gritty, how exactly are the programmers defining “British”?We all know the jaw-dropping conversations taking place in GB News-adjacent circles about national identity. TheTory-to-Reform defectorsRobert Jenrick and Suella Braverman seeEnglishness as an ethnic identity. If this definition wins out, which is quite conceivable, what will happen then? A playlist cull that will leave little apart from the musical equivalent of sliced white bread?There are more fascinating questions to ask. There hasbeen an on-off debateabout whether Britpop was partly responsible for Brexit. As the writer of abook about that cultural wave, I have always clung on to the idea that because its nationalistic(ish) animus was focused on the US, and the demographics of Leave voters do not map on to the Britpop generation, no one had any case to answer. But this latest development brings on a slight pang of unease. In retrospect, the large-scale whiteness of Britpop was, as we say these days, rather problematic. On a musical level, it accounts for its chronically limited range of influences and inputs, which led to it burning out pretty quickly. But it also left it open to what might turn out to be a belated act of appropriation: whatever music the new station plays, I would imagine that Oasis, Blur, Pulp et al will be an integral part of its output. Put another way, the Farage-ist tanks are now surely heading for Britpop’s metaphorical lawn.That piping hot new TV show I just watched? I can’t recall a thing about it | Zoe WilliamsRead moreInquiries to a couple of music lawyers established that musicians cannot stop radio stations that possess the relevant licences and pay the required royalties from playing their material. Self-evidently, however, they could quite easily express their displeasure at the prospect of being part of a constant Farage-ist soundtrack. In the excellent new Oasis documentary, Don’t Look Back in Anger, Noel Gallagherrightly saysthat his band was never “a rightwing thing … All are welcome. It’s we and us.” In the context of GB Music Radio, he should translate that into something slightly more specific. So should the already embattled Ed Sheeran, Adele, what remains of the Rolling Stones, the former members of Dire Straits and everyone else who is – and isn’t – mentioned in the station’s launch statement. The music all of them make, after all, is founded on precisely the kind of cultural mixing that so many voices associated with GB News take against.Oh, and one last thing. This message needs to be out there in the fabric of people’s lives, not only pouring out of their phones, but arriving in their towns. The West Runton Pavilion was demolished in 1986. But imagine some modern equivalent of Militant Entertainment pitching up on the Essex coast, the old Nottinghamshire coalfield, the seaside towns of Kent, or any number of Reform’s supposed heartlands. Is that really now as inconceivable as it seems?John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGB NewsOpinionReform UKOasisPop and rockcommentShareReuse this content

title: Too much Overlap? Gary Neville’s podcast empire knows no bounds | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The Overlap has gone daily, with Steven Gerrard and Joe Hart among the latest additions to an ever-growing family
Author: John Brewin
Headline: The Overlap has gone daily, with Steven Gerrard and Joe Hart among the latest additions to an ever-growing family
Content: Ian Wright (left) and Gary Neville have helped give The Overlap a TV family dynamic.Photograph: The OverlapView image in fullscreenIan Wright (left) and Gary Neville have helped give The Overlap a TV family dynamic.Photograph: The OverlapSoccerToo much Overlap? Gary Neville’s podcast empire knows no boundsThe Overlap has gone daily, with Steven Gerrard and Joe Hart among the latest additions to an ever-growing familyJohn BrewinWed 21 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleViewed in 2026, Nathan Barley, Chris Morris’s 2005 sitcom, showsremarkable prescienceabout the last two decades of metropolitan life, from smartphone addiction and digital derangement to sheer existential vapidity. When Barley’s character referred to his occupation as “self-facilitating media node”, Morris and co-writer Charlie Brooker were way ahead on the creator economy. What the pair failed to predict was ex-footballers joining the sector in droves. These days, if you are a former footballer without a podcast or YouTube channel, then did you ever really play the game?Setting aside the Gary Lineker Goalhanger empire, manspreading its centrist-dad agenda into issues way beyond guffaws with Micah Richards and Alan Shearer, there isGary Nevilleto rule them all. Manchesterism’s second-most influential practitioner has been on heavy manoeuvres. Unlike Lineker’s productions, the Overlap’s output continues to stick largely to football; a rugby podcast was mothballed in February, though its cricket equivalent continues.Dwight Yorke: ‘I’m not a kid trying to get into management – I’m a manager’Read moreHaving snatched Wayne Rooney from the BBC in the summer for a Manchester United-based two-hander with the YouTuber Mark Goldbridge, last week the Overlap went daily, extending the output to 4pm Monday to Friday. An online launch had Jamie Carragher baiting Goldbridge, real name Brent Di Cesare. The former policeman shunned a “no comment” approach during his interrogation, biting back during an exchange that had Neville choking on his Huel in laughter. Clipped up, the send button pressed, job done.The Overlap has gained a TV family dynamic, a chorus line of familiar characters. Neville and Carragher are mummy and daddy bear, football’s Richard and Judy. Jill Scott is the dotty aunt, Roy Keane the irascible uncle, smirking along with Ian Wright in picking over the latest gossip. It has been highly popular, occasionally agenda-setting, softening Keane’s image, even making a cultish figure of production hand Kiaran Saunders, supplier of biscuits and blueberries. Neville’s empire-building, though, is boundless, his tanks bulldozing into the already packed football podcast space, with newsletters to follow. The Overkill, anyone?The family has been extended. Mondays have Steven Gerrard reviewing the weekend’s action with Becky Ives, this week offering a defence of Florian Wirtz: “Don’t give up on him.” Tuesdays have Kelly Cates and Ashley Young in tandem. Tim Sherwood and Jamie Redknapp are Wednesday’s pairing. Not the first time the Sky mainstays, one-time Tottenham midfield partners, have diversified. In the mid-2000s, they ran Icon, a lifestyle magazine initially only available to professional players. A combination of high-end advertising, onanistic photography and Redknapp’s purring interviews with A-list sportspeople fell flat, even after it became available in airport first-class lounges.View image in fullscreenBecky Ives and Steven Gerrard breakdown the weekend’s action.Photograph: Global Media / Sky VegasTwo decades on, such cologne-fragrant exclusivity has been swapped for the ubiquity of Bury’s most famous son piling it high. The quarter-zipped ex-Spurs duo are not alone as 1990s footballers taking the Neville shilling. Mark Crossley and Duncan Ferguson make an unlikely – but promising – pairing. Previously most famous for being the only goalkeeper to save a Matthew Le Tissier penalty, Crossley has made a successful after-dinner speaking career of Brian Clough anecdotes and “young man” impressions. “Big Dunc” completely refused to speak to the media when a player but he was a hit within ITV’s World Cup 2026 coverage.On last week’s edition Ferguson suggested Gianluigi Donnarumma might be over the hill. “He’s 27, actually,” said Crossley before a classic game’s gone discussion of video assistant referees ruining the sacred art of smashing into the opposition at goal-kicks. Just what the listener came for, eating perhaps into the Under The Cosh’s market share of real football man podcasts. Whether Ferguson’s appointment as Glentoran manager breaks up the band is unclear, though management never halted Robbie Savage’s many media ventures.Two further goalkeepers have signed up. Last week’s Friday edition had Joe Hart and Peter Schmeichel entering the Manchester City charges chat. While admitting to mistakenly burying the lead when Lisandro Martínez was willingly dishing the dirt on Manchester United while serving as CBS’s Champions League interviewer in Madrid last Tuesday, Schmeichel gave Hart a far harder ride. “It’s tough to be a Manchester City person,” Hart said. “I love the club … we’re in it together.” Schmeichel stayed insistent on City’s owners: “They’re letting Manchester down, they don’t understand what this place is. They have built a lot of towers and homes and all that but they don’t get this place.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I’ve worked closely with Khaldoon [al-Mubarak] and he does get this place, that’s my reference point,” said a hesitant Hart. “He’s an incredible person.” More good, strong, clip-up content.The City affair will ask former players to intersect with uncomfortable issues for some while yet. That Neville’s further business interests include building projects running parallel to the Abu Dhabi-funded developments in Manchester is another example. Overlaps have become unavoidable in more ways than one.Explore more on these topicsFootballGary NevillePodcastingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He had this electrical charge’: the short life and long legacy of Jason Molina, master of Americana | Music | The Guardian
description: As a documentary celebrates the late US musician, friends and collaborators describe an incomparable storyteller who brought ‘myth and magic to everyday life’
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: As a documentary celebrates the late US musician, friends and collaborators describe an incomparable storyteller who brought ‘myth and magic to everyday life’
Content: ‘These are all time country songs’ … Jason Molina performing as The Magnolia Electric Co at All Tomorrows Parties in 2007.Photograph: Gary Wolstenholme/RedfernsView image in fullscreen‘These are all time country songs’ … Jason Molina performing as The Magnolia Electric Co at All Tomorrows Parties in 2007.Photograph: Gary Wolstenholme/RedfernsMusic‘He had this electrical charge’: the short life and long legacy of Jason Molina, master of AmericanaAs a documentary celebrates the late US musician, friends and collaborators describe an incomparable storyteller who brought ‘myth and magic to everyday life’Daniel Dylan WrayWed 21 Oct 2026 11.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJason Molina grew up in a trailer in the working-class city of Lorain, Ohio. The city’s skyline once flickered with blue flames and a warm orange glow emanated from clattering steel mills, but by Molina’s teenage years, Lorain was in a tailspin. “Things were really on the economic decline,” says Tommy Nickoloff, Molina’s childhood friend and director of a new documentary: You Fuckers Figure It Out: A Jason Molina Story. “Nobody had any money and we were encouraged to get out. It’s a place where the American dream was born and died. And we watched it die.”Molina did indeed get out: the singer-songwriter released almost 20 studio albums and numerous EPs, primarily under the monikers Songs: Ohia and Magnolia Electric Co, spanning lo-fi to slowcore via polishedAmericanaand alt-country. By 2009, he estimated he had written thousands of songs. But he died in 2013, aged 39, after years of alcoholism.View image in fullscreen‘It still shocks me how few people are aware of Jason and his legacy’ … Tommy Nickoloff.Photograph: Courtesy Tommy NickoloffThe documentary is a warm and intimate look back on Molina’s early life and how his rust belt upbringing, along with notions of home, place and landscape, became recurring themes in his bountiful songs. The audience for them has kept growing after his death: there’s been a biography, cover albums, a touring tribute band titled Magnolia & Johnson Electric Co made up of ex-bandmates, and he’s got a new generation of fans in Phoebe Bridgers, MJ Lenderman, Clairo, Kevin Morby, Waxahatchee and hyped young singer-songwriters such as Greg Freeman. “You have a moment with a handful of artists in your life where you hear their music and it clicks and you immediately fall in love,” says Freeman. “That happened with Jason’s music.”But this wasn’t always the case. “It still shocks me how few people are aware of Jason and his legacy, especially around home,” says Nickoloff, recalling a 2006 show in nearby Cleveland that drew just 70 people.When Songs: Ohia started in the mid-1990s, it was via lo-fi skeletal songs recorded to tape that were tender yet raw and delivered with a quivering high tenor reminiscent of Neil Young and soon-to-be collaborator Will Oldham. As grunge and alt-rock boomed, Molina went against the grain. “There was nothing less cool than a ukulele in 1994,” laughs his former bandmate Max Winter in the film. “Holy shit, he may as well have been playing bagpipes.”But Molina was unique from a young age. A voracious reader as a child, he consumed everything from instruction manuals to foreign language poetry. His teenage years were spent as a metalhead and by the time he was at college, his fervent, enthusiastic – sometimes annoying – energy earned him the nickname “sparky”. Now writing a song a day, he would sometimes play impromptu 5am shows on a roof or porch to show them off. “I’ve never met anyone like him,” says Nickoloff. “He’s like a 20-sided die in Dungeons and Dragons. Most people are lucky if they have six sides.”Chris Swanson, co-founder of record label Secretly Canadian, heard Molina’s first single, Nor Cease Thou Never Now, and was besotted. “We obsessively played it and drove 19 hours to New York to go see him,” he says. Songs: Ohia was the label’s second ever signing and a lifelong relationship began. “Without him there would be no us – plain and simple,” the label said after his death. A pattern of releasing at least an album a year followed, including 2000’s The Lioness, in which he decamped to Scotland to work with Alasdair Roberts and members of Arab Strap on a ghostly yet beautiful record of post-rock-folk-blues.Emma Niblett, who performs as Scout Niblett, was a friend, collaborator and touring partner of Molina’s. “He had this electrical charge around him, which matched his nickname,” she recalls. “And he had this ability to bring myth and magic to everyday life as a master of storytelling. You never quite knew if his stories were true or fantasy or a bit of both.”The late producer Steve Albini, who worked with Molina, also recalled this blurring of truths. “He was a big bullshitter,” Albini said in 2014. “A lot of the things that he said were fantastic and it seemed like he wanted things to be magical and awesome, and that he needed to create fables for himself to inhabit in order to do that.” Swanson describes this unusual quirk as “the elephant in every room with Jason”, adding: “He was just a consummate storyteller and if that meant him saying he was bitten by a tarantula which ended up quasi-paralysing him, then that’s the story.”This seeped into his songwriting too: Molina’s obsession with ghosts and hauntings added an otherworldly element to his work. “The songs belong in his own secret world,” says Freeman. “There’s an internal logic and language to his songwriting, the way motifs reappear and build this imaginary psychic place. Like he’s painting a dream.” Niblett describes him as “a magician”, “incomparable” and “a one-off, playing in a major league by himself”.In 2003, Molina released his magnum opus, Songs: Ohia’s The Magnolia Electric Co (confusingly, the name of the album then became the name of the band afterwards). Mike Brenner’s stunning, shimmering lap steel is all over the record. “When I was sent the demos, I was stunned by how much of a quantum leap it was,” he says of the progress from the previous record. “It sounded like a whole different game.” Swanson felt similarly. “You can hear it in the demos but when they made the album, it just became effervescent,” he says. “The songs had stepped up by a full magnitude of order and they just sounded timeless. It was like, holy shit! These are all-time country songs.”View image in fullscreen‘Supernatural powers’ … Jason Molina on stage at Primavera Sound in 2009.Photograph: Jordi Vidal/RedfernsProduced by Albini, with a full band, it was a lightning in a bottle moment for all involved. “The most otherworldly experience I’ve ever had in a studio,” says Niblett. “It felt like some supernatural powers were present. His writing felt like pure channelling. It was so clear, vulnerable, yet insightful, and undeniable. We all knew that something special was occurring.”However, changing your name halfway through your career is not an ideal scenario to help boost your profile. “It was very tricky,” says Swanson. “And this was also during the era when he’d go on tour and not play any songs from the album he’d just released, and only play ones that no one’s heard before.” Molina was driven, prolific, and at times stubborn and impatient: “He wasn’t super interested in doing things twice,” says Brenner.He was also capricious, says Brenner, which Swanson also recalls. “Very generous, sometimes to his own detriment,” he says. “He’d be like, ‘I just gave away our guarantee [fee] for the show to someone on the street who looked hungry.’ He would do very irrational things out of a generous impulse.”Molina continued to release albums and EPs at a remarkable pace but by the end of the 2000s things slowed down. “The later it got in the story, the more stressful and darker the touring became,” says Brenner. “It became less enjoyable and I don’t think the quality of the shows were at the forefront of his mind.” Niblett recalls seeing a change when watching him perform. “He seemed to slowly disappear,” she says. “Although he was present on stage, his presence diminished. He started leaning on the band to take the weight, so his powerful, unique, and nuanced way of carrying a song was fading. I could hear and see he had lost himself. He was literally hiding behind his band in the later years.”Unbeknown to many, Molina had begun to drink heavily. “He was a very light drinker in his 20s,” says Swanson. “But in his 30s, he went whole hog.” This eventually led to debilitating alcoholism that meant he retreated and stopped releasing music in 2009. The last four years of his life are described by his family as “pure chaos” in the documentary. For those who knew the young Molina, “it was unbelievable,” says Nickoloff. “It made zero sense. To the degree it was like: I don’t know anybody else named Jason Molina but they have to be talking about that person.”‘His ache is real’: Bob Dylan and more on the wild genius of honky-tonk hellraiser Gary StewartRead moreSwanson recalls visiting him a few months before his death in Indianapolis. “He had given away all his belongings, which was something he would do routinely,” he says. “So he was living in a shell. We made the decision to move him to Bloomington, where he had more of a community, as his community was with street people in Indianapolis around the projects he was living in.”But a week after that decision was made, Molina died of organ failure related to his alcoholism. “I honestly wouldn’t have believed it if you’d have told me years earlier that’s how his life would end,” says Niblett. “I don’t think the shock ever leaves.”Despite being a heartache of enormous magnitude, for Nickoloff it ended up changing his life in numerous ways. “Jason’s death saved my life,” he says. “I was in a terrible spot emotionally and psychologically. He’d always been this beacon for me, and then he’s gone. But as a kid he was the only voice that was encouraging and believed in me to do something. So, in that spirit, we made this film and what a tremendous pleasure it is to be a small vehicle in helping make people more familiar with him, his work and his life. He was my homeboy.”You Fuckers Figure It Out: A Jason Molina Story premieres 25 October (Rio Cinema) and 8 November (ICA) at London’s Doc’n Roll film festivalExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockIndieMusic documentaryAmericanafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best Kindles in the UK for every bookworm and budget – tested | Kindle | The Guardian
description: Whether you want a colour screen, somewhere to scribble notes or a child-friendly model, here’s what we recommend from Amazon’s e-reader range
Author: Andrew Williams
Headline: Whether you want a colour screen, somewhere to scribble notes or a child-friendly model, here’s what we recommend from Amazon’s e-reader range
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterKindleReviewThe best Kindles in the UK for every bookworm and budget – testedWhether you want a colour screen, somewhere to scribble notes or a child-friendly model, here’s what we recommend from Amazon’s e-reader rangeThe best e-readersAndrew WilliamsWed 21 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom that fresh paperback smell to the wrinkles in the spine, nothing beats a real book. But if you’re sick of the space they take up in your home, or the weight they steal from your holiday luggage allowance, it might be worth considering an AmazonKindle. It can fit thousands of weighty reads into as little as 158g, and as tech goes, it’s almost immune to the sort of pathological time-wasting features that come with modern phones and tablets.Amazon Kindles have been available in the UK for more than 15 years, so they’re an old-school gadget at this point. But in 2024, the biggest update yet arrived: colour, which added an important extra option to the existing Kindle lineup, alongside readers for children, for note-taking and for tighter budgets.With so many modern versions available now, I spent months testing them to analyse their pros and cons to help you find the best Kindle for your needs.A note on Kindle’s next generationAmazon clearly has a sense of humour, because no less than one day after I’d finished writing this guide the brand announced a whole new range of Kindles. I will keep this page updated with how the new line compares once I have fully tested them.Available to preorder ahead of their release on 11 November, theKindle PaperwhiteandColorsoftwill be a little lighter and thinner than their predecessors, with a fetching new array of colours.More significant changes have been made to the Signature Edition models, trading plastic backing for an aluminium one. But it’s the basic Kindle that’ll get the biggest upgrade, with the raised screen border replaced for a flat end-to-end design like the Paperwhite. There are Kids editions of thesee-readerscoming, too.The good news about fresh launches is that the models tested here are far more likely to be slashed in price, so you could save some money.At a glanceBest Kindle overallKindlePaperwhite (2024)£184.99 at AmazonBest budget KindleAmazonKindle (2024)£134.99 at ArgosBest Kindle for kidsKindleColorsoft Kids£274.99 at John LewisBest Kindle for note-takingKindleScribe Colorsoft£569 at AmazonBest budget Kindle for kidsKindleKids£159.99 at John LewisBest colour KindleKindleColorsoft (2024)£239.99 at AmazonWhy you should trust meI’m a long-term e-reader user; I first tried one in place of paperbacks in 2009, the Sony PRS-505, a year before the first Kindle arrived in the UK. Since then I have tested almost every member of the Kindle family going. From theKindle Fire HD(which some say never deserved the Kindle name at all because it’s more tablet than e-reader) to fondly remembered classics such as the Kindle Voyage and Oasis, I’ve lived with them all, for better and worse. I keep coming back to Kindles over other e-readers for their simplicity and reliability – and for Amazon’s ever-changing Kindle book sales.Most of my book reading is done on e-readers these days. Light, portable and ideal for bedtime reading, e-readers are among my favourite pieces of tech – even if nothing can quite replace the nostalgic charm of a real paperback.How I testedView image in fullscreenWell read: some of the Kindles were tested for about six months.Photograph: Andrew Williams/The GuardianTo test a Kindle, you need to live with one for a while. Many keep ebook readers for a decade or more – they can be remarkably long-lasting – so a cursory test wasn’t going to cut it.While I’ve tried each of these devices as my personal e-reader for several weeks (at the very least), I’ve used the key Colorsoft and Paperwhite readers for about six months, on and off. And for the Kindles designed to offer more than just reading, such as the Kindle Scribe, I wrapped them into my day-to-day routine, using the Scribe (for example) in place of a paper to-do list.Unlike a tablet, raw power is not important in e-readers. Page-turn speed does matter, but is now good across the whole Kindle lineup. What matters more is how comfortable the screen is to read from, how comfortable the e-reader is to hold, and of course how well it slots into your day-to-day life.Any remaining devices from this Kindle group test will be donated to Cancer Research UK.The best Kindles in 2026View image in fullscreen‘Still Amazon’s best e-reader’: the Kindle Paperwhite.Photograph: Andrew Williams/The GuardianBest Kindle overall:Kindle Paperwhite (2024)KindlePaperwhite (2024)from£184.99£184.99 at John Lewis£184.99 at AmazonWhat we loveThe reading experience and practicality are hard to beatWhat we don’t loveSo familiar that it’s a bit boring in 2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£184.99 at John Lewis£184.99 at AmazonTo my mind, Amazon’s best Kindle e-reader is still the Paperwhite. It has been around since 2012, and has been slowly, gradually and conservatively tweaked since. You can’t mess with perfection all that much, apparently.This best overall ranking is based on one key assumption: above all else, you want to use your Kindle to read novels.Why we love itAmazon’s 2024 Paperwhite has a 7in screen, which is fractionally bigger than the previous version. It’s exceptionally clear and clean-looking, with a whiter, less fuzzy-looking page background than the Colorsoft, which makes it easier to read outdoors in direct sunlight.This is one of the highest-contrast screens you’ll find in the e-reader kingdom, which is pretty important when one of the original selling points of e-readers was lower eye strain. A Paperwhite makes an hour with Agatha Christie feel like moisturising your eyeballs, relatively speaking.This is also as close as you get to a take-anywhere e-reader. It has excellent water resistance and weighs only 211g. For frequent getaway travellers, it could pay for itself purely in Ryanair’s oversized baggage fees.How waterproof is it? The official line is the IPX8 design can handle “2 metres of fresh water for up to 60 minutes and 0.25 metres for 3 minutes in seawater”. I haven’t dropped it in the sea, but may have dropped the Paperwhite in the bath a few times without incident.Its ergonomics are simple but excellent – one-handed reading is a joy – and while the interface hasn’t changed all that much in years, it’s easy to understand.It’s a shame that …there’s no pen stylus support for note-taking, or speaker for audiobooks. It’s all unnecessary fluff if you’re here for reading, and you can stream audiobooks to headphones or a speaker over Bluetooth,but it is worth noting.The real reader’s conundrum: how much of a turn-off is it that you can’t borrow books from UK libraries? It’s on offer in Kobo and PocketBook models, but not here, or on any of Amazon’s Kindle line.A Paperwhite could have also been the perfect vehicle for two features it lacks: page-turn buttons and a textured glass screen.Buttons let you move your hands even less when turning the page, and glass is much harder than the plastic screen on the Paperwhite and therefore less susceptible to scratching. And while glass could add to the weight, the older glass-screened Kindles – the Voyage and Oasis – were actually lighter than this Paperwhite, at 180-188g.Display:7in monochrome E InkStorage size:16/32GB (Signature Edition)Dimensions:127.5 x 7.8 x 176.7mm (WDH)Weight:211gKindlePaperwhite (2024)from£184.99£184.99 at John Lewis£184.99 at AmazonWhat we loveThe reading experience and practicality are hard to beatWhat we don’t loveSo familiar that it’s a bit boring in 2026Best budget Kindle:Kindle (2024)AmazonKindle (2024)from£134.99£134.99 at Argos£134.99 at AmazonWhat we lovePocketable, affordable and lightWhat we don’t loveNot slick-looking or – more importantly – water resistantView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£134.99 at Argos£134.99 at AmazonThis is Amazon’s smaller, humbler, more affordable Kindle, but it is still an excellent e-reader. In fact, for reading, the basic Kindle beats some more expensive models in some important display quality features.It has a 6in display rather than the Paperwhite’s 7in; the screen has a raised bezel rather than a flush front; and the light doesn’t have adjustable warmth, just intensity.Why we love itThe basic Kindle is near-unbeatable as an e-reader that’s large enough to act as your sole reading device, yet small enough to fit in a surprising array of pockets (especially now that skinny jeans have more or less been exiled to fashion’s Room 101).It also needs less careful treatment than some other Kindles. Its raised border means you can place it face down on a table without worrying as much about sand or grit scratching the screen. While e-reader screens are fairly resilient, they’re not immune to surface scratches.I found that contrast, text clarity and overall punchiness of the screen are on the same level as the Kindle Paperwhite, too. In testing, it was clear as anything, day or night, thanks to the front light.It’s a shame that …the Paperwhite is not a glamorous piece of tech, but it does offer some advantages over this more basic model. The Kindle’s raised bezel casts a shadow on the screen in some light conditions that may annoy some – although I can almost guarantee you’ll get used to it.There are two obvious practical concessions to consider, too. No water resistance means caution is required at bath time, and a smaller screen also means more page turns unless you can make do with smaller text. The larger you like (or need) your text, the more this stands out. For bedtime, a larger screen can be more comfortable in the weight-to-page-turn ratio.Display:6in monochrome E InkStorage size:16GBDimensions:108.6 x 8 x 157.8mm (WDH)Weight:158gAmazonKindle (2024)from£134.99£134.99 at Argos£134.99 at AmazonWhat we lovePocketable, affordable and lightWhat we don’t loveNot slick-looking or – more importantly – water resistantBest Kindle for kids:Kindle Colorsoft KidsKindleColorsoft Kidsfrom£274.99£274.99 at John Lewis£274.99 at CurrysWhat we loveIt’s an educational tool with just enough of a fun edgeWhat we don’t loveNot cheap, and colour is a little mutedView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£274.99 at John Lewis£274.99 at CurrysSome will say the ideal Kindle for kids is the cheapest one. But parents are in a war for reading v TikTok, YouTube and God knows what else. A Kindle Colorsoft Kids is arguably the most benign screen going.This is actually the same hardware as the standard Kindle Colorsoft, bundled with a loud and colourful case and a slightly different two-year warranty. That means it can grow with them – or you can co-opt the reader yourself if your child loses interest.Why we love itMany will have memories of rifling through books to find the illustrations as a child, or picking a book solely on the merits of its cover. A Kindle Colorsoft Kids retains more of that charm than the monochrome alternative thanks to its colour screen and vibrant case.A 12-month Amazon Kids+ subscription is included with the Kindle Colorsoft Kids, helping you make the most of that too. After the first year, it costs £7.99 a month (or £6.99 if you’re a Prime member) and grants access to loads of child-friendly content, including games and apps as well as books. Parents of comic book obsessives will probably have to pay for some of that content separately because the Kids+ library is mostly limited to primary-school-age-appropriate content, whileKindle Unlimited(£9.49 a month) includes lots of Batman and Spider-Man graphic novels for slightly older kids.The water resistance and all-round ruggedness of this e-reader pair well with Amazon’s“worry-free” warranty – “if it breaks, we’ll replace it,” to use Amazon’s own wording. While the warranty does come with caveats, it still offers some peace of mind.It’s a shame that …children aren’t always the best at managing their expectations, and some may be disappointed with the Colorsoft Kids as a result. Its colour is muted, which is all the more obvious if they also have access to a tablet or smartphone.A screen this size is also not ideal for comics and graphic novels, as it’s much smaller than they were designed to be read. It’s best described as a gadget for novels that can also handle other content.Display:7in colour E InkStorage size:16GBDimensions:132.2 x 12.7 x 178mm (WDH, including case)Weight:334g (including case)KindleColorsoft Kidsfrom£274.99£274.99 at John Lewis£274.99 at CurrysWhat we loveIt’s an educational tool with just enough of a fun edgeWhat we don’t loveNot cheap, and colour is a little mutedBest Kindle for note-taking:Kindle Scribe ColorsoftKindleScribe Colorsoftfrom£569£569.99 at John Lewis£569 at AmazonWhat we loveColour note-taking is great, and we finally get easy OCRWhat we don’t loveIt costs a small fortune considering its limitationsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£569.99 at John Lewis£569 at AmazonThink of the Scribe Colorsoft as the grownup version of my top pick for kids. It includes a stylus for highlighting text and writing notes, and you can email your notes as PDFs with or without OCR (optical character recognition), which turns your handwriting into standard text for copying and pasting into documents.Why we love itThe Scribe series is where Amazon lets more tablet influence enter the wider Kindle series design. It has a slim aluminium rear casing, which recently became an option in the Signature Editions of Amazon’s new-for-2026 models. It’s slick and super-slim at just 5.4mm thick.A Kindle display will never have the slight give of a paper notebook, but you become accustomed to scrawling on it fairly quickly. And unlike an iPad, the stylus is included rather than costing a small fortune.The screen is a stylus-friendly, smooth textured glass for a paper-like drawing and handwriting feel. But it has an end-to-end flat design, so it should be used with caution to avoid scratches.Drawing or writing with it has minimal lag, even though the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft is nowhere near as powerful as an iPad.Sticking to the style seen throughout the series, Amazon keeps things simple with the Scribe Colorsoft. You can annotate books and PDFs and create your own notebooks. Since its UK release in April 2026, it has evolved to turn handwritten text into digital text you can copy and paste without emailing it to yourself – which always felt desperately clunky to me in the Scribe’s early days.It’s a shame that …the Scribe Colorsoft is Amazon’s most expensive device in this class, and it doesn’t have any form of water resistance, unlike the more ordinary e-readers. Sure, you’re less likely to need a Scribe in the bath, but it’s a shame nevertheless.Some will also feel hemmed in by the software, which – despite Amazon’s deployment of the buzzword “AI” in the marketing – does not feel all that smart. Sketched objects beyond basic shapes can’t be cleaned up into digital object equivalents, and there’s no support for layers, which is standard stuff for graphics tablets and lets you edit elements of a piece of digital art separately.This is the other side of the Scribe series’ inviting simplicity. It could also be seen as basic or, in some areas, clunky. Given the very high cost, that may well sting.Display:11in colour E InkStorage size:32/64GBDimensions:189 x 5.4 x 245mm (WDH)Weight:400gKindleScribe Colorsoftfrom£569£569.99 at John Lewis£569 at AmazonWhat we loveColour note-taking is great, and we finally get easy OCRWhat we don’t loveIt costs a small fortune considering its limitationsBest budget Kindle for kids:Kindle KidsKindleKidsfrom£159.99£159.99 at John Lewis£159.99 at AmazonWhat we loveWorry-free guarantee provides peace of mindWhat we don’t loveThe design could and should be a bit more funView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£159.99 at John Lewis£159.99 at AmazonThe Kindle Kids deserves a nod for those shopping for a younger crowd, not least because the price of my top kids’ pick may have left a few open-mouthed.This is effectively the basic Kindle model set up as a child-friendly e-reader by default, with a better warranty and a bundled cover. For a bit extra, it’s a sound deal.Why we love itLike the Kindle Colorsoft Kids above, this model features Amazon’stwo-year“worry-free”guarantee, which assures customers “if it breaks, we’ll replace it”. Add the included sturdy flip-cover case plus six months of the up-to-£7.99-a-month Kids+ subscription, and the £25 bump from the basic Kindle seems like a steal.There’s nothing stopping you from using the Kindle Kids as an adult e-reader if your child grows out of it or gets bored either. You just switch to an adult profile.It’s a shame that …colour in the Kindle Kids design is limited to the bundled cover. The device body is black only, even though the adult Kindle comes in green too – granted, this would probably clash horribly with the cases.And while we’re at it, how about a few more case options? There are only three, and two are roughly sea themed – you can call it a “space whale”, but we’re still looking at a creature of the ocean.Display:6in monochrome E InkStorage size:16GBDimensions:114.4 x 13.6 x 158.8mm (WDH)Weight:256g (including cover)KindleKidsfrom£159.99£159.99 at John Lewis£159.99 at AmazonWhat we loveWorry-free guarantee provides peace of mindWhat we don’t loveThe design could and should be a bit more funBest colour Kindle:Kindle Colorsoft (2024)KindleColorsoft (2024)from£239.99£259.99 at Argos£239.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s what many of us have always wanted: a colour e-readerWhat we don’t loveRubber border deteriorated during testingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£259.99 at Argos£239.99 at AmazonMany long-term e-reader fans had been waiting for years for a colour Kindle when it finally arrived in the UK in 2024. At long last, we could judge books by their colour covers instead of monochrome ones. And the dream, for some, of reading comics on the go without tablet eye strain was realised – sort of.Why we love itAmazon technically gave us what many people were asking for before the Colorsoft arrived – a Paperwhite, but with a colour screen. Almost everything else remains the same.The design, weight, and in-hand feel while reading are all similar, letting Paperwhite owners transition as comfortably as possible. And even though its battery is rated a little lower – eight weeks compared with the Paperwhite’s 12 – I didn’t find the drop too obvious in testing.It’s a shame that …many people I’ve shown the Colorsoft to have been, to be blunt, disappointed. The technology here is a work in progress, and as with a lot of current-generation colour e-readers, its punch and depth are muted and gradients tend not to look all that refined.That’s because its colour is produced using a separate screen layer that ends up making the “white” of your e-reader page far more grey than a Paperwhite. That means you really need to use the display light all the time, which can impact battery life. I still found it to be a long-lasting device, however.A word of warning: I don’t recommend using a Kindle Colorsoft without a case. After six months of testing, the protective rubber border between the screen and the casing became extremely tatty.Display:7in colour E InkStorage size:16/32GBDimensions:127.6 x 7.8 x 176.7mm (WDH)Weight:16GB, 215g;32GB, 219gKindleColorsoft (2024)from£239.99£259.99 at Argos£239.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s what many of us have always wanted: a colour e-readerWhat we don’t loveRubber border deteriorated during testingThe best of the restKindle Scribe (2024)KindleScribe (2024)£279.99£279.99 at AmazonWhat we loveA savvy choice if you’re looking for a digital notebookWhat we don’t loveThe Scribe Colorsoft is a better option for most peopleView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£279.99 at AmazonBest for:a digital notebookThis isn’t quite the Scribe Colorsoft minus the colour screen, as it has a slightly different design. Amazon’s monochrome model has a chunky thumb grip on one side in its 2024 iteration, which was binned in a2025 design refresh. At the time of writing, you can buy either model, but I tested the older variant.A premium stylus (worth £79) is included with this model, making it an all-in-one package that makes a lot of financial sense if you plan on using it as a digital notebook and aren’t too fussed about having a colourful display.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s a simple one. I felt colour may have an even bigger impact for Scribe users than Paperwhite ones. Colour only makes occasional meaningful appearances in novels. But for note-taking, PDFs and looking over presentation documents? It’s a big part of the equation. If you’re looking for a note-taking Kindle, I’d suggest the Scribe Colorsoft.That said, those not bothered about colour should obviously pick the standard Scribe as it is significantly cheaper. And it also has higher display contrast.Display:10.2in monochrome E InkStorage size:64GBDimensions:196 x 5.7 x 230mm (WDH)Weight:433gKindleScribe (2024)£279.99£279.99 at AmazonWhat we loveA savvy choice if you’re looking for a digital notebookWhat we don’t loveThe Scribe Colorsoft is a better option for most peopleWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenPaws for thought: from library books to refurbished models – what to consider when buying a Kindle.Photograph: Andrew Williams/The GuardianCan you borrow library books with a Kindle?Kindles cannot borrow ebooks from digital lending libraries in the UK.The two common digital book-borrowing services used across the UK are BorrowBox and OverDrive’s Libby. Unfortunately, Kindles don’t support either of these platforms in the UK. Kindle users in the US do, however, get to borrow books through OverDrive.To get library book loans, consider aKoboorPocketBook e-reader. Both support Libby. Head to your local library to see whether it supports such loans with a membership.What Kindle accessories are worth having?A case is highly recommended, particularly if you use a Kindle Colorsoft or Paperwhite. I learned the hard way. These e-readers have a border layer of rubbery material that sits between the rear casing and the screen. It acts as handy impact protection, but can become tatty through general wear in a few months if there’s no case to help out.Amazon’s own Kindle cases are good quality, if a little expensive, but alternatives are available. If you mostly read in bed, you may want to try one with a hand strap, which I’ve enjoyed using in the past.Does a Prime membership come with free Kindle books?An Amazon Prime membership doesn’t include Kindle Unlimited, but Prime Reading does provide access to a rotating but limited library of titles – the number of included novels tots up to a figure in the low thousands.That’s plenty to be getting on with for the casual fiction fan, but it’s going to be down to luck if a book you already want to read happens to be in there. It has never happened to me.Prime Reading is a borrowing service. You don’t have permanent access to these books once you pick them, but you can borrow up to 10 at a time for as long as you have an active Prime membership.Is Kindle Unlimited worth it?Kindle Unlimited costs £9.49 a month and includes “unlimited access” to a large number of books, audiobooks and magazines.There are a couple of limitations, though. You can borrow up to 20 titles at once, but unlike a library loan, there are no return dates. For most, this won’t be a major limitation, especially since you can just “return” one of the books if you hit the limit and want something new.The Kindle Unlimited collection doesn’t encompass the entire Kindle library either, giving access to about 4m titles. (Amazon doesn’t publish stats on how many books are in the full Kindle library, but some estimates have the figure at above 10m.) As such, if you are the kind of person who gets your heart set on reading something specific, you may find Unlimited frustrating.Happy to have a browse and pick something from a glance at its cover, summary or reader reviews? It could end up a real bargain for the voracious readers out there. You can try a month for free, and occasionally longer trials are available too. You can check over at theKindle Unlimitedlanding page.What to do with your old KindleKindles can fetch a good price secondhand on platforms such as eBay or Vinted. The main turn-off for buyers is usually scratches or damage to the screen. Alternatively, CeX accepts Kindles, although phone trade-in fave musicMagpie does not.If this sounds like too much effort, Amazon has a trade-in scheme for many sorts of Kindles – although you won’t get much for older-generation models – and you’ll get a 20% discount off a new Kindle. Digging a little deeper into the terms and conditions, your old Kindle needs to work, hold charge, be free of cracks and defects, and have no stickers or decals on the screen. Otherwise, your trade-in value will tank.How do you get a refurbished or cheap Kindle?Amazon sells refurbished Kindlesat a slight discount. And while you don’t quite get the level of promised quality that Apple’sCertified Refurbished iPadshave – including a guaranteed new casing and battery, for example – Amazon does claim a refurb should “look and work like new”.If you’d rather buy a brand-new device, it’s probably a good idea to wait for one of Amazon’s sales. Such sales periods are the best time to buy a Kindle.These are typically Black Friday in November and Prime Day in the summer, with additional sales in October and around Christmas. I’ve seen sub-£100 refurbishedKindle Paperwhitesduring these sales, representing £44 off the current refurbished price, £85 off the “new” cost.What are Kindle ads and can you remove them?When you buy most Kindles, you have the option to buy it “with ads” or without, and there’s a £10 to £15 saving if you pick the ads version. That means adverts will be displayed on the lockscreen when the e-reader is not in use.They are pretty inoffensive, as ads go, typically advertising a book – and are not shown while you are actively reading.However, you can also upgrade a Kindle with ads to ad-free software for a one-off fee whenever you like.Are Signature Editions worth it?ThePaperwhiteandColorsoftare available as Signature Edition models at a price bump.Upgrades include wireless charging, double the storage and an auto-adjusting front light. By tech standards, it’s not a pricey upgrade. However, none are all that noticeable unless you’re a real wireless-charging household.Kindle batteries last for several weeks, and getting close to running out of storage isn’t something most need to worry about. And the auto-screen-brightness feature is far less reactive than that of a phone, at times making you wonder if it’s doing anything at all.How much recycled material do Kindles use?Like several of the key tech manufacturers, Amazon likes to talk up the recycled materials used in its key products. All Kindle packaging uses 99% materials from “responsibly managed forests or recycled sources”. Here’s how the devices themselves stack up:Kindle Paperwhite (2024) – 29% recycled materials in total, internal frame is 90% recycled magnesiumKindle Colorsoft (2024) – 28% recycled materials in total, battery uses 100% recycled cobaltKindle (basic) – 75% recycled plastics, 90% recycled magnesiumScribe (2024) – 18% recycled materials in total, 100% recycled aluminiumScribe Colorsoft (2025) – 11% recycled materials in total, battery uses 100% recycled cobaltAmazon provides a sustainability data sheet for all key models on itssustainability website.For more, read thebest e-readersand the100 best novels of all timeAndrew Williams is a consumer journalist who has written about technology since before the first iPhone came out. As his flat is filled with the cardboard boxes of gadgets, he tries to get out for a run whenever possible to avoid them – often while testing a fitness tracker and a phone camera at the same timeExplore more on these topicsKindleThe FilterE-readersGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Energy secretary leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfield | Oil | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaigners
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaigners
Content: Miatta Fahnbulleh with Douglas Alexander (left), the Scotland secretary, and John Healey, the chancellor, on a visit to a Shell gas terminal in Peterhead on Wednesday.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAView image in fullscreenMiatta Fahnbulleh with Douglas Alexander (left), the Scotland secretary, and John Healey, the chancellor, on a visit to a Shell gas terminal in Peterhead on Wednesday.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAOilEnergy secretary leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfieldExclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaignersKiran Stacey,Jessica ElgotandFiona HarveyWed 21 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 08.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMiatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the giant Rosebank oilfield, sources have told the Guardian, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners.Afterapproving the smaller Jackdaw gasfieldon Wednesday, officials say the energy secretary is leaning towards refusing approval for what would be one of the biggest oilfields in the North Sea.But she could still be overruled by Andy Burnham, who may hear different representations from the chancellor, John Healey. A final decision is expected before the end of this year.In comments that will be read as a signal of her intent, Fahnbulleh told the Guardian that the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it.“One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.”In contrast, Healey told ITV he expected “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, a suggestion he is anticipating new oil revenues. Burnham would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision.A map showing active oil and gas fields in UK watersLabour MPs warned on Wednesday there would be a major pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessity as part of the transition to net zero.MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent.Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet taken a final decision on Rosebank. The field would emit about seven times the carbon of Jackdaw and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe that it would do less for UK energy security, given most of the oil would be exported.A spokesperson for the Department forEnergySecurity and Net Zero said: “This is speculation. As the energy secretary has said, each project will be assessed on its own merits.”On a visit to Aberdeen, Fahnbulleh said she had been satisfied that Jackdaw, which is due to begin producing gas within weeks and will add an estimated 36m tonnes of carbon emissions, would not violate the UK’s climate commitments.“As we make the transition, we are going to need gas,” she said. “At a point when we have got conflict in the Middle East that is triggering an energy crisis, energy security is vital, and homegrown energy is key.”She admitted, however, it would not help achieve the government’s main energy target of bringing down bills, saying: “This is not about bills.”View image in fullscreenFahnbulleh on a visit to St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeen on Wednesday.Photograph: Lauren Hurley/No 10 Downing StreetTheUN Environment Programmehas recommended that global carbon emissions be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin.The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-eastScotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.One Labour MP close to the energy secretary said she knew her credibility was “on the line” and that she was able to show she was pragmatic by approving Jackdaw but drawing the line at Rosebank. “She’s putting up a fight and I want to be supportive of Miatta – I understand what she is fighting,” they said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut they said the decision would ultimately come down to Burnham. “Andy is not a climate guy – he is under pressure. If he wants to do it, he’ll do it.”Several serving ministers have said they would find Rosebank a more difficult decision to back and it would cause greater problems in their constituencies.The former minister Catherine West said climate change “is not a future threat but a present reality” and that the answer to job losses in the North Sea was not to “double down on new fossil fuel developments”.Afzal Khan, the Labour MP for Manchester Rusholme and chair of the all-party parliamentary group on climate change, said: “Approving projects on the scale of Rosebank, on top of today’s decision to approve Jackdaw, cannot be justified.”Burnham is seeking more ways to lower energy bills, telling MPs on Wednesday that ministers would consider whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills to ease cost pressures on households.While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfield project have sought approval for existing licences.The Greens said on Wednesday they intended to fight seats directly on the issue of Jackdaw and Rosebank. The Green MP Carla Denyer said: “We have identified dozens of seats where we are Labour’s main challenger and the climate is one of the top issues and voters have been mobilised by the heatwave and wildfires.“Our strong advice to Labour MPs is to stand up to Andy Burnham and his act of climate violence, both to save your seats and, far more importantly, to protect the planet for future generations.”Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through a new energy wealth fund. She said the fund would be given £2bn in the budget.“When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes.However, she could not say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the new fund, or how much that might generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said.Explore more on these topicsOilMiatta FahnbullehLabourFossil fuelsGasEnergyEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: Committee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decade
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Committee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decade
Content: It took the UK destroyer warship HMS Dragon more than three weeks to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt took the UK destroyer warship HMS Dragon more than three weeks to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesDefence policyRoyal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warnCommittee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decadeDan SabbaghDefence and security editorWed 21 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability ofRoyal Navysubmarines and warships, MPs on the defence select committee have said.The committee focused on the slow deployment
