of HMS Dragon to Cyprus this spring, declining numbers of frigates, and reports that all five Astute-class attack submarines were in dock this summer as evidence of a navy under-resourced for the threat.“The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the high north,” said Tan Dhesi, the committee chair. “Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments.”The high north, the seas beyond Scotland, have become increasingly strategically significant amid growing Russian interest in energy pipelines and undersea cables at a time when Arctic seaways are opening up because of global heating.The navy shadowed a Russian spy ship, the Yantar, operating inside the UK’s economic waters inNovemberandJanuarylast year, accusing sailors onboard of trying to map strategic cables and shining lasers at RAF pilots monitoring them.Map of high northRussia also wants to assert control over the emerging northern sea route, a 3,500-mile (5,600km) shipping lane running along the country’s Arctic coast. It is the quickest maritime route from China to Europe, navigable last year for four and half months.The MPs argued the UK needed to make “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade, and they called on theMinistry of Defenceto draw up a plan to ensure more warships and submarines are at sea by 2030.The problem would be particularly acute, the committee added, if the US did not support the UK in a crisis, a rare cross-party acknowledgment that under Donald Trump, US military help cannot be relied on, particularly if a small Nato member in the region was threatened or attacked.“There would be critical military gaps if the United States were not involved in countering such [Russian] aggression,” the MPs said, and they argued that the UK, as the next largest Nato military in the region, had to be prepared to increase its navy.It took more than three weeks for HMS Dragon, a destroyer, to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean in March after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone. No warships were available and Dragon had to be hauled out of dry dock to deploy.The navy has five frigates with sonar dedicated to detecting Russian submarines at distance, the committee noted, lower than a target of eight, as ageing warships have been scrapped without replacements coming into service. It could take until 2037 before it reaches its stated requirement, the committee added.None of Britain’s five Astute submarines, also used to track Russian maritime activity, were at sea from June and into the summer. They were in dock for a mixture of short-term and long-term refits, the committee noted, and they also lack the capability to operate under ice, unlike their Russian equivalents, although certification exercises are in progress.However, no significant extra money is expected to be available for defence until the next decade, with Andy Burnham’s government committed to medium-term spending plans agreed under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer.Though Starmer agreed to lift defence spending by about £30bn a year to 3.5% of GDP in 2035, he would only sign off spending to the lower level of 2.7% by 2030. That prompted the resignation of John Healey as defence secretary, only for him to return as chancellor under Burnham, with the old spending plans intact.In response to the report, an MoD spokesperson highlighted a recent £330m investment to protect undersea infrastructure, and noted that Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, had visited Iceland this month and watched how HMS St Albans, a frigate, tracked Russian submarines in the north Atlantic. “We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses,” they added.Explore more on these topicsDefence policyRoyal NavyMinistry of DefenceMilitarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Aneurin Bevan’s personal security file was ‘remarkably tame’ – National Archives | Labour | The Guardian
description: Some in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interest
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Some in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interest
Content: Aneurin Bevan came to the attention of MI5 in the 1930s.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenAneurin Bevan came to the attention of MI5 in the 1930s.Photograph: PALabourAneurin Bevan’s personal security file was ‘remarkably tame’ – National ArchivesSome in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interestCaroline DaviesWed 21 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAneurin “Nye” Bevan, the WelshLabourfirebrand who spearheaded the creation of the NHS, was monitored by security services for more than two decades, though his personal file was “remarkably tame”, according to official files released to the public.Bevan came to MI5’s attention in the 1930s over concerns about his links with known communists, papers released to theNational Archivesshow. Monitoring continued even after he became a minister in the postwar Labour government that created the NHS.At one point, his links to a known Russian spy led to the then director general ofMI5approaching prime minister Clement Attlee to warn him.However, the papers show, some in the security services questioned why Bevan was of interest. Although there is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, one officer wrote in 1943: “I do not think that Bevan’s activities are a matter in which we, the Security Service, should be involved.“In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently, as any copy of Hansard will show, and it would not therefore be possible to do anything positive.”Reviewing the file after his death in 1960, another MI5 officer noted: “Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame.”MI5 first opened a personal file on the backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in South Wales in 1933. He was described in one entry to have “inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the communist cause.”He was also noted to have been “in close touch” with Harry Pollitt, general secretary of the Communist party of Great Britain, and others in the party who backed his plan to organise “workers’ freedom groups” to defend against “capitalists”.Bevan fell out with his communist allies who had complained he was not interested in workers’ unity and was intent on building “a movement of his own”. But by 1936 they had reconciled, with Bevan supporting an application by the Communist party to affiliate with the Labour party.In 1949, MI5 became concerned about Bevan’s friendship with Wilfred Macartney, who had been convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.Recordings of Macartney’s conversations suggested he was passing on information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt. It led the director general Sir Percy Sillitoe to approach Attlee, who dismissed Macartney’s claims as a “tissue of lies” but agreed to “warn” Bevan about Macartney.The file was finally closed in 1975, 15 years after Bevan died.Other newly released papers show MI5 feared communists could attempt to disrupt the coronation of King George VI, with Communist party activists closely watched before the Westminster Abbey ceremony in 1937.While the party prepared a propaganda drive and printed a million anti-monarchist leaflets to be distributed during coronation week, members were warned to avoid antagonising a largely pro-royalist public.One MI5 report from April 1937 noted that a “comrade” in Manchester had been “severely censured” for proposing a series of demonstrations as it would be “playing into the hands of the fascists and police”. “It has been pointed out that members will be ‘going against the stream’ in doing this and they must be careful to speak in such a way that they do not make themselves unpopular with their neighbours.”Sir Michael Tippett, a leading British composer of the 20th century and a famed pacifist, was also monitored by MI5 as a suspected Trotskyist revolutionary, according to the files.MI5 believed he joined first the Communist party and then the Trotskyists in the 1930s, and remained an active supporter until the end of the second world war.The files suggest, however, he was unconvincing as a revolutionary. In one intercepted letter to a Communist party organiser in London, he complained of the difficulties of trying to combine his work as a communist with his life as a music teacher living in rural Surrey. His evening commitments meant that it was “quite impossible” for him to attend “cell” meetings in London, he complained.A report from 1955 noted that Tippett “has not come to notice in connection with communist or Trotskyist affairs”.However, his radical past meant that as late as 1959 he was blocked from taking up a Foreign Office-sponsored lectureship in Germany, and it was only in the 1960s that MI5 were prepared to give him a clean bill of health. In 1966, he was knighted for services to music. He died in 1998 aged 93.Explore more on these topicsLabourMI5National ArchivesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Heidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attack | Israel | The Guardian
description: US photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incident
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: US photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incident
Content: Heidi Levine in her hospital bed on Wednesday before she was discharged.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHeidi Levine in her hospital bed on Wednesday before she was discharged.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianIsraelHeidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attackUS photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incidentJulian BorgerandQuique Kierszenbaumin Petah TikvaWed 21 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 20.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured byIsraeli settlers in the West Bank on Fridayhas described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians.Heidi Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds when she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by a crowd of masked settlers while she and other journalists were covering the olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.It is unclear whether the puncture wounds were caused by knives or other weapons. Levine said a witness to her attack had seen nails sticking out of some of the wooden clubs wielded by her attackers.Levine, 64, has covered multiple wars and had just returned from an assignment in Ukraine before Friday’s attack. She said she would most likely have been killed had she not been wearing protective body armour and a helmet.“I probably would have been dead, because for sure it doesn’t take much to kill a person with blows to the head,” she said shortly before being discharged from hospital on Wednesday in the Israeli city of Petah Tikva.Levine pointed out that Palestinians did not have such protection and more than 20 had been killed in settler attacks so far this year, in the course of an escalating campaign of aggression –described as terrorismby Israeli security leaders – across the West Bank, aimed at driving Palestinians from their land.“Every single journalist who looked at [the attack on me] are thinking they and I have gone to so many funerals of Palestinians killed by settlers,” Levine said.She said the olive harvesting at Abu Falah had begun peacefully but at some point a group of young masked settlers appeared on a nearby hilltop watching the group of Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying them. Levine said the attack began only after the Israeli army arrived on the scene.“Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said. “Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw teargas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me.“I managed to keep my face to the ground, and I don’t know if I took that position to protect myself with my face down or it was their initial blow. Otherwise my whole face would have been broken and I could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye.“They started kicking me and beating me with sticks. I can’t even count how many times, probably more than a hundred times. I actually tried playing dead so that they would stop. But it didn’t work.”1:57American photojournalist recounts Israeli settler attack in the occupied West Bank – videoWitnesses said the beating only ceased when young Palestinian men used slingshots to aim stones at settlers forcing them back, allowing another American journalist, Jasper Nathaniel, to reach Levine and, with other reporters, help her to safety.“Theshabab[Palestinian youth] put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing. It was like a biblical battle,” Levine said.After the attack,Nathaniel wrote: “Had theshababnot stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead. It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s.”He said the army pursued the young Palestinians after the incident, rather than the settlers. Palestinians risk being shot by settlers or soldiers if they try to resist attacks, and can face long periods in detention without charge.Levine, who has lived in Israel for four decades, said she would go back to reporting on theWest Bankas soon as she recovered. “My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.”Since the attack, she has received letters from Israelis expressing regret, and an apologetic phone call from the president, Isaac Herzog.“He was a teddy bear on the phone,” she said. “He kept saying I just want to give you a big hug and these are not representative of who this country is, they’re a dark stain, and he called them thugs.”The office of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, however, put outa statement on Xseeking to cast doubt on witness and video accounts of what he called an “alleged attack”.Levine was particularly angered by Netanyahu’s claim that some video footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”.“That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why,” Levine said. “They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me.”The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee,called the attacka “despicable act of terror” and demanded prosecutions. Israeli police arrested 10 suspects after the Abu Falah incident and another attack on Saturday aimed at European diplomats near the West Bank village of Taybeh.On Wednesday an Israeli court released four suspects in the attack on Levine and put them under house arrest, on the grounds there was insufficient evidence to keep them in custody.Asked if she expected her attackers to be brought to justice, Levine said her level of confidence was “two out of 10”.“I am not very hopeful,” she said. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it. But it’s not just arresting these teenage thugs. It’s going after their leaders, the rabbis, and how they’re organised.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelWest BankPalestineJournalist safetyWashington PostBenjamin NetanyahuUS press and publishingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jeffrey Donaldson investigated over alleged rape in UK parliament | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Met police investigating after referral from PSNI about allegation former DUP leader raped woman in 2016
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Met police investigating after referral from PSNI about allegation former DUP leader raped woman in 2016
Content: Jeffrey Donaldson was the leader of the DUP between 2021 and 2024.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenJeffrey Donaldson was the leader of the DUP between 2021 and 2024.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PANorthern IrelandJeffrey Donaldson investigated over alleged rape in UK parliamentMet police investigating after referral from PSNI about allegation former DUP leader raped woman in 2016Aletha AduWed 21 Oct 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Metropolitan police are investigating an allegation that the former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson raped a woman inside parliament in 2016.Scotland Yard confirmed it received a report from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) on 13 October about an alleged rape in the Palace of Westminster involving a man now aged 63.The Belfast Telegraph first reported the allegation concerning a woman from Northern Ireland. The newspaper reported that Donaldson invited the woman on a tour of the Commons where he introduced her to high-profile figures. He was said to have taken her for dinner before bringing her into the DUP’s offices in parliament.The newspaper also reported that the woman received a photo of Donaldson during the Covid lockdown showing a filter on Snapchat across his face with a message saying: “Ready to face the world as soon as this isolation lark is over.”The woman has been interviewed by PSNI officers, who referred the case to the Met because the alleged offence was said to have taken place in London.The Met confirmed that the alleged rape was reported to have taken place inside parliament in 2016.A Met spokesperson said: “On Tuesday 13 October, the Met received a report, referred to us by Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), relating to an allegation of rape in 2016, by a man now aged 63.“The allegation relates to one victim who is being supported by specialist officers. The investigation is in its early stages. No arrests have been made and inquiries remain ongoing.”Donaldson was the leader of the DUP from 2021 to 2024.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandDemocratic Unionist party (DUP)newsShareReuse this content

title: Orangutans prefer food associated with sounds of laughter, study suggests | Animal behaviour | The Guardian
description: Apes in study more likely to choose treats linked to sound of peers having fun, suggesting emotions influence learning
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Apes in study more likely to choose treats linked to sound of peers having fun, suggesting emotions influence learning
Content: An orangutan tucks into a treat. The study suggests positive emotions could influence how the great apes learn and make decisions.Photograph: Elisabetta A Villa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn orangutan tucks into a treat. The study suggests positive emotions could influence how the great apes learn and make decisions.Photograph: Elisabetta A Villa/Getty ImagesAnimal behaviourOrangutans prefer food associated with sounds of laughter, study suggestsApes in study more likely to choose treats linked to sound of peers having fun, suggesting emotions influence learningNicola DavisScience correspondentWed 21 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOrangutans base their food choices on whether others appear to be having a good time, research suggests.Scientists studying captive orangutans have found that when the great apes heard the sound of their peers laughing before they searched a bowl for a tasty treat, they valued the reward more highly.Erica Cartmill, a professor of anthropology and cognitive science at Indiana University and senior author of the work, said the study is part of a larger project exploring whether animals feel joy and what the implications of those emotions are in areas such as cognition and learning.“One of our big motivations … is building on human research that shows that emotion has important effects on rational thought – and that they aren’t two separate things; they really influence one another,” she said. “We wanted to extend that to animals – in this case to orangutans.”Writing in the journal Biology Letters, Cartmill and her colleagues report how they worked with six orangutans based at two zoological institutions.The researchers first trained the orangutans to search through bowls to find food treats. They then presented each orangutan with two bowls. One contained a tasty morsel buried under a harmless substance such as moss or sawdust, while the other contained a different type of material but no treat.Crucially, just before the researchers presented the bowls to the orangutans, they played a recording. This was either the sound of orangutans playing and laughing or environmental sounds such as wind, with the choice of soundtrack depending on which of two substances was used to cover the food that day.On the fifth day the team presented the orangutans with two bowls, but this time each contained a treat buried beneath one of the two food-covering substances. They then asked the orangutans to pick a bowl.The results from multiple trials revealed that, overall, the apes preferred to pick the bowl containing the substance associated with the sound of laughter, with four of the six orangutans showing a clear preference.Cartmill said the preference could be rooted in the sound of laughter putting the orangutans in a more positive emotional state when they learned to associate the substance with food.Dr Adriano Lameira, a primatologist and evolutionary psychologist at the University of Warwick, who was not involved in the work, described the results as fascinating.“Effectively, hearing others clearly having a good time, orangutans placed their food order: ‘I will have what they are having, please!’” he said.Cartmill added the results suggest it is not only the quantity or frequency of a reward that can be important when learning associations.“What our work is showing is that it’s also about the state of the animal when they are learning that association,” she said.“Who you are in that moment – the context, the emotional states, what you’re feeling, what you’re thinking about – can also influence and can carry over in how you remember these things that you’ve learned.”The findings, she added, could have applications to humans, including in educational environments.“Students might learn at similar rates if they are in a good mood or not, but our research suggests that they would value information more if they learn it when they are in a good mood,” Cartmill said.She added that could be useful in helping to understand why some information is more trusted or why students choose to continue studying certain subjects.“If a student is anxious when they are learning maths for example, it might impact whether they prefer maths versus other subjects when choosing what to pursue in the future,” she said.Explore more on these topicsAnimal behaviourPrimatologyAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope will not need further cancer treatment, doctors say | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: Medics indicate pontiff’s tumour had not spread, but doubts remain about planned trip to South America next month
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Medics indicate pontiff’s tumour had not spread, but doubts remain about planned trip to South America next month
Content: Pope Leo delivered his weekly address on Wednesday as he gradually resumes normal duties.Photograph: Franco Origlia/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPope Leo delivered his weekly address on Wednesday as he gradually resumes normal duties.Photograph: Franco Origlia/Getty ImagesPope Leo XIVPope will not need further cancer treatment, doctors sayMedics indicate pontiff’s tumour had not spread, but doubts remain about planned trip to South America next monthNadeem BadshahWed 21 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 17.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePope Leo will not need any further ⁠treatment after undergoing lung cancer surgery last week, his doctors said, indicating ⁠that his tumour had ⁠not ​spread.Pope Leo lung cancer surgery: what kind of operation did he have and what happens next?Read moreThe ⁠71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his ​right lung removedon 13 Octoberand was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most ‌common form of lung cancer.Final histological examinations and molecular biology analyses of the tissue removed confirmed the diagnosis, with the disease remaining localised, the doctors said in a statement released by the Vatican.“A subsequent ‌oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the pope’s lead surgeon, ​Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said.However, it was still unclear whether the pope would ⁠proceed with a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, scheduled for 6-17 November.Leo was discharged from hospital on Saturday and isgradually resuming his normal duties. On Wednesday, he returned to ⁠St Peter’s Square for his weekly audience with ​pilgrims.The pope had been working from hospital, including making a phone call last Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.Last Sunday, the pontiff told a crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square that he would “gradually resume” his activities.He also thanked those who had prayed for him, saying that he appreciated the support while adding that the experience had made him feel especially close “to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity”.Margaritora said ​last week there ​were “no clinical reasons” preventing the pope from travelling ​to South ‌America, but ​the Vatican’s ​secretary of state indicated that the pontiff may need to adjust the pace of his schedule to aid his recovery.Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys playing sports including tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.In May last year, Leo became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church.Explore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVThe papacyCancerReligionHealthCatholicismChristianitynewsShareReuse this content

title: No surprise and lasting anger: families of people who died in care homes react to Covid inquiry report | Covid inquiry | The Guardian
description: Relatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policy
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: Relatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policy
Content: The Covid memorial wall in London.Photograph: Matt Crossick/PAView image in fullscreenThe Covid memorial wall in London.Photograph: Matt Crossick/PACovid inquiryNo surprise and lasting anger: families of people who died in care homes react to Covid inquiry reportRelatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policyEsther AddleyWed 21 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“At the time it felt like a devil’s bargain – it was horrible, but it was what [we thought] we had to do to keep people safe,” says Amy of the “devastating” and “terrifying” restrictions that led to her maternal grandparents being locked down in separate care homes during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.Eva and Eric had been married for more than 60 years when her dementia and his increased frailty meant they needed separate residential support. When the first lockdown was announced in March 2020, however, it in effect cut them off from each other and their granddaughter, to whom they had been especially close after the early death of Amy’s mother.“I spoke to Grandad on the phone when it was possible – it often wasn’t possible due to staff not being able to take him a phone – and he was desperately lonely, isolated in his room, unable to talk to anyone because they were worried about [the spread of Covid],” says Amy, 39, who lives in Milton Keynes and works for a large software company. “I consoled myself that they were keeping him safe. That all the isolation was necessary.”Instead, she says, he was depressed and very afraid until he finally caught the virus in 2022. Amy saw him for the first time on a Covid ward, “when I had to beg and beg and beg the hospital staff to let me visit him”. Eric died shortly afterwards.View image in fullscreenEva and Eric.Photograph: SuppliedSix years after Covid struck, the latest report from the public inquiry into the pandemic, published this week, has convinced Amy that the policy of isolating residents was “cruel and pointless”, she says. “I want to smash something. I can never get that time with them back.“The impression I had at the time was that [the government] were doing their best in the face of an unstoppable tidal wave, but it sounds like they put out a hand and expected it to stop the ocean.”The inquiry concludedthat the entire care sector had been an “afterthought” to government planners, and that a claim by the then health secretary, Matt Hancock, to have put a “protective ring” around residents was entirely unfounded. Instead, the decision to discharge untested patients from hospitals into care homes led to the virus spreading “like wildfire”, while blanket restrictions on outside contact led to “immense emotional harm” and “profound isolation” for vulnerable residents.The findings are no surprise to the family members of care home residents, many of whom have told the Guardian of the immense distress their loved ones went through. Roger Dennison’s father, Lucius, was a sprightly 90-year-old care home resident when the first reports of the coronavirus emerged; they watched the news together in Lucius’s room and wondered how quickly it would peter out.Weeks later, Lucius’s care home had firmly locked down, and the only way Dennison could talk to his dad was through a window that had been opened a few inches at the top. “You’re standing on tiptoe, trying to shout in and then be heard on the other side,” he says. “It was very confusing. It wasn’t very happy as an experience.” They tried it just once but stopped because it was too distressing for Lucius.Lucius Dennison.Photograph: Roger DennisonAfter that, Dennison, who had previously visited every other day, was reliant on passing messages through staff, while Lucius was “in his room, largely on his own”. The disease “became a growing apprehension for me once it became clear people were coming into the home and bringing it with them”, says his son. “I think there was a sense of inevitability.” Lucius caught Covid in the first wave and died in hospital in April 2020.To care workers, too, the situation was terrifying and immensely distressing, says Nick (not his real name), who was a senior worker at a home in West Yorkshire. “The situation from the very start was frightening because we all thought that if you got Covid, you died or were going to be seriously unwell. I remember having to strip naked at the back door of my house because we had a resident return from hospital who had shared a ward with Covid patients. As a care home, we tried to refuse their return based on the risk of infection but were told [by the hospital] that we couldn’t.”From that point, he says, “all hell broke loose”. “Our first case of Covid was about a week later.” They had already run out of personal protective equipment, he says.‘Superficial damp squib’: Covid inquiry recommendations fail to impress bereaved familiesRead more“The mental health impact on all staff was huge. Watching people die at such a high rate in such a small space of time; having to say goodbye to so many people we came to know and love; putting our own health on the line every day and then quite possibly carrying that home to your family. Mentally, we were all spent.”Like many, Catherine Bennett, a retired teacher from Lewes in East Sussex, says she was not shocked by the inquiry’s findings: “We knew what was happening. I am, however, very angry.” Her father, who had been in a care home since 2018, “felt a terrible sense of abandonment” that no one was able to visit and became paralysingly afraid of catching the virus.“For a long time he didn’t go down for meals; he stopped doing all his activities so he wouldn’t meet anybody.” After some months, she says, the care home built a room where residents could talk to relatives through a glass panel and speakers. It was, she says, “very distressing for a man of his age to be separated from his loved ones in that way, to be able to see us through the glass but not be able to touch us or have any meaningful contact”. Her father died in the home in 2022.Diana, a retired social worker from Derby, feels a similar lasting anger about the experience of her sister, Helen, whose mental health needs meant she was living in a care home in Carlisle when the pandemic struck, and who experienced a similar bewilderment at her sudden isolation. The first time Diana was able to sit with her was after a year of lockdown when Helen was very unwell; she died the same day.“I just think they threw care homes under a bus while they partied in Downing Street, and I do feel rather cross about that,” says Diana. “I think it is a major trauma for this country and I think it should never be forgotten.”Explore more on these topicsCovid inquiryCoronavirusSocial careCare workersOlder peopleHealth policyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Steve Witkoff’s flattery of the Russian leader could be just the start of a mendacious stratagem from a US president who says Moscow ‘has been fine on Ukraine’
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Steve Witkoff’s flattery of the Russian leader could be just the start of a mendacious stratagem from a US president who says Moscow ‘has been fine on Ukraine’
Content: Students and teachers in the hallway at an underground school in Kharkiv, Ukraine.Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStudents and teachers in the hallway at an underground school in Kharkiv, Ukraine.Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The GuardianUkraineAnalysis‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and dieAndrew Rothin KharkivSteve Witkoff’s flattery of the Russian leader could be just the start of a mendacious stratagem from a US president who says Moscow ‘has been fine on Ukraine’Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.57 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.54 EDTShareThey say the first casualty of war is truth. For theTrump administration, the road to peace with Russia now encompasses some extraordinary lies.Steve Witkoff delivered one as he sat down withVladimir Putinin St Petersburg on Wednesday, aiming to close the deal on Russia’s land grab in Ukraine with the White House’s strategy of maximum pressure on Kyiv and saccharine flattery of the Kremlin.“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” said Witkoff, a real-estate mogul who, thanks to being Trump’s friend, is now the US’s senior envoy and diplomat to end the largest European conflict since the second world war. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”In Putin’s 26 years in power, it is a rare moment when he has been granted that specific honour. Skim through Russia’s past wartime exploits – from the bombing campaigns in Chechnya and Georgia and Syria, to the thousands of Russian citizens jailed for dissent, to the violent deaths of prominent opposition journalists and politicians in barely disguised assassinations and poisonings – and it will be difficult to identify Putin’s credentials as a humanitarian.View image in fullscreenVladimir Putin and Steve Witkoff meet in St Petersburg.Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/ReutersAnd that is before looking to Ukraine, where Russia chose to launch a full-scale invasion that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. The Guardianrecently obtained a Russian strategy documentshowing the Kremlin’s potential to black out Ukrainian cities this winter, cutting off up to 90% of electricity to cities such as Kyiv and Odesa and Kharkiv – where millions of people live – to intentionally create a humanitarian catastrophe. And judging by the nightly barrages levelled at power plants for cities across Ukraine, the Kremlin has decided to move forward with that strategy until Kyiv surrenders.As Witkoffmet Putin on Wednesday, schoolchildren in Kharkiv hastened down a reinforced stairway, sirens announcing the arrival of Shahed drones overhead. This is no ordinary bomb shelter; it is one of 10 underground schools Kharkiv has constructed because of Russia’s regular bombing of the city less than 20 miles from the border.Parents had welcomed the schools because they were safe, said teachers, and this was the one way that young people could have an uninterrupted school day during a war that could last years more – and reignite even if a shaky peace deal is reached.View image in fullscreenStudents and parents arrive and depart from the entrance to an underground school in Kharkiv.Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The Guardian“We all believed in Trump. We all really had hopes for America and for Trump to stop this monster Putin,” said Olena Svytlychna, the head of the education department of the Novobavarskyi region in Kharkiv, sitting in the school’s cafe on Wednesday.“And now we have doubts, we don’t believe them. And we are very scared.”As Witkoff spoke, the families of six people killed in a drone strike in a park near Kharkiv this week were holding funerals. The youngest victim of the strike was a one-year-old girl, Anhelina, who was killed as she was sitting strapped into her stroller in a playground. Her mother, Inna Mariukhna, a local schoolteacher, was also killed in the strike. The final death toll was four adults and two children, Anhelina and an 11-year-old girl.View image in fullscreenA destroyed building in Kharkiv after an air attack on Tuesday.Photograph: Sergey Bobok/AFP/Getty ImagesThose lives have barely earned a mention from the White House as it pushes forUkraineto capitulate as quickly as it can this week – and crucially before the 3 November midterm elections when voters will deliver a referendum on Trump’s leadership for the last two years.Shortly after the bombing, Trump told reporters on the White House lawn that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine”. After taking criticism for that remark, he mentioned the attacks in passing just to downplay the shelling of civilians: there were “some people in a town that got hit or whatever, but mostly young soldiers” died, he said from the Oval Office on Tuesday.For the White House, those words cost little. Witkoff’s goal was to bring home a US citizen, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, who had been detained in Russia. But if Witkoff wants to buy a peace deal by 3 November through flattering Putin, then this will only be the White House’s opening salvo in its war on truth.Explore more on these topicsUkraineUS foreign policyEuropeTrump administrationRussiaVladimir PutinDonald TrumpanalysisShareReuse this content

title: What is Black journalism for? | Media | The Guardian
description: In honour of Claudia Jones’ memory, I reflect on how diasporic reporting provides community and avoids being defined by the western white experience
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: In honour of Claudia Jones’ memory, I reflect on how diasporic reporting provides community and avoids being defined by the western white experience
Content: Navigating around subsumption … so much exists beyond the reach of a right-wing columnist.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Corbis/Getty Images/ Schomburg Center for Research in Black CultureView image in fullscreenNavigating around subsumption … so much exists beyond the reach of a right-wing columnist.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Corbis/Getty Images/ Schomburg Center for Research in Black CultureThe Long WaveMediaWhat is Black journalism for?In honour of Claudia Jones’ memory, I reflect on how diasporic reporting provides community and avoids being defined by the western white experienceDon’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNesrine MalikWed 21 Oct 2026 09.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 09.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis week, I had the great honour of delivering the Claudia Jones memorial lecture, hosted by the UK National Union of Journalists. It is partly inspired by the Long Wave and the extraordinary response it continues to receive from readers. As the newsletter turns two, I reflect, in the abridged version of the lecture below, on the importance of making space in an embattled political climate.View image in fullscreenA broader denial … it took time for the existence of institutional racism to be widely accepted.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/Getty ImagesIt feels like a particularly difficult time to say anything with much certainty. We stand today in the shadow of the Black Lives Matter Movement – as well as the wreckage brought about by neoliberalism, the rise of the far right, and ongoing culture wars. In the last decade, several moments have swelled with possibility and then melted away – not quite into nothing, but certainly, less than we would like. Where do we go from here?It feels to me, as someone who began writing as a columnist and journalist proper less than a decade ago, that I broadly could always tell what my marching orders were – who the antagonist was. In Britain, a Conservative government enacted large-scale cuts to public services, and the police and Security Service institutionalised Islamophobic and anti-Black policies such as the Prevent duty and stop and search. It was a hostile environment that meted out treatment so cruel that I am still haunted by some of the stories I heard from victims I met while reporting on it. And it was a broader political culture that refused to acknowledge that institutional racism existed. Things were said to us, and about us, while we lived an entirely different reality. The sense was of a particular sort of psychological agony, one which powered much of my writing.I remember when the lies began, after what appeared to be giant breakthroughs in 2020. There were always lies but these had a different quality – a coordinated feel. The Daily Mail would print something, and then Tory ministers would run with it, conveying outrage and dismay at the special treatment Black people were supposedly demanding and receiving. Then, the airwaves and social media would hum with discourse and debate for days in the aftermath. One particular episode comes to mind: when the BBCshortened itsLast Night of the Proms broadcast due to Covid-related precautions, and the rightwing media claimed Land of Hope and Glorywas cancelledbecause of the BLM movement. Even then-prime minister Boris Johnson joined the condemnation.What happened after 2020?View image in fullscreenPlaying whack-a-mole … reporting Black concerns is taken as recruitment into war.Photograph: Justin Lane/EPAAfter the death of George Floyd, similar stories followed. Trying to correct and counter media coverage, rightwing myths, and mainstream discourse about race became like playing whack-a-mole. The right and those influenced by them worked together to produce a blanketting account of Blackness. If you challenged or complained, you were labelled as entitled, and addicted to a victimhood that the government had disproved once and for all in the form of anofficial report. Even if you said or did nothing, stories would be made up about you for sport.The progressives were the most infuriating of all. Posting black squares and taking the knee when the cost was low and reward was high, but then retreating to the pompous and disingenuous argument of “going high” in the face of Black vilification because culture wars aren’t “salient” to voters. They were pretty salient to Black people. I experienced this time as one of almost physical savaging.In hindsight, I see we were rapidly boxed in, with no room for manoeuvre. I felt a sinking realisation in my work: every objection I wrote or spoke was happily gobbled up by the very ecosystem it fought. Journalism regarding Black concerns and public figures became a matter not of reporting and opinion, but instant recruitment into a war. Our opponents were a disparate bunch, but were the product of a majority white establishment that just did not want to listen to the experiences of Black people, to thefactsabout disproportionate policing and racial profiling, and vastly unequal maternal health, unemployment, education and income. It felt like a trap. In responding to this climate, our orientation was not towards each other, even though it felt like we were defending each other. We needed to turn away from white-facing discourse and into Black-facing and intra-communal discourse. A step back became necessary. What was journalism for?How can multi-faceted Blackness take up space?View image in fullscreenGathering in the spirit … the legacy of Claudia Jones informs our in-depth reporting of the diaspora.Photograph: FPG/Getty ImagesIn 2024, we began publishing the Long Wave. I have learned a lot in the past two years, but the main lesson is just how much more distinctive the Black experience is, even more than I thought or intuited, because no other people were enslaved, traded and removed from their lands in such numbers and over such a long time. The Black diaspora is among the largest and most sprawling of them all, connected by similar histories that often shock myself and the team with the specificity of practices, ways of living and challenges on entirely different continents. Whether it was in common linguistic heritage, musical influences, resistance politics, and in oneparticularly bewildering report, shared mystical pre-Abrahamic practices.Diaspora is not a people scattered from a homeland, but a homeland that has travelled with the people and remains, in different forms, still within them. It makes space for a multifaceted form of Blackness, which can incorporate co-existing identities. For me, these identities have included being Sudanese, from a certain tribe, and Muslim. Following that, I have found other ways of self-defining – African, pan-African, and Black. I have found that Black can mean belonging to part of something bigger. Acknowledging this followsthe legacyof Claudia Jones herself, who inspired this speech. Jones’s journalistic endeavours at the West Indian Gazette supported anti-racism in the UK, but also fostered dialogue between West Indians and international freedom movements. And in establishing the precursor to Notting Hill Carnival, she also galvanised a form of Black culture that insists on its endurance on its own terms.In these forms of thinking, writing, organising and community-building, we might find that space for manoeuvre. That breathing space as a Black British journalist, and a Black Briton who gives a damn. That space to be Black and care and write about racism – because it is simply a fact of one’s life. That space to do so without being limited by it and defined by it. And that space to be confident and ambitious and global with our own stories, without having to worry about how this looks to “them”. This feels all the more pressing to me as a Black journalist who is also Muslim and Arab. None of this will change the media or the environment we live in, but it will help us navigate it without being subsumed by it.This is the process of identifying with a diaspora, and actively seeking ways in which we can re-connect with it. It is also a process of divesting from the particular, and embracing something more whole. To think in different strategies and approaches to surfacing Black life beyond its treatment by white majorities and hegemonic histories. To understand that wherever we feel kettled in, suffocated and disempowered, so much exists beyond the reach of the online troll or rightwing columnist. There is history, literature, political activism, carnivals, music, travel and, wherever we stand – community and gathering in the spirit of what Claudia Jones created. There are also vast opportunities for journalism that reports the diaspora not simply as an addendum to a western white experience. What is journalism for? For me, it is to exist on your own terms.To receive the complete version of The Long Wave in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCompetitionView image in fullscreenJason Okundaye’s book Revolutionary Acts: Love and Brotherhood in Black Gay Britain.Next week, the Long Wave marks its second anniversary. What, to you, is the most memorable edition of the Long Wave? Perhaps there was a piece you deeply related to, or one that drew your attention to a shared diaspora experience?Send us your name, location, your chosen edition, and 3-5 sentences explaining why. Our favourite responses will receive a copy of former Long Wave editor Jason Okundaye’s book Revolutionary Acts: Love and Brotherhood in Black Gay Britain – part of the Guardian bookshop’sBlack History Month collection. They may also be published in next week’s anniversary edition of the Long Wave.Entries should be submitted tothelongwave@theguardian.comby 9am on Monday 26 October.Diaspora discussesLast week, Long Wave editor Micha Frazer-Carrollshared her experienceof attending a Jamaican Patois class, and the barriers to Caribbean diasporans learning Creole languages. Here’s what readers thought:double quotation markLiving in Scotland, I rarely speak patios, but I enjoy hearing it and sharing a few words. Its etymology is what fascinates me. I cried when I learned thatnyam, our word for eat, comes from the Fulani word,nyami, meaning to eat. Alsounuis plural for “you” in Yoruba. I cried because it brought home all those lost voices, words from home, and people displaced against their will.Pauline Brown, based in Glasgow, Scotlanddouble quotation markI grew up also surrounded by Indo-Guyanese English Patois. My grandmother’s Patois included many Bihari, Sanskrit, West African and Indigenous Arawak terms. I remember speaking on my first day of kindergarten and my teacher being quite confused. My grandmother died a few years ago and when she was admitted to hospital the staff did not know what language she spoke. Her doctor very rudely joked: “we thought she was from another planet and that she was speaking some Martian language.” I feel that she could’ve lived many more years had there not been a perceived language barrier during her care.Rajendra Kapila Basdeo, based in Montréal, Québec, Canadadouble quotation markI’m a Jamaican living in Canada, but I go to Jamaica every year. In Canada, the Jamaican language is much more recognised, taught at the university, translated into the New Testament and celebrated thanks to the work of many people. I write poetry in Jamaican (the term that marks it as a language as opposed to a dialect). I think we have come some way away from the stigma. You should hear my Canadian born 10-year-old grandson speak it as his mother practices with him and teaches him the grammar!Jennifer Walcott, based in Toronto, Canadadouble quotation markI am pleased to know someone is teaching Jamaican Patwa, but I did not agree with parts of this newsletter’s description. I doubt that anyone would overstandkinfor “skin” orkalpfor “skyalp” (the usual pronunciation). For me, when I returned from England speaking “the Queen’s English” I learned Patois by being in and around Patois speakers. It blended into my language and musical rhythm until it is completely a part of how I now speak. However, may the students press on. Learning more languages is always good for everyone.Barbara Blake-Hannah, based in Kingston, Jamaicadouble quotation markAs someone born and raised in Jamaica, I’ve never even thought about how Jamaicans born and raised abroad may feel about speaking Patois. This newsletter was enlightening and opened my eyes to how they suffer a pain that I cannot understand, and instead of teasing them about how they sound when they try to speak like a native Jamaican, I need to give them grace and help them with their Patois. I’ll make sure to tell my friends as well.David P.A. Mullings, based in the US and JamaicaExplore more on these topicsMediaThe Long WaveNewspapers & magazinesNewspapersActivismBlack Lives Matter movementAfricaCaribbeannewslettersShareReuse this content

title: The Experiment review – easily the most disturbing thing on TV | Television | The Guardian
description: As members of the public tour a fake ‘residential home’ for disabled people riddled with Nazi ideology, you desperately hope someone will speak up. Prepare for the most excruciating viewing of your life
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: As members of the public tour a fake ‘residential home’ for disabled people riddled with Nazi ideology, you desperately hope someone will speak up. Prepare for the most excruciating viewing of your life
Content: Mat Fraser and Sophie Morgan watch events unfold on monitors.Photograph: Kalel ProductionsView image in fullscreenMat Fraser and Sophie Morgan watch events unfold on monitors.Photograph: Kalel ProductionsTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Experiment review – easily the most disturbing thing on TVAs members of the public tour a fake ‘residential home’ for disabled people riddled with Nazi ideology, you desperately hope someone will speak up. Prepare for the most excruciating viewing of your lifeFrances RyanWed 21 Oct 2026 18.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave never had to pause a programme halfway through before to catch my breath. That is until The Experiment – Channel 4’s highly controversial social exercise designed to find out “how susceptible the British public are” to Nazi ideology about disabled people. This is a show so disturbing, timely and surreal that within 90 seconds of viewing it alone, I am looking around for confirmation from an empty room that any of this is happening.We start with a clip of Hitler. Against a backdrop of growing anti-benefits and ableist rhetoric, presenters Mat Fraser and Sophie Morgan fear the disabled community globally are once again being framed as a financial burden. Their question is: can the British public be persuaded that disabled people should live in “money saving” segregated institutions and be given low-skilled jobs to be productive?Cue “Segrilife”, a residential home for disabled people that members of the public are invited to tour. In fact, every resident is a disabled actor, and the creepily jovial corporate films and posters are made using AI. Fraser and Morgan are watching events unfold on monitors in another room.Each part of the tour is based on a different piece of Nazi ideology, much of which has a menacingly clear link to some modern-day ideas. First off, the group are shown “the workshop”, where disabled people are placing beads on to string to earn an allowance. “I used to be in marketing. I don’t know why I’m in this room now,” a character called Sonia says, threading monotonously in her wheelchair.Soon, we are touring a dormitory (or “the nest”) – a room with threadbare beds lined up in a row for disabled people to use as a communal bedroom, with cameras placed on the walls to monitor them. “It’s safe,” one woman in the tour group says, approvingly. “That’s what the people we’ve just met need.”On the walls are posters repackaging 1930s fascist concepts with a glossy contemporary face – the price tag of a disabled person’s care package in bold font next to their smiling photo, with mantras such as: “Normal life isn’t for everyone.”It is excruciating and sinister and there is little letup, the producers building the tension methodically as viewers witness dehumanisation being normalised in real time.View image in fullscreenVisibly distressed … Fraser and Morgan in The Experiment.Photograph: Kalel ProductionsFew TV moments this year have been more disturbing than when three members of the public and a manager (an actor) discuss the “cost” of a young disabled woman as she sits silently in the same room, with the “savings” the state has made by putting her in an institution glowing on an iPad.You are, of course, waiting desperately for someone – anyone – to speak up. It’s a long wait. There are a couple of women who show some concern but it’s all rather tame given what they’re seeing. By the time one man on the tour finally declares, “This is hell on earth,” I don’t know whether to cheer or cry.Threaded between these scenes is a harrowing history of “Aktion T4” – the Nazi’s programme to systematically segregate and murder disabled people. Fraser – visibly distressed – and Morgan visit Hartheim Castle in Austria, one of six facilities in which tens of thousands of so-called “mercy killings” of disabled people occurred in gas chambers from 1939.You could argue that the programme-makers controversially pairing Nazi killings with 2026 rhetoric is counterproductive to winning over hard-to-reach critics. That the horrors of the past are of such unique depravity that discussing them in a modern context will let the Daily Mail et al dismiss the whole thing as woke hysteria. And yet you could also claim that’s the point: it is comforting to tell ourselves fascism and democratic ideas are always neatly defined, that the beliefs strangers held 80 years ago bear no relation to what our relatives post on Facebook today.There is the standard reassuring reveal at the end of the programme, in which the participants discover the truth and make all the right noises to suggest they have learned something. But it is hard to shake off what we’ve seen: most of the public who take part are convinced it is quite rational to treat disabled people as less than human, and with remarkable ease.Some excuse it for the strain on the taxpayer. Others say institutionalisation is for disabled people’s own sake. As one woman concludes, it’s “incredible” they are being looked after and “kept occupied”.That’s the thing about prejudice towards disabled people. It is not always violent or cruel. Much of the time, it is an almost well-meaning belief that disabled people are not quite like other people. Not as complex. More infantile. Of less value.There is a moment when Morgan covers her eyes with her open fingers, barely able to watch through the monitors what has been unleashed. Viewers would be forgiven for doing the same. But acknowledging that these attitudes still exist is the only way we might begin to rid society of them. None of us should look away.The Experiment is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDisabilityreviewsShareReuse this content

title: What an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountain | Recycling | The Guardian
description: This summer alone, 26 local authorities in the UK had to stop accepting fridges and freezers for recycling. Now the appliances are piling up around the country – with no proper disposal date in sight
Author: Sam Wollaston
Headline: This summer alone, 26 local authorities in the UK had to stop accepting fridges and freezers for recycling. Now the appliances are piling up around the country – with no proper disposal date in sight
Content: A chilling sight … some of the 3,000 fridges and freezers at the former Mayton Wood recycling centre in Little Hautbois, Norfolk.Photograph: James Linsell Clark/SWNSView image in fullscreenA chilling sight … some of the 3,000 fridges and freezers at the former Mayton Wood recycling centre in Little Hautbois, Norfolk.Photograph: James Linsell Clark/SWNSRecyclingWhat an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountainThis summer alone, 26 local authorities in the UK had to stop accepting fridges and freezers for recycling. Now the appliances are piling up around the country – with no proper disposal date in sightSam WollastonWed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot much is happening in the tinyNorfolkhamlet of Little Hautbois on the day I visit. The pub, once popular with airmen from RAF Coltishall, stopped being a pub a long time ago, even before RAF Coltishall stopped being RAF Coltishall. It’s not Saturday, so there are no weddings at Hautbois Hall. Nor is it 19 May, so the restless, headless ghost of Thomas Boleyn isn’t driving his carriage across the bridge over the River Bure, as he is said to do on the anniversary of the execution of his daughter, Anne. Today, a lovely autumn one, all is as it should be.But half a mile down a narrow country lane is an incongruous and baffling sight: a strip of gentle hillside made up of large white rectangular blocks, piled up and sparkling in the sunshine. A glacier, you might think, if you were in Norway rather than Norfolk. (And ice is involved, as it happens.) As you get nearer, the picture becomes clearer; the blocks have coils on one face, doors and handles on the opposite one, plus the manufacturers’ names. It’s a glacier of fridges, more than 3,000 of them.Kate Murrell, the assistant director of waste management at Norfolk county council, is here to let me in. The fridges are surrounded by a security fence with CCTV cameras. “It’s not what we want to see here, or what the local residents want to see either,” says Murrell. The nearest local resident, Stuart Brown, tells me over his garden fence that it is “a bit of an eyesore”.These eyesores are not particular to Norfolk. All around the UK, old fridges are piling up, including in Nottinghamshire, Durham, Oxfordshire, Gloucestershire and Newport, the last of which found itself with a mountain of 80,000 appliances over the summer. So what is behind it?View image in fullscreenA blot on the landscape … with recycling centres unable to take fridges, fly tipping is increasing.Photograph: Justin Kase zsixz/AlamyIn part, it is because fridges and freezers are difficult to dispose of. David Santillo, a senior scientist with Greenpeace Research Laboratories, based at the University of Exeter, explains that they contain gases and materials that are harmful to the environment if the appliances are not dismantled correctly. Thus, by law, fridges have to be dismantled at specialist processing plants. The problem is that the number of these plants is shrinking rapidly in the UK.In Norfolk,a fireat an electrical waste and treatment facility in Thetford in April meant there was nowhere to recycle fridges and freezers for two or three months, which caused a pile-up. “If you got a new fridge and took the old one to the tip, they turned you away,” says Murrell. Then came this summer’s record-breaking temperatures, which caused more fridges and freezers tobreak down– and some processing plants to shut temporarily. As Murrell says: “During Covid, people upped their refrigeration capacity at home,” so there are even more appliances to deal with.double quotation markIt’s nationwide. I’m hearing more and more reports of councils strugglingAfter the Thetford fire, Norfolk council ran out of treatment facilities to which it could send fridges. Thetford was one of just eight full-scale processing plants for fridges in the UK; another major plant in south Wales shut down when the recycling companyUnimetals filed for liquidationand a plant in the West Midlands closed in February due to a fire. This summer alone, 26 local authorities had to stop accepting fridges and freezers. Compared with Newport’s 80,000 fridge mountain, this Norfolk site maybe doesn’t look so terrible, though the stark contrast with its bucolic surroundings certainly adds to the shock value.“It’s nationwide,” says Jon Hubbard, the chair of the Local Government Association’s neighbourhoods committee. “I’m hearing more and more reports of councils struggling. In my own local authority in Wiltshire, I see large quantities of fridges and freezers piling up. It’s certainly not getting any better.”Santillo says the main danger with these appliances is the refrigerants. “Lots of different chemicals are used as refrigerants. Very old fridges could contain CFCs, which are ozone-depleting substances. There are almost certainly going to be HFCs, which are potent greenhouse gases. Others will contain propane and isobutane. Commercial fridges can contain ammonia.”Once removed and isolated, he says: “The refrigerants can be recycled and reused or, in the case of some of the old ones, they would need to be incinerated. Then you have the foams used for insulation, which can contain hazardous substances such as fluorinated compounds that also have to be recycled or incinerated.”While some of the fridges at Little Hautbois are clearly quite old, others look pretty recent – in working order even. Murrell says they probably are. Often the fridges are disposed of because the owner wants an “upgrade, or it’s a new kitchen and they want one that fits in with this, not that”. Some just aren’t built to last or are impossible to repair.View image in fullscreen‘Often the fridges are disposed of because the owner wants an upgrade’ … Kate Murrell, assistant director of waste management at Norfolk council.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianSantillo says manufacturers could do a lot more to stop fridges and freezers needing to be disposed of. “They could find ways of making them last longer. They’re a significant investment and some of them aren’t very robust.” It doesn’t help that we no longer get things fixed. “The weakest link is always the compressor; once that goes, it becomes so expensive to fix that people tend to just get a new fridge.”double quotation markPeople claim to be legitimate waste disposal organisations, collect your fridge and then dump itHubbard points a finger in another direction – at the producer compliance schemes that coordinate the collection, recycling and disposal of fridges and freezers in the UK. The idea is that the polluter pays, but because treatment capacity has been hit so hard, producers haven’t been able to keep up, so councils are having to handle and fund the collection, storage and treatment of these goods. “We’re picking up the phone, and they’re not answering,” says Hubbard of the schemes. “They need to come up with a proper business plan to get back up to full-scale recycling again. In the short term, they need to come up with a solution to storage.” At the moment, this is also falling to local authorities. “It’s costing money that should be spent on libraries, sports centres, fixing potholes, delivering health and social care,” he says. Murrell says more help needs to come from central government: “What the country needs is a more resilient infrastructure to deal with fridges and freezers at the end of their lives.”The other worry, says Hubbard, is the risk of fly-tipping when council disposal services are forced to halt. “Council-tax payers are being scammed by people who claim to be legitimate waste disposal organisations, collect your fridge and then dump it where they shouldn’t. And if that fridge can be tracked back to a resident, it’s the resident who gets prosecuted.” He advises people to take photographs of any disposal company’s licence.View image in fullscreenGoing nowhere … fridges and freezers at Mayton Wood recycling centre, Little Hautbois, Norfolk.Photograph: Joshua Bright/The GuardianAnd the piles of fridges building up? “Recycling fridges should be about containment,” says Santillo. “You have to take the refrigerant out, contain it, then that goes on for further treatment. That’s clearly broken down and they’re just being dumped. They certainly shouldn’t be left to fall apart and fragment in the environment.”He has an additional concern. “If you have piles of fridges and freezers, they’re going to become home to wildlife; they’re great places to attract animals that like to live in small spaces.” Murrell says that here in Norfolk, pest control come in regularly and haven’t discovered any new residents, gnawing away at fluorinated insulation. But looking up at the kestrel hovering overhead, I wonder. I don’t think it’s after putrefied turkey twizzlers.Norfolk is now accepting fridges, but only at seven of its 19 recycling sites, which is all that can be managed. “That’s a way of reducing the volumes we get in,” says Murrell. “Customers might have to travel a bit further and so think twice about disposal at the moment.”A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs says these delays are “frustrating” and that the minister responsible for waste crime has written to producer compliance schemes asking them “to take all reasonable steps to fix this fast, as this cannot go on any longer”.Safe and easy ways to recycle electricals – and even get money for your old gadgetsRead moreThe spokesperson added: “We appreciate the challenges facing local authorities, and are working closely with them, the Environment Agency and industry to manage the impact of capacity shortages, including allowing temporary storage sites and looking at long-term solutions to ensure this does not happen again.”In the meantime, the site here outside Little Hautbois is full, with no room for any more fridges. Nor are the ones already piled up here going anywhere at the moment, and Murrell is not hopeful that this will change any time soon. “Until we see national capacity really increase, councils like us are going to see disruption to the services. I think this one’s stuck for quite a while.”Chances are then that next 19 May, when Thomas Boleyn comes riding through with his phantom horses and carriage, he’ll look to the side of the road and think: “What an eyesore!”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: don’t want to get your Big Winter Coat out just yet? Try ‘onion dressing’  | Fashion | The Guardian
description: It’s time to learn the art of layering – and we’re talking a crew neck with a ballet wrap and blazer, not full-on outdoor explorer
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: It’s time to learn the art of layering – and we’re talking a crew neck with a ballet wrap and blazer, not full-on outdoor explorer
Content: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Melanie WilkinsonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jess Cartner-Morley on fashionFashionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: don’t want to get your Big Winter Coat out just yet? Try ‘onion dressing’It’s time to learn the art of layering – and we’re talking a crew neck with a ballet wrap and blazer, not full-on outdoor explorerJess Cartner-MorleyWed 21 Oct 2026 11.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs layering an art? Probably not in the traditional sense. We are not talking theBayeux tapestryhere. No one is going to queue round the block to admire the subtle interplay between your Uniqlo Heattech and your cashmere crewneck. Still, I think it’s nice to romanticise this stuff. The deeply unpoetic truth is that it is going to get cold and wearing one item of clothing at a time simply isn’t going to cut it. So let’s pretend that the sliver of white T-shirt beneath a jumper, the shirt collar poking out above a cardigan, or the ballet wrap over a snug top are not acts of basic thermal self-preservation, but composition. A creative statement about proportion, texture, colour and self-expression. If you have to wear half your wardrobe at once, you may as well make a masterpiece out of it.The avant-garde layering term to drop in order to sound like a connoisseur this season is onion dressing. Not the most romantic name, but a clear visual for the most refined form of layering, which is fine layers rather than hefty ones. And instead of the top layer covering all beneath it, each piece should be visible. As if we were slicing through the onion and looking at a cross-section if you will excuse me labouring the allium thing. This is layering with finesse rather than brute force. Hems and collars and cuffs give an outfit depth and texture without adding too much bulk. You want to look intriguing and multi-dimensional, not likeJoey in Friends wearing all of Chandler’s clothes.double quotation markConsider either the middle or top layer being sleeveless to avoid feeling like you’ve been stuffed like a Christmas turkeyOnion dressing is your sartorial safety blanket in an increasingly uncertain climate. Autumn was unpredictable enough to start with, and our new weather reality is constant chaos. The merry-go-round keeps spinning even when you are indoors: will the train carriage be arctic and draughty or stuffy and overheated today? Who knows, comrades. You are invited for Sunday lunch, but will your pals have their heating on full blast or not at all? One can neither ask in advance, nor comment. Best to be stylishly prepared for all eventualities.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The GuardianThe greatest joy of onion dressing is that you can put off the moment when you start wearing your Big Coat. As a psychological upside, this is not to be sniffed at. In January and February you will be stuck in that thing, so you don’t want to be sick of the sight of it by then. Imaginative combinations of less bulky pieces can keep you warm, offer temperature flexibility, make getting dressed less dull, and get some extra use out of jackets that would otherwise be sidelined for six months.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: now is the perfect time to flash some laceRead moreStart with the science. The allure of layering is looking relaxed, effortless and ready for anything. Red-faced, sweaty and unable to move your arms because your sweater is too bulky for the sleeves of your jacket is not elegant. Follow the principles of hardy folk dressing for the outdoors and start with a fine base layer, something breathable to keep you warm without cooking you. A polo neck is extra cosy, but a crewneck looks chic. Check that the neckline is clean and tidy, because this part will be on show and that needs to look deliberate. Then a middle layer: this could be a plaid or plain cotton button down shirt, or an interesting cardi, or a sweater. Outdoors, all you need now is a “shield” layer: an easy on-and-off piece, which could be a blazer, a chore jacket or a puffer vest. Oh, one last practical point: consider either the middle or top layer being sleeveless to avoid feeling like you’ve been stuffed like a Christmas turkey.You need some flair, too. This is style, not pass-the-parcel. If all the layers are utilitarian the effect can veer a bit “Duke of Edinburgh award”. A pop of colour works. Contrasting textures will add sophistication. A collar or layered necklines are good for elevating the vibe. Layering is not going to get you a retrospective at the Tate, but it does take an eye for colour, composition and texture. Keeping warm is much more interesting when you use your imagination.Model: Imogen May at Milk. Styling: Melanie Wilkinson.
