title: Ilford Boy review – Barbra Streisand teaches teen to smile about the way we are | Theatre | The Guardian
description: In Danny Lee Wynter’s drama, a quiet boy struggles amid the swirl of his family until a mercurial friend offers him another future
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: In Danny Lee Wynter’s drama, a quiet boy struggles amid the swirl of his family until a mercurial friend offers him another future
Content: Debut … Leo Whitfield Harris in Ilford Boy.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreenDebut … Leo Whitfield Harris in Ilford Boy.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewIlford Boy review – Barbra Streisand teaches teen to smile about the way we areDonmar Warehouse, LondonIn Danny Lee Wynter’s drama, a quiet boy struggles amid the swirl of his family until a mercurial friend offers him another futureKate WyverWed 21 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBroad Essex accents fill the stage in Danny Lee Wynter’s sprawling family drama. The busy script from theBlack Superheroplaywright is crammed with a fractious extended family treading heavily over old arguments, but the production sings when an old friend swans back into town. Set across the 80s and 90s in the shadow of the Aids crisis, this story’s beating heart travels around on tap shoes.Quiet teenager Ted (Leo Whitfield Harris in his stage debut) is surrounded by the loud swirl of his feuding family, with everyone’s rusty views on queerness, race and masculinity grating against each other as they clear out his showtune-loving nanna’s house in Ilford. His father (a bolshie Gershwyn Eustache Jr) is pushing him towards boxing and girls, so Ted grits his teeth and resists anything seen as weakness, but in doing so he resists kindness too.View image in fullscreenA chaotic neon home … Peter McKintosh’s set for Ilford BoyPhotograph: Helen MurrayThere is sharpness and humour within the core family’s spiky arguments, with an abundance of anguished love offered by Ted’s mum (Ria Zmitrowicz), though some of the wider family could have more substance. Flashbacks build up backstory, enabling the creative team to have fun with costumes and hair. In both timelines, Tim Sheader’s direction scatters the family across Peter McKintosh’s surprisingly sparse double-decked neon home that doesn’t quite reflect the chaos – or the occasional warmth – within.View image in fullscreenEffervescent … Craig Stein.Photograph: Helen MurrayBut then there’s Pat, Ted’s mum’s old friend, played by the mercurial Craig Stein. While everyone else is telling Ted how to be, here is a Black gay man showing him another way. As Ted is drawn in by Pat’s knowledge of Barbra Streisand, the play begins to move away from the more predictable father-son dynamics and towards something more effervescent.There’s a whole life in the way Pat looks with disgust at Ted’s father, in how he talks about his lost love, in the hand he stretches out to Ted when the teenager asks him to dance. Illuminated in a brilliant moment of boldness from the script, with glorious movement by Ebony Molina, this is the image we’re left with long after Pat’s left the stage and the rest of the family have turned away: a beautiful man, up above the audience, leg kicked high in the air, radiant with life.AtDonmar Warehouse, London, until 28 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreDonmar WarehouseEssexWest EndBlack British culturereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Why is Liz Truss trying to be Danny Dyer with her new book? | Liz Truss | The Guardian
description: Bank Job, the former prime minister’s forthcoming publication, is about a shady cabal that brought down the bond market. Seemingly she has forgotten that this was her doing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bank Job, the former prime minister’s forthcoming publication, is about a shady cabal that brought down the bond market. Seemingly she has forgotten that this was her doing
Content: Banging the same drum … the cover of Liz Truss's new book.Photograph: Liz TrussView image in fullscreenBanging the same drum … the cover of Liz Truss's new book.Photograph: Liz TrussPass notesLiz TrussWhy is Liz Truss trying to be Danny Dyer with her new book?Bank Job, the former prime minister’s forthcoming title, is about a shady cabal that brought down the bond market. Seemingly she has forgotten that this was her doingWed 21 Oct 2026 11.04 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Liz Truss’s Bank Job.Age:Forthcoming.Appearance:Etiquette dictates that you should never judge a book by its cover.Yes, but do it anyway.It looks like a poster for one of those bad gangster films Danny Dyer used to make, featuring a shadowy set of tough guys – except, instead of Dyer front and centre, there’s Liz Truss.So you’re saying this is a book – byTruss?Yes. The former prime minister’s new book is out next week. Its subtitle is A Short Book on How the Bank of England Broke the Bond Market and Brought Down the Government.I have so many questions.Who wouldn’t?The response to her first book, Ten Years to Save the West, didn’t seem to guarantee that she’d get to publish a second.‘Five-year-old on acid’: Liz Truss’s Ten Years to Save the West, digested by John CraceRead moreOK, first: how short is short?Amazon states that the book comes in at just 99 pages. For reference, that’s about 13 times shorter than War and Peace, or three times shorter than the 2012 memoir byTulisa from N-Dubz.Next:who onearth is publishing this?That would be Free Speech Press, which says it is “dedicated to publishing books that challenge conventional thinking”. Its authors includeJennifer Arcuri, who you might remember as that woman who claimed she had an affair with Boris Johnson, and the guy who went viral for sayingyou can grow concrete.Mike Graham?That’s him. Actually, this is an interesting link: Graham also owns UKLive, the YouTube channel that now hosts Truss’s show.Is that still going?Sadly yes. And by the look of recent videos – which include “Why Britain’s political system is completely broken”, “Britain is becoming a LOW-TRUST society” and “Defund the BBC” – she’s still scratching around the US right’s favourite talking points in the hopes that someone will love her again.Whathas been the response to the announcement? Are people excited?Well, when Truss announced Bank Job on X, just six days before its publication date, replies variously retitled it as “Bankrupt” and – inevitably – “Lettuce Job”.I suppose we should ask what the book is actually about.It’s the same drum that Truss has been banging since her embarrassment as PM: the country is secretly run by the Bank of England, the Treasury and the Office for Budget Responsibility, with this unelected cartel ensuring that Britain will never change.Still, at least it’s nice and short.Exactly – it’s a toilet book, in the sense that it will probably do in a pinch if you run out of Andrex.One last question.Go ahead.The book is about breaking the bond market, and bringing down the government,but …But wasn’t it Truss who did that? Yes, it was her.Do say:“Liz Truss knows who broke the bond market.”Don’t say:“Presumably because Liz Truss owns a mirror.”Explore more on these topicsLiz TrussPass notesPolitics booksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: This foolish decision undermines hopes that this government will take the necessary steps the climate crisis demands, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: This foolish decision undermines hopes that this government will take the necessary steps the climate crisis demands, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Illustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianOpinionClimate crisisBurnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a penZoe WilliamsThis foolish decision undermines hopes that this government will take the necessary steps the climate crisis demandsWed 21 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 21.29 EDTShareWhen the news broke that theUK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield, I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately, the theme suggested by readers was what can the public actually do in the face of what feels like paralysing climate doom?There is so much going on that is hopeful: biodiversity tracking, river protection, rewilding. Shruti Suresh, from the independent watchdog Global Witness, told those in attendance that if they wanted to effect change, they should protest against Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project. The message was so well understood that it didn’t need labouring.The mood in the room when the news came in was one of audible dismay. People had just watched the minister for climate transition declare that she could see the challenges ahead and was ready for them. The Jackdaw announcement will face immediate protest and legal challenge, but it sends a very clear signal from the government: we don’t mean what we say about ending emissions.It turns out you can take all imaginable personal responsibility to arrest the climate crisis, make lifestyle adjustments that even five years ago you wouldn’t have dreamed of, miraculously summon the energy to take collective action from what is often private despair, but it will be insufficient as long as corporations – assisted by the government – are working against you, in effect with impunity. At some point, you need to get the people you elected to do what we all know – and they acknowledge – is necessary.The Jackdaw decision had been quietly parked during the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when the threat of the Greens seemed greater to Labourthan it turned out to be. But while Labour successfully buried the issue during the campaign, the underlying issues surrounding Jackdaw – and Rosebank, which is yet to be decided upon – persist.Since the 2015 Paris agreement, we have been committed to try to limit temperature rises to 1.5C, and we’ve known for at least five years that means the vast majority of fossil fuels have to stay in the ground. As of 2024, there’s been scientific consensusthat the target of 1.5C is “deader than a doornail”, whilethis week’s emissions-gap reportcould not be clearer: the threshold will be breached and it will cause unimaginable damage, yet with urgent emissions reduction, there is a way back from the abyss. There is no workable argument that runs: “Everyone has to leave their fossil fuels in the ground, as a matter of the utmost urgency, except for us; everyone has to prioritise the long-term survival of a livable planet over energy bills, except for us; we all need to reach carbon neutrality and worry about high-skilled jobs later, except for us.” The Jackdaw field isn’t huge, will peak in a short timeand won’t on its own reduce energy bills, which are determined by global markets. So it’s tempting to shuffle it off as a side-order issue, but it matters: it destroys our moral authority as a nation and it extinguishes hope.The climate debate operates on two tracks that don’t meet. On the one hand, we talk about non-linear irreversible tipping points whose effects would be so seismic that the question of mitigation is too vast and, frankly, too painful to consider. The only bearable discussion of thecollapseof the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) – a system of currents within the Atlantic Ocean – is how to avoid it, and the contested matter of whetherthat is even possible. We talk aboutheat deaths across 854 European citiesover the past summer, and we talk about areas in the UK of environmental deprivation, flood risks and poorly insulated housing. We also talk about food security both in the short term, with potato crops destroyed by the weather, and in the long term, with supply chains subject to the incomprehensible devastation of every country going through its own particular climate crisis simultaneously.We look at the social unrest across Europe– which is thefastest-warming continent– and ask to what extent the deprivation created by an unstable climate is being weaponised by a far right hell-bent on choking off climate action.Then we gate off all that knowledge, all that anxiety, all that will to action, and turn our attention to the UK’s immediate energy compromises. The arguments here run that since we’re going to import gas from somewhere anyway, because any transition will take time, we may as well get it at home. Even though it’s well known that household energy priceswon’t be reduced, the government can use the tax take to reduce VAT. Some categories of emission are lower from UK gas than they would be from energy imported from the Gulf.We need to bring these conversations together, because what they describe is one shared reality. Alongside the carbon that Jackdaw and Rosebank would release, they’ve “sucked all the oxygen out of the debate around what to do about climate change”, Chris Stark, the former CEO of the Climate Change Committee, has said. A warm homes initiative would create vastly more jobs,research recently found, and by reducing bills would also bring far more prosperity, with the additional advantage of not undermining the climate goals we claim to hold.Thinking of agriculture alone, the headroom, investment and planning we’re ploughing into carbon extraction could make an immeasurable difference to building resilience for an already uncertain future. The most meaningful way to reduce household bills is to reduce reliance on increasingly turbulent world markets, by separating the renewable price from the fossil fuel price, which would immediately boost the already flourishing wind and solar sectors.Gas and oil proponents beg us to be pragmatic, while their own arguments are floridly impractical: conducted as though the outside world doesn’t exist; as though carbon emissions are tomorrow’s problem; as though there aren’t better solutions for high prices and insecurity everywhere you look; as though we have time to quickly exhaust all our bad answers before we move on to good ones.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne depressing aspect of the Jackdaw announcement – although by no means themost depressing – is that it’s all about the optics. Even its most trenchant supporters would admit that it’s not a long-term solution to energy security. Rather, it’s a flag to the fossil-fuel industry that the government isn’t an enemy. It’s a toxic smoke signal to the US that the UK might not be with it, but definitely isn’t against it. It’s a feeble attempt at domestic politicking byLabour, trying to deflate the Conservatives’ anti-net zero bubble. It’s a statement of intent to make no trouble, when the trouble is already upon us.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: From strife-torn France to the UK, rightwing populists win when they stir chaos while promising order  | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: Marine Le Pen and Donald Trump are arsonists who play at being firefighters. Nigel Farage is finding that act harder to pull off in Andy Burnham’s Britain, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: Marine Le Pen and Donald Trump are arsonists who play at being firefighters. Nigel Farage is finding that act harder to pull off in Andy Burnham’s Britain, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionMarine Le PenFrom strife-torn France to the UK, rightwing populists win when they stir chaos while promising orderRafael BehrMarine Le Pen and Donald Trump are arsonists who play at being firefighters. Nigel Farage is finding that act harder to pull off in Andy Burnham’s BritainWed 21 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 07.08 EDTShareAn election where one side represents chaos will nearly always be won by the party that promises order instead. Public fatigue after years of turbulent Tory rule accounted for Labour’s 2024 landslide victory more than any policy in Keir Starmer’s manifesto. Across the Channel, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally (RN), is currentlyon course to winnext year’s presidential poll with a pledge of “restored authority and security” for a country that has spent years cycling between enervating stasis and explosive crisis.Le Pen has been boosted in recent days byscenes of city centres ablazeand shops being looted as student demonstrations mutated into riots. Street confrontation is a more standard feature of the political repertoire in France than in most settled democracies, but the destruction was disturbing by any measure.President Emmanuel Macron’s government, debilitated by the lack of a parliamentary majority, looked unprepared for the scale of the unrest. There was ample indication that something big was brewing. What began with high school students despairing at the neglected state of secondary education evolved into a general mobilisation of anger at high living costs and a lack of economic opportunities. Aggressive police tactics radicalised the crowd. As night followed day, and just as predictably, political fury gave way to opportunistic pillaging.Prime minister Sébastien Lecornuaccused “ultra-left” provocateursof stirring disorder as part of a strategy to render the country ungovernable in the run-up to next year’s elections. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the populist left’s presidential candidate, countered thatviolence was the natural byproductof a degenerate repressive state that conspires to discredit resistance, and that the protests channelled the heroic spirit of May 1968.At 75, Mélenchon is old enough to remember that Paris spring of revolutionary fervour. He has a keen following in the current generation of activist students, but the insurrectionary rhetoric unsettles swathes of conservativeFrance. His pungency could put Le Pen in the Élysée Palace.In the past she has been locked out of the presidency bycoalitions of moderate and left voters rallying, often without enthusiasm, behind the candidate best placed to stop her. RN’s advances in parliament have been checked in the same way, although it is currently the biggest party.Macron has twice been the beneficiary of that dynamic, but he can’t run again, has no obvious successor and is so radioactively unpopular that the whole liberal centre ground is contaminated by his standing on it.Current polling indicates that the “republican front” would unravel if the only names in a second-round run-off were Mélenchon and Le Pen. The centre-right would break for the RN leader. It probably wouldn’t even be close.France’s crisis has not escaped notice across the Atlantic, where it is viewed through the warped lens of Maga ideology.Donald Trump explainedthat “France is burning” because the country has been overrun by immigrants “with hatred in their hearts”. JD Vanceagreed that“western liberals” were to blame for opening European borders to “the third world” and advised American voters to view French misfortune as a premonition of the future if Congress is captured by Democrats in midterm elections next month.Republican efforts to cast their rivals as catalysts of national ruin have limited traction when Trump is the obvious engine of chaos. Democrats didn’t start the war in Iran. Nor did they author a deranged trade policy that alienated the US’s friends, turning even Canada into a foe.This is a common problem for incumbent demagogues. In opposition, simple solutions are proposed for complex problems: tariffs as the remedy for industrial decline; expelling illegal immigrants as the answer to every social and economic grievance; trusting in the leader’s judgment as the answer to everything else.In office, those mechanisms fail to deliver the promised benefits. Someone needs to be blamed. The categories of undesirable element grow. Media, universities, courts and opposition parties are called crooked or treasonous. But purges disrupt the smooth running of a country. They are bad for the economy. This is how the insecure leader goes through the gears of tyranny. A craving for control generates dissent, which is attacked as a menace to society, requiring more draconian law enforcement. When that provokes more determined opposition, the dissenters are denounced as extremists who jeopardise public safety.Trump has travelled some way down that road already. He might accelerate a lot further after the midterms. One option is to make bogus claims of election fraud, denying the validity of results that, if allowed to stand, would empower Democrats to hold a rogue president to account. His despotic temperament and his record of refusal to admit any electoral weakness suggest he would rather trigger a constitutional crisis of existential dimensions for American democracy than acquiesce to cohabitation with an unfriendly Congress. He will plunge the country deeper into chaos and insist that the nation rally around him as the only one capable of restoring order.That is standard authoritarian operating procedure. The arsonists affect dismay at the conflagrations they ignite. They cavort in firefighter costumes and hose the flames with petrol.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is the role Le Pen is readying herself for now in France. If she wins next year’s election, the backlash from the left will be ferocious. That challenge will be eagerly confronted by an incoming president likely to be looking for pretexts to declare a national emergency and remake the republic as a vehicle for her personal authority.Britain’s radical right parties dream of an equivalent opportunity. They revel in lurid imagery of societal breakdown. Sometimes the fantasy is camouflaged as a warning about the dangers of unchecked immigration, but impatience for a violent reckoning is never far from the surface. ForRupert Lowe, leader of Restore Britain, there is seemingly no effort to conceal the relish. He told his followers on X last week that his agenda would certainly trigger “civil unrest and rioting,” and that “what needs to happen will be incredibly painful”.Lowe is still a relatively fringe figure but he exerts disproportionate influence in the conservative digital ecosystem thanks toamplification on X by Elon Musk, the platform’s oligarch proprietor. Lowe’s candidate beat the Tories and Liberal Democrats in Manchester’s mayoral byelection earlier this year. By competing for votes with Reform UK, Restore Britain has drawn Nigel Farageinto an arms racein fanatical anti-migrant rhetoric.Farage’s status as a more serious contender in the electoral arena allows him to launder ideas that were once self-evidently extreme – mass deportations, for example – as mainstream policy. That doesn’t automatically make them popular. There is an audience for ethnically selective nationalism but it has a ceiling. The voters who are motivated by determination to thwart Farage outnumber those who want him installed in Downing Street.That tactical coalition is easily galvanised because prominent figures on the British right wear their arsonist intent so brazenly. Also, a stable Labour government isn’t giving them opportunities to play at being firefighters.To advance on power, Reform UK has to win over the kinds of voters that Le Pen sees heading her way through the smouldering rubble of French politics: people exhausted and bewildered by the system unravelling, without hope that incumbent authorities can get the country back on track, and amenable to the argument that fanatical leftists are the more menacing agents of chaos. Thankfully, those are not the conditions of British politics. Andy Burnham’s every step should be guided by the need to keep it that way.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsMarine Le PenOpinionFranceEuropeNigel FarageRupert LoweThe far rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: Gas go-ahead ignites oily response from Trump, while speaker seems ready to blow  | John Crace | The Guardian
description: The energy secretary’s trip north provokes Hoyle’s futile rage, while ITV’s Reform exposé leaves Zia Yusuf immensely sad
Author: John Crace
Headline: The energy secretary’s trip north provokes Hoyle’s futile rage, while ITV’s Reform exposé leaves Zia Yusuf immensely sad
Content: At PMQs, Kemi Badenoch was struggling against Mr CongenialityPhotograph: House of Commons/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAt PMQs, Kemi Badenoch was struggling against Mr CongenialityPhotograph: House of Commons/AFP/Getty ImagesThe politics sketchHouse of CommonsGas go-ahead ignites oily response from Trump, while speaker seems ready to blowJohn CraceThe energy secretary’s trip north provokes Hoyle’s futile rage, while ITV’s Reform exposé leaves Zia Yusuf immensely sadWed 21 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTShareWhen is a licence not a licence? When it’s a new licence that is an old licence. After months of faffing around – there were the small matters of a party conference and a byelection to negotiate first – the government finallygave the go-aheadto drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. What swung it wasn’t so much the irresistible excitement of creating 27 new jobs and securing 2% of the UK’s gas supply for the next 10 years, it was the politics. If other countries were going to carry on drilling then we might as well do so, too.There would still be the same amount of greenhouse gases created and we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else for our gas supply. Though we would for the other 98%. Small steps and all that. At a time of global insecurity and rising energy costs, it was time to drill, baby, drill. So the inconvenience of a Labour manifestothat promisedno new North Sea licences could be rethought. It was now merely re-allowing a licence that had already been granted and then deemed unlawful by the courts. AKA dancing on the head of the pin.Donald Trump greeted the decision with wild enthusiasm. Though he appeared to be under the impression Jackdaw would be drilling for oil and would turn the UK into a land of plenty overnight. No one in the UK could quite bring themselves to enlighten him. Fair to say, that not everyone in the UK was quite so thrilled. Not least Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, andMiatta Fahnbulleh, the current one.Miatta had sought permission to be as far away as possible from Westminster for prime minister’s questions and the subsequent ministerial statement on Jackdaw. So she had taken the trouble to go all the way to Aberdeen to make a television statement that she could have made in her own department. And she is the one worried about her carbon footprint.View image in fullscreenMiatta Fahnbulleh with ministerial colleagues Douglas Alexander (left) and John Healey in Aberdeen on Wednesday.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAOnly it turns out that any amount of emissions is a price worth paying for a minister anxious not to have the hypocrisy of her former opposition to Jackdaw replayed to her by many of her own backbench MPs. Life comes at you fast when you’re a politician climbing the greasy ministerial pole. You find yourself in some awkward places, the most awkward being theHouse of Commons. Hence the – ahem – unfortunate diary clash.The speaker wasless than impressed. Lindsay Hoyle sounded as if he had swallowed a fistful of amphetamines and steroids and was mid-roid rage. He only just stopped short of calling the Labour frontbench a bunch of fucking fucks. Maybe he was just having a bad day.For decades now, governments of all colours have been going out of their way to make sure that junior ministers take the flak to save their bosses the embarrassment of an hour’s humiliation at the dispatch box. The parliamentary equivalent of droit de seigneur. Lindsay demanded assurances this would never happen again, and the junior energy minister Michael Shanks duly nodded sheepishly. Not that he cared. He mainlines oil for breakfast. Inside, he was just counting down the seconds till the speaker had calmed down a bit. And then carried on as normal. Of course it will happen again. Maybe even next week.PMQs itself also took on a familiar look, with Kemi Badenoch unable to make any inroads into Andy Burnham. You could even sense her frustration. There were times when she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, but now both she and theLabourparty have seen him off, she is faced with Mr Congeniality.Against him, Kemi’s attack lines feel half-arsed. Not properly thought through. Everything she tries just bounces off him. He seems almost untouchable. Mostly because he’s a better politician, but also because he has the air of a reasonable grownup. Someone you feel is doing his best and comes across as someone you can trust. Well. As close to honest as you get in Westminster.By contrast, Kemi feels like a second-rate opportunist. She tried making something of Labour taking years to approve the Jackdaw licence, a charge that rather melted away when Burnham pointed out we could have been drilling ages ago if the Tories had bothered to get the necessary legalities right in the first place. This was about putting pragmatism before ideology, Andyinsisted. Fair enough. Though expect him to say precisely the opposite when it comes to the Rosebank oilfield. Then ideology will take precedence over pragmatism. Fahnbulleh had alreadyas good as confirmedthat Rosebank was dead in the water.Reform UK fined for failing to declare it was publisher of campaigns materialRead moreFor the rest ofPMQs, it was Kemi who was dead in the water. Seemingly having no other real questions she wanted to ask. It felt like she was sulking. Or underprepared. Her pre-budget attack lines went nowhere. First Andy pointed out that he was the only one with a plan to ditch the triple lock and sort out social care – still more vibes than policy – and ended by making fun of Liz Truss’s forthcoming new book on the mini-budget.It wasn’t her who had screwed the country, apparently. Liz had been captured by the Blob. But it could have been any number of the current members of the shadow cabinet. Including the shadow chancellor who was part of the Trusster’s team. Incidentally, Liz was due to be interviewed by a robot on Wednesday afternoon at a Lincolnshire fair. But how would we know which was which?That just left time for Burnham to take one question from a Labour backbencher aboutthe ITV exposéof Reform. Though Nigel Farage had already left the chamber by then, so he couldn’t get all heated and declare that it was all a London plot and that it was perfectly normal for people to be as racist as possible in the comfort of their own homes. It was political correctness gone mad.As if by telepathy, Zia Yusuf had chosen just that moment to post a video on social media in which he expressed his immense sadness that the media had stooped so low. He would be reporting ITV to the police, he insisted, because they had betrayed the racist code of honour.How could everyday racists feel comfortable expressing their racism in the workplace if they couldn’t be sure that their colleagues weren’t undercover journalists looking to expose them? The world had gone mad. Who would have guessed that deep down, Zia – the man even the Reform elite have come to hate – was a snowflake at heart.Explore more on these topicsHouse of CommonsThe politics sketchPMQsMiatta FahnbullehLabourConservativesReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: I’ve booked my first proper holiday – and it’s pulled me out of winter grimness like a magic spell  | Bim Adewunmi | The Guardian
description: Anticipating a potential spring in which I am bathed in sun on a Greek island is giving me the kind of glee that makes anything feel possible
Author: Bim Adewunmi
Headline: Anticipating a potential spring in which I am bathed in sun on a Greek island is giving me the kind of glee that makes anything feel possible
Content: The Greece of my dreams …Photograph: Georgios Tsichlis/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Greece of my dreams …Photograph: Georgios Tsichlis/AlamyOpinionLife and styleI’ve booked my first proper holiday – and it’s pulled me out of winter grimness like a magic spellBim AdewunmiAnticipating a potential spring in which I am bathed in sun on a Greek island is giving me the kind of glee that makes anything feel possibleWed 21 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 20.16 EDTShareReader, it’s important to tell you that I’ve never been to Greece in my life. Not once. But Imightbe going, for the very first time, in the spring. And so, for the last week or so, all my dreams have featured fresh fish cooked to flaky perfection, a swimming pool into which I shall venture no deeper than my waist (I can’t swim), and the heat of the sun that not even the climate crisis can make happen in the UK in April.I don’t come with a history of exotic foreign holidays. Travelling abroad fell under the umbrella of familial duty: “Going Home”, AKA a brief return to the place where my parents were born (and coincidentally more and more foreign to them the longer they lived in the UK) in order to keep the ties of kinship going and remind us of our roots. I should say we didn’t do idyllic UK-based holidays either. I read about caravans in Enid Blyton books and watched Vaseline-lensed ads for CenterParcs and knew neither was in my immediate future. I made peace with it. We just weren’t a “going on holiday” type of family. It didn’t bother me. I harbour no resentment, and honestly, feel largely equanimous when I consider this “gap” in my life experience.But this potential Greece trip? It’s been on the back burner of my mind for years. A low-level, always-running app on my personal CPU, taking up very little energy but alive and constant. Almost as soon as I found out I was pregnant, I had a full-fledged fantasy. Picture it: somewhere in Europe 2027. A villa, a group of friends, two weeks of deep chats, delicious local cuisine, reading books and afternoon swims (remember, I can’t even swim). Our children? I dunno, somewhere safe and/or soundly asleep. My mind? Unencumbered, dreaming up the outline of my next play. My body? Relaxed but strengthened by the daily yoga session that also magically happens shortly after every sunrise. Before you ask, yes, I can hear myself. I know I sound insane. And I’m fine with it!My friend, newly a mother of two also, is the planner of this Greece trip. She sees the vision, works at the same foolish bank of romantic illusion where I have my account. But she’s not just a dreamer. She’s done solid, boots-on-the-ground research. She’s checking dates, curating the invite list: who likes cooking? Whose vibe matches our knackered-but-trying-to-be-a-good-friend situation? How many childfree adults can we ethically invite until we have the optimal number of eyes to cover all the children who’ll be around? She’s checking availability, organising the group chat, working to makemydreams a reality. I could kiss her. And perhaps in Crete, with the permission of all affected parties, I shall.Autumn is here, and I’ve got five micro-moments of joy to see us throughRead moreMore than the treat of a fortnight somewhere far away and yet in the company of old, dear friends, what I’m feeling most acutely is the pleasure of a promise. Having something to look forward to? A balm in the best of times. But especially so right now. I am re-emerging from beneath the cloud of the fourth (and fifth!) trimester. I read – and finished – a book the other week. I worked out with a kettlebell at some point in the past month. I went to a gig! Things are feeling viable again.Outside of my little sphere, having something pleasurable on the horizon feels like a magic spell. There is a grimness to reading headlines in the morning that can’t be shaken off. Going on holiday clearly won’t solvetheseproblems but my Cretan dreams give my soul small moments of uncomplicated anticipatory glee that make life worth living despite the horrors of near and far. Spring will come again, as it always does. The human race trudges on.Perhaps I feel my most human when I am anticipating. Inside of that anticipation is the incredible knowledge that while everything is possible, sometimes I get to imagine only delightful things. It’s an excellent exercise. Like I said, a magic spell.So here goes: I might be going to Crete with my children. What if we have an amazing time? What if this is the beginning of a new family tradition? What if the baby takes his first steps there? Could I master a couple of new recipes with new ingredients before we return home? Will 2027 be the year I start and finish Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan quartet? In Crete, anything could happen.Bim Adewunmi is a freelance journalistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: A gen Z protest movement could be about to oust Serbia’s strongman. Here’s why that will shake Europe | Misha Glenny | The Guardian
description: Student activists seem set to defeat Aleksandar Vučić at the ballot box this Sunday. The EU should never have written off Serbian democracy , says journalist Misha Glenny
Author: Misha Glenny
Headline: Student activists seem set to defeat Aleksandar Vučić at the ballot box this Sunday. The EU should never have written off Serbian democracy , says journalist Misha Glenny
Content: A student-led protest in Belgrade, Serbia, 7 October 2026.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersView image in fullscreenA student-led protest in Belgrade, Serbia, 7 October 2026.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersOpinionSerbiaA gen Z protest movement could be about to oust Serbia’s strongman. Here’s why that will shake EuropeMisha GlennyStudent activists seem set to defeat Aleksandar Vučić at the ballot box this Sunday. The EU should never have written off Serbian democracyWed 21 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.06 EDTShareHistory may not be about to repeat itself inSerbia, but it is beginning to rhyme. Just over a quarter of a century ago, Serbian citizens turned out to vote in large numbers to inflict a historic defeat on the then strongman in Belgrade, Slobodan Milošević, who was seeking re-election as president. He lost despite his extensive control over the media, the judiciary and the security forces. When he was reluctant to leave office, Serbs poured on to the streets in their hundreds of thousands, finally forcing him to go.On Sunday, a new generation could have the decisive voice in an equally fateful election, this time for the national parliament. Today’s strongman, Aleksandar Vučić, recentlyresigned as president to fight the electionwith the aim of swapping the locus of power from the presidency to the prime minister’s office.But Vučić, who has been in almost total control of Serbia for 14 years, finds himself on the back foot for the first time since he assumed power, just as Milošević did in 2000. Like his close friend, Viktor Orbán, who wasdecisively beaten in electionsearlier this year, Vučić has felt compelled to pull out all the stops to halt the opposition electoral coalition, known as the Student List (SL).Unlike Orbán’s Fidesz party, Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) is unlikely to be humiliated in Sunday’s vote. Opinion polls vary widely – some giving the SL alead of almost 10 percentage points, others suggesting the race is neck and neck. Pollsters also suggest that the higher the turnout, the greater the chances for the opposition. Some fear that the aftermath could even be violent.Vučić is throwing the kitchen sink at the campaign to skew the result his way. He has tightened his grip on the media bysupporting a change in ownershipof what was until recently the most important independent news group, United Media. Last weekend,10 prominent journalistsfrom its most important outlet, the TV station N1, resigned in protest against senior editorial appointments believed to favour Vučić and the SNS.N1 had been key in reporting the rapid rise in support for the student protest movement since itemerged spontaneously in November 2024. Students first took to the streets when the canopy over the main rail station in Novi Sad in the north of Serbia collapsed, killing 16 people. The tragedy occurred just months after a Chinese consortium had finished renovating it in what critics claim was a corrupt deal.View image in fullscreenMass silent protest outside Novi Sad railway station to mark the first anniversary of the canopy collapse that killed 16 people, 1 November 2025.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersAt first, Vučić’s response was to wait until the demonstrations petered out. But despite various attempts to coerce the students to retreat from the streets, the protests grew throughout 2025 and 2026. In March 2025, during a 15-minute period of silence to honour the victims of the Novi Sad disaster, protesters alleged thatpolice deployed a sonic weapon, the US-made LRAD 450XL, causing the crowd to disperse in panic. The government denied the use of the weapon and later the interior ministryfiled a criminal complaintagainst one military analyst over his claim that a sonic weapon was probably used.The demonstrations have showed no sign of letting up in the past two years. The big challenge facing the students was how to channel the undoubted energy they generated through the movement into a coherent political force capable of challenging Vučić. The old opposition parties were riven by factionalism and lacking dynamic leadership. But this summer the students announced they had selected candidates to stand in a new formation, the Student List, including prominent academics, engineers, workers, cultural figures and students. Their straightforward slogan is “Serbia or the mafia”.Vučić has responded to the challenge by cranking up the nationalist rhetoric in recent months in order to mobilise the far right. He haswelcomed the supportof his neighbour, Milorad Dodik, the de facto leader of Republika Srpska, the Serbian entity in Bosnia. Dodik has long been regarded as Vladimir Putin’s main man in the Balkans and more recently hascosied up to Donald Trump, whose associates are investing in a gas pipeline with his help.Vučić, too, has been cultivating support from Moscow. Personal relations between Putin and the Serbian leader have been strained in the past. Vučić has been supplying Ukraine with a significant amount of munitions while playing his complex game of trying to balance friendly relationships with the west and Russia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRevealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump businessRead moreBut with the gloves off, the Serbian leader has become less coy. Another sign of how seriously he views the students’ challenge was his decision to allow the recent nationalist jamboree ofa state funeralfor the man known as the “Butcher of Bosnia”, convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić, with the aim of bolstering his support among nationalists.If despite all this the Student List emerges victorious at the election, the shock waves will be felt as powerfully acrossEuropeas they were when Orbán was defeated.Above all, it opens the possibility of a swifter integration with theEuropean Union, a move that would be welcomed not just in Brussels but in London as well. Successive British governments are concerned that the Balkans represents the soft underbelly of European defence where Russia can exert significant pressure. Since Brexit, Britain’s influence here is limited politically but it has been active in promoting security cooperation across the region, with Nato and the EU.Student activists and their supporters have been disappointed by an apparent indifference on the part of the EU to their political struggle and a general perception in the outside world that Serbia’s democracy is a lost cause. On Sunday, they aim to prove them wrong.Misha Glenny is a former central Europe correspondent for the Guardian and the BBCExplore more on these topicsSerbiaOpinionProtestEuropeEuropean UnioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City have been a joy to watch but they became detached from their roots | Soccer | The Guardian
description: City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward
Author: Philipp Lahm
Headline: City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward
Content: Manchester City created world stars such as Kevin De Bruyne and Rodri, pictured after winning the Premier League in 2024.Photograph: Alex Livesey/Danehouse/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester City created world stars such as Kevin De Bruyne and Rodri, pictured after winning the Premier League in 2024.Photograph: Alex Livesey/Danehouse/Getty ImagesSoccerManchester City have been a joy to watch but they became detached from their rootsPhilipp LahmCity behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forwardWed 21 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTShareDo we have to reassessManchester Citynow? In my columns, I have repeatedly engaged with this club and its key figures. Looking back at what I have written over the years, I believe it remains beyond question that the team have achieved greatness. I always loved watching them: they were a true unit on the pitch, a finely tuned orchestra.I would also write all over again that the conductor, Pep Guardiola, masters his craft like few others. I could recognise his teams even if they were wearing the wrong shirts and the game was broadcast in black and white – by the passes, the distances between the players and the intelligence of their interplay. It is no wonder Guardiola inspires others to become managers; look at Vincent Kompany, Mikel Arteta, Enzo Maresca, and perhaps some time Ilkay Gündogan and Rodri.As a player and a columnist, I never had an issue with Manchester City – precisely because, for many years, the club avoided buying the most obvious superstars. Guardiola said it himself: the most valuable of the valuable do not go to a club such as City, who aren’t even the biggest football brand in their own home town.Football regulator has ‘absolute power’ to force Manchester City sale if verdict upheldRead moreMany became world stars in Manchester. Kevin De Bruyne had been discarded by Chelsea, Rodri’s true class was overlooked in Madrid for a long time, Gündogan’s career was on the brink after injuries, and most recently Gianluigi Donnarumma was no longer wanted in Paris. In Germany, City signed players from Hamburg, Frankfurt and Wolfsburg. Erling Haaland in 2022 was the first player they targeted who was also pursued by Bayern Munich. City did not operate like Paris Saint‑Germain did in the era before Luis Enrique.From the outside, City fundamentally did not do much differently from the other 10 or so top European clubs. But what are achievements on the pitch worth if they are accompanied by rule-breaking? The clubhave been found guiltyof breaching the Premier League’s financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. It allegedly invested almost €1bn more than allowed and declared. The league leaders face potential forced relegation or titles being stripped. City continue to deny wrongdoing and are appealing against the decision.It is right for the Premier League to crack down on unfair competition. I also appreciate that Germany is holding on to the 50+1 rule, which the federal cartel office recently upheld. It ensures that the majority of voting rights must remain with the parent club – the non‑profit section of a professional club. The exceptions that have applied to Leverkusen and Wolfsburg are under review.View image in fullscreenA Manchester City fan holds up a banner during the club’s Premier League match with Ipswich at the Etihad Stadium.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesThe bedrock of our football culture is 50+1. This rule exists only in Germany, yet it speaks to a spirit that fits perfectly with the European sports model: 50+1 maintains a balance; on the one hand it allows for investment, on the other it guarantees participation. It strengthens the rights of members and fans. Perhaps it is because of this rule that the average attendance in Germany is higher than anywhere else in the world.What is the ultimate purpose of football? It is a business, but its infrastructure is still developed by the general public. That is how I have always understood sport. Even as a professional, it was clear to me that my privileged life was made possible by many people working on a voluntary basis. Through my role as tournament director of the European Championship, these political connections have become even clearer to me.The stadium and football clubs can remain the final places where people gather and society debates its issues only if the elite and the grassroots stay connected, and the public is involved in the process. Football must not be detached from its roots, as was the case with Manchester City. This becomes possible when rules are enforced by an institution. Ideally, not by a commercial entity but by a non-profit one such as Uefa.In business, as in politics, I am observing a shift in mindset. Today, it is deemed necessary to invest in non‑profit institutions. More and more companies realise that football allows for a genuine exchange with the population – that it provides the perfect vehicle to set up corporate social responsibility projects.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is what is needed in these politically turbulent times. In our fragmented world, political parties, churches and the media have lost credibility. In sport, however, people still come together. It is a tool to foster social cohesion. Therefore, I consider 50+1 to be a distinct competitive advantage for the Bundesliga.I also welcome the fact that rules mean something in another case. Uefa is standingfirm against Gianni Infantino, who recently wanted to privatise the World Cup and its profits. Along with his friend Donald Trump, he was seen by many as breaking the normal ruleswhen Folarin Balogun’s suspensionwas lifted. The outcry from the global football community was loud, and it is possible that the Fifa president will fall.When behaviour such as that in Manchester and at Fifa is punished, it is a good thing. Football must prevent questionable ideas from distancing it even further from its grassroots. Only then can it drive engagement in civil society, and only then can it strengthen Europe.Philipp Lahm’s column was produced in partnership with Oliver Fritsch at the German online magazineDie Zeit.Explore more on these topicsFootballManchester CitycommentShareReuse this content

title: After three disastrous years, Israel needs to rethink itself. A new government would be a start | Dahlia Scheindlin | The Guardian
description: Only a clear opposition victory would let us begin to heal, strengthen democracy and establish Palestinian rights, says Dahlia Scheindlin, a Tel Aviv-based political analyst
Author: Dahlia Scheindlin
Headline: Only a clear opposition victory would let us begin to heal, strengthen democracy and establish Palestinian rights, says Dahlia Scheindlin, a Tel Aviv-based political analyst
Content: A print worker produces an election poster featuring Benjamin Netanyahu for the Likud party in Rosh Haayin  on Thursday.Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA print worker produces an election poster featuring Benjamin Netanyahu for the Likud party in Rosh Haayin  on Thursday.Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesOpinionIsraelAfter three disastrous years, Israel needs to rethink itself. A new government would be a startDahlia ScheindlinOnly a clear opposition victory would let us begin to heal, strengthen democracy and establish Palestinian rightsDahlia Scheindlin is a Tel Aviv-based political analystWed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 07.50 EDTShareIsrael’s 27 October election is fast approaching, with little clarity about who will win. But Benjamin Netanyahu ismore likely to lose. Hispolling is poor, and the fractious opposition parties may yet find a way to form the next government.What would such a government do? Most of the Zionist opposition parties, the frontrunners to lead such a coalition, have offered bromides about good governance and unifying the country. Others have focused on more specific plans to establish a state commission of inquiry into the government’s failures around the attacks of 7 October 2023, and end the exemption from military service enjoyed by most ultra-Orthodox Jewish men.But if a new government truly plans to build a better future,Israelneeds more profound changes. Simply ousting Netanyahu will not be enough.The two issues the opposition has highlighted are understandably important to Israelis. For so many citizens, the disaster of 7 October and subsequent two-year hostage crisis became a crisis of faith in the state itself. Without accountability through an independent inquiry, society cannot move on. And even staunch supporters of peace cannot tolerate the rank injustice of some citizens serving and dying in wars while others are systematically let off the hook.But what then? Israel’s war in response to 7 October has continued to devastate Palestinian society. But the past few years have damaged Israel internally as well.Social solidarity in Israelis abysmal. Hundreds of thousands of reservists have served for months, interrupting their studies, family life and income. Up to 30,000 people have been wounded, according to Israel’sministry of defence.Meanwhile, the current government hasslashed social-service budgetsin favour of defence spending. The psychological toll is immense, yet Israel had a shortage of psychiatristseven prior to the war. Dr Graciela Cors, a youth and child psychiatrist, told me: “The mental health situation is catastrophic, and so are the social systems that are supposed to support mental health, like outpatient clinics andKupot Holim[Israel’s state-mandated health funds].”These problems are urgent, but addressing them would amount to damage limitation. Without deeper change, better-funded services and greater conscription would do little more than help Israel cope with the next round of seemingly endless wars.View image in fullscreenAn election billboard featuring the centrist Yashar party leader, Gadi Eisenkot, in Tel Aviv.Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty ImagesIsrael desperately needs to confront the factors that brought the country to this point to begin with.Before Hamas’s attack, 2023 was already the year these long-festering problems burst into full view. Society was torn apart by two unreconciled, deeply interconnected questions: what kind of democracy Israel should be, and what is the future for the Palestinians?Historically, Israel has demonstrated aflawed, ambiguous commitment to democracy. It avoided writing a constitution, and has no law that explicitly guarantees equality to all citizens. But over roughly the past 15 years, that ambiguity has given way to a full-blown assault on democratic institutions. Attacks on the judiciarycame from top governing officials, culminating in Netanyahu’s government’s plans in 2023 to drasticallyweaken judicial independence.That top-down assault fell on fertile ground because of a deeper problem: the erosion of democratic values, shaped in part by education. Or Kashti, the former longtime education correspondent for Haaretz (where I also write), told me that the seeds of the judicial assault are found in the newcivics textbook adopted in 2016. He has traced a shift from vague treatment of democracy in earlier decades, to what he describes as “indoctrination”, with greater emphasis onJewish identityandstate power. This is a thin and misguided view of democracy, one that risks elevating the will of the majority above all other democratic values.The curriculum can also be alarmingly parochial. Kashti says that historymatriculation examsfocus on the second world war and the Holocaust, the wars of modern Israeli history and the establishment of the Zionist movement. “All other topics in history of the world are marginal,” he says. Religion, he adds, infiltrates unrelated subjects. “In geography or weather lessons, children are told to learn the prayer for rain. What’s the connection between prayer for rain and a lesson on geography and climate change?”This narrow conception of democracy helps explain how, in 2022,halfthe countryelected partiesthat sought to hobble judicial institutions as part of the coalition government’s programme. And when education gives barely any attention to human rights, civil liberties and the equality of all citizens – it becomes easy to see why Palestinian self-determination has dropped off the Israeli agenda entirely.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor decades, Israeli society has increasingly acted on the assumption that Palestinians could be contained through military force or control. In the years before 7 October, most Israelis saw no contradiction between democracy at home and their active military occupation regime effectively ruling over all Palestinians, without giving them rights or representation.Netanyahu’s current government has pursued the logical end of occupation –permanent annexation, ever-expanding settlements and ethnic cleansing. To do that, the government had to destroy the final guardrails on its power. The 2023 assault on the judiciary finally galvanised many Israelis, who feared that their own liberties were under threat. Massive protests followed, plunging the country into prolonged social turmoil.No Israeli government can offer a different future without fundamental and comprehensive change on these deepest issues. What is needed is a fundamental reassessment of the country’s entire social ethos.The good news is that such change is absolutely possible. Education curriculums can be rewritten to embrace the principles of a modern liberal democracy. Teachers, politicians andeven religious leaderscan embrace human and civil liberties, minority rights, checks and balances, good governance and the universal values that too many Israelis disdain today. Societies and people can change.In such a society, it would be the occupation, rather than democracy, that would become an unsustainable affront to the values of Israel. This is a long way off; the current opposition leaders demonstrate no vision leading to such an outcome, and change is needed much more urgently. Israel’s right wing and many ordinary citizens, shaped by years of fear, would fight any change favouring Palestinian independence. But without embarking on the path, the country will never get there; needless to say, Palestinians will never be free.None of this will transpire if Netanyahu wins or if Israel’s elections yield a stalemate. But an opposition victory should be the day when the hardest, yet most hopeful, work will begin.Dahlia Scheindlin is a Tel Aviv-based political analyst and author of The Crooked Timber of Democracy in IsraelDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on drilling in Jackdaw: a truly pragmatic approach would focus on Britain’s green transition | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Opening the North Sea gasfield will deliver minimal benefits for households, while sending a dismal signal before next month’s Cop summit
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Opening the North Sea gasfield will deliver minimal benefits for households, while sending a dismal signal before next month’s Cop summit
Content: (L to R) Scottish secretary Douglas Alexander, energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and chancellor John Healey visit a gas terminal in Peterhead on Wednesday.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAView image in fullscreen(L to R) Scottish secretary Douglas Alexander, energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and chancellor John Healey visit a gas terminal in Peterhead on Wednesday.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAOpinionEnvironment policyThe Guardian view on drilling in Jackdaw: a truly pragmatic approach would focus on Britain’s green transitionEditorialOpening the North Sea gasfield will deliver minimal benefits for households, while sending a dismal signal before next month’s Cop summitWed 21 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.53 EDTShareThis week a report from the UN Environment Programmeconcludedthat holding global temperatures to a 1.5C warming limit – the centrepiece commitment of the Paris climate agreement – is no longer achievable. If the disastrous consequences of a significant overshoot are to be mitigated, it argued, governments must start delivering the short-term actions to meet long-term targets on reducing fossil fuel consumption.Disappointingly, Andy Burnham and his energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, took a different view of short-term priorities on Wednesday. Before the November Cop summit, where regaining lost momentum on climate action will be crucial, theirdecisionto approve new drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield sent a dismal signal. The prime ministerjustifiedit as a pragmatic move “at a time when people are really struggling”. But the pragmatic arguments don’t stack up.View image in fullscreenMichael Marra.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAGoing ahead with Jackdaw will have no impact on bills this winter and little in the longer run. It willdeliveronly a small number of jobs for a very limited period. Tax revenues from new drilling will be substantially negated by the various concessions and breaks enjoyed by the oil and gas industry. Claims that Jackdaw will enhance the UK’s national energy security are hugely overblown, given that it will satisfy a mere 2% of national demand. The country’s heavy reliance on natural gas imports will remain unaltered.So why? Mr Burnham would doubtless have preferred not to be landed with the judgment call on either Jackdaw or the much larger Rosebank oil and gas field (on which an announcement has yet to be made). Both were already in the licensing system, having beenapprovedby Rishi Sunak as he sought a dividing line with Labour. A successful legal challenge meant the final decision fell in the present prime minister’s lap.On Jackdaw at least, Mr Burnham appears to have judged that political expediency, particularly in Scotland, was best served by waving it through. A failure by governments to invest gamechanging sums in the green transition has made the politics of net zero more fraught. The recent Tory byelectionvictoryin Aberdeen South followed a campaign focused on reviving oil and gas production in the North Sea. One of the first acts of Scottish Labour’s new leader, Michael Marra, has been tobackboth the Rosebank and Jackdaw developments.Mr Burnham inherited this complicated set of circumstances. But rather than rubber-stamping a regressive rearguard action by the fossil fuel industry, he should be using his rhetorical gifts to make the pragmatic case for Britain’s green energy future. As research by the E3G thinktank haslaid out, the dubious benefits of drilling for disappearing oil and gas reserves are dwarfed by the potential economic impact of insulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps. The government’swarm homes plan, it estimated, would significantly reduce household energy bills and generate 50,000 new jobs. Yet Ms Fahnbulleh isreportedlyunder pressure to find cuts so spending can be diverted to defence.The best way to achieve energy security, back British workers and bring down bills – the three imperatives identified by Mr Burnham in his statement on Wednesday – is to invest ambitiously in the country’s climate goals. Proceeding with Jackdaw does not, in itself, signify a prime ministerial reluctance to do that. But this decision suggests there are grounds for concern about which way the wind is blowing in Downing Street.Explore more on these topicsEnvironment policyOpinionAndy BurnhamLabourCop31Renewable energyEnergyFossil fuelseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the Republicans’ midterms struggle: Trump has circuses, but voters also want bread | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Editorial: As prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promised
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Editorial: As prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promised
Content: Donald Trump at a midterm campaign rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at a midterm campaign rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesOpinionUS midterm elections 2026The Guardian view on the Republicans’ midterms struggle: Trump has circuses, but voters also want breadAs prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promisedWed 21 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.27 EDTShareIt is no great revelation that Donald Trump is enriching himself as president. Heraked in $2.2bnin 2025, with his position and his personal interests frequently overlapping. Yet this week’s poll finding that 34% of Republicans (and 66% of all American voters)thinkthat he is using his position to make himself rich merits attention.Separately, voters in a Fox News poll last week putgovernment corruptionat the top of their list of concerns – just ahead of inflation and high prices.Mr Trump pledged that people would be better off if they voted for him. Billionaires are; not the rest. He promised to lower grocery costs (they have risen) and to cut the price of gasoline to below $2 a gallon. It’s more than double that, thanks to his illegal war on Iran. Tariffs haven’t helped. Incumbents struggle when life feels unaffordable, andpolling for the Guardianhas shown the disenchantment of key voting groups. The gulf between his own prosperity and the lives of his base now looks less like an inspiration and more like an insult. Cash offers seem unlikely to help much.The president’s popularity rating sank toa record low of 36%in a poll on Wednesday. Mr Trump, of course, is not on the ballot. But he istouring red statesas he seeks to shore up the vote in places where the idea of a Democratic victory looked laughable two years ago. Democrats are rightly cautious about their midterms prospects, having been burned too many times. But less than a fortnight from 3 November, with many votes already cast, polls suggest that they will take the House and could well claim the Senate too.View image in fullscreenJames Talarico.Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesThe party is still unpopular, though impressive candidates are performing far better than anyone expected in surprising places – notably Texas and Kansas. But they are nowmore trusted on economic issues. Independents are turning away from Mr Trump and his party, and many Republicans seem unenthused, for multiple reasons. The “Maga-sympathetic” pollster Rich Barisarguesthat “Donald Trump did this to himself”. His base believed Mr Trump was their champion. Now they suspect that he is “just another politician”.There is merited concern about how the president has already used his powerto tilt the midterms, and more about what he may do if his party fares as badly as forecast. Republicans still hope to reclaim ground through traditional if unsavoury means, massively outspending Democrats.Yet whilesome polls are tightening, culture war attacks and salacious lies about opponents such as James Talarico in Texas do not seem, at least so far, to be as powerful as Republicans hoped. That’s not just because Democratic candidates are repositioning themselves. The toxic messaging of the presidential race – that Kamala Harris “is for they/them, President Trump is for you” – doesn’t land if voters believe that he’s actually for himself and his friends.Republicans nowpoint to France’s unrestand claim that a Democrat-dominated Congress would bring chaos and destruction to America. Their fearmongering has often motivated core voters. But while Democrats stick to the economic attack, Republicans are trying to change the subject instead of offering answers. Mr Trump’s bread-and-circuses politics is floundering,cage fights on the South Lawnof the White House notwithstanding, as voters ask what happened to the bread.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionTrump administrationDemocratsUS politicseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: In the age of AI, learning maths is even more vital | Mathematics | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers react to Simon Jenkins’ article that said it’s more important for children to learn how to speak fluently than study mathematics
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers react to Simon Jenkins’ article that said it’s more important for children to learn how to speak fluently than study mathematics
Content: ‘Maths … teaches us to reason, analyse evidence, solve unfamiliar problems and question whether an answer makes sense.’Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Maths … teaches us to reason, analyse evidence, solve unfamiliar problems and question whether an answer makes sense.’Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesMathematicsLettersIn the age of AI, learning maths is even more vitalReaders react to Simon Jenkins’ article that said it’s more important for children to learn how to speak fluently than study mathematicsWed 21 Oct 2026 12.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTShareSimon Jenkins must have had a deeply unpleasant experience of learning maths at school because he seems to have a pathological antipathy towards it (We are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently?, 16 October). I have no qualms with his insistence on the importance of oracy. But his argument breaks down with the claim that it is either oracy or maths, but not both. This is nonsense. Oracy and maths skills should exist side by side. Both contribute to a person’s ability to realise their full potential, and to employment opportunities.Maths drives the understanding of the natural world and contributes vastly to the solutions of problems that humanity needs to solve to exist. It is fundamental to science and technology, health and medicine, communications, the study of the Earth, finance and economics, distribution of resources and supply chains, architecture, warfare, and much else besides.The negative economic, social and health and wellbeing impacts of poor maths skills in adult life are well known, yet the maths skills gap – the difference between the numbers of mathematically literate people we need and the number we have – remains too large in the UK.Many young people suffer from maths anxiety, but that is not an argument for not teaching maths and its importance. It is a social problem that needs addressing by improving the quality of schooling and attacking the root causes of social issues that affect how young people engage with society.Dr Jack AbramskyLondonThe idea that calculators and AI reduce the need to learn maths is mistaken. Maths is about far more than calculation. It teaches us to reason, analyse evidence, solve unfamiliar problems and question whether an answer makes sense. These abilities are more important, not less, when technology can produce apparently authoritative answers in seconds. The public need to know when they can trust those answers, and maths underpins that.The government’s2025 curriculum and assessment reviewrecognised this, stating that “Being secure in core subjects such as Maths and Science will remain pivotal for young people, now and in the future”. The review also highlighted the growing importance of critical thinking and digital skills in a world increasingly shaped by AI.Maths is also fundamental to the economy.Analysis by the Academy for the Mathematical Sciencesfound that more than 5 million people worked in mathematical-science occupations in 2024, contributing £489bn, or 19% of the UK’s total gross value added. Ensuring young people develop strong maths skills is therefore important not only for individuals, but for the UK’s future productivity and prosperity.We should strengthen young people’s ability to communicate, but not at the expense of their ability to reason mathematically. In the age of AI, both are more important than ever.Mark ChaplainPresident, London Mathematical SocietyHeather TewkesburyPresident, Institute ofMathematicsand its ApplicationsMuch as I understand the advantages that oracy confers, it is no gift when it is combined with entitlement and dishonesty. It was Boris Johnson’s silver tongue that got him into Downing Street and kept him there, despite outlandish transgressions and fabrications. I would prefer that schools embedded behaviour, integrity and sincerity into the curriculum. These are the building blocks for sound character.Mona SoodSouthend-on-Sea, EssexI think Simon Jenkins may be slightly behind the times. My five-year-old child goes to a state foundation primary with two sites in south London. Oracy is a core part of the curriculum. Her professional state-educated parents attended the workshop the school provided on the subject; it was certainly not something familiar to our own education.Our daughter has flourished in confidence and speech. Previously a naturally shy child, she now regales kind strangers on public transport with stories. Her teacher encourages simple but critical interaction daily – each child says hello and goodbye to their teachers and each other in a way that is comfortable to them and respectful to others. This is in a classroom that has lots of children with education, health and care plans, who qualify for free school meals, and who have English as a second language and parents who do not speak English. The benefits are obvious, but Winchester it is not.Dr Elaine SeymourLondonAll public schools know the answer to Simon Jenkins’ question, hence their debating societies. All state primary schools also know how to develop confidence and ensure that all have the opportunity to take part in community events.Never overlook the importance of early-years festive productions, class assemblies, concerts, school councils and school plays. These vital aspects of our state curriculum need to be celebrated. Never forget the insignificance and misery of log tables and slide rules.Sally BatesRetired primary headteacher, Cotgrave, NottinghamshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: A plan to ensure energy is affordable for all | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Letter: Dr Alex Chapman calls for a government-funded price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas, in response to an article by Nils Pratley
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Dr Alex Chapman calls for a government-funded price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas, in response to an article by Nils Pratley
Content: ‘Every household should be able to afford the energy essentials: enough warmth to survive a winter; enough electricity to switch on the lights and run a fridge.’Photograph: Jacob King/PAView image in fullscreen‘Every household should be able to afford the energy essentials: enough warmth to survive a winter; enough electricity to switch on the lights and run a fridge.’Photograph: Jacob King/PAEnergy billsLettersA plan to ensure energy is affordable for allDr Alex Chapmancalls for a government-funded price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas, in response to an article by Nils PratleyWed 21 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.33 EDTShareNils Pratley thinks that the secretary of state, Miatta Fahnbulleh, should “keep things simple” and develop a targeted social tariff to protect vulnerable households from surging energy bills (The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff, 14 October). Unfortunately, there is nothing simple about such a scheme.Pratley’s proposal would mean creating a new benefits system inside our privatised energy industry. If the interminable debates about our current benefits system were not enough to put him off, we can look to the failing social care system to see where it might lead. Andy Burnham has made it his life’s mission to dismantle this lottery that can strip pensioners of their savings and the family home. Just as he now plans a universal public provision of adult social care, we at the New Economics Foundation have such a plan for energy.Every household should be able to afford the energy essentials: enough warmth to survive a winter; enough electricity to switch on the lights and run a fridge. We should recognise this as a universal right rather than waste time tinkering with a targeting system that arbitrarily separates the “worthy” from the “unworthy” (the “rough justice” of the Resolution Foundation’sproposal, which penalises households based on the income of the highest earner, is a case in point).The long-term design of a universal offer can be debated. But as another energy crisis bears down on us, we should keep it simple: have the Treasury fund a true price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas. This would be a policy from which everyone wins (especially if electrically heated homes are allowed to transfer across their gas allowance).In the longer term, one way to help pay for this could be to charge households with very high energy consumption more. But there are other ways. The Australian “solar sharer” scheme gives every household three hours of free electricity in the middle of the day, bringing hope that renewables could soon give true energy security.Dr Alex ChapmanHead of economic and environmental policy,New Economics FoundationHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
