title: The Green party hasn’t lost its way, it’s just broadening its appeal | Green party | The Guardian
description: Letters: Marianne Gemmeke and John Ashby respond to criticism of the party and its leader, Zack Polanski
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Marianne Gemmeke and John Ashby respond to criticism of the party and its leader, Zack Polanski
Content: ‘Social justice has always been at the heart of the Greens’ policy.’Photograph: Hiba Kola/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Social justice has always been at the heart of the Greens’ policy.’Photograph: Hiba Kola/ReutersGreen partyLettersThe Green party hasn’t lost its way, it’s just broadening its appealMarianne GemmekeandJohn Ashbyrespond to criticism of the party and its leader, Zack PolanskiWed 21 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.33 EDTShareThe two eloquent letters on the super-rich (The problem with living in a rich man’s world, 14 October) explain perfectly why I, as a longstanding Green party member, could not agree less with the letter writers who claim that the party has lost its way (Has Zack Polanski forgotten what the Green party is for?, 14 October).Social justice has always been at the heart of the Greens’ policy, which also means that unless we have a change in our dysfunctional economic system, we cannot achieve the green agenda. The Green movement has always been about having a moral framework, standing up for oppressed people and bringing about a more just society both at home and abroad.People tend to know about the green agenda; it is the other messages that need clearer communication, which is where recent campaigns have focused, leading to a surge in membership.Marianne GemmekeEastleigh, HampshireThe complaint about theGreen partyused to be that it was a single-issue pressure group. In response, it diversified into general politics, and now the complaint is that it talks about things other than climate change. You just can’t win.John AshbyOxfordHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Getting into the swing of playing golf | Golf | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Adrian Chiles’s article on his antipathy to the game
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Adrian Chiles’s article on his antipathy to the game
Content: ‘After more than 50 years of playing without any discernible improvement, I still soldier on o’er hill and dale, wielding my mashie niblick.’Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘After more than 50 years of playing without any discernible improvement, I still soldier on o’er hill and dale, wielding my mashie niblick.’Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesGolfLettersGetting into the swing of playing golfReaders respond to Adrian Chiles’s article on his antipathy to the gameWed 21 Oct 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTShareI have some sympathies with Adrian Chiles’s war of attrition with golf (I hate golf, 14 October). I too have suffered with shots to the right followed by shots to the left, and have had rounds with many bad shots, only to then have a perfect drive down the middle, or by sinking a 20-yard putt on the last green that inevitably brought me back the next week thinking that I had finally cracked it.Over the 60 years that I have been playing, I have learned that it is possible to master some of this game some of the time, but not all of the time. There are many other pluses to this wonderful game. I have played golf on many courses in this country and in Europe, enjoying great views and friendships along the way.At 81 years of age, I still play twice a week, walking just over five miles each time, and still play to a respectable nine handicap. Come on Adrian, look on the bright side and continue your search for the perfect swing, even if it’s only one per round.Bob DawsonGreenmount, Greater ManchesterAdrian Chiles has it all wrong. If he removed the competitive element from his approach, he would see that golf doesn’t sit in isolation from the world around it. I was coerced into playing golf for the first time at the age of 60. I didn’t have that elusive isolated “Wow!” moment. The whole round, from a golf point of view, was lousy. But I loved the camaraderie, the walk through nature, the science attached to equipment and performance, the exercise on most fronts and the knowledge that, even with time against me, I could get better. I did … and plateaued. I fully expect to get worse as age takes over – I don’t care. As has been said, golf is not a game of being perfect, it is a holistic experience that is hard to match.Joe WaddleBedlington, NorthumberlandI can readily identify with the myriad frustrations that Adrian Chiles identifies in his experiences of playing golf. However, after more than 50 years of playing without any discernible improvement, I still soldier on o’er hill and dale, wielding my mashie niblick.I do so because of all the positive benefits to be gained from a four-hour walk unspoiled: the exercise, the beautiful scenery, the fresh air and, as much as anything, the banter and bonhomie with my old schoolmates as we mercilessly mock our collective inability to master the game.Get back out there, Adrian Chiles, it’s fun and good for your mental health!Kev WardQuorn, LeicestershireI stopped playing baseball at the age of 65 (exploded achilles tendon); ice hockey at 70 (Covid). I took up golf. Now five years in, I’m a reliable bogey golfer. I’m not a great athlete, absolutely average in size (5ft 9in) and took one formal lesson. But God bless YouTube. All the answers are there. Play with people who are better than you (not difficult in my case) and be willing to improve gradually.There are tons of people who can tell you what you are doing wrong. Find one person who simplifies the game and follow them exclusively. For me, it’s a YouTube star called Jimmy Tropicana. And his best skill is making you believe you can play the sport well.And stop keeping score until you develop some consistency. Just think about the next shot – not the good or bad ones already taken. The score will settle itself.Chris GarganVerona, Wisconsin, USExplore more on these topicsGolfFriendshiplettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Angry’ Carrick on the brink as Fernandes hits out at Manchester United tactics | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: The manager apologised to Manchester United fans after the 4-1 defeat in Como, while his captain criticised the team’s tactical approach
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: The manager apologised to Manchester United fans after the 4-1 defeat in Como, while his captain criticised the team’s tactical approach
Content: Michael Carrick offered a mea culpa to those Manchester United fans who stayed past the final whistle in Como.Photograph: Alessandro Garofalo/ReutersView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick offered a mea culpa to those Manchester United fans who stayed past the final whistle in Como.Photograph: Alessandro Garofalo/ReutersManchester United‘Angry’ Carrick on the brink as Fernandes hits out at Manchester United tacticsManager apologises to fans after 4-1 defeat in ComoCaptain criticises ‘decision from the staff’ not to pressJamie Jacksonat the Giuseppe Sinigaglia StadiumWed 21 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick’s future asManchester Unitedmanager is in the balance after a humiliating 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como on Wednesday night.Before Bournemouth’s visit to Old Trafford on Sunday his future may be discussed by Jason Wilcox, the director of football, Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the co-owner who controls sporting policy.Como demolish dismal Manchester United to pile more pressure on CarrickRead moreOn a torrid night an “angry” ­Carrick insisted afterwards that he had not given his position any thought and was forced to defend himself against Bruno Fernandes after his captain questioned the manager’s tactics of not pressing against Cesc Fàbregas’s team. Carrick also criticised his side for not running. The defeat by Como in the third Champions League group game leaves United with only two wins all season from 11 games. ­Carrick’s side are in 13th place in the Premier League and wereeliminated from the Carabao Cuplast month.The 45-year-old was asked if he fears for his job. “Listen, I’ve not given my own position any thought,” he said. “[My thoughts are] for the supporters – I was one of them watching that and I wasn’t happy at all.”Carrick was then asked if he could walk away following the latest defeat in Europe. “No. It’s not about me right now and my feelings in that regard,” the manager said. “It’s more of as a team and as a football club, what we want to look like, what we should look like. And as I said, the results can come and go at times, but you got to do it in a certain way. And that wasn’t it.”700 United sup­porters travelled. At the end around 200 remained and Carrick went to ­apologise to them, noticeably ­ignoring his players. After United conceded Nico Paz’s second-minute goal, Carrick’s men were unable to mount any resistance. By 57 minutesComoled 3-0, due to Tasos Douvikas’s strike and Paz’s second, before Jacobo Ramón completed the scoring for the Italian side on 76 minutes. Joshua Zirkzee netted in added time for the visitors.Fernandes openly challenged ­Carrick’s strategy during the match. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” he said.The captain was asked if Carrick’s tactics were wrong. “That’s on the manager and staff to see, not me,” he said. “Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable. As you saw with them, the centre-back was coming to mark me in my own half. We need to do that as a team but we were unable to.”Fernandes’s criticism was put to his manager after the match. “We actually half-pressed man-to-man the second half and then conceded a goal from that,” Carrick said.“Whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCarrick was asked how he can raise the mood before Bournemouth’s visit.“I’m bitterly disappointed, I’m frustrated; more than frustrated, I’m really angry. But you’ve got to move on. You got to deal with what’s next and see what that looks like.“At this moment in time, there’s a lot to do before that next game to get the team ready because that was a difficult night for everyone. I have to apologise to the supporters.”View image in fullscreenBruno Fernandes and his United teammates were second-best throughout.Photograph: Alessandro Garofalo/ReutersExplore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickComoCesc FàbregasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal’s Declan Rice strikes late to deny Bayern Munich after Harry Kane penalty | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Declan Rice’s late equaliser rescued a 2-2 draw for Arsenal in a blockbuster contest at Bayern Munich after Harry Kane had scored from the spot
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Declan Rice’s late equaliser rescued a 2-2 draw for Arsenal in a blockbuster contest at Bayern Munich after Harry Kane had scored from the spot
Content: Declan Rice knee-slides across the turf after scoring Arsenal’s equaliser late in the second half.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDeclan Rice knee-slides across the turf after scoring Arsenal’s equaliser late in the second half.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueArsenal’s Declan Rice strikes late to deny Bayern Munich after Harry Kane penaltyDavid Hytnerat the Allianz ArenaWed 21 Oct 2026 17.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is as if Harry Kane cannot get enough of tormenting Arsenal. TheBayern Munichstriker has plenty of form from his Tottenham days. He remains the top scorer in north London derby history with 14 goals. He made an impact yet again here and yet it was not a night when he had the final word. That honour fell to Declan Rice, the Arsenal midfielder storming into the Bayern area in the 82nd minute to guide home a low finish that Kane would have been proud to call his own.Arsenal were hunting their latest statement result. Only once had they ever won away against Bayern – the 2-0 in theChampions Leaguelast 16 second leg in 2013, although it did not prevent an away goals exit. Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player that night. When Eberechi Eze, who came on for the injured Bukayo Saka in the 10th minute, gave them the lead midway through the first half, their hopes surged.‘It doesn’t look good’: Mikel Arteta concerned as Bukayo Saka limps off against BayernRead moreEnter Kane. He wore his playmaker’s hat; some of his passing was sumptuous and it was his assist for Alphonso Davies that helped Bayern to draw level. He wore his finisher’s one, too, scoring from the penalty spot to put his team in charge. It meant he had scored in 10 consecutive Champions League games; one short of Cristiano Ronaldo’s record. There is a reason why Kane is the favourite to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday. He now has 16 goals against Arsenal; he has only scored more against one club – Leicester, against whom he has 20.Rice loosened Bayern’s grip. It was a lovely goal from him and Arsenal even hinted at a late winner, Jurriën Timber drawing a tip over from Manuel Neuer in stoppage time. That would have been too much because Bayern shaded an absorbing tie in terms of clear chances created. But Arsenal made their point. They were value for it.Arsenal knew they were inside a fortress. Bayern had not previously lost a Champions League group or league phase match at their own stadium since the 3-2 reverse against Manchester City in December 2013, 40 games ago. The following 39 featured 37 wins and two draws. Arteta’s players were not intimidated. They bristled with assurance at the outset and Rice rewarded their never-say-die spirit. Bayern had wanted revenge for their3-1 defeat at the Emirates Stadiumin the league stage last season. They did not get it.Arteta’s idea was to go pretty much as strong as possible with his lineup. He made just two changes, Timber for Ben White and Noni Madueke for Eze, albeit the latter was not on the bench for long. Saka had tussled with Davies and it looked innocuous. The alarm bells rang when Saka grabbed his thigh and went to ground, waving his hand in the air.View image in fullscreenBukayo Saka receives treatment after going down injured early on.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesWas it possible for the Arsenal support to think that Bayern had been stripped of their fear factor in the line behind Kane? Michael Olise was suspended, Jamal Musiala was injured and Luis Díaz was a substitute. He came on in the 68th minute only to be forced off before the end. Bayern were without the midfielder Joshua Kimmich for personal reasons.Arteta moved Madueke over to his more natural position on the right wing when he introduced Eze on the left and Bayern will still be wondering how the latter was afforded so much space up the inside channel on that flank to put Arsenal in front.It was a fabulous ball from Martin Ødegaard, who was in the mood, full of sharp turns and urgency, and Eze had the time to let it bounce before shooting first time into the far corner. An offside flag killed the Arsenal celebrations and there was one of those weird waits before the video assistant referee ruled that Eze was in fact onside.Kane was booed by the Arsenal fans. Of course he was. He dropped deep to link the play and there was a moment in the 17th minute when he started a move with a pass from inside his own penalty area. There was a glorious ping over Gabriel Magalhães, who was the last Arsenal defender, for Ismael Saibari on 23 minutes, although his teammate could not control, and Kane’s fingerprints were all over the equaliser. He was on halfway when he sculpted the low through ball for Davies which took Timber out of the equation. The Bayern winger’s finish was clinical.View image in fullscreenHarry Kane lashes in from the spot to put Bayern Munich 2-1 ahead.Photograph: Michael Zemanek/ShutterstockBayern had other chances in the first half, none better than the one for Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, in the 21st minute. It was Kane who began the attack, taking a quick goal kick – yes, really – and Gnabry was the man over on the right when the Bayern forwards worked it that way. Gnabry’s shot was too close to David Raya. Kane also saw Ezri Konsa produce a fine block to keep him out.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is never anything other than a pleasure to be at the Allianz for a showpiece match. All the staples were present and correct. The en masse scarf waving. The slightly slapstick oompah band notes. The fans at either end of the ground calling to each other. The non-stop drumbeat and songs from the Südkurve, who also bounced as one at times.The pre-game surprise had been the sight of Vincent Kompany in the Bayern dugout; the manager made a Lazarus-like rise from his sickbed and the action after the restart kept the blood pumping. Arsenal thought they had gone back ahead when Bruno Guimarães rose to meet Rice’s corner only for Neuer to produce an extraordinary save.The goalkeeper touched the ball up and on to the crossbar and away. Shades of Gordon Banks against Pelé. It was Raya’s turn next; his save to keep out Dayot Upamecano’s close-range header from Gnabry’s cross was of the highest order.View image in fullscreenMikel Arteta applauds the travelling fans after the final whistle.Photograph: Tiego Grenho/Every Second Media/ShutterstockIt was interesting to watch Kane after the penalty was awarded for handball against Timber. Bayern had worked the ball back to their No 9 and, when he shot, Timber’s arm was outstretched. Kane went through his mental processes. He could see that Raya did not retreat to his line for what felt like an age. Kane delayed even longer. He was in total control. He stuttered before banging the ball hard into the right-hand corner.Bayern were close to putting the game to bed. Konrad Laimer dragged narrowly past the far post when well-placed but it was Arsenal who produced the sucker punch. Eze was dangerous throughout. And when the opportunity knocked for Rice after a pass from the substitute Viktor Gyökeres, he made no mistake.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueBayern MunichArsenalmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Jimmy Anderson set to retire from cricket as Lancashire opt against renewing contract | Jimmy Anderson | The Guardian
description: Jimmy Anderson is expected to call time on his remarkable career at the age of 44 after being told his contract at Lancashire will not be renewed
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Jimmy Anderson is expected to call time on his remarkable career at the age of 44 after being told his contract at Lancashire will not be renewed
Content: Jimmy Anderson claimed 50 wickets in just 11 county matches at an average of 17.68 as the Red Rose finished second bottom of Division Two.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJimmy Anderson claimed 50 wickets in just 11 county matches at an average of 17.68 as the Red Rose finished second bottom of Division Two.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesJimmy AndersonJimmy Anderson set to retire from cricket as Lancashire opt against renewing contractEngland bowler may have played last game at age 44Lancashire tell Anderson he does not fit their plansAli MartinWed 21 Oct 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJimmy Anderson is expected to call time on his remarkable career at the age of 44 after being told his contract at Lancashire will not be renewed for next season.A change of direction is under way at Old Trafford after the club finished second-bottom of Division Two in the County Championship this year and failed to get out of the group stages in both men’s white-ball competitions.The Spin | Writing a book with Chris Woakes showed the inner steel of the nicest man in cricketRead moreRichard Kenyon has since arrived from Nottinghamshire as Lancashire’s new chief executive and hired Paul Farbrace from Sussex as director of cricket. While Farbrace does not start officially until next month, the pair informed Anderson on Monday that he does not feature in their plans, as first reported by the Times.Anderson had been on season-by-season contracts with his boyhood club following his retirement from England duty in 2024, and he captained the first team in their most recent campaign. He combined this with 50 wickets at a princely average of 17, even if it could not prevent the club’s lowest finish in the two-division era.Unless an overseas deal follows this winter, or a hopeful county comes calling, it appears Anderson has played his final game of professional cricket. If so, then he will finish with 1,193 first-class wickets, and more than 400 in limited-over matches, to go with the knighthood he was awarded 12 months ago for services to the sport.View image in fullscreenJimmy Anderson poses for a portrait in the Old Trafford changing rooms in 2021.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianReports at the end of the season suggested Anderson was unlikely to remain as Lancashire captain but there were also indications that he wished to play on. This was only ever going to hinge on the new leadership’s view, however, after Daniel Gidney stood down as chief executive and Mark Chilton lost his job as director of cricket.The call has now been made by Chilton’s successor, Farbrace, who was head-hunted to revive the ailing county. Farbrace, a former England assistant coach, had been poised to remain at Sussex on a part-time basis – a new arrangement triggered by their financial difficulties – only to be swayed by the lure of a Test county.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor all that Anderson has raged against his advancing years, the decision is a bold one that has put sentiment to one side. A product of Burnley cricket club, and having made his first-team debut for Red Rose in 2001, there will doubtless be a large section of the membership who would have wanted one more season.The same went for a significant number of England supporters two years ago when Anderson was ushered into retirement by Rob Key, Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes. With 704 Test dismissals he finished as England’s record wicket-taker and the third highest in history overall – even if he personally remained unsated.Explore more on these topicsJimmy AndersonLancashireCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barkley and Buendía on target as Aston Villa sink Viking to maintain perfect start | Champions League | The Guardian
description: An own goal from Henrik Heggheim completed Aston Villa’s 3-1 Champions League victory against Viking, their third consecutive win of the league phase
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: An own goal from Henrik Heggheim completed Aston Villa’s 3-1 Champions League victory against Viking, their third consecutive win of the league phase
Content: Ross Barkley soaks in the cheers after giving Aston Villa a first-half lead.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoss Barkley soaks in the cheers after giving Aston Villa a first-half lead.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersChampions LeagueBarkley and Buendía on target as Aston Villa sink Viking to maintain perfect startNick Amesat Villa ParkWed 21 Oct 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a little over 20 minutes, Aston Villa could look down on the rest of Europe. They had scaled theChampions Leaguesummit on goal difference when Henrik Heggheim put through his own net and the fact was not lost on the Holte End, who reflected their position in song and perhaps allowed themselves another glimpse back to the days when their supremacy was undisputed. “We’ve conquered before, we’re prepared for more,” the pre-match tifo display had read.Perhaps Villa really will rekindle the spirit of 1982 but the frustration here, albeit minor in the wider scheme, was that they could not maintain their bird’s-eye view over the continent. A superbly taken volley by Peter Christiansen, awarded by the video assistant referee after initially being disallowed for offside, gave Viking a consolation their second-half display deserved and meant Unai Emery’s side must make do with slumming it just behind Paris Saint-Germain.Declan Rice strikes late for Arsenal to deny Bayern Munich in blockbusterRead more“Collectively and individually we did a good job and some players also made a step forward in their confidence,” said Emery, who was pleased with Villa’s seriousness against opponents still finding their way in a first campaign at this level. “Each match has an objective to get better, to be consistent and be very demanding.”The hard work had been done in an opening period whose scoreline hardly did justice to Villa’s total dominance. Viking had drawn at home with Bayern Munich in their previous game, a fact that would look more explicable when they emerged from their shell later, but were barely afforded a kick and looked vulnerable every time the ball was delivered from wide.Nicolas Jackson, electric in the6-0 thrashing of Fenerbahce, fluffed two free headers in the opening seven minutes and a similarly resounding win came to appear possible. Emery had made four changes but Villa, working the play smoothly from side to side, were a consistent threat and unfazed by opponents whose attacking ambition was initially minimal.The breakthrough arrived after a spell of pressure sparked when a cross from João Gomes, the makeshift right-back, deflected on to the bar. Two corners later, an inswinger from the livewire 18-year-old Ibrahim Mbaye was met by Ross Barkley, who leapt highest to plant a firm header across Arild Østbø at the near post.Barkley had scored twice in the previous week’s big win but the rest of the first half resembled a quest for Emiliano Buendía to put his mark on the scoresheet. Straight after the opener Buendía looped a header wide of the vacant goal after Østbø had parried from Alysson, who was a rangy threat throughout, and then he charged on to a clever John McGinn corner only to aim straight at the keeper.View image in fullscreenRoss Barkley heads Aston Villa’s opener from Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAIt was third time lucky when the VAR reviewed a needless challenge by the Viking captain Zlatko Tripic on Alysson, who had run into traffic in the box, and led the referee Sebastian Gishamer to award a penalty. Buendía rolled it in, his fourth goal in consecutive European games; 37 minutes had passed and Viking had still not produced a meaningful attack.After the restart they showed some of the intensity and verve that had ruffled Bayern, the richly promising midfielder Tobias Moi warming Zion Suzuki’s midriff and seeing a goalbound effort blocked. Suzuki also beat away a Tripic drive. But Villa could now exploit space in behind and, after flashing an angled effort just wide, Alysson got away once again to create the third. This time his attempted centre snicked off Heggheim, who was desperately trying to recover, and gave Østbø no chance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNow Villa were, as the home choirs gleefully announced, top of the league and they received further opportunities to hammer home the point. Alejandro Garnacho saw one of them saved by Østbø after a strong run but Viking remained a threat and Christiansen’s finish, emphatically converting Kristoffer Askildsen’s deep cross, was by some distance the best of the night.“The second half was much more like the Viking we want to be,” said Morten Jensen, whoco-manages the Norwegian championsalongside Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim. “Maybe we had too much respect for them in the first half, they were all over us.”View image in fullscreenEmiliano Buendía calmly doubles Aston Villa’s lead from the penalty spot.Photograph: Alex Livesey/AVFC/Getty ImagesNine points from nine, not to mention 12 consecutive home wins in Europe, mean Villa are flying. Sweeping Fenerbahce and Viking aside can “give us confidence and comfort for the next challenges,” Emery said. They will need plenty of it given a trip to Barcelona follows the relatively soft run presented so far. Maybe the peak is yet to come.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueAston VillaViking FKmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: No sour grapes: Venter on vintage form as he lays out Saracens vision | Saracens | The Guardian
description: The head of rugby culture and wine consultant wants people to see ‘the bigger picture’ as he builds the club to win the Prem again
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: The head of rugby culture and wine consultant wants people to see ‘the bigger picture’ as he builds the club to win the Prem again
Content: Brendan Venter would rather talk about wine than rugby but admits: ‘I’ll never master either of them.’Photograph: Andrew Redington/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrendan Venter would rather talk about wine than rugby but admits: ‘I’ll never master either of them.’Photograph: Andrew Redington/Getty ImagesSaracensNo sour grapes: Venter on vintage form as he lays out Saracens visionHead of rugby culture and wine consultant wants people to see ‘the bigger picture’ as he rebuilds club to win the PremGerard MeagherWed 21 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArm wrestling with Chas & Dave. Youth hostelling with Chris Eubank. Wine tasting with Brendan Venter. Two of those are among the suggestions made by a flailing Alan Partridge in the famous “smell my cheese” sketch, the other took place on a chilly Tuesday night in north London this week. No prizes for guessing which, given recent events, but 12 months ago it would not have been so easy. Things move fast in theSaracensworld, however.When the invitation arrived, you could not help but smile. Saracens would dispute that Venter’s temporary job title change from director of rugbyto head of rugby culture and wine consultantwas, to put it bluntly, taking the mickey. But, still, there was something delicious about it. Curiosity took hold, invitation was accepted. A poisoned chalice or a peace offering?Red Roses drop Kildunne to bench for Canada rematch as Mitchell seeks England resetRead moreIt soon became clear this was a charm offensive. Saracens have been through the mill of late and felt the need to issue a fierce statement this week defending themselves. To recap, they were fined because Prem Rugby executives felt Venter was dodging media obligations. They have endured mixed results to date butthe performance against Sale, witnessed by a worryingly sparse crowd, was cause for concern. And theysacked the 21-year-old Totoa Auvaaafter his latest brush with the law. Accordingly, Saracens threw open the doors and wheeled out the big guns. Chief executive, chairman, owner, Owen Farrell, Ben Earl and George Martin and, of course, Venter, in his element with dozens of bottles of red to get stuck into.Venter’s reasons for not wanting to fulfil media duties are roughly threefold. One, because he does not like the banality of it all. “What are your thoughts on that match?” is a question for which life is too short. Two, he wants to promote his coaches such as Joe Shaw. Three, he does not trust himself to bite his lip and avoid disciplinary proceedings.The first two points are more persuasive than the third but Venter has acknowledged things played out regrettably and here we are, in Saracens’ home dressing room about to discuss notes and tones. Venter is deeply passionate about wine and that he loves to talk about it. “You get to explore wine,” he says.View image in fullscreenNoah Caluori has his head in his hands after Saracens’ defeat against Connacht in the Champions Cup.Photograph: Thomas Flinkow/Sportsfile/Getty Images“It’s like rugby, you’re never going to beat rugby, there are always better ideas and different permutations. I know I’ll never master either of them. Just when you think you’ve got it, you don’t have it and it slips away. Just when you think you’ve figured it out then you are humbled.”We are blind tasting to avoid preconceptions, just as he did with the Saracens squad during pre-season, before running out on to the training field. “We are so subjective as human beings,” adds Venter. “We can’t help it. We see things, we hear things, and we are influenced. When I tell you this wine costs £100, or it’s this fancy label, or it’s this old, or it comes from this country, you will think it is a good wine.“The lesson was brilliant for [the players] that day. I am not going to know how much you earn. I don’t want to know how old you are. I’m going to measure you by how you taste, and it was for the players then to get an opportunity to get a seat at the table. If you’ve got a seat at the table, you are going to be up for selection.”Venter is in full flow. Cabernet is the base of most Bordeaux, he says, and as a result, represents the defence. Merlot, by virtue of being softer, is the attack. Cabernet franc represents kicking, petit verdot and malbec the unseen work that knits everything together. South Africa wines, in Venter’s eyes, are big, meaty and they’re the props.“The Italians would without doubt be the wings, the flamboyant style,” he says. “The French would be the centres, the same thing, the Aussies would be the meticulous people, the scrum-halves, the fly-halves, the New Zealanders would be the sevens, really tough. And then the Georgians would be the hookers.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Breakdown | ‘Freer’ Red Roses resolve to come back stronger after Canada end epic runRead moreVenter’s stock at Saracens is sky-high despite indifferent results this season. The wonders he worked in his first spell, laying the foundation for players such as Farrell, Maro Itoje, Jamie George and the Vunipolas – Mako and Billy – to form England’s most dominant team for more than a decade make sure of that. Put simply, he has returned to do so again.“In rugby we see today so much, we don’t see the bigger picture,” he says. “The bigger picture is developing people over a longer period to try and win a Premiership. We need to build again. If you think about it, we were so good for so long with these superstars. And they’re at the end of their time and we need a new group. They’re not going to fall from the air, we need to develop them.”Farrell is one of the few remaining. He has taken his first steps into coaching – the smart money is that he is still at the club long after hanging up his boots – but he too sees reasons for optimism in Venter’s second stint. “We’re doing it in a bit of a different way from what we’ve been used to but we feel like that will benefit us in the long run. We did the same thing with the wine tasting and then we went out to train after. I can’t remember if it was one of our best sessions. Not because I had too much! He’s very clear and makes it about what we’re doing now – not about what’s been before.”Time will tell if Venter’s second stint is a success but in wine, there tends to be truth.Explore more on these topicsSaracensRugby unionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Paris Saint-Germain sparkle on the pitch while the city of light burns around them | Paris Saint-Germain | The Guardian
description: PSG, the pet project of the state of Qatar, expresses the dualism of the city, a place of deprivation where the centre is perfect
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: PSG, the pet project of the state of Qatar, expresses the dualism of the city, a place of deprivation where the centre is perfect
Content: PSG fans’ tifo sends a chilling message before their game against Barcelona.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAView image in fullscreenPSG fans’ tifo sends a chilling message before their game against Barcelona.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAParis Saint-GermainParis Saint-Germain sparkle on the pitch while the city of light burns around themBarney RonayPSG, pet project of the state of Qatar, expresses the dualism of the city, a place of deprivation where the centre is perfectWed 21 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.55 EDTSharePASSION!GOOOOAL!MVP!The security deployment will be massive.Those who sought to bring down the Republic will have to answer for it.Tell you who would have loved this? Who would have been utterly engrossed scrolling the hashtag #Paris on Tuesday night as two things happened simultaneously, theharrowing of the Barcelona defenceat the Parc des Princes, and the harrowing of Paris itself via tales of city-centre thuggery and end-of-days political doom‑mongering.The big man, Guy Debord himself. The Society of the Spectacle, you say? Actually, I think we’re past that now. Hold the society bit. We’ll just take the spectacle.The great Parisian Situationist philosopher wasn’t really one for managed fun. But it was impossible not to be bowled over by the extraordinary pre-match show for Paris Saint‑Germain versus Barcelona,Champions LeagueMatchday Three.Kvaratskhelia asks ‘why me?’ after ACL rupture in most serious of three PSG injuriesRead moreThe wild pyrotechnics, the plumes of smoke, the full-wrap light show, the lime-green robo‑text spelling out every player’s name on the pitch. Although not the Barcelona names, sadly, for anyone with an unrealised desire to see the words “ANTHONY GORDON” projected in vast letters for the delight of a shrieking crowd.Admittedly, the Halloween‑themed tifo banner showing a maskedParis Saint-Germainserial killer-type literally butchering the Barcelona badge to death with his bloodied chainsaw was perhaps a bit much. As were the Barça Puta signs, which are now reportedly the subject of a complaint to Uefa.But it was a wild and all‑consuming spectacle, annihilating every other impulse in your head to a green thought in a green shade. And in the process capturing the profound sense of cognitive dissonance in the city.View image in fullscreenPSG fans light flares after their team took the lead against Barcelona.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty ImagesJust walking around the streets of central Paris earlier in the day generated its own mild whiplash. On the face of it this was still the same city offlâneursand tourists and everyday bistro business, and not, repeat not, a civil war drama or some kind of emergent military caliphate.But the sense of dread was also tangible. You still got the occasional crunch of glass underfoot. Here and there charred bikes and scooters had been politely piled to one side. Even close to the Parc, away from the main hotspots, shopkeepers could be seen emerging warily into their doorways at the sound of a police siren.By Tuesday night, a total of 2,513 people had been taken into police custodyafter the events of the weekend. At least 420 rental bikes had been destroyed or maimed. Liberated high-value retail goods were already being sold on Vinted, a commendable show of entrepreneurial energy from the maligned younger generation.Not that you’d suspect these two worlds had any kind of overlap, lost in the booming triumphalism around PSG’s 4–2 win, one of the most beautifully luminous football matches you’re ever likely to see. Or indeed reading the coverage of an event that seems to have been treated in France like its own clear, clean space, floating above the flames, all the chat about the brilliance of Monsieur Dynamite, Désiré Doué, the wonderful television audiences on Canal+ TV, the whole of European football “kneeling before the machine” (are we sure this isn’t to do with anarchic rejection of social control?). “Paris est insubmersible!” was the headline in Le Parisien. But is it?Remember when football used to reflect the world? Or just provide clues, a commentary, some kind of metaphor? This is no longer the case. At a time when even the most thunderous of commentators is struggling to summarise all this in suitably trite and damning terms, it was hard to avoid the feeling Paris Saint-Germain, the pet power football project of the state of Qatar, expresses this dualism perfectly.Sometimes you just have to let football tell you things. “People who want to cause trouble in the city centres next Saturday will be prevented,” Emmanuel Macron announced on Tuesday evening, speaking, as it happens, from Doha, where he met Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, ultimate owner of PSG.View image in fullscreenDésiré Doué (left) with João Neves after scoring PSG’s first goal against Barcelona.Photograph: David Ramos/Uefa/Getty ImagesMacron is said to be considering deploying the French military to keep the peace on the streets before the next planned protests, although even here he may have to ask Qatar’s permission if he wants to deploy any of the French troops currently deployed working its missile systems, or embedded in the Doha security services.The key event Macron is tooling up for is this Saturday night, 24 October, the date thegiletsjaunessocial media feed has set for an even greater swell of disorder. And again this will be football adjacent, with PSG playing Lyon at home on Sunday, a top‑of‑the-table capital‑city clash played out against whatever wreckage is left, however many thousands of Dot bikes are savaged, whatever guerrilla skirmishes are still playing out in the Marais.What does this really have to do with football and theIci C’est Parisbrand appropriated by a state outreach project? Well, what are these demonstrations anyway? There have been many theories put forward as to what exactly is happening here, what is the spark, the kindling, the fire behind this disorder. School protests were the original line. Others have now roped in some kind of nebulous omni-cause, Instagram-activism, perhaps even a barbarian takeover, the decline of the west, savagery at the gates, of the type Donald Trump pretends to see.Do you need a single reason? Take a look around. Modern life is pretty alarming on a minute‑to‑minute basis. Disaffection, alienation, a sense of being transformed in real time into a passive economic consumer unit, a set of eyeballs, an avatar of consumption. French youth unemployment is close to 20%. Robots nobody wants are being lined up to take jobs that don’t exist. Why don’t these young people want to join a youth club? Why don’t they sign up for the Liberal Democrats? Why are they enjoying empowered disorder? Maybe because nothing is yours around here, not even the things thrust into your brain as digital distractions. So why not grab something when you can? Debord would have called this “a vicious circle of isolation”, lonely crowd, technologies based on isolation.On the other hand, what is PSG in Paris, other than the perfect expression of this? It often seems to surprise people that celebrations of PSG victories end up with riots and burnt-out cars. But Paris is both a beautiful and deeply dysfunctional city, a place of make‑believe and deprivation, where the centre is a perfect, performative relic, the suburbs shunted out to the ring roads, a life lived inside a box, noses pressed up against the glass, peering through your binoculars at the city of someone else’s love.Paris is the divide between overclass and churn expressed in a single city. It’s everything you might have had but never will. And PSG represent this like no other entity, a football club owned as an act of outreach by a staggeringly rich inherited monarchy, weaponised passion, borrowed culture, engineered spectacle, deeply cynical but also deeply seductive.View image in fullscreenDamage after the riots in Place de la République.Photograph: Telmo Pinto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockWhy are the Qataris splurging hundreds of millions into this project? Because they just really like high-pressing positional football? Qatar is the indentured labour state that employs Colin Kaepernick to promote its outreach projects. It will hymn its connections to the footballers of thebanlieue, which is true and real and valuable, but not because of anything this political project wants or needs other than public relations.It is in its own way a perfect human lab experiment, synthesised beauty, collectivism, with a cold, cold hand at its heart. And this is why there weren’t two versions of Paris in evidence on Tuesday night, just the same one, the dark side and the shiny side, an engine of the same divisions, the same kind of violence, right down to the sight of kids in PSG training gear dodging the police or taunting the barricades at the Place de la République.And now we have Sunday night to come, moreIci C’est Paris, more PASSION. What kind of background will it be played out against? Does it matter under the lights? Will anyone notice?Le Monde has described these events as a very basic test of the republic, its ability to bend, to remain essentially itself, the state’s willingness to pit itself against its own people. Football, as ever, holds these answers already. PSG’s Qatari owners have spent the past 15 years flaunting this city like a global luxury brand, extending its reach, creating its own ideal of conspicuous consumption, spectacle, triumph,son et lumière, bread and roses. As ever, if you want to know how and why, football has the answers.Explore more on these topicsParis Saint-GermainChampions LeagueFranceEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Red Roses drop Kildunne to bench for Canada rematch as Mitchell seeks England reset | England women's rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Ellie Kildunne is on the bench for England’s third and final Test against Canada as the Red Roses look to bounce back from their first loss in four years
Author: Sarah Rendell
Headline: Ellie Kildunne is on the bench for England’s third and final Test against Canada as the Red Roses look to bounce back from their first loss in four years
Content: Ellie Kildunne surges forward for England in their two-point defeat by Canada but will not start in Ottawa.Photograph: Ka Lok Ng/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEllie Kildunne surges forward for England in their two-point defeat by Canada but will not start in Ottawa.Photograph: Ka Lok Ng/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockEngland women's rugby union teamRed Roses drop Kildunne to bench for Canada rematch as Mitchell seeks England resetStar back loses starting place following 24-21 upsetHead coach: ‘She adds huge value – she will get back’Sarah RendellWed 21 Oct 2026 08.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEllie Kildunne has been dropped to the bench for England’s third and final Test against Canada on Friday as the Red Roses look to bounce back from their first loss in four years.The Maple Leafs defeatedEngland 24-21 last Fridayto end the Red Roses’ 41-game unbeaten streak. Kildunne starting from the bench, with Emma Sing at full-back, is one of four changes the head coach, John Mitchell, has made to his starting XV for the Test in Ottawa.“She [Kildunne] adds huge value, she is just going through a difficult period at the moment,” Mitchell said. “It’s important for us to help her through that. She has to become consistent as well. She will get back. It is also important to create competition and to recognise that you have to become more consistent, especially when you are competing in the Red Roses.“It’s really important to reinforce the behaviours we think are necessary to our game. That goes for everyone.”The last time Kildunne did not start for England was in the 2025 Rugby World Cup quarter-final against Scotland after she suffered a concussion in the previous match. Kildunne has started the nine games England have played so far in 2026 but last Friday she committed four knock-ons and Canada managed to stifle England’s standout player.Sing will win her 18th cap for England, with her last start for her country coming against Italy in the Six Nations. In that match,which the Red Roses won 61-33in Parma, the 25-year-old played at full-back with Kildunne starting on the wing.Quick GuideEngland team to face CanadaShowSing; Breach, Jones (captain), Rowland, Venner; Harrison, Packer; Botterman, Cokayne, Bern, Talling, Campion, Burton, Kabeya, FeaunatiReplacementsField, Carson, Muir, Short, Matthews, Robinson, Aitchison, KildunneWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The other changes see Sadia Kabeya starting ahead of Alex Matthews, who is on the bench, with Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and Tatyana Heard dropped from the matchday 23 as Mia Venner and Helena Rowland start.Of Moloney-MacDonald and Heard’s reactions to being dropped, Mitchell added: “Their response has been outstanding. Both individuals have different cases, that is between myself and them.”The captain, Meg Jones, added the team have had “honest conversations” as well as allowing players to “feel sad, happy or indifferent” about the loss.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Now we have the opportunity to not be defined by the outcome [the loss last Friday] and really solidify where your two feet are and where you are is the most important. That is where you find courage and bravery to stick where you are in the present moment. That is going to be huge for us this weekend.”Canada lead the series against England after last Friday’s defeat and the26-26 draw at Exeterin September.The Red Roses have travelled to Ottawa to take on Canada again and while it will be the final time they play their rivals in this WXV Global Series, England’s matches do not end there. They face the USA on 30 October for their final match until the Women’s Six Nations in April.Explore more on these topicsEngland women's rugby union teamWomen's rugby unionCanada women's rugby union teamRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mark Allen reveals he made snooker return after 10-week stay in mental health clinic | Snooker | The Guardian
description: Mark Allen has revealed he spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic before discharging himself to play in this week’s Northern Ireland Open
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mark Allen has revealed he spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic before discharging himself to play in this week’s Northern Ireland Open
Content: ‘I didn’t see a future in anything. My daughter kept me going,’ says Mark Allen.Photograph: Richard Sellers/PAView image in fullscreen‘I didn’t see a future in anything. My daughter kept me going,’ says Mark Allen.Photograph: Richard Sellers/PASnookerMark Allen reveals he made snooker return after 10-week stay in mental health clinicFormer world No 1 vows to show ‘fighting qualities’‘I see the light now that I couldn’t see before’Press AssociationWed 21 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Allen has revealed he spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic before discharging himself toplay in this week’s Northern Ireland Open. In a long statement posted on X, the 40-year-old said he was “not OK” but vowed to show his renowned “fighting qualities” as he continues his recovery.Allen’s 4-2 defeat by his friend and compatriot Jordan Brown on Tuesday was his first match since his world championship semi-final loss to Wu Yize in April, whenhe missed a black off its spotthat would have given him the win.‘I’m in a bad place’: Mark Allen says his snooker career may be over after defeatRead moreAfter losing to Brown, Allen conductedan emotional interview with TNT Sportsin which he said he was “really overwhelmed”, and suggested his career could be over. He wrote on Wednesday: “Everything I said in that interview was true. However, rest assured I’m doing my best to turn things round.“I have been in a mental health clinic for the last 10 weeks, finally discharging so I could attempt to play in Belfast. I owed that to my family, in particular my daughter to see me play for what could be the last time … I also owed it to the fans who have supported me throughout my 21 years on tour.“I also owed that to WorldSnookerwho have been amazing from day one in all this, in particular [chief executive] Simon Brownell and [WPBSA Players chief operating officer] Neil Tomkins who have remained in touch regularly, even Simon paying me a visit in the clinic itself.“I’m not OK, but I’m OK in that itself. I’ve been much worse in the last few months than you saw yesterday. I literally didn’t see a future in anything. My daughter kept me going, the therapists, staff and all the other patients were amazing and helped me through some really dark days.“I see the light now that I couldn’t see before but I do now. I also know it won’t happen overnight. I’m a work in progress. My fight and determination on the table has always been there for ones to see. I need to show those same fighting qualities off it now for a while.“Please don’t detract anything from Jordan yesterday, he’s been aware of my struggles and that can’t have been easy to play in but he handled it with grace and skill as I knew he would. I’m proud to call him a friend.“I hope the rest of the event is a success and I will continue my treatments going forward and then see what’s ahead.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSince his defeat by Wu, Allen has stayed away from the tour for unspecified personal reasons that are understood not to relate to any repercussions from the manner of his defeat at the Crucible.Allen has won both UK and Masters titles in a total of 12 ranking tournament wins, and has reached the world championship semi-finals three times. He was ranked world No 1 for four months in 2024.In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat988lifeline.org. In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978Explore more on these topicsSnookerMental healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Austin GP is about much more than potential for Antonelli’s first F1 world title | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The young Italian driver’s maiden championship is all but secured but Mercedes upgrades will inform next year’s run to the line
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The young Italian driver’s maiden championship is all but secured but Mercedes upgrades will inform next year’s run to the line
Content: Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli is primed to become F1’s youngest champion – but his team’s dominance is under threat for next season.Photograph: DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMercedes’ Kimi Antonelli is primed to become F1’s youngest champion – but his team’s dominance is under threat for next season.Photograph: DPPI/ShutterstockFormula One 2026AnalysisAustin GP is about much more than potential for Antonelli’s first F1 world titleGiles Richardsin AustinYoung driver’s maiden championship is all but secured but Mercedes upgrades will inform next year’s run to the lineWed 21 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 15.45 EDTShareThere is nothing quite like a potential title decider to bring the fiercest of spotlights to bear as doubtless Kimi Antonelli will discover when he attempts toseal his first championshipat the United States Grand Prix this weekend.For the young Italian the goal is straightforward and the culmination of a childhood dream. However, for his Mercedes team there will be scrutiny over performance in Austin that has significant implications going into next season.F1 returns to Africa for first time since 1993 with 10-year Rwanda deal from ‘early 2030s’Read moreThe 20-year-old Antonelli holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton is fifth or lower. It is not an entirely impossible scenario but even if he does not clinch the title in Texas, in all likelihood he will be crowned in Mexico a week later.Antonelli has been exceptional in only his second season in F1, but also enjoyed what was for the opening half of the season an all but untouchable car. Mercedes can no longer boast that advantage. Max Verstappen has won the past two races as Red Bull’s upgrades finally unlocked the performance they felt was there to be exploited.Ferrari, too, are now close to Mercedes, capable of beating them and have a raft of aerodynamic upgrades arriving in Austin. McLaren, having dropped back a tad in recent races, have repeatedly proved to have the measure of the championship leaders and have upgrades planned for the coming triple-header in the US, Mexico and Brazil.Mercedes had not had it all quite their own way then when they brought their second and final improvements to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. Yet an expected uplift of as much as three-10ths a lapwas met with disappointment. The upgrades did not deliver as expected and the car became a handful to drive, gains in lap time unsurprisingly elusive.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli finished third in Singapore, enough to maintain a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell.Photograph: Yichin Hou/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe Mercedes is less forgiving, switching between understeer and oversteer in a narrow window, working the tyres harder.Such was the discrepancy between what occurred on track and what was expected that after Malaysia they reverted to using the old spec on Russell’s car and the new one on Antonelli’s to better assess the issues atthe following Singapore GP, after which the Italian felt there had been an improvement.All of which is part of the development process, especially in a season of new regulations. But as the Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, noted these updates were not only intended to enhance and improve but were of paramount importance because they would inform next season’s car.“Was it an easy car like the previous one? I don’t think it was. Does it have the performance that we were hoping the upgrade would bring? I don’t think so yet. But it was a step in the right direction,” Wolff said after Singapore. “In Austin, we should see whether we can continue to consolidate that and whether it has more performance, because it’s crucial for the development direction for the next year.”View image in fullscreen‘In Austin, we should see whether the Mercedes has more performance, because it’s crucial for the development direction for the next year,’ says Toto Wolff.Photograph: DPPI/ShutterstockWhile Malaysia and Singapore might be considered outliers, Austin is a typical circuit, with medium- and fast-speed corners on a flowing track where good balance and a quick, well-behaving car is rewarded – the type of track where Mercedes were in control for the much of the season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat said, some at the team may be forgiven for experiencing a discomforting sense of deja vu. In each of the previous four years, with many upgrades not delivering as expected and in some cases setting the team back.Kimi Antonelli admits he can taste F1 glory after Verstappen wins Singapore GPRead moreTo be fair, Mercedes are far from such straits now and are still quick. Yet they have nowhere near the level of dominance they enjoyed in the 2014-2020 period when they remained all but untouchable and missteps along the way were almost unheard of.At the time the opposition closed on them but in most cases that was because Mercedes were already switching resources to the following year, confident they were ahead of the game and in where they needed to go with next year’s model.As this season draws to a close there is no such clearcut advantage. The frontrunners are all still feeling their way toward exploiting the maximum from the new regulations. The direction for 2027 is vital because the field is far more closely matched and developing at a fearsome rate, as Red Bull have demonstrated.Mercedes’ lead this season is nonetheless formidable and while they cannot seal the constructors’ championship this weekend, Antonelli’s drivers’ title is surely all but done and dusted. Austin, however, might yet suggest whether they can repeat the feat in 2027.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Kimi AntonelliMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s approval rating drops to 36% two weeks before midterms, poll finds | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of economy and cost of living, says poll in new low recorded by NY Times/Siena
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: Voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of economy and cost of living, says poll in new low recorded by NY Times/Siena
Content: Melania and Donald Trump walk to sign an executive order signing in the Rose Garden of the White House on Monday.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMelania and Donald Trump walk to sign an executive order signing in the Rose Garden of the White House on Monday.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump’s approval rating drops to 36% two weeks before midterms, poll findsVoters disapprove of Trump’s handling of economy and cost of living, says poll in new low recorded by NY Times/SienaAriana BaioWed 21 Oct 2026 10.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s approval rating sank to 36% just two weeks before themidterm elections, the lowest recorded in a poll by theNew York Times/Siena College, with most respondents expressing frustration over his handling of the US economy, cost of living and Iran war.In an October survey of approximately 3,494 likely voters, 59% said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of his job, and 52% said they planned to vote for the Democratic candidate in the upcoming election.Much of the disapproval toward the US president was associated with frustrations over Trump’s handling ofeconomicand cost-of-living-related issues. On gas prices, 73% of registered voters said they disapproved; on the cost of living, 69% said they disapproved, andon the economy, 64% said they disapproved.Key US voters say economy is getting worse ahead of midterms, exclusive poll findsRead moreApproximately 65% said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of theIran war, which hasdragged on for nearly eight monthsand pushed gas and oil prices up.The new polling numbers paint a gloomy picture for Trump andRepublicans, who have embarked on an uphill battle to defeat Democrats in the upcoming midterms to maintain their majority control in Congress.Trump, whose name recognition has largely helped Republican candidates in past elections, has been on the road campaigning for Maga-aligned candidates. However, some candidates havesought todistance themselvesfrom the president, who has become increasinglyunpopularover his economic policies.In 2024, Trump promisedtolowereverydaycostsfor Americans,keep inflation lowand to keep the US fromstarting more wars abroad.But as of 21 October, gas prices weremore than $4.25 a gallon, inflation increased to 3.7% last month and the president’s war with Iran remained steady.BetweenSeptemberand October, the US president’s approval rating decreased by two percentage points in the New York Times/Siena College polls.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDemocratic candidates, meanwhile, haveseized onthecost-of-livingissuesto appeal to independents and undecided voters, promising to rein in the president’s policies that have pushed costs up, such as tariffs.While polling from the New York Times/Siena College indicates Democrats have the upper hand headed into next month’s election, the party is still fighting against a massive financial war chest incompetitive racesinTexas,Ohio,New York,AlaskaandIowa.The Guardian has asked the White House for comment.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS midterm elections 2026US politicsRepublicansUS economyUS-Israel war on IrannewsShareReuse this content

title: Officials confirm flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite found in US wildlife | Texas | The Guardian
description: USDA says screwworm found in elk in Texas, and warns hunters and ranchers to be vigilant to help stop spread
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: USDA says screwworm found in elk in Texas, and warns hunters and ranchers to be vigilant to help stop spread
Content: A New World screwworm and other botfly specimens under the microscope at a lab in Kerrville, Texas.Photograph: Kaylee Greenlee/ReutersView image in fullscreenA New World screwworm and other botfly specimens under the microscope at a lab in Kerrville, Texas.Photograph: Kaylee Greenlee/ReutersTexasOfficials confirm flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite found in US wildlifeUSDA says screwworm found in elk in Texas, and warns hunters and ranchers to be vigilant to help stop spreadGuardian staff and agencyWed 21 Oct 2026 19.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Department of Agriculture (USDA) said on Wednesday it had ⁠confirmed the ⁠first detection ​of flesh-eating parasite the New World screwworm in US wildlife in an ⁠elk in Pecos county,Texas.The elk was located on a game ⁠ranch and was reported after being harvested by ​a hunter, the ‌USDA said ‌in a statement.The Texas animal health ‌commission will modify a previously established infested zone, and the USDA and the Texas parks and wildlife department is conducting additional wildlife surveillance in the area, the USDA said.“We encourage all hunters and landowners to be vigilant for signs of New World screwworm while they are out in the field this season,” Texas wildlife division director Alan Cainsaidin a statement.Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central ​America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports.The US halted livestock imports ⁠from Mexico last year to keep out screwworm, ​but ​resumed trade in August ​at an Arizona port as part ​of a ‌phased reopening ​plan.The halt has tightened US cattle supplies and pushed beef prices to record highs for American consumers.Despite those efforts, the screwworm was detected in June on a calf in Texas’s Zavala county, located near the US-Mexico border. There have since been dozens of cases detected in the US this year, including on a horse and on a dog.Explore more on these topicsTexasUS politicsWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cut the umbilical cord’: Bougainville’s bid to break away from Papua New Guinea faces reckoning | Bougainville | The Guardian
description: MPs in PNG to decide on ratifying a 2019 referendum in which Bougainvilleans voted overwhelmingly in favour of independence
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: MPs in PNG to decide on ratifying a 2019 referendum in which Bougainvilleans voted overwhelmingly in favour of independence
Content: People queue to vote in Bougainville’s capital Buka during the 2019 independence referendum.Photograph: Ness Kerton/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople queue to vote in Bougainville’s capital Buka during the 2019 independence referendum.Photograph: Ness Kerton/AFP/Getty ImagesBougainville‘Cut the umbilical cord’: Bougainville’s bid to break away from Papua New Guinea faces reckoningMPs in PNG to decide on ratifying a 2019 referendum in which Bougainvilleans voted overwhelmingly in favour of independenceBen DohertyWed 21 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor decades, the distant island of Bougainville has fought for secession fromPapua New Guinea, for a future as an independent nation of its own.This week, that long-running aspiration faces further challenge, with PNG’s parliament slated to debate the ratification of Bougainville’s 2019 UN-sanctioned referendum, in which nearly 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence.That referendum was a key element of the 2001 Bougainville Peace Agreement, which ended a 10-year long civil war estimated to have killed as many as 15,000 people.‘No one will stop our people’: Bougainville president defiant in push for independenceRead moreEven as violence has reemerged around the controversial Panguna mine – a catalyst for the conflict, but now seen as critical to the island’s independent financial future – Bougainville’s government has insisted it will not be deterred from secession. It has committed to “self-government” from next year, and to breaking away from PNG, as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.Sources in Port Moresby and Bougainville say they expect the independence referendum result to be rejected on the floor of the PNG parliament, given the threshold for ratification has been raised to three-quarters of all MPs, not the two-thirds usually required for constitutional amendments.The autonomous island of Bougainville, PNG’s easternmost province and about 1,000km from the capital, is home to about 300,000 people, culturally and ethnically distinct from the rest of the PNG archipelago. It has for decades, sought to break free of rule by Port Moresby.Map of PNG and BougainvilleDivided opinionPort Moresby has long resisted acting on Bougainville’s post-conflict independence, anxious not to establish a precedent for the break-up of PNG’s vast and culturally diverse archipelago, or to lose a resource-rich and potentially lucrative province.Bougainville’s attorney-general and vice-president, Ezekiel Masatt, said that theMP vote threshold was “crafted” by the PNG government to defeat the vote.“There is a national government strategy to poison the waters and make it impossible to come close to reach the voting threshold,” he said in a June statement.Opinions in PNG’s parliament were divided ahead of the referendum vote.Dr Allan Marat, chair of a bipartisan committee on Bougainville matters, told parliament last month that the island had met all the conditions outlined in the 2001 peace agreement and deserved its independence.“It seems there is only one humane option for us members of this honourable house to do … to cut the umbilical cord connecting baby ‘Bougainville Independence’ to PNG,” he said.Others are fiercely opposed. Former deputy prime minister Belden Namah, who served in the PNG army during the Bougainville conflict, said the question went beyond a political debate.“It is an issue of national sovereignty, it is an issue of constitutional integrity, it is an issue of peace, unity, sacrifice and the future survival of Papua New Guinea as one nation,” he told the same parliamentary sitting.In June this year, Bougainville’s president Ishmael Toroama presented his government’s “final position” on the island’s political future.He said Bougainville would enter a stage of “self-government” from 1 September 2027, before declaring itself independent “separate from the state of PNG” in 2030.Toroama said he did not want a return to violence or conflict with Port Moresby. “Our objective has never been confrontation,” he said. “Our objective has always been reconciliation, partnership and a peaceful transition founded on law and mutual respect.”View image in fullscreenPresident Ishmael Toroama says Bougainville will enter a stage of ‘self-government’ from September 2027.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianThe Bougainville government hopes the controversial Panguna gold and copper mine will fund independence. Carved from a mountain in the centre of the island, it was once one of the largest gold and copper mines in the world, and still has an estimated $60bn in unrealised reserves.“We closed the mine because of oppression,” Toroama told the Guardian in aninterview last year. “Today the mine is the key to our economic growth and settling all unresolved issues from the war.”Q&AWhat caused the Bougainville civil war?ShowBougainville, a group of islands off Papua New Guinea to the north of Australia, has been variously controlled by Britain, Germany, Japan, Australia and PNG.It declared independence in 1975 as the Republic of North Solomons, but was absorbed into the newly independent PNG weeks later.Its close ethnic ties and proximity to the Solomons archipelago means it has always sat uneasily with Port Moresby’s rule.That discontent came to a violent head in 1988 after a long-running dispute over the lucrative Panguna copper and gold mine.The mine, carved from a mountain in central Bougainville, was critically important to PNG, at one point generating more than 45% of the country's national export revenue.Multinational Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly US$2bn from the mine over 17 years of operation. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands had been destroyed by it.Under the leadership of a former mine worker, Francis Ona, disaffected Bougainvilleans ran a sabotage campaign which forced the mine’s closure in 1989.The PNG Government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war that ran for a decade, and saw as many as 20,000 people die.PNG later hired international mercenaries to end the conflict (the notorious Sandline affair), before a peace agreement was signed in 2001.In a 2019 referendum, 97.7% of Bougainvilleans voted in favour of independence. Many argue that reopening Panguna mine will be key to the island’s economic future as an independent nation.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Multinational Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it. The mine and surrounding river deltas remain dangerously polluted. Rio Tinto hassigned an MOUwith the Bougainville government to address the ongoing environmental and human rights impacts of the dormant mine.Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as ‘the crisis’ – that ran for a decade.Violence returned to the mine last month, when up to 30 men carrying high-powered rifles drove into the sprawling Panguna pit site and set fire to nearly 40 heavy haulage trucks, excavators and water tanks owned by the newly appointed contractor, India’s Lloyds Metals and Energy.View image in fullscreenAerial photo of Panguna open pit mine in Bougainville, Papua New Guinea.Photograph: Awol Imagery/AlamyToroama said violence would not intimidate his government from redeveloping the mine.“We will not cower to terroristic acts of violence designed to cause disunity and distract us from our agenda of creating a socio-politically and economically viable Bougainville,” he said after the incident.Oliver Nobetau,Pacific islandsprogram director at the Lowy Institute, an Australian thinktank, said it was well known across the island that “not everyone is on-side to reopen the mine”.He said the incident, while relatively minor, had damaged the independence cause by affirming Port Moresby’s often-overstated concerns that Bougainville was not ready for independence, including that the island had not fully disarmed.Nobetau said a “no” vote was looking increasingly likely in PNG’s parliament.“My assessment is that it’s not going to spill over into actual conflict and fighting the way that people fear,” he said. “I think there’s going to be a lot of social tensions, a lot of political tensions, but I think eventually they’ll come back to the table to discuss how to move forward.”Nobetau said the independence movement on Bougainville would not be deterred by resistance from Port Moresby.“I think most likely they will try to go at it alone through the self-government model and then rolling out a three-year plan towards independence by 2030.”Explore more on these topicsBougainvillePapua New GuineaPacific islandsAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Woman told Russell Brand he treated her ‘like an animal’, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women
Content: Russell Brand and his wife Laura Gallacher leave  Southwark crown court.Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRussell Brand and his wife Laura Gallacher leave  Southwark crown court.Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesUK newsWoman told Russell Brand he treated her ‘like an animal’, court hearsBrand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six womenEmine SinmazWed 21 Oct 2026 11.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman said Russell Brand degraded her and treated her like “a piece of meat” when he raped her at his London townhouse, a court has heard.She alleged she repeatedly begged the 51-year-old comedian to stop the assault which left her bleeding for days and in pain.Months later she bumped into Brand who texted her saying: “You’re dirty and I wanna push you further.”Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009.
