He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.The TV personality listened intently in the dock as the woman gave evidence from behind a screen at Southwark crown court on Wednesday.Brand is accused of anally raping the woman at his three-storey Victorian townhouse after picking her out from a crowd at one of his stand-up performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009.The woman told police she was a “massive fan” of Brand and had performed oral sex on him after the gig despite having a boyfriend at the time. Days later, she went to Brand’s home in Hampstead, north-west London, knowing she would have vaginal sex with him. But she alleged Brand anally raped her after consensual vaginal sex.In tense exchanges with Brand’s barrister Ian Winter KC during cross-examination, the woman denied she had consented to anal sex but later regretted it because she was in pain and feared she had contracted HIV.The woman told the court that Brand “didn’t act like he’d done something criminal” after the alleged attack, to which Winter replied: “That’s because you consented.”She insisted she had not, telling the barrister: “We’re not here to discuss my morality.”“I didn’t consent to what happened to me,” she continued. “I have said that repeatedly in questioning. I made it very clear that I thought I was going to have penetrative vaginal sex with a condom.“I agree that I haven’t painted myself in a very good light. I did just meet Mr Brand at the Hammersmith Apollo and I did have a partner who I really loved and I made a huge mistake.”The woman was also questioned about her pre-recorded police interviews which were played to court on Tuesday and Wednesday. She told officers she ran into Brand at the Edinburgh Festival months after the alleged rape, and then received a “random” text from the comedian.The woman, who was in her early 20s, said she challenged Brand: “Why are you even messaging me?” She claimed he responded: “Because you are dirty and I want to push you further.”She said she replied saying: “I think you’ve pushed me far enough, you treated me like an animal,” to which Brand responded: “I’m sorry.”She told police: “I feel how I’d felt at his house, that I felt completely degraded and fucking treated like an animal, like a piece of meat.”Winter questioned why she had not replied to Brand saying he had raped her. He told the woman: “That’s because he had pushed you and probably had treated you like an animal, but he didn’t rape you.”“I didn’t consent,” the woman replied.Earlier, Winter said the woman was aware of Brand’s reputation, to which she replied: “I had not heard about Mr Brand raping somebody.”Winter replied: “Of course not. You knew that he was extremely sexually active with multiple women. You knew that he won the Sun newspaper’s Shagger of the Year three years running.”He went on to describe how Brand’s show at the Hammersmith Apollo was “extremely sexually explicit” and that women were throwing their bras at the comedian and flashing their naked breasts. “I didn’t do that,” the woman replied.The barrister said that after the show the woman had performed oral sex on Brand “who was effectively a total stranger, because you were obsessed with him at the time”. She replied: “If what you are asking is, would I have met someone … and then perform oral sex on him had he not been the person that he was, the answer is no.”The barrister said the woman was aware that Brand was interested in “transactional” sex when he persuaded her to go to his house after the gig. “I didn’t think I was going to be his girlfriend,” she replied.But the woman denied Winter’s suggestion that Brand had told her he wanted to have anal sex with her.Winter said: “In a way, you went along with what he wanted because you were young and impressionable and obsessed with him. I’m putting to you, you agreed to do that.”She replied: “I didn’t agree to do that.”“The reason I made the comment about going there willingly and regretting it afterwards was because I did not consent to that,” she said.The woman said she had not been able to immediately tell Brand to stop the alleged rape because she was in shock and pain. “In the very first instant I couldn’t speak, I couldn’t breathe,” she said.She said she carried a lot of guilt and shame about what had happened, saying: “Because I went to his house willingly, because I engaged in a consensual type of sex, I didn’t feel I had as much right to feel as bad about it as I did.”When Winter pressed her, she replied: “I felt a lot of burden. I carried that feeling of guilt and shame and I felt lots of things but particularly for exactly the reason that you are doing right here, making me feel like I brought it on myself. That just because you go somewhere willingly and the outcome in the end is not consensual – it’s a different scenario.”The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agenda | The far right | The Guardian
description: Nationalist leaders are framing unrest as consequence of failed liberal governance and open borders
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Nationalist leaders are framing unrest as consequence of failed liberal governance and open borders
Content: A fire burns as police officers in riot gear stand guard in Paris.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersView image in fullscreenA fire burns as police officers in riot gear stand guard in Paris.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersThe far rightEurope’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agendaNationalist leaders are framing unrest as consequence of failed liberal governance and open bordersJon Henleyand Guardian correspondentsWed 21 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope’s far-right leaders have jumped on the violence that rocked numerous cities last weekend, framing it as the inevitable consequence of failed liberal governance and open-border policies and insisting only they can restore law and order.Months away from key elections in Spain,Franceand Italy, authoritarian nationalists are eager to weaponise the wave of street unrest, originating in peaceful protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services but hijacked by violent rioters.View image in fullscreenJordan Bardella, the president of the National Rally in France, said the government was ‘impotent’ in the face of widespread rioting and looting.Photograph: Nicolas Messyasz/Sipa/ShutterstockThose in opposition have not held back. In France, where cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon faced widespread rioting and looting, the far-rightNational Rally(RN) has denounced centrist incompetence and promised a crackdown.‘A powerful warning’: will Europe’s angry protests lead to real political change?Read moreThe party’s president, Jordan Bardella, said the government was “impotent”. The RN leader,Marine Le Pen, said on Wednesday the state was “collapsing” and had “lost control of everything” amid “migratory, budgetary and security chaos”.Ahead in presidential polls and seeking voters beyond her base, Le Pen has resisted explicitly racialising the unrest, but has framed it more broadly as a result of state and policy failures leading to “anarchic immigration” and “a total loss of authority”.In Germany – where there were no major protests – the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has stoked fears rioting could spill over the border. Its co-leader Alice Weidel said France’s “violent excesses” were a “warning for Germany”.View image in fullscreenThe AfD co-leader Alice Weidel linked the unrest to immigration.Photograph: Hesham Elsherif/Anadolu/Getty ImagesWeidel also linked the unrest to immigration, posting: “The dangerous mix of mass migration and leftwing extremism threatens to lead to civil war-like conditions here too … There will only be a turnaround on migration with the AfD!”In Portugal, populists have used peaceful protests to blame immigration for the country’s housing crisis, which André Ventura of the far-right Chega partysaid was chiefly a consequenceof an “uncontrolled influx of people from abroad”.In Spain, where the housing crisis has led tohuge protestsand a Madrid encampment, and prompted the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez,to call a snap electionnext month, the far-right Vox party has sought to demonise the protesters. “They’re not defending the right to housing, or asking for work, they’re serving Pedro Sánchez,” the party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said. “They’re Sánchez’s militias.”Vox has also attempted to link the housing issue to migration. In a message posted on social media last month, the party falsely suggested that the 87-year-old womanwhose evictionsparked the mammoth protestswould have had a homehad she been an immigrant from north Africa.InBelgium, where cost of living protests also escalated into street clashes in Brussels and Liège, the far-right Flemish nationalists of Vlaams Belang framed the rioting as a failure of integration and open borders, characterising it as “imported violence”.Italy’s prime minister,Giorgia Meloni, has adopted another strategy – as head of a far-right government she has headed for four years, she cannot simply blame failures of the state. Instead, she has expanded her law-and-order agenda, and framed rioters as extremists.“Demonstrating is a right, but setting our cities ablaze is not,” Meloni said after rioting in Milan and Bologna. “Hooligans have exploited the protests to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security, and hold entire cities hostage.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAs head of a far-right government she has headed for four years, Giorgia Meloni cannot simply blame failures of the state.Photograph: Pier Marco Tacca/Getty ImagesMeloni has previously enactedsweeping security measuresaimed at hindering public dissent, including jail terms for blocking roads, tough sentences for resisting police officers, and pre-detention for demonstrators thought likely to cause trouble.This weekshe passed emergency decreescreating an offence of violent participation in ⁠a demonstration, imposing tougher penalties on ⁠rioters and organisers of violent groups, and penalising parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.But she too has highlighted immigration as a factor, noting that “nearly half of those stopped or arrested” after the Milan riots were “of immigrant background, including individuals born abroad and second-generation children of immigrant families”.Beyond Europe’s orthodox far-right parties, anti-immigration polemicists have gone further, interpreting the violence not as state and policy failures but as evidence of a looming civilisational war fuelled by multiculturalism and non-EU immigration.Éric Zemmour, the founder of France’s Reconquête! (Reconquest) party, demanded an immigration halt and the deportation of “foreign delinquents”, declaring: “These are not riots, but the warning shots in an ethnic war. Either we establish absolute order or we yield.”The far-right narrative has been reinforced by similar comments from the US, where both the president and vice-president have sought to turn the unrest in France in particular into a cautionary tale for voters before midterm elections.Donald Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”, adding on social media that immigration “has shattered that once great country”.JD Vance echoed the same view, saying: “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion.” In doing so, they “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”, he said.Deborah Cole in Berlin, Angela Giuffrida in Rome and Sam Jones in Madrid contributed reportingThis article was amended on 21 October 2026. An earlier version incorrectly attributed a quote from Portuguese prime minister Luís Montenegro to opposition leader André Ventura. This quote has been removed.Explore more on these topicsThe far rightEuropeProtestNational RallyMarine Le PenAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)FrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: NSW passes ‘human compost’ laws with several MPs saying they will utilise practice after they die | New South Wales politics | The Guardian
description: Australia-first laws provide a third legal option other than burial and cremation for the treatment of bodies
Author: Nino Bucci
Headline: Australia-first laws provide a third legal option other than burial and cremation for the treatment of bodies
Content: Libertarian MP John Ruddick said he would likely choose terramation over burial or cremation when he dies.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLibertarian MP John Ruddick said he would likely choose terramation over burial or cremation when he dies.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianNew South Wales politicsNSW passes ‘human compost’ laws with several MPs saying they will utilise practice after they dieAustralia-first laws provide a third legal option other than burial and cremation for the treatment of bodiesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastNino BucciWed 21 Oct 2026 15.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeveralNew South WalesMPs say they want their own bodies turned into “human compost” after Australian-first laws were passed allowing the unusual practice.The laws, passed on Wednesday, provide a third legal option other than burial and cremation for the treatment of bodies.The private member’s bill was introduced by independent Sydney MP Alex Greenwich, who travelled to Germany and the US to research the practice, which is allowed in some parts of both countries.Breaking it down: how to limit the environmental impact of your body after deathRead moreThe practice, known as natural organic reduction, terramation or human composting, involves placing the body in a temperature-controlled vessel with organic matter such as alfalfa, straw or mulch.Once inside, the vessel is turned or rocked to circulate air. The introduced matter reacts with the air and feeds the body’s naturally occurring microbes to rapidly decompose the body.The process creates heat that, after about 30 days, transforms the body into soil. When rested for about 30 days more, the vessel contains about 110kg of “dry, rich soil that is fertile and free of pathogens”, Greenwich told the legislative assembly earlier this year.View image in fullscreenA display near a composting vessel at Recompose, a green funeral home specialising in human composting, in Seattle, Washington.Photograph: Mat Hayward/Getty Images for RecomposeIn the legislative council on Wednesday, John Ruddick, a Libertarian MP, said he backed what Greens MP Dr Amanda Cohn said in supporting the bill: he thought it was likely he would choose terramation over a burial plot or cremation.“Terramation will be voluntary. It is a choice. A lot of people may not choose it … I am pretty sure that I will put in my will that I wish to be terramated,” Ruddick said.“I like the idea of being buried somewhere and having a nice big gum tree grow there for 100 years.“The idea of being cremated or buried has always freaked me out. This is a much better option.”View image in fullscreenCameron Murphy says he looks forward to ‘being able to utilise this service in the long-distant future after it becomes law’.Photograph: Carly Earl/The GuardianThe Labor MP Cameron Murphy also said: “I look forward to being able to utilise this service in the long-distant future after it becomes law”.Liberal MP Susan Carter urged the government to consider when it implemented the bill how to ensure the dead were respected.“Terramation should not simply become a human compost bin,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Like all the many ways in which we approach death, it should help those who remain to mourn, and the respect shown to that person in life should continue into death.“It is important for that person, for their family, and for the whole way in which we go forward as a society.”Emma Hurst MP, the Animal Justice MP who introduced the bill into the legislative council, told parliament on Wednesday that terramation had significant environmental benefits.She said it could avoid the need for large burial plots and can be wholly carbon neutral, compared with cremation, which she said was energy intensive and released substantial greenhouse gas emissions.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Terramation provides possibilities to grow living things, like trees and plants, in honour of a life,” Hurst said.“Because terramation is a slow process, there are multiple opportunities for ceremonies, including for the laying of the body in the vessel and for opening the vessel after a body has been terramated.“Facilities overseas have allowed families to visit during the terramation process. It is a natural and gentle process that, for some, can help with grieving.”The bill passed on Wednesday gives the NSW government 18 months to create regulations to control the practice, which would be limited to specialised facilities.Explore more on these topicsNew South Wales politicsNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Giant tunnel proposed to tackle Windermere sewage discharges | Water | The Guardian
description: United Utilities, Environment Agency and local campaigners say 12-mile tunnel could take sewage away from England’s largest lake
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: United Utilities, Environment Agency and local campaigners say 12-mile tunnel could take sewage away from England’s largest lake
Content: A view of Lake Windermere and Waterhead Bay in Ambleside in the Lake District national park.Photograph: Ashley Cooper/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA view of Lake Windermere and Waterhead Bay in Ambleside in the Lake District national park.Photograph: Ashley Cooper/Getty ImagesWaterGiant tunnel proposed to tackle Windermere sewage dischargesUnited Utilities, Environment Agency and local campaigners say 12-mile tunnel could take sewage away from England’s largest lakePippa NeillEnvironment reporterWed 21 Oct 2026 06.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlans are under way for a new giant tunnel to transport sewage away from Windermere, England’s largest lake.Windermere, in the Lake District, has suffered from widespread raw sewage and bacterial pollution driven bydischarges from United Utilities. Campaigners say this pollution has caused more frequent toxic blue-green algal blooms, withthe public advisedto avoid swimming in the lake.Modelling indicates the climate crisis will exacerbate these challenges, with the catchment expected to experience more intense rainfall over the coming years, placing further pressure on the wastewater infrastructure.View image in fullscreenFish feed from sediment from a combined sewer overflow pipe as it discharges into the River Brathay, which feeds into Windermere.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesA new project, backed by United Utilities, theEnvironment Agencyand local campaigners, has set out a vision to end sewage discharges into the lake by building an 12-mile (19km) tunnel to transport sewage away from the lake.The water company said the use of tunnelling techniques would minimise the disruption to local communities.Windermere is at the heart of theLake DistrictUnesco world heritage site and has been the inspiration for poets, storytellers and lyricists for generations, with an estimated 17.7 million people visiting every year.The treated effluent would then be discharged into either the River Leven or the Irish Sea at Ulverston. It is estimated the project will cost £3.6bn, withUnited Utilitiesto seek permission from the government to raise customer bills to pay for it. It said the programme could add up to £3.17 a month to water bills in 2035.The project will now enter the detailed design phase during which specialised engineers will work out the technicalities of the build, which is expected to take two years.If granted permission to raise bills to pay for the project, United Utilities said the project could be complete within seven years and would provide a “one and done” solution with an immediate impact.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMatt Staniek has been calling for the end of sewage discharges into the lake for more than five years.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverMatt Staniek, a campaigner at Save Windermere, which is a partner on the project, said creating the feasibility report had involved weekly meetings over 15 months.Staniek, who has been calling for the end of sewage discharges into the lake for more than five years, said he was concerned at first about partnering with the company causing the pollution, but said they were the only people who could actually fix it. “This has demonstrated that it is possible not to dump sewage in Lake Windermere,” he said.In planning for the project, the team considered the transformation of Lake Annecy in France, which is widely recognised as one of thecleanest lakesin Europe. In the 1950s, Annecy faced similar pollution problems, butthe authorities investedin long-term infrastructural improvements to eliminate the sewage discharges.“This is up to the government now. The plan is there, it’s in place, we’re not going to stop until Andy Burnham is on the shores of Lake Windermere with a spade announcing that the construction has begun on this project,” Staniek said.Explore more on these topicsWaterLake DistrictUnited UtilitiesWater industryPollutionEnvironment AgencynewsShareReuse this content

title: Firefighters voice growing concerns over water supplies to tackle UK wildfires | Firefighters | The Guardian
description: During a summer fire that destroyed homes in Stourbridge, low pressure meant filling a water carrier took 40 minutes
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: During a summer fire that destroyed homes in Stourbridge, low pressure meant filling a water carrier took 40 minutes
Content: Firefighters douse the smouldering remains of a home near Stourbridge in August.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFirefighters douse the smouldering remains of a home near Stourbridge in August.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesFirefightersFirefighters voice growing concerns over water supplies to tackle UK wildfiresDuring a summer fire that destroyed homes in Stourbridge, low pressure meant filling a water carrier took 40 minutesPippa NeillEnvironment reporterWed 21 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConcerns have been raised about how drought affects the UK’s ability to cope with wildfires after MPs were told firefighters struggled for water supplies during this year’s record summer.The government has been urged to set out water companies’ statutory responsibilities during major fire incidents to improve the country’s preparedness for the years ahead.The UK experienced itshottest-ever summerthis year, with prolonged dry periods and extreme heat fuelling wildfires across the country.Figures releasedearlier this month showed a clear upward trend in the number of fires recorded each year.The chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFFC), Phil Garrigan, told MPs on the environment, food and rural affairs (EFRA) committee that fires developed more quickly because of limited water supplies. He said concerns about water availability had grown during his 37 years in the fire service.During a wildfire inStourbridgein the West Midlands that destroyed several homes, replenishing a water carrier took almost 40 minutes because of reduced water pressure.In tackling a separate wildfire in theNew Forestin August, the fire service said maintaining water supply had been a significant challenge.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSevere drought declared in six areas of England as reservoirs run lowRead moreFire services take water from mains and open sources such as lakes and rivers. With levels in the latter extremely low as result of the drought, the fire service’s access was restricted. It also faced pressure to limit its use of mains water to avoid shortages for paying customers.“In summers like this year, we would normally ask for more resources, but those resources aren’t always available and we’re having to wait longer for additional resources or we’re having to find other ways to deal with the fire,” said Dave Swallow, the NFCC’s deputy lead on wildfires.A survey of UK fire and rescue services in the summer found that 81% of respondents had changed their emergency response plans in areas where access to water was a concern.Could England and Wales ever run out of water?Read moreThe NFCC, which conducted the survey, said growing pressure from climate breakdown, population growth, housing development and emerging infrastructure such as datacentres, was increasing demand on an already stretched water network.“Firefighters cannot fight fires without water. That sounds obvious, yet our evidence shows four in five fire and rescue services have had to change response plans because of concerns about firefighting water supplies,” Garrigan said in the summer.As the climate crisis worsens and demand for water increases, the Environment Agencyestimatesthat England’s public water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055 without urgent action to future-proof resources.The EFRA committee has called for water for firefighting to be recognised as a critical public safety requirement. It said the government should establish a statutory framework and national protocol setting out water companies’ responsibilities during major fire incidents, including minimum expectations for water supply and pressure, communication and operational coordination with fire and rescue.The committee also said water companies should be required to assess, test and verify their ability to support firefighting operations.“Water companies must be relied upon for adequate supply,” the committee chair, Alistair Carmichael of the Scottish Liberal Democrats, said.A government spokesperson said: “Improving wildfire preparedness is a major government priority. That’s why this week we are holding a summit with government ministers, fire and rescue leaders, land managers and other partners to understand how we can strengthen the response to this increasing risk.”A government-fundedUK wildfire conferenceis scheduled to take place in Leeds on 10 and 11 November.Explore more on these topicsFirefightersDroughtClimate crisisExtreme weatherWaterWildfiresEmergency servicesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shark trapped for a month in South Korean canal is finally freed | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Bukang-i successfully guided out after month in which it drew 1.6m visitors and was watched over by YouTubers
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Bukang-i successfully guided out after month in which it drew 1.6m visitors and was watched over by YouTubers
Content: Shark in the canal during operation to guide it out in Busan, South Korea, on Wednesday.Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersView image in fullscreenShark in the canal during operation to guide it out in Busan, South Korea, on Wednesday.Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersSouth KoreaShark trapped for a month in South Korean canal is finally freedBukang-i successfully guided out after month in which it drew 1.6m visitors and was watched over by YouTubersRaphael Rashidin SeoulWed 21 Oct 2026 07.41 EDTFirst published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInSouth Korea, they call themjagyeongdan, a word whose meaning sits somewhere between vigilante group and neighbourhood watch. Each night they put on hi-vis vests, picked up their selfie sticks and gathered around the harbour in Busan to keep watch over an unlikely charge: astranded sharkaffectionately known as Bukang-i.On Wednesday, after more than a month in the canal and at the third attempt, the shark was successfully guided out, South Korea’s oceans ministry said. Officials expect her to move into open water in time.For the month that she was stranded, the group of self-appointed guardians took turns to protect her, patrolling the waterfront at night for visitors who might disturb the animal.Most are YouTubers who livestreamed the waterway, where the shark became a national celebrity. They stayedup through the night, calling out anyone shining torches or lasers into the water. Some of their videos have been watched hundreds of thousands of times.View image in fullscreen(Left to right) The YouTubers Kim Jong-hwan, Choi Won-jin and Na Tae-soo, who have been keeping watch over the trapped shark in BusanComposite: Supplied/ Yonhap News Agency“They bring fishing lamps, or the kind of lights people use at a campsite,” saidChoi Won-jin, one of the shark’s protectors. He would arriveas the lights went out along the canal and wait for the offenders Koreans online call “lantern villains”.The shark had been marooned in the canal since 18 September. Named after Bukhang, the Korean name for the city’s North Port, and about 3 metres long, the female dusky shark was one of a species classed as endangered worldwide. More than 1.6 million visitors came to see her, the city said, at a park that used to draw about 2,000 people on a busy Saturday.View image in fullscreenVisitors watching the shark trapped in a waterway in the south-eastern port city of Busan.Photograph: Jung Yeon-Je/AFP/Getty ImagesAuthorities had twice tried to guide her back out to sea and failed. Until she left, the shark remained in the canal, drawing crowds by day and leaving a handful of men to keep watch after dark. They patrolled the canal’s park to check everything was in order, ate snacks as the night wentby, and shared their grievances on air about the behaviour they witnessed.“We’re ordinary members of the public,” said Choi, who has had a YouTubechannel for 10 years and covers trending issues in South Korea.“So we have no choice but to put it nicely, and get them to understand as best we can.”“Don’t, please don’t switch the torch on,” said one of them, a YouTuber who lived nearby and went by the nameNa Tae-soo. Most people complied, he said. “The animal thrashes about at night because of the torches, and it’s dangerous.”View image in fullscreenCrowds flocked to the waterfront park in Busan to see the shark.Photograph: Yonhap/EPAHis footagecaptured the shark twisting sharply away from a beam of light at 2am and striking the side of the canal. The national institute of fisheries science later confirmed an abrasion on her snout and said a visitor’s torch was likely to have startled the shark into injury.Korean media reported that 105 officials from seven agencies watched over her, with a team on standby to reach the water within three minutes. Choi disputed this, saying that after dark it wasalmost up to him and the others.The waterfront was closed to the public from midnight until 5am, a restriction the YouTubers said was impossible to enforce across a park that size. One night, livestreaming from the walkway, Choi filmed a man tipping food waste into the water.Nobody saw the shark feed, though experts said feeding could happen in an instant and sharks her size did not need to eat often.Further attempts to free the shark had been paused on the grounds that more force would distress her.Cooler water had been expected to prompt her to move on. Dusky sharks prefer water between 18C and 26C, the fisheries institute said. Experts put 15C as the point below which her physiological functions would start to decline, and about 11C as the point at which survival would become precarious. Busan city officials had expected the canal to reach that temperature after the middle of November.View image in fullscreenThis aerial photo taken on 29 September shows South Korean coastguard boats spraying water in an attempt to guide the shark back to the sea.Photograph: Yonhap/AFP/Getty ImagesThe fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributed to warmer seas and more of the fish that sharks feed on.The affection for Bukang-i has meanwhile become an industry, with a commemorativesoju, a baseball mascot in a shark cape and an honorary city ambassadorship, and nearby shops reporting a surge in sales. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, visited the canal in mid-October.None of the shark’s guardians thoughtshe should be forced out. Choi said the city should protect her where she wasuntil she left of her own accord.Kim Jong-hwan, who runs a small business, keptwatch by day as well and livestreamed her almost every day. “I went to pass on information [to my followers], and after that I started observing her”, he said. “Watching her over time, with the water pumps being fired and then the nets, I came to find those things being done to her objectionable. So we ended up cheering her on.”“She’s just an animal, and she came in by her own choice,” Kim said. “If it gets cold, if there’s no food, if the water doesn’t suit her, she’ll leave by herself. I’d like her to just be left alone, to rest there comfortably until then, and go.”Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaSharksMarine lifeWildlifeAnimalsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shabana Mahmood urged to ‘read the room’ on Labour opposition to immigration policy | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: No 10 declines to rule out watering down plans to extend waiting period for indefinite leave to remain as cabinet split widens
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: No 10 declines to rule out watering down plans to extend waiting period for indefinite leave to remain as cabinet split widens
Content: Labour Party Conference 2026 in Liverpool - Day TwoSecretary of State for the Home Department Shabana Mahmood gives a speech on the second day of the Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, United Kingdom on September 28, 2026.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLabour Party Conference 2026 in Liverpool - Day TwoSecretary of State for the Home Department Shabana Mahmood gives a speech on the second day of the Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, United Kingdom on September 28, 2026.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumShabana Mahmood urged to ‘read the room’ on Labour opposition to immigration policyNo 10 declines to rule out watering down plans to extend waiting period for indefinite leave to remain as cabinet split widensRowena MasonandMatthew WeaverWed 21 Oct 2026 13.33 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood has been urged to “read the room” on Labour opposition to her immigration policy, as No 10 declined to rule out watering down her plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residencecould be watered downby exempting care workers from the new rule.However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”View image in fullscreenMiatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, on Wednesday repeatedly refused to back the plan to make foreign workers wait 15 years to claim permanent residency.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesThere is already a cabinet split over the policy, which deepened on Wednesday whenMiatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, repeatedly refused to back the specific plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to claim permanent residency in the UK.This week it was reported thatFahnbulleh appeared to criticise the planson her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”This year the housing secretary, Angela Rayner,publicly criticised the plans, and dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.View image in fullscreenMPs believe they have a chance of convincing Burnham to exempt care workers from Mahmood’s proposals.Photograph: 10’000 Hours/Getty ImagesMPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, theHome Officehas said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the reforms.Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn her interview with Sky News on Wednesday, Fahbulleh repeatedly avoided the question on whether she would back an increase in the waiting period for permanent residency to 15 years. She said: “We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution. And so there is a package of reforms. The home secretary has been consulting on this. She’s looking at the range of responses, and she will come out with the measures that we take forward.“No one can look at our immigration system – and I say this as someone that came to this country as a refugee – and not believe that it’s broken and not believe that we need to fundamentally reform it.“But our principles has to be a system where we’ve got control, but ultimately a system that when people do come to this country, they are able to integrate, they are able to contribute, and that we both respect but also value that contribution.”She said she supported “reforms that say that people have to contribute and make a contribution to this country in order to get citizenship”, adding: “I 100% back Shabana Mahmood and everything she is trying to do.”But she avoided multiple questions on the prospect of a 15-year wait. When it was put to her that she did not back that specific proposal, Fahnbulleh said: “Don’t … put words in my mouth.”A government source said that “the minister clearly supported the policy and process” in her interviews, “but while subject to review of the consultation, the final policy is not set – so ministers cannot offer opinions on specific parts of it”.A Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumMiatta FahnbullehShabana MahmoodHome OfficeLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Tory election candidate suspended over contract killing claims | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Jack Ross was filmed allegedly discussing with an undercover reporter violent options to deal with enemies
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Jack Ross was filmed allegedly discussing with an undercover reporter violent options to deal with enemies
Content: Jack Ross at a London vigil after the murder of Charlie Kirk. He told Al Jazeera that his comments to its undercover reporter were not serious.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyView image in fullscreenJack Ross at a London vigil after the murder of Charlie Kirk. He told Al Jazeera that his comments to its undercover reporter were not serious.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyConservativesFormer Tory election candidate suspended over contract killing claimsJack Ross was filmed allegedly discussing with an undercover reporter violent options to deal with enemiesBen QuinnandHenry DyerWed 21 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 15.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former Conservative election candidate has been suspended from the party after he was seemingly filmed discussing the cost of hiring contract killers and offering to “broker” the services of a far-right activist with alleged paramilitary links.Jack Ross was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter “What do you want done?” before listing the type of violent options that could be bought.Ross appeared to tell the Al Jazeera journalist: “They can just kick the fuck out of someone. That’s a certain amount. They can start cutting people’s faces up, that’s another amount. And they can stab someone. They can shoot someone. They can kill someone.”Police inScotlandsay they will be reviewing and assessing the Al Jazeera documentary – Contract Killers and the Far Right – for any criminality.Ross is the chief executive of Turning Point UK, a spin-off from the campaign group founded by the murdered US Republican commentator Charlie Kirk.Footage released by TPUK last year showed Ross and others from the group meeting Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, after Kirk’s death.A profile page for Ross on the website of the Bow Group, a Conservative thinktank that lists him as a research fellow, states he has advised MPs and candidates on political and digital strategy. He has been pictured alongside Boris Johnson and other high-profile figures including James Cleverly, Jacob Rees-Mogg and Liam Fox.Ross wasreported by Al Jazeerato have introduced an undercover reporter to a violent criminal from Glasgow with links to the paramilitary Ulster Volunteer Force, who offers to have people killed for money.Al Jazeera approached Ross with a fictitious family problem where a deceased uncle’s business was at risk of being taken over by a gang, whose members were supposedly warned they would “get fucked” if anything happened.Ross replied to this: “Yeah, you have to deliver on that as well. You’ve got to explain to me what’s needed … I can then go and broker from there. But I’ve got to say, even to myself … if there’s lashback I’ve got to keep my name out of it.”The Scottish paramilitary contact was then filmed at a London hotel offering to arrange different types of killings, ranging from a hit-and-run that could be made to look like drink-driving to a stabbing.The meeting took place after Ross, apparently acting on behalf of the Zimbabwean government, had reportedly paid thousands of pounds to the Glasgow activist to organise a fake political rally in support of lifting UK sanctions imposed on the African country.Ross said: “I have had a few things and some of the Zims [Zimbabweans] have said to me they want stuff done. They wanted a fucking shooter.”He said he had asked them to talk to the paramilitary, adding: “I said I was not putting fucking prints on anything.”While TPUK was launched as a student movement, it has become increasingly involved in anti-migrant street protests. Its chief operating officer is Nick Tenconi, the leader of the far-right UK Independence party, who visited the Conservative conference in 2022 with Ross.Ross was filmed in 2022 telling an undercover reporter they should chat to him about what they wanted, adding “keep it simple” and then listing the various violent options that could be bought for cash, including murder.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Conservative party spokesperson said: “Mr Ross’s membership of the Conservative party has been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation. We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing.”At another point, Ross expressed concerns that journalists could be recording the sort of things he was saying and could pass them to police.“The journalist will put it out there and then the police will pick it up and fuck you,” he said. “You’ve got to think that what we were talking about and had someone film it we’d be fucking done for conspiracy.”Tenconi was filmed alongside Ross as they outlined a plan to use football hooligans to stir up trouble.Tenconi said: “So let Labour get in. So we build the new right and we have these armies … so, three-pronged. We keep winning MPs over. Then we build the second prong, we build an army, and that’s street demos, protest, just fuck things up, basically.”A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the documentary. It will be reviewed and assessed for any criminality.”Al Jazeera reported that Ross had “completely” denied its investigation’s findings, claiming that everything he said to the undercover reporter was not meant seriously.Ross, who was a local elections candidate for theConservatives, was approached by the Guardian for comment through TPUK. Tenconi was also approached for comment via his party.Explore more on these topicsConservativesUK Independence party (Ukip)ScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform UK fined for failing to declare it was publisher of campaigns material | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Party given additional penalty by Electoral Commission for not paying original fine on time
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Party given additional penalty by Electoral Commission for not paying original fine on time
Content: Reform UK was fined after four items of elections material were missing an ‘imprint’ – a declaration of the publisher so voters know who paid for the promotional message.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenReform UK was fined after four items of elections material were missing an ‘imprint’ – a declaration of the publisher so voters know who paid for the promotional message.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAReform UKReform UK fined for failing to declare it was publisher of campaigns materialParty given additional penalty by Electoral Commission for not paying original fine on timeRowena MasonWhitehall editorWed 21 Oct 2026 12.31 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK has been fined more than £2,000 for failing to declare it was the publisher of campaign material seen by voters – including an additional penalty for failing to pay on time.Nigel Farage’s party was sanctioned by theElectoral Commissionafter four items of election material were missing an “imprint” – a declaration of the publisher so voters know who has paid for the promotional message.It was due to pay £1,750 on 23 September, but the fine was increased by a quarter to £2,187 because Reform missed the payment deadline. The penalty was eventually paid on Tuesday.Jackie Killeen, the commission’s director of electoral administration and regulation, said: “The UK’s political finance and imprints laws are there to ensure transparency in both the finances of political parties and the materials produced to influence voters.“As a regulator, we take proportionate action based on the facts and circumstances of each case, as set out in our enforcement policy. We seek to support compliance and deliver transparency, and we will take enforcement action where necessary.”The fine related to three social media accounts run by Reform, on X, Instagram and LinkedIn, that did not have digital imprints between at least November 2025 and January 2026.The party also published an advertisement in the Telegraph in February 2026 without an imprint, promoting its shadow chancellor, Robert Jenrick. The watchdog’s investigation found that the purpose of the advertisement was to promote Reform and its electoral success in the May 2026 elections, so the ad required an imprint.There has also been a separate complaint about the Reform candidate’s election material in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February this year.On that occasion, the party sent out a letter designed to look as if it had been handwritten by the local resident Patricia Clegg, who said she no longer wanted to vote Labour, but who was in fact working for Reform – without including an imprint.The party said it was caused by a printing error, and that the company had accidentally left the imprint off the material.Reform’s censure from the Electoral Commission came as the party said it had reported ITV to the police after the broadcaster’s exposéwhich revealed racist remarksby members of the party.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReform candidate filmed saying asylum seekers should be put in ‘concentration camps’Read moreZia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, announced it would also launch a legal challenge against the ITV journalists involved and the broadcaster’s board of directors.The channel’s undercover investigation included footage of Reform councillors and candidates using racist language.In one excerpt, black children were referred to as animals, while in another a Reform member said his area had become infested with Asian families.In a social media video, Yusuf said: “We have reported multiple ITV journalists and their board of directors to the police, and will be taking legal action against all of them. Journalists are supposed to report the news. These ones set out to create it.”He claimed that the undercover ITV reporter who became employed as a Reform press officer had “doctored” her passport to gain the job.He also said two undercover reporters who joined Reform members campaigning in Portsmouth had been reported to the police, as it is illegal to pay someone to canvass for a candidate.An ITV spokesperson said: “ITV stands by its journalism. The programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom broadcasting code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest.“All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme’s producers. Should the police get in touch, we would fully cooperate.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKElectoral CommissionParty fundingPress regulationNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It feels quite frightening’: readers rush to snap up Sally Rooney books as stocks dwindle amid Palestine Action ban | Books | The Guardian
description: Booksellers have reported selling out of the Irish novelist’s works after it was announced that her books would be withdrawn from sale in the UK
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Booksellers have reported selling out of the Irish novelist’s works after it was announced that her books would be withdrawn from sale in the UK
Content: Sales of Sally Rooney’s books have been halted in the UK over her support for Palestine Action.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSales of Sally Rooney’s books have been halted in the UK over her support for Palestine Action.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesBooks‘It feels quite frightening’: readers rush to snap up Sally Rooney books as stocks dwindle amid Palestine Action banBooksellers have reported selling out of the Irish novelist’s works after it was announced that her books would be withdrawn from sale in the UKEmma LoffhagenWed 21 Oct 2026 14.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBooksellers have reported selling out of copies of Sally Rooney’s novels, following the news that her books would bewithdrawn from salein the UK, given her support for the banned group Palestine Action. Sales shot up nearly 300% in a week, asa host of high profile writerssigned letters in support of the Irish author, including Zadie Smith, Annie Ernaux, Arundhati Roy, Ali Smith and Kamila Shamsie.Bookmarked, an independent bookshop in Bristol, had three Sally Rooney novels in stock whenFaber announced last weekthat it would stop supplying the author’s books. Within hours, customers had bought all of them. Now the shop has none, and it cannot get any more. “In retrospect, I feel like we should have put them behind a glass casing, forever on display until the law is overturned,” says the shop’s general manager Evelyn.Faber’s books “have just been immediately taken down from the suppliers’ website, which feels really eerie”, she adds. “What worries me most is the precedent that it sets … We’re becoming increasingly used to seeing this type of stuff happen in other countries, but this is happening on our doorstep.”Rooney is arguably the best-known literary novelist of her generation. Normal People alone has sold more than a million copies in the UK, and each new book is treated as a publishing event, with launch-day queues and early openings. Now, her work is disappearing from British shelves.Last year,Rooney said that she would use proceedsfrom her books and their BBC adaptations to support Palestine Action. The direct action groupwas proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025, and supporting it is now a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison (the high court ruled the proscription unlawfulin February,but thecourt of appeal overturned that decisionin June and the ban remains in force). Last week, Faber said UK legislation meant it could not pass on UK earnings to Rooney, and that it had decided, with her full agreement, to stop supplying her work. Copies already in shops can still be sold, they just cannot be replenished.View image in fullscreenSally Rooney in 2020.Photograph: Erik Voake/Getty Images for HuluReaders have rushed to buy what was left. Nielsen BookScan told the Guardian that Rooney sold 4,531 copies last week, up 291% from the week before the announcement.Restocking is now the problem. When a customer came into The Best of Times, a new bookshop and cafe in Kent, asking for Rooney, owner Gavin Boyter went to re-order. On the website of Gardners, the UK’s main book wholesaler, every one of her titles was marked as unavailable to order.“Farcically, I can order Bucknell University Press’s Sally Rooney: Perspectives and Approaches for a mere £96,” he said. “I guess we’ll be out of stock for the foreseeable future, which is a great shame.”“I can still order four different versions of Mein Kampf, though,” he added, which illustrates the “absurdity” of the situation.In August 2025, weeks after Palestine Action was banned, Rooney wrote in the Irish Timesthat if supporting the group made her “a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it”. She has sincesaid she could no longer safely travel to the UKwithout facing arrest, sending her editor to collect an award in London on her behalf.At Juno Books in Sheffield, Alim Kheraj said the situation felt unprecedented. “We’ve had people coming in asking if they can buy the books specifically to support Rooney,” he said. “But we’re completely sold out. I can’t think of another time where a publisher has had to pull a book because of comments [an author has] made about a specific organisation,” he added. “It feels quite frightening.”Across the Irish Sea, a kind of book smuggling – entirely above board, as far as the booksellers involved understand it – has sprung up almost overnight.Kennys Bookshop in Galway, which ships worldwide, says its Rooney sales have risen tenfold since the announcement. Almost none of the new buyers are Irish: 95% of the increase, owner Tómas Kenny said, has come from Britain. “It’s almost exclusively the UK”.British booksellers are also trying to get stock in by the back door. Kenny, who works closely with UK shops through theBooksellersAssociation, said he had been contacted by “lots of people” looking to get hold of books.For him, the reversal is striking. He grew up in an Ireland where books were banned for blasphemy. “Britain was where people escaped to, to read and watch what they wanted,” he said. “We’re in a scenario where it’s the opposite”.Northern Ireland, which has access to both the UK and Irish markets after Brexit, has become a conduit. Some booksellers there are openly continuing to stock Rooney by sourcing her books from the Republic, and then posting them across the water. Lesley Price, who runs Bridge Books in Co Down, says she has been “inundated” with website orders, most of them heading to Britain, and that sales were up “tenfold, if not more”.“I don’t believe in book banning,” she said. “I know it’s not a ban, but I guess it is a censorship of sorts, and that does not sit well with me.” When she posted online that Bridge Books would continue to stock Rooney’s books, she says the response has mostly been positive, with some exceptions. “There have also been quite a lot of people calling me a terrorist sympathiser and wishing harm on my business.”Writers have also rallied behind Rooney. An open lettersigned by hundredsincluding Patrick Ness, Damian Barr and Juno Dawson called on the government to act. A second letter,published by the New Statesmanand signed by writers including Zadie Smith, Annie Ernaux, Naomi Klein and new Nobel literature laureate Anne Carson, declared: “Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist.”Normal People stars Daisy Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal are also signatories, along with Gary Lineker.“I am troubled at this Orwellian suppression of ideas, all writers should be,” says Dawson. “Both throughout history and today, clampdowns on artistic freedom are a hallmark of rising fascism.” Nikesh Shukla said he signed to draw attention to what he sees as the wrongness of the ban on Palestine Actionitself, which he said was “now damaging the arts sector, literature and freedom of speech”.Proscribing Palestine Action “highlighted that the Terrorism Act is too broad in structure and application,” says Jemimah Steinfeld, chief executive of Index on Censorship. “The arrests of thousands of peaceful protesters that followed made this point even stronger.”“This is really a test case,” she continued, adding that Faber’s caution was “fully understandable” because “we’re on new ground”. Ireland’s foreign affairs minister, Helen McEntee, has said she will raise the matter directly with the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband.The real test will come with her next release. Rooney’s latest novel, Intermezzo, was published two years ago. “What happens when she has a new book coming out, which I would say is not that far away?” Kenny said. “Will it be available in the UK? That, to me, will be a far bigger story.”For independent shops, the stakes are high. “It’s really some titles, like Sally Rooney, that will make or break your year.”Explore more on these topicsBooksSally RooneyPalestine ActionBooksellersPublishingFictionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nancy Pelosi’s office latest recipient of letter containing white powder | Nancy Pelosi | The Guardian
description: Former speaker is latest target of mailings sent to various Congress members in the lead-up to the midterm elections
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Former speaker is latest target of mailings sent to various Congress members in the lead-up to the midterm elections
Content: Nancy Pelosi at the US Capitol on 20 November 2025.Photograph: Tasos Katopodis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNancy Pelosi at the US Capitol on 20 November 2025.Photograph: Tasos Katopodis/Getty ImagesNancy PelosiNancy Pelosi’s office latest recipient of letter containing white powderFormer speaker is latest target of mailings sent to various Congress members in the lead-up to the midterm electionsDani AnguianoWed 21 Oct 2026 18.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCalifornia representative Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious letter” on Wednesday in what appears to be the latest incident of ill-intentioned mailings targeted at US Congress members before the midterm elections.The offices of more than three dozen members of Congress across the political spectrum havereceived envelopescontaining white powder in recent days. One lawmaker’s office said preliminary tests indicated the powder was not hazardous.More than three dozen Congress members’ offices sent envelopes containing white powderRead moreA spokesperson for Pelosi said the letter was “consistent with mailings reported by other congressional offices” and that everyone in the office was safe.“Speaker Pelosi remains focused on serving the people of San Francisco and is concerned for the members and staff whose offices have experienced similar incidents,” Nicholas Martin, a spokesperson for the speaker emerita, said in a statement.“She is grateful for the efforts of the US Capitol police, the San Francisco police department and other law enforcement agencies to thoroughly investigate this series of intimidation across America.”More than 100 letters thought to contain white powder were reportedly thought to be circulating in the US mail system. Election offices across the US have also reported receiving suspicious mail.The mailings are under investigation by the FBI, the Capitol police and the US Postal Inspection Service. The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement earlier this week: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.”Explore more on these topicsNancy PelosiHouse of RepresentativesUS CongressUS crimeUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Epstein’s attorney and accountant accused of ‘facilitating and concealing’ his crimes in lawsuit | Jeffrey Epstein | The Guardian
description: New Mexico lawsuit claims ‘in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project, his associates received generous salaries’
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: New Mexico lawsuit claims ‘in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project, his associates received generous salaries’
Content: Raúl Torrez, New Mexico’s attorney general, at a news conference on Capitol Hill in Washington DC on 14 April.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreenRaúl Torrez, New Mexico’s attorney general, at a news conference on Capitol Hill in Washington DC on 14 April.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APJeffrey EpsteinEpstein’s attorney and accountant accused of ‘facilitating and concealing’ his crimes in lawsuitNew Mexico lawsuit claims ‘in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project, his associates received generous salaries’Anna BettsWed 21 Oct 2026 14.40 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe attorney general of New Mexico on Wednesday filed a civil lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s longtime attorney, Darren Indyke, and Epstein’s longtime accountant, Richard Kahn, accusing them of having “facilitated and concealed” Epstein’s crimes, and is seeking to stop them from being paid by Epstein’s estate while the litigation plays out.Thelawsuit, filed in the US district court for the district of New Mexico, names Kahn and Indyke as defendants both in their individual capacity, and in their capacity as co-executors of Epstein’s estate. The complaint also names Epstein’s estate, and the 1953 Trust, which holds the estate’s assets.“Epstein, with the help of his associates, trafficked, isolated, and abused survivors at alluring locations” including at Epstein’s ranch in Stanley,New Mexico, known as Zorro Ranch, the complaint claims. It goes on to allege that “in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project and remaining silent about it, his associates received generous salaries, access to elite social circles, and lavish gifts, including being named beneficiaries of his multimillion-dollar estate”.In a statement on Wednesday, an attorney for Indyke shared a statement on behalf of both Indyke and Kahn saying that they “emphatically reject the New Mexico Attorney General’s allegations that they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr Indyke nor Mr Kahn was present.“Not a single woman has ever accused Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse, nor claimed at any time that she or anyone else reported to them any allegation of Mr Epstein’s abuse,” the statement added. “The New Mexico Attorney General’s complaint does not allege anything to the contrary.”The statement goes on to say that “neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General’s investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit”.Earlier this year, Kahn and Indyke told the US House committee investigating Epstein that they hadno knowledgeof Epstein’s crimes during their employment.Among the demands the lawsuit seeks is a court order preventing Indyke and Kahn from receiving estate payments while the case proceeds.The complaint alleges that both men profited personally from their relationships with Epstein. It alleges that from 2011 to 2019, Indyke received more than $16m from Epstein and related entities and that Kahn received more than $10m.In a statement on Wednesday, Raúl Torrez, New Mexico’s attorney general, said that Epstein “did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible”.“The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico,” he said. “Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences.”In the complaint, Torrez wrote that “through this action, the State seeks to hold these individuals accountable to the fullest extent possible and to ensure that Epstein’s assets are distributed to the survivors of his horrific crimes”.Several survivors of Epstein’s abuse signed a letter on Wednesday in support of Torrez’s lawsuit “because it can expose what roles Indyke and Kahn played in Epstein’s operation, examine how they handled survivors’ claims, and prevent Epstein’s trusted loyalists from being rewarded for their roles in Epstein’s organization”.“Survivors deserve accountability and answers under oath. Epstein’s chosen confidants should not get the last word – or the money,” they added.At a news conference on Wednesday about the new filing, Epstein survivor Anouska De Georgiou thanked Torrez for “standing with survivors”.“We have carried this burden for long enough,” she said. “It is time for those responsible to answer for their part in it.”The announcement on Wednesday comes amid a separate ongoing dispute between New Mexico officials and the Department of Justice over files Torrez is seeking as part of the state’s investigation intoEpstein’s possible crimes in the state, including at his ranch outside Santa Fe, where multiple survivors have said they were abused.Torrezsued the Department of Justicein August, accusing the department and Todd Blanche, the attorney general, of “stonewalling” the state’sinvestigation, which was reopened in February. Torrez asked the court for access to unredacted Epstein-related files held by the justice department, and said in its filing his prosecutors had requested access to the records but had “faced sustained resistance” from the department.The case is ongoing and the justice department recently filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that “decisions about law-enforcement information sharing are committed to the agency’s discretion” and that turning over unredacted files would violate victims’ privacy.Epstein’s Zorro Ranch cameunder renewedscrutiny after the justice department’s release of roughly 3m files related to Epstein late last year and early this year. TheGuardian reported in early Februarythat the newly disclosed Epstein files contained thousands of references to Zorro Ranch, and numerous photos of men and young girls at the property, and that several survivors of Epstein’s abuse had also previously given testimony about abuse they say they were subjected to there.TheGuardian investigationalso revealed that, unlike Epstein’s other properties in Palm Beach, in New York and on his private Caribbean island, federal authorities had apparently never searched the New Mexico ranch.Epstein, whodiedin a Manhattan jail in 2019 while awaiting trial onfederal sex-trafficking charges, bought the property in New Mexico 1993. It was later sold by his estate in 2023.In late February, Torrez announced thatNew Mexico would reopen its investigationinto Epstein’s activities at the ranch, after the state’s initial investigation was put on hold in 2019 at the request of federal prosecutors in New York, who were pursuing the investigation into Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation that led to his arrest. In March, New Mexico authoritieslaunched a searchof the ranch.Torrez has said that he wants to establish what took place at Zorro Ranch. New Mexico lawmakers also established a “truth commission” to examine activities at the ranch.Explore more on these topicsJeffrey EpsteinNew MexicoSex traffickingUS justice systemRape and sexual assaultUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted | Guinea-Bissau | The Guardian
description: Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’
Author: Melody Schreiber
Headline: Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’
Content: A woman stands in a shared room at a residential care facility for pregnant mothers in Gabu, Guinea Bissau, on 22 May 2012.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APView image in fullscreenA woman stands in a shared room at a residential care facility for pregnant mothers in Gabu, Guinea Bissau, on 22 May 2012.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APGuinea-BissauControversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns haltedHepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’Melody SchreiberWed 21 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher,wroteon LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previouslydeniedthat the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when theysearchedthe offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.It was vital to supportGuinea-Bissauin rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.View image in fullscreenThe Minister of health, Quinhin Nantote, at the presidential palace in Guinea-Bissau on 29 November 2025.Photograph: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP/Getty ImagesSuch a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the WorldHealthOrganization (WHO).“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who hasco-publishedresearchraising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”Explore more on these topicsGuinea-BissauAfricaHepatitis BVaccines and immunisationHealthChildren's healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Indian court orders release of two leaders of Cockroach movement | India | The Guardian
description: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdown
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdown
Content: Saurav Das (centre) and Ashutosh Ranka (right) leave a police station after seeking approval for a protest earlier this month.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSaurav Das (centre) and Ashutosh Ranka (right) leave a police station after seeking approval for a protest earlier this month.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesIndiaIndian court orders release of two leaders of Cockroach movementSaurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdownHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiWed 21 Oct 2026 11.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka,had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jailafter being arrested by Delhi police last week.On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison.
