They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, which led to the barricading of central Delhi andthousands of young peoplebeing detained.11:32India’s Cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown - The LatestDas and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the rulingNarendra Modigovernment, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streetsRead moreThe CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have beencalling for the resignationof the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced theresignation of Modi’s education ministerafter sustained demonstrations.Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was alsodetained on Fridayafter he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaProtestNarendra ModiSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Tesla beats earnings projections after Musk floats SpaceX merger plan | Tesla | The Guardian
description: Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but he declined to elaborate
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but he declined to elaborate
Content: A Tesla dealership in Santa Clarita, California. Wall Street has projected Tesla to report $27.9bn in revenues.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Tesla dealership in Santa Clarita, California. Wall Street has projected Tesla to report $27.9bn in revenues.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesTeslaTesla beats earnings projections after Musk floats SpaceX merger planMusk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but he declined to elaborateDara KerrWed 21 Oct 2026 19.03 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInvestors were paying close attention to Tesla’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executiveElon Muskfloated the idea of merging the car company with his rocket and AI company, SpaceX. But they didn’t glean further information after the company announced there would be no questions on the matter.“With regard to a potential merger withSpaceX, I think I said everything that should be said yesterday,” Musk, the CEO of both companies, said on Tesla’s earnings call. He repeated a phrase he said on Tuesday: “I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.”On acall with SpaceX investorson Tuesday, Musk said it would be a “good idea” to combine the two companies and that “there’s a lot of merit” that would come with it.Musk said on Tuesday that the board of directors for both of his businesses had put together special committees to explore the potential merger, but had not yet reached an agreement on the terms of the transaction. The move would require the approval of 50% of allTeslashareholders.Tesla and SpaceX explore merger as Elon Musk gives backingRead moreOn Wednesday, Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings, with a reported revenue of $28.05bn and $0.48 on earnings per share. That beat Wall Street’s projections of $27.9bn in revenue, with $0.43 on earnings per share. Still, the company came in at aslightly lower revenue than last quarter, which was $28.23bn. And its automotive revenue dropped 3% from the year prior.“We maintained strong momentum on many projects spanning Super Intelligence (SI), robotics and renewable energy that will be critical to building a future of Amazing Abundance,” the company wrote in itsreport.Despite the stronger-than-anticipated quarter, Tesla has experienced a rough year with falling stock and increased competition from cheaper Chinese automakers. The company’s share price has fallen by more than 11% this year, although it appears to have rebounded some since last week with the news of the possible SpaceX merger.Last week, Muskunveiled the company’s electric sports car, the Roadster 2, which he said uses technology from SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”. At a demonstration at a SpaceX facility in Texas, a remote-controlled version of the car drove up a steeply curved ramp and then used jet-like thrusters to flip over, hover and land. The vehicle is priced at upwards of $200,000.“Flying cars are real … It can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics,” Musk said at the event, adding: “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions.”During Tesla’s earnings call on Wednesday, he added that the event was “the coolest demo of any product ever”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTesla’s vehicle sales are not as crucial to its market performance as they once were, as the company has pivoted towards robotics, autonomous driving and AI. Tesla’s Optimus robot has faced production hurdles, however; and its driverless taxi service, Robotaxi, has hit road blocks in scaling its fleet and expanding to new cities.“Tesla’s leaders continue to make big claims about autonomous mobility and physical AI. The company has achieved remarkable things but continues to miss some of its leaders’ bolder bets,” said Paul Miller, a principal analyst for market research firm Forrester. “Tesla robotaxis are undeniably carrying passengers, but not yet at anywhere near the levels the company promised.”Musk has long declared the Robotaxi will have near-infinite demand and that “probably half the population of the US” would be using the autonomous ride-hailing service by the end of 2025. Similarly, the CEO has forecast the manufacture of as many as 1m Optimus robots each year. As Miller pointed out with Musk’s promises, he has failed to reach those lofty targets and rollout has been slow.Musk once again touted the robots on Wednesday, saying: “I remain convinced that Optimus will be the biggest product on earth and humanoid robots in general will be the biggest product on earth.” He added that no other company compares to Tesla in developing humanoid robots – this is despite Chinese competitorsmaking vast stridesin the technology.Explore more on these topicsTeslaQuarterly resultsElon MuskSpaceXnewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta ordered to pay $25bn to New Mexico in Cambridge Analytica data-privacy case | Meta | The Guardian
description: Jury had found Meta misled consumers after Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign obtained user data without consent
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jury had found Meta misled consumers after Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign obtained user data without consent
Content: Meta’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, speaks at the Meta Connect conference in Menlo Park, California, on 17 September 2025.Photograph: Benjamin Legendre/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMeta’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, speaks at the Meta Connect conference in Menlo Park, California, on 17 September 2025.Photograph: Benjamin Legendre/AFP/Getty ImagesMetaMeta ordered to pay $25bn to New Mexico in Cambridge Analytica data-privacy caseJury had found Meta misled consumers after Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign obtained user data without consentGuardian staff and agencyWed 21 Oct 2026 19.33 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA judge inNew MexicoorderedMeta Platformsto pay $25bn on ⁠Wednesday after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved inDonald Trump’s2016 presidential campaignobtained data from millions of Facebook users ⁠without their consent.“Facebook’s wrongdoing – ⁠over the course of ​years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219bn was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25bn.A spokesperson forMetadid not immediately respond to a request for comment.Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensifies days before Brazil presidential runoffRead moreSettlements over the social networks’ safety are growing so large that Meta is reporting significant drags on its business. In its quarterly earnings report, issued the same afternoon as the announcement of the judge’s order, the company said its net income came in significantly below Wall Street analysts’ expectations because of a $9.9bn settlement payment in the US. In August, the social media giant agreed to pay $17bn to settle a nationwide lawsuit by dozens of state attorneys general, who alleged it intentionally designed addictive products that harmed children. Despite the hefty payments, Meta still reported a 26% increase in quarterly revenue up to $64.6bn.New Mexico’s attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations thatCambridge Analytica, ⁠a British political consulting firm, had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.The state accused Meta ​of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had ‌access to their data, how the ‌company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform, and other internal policies. The company knew that third parties had broad access to ‌users’ personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company’s bottom line, the state said.Meta has faced a wave of lawsuits over the course of the year related to user safety, with the culmination of several cases beingreferred to as a big tobacco momentfor social media. The company will report its third-quarter earnings on Wednesday.Jurors on 25 September found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43m violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement.State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 per ‌violation, and directs that all of the money go to New Mexico’s school system, New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, told reporters after the verdict. At a hearing on 1 October, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had ​asked Mathew to award the state between $35bn and $40bn, saying that would be supported by the US constitution’s protections on due process and the jury’s verdict.“This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price,” McGinn said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45bn, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the ⁠state. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove ​that any consumer had actually been misled, the ​company said in court filings.The ​verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the ​state of New Mexico against ‌Meta Platforms.In the first trial, ​which ended in March, a ​Santa Fe jury found Meta misled users about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay $375m in civil penalties.After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay $567m into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico.Explore more on these topicsMetaUS elections 2016Donald TrumpFacebookCambridge AnalyticaPrivacySocial networkingnewsShareReuse this content

title: French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets | Bonds | The Guardian
description: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests
Content: Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities in France.Photograph: Michel Euler/APView image in fullscreenInitially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities in France.Photograph: Michel Euler/APBondsFrench borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook marketsYield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protestsPhillip InmanSenior economics writerWed 21 Oct 2026 09.17 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 09.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone.The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known asobligation assimilables du Trésor(Oat), issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%.The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasinglyviolent street protestsin recent weeks.Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living.Initially calm protests have often been met withaggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities. Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges.No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called asnap election in 2024. The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending.France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action.International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMatthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at the currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies.“The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said. “It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.”Explore more on these topicsBondsEurozoneFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Booking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scams | European Union | The Guardian
description: European Commission calls accommodation website’s approach to fraudulent listings and phishing scams as ‘absolutely substandard’
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: European Commission calls accommodation website’s approach to fraudulent listings and phishing scams as ‘absolutely substandard’
Content: Booking.com said it was engaging constructively with the commission.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenBooking.com said it was engaging constructively with the commission.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersEuropean UnionBooking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scamsEuropean Commission calls accommodation website’s approach to fraudulent listings and phishing scams as ‘absolutely substandard’Jennifer RankinWed 21 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEU regulators have opened an investigation into Booking.com, alleging that the accommodation website has not done enough to protect consumers from fake listings and scams.TheEuropean Commission, which regulates the world’s biggest tech companies operating in the EU, said Booking.com may have breached the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) with its “absolutely substandard” approach to tackling fraudulent listings and phishing scams, where criminals impersonate a third party to trick people to hand over money.A commission official said Booking.com should be carrying out risk assessments and acting to prevent fraud as required under the DSA. “We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” said the official. “Although they take measures, they could go much further and they could have much more solid systems to prevent fraud.”EU officials will also investigate whether Booking.com has breached advertising transparency rules, by potentially not making clear to users that some accommodation providers had paid to make their business more visible on the website.View image in fullscreenHenna Virkkunen, the European Commission’s executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy.Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPAUnder the EU’s DSA, whichaims to protect peoplefrom harmful and illegal internet content, a company could be fined 6% of its worldwide annual turnover.The commission said that opening the investigation did not prejudge the outcome.Booking.com, which is headquartered in Amsterdam and claims to have 28m accommodation listings, said it was engaging constructively with the commission. “Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com,” a company spokesperson said. “We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to ‌combat cybercrime and online fraud, and protect travellers and partners.”The investigation comes after researchers at the UK consumer group Which? exposed security lapses at Booking.com when they used the site to set up –and accept payment for– a fake offer to stay at 10 Downing Street.EU officials are investigating similar scams, with less high-profile addresses, where consumers thought they had booked a stay, only to find on arrival at a property that it had been fraudulently listed on Booking.com.Officials are also assessing a second category of scams, dubbed “reservation hijacks” where scammers use hacked data to impersonate an accommodation provider. Criminals send WhatsApp messages and have even used Booking.com’s own platform to request payments from Booking.com’s customers, supposedly to secure a stay. Casesseen by Guardian Money in 2025involved the theft of several hundred pounds.EU officials will examine whether the company has sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said it had received 200 reports of scams costing people €65,000 that involvedBooking.comin 2025, up from 89 reports worth €25,000 the previous year. These cases were “just the tip of the iceberg”, it said, as many victims would not report to its fraud helpdesk.Booking.com told the BBC in 2024 it had seena 500 to 900% increase in scamsin the previous 18 months, driven by generative AI tools that enable fraudsters to create very realistic-looking fake emails and internet booking links.Agustín Reyna, director general of the pan-European consumer group BEUC, said: “It is positive to see the European Commission investigating Booking.com for failing to meet EU digital rules. This is a systemic problem.”Henna Virkkunen, the commission’s lead official on tech policy, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionEuropeEuropean CommissionInternet safetyScamsCybercrimeIdentity fraudnewsShareReuse this content

title: Standup Jon Richardson on turning his dark teenage diaries into a tearjerking memoir: ‘I couldn’t sugarcoat those years’ | Jon Richardson | The Guardian
description: While facing grief, illness and a very public breakup, the comic reached for his diaries – and found a happy kid who spiralled into despair. Inspired by a Nobel laureate, he wrote a frank, funny book about that boy and what he grew into
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: While facing grief, illness and a very public breakup, the comic reached for his diaries – and found a happy kid who spiralled into despair. Inspired by a Nobel laureate, he wrote a frank, funny book about that boy and what he grew into
Content: ‘I have accumulated a horrific amount of paraphernalia from my own back story’ … Jon Richardson now and during his younger years.Composite: Ray Burmiston; SphereView image in fullscreen‘I have accumulated a horrific amount of paraphernalia from my own back story’ … Jon Richardson now and during his younger years.Composite: Ray Burmiston; SphereJon RichardsonInterviewStandup Jon Richardson on turning his dark teenage diaries into a tearjerking memoir: ‘I couldn’t sugarcoat those years’Brian LoganWhile facing grief, illness and a very public breakup, the comic reached for his diaries – and found a happy kid who spiralled into despair. Inspired by a Nobel laureate, he wrote a frank, funny book about that boy and what he grew intoWed 21 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt begins on Christmas Day, 1996: “It’s been a lovely day … I realised how much I love my family.” It ends three years later: “I’m lying on the floor in floods of tears and all I want to do is die.” Say what you like about adolescence but it is nothing if not an emotional tumult. “If I’d known as a teenager,” saysthe comedian Jon Richardsonruefully, “that I’d one day write a book about them, I couldn’t have bookended my teenage diaries with better quotes to show what a storm of shit those years can be.”The book is The Teenage Diaries of a Stand-Up Comedian, and it has been two years in the making. Two years that, if not quite the hormonal rollercoaster the book itself records, have been quite the ride. The project is borne of a crossroads moment in the Lancashire man’s midlife, after he experienced bereavement, serious illness among family and friends, and the breakdown of his marriage to fellow comic Lucy Beaumont. The last was an inevitably very public ending, splayed across the tabloids, to a relationship which itself played out in public, courtesy of the couple’s acclaimed mockumentary about their domestic arrangements,Meet the Richardsons.double quotation markIt’s a handbook – a way to make sure your kids don’t turn into me“There was a lot going on,” he recalls, “some of which called for self-reflection, and some that was completely beyond my control – to do with getting to a certain age, when the people around you get frailer, and you start looking differently at your relationships with your parents and your own childhood. So I was in quite a reflective period anyway.” But in Richardson’s case, there was a specific focus for that reflection. “I have genuinely accumulated a horrific amount of paraphernalia from my own back story,” he says. An inveterate hoarder, the 44-year-old had cupboards full of detritus (ticket stubs, photos, certificates, VHS videos, letters and emails – and of course, his teenage diaries) salvaged from the early years of his life.View image in fullscreenA relationship that played out in public … Richardson and his then wife, Lucy Beaumont, in 2019.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian“I felt like there must be a reason I’ve kept it,” says Richardson. “And perhaps the reason is that, one day, if you’re lucky enough to have the time, you can work out: what is of meaning, why did you keep certain things, what can you afford to get rid of? That’s the journey of the book really. It’s in the present tense because it documents me doing the reflecting and the clearing out. But it’s about those first 20 years and how much of them you carry over.”While writing, the comic deep-dived into teenage memoirs fromRae Earl’s My Fat, Mad Teenage Diary, via the works of Nobel prize winnerAnnie Ernaux(thanked by Richardson in the acknowledgements), to the recentComing of Age: How Adolescence Shapes Usby psychologist Lucy Foulkes. The resulting book may not be the one you’d expect from the neurotic standup once branded “the nation’s favourite worrier”, or from the team captain on Channel 4’s 8 Out of 10 Cats, or even from the presenter of popular documentaries about OCD. This is not a book to nestle snugly in the humour section of Waterstones, nor one that jauntily glosses the anxieties of adolescence.“I’m always very aware my job is to make people laugh,” says Richardson, “and I hope there is plenty of humour in the book.” There is. Its structure – diary extracts followed by grownup Jon reflecting ruthlessly thereupon – offers Richardson endless opportunities for entertaining self-abasement. And there is nostalgic delight to be had in the period detail: “Blockbuster video, Tupperware parties and Ann Summers.” And there is droll dramatic irony too, as per Richardson’s favourite entry, aged 14, apropos of nothing: “I’ve decided that although I’ll probably end up being a teacher, I’d love to be a comedian.”double quotation markA lot of kids just need to be told that it’s OK to be sad or strugglingHe says now: “But in terms of the emotions, I couldn’t sugarcoat what those years were. Very few people become comedians because they’re well-adjusted and just want to spread joy in the world. Going back to the 60s and 70s, and those people who now have BBC Four documentaries made about them, people tend to come to comedy through having unscratched itches, or to make amends for some shortcoming in themselves. And I’m no different.”In the book, we follow Richardson’s teenage self from 14 to 17. “I think I watched Zack Morris on [the sitcom]Saved By the Bell,” he recalls, “and thought, ‘Oh, teenagers are supposed to keep secret diaries.’ But those early entries don’t have anything to say. I’m in my room playing Mario Kart most of the time.” At first, teenage Jon comes across as kind, bright, tentatively happy. But as time passes, his diary increasingly records a sense of isolation, frustration and low self-worth. He goes to a single-sex school. He feels ugly. He is growing up in a town – Morecambe, Lancashire – that seems to him like the dead-end back of beyond. His parents are separated and, in a book that is eloquent on poverty and class, money is tight.View image in fullscreenIn a stir … Richardson on The Great Celebrity Bake Off in March.Photograph: Laura Palmer/Channel 4These are all factors in Richardson’s spiral into a dark place. “There were an awful lot of happy times that I never wrote about,” he insists. But “very quickly the diary becomes a place to put the emotions that you don’t want to burden other people with, a place where you only talk about the struggle. It can become quite unhealthy.” In the book’s final chapter – ring-fenced from the earlier material, says Richardson, because it’s hard to be funny about – diary entries show teenage Jon considering suicide.In 2023, alongside the former athlete Jessica Ennis-Hill and broadcaster Dan Walker, Richardson launchedBright Young Dreams, a fundraising campaign to support youth mental health – into which he will “put more of my energy over the next few years than anything else”. When I ask what might have made life more bearable for junior Jon, he would not, he replies, have changed any of the material circumstances of that boy’s life. What would have helped, he says, is “some understanding that it’s OK to be struggling and to be sad. A lot of kids just need to be told that, yes, itisreally hard, thesearedifficult years”.As the parent myself of a boy on the precipice of his teens, the book terrified me about what’s in store – while rallying my resolve to care for him through it. “If nothing else,” says the comic, “consider this a handbook for parents to make sure their kids don’t turn into Jon Richardson! That is a great gift I bestow on the nation.” But if his book offers a sobering reminder of the trials of teenagedom, it is also very affecting on family love. Its heroes, alongside the foundering teen centre-stage, are Richardson’s mum, dad and sister.“You can’t talk about those years without bringing other people’s lives into it,” he says. “My main concern was protecting the privacy of people who haven’t chosen to write a book.” But his loved ones, off the page as on it, have been unstintingly supportive. “I write about my dad’s depression in the book, and I had to say to him, ‘Do you mind if I tell that story?’ And he said: ‘You do what you want to do.’” That conversation, says Richardson, was easy. Far harder for this working-class northern male was having to address his family about – ugh – their love for one another. Towards the end of the book, he reprints an email from his sister, sent at a fragile time of Jon’s life, that is so trenchant and loving in its support of her wee brother, that I couldn’t read it without welling up.View image in fullscreen‘Now I take a difficult emotion and, instead of blurting it out on a page, I convert it into punchlines’ … Richardson performing in 2015.Photograph: Publicity image“It had the same impact on me,” says Richardson. “But my sister doesn’t know yet that it’s in the book. I haven’t been able to have that conversation. It’s easier to just put it in and not talk about it. ‘I love you. It’s in a book, so it’s a fact. Bye!’”Now living a life his teenaged self could scarcely have dreamed of, is Richardson still keeping a diary? He is not – give or take the purely factual records he keeps, in an array of journals behind his head on our Zoom call, of his every gig since taking up standup in 2003. Grownup friendships and counselling have all supplanted the role diaries once played in his life. “They ended,” he says, because “I started going to the pub and hanging out with people.” And then he discovered standup, which was “transformative”.“My approach to standup has always been: ‘How do I feel at this moment, and how do I package it in a way that’s interesting and amusing?’ It’s like a house conversion, like walking into a dilapidated wreck and turning it into something presentable. I take a difficult emotion and, instead of blurting it out on a page, I get to talk to people every night who’ve had similar experiences, and convert it into punchlines. And I can see people laughing and having a good night because I’ve confronted this emotion. And that,” says the tormented teenager, the teacher manqué turned comic and now memoirist, “has done wonders for my wellbeing.”The Teenage Diaries of a Stand-Up Comedian by Jon Richardson (Little, Brown Book Group, £25). title: Ellie & Natasia review – please give us more of this irresistibly weird comedy  | Television | The Guardian
description: The hilarious duo are back with deeply silly sketches about an evil trad-wife, Lime bike addicts and Dubai chocolate. There are only three episodes, but each one is gloriously unsettling – and packed with ridiculously good guest stars
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: The hilarious duo are back with deeply silly sketches about an evil trad-wife, Lime bike addicts and Dubai chocolate. There are only three episodes, but each one is gloriously unsettling – and packed with ridiculously good guest stars
Content: Eccentric … Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in season two of Ellie & Natasia.Photograph: BBC/Nit TV/Jack BarnesView image in fullscreenEccentric … Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in season two of Ellie & Natasia.Photograph: BBC/Nit TV/Jack BarnesTV reviewTelevisionReviewEllie & Natasia review – please give us more of this irresistibly weird comedyThe hilarious duo are back with deeply silly sketches about an evil trad-wife, Lime bike addicts and Dubai chocolate. There are only three episodes, but each one is gloriously unsettling – and packed with ridiculously good guest starsHannah J DaviesWed 21 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2022, comics and actors Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou starred in six bite-size episodes of their self-titled sketch show. Among the highlights: a woman who makes wild swimming her whole personality before realising she hates freezing water; a pair of overbearing, overopinionated mums who vlog from a sterilely clean kitchen (“you’re not a real mum unless you’re redecorating or knocking through at least six times a year”) and, of course, Internet Nails, about two decidedly useless eastern European beauty entrepreneurs who were branching out into a variety of business ideas (“please let us scratch you with our ink today, and if you change your mind we can burn the tattoo off with professional match”). It was often hilarious, and was definitely weird, with many parallels to the offbeat Channel 4 series Stath Lets Flats (which White and Demetriou starred in alongside the latter’s brother, its creator Jamie).Four long years later – reportedly due to scheduling clashes – the duo are back. Ellie & Natasia series two comprises just three episodes, although – gladly – these episodes are now half an hour long rather than a mere 15 minutes. Internet Nails, in particular, remains a crucible for unsettling comedy, with the salon having become a “premiere relax styling and elegance lounge for all makeup, hair straightening and spray tanning mother-baby needs”). The fact that both women were pregnant at the time of filming only makes it funnier, and the low-rent experience (“100% birthing penthouse with perfect lukewarm Jacuzzi”) is deeply silly and – for anyone who has gone to a slightly shonky beauty shop before – astutely observed. The judgy mums are back, too, complete with advice on how to make your wardrobe stretch from “conception to birth, birth to night, night to bed, bed to menopause, menopause to coffin, and coffin to hell …”Influencers have become even more inescapable since White and Demetriou’s first series, and the parodies are plentiful. These include two women who speak gobbledegook into their podcast microphones, while their hats get bigger and bigger with every scene (“don’t just dress for the job you want,” White implores. “If you want the dress, job for it”). There’s also a bit about a sack-wearing, trad wife-style content creator (White) who enjoys eating croissants, making collages and, er, keeping the woman her boyfriend cheated with locked up in her basement. So silly, so irresistible.View image in fullscreenSo silly … Ellie & Natasia.Photograph: BBC/CPL ProductionsOf course, this is a sketch show, so not everything lands. The two women who spend hours in posh shops fondling candles and cooing are relatable but the concept wears thin, even when Sian Clifford pops up as a wonderfully exasperated shopkeeper. An OnlyFans parody that involves the pair eating grapes and mashed potatoes out of their cleavages feels more like an in-joke. See also: Mary Poppins at the gynaecologist, complete with what can only be described as dangerously cavernous nether regions. Unfortunately, that four-year gap also means that Mitchell and Webb pipped them to the post with a Repair Shop send-up in Mitchell and Webb Are Not Helping, even if White and Demetriou’s version is funnier, with a better payoff.‘It was like your worst nightmare’ – Ellie and Natasia on mums, music … and failing to make Bob Mortimer smileRead moreLuckily, there’s much that does work – eccentric and sometimes touching vignettes of life that don’t punch down but do cock a snook at almost every area of society, from a “wee little shop selling tiny mini wee things” in Scotland to Lime bike addicts to aspirants like Donna and her cousin Nikki, who composes a rap about Dubai chocolate’s pistachio filling. A Crystal Maze-style gameshow about a man who needs to get rid of all the snakes that are ruining the foundations of his house (“I sleep with a knife on a stick!”) probably doesn’t say much about anything, actually, but it is totally hysterical. Ditto a Fonejacker-esque recurring bit where Demetriou pops up to declare “I made it, it was me!” about everything from a pot plant to a high-rise building to a pen. A special mention, too, for “Women’s-Only Only Fools and Horses”, a new musical stage adaptation of the TV series (a sheepskin-clad Demetriou explains: “Strip it back and at its heart it’s a very serious story about three generations of working-class men …”).The series also manages to pack in a ridiculous surfeit of British comedy talents, from Jamie Demetriou to Steve Coogan, Katy Wix to Asim Chaudhry, Kiell Smith-Bynoe to Vicki Pepperdine. But, of course, its brightest lights are White and Demetriou. “Pregnant and doing a sketch show? Does that make it funnier?” asks Demetriou in one of the transition scenes where the two women natter to each other. Not necessarily, but I could easily watch another 10 episodes.Ellie and Natasia aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Clayface review – flesh-stretching DC body horror is very gory but not very good | Horror films | The Guardian
description: Liverpool makes for an unconvincing Gotham City in this effectively gross but otherwise middling attempt to milk money from a lesser-known Batman villain
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Liverpool makes for an unconvincing Gotham City in this effectively gross but otherwise middling attempt to milk money from a lesser-known Batman villain
Content: Tom Rhys Harries in Clayface.Photograph: Warner BrosView image in fullscreenTom Rhys Harries in Clayface.Photograph: Warner BrosHorror filmsReviewClayface review – flesh-stretching DC body horror is very gory but not very goodLiverpool makes for an unconvincing Gotham City in this effectively gross but otherwise middling attempt to milk money from a lesser-known Batman villainBenjamin LeeWed 21 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 15.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsense of desperation is understandably in the air over at DC, the company, like Marvel, slowly realising that the mass superhero fever has finally broken. There’s still interest there, of course (this summer’s Spider-Man is now the biggest film of all time in the US after all), but it’s no longer good enough to leave a high-speed conveyor belt unmanned, purpose and quality control be damned. 2019 saw a staggering 10 superhero films released in cinemas, and the inevitable exhaustion that followed, also fueled by Covid, led to a gradual winding down, monster hits turning into minor ones and sure bets often becoming expensive flops.The Cycle review – forensic scientist autopsies her dad in grisly psychodrama that turns supernaturalRead moreAs Peter Parker winged his way to box office records this summer, DC’s Supergirl bombed so hard that experts believe it might have cost Warners upwards of $200m in losses. It was just the latest disappointment for the brand after Black Adam, Joker: Folie à Deux, Blue Beetle and The Flash all underperformed while even last year’s much-heralded Superman reboot only grossed a solid $618m, a far cry from the $1bn heyday of the genre (things got so bad that even a fully filmed Batgirl adventure wasdeleted for the tax break). Notably, the last DC film to swoop past that magic figure was Joker in 2019, a darker, lower-budget attempt to spotlight a villain rather than a hero, a big swing with relatively low stakes. Todd Phillips’s film might be best known by some for being brave enough to ask the question, “What if Taxi Driver sucked?” but for all of its many issues, it brought buzz and prestige and, shockingly, Oscars, to an easily ridiculed universe. It was also, crucially, something rare in that world: a close-to-good idea.The evolution of Clayface, another R-rated villain origin story with a markedly lower budget than the DC norm, was not in direct response to Joker (it is allegedly the first in a new “Gods and Monsters” strand) but its path is one that head James Gunn would clearly like to emulate, albeit financially rather than awards-wise. One of many thoughts I had during Clayface, other than what I should have for dinner and how long I might be able to make a small popcorn last, was just how striking Phillips’s film stands in comparison. It remains shallow and smug and cursed with a grating lead performance, but it was visually punchy and, like the very best comic book adaptations, genuinely transporting, rich on dank atmosphere and thoughtfully curated production design. It was an undeniable moment.Clayface is overwhelminglynota moment. Admittedly its targets are way lower (Mike Flanagan’s original script, allegedly more texturally complex, wasentirely rewritten) but even as a similarly new way in, as a relatively standalone horror movie for those who wouldn’t now rush toward a superhero caper, it’s a clumsily missed opportunity and another reminder that those at DC don’t seem to know what they’re doing and why they’re doing it.Rather than feeling like a lower-budget DC movie (it was made for around $40m), it looks closer to a network TV series, more Fox than HBO Max, more Gotham than Lanterns. With the standard there now so high (The Penguin looked every bit a blockbuster movie), the distractingly tinny aesthetic and lack of confident directorial style is disappointing both as a horror (especially at a time of micro-budgeted films such as Obsession and Backrooms looking so very distinctive) and as a tale that takes place in the DC universe. Liverpool was used as a stand-in here and if, like me, you found Manchester to be an unconvincing New York in Brand New Day, you won’t realise how good we had it …Gotham is where working-class boy done good Matt (Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries, fine enough) is from and a place that he was desperate to leave. He’s a rising movie star, riding high after his first Oscar nomination (“Nominees don’t wait in line!”) and on a trip back to his home town, he makes the mistake of sleeping with the girlfriend of a violent gangster, introduced by Goldfrapp’s Ooh La La, one of the film’s many dated attempts at cool. As a result, he has his money-making face sliced up by goons and his career soon crumbles, back to a bedsit with all his money wasted on useless surgeries orchestrated by his viperous lawyer.Matt is desperate for revenge and resurrection, and after stumbling upon a doctor working on experimental skin surgery (Naomi Ackie, trying her hardest), he thinks he’s found his chance. But before you can say Substance (the elixir is at least red here over Brat green), things go horribly wrong …View image in fullscreenHarries as Matt, who is seeking revenge and resurrection.Photograph: Warner BrosWhat the film does do is successfully gross us out, as Matt’s skin starts to morph in tune with his emotional state, which might be enough for some, and in the screening I attended, mostly filled with rowdy non-journalists, there was a vocal response to the goriest and gloopiest moments. The trailer scene, of Matt trying to cut through flesh growing over his eyes while on a bumpy flight, is brilliantly awful to watch, and it’s in these more intimate, uneasy moments where director James Watkins shows off his dusty genre mettle. His best films have been his earlier, smaller attempts – 2002’s genuinely creepy and forward-thinking reality TV horror My Little Eye and 2008’s brutal hoodie thriller Eden Lake – but he’s less assured when the canvas is expanded.Clayface is as poorly lit and junkily made as the very blandest of streaming movies and never once do we feel transported to Gotham with a cast of exclusively non-American actors trying to out-accent each other (Eddie Marsan, as ever, loses that game). It doesn’t help that what could have been interesting at one point (perhaps when Flanagan was the sole author) with briefly pointed at issues of AI, unreality and method acting, has been sanded down to a kill-by-numbers revenge thriller led by a character who feels like an off-brand swirl of Venom, Hulk, Joker and Mystique. His abilities, and the rules of how they work, are so poorly defined, that he just becomes a screenwriting device, able to do whatever is needed in the moment.Any tragedy that could and should have come from the character and his journey – boy from the wrong side of the tracks to privileged Oscar nominee to flesh-stretching, face-changing supervillain (!) – is excised for an easier video game trajectory, from one familiar level to the next (despite those involved comparing this to The Fly, this is very muchnotthat). Clayface might be the start of a “bold” new era for DC’s superhero output but for anyone outside of a boardroom, it’s a face we have seen many times before.Clayface is out in Australian cinemas on 22 October and in US and UK cinemas on 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsDC ComicsThrillersEddie MarsanSuperhero moviesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ghosts: The Possession of Button House review – new levels of giddiness unleashed in spooky spin-off | Movies | The Guardian
description: Picking up not long after the events of the final episode of the BBC’s haunted house comedy, this glorious new film is every bit as warm and comforting as the TV sitcom
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Picking up not long after the events of the final episode of the BBC’s haunted house comedy, this glorious new film is every bit as warm and comforting as the TV sitcom
Content: Each and every ghost could single-handedly power a 90-minute script … Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.Photograph: Courtesy of Mandozzi PhotographyView image in fullscreenEach and every ghost could single-handedly power a 90-minute script … Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.Photograph: Courtesy of Mandozzi PhotographyMoviesReviewGhosts: The Possession of Button House review – new levels of giddiness unleashed in spooky spin-offPicking up not long after the events of the final episode of the BBC’s haunted house comedy, this glorious new film is every bit as warm and comforting as the TV sitcomCath ClarkeWed 21 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 09.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat on earth is happening at Button House? Kitty has tasered a police officer. Fanny is pulling down her capacious Victorian drawers to show off her bottom. Robin the caveman has fallen in love with a crusty eco activist (to be fair she looks quite a bit like him). If you’ve never watched theBBC’s haunted house comedy Ghosts– one of the finest family television shows in recent memory – none of the above will make the slightest bit of sense. Neither perhaps will this glorious new film, which picks up with the ghosts not long after the events ofthe final episode in 2023.Often when British sitcoms get a spin-off what happens is the gag-to-runtime ratio dips. But breaking out of the 30-minute episode structure seems to have freed up the writers to unleash new levels of giddiness with added spoonfuls of silliness. The jokes keep coming, and it’s every bit as warm and comforting as on TV.It’s been a few months since Alison and Mike (Charlotte Ritchie and Kiell Smith-Bynoe) left Button House, selling the crumbling stately pile to a hotel chain. But work on the refurb has stalled, and the ghosts are pining after Alison, the only living person who can see them (long story). One of the joys of Ghosts is the competing main character energy of Button House’s deceased residents, played to perfection by an unassailable cast. There’s the sleazy Tory MP with no trousers, Julian Fawcett (Simon Farnaby), forever caught with his pants down. And scoutmaster Pat (Jim Howick) with an arrow through his neck. It feels mean to leave out the rest; each and every ghost could single-handedly power a 90-minute script. To say anything about the plot would ruin the fun. (I watched with a nine-year-old who hooted throughout.) It really is a delight.Ghosts: The Possession of Button House is in UK and Irish cinemas from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsScience fiction and fantasy filmsBBCTV comedyComedyTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Scream review – Wes Craven meta horror remains super smart and scary 30 years on | Movies | The Guardian
description: Self-aware romp through the genre is redolent of the 90s but its ghost-masked killer is as alarming as ever
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Self-aware romp through the genre is redolent of the 90s but its ghost-masked killer is as alarming as ever
Content: Shocking sights … (from left) Courteney Cox, Jamie Kennedy and Neve Campbell in Scream.Photograph: Dimension/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenShocking sights … (from left) Courteney Cox, Jamie Kennedy and Neve Campbell in Scream.Photograph: Dimension/Sportsphoto/AllstarMoviesReviewScream review – Wes Craven meta horror remains super smart and scary 30 years onSelf-aware romp through the genre is redolent of the 90s but its ghost-masked killer is as alarming as everPeter BradshawWed 21 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 30th anniversary re-release of the original Scream, from screenwriter Kevin Williamson and directorWes Craven, brings us to a locus classicus of the 90s: a self-aware romp through the horror genre. It features Skeet Ulrich’s high schooler Billy Loomis announcing that reality is “all one big movie – but you can’t pick your genre”, which is the meta-slasher equivalent of Jacques Derrida’s belief that there is nothing outside the text.A ghost-masked killer is murdering and terrorising the bland Californian town of Woodsboro, and we begin with his gruesome assault on Casey (Drew Barrymore); he makes chilling calls to people’s landline phones, in an era where that meant you more or less had them pinned them down to a certain location. (The existence of “cellular” phones was still an exotic novelty.) The mother of teen Sidney (Neve Campbell) had been brutally killed previously, a crime pinned on local man Cotton Weary (a cameo for Liev Schreiber) who is now in jail. But was he really guilty? Now Sidney is at risk like everyone else.Yet as one of the local horror fans points out: you’re safe as long as you stick to the three scary-movie rules: stay a virgin, avoid drink and drugs, and don’t utter the hubristic phrase “I’ll be right back”. (Perhaps someone could also have pointed out the difference in vulnerability-level between blondes and non-blondes.) So when Sidney has sex, she puts herself in mortal danger. Meanwhile, brash local TV reporter Gale Weathers (played by Courteney Cox, already a star from Friends) figures she can crack this case wide open, and she has a tendresse for the goofy young cop deputy Dewey Riley, played by Cox’s future husband, David Arquette.The self-aware references are many, and the action of Scream is often wittily juxtaposed with narrative sequences from a classic such as Halloween. What comes across from watching the original Scream 30 years on is that there is one horror classic that could be an influence but isn’t referenced, perhaps because it isn’t canonical in the purist slasher-film sense: Truman Capote’s reportage history In Cold Blood. (I think of this, when one character here dismisses the idea of “motive”.)What also emerges, perhaps not entirely intentionally, is how very obnoxious, and very possibly sadistic, male movie fandom can often seem in itself. It’s very apparent when the killer smugly challenges his victim with a trick question about who the killer is in the first Friday the 13th. This film is brash and smart in that distinctive 90s way – and the title sounds like an order.Scream is in UK cinemas from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsWes CravenDrew BarrymoreLiev SchreiberreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine review – turgid tribute to pioneering star | Classical music | The Guardian
description:
Barbican Hall, London
Julia Bullock is magnetic in this discourse on Josephine Baker, but the 100-minute piece is slow-moving and lacking in intimacy
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Barbican Hall, LondonJulia Bullock is magnetic in this discourse on Josephine Baker, but the 100-minute piece is slow-moving and lacking in intimacy
Content: Transgressive … Julia Bullock in Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenTransgressive … Julia Bullock in Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewPerle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine review – turgid tribute to pioneering starBarbican Hall, LondonJulia Bullock is magnetic in this discourse on Josephine Baker, but the 100-minute piece is slow-moving and lacking in intimacyErica JealWed 21 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosephine Bakerwas many things: a civil rights activist; a spy for the French resistance; a woman who, born into poverty, became the best-paid stage star in Europe. But before she was any of these, she was an entertainer. So one wonders what on earth she would make of Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine, a turgid 100-minute piece developed by the soprano Julia Bullock, composer Tyshawn Sorey, poet Claudia Rankine and director Peter Sellars.This was its UK premiere, although Bullock and Sorey have been performing versions of it in the US and elsewhere over the past decade. It isn’t a tribute in the usual sense, but a discourse on racial discrimination, in Baker’s day and our own. Bullock, magnetic as ever, sings and speaks alongside six musicians, who include Sorey himself on piano, drum kit and percussion, plus electric guitar, violin, alto flute, saxophone and bassoon. On a platform, in front of a saturated square of brightly coloured light, Bullock declaims Rankine’s words and sings Sorey’s music, in which Baker’s songs are deconstructed, reformed, and mostly slowed right down. A riff on Bye Bye Blackbird has guitar and saxophone sounding suspiciously like the playout on a 1980s power ballad. Later, more rewardingly, the guitar gives a highlife flavour to a version of Je t’aime. But mostly the score is bloated and the instrumental episodes don’t unify the piece so much as draw it out. Ear-splitting bass drum and tam tam indicate emotional climaxes. Everyone is mic’d up, which works against any sense of intimacy.View image in fullscreen‘Baker’s songs are deconstructed, reformed, and mostly slowed right down’ … Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Mark AllanSurtitles translate the French, laying bare the sentiments that she slipped into unsuspecting ears. “Should I be white to please you more?” Bullock sings, holding a half bow and gazing out as if simultaneously accusing us and seeking our approval. One episode alludes to Baker’s famous “danse sauvage”, for which she wore a skirt made of rubber bananas, and almost nothing else. Braless under the sheer fabric at the top of her jumpsuit – and yes, the sight of a woman’s breasts is more transgressive on theBarbicanstage today than it was in the Folies Bergères a century ago – Bullock dances, making some of Baker’s grotesquely caricatured “savage” moves, and the effect is properly disturbing. Here, Perle Noire is hard-hitting. Otherwise, it’s hard going.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicJosephine BakerBarbicanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Popcorn with your Puccini: can opera on screen ever work?  | Music | The Guardian
description: Composers have harnessed TV and cinema since Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors pulled in five million viewers 75 years ago but for my money Kombat Opera’s satire showed us how to do it best
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Composers have harnessed TV and cinema since Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors pulled in five million viewers 75 years ago but for my money Kombat Opera’s satire showed us how to do it best
Content: ‘There are huge gains in seeing close up what the singers are doing as actors’ … people watch Madame Butterfly, projected live in Times Square, New York, in 2006.Photograph: Dima Gavrysh/APView image in fullscreen‘There are huge gains in seeing close up what the singers are doing as actors’ … people watch Madame Butterfly, projected live in Times Square, New York, in 2006.Photograph: Dima Gavrysh/APTom Service on musicMusicPopcorn with your Puccini: can opera on screen ever work?Tom ServiceComposers have harnessed TV and cinema since Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors pulled in five million viewers 75 years ago but for my money Kombat Opera’s satire showed us how to do it bestWed 21 Oct 2026 11.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.17 EDTShareIt’s not even Halloween, but here’s an operatic Christmas story for you. This is the 75th anniversary of the first opera made for television: Gian Carlo Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors, broadcast at Yuletide in 1951 and watched by five million people across the US in a production sponsored by Hallmark.You can watch the original broadcast on YouTube: it was introduced with wit, self-deprecation and early 50s elegance by Menotti himself (vastly less charmingly, the role of King Balthazar was played by a singer in blackface). Chet Allen’s performance as the boy, Amahl, is staggering, and even more moving is Rosemary Kuhlmann’s Mother, especially in her aria, All That gold!.Amahl is “an opera for children because it tries to recapture my own childhood”, Menotti said. It was played on US TV every Christmastime throughout the 50s, and was recorded and remade in new productions the next decade, while the BBC picked it up in 1953, and there was even an Australian TV version. Less than an hour long, Menotti’s festive fable works because of the intimacy of its story, and its refusal to patronise its intended audience.View image in fullscreenPatronising-free: the 1963 made-for-TV production of Carlo Menotti’s Amahl and the Night VisitorsPhotograph: No creditBut Amahl was a high-water mark. Another opera-made for-telly anniversary this year isBenjamin Britten’s Owen Wingrave, composed for the BBC and first broadcast 55 years ago. Britten’s piece definitely wasn’t made for children. Based on a gothic novella by Henry James, it’s the story of the pacifist Owen Wingrave’s struggles against his military forebears and his fiancee who is ashamed of him. Britten’s opera is uncompromisingly claustrophobic and intense, one of his most underrated scores – but it’s a piece that wasn’t designed to capture Amahl’s popularity on screen.The later story of operas made for TV in Britain is more about exploration of the possibilities of the medium rather than following in Menotti’s audience-first footsteps: in the 90s and 00s there are pieces composed for TV includingJudith Weir’s Armidaor Jonathan Dove’sWhen She Died …, written on the fifth anniversary of the death of Princess Diana, and there were filmed productions of existing operas especially remade for television, such as the director Margaret Williams’s scintillating versions of Thomas Adès’sPowder Her Faceor her version ofBritten’s Owen Wingrave, produced for Channel 4 in 2001 to mark the opera’s 30th anniversary.These days, opera is more often found on the big screen: cinemas all over the world can take you to a night at the opera, and here’s another anniversary for you – this autumn marks 20 years since theMetropolitan Opera started streaming its productions to cinemas, an innovation that the Royal Opera House in London quickly followed, finding new audiences, as well as a parallel stream of income and impact.View image in fullscreenThe mechanics of opera work through the other end of the telescope … Madame Butterfly in Times Square, New York, in 2006.Photograph: Dima Gavrysh/APThe Met: Live in HD has been controversial: Peter Gelb, the Met’s general manager suggested in 2013 that the cinema audiences were “cannibalising” the audience for live shows; but surely, from Japan to Brazil, and here in the UK, these broadcastsreach opera-loverswho are unable to go to the Met in person.On cinema screens there are huge gains in seeing close up what the singers are doing as actors, subtleties of facial expression and the relationships between the characters on stage that you can’t pick up when you are sitting at the back of the gallery. But the essential problem with broadcasting live opera on any screen remains the same as it was in 1951. We are watching performers who are projecting through the acoustic miracles of their voices into an auditorium that seats thousands.The intimacy of film, and especially TV, requires precisely the opposite mode of delivery. In drama on TV or film, the wonder and the illusion lies in sharing an intimacy of space and feeling with the actors, whereas the mechanics of opera work through the other end of the telescope, zooming out from their voices towards us in the audience, rather than zooming us in to be with them in each scene.Operaand film are essentially made for entirely different purposes.But if you do want to see what happens when opera is made for television from the ground up, there’s another anniversary to tell you about: it has been 19 years since Richard Thomas’s Kombat Opera Presents, half-hour shows broadcast in 2007 that sent up TV staples fromThe Apprenticeto theSouth Bank – Bragg! – Show. Thomas was hot on the heels of the success of his theatre show with Stewart Lee -Jerry Springer: The Opera, but the origins of Kombat Opera also go back to sketches in Simon Munnery’s Attention Scum series that aired on the BBC in 2001, with the soprano and contemporary music catalyst Loré Lixenberg, who made a new art-formdressed as a gothic uber-diva, filmed on the white cliffs of Kent.Lixenberg, and trained singers including Leigh Melrose, Janis Kelly and Sophia Ragavelas made every half-hour long episode of Kombat Opera their own, but it’s the way Thomas included parts for actors including Kevin Eldon, Hugh Dennis and Jon Culshaw, and mixed all the media together, that makes these shows so compelling.The format never feels as if it is selling either medium short: the heightened emotionalising and ridiculousness of opera serves the satire perfectly, joyously and concisely. Seems opera on screen works best when its turns its attention to the screen itself.***Talking of taking the artform into new places, Raymond Gubbay celebrates his 80th birthday with the Choir of King’s College, Cambridge atWigmore Hall, Londontonight. Gubbay’s Classical Spectaculars, his Christmas shows, his operas at the Royal Albert Hall – which included flooding the arena with 65,000 litres water every night for Puccini’s Madame Butterfly, a Turandot at Wembley Arena in collaboration with the Royal Opera House, and even hisSavoy Opera venture, a brave but doomed attempt to make repertory opera work in the West End without subsidy, are some of the most brilliant, energetic, and imaginative ways of popularising classical music over the last 60 years.View image in fullscreenSubsidy-free business model:  Raymond Gubbay, photographed for the Guardian in 2015.Photograph: David Sillitoe/The GuardianTo make large-scale classical music profitable is a vanishingly rare phenomenon. (Even if, while it’s true to say that as a business, Gubbay never took a penny from any Arts Council, most of the musicians and orchestras he worked with wouldn’t exist without it.) Gubbay’s 80th birthday concert will give its profits to another now Arts Council-free organisation, Wigmore Hall itself. Gubbay’s subsidy-free business model remains an impossible dream for most, but Wigmore Hall is an unlikely contemporary torchbearer for the same spirit of entrepreneurship.This week Tom has been listening to:Anna Meredith’s Dusky, the single from her new album.You know that feeling when you’re on the summit of the rollercoaster Stealth at Thorpe Park, and there’s that microsecond where your heart’s in your mouth before the drop? Dusky is like six and a half minutes spent in that place of delirious freefall, as rhythms grind against each other, melodic arcs rising and falling, to make time warp and your stomach pitch and yaw.Explore more on these topicsMusicTom Service on musicClassical musicOperacommentShareReuse this content

title: As fans reject AI-generated music, even boosters are drawing the line | Music | The Guardian
description: Enthusiasts like Grimes and A$AP Rocky may embrace AI-generated content, but they won’t produce it themselves
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Enthusiasts like Grimes and A$AP Rocky may embrace AI-generated content, but they won’t produce it themselves
Content: Grimes and A$AP Rocky.Composite: Getty imagesView image in fullscreenGrimes and A$AP Rocky.Composite: Getty imagesMusicAnalysisAs fans reject AI-generated music, even boosters are drawing the lineBlake MontgomeryEnthusiasts like Grimes and A$AP Rocky may embrace AI-generated content, but they won’t produce it themselvesWed 21 Oct 2026 09.22 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTShareStreaming services, notable musicians and fans are confronting the growing presence of AI-generated music and drawing lines in the sand.On Tuesday,Spotifyannounced it had removed about 50m songs consideredAIslop from its recommendations to users over the past year.“Our editors hold the same standard and don’t program content identified as slop or spam,” a statement from the company read.Spotifyrequires “AI persona” badges on artist profiles that don’t represent a real human being, but it does not require individual songs generated by AI to be labeled. Other streaming services have taken more stringent stances.Though it is cracking down on slop tracks, Spotify is far from AI-shy. The company allows users to create playlists with generative AI and has promised a tool for making AI-generated remixes and cover songs.Cyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’Read moreUnable to ignore the tide, even early AI boosters like the singer and producerGrimes, former paramour of Elon Musk and mother to three of his 14 children, have declared their limits on allowable amounts of AI. She and other musicians say they are open to AI-generated music but wary.Fans, by contrast, have little tolerance for it. They are voting with millions of streams against artifice in music. Songs and albums harkening back to analogue instrumentation are dominating the Billboard charts, no futurism wanted.Both A$AP Rocky, rapper and partner to Rihanna, and Grimes have taken the same position: accepting AI-generated music but not making it.“I prefer to do things myself, practically,” A$AP Rocky toldBillboard: “If somebody does a totally AI-generated song where all they did was prompt something, then I think that’s their thing. But who am I to say what’s standard and what’s not? I’m just doing me out here, and I’m doing my music practically – the right way.”Kelly Clarkson similarly outlined her own boundary while expressing enthusiasm for AI.“I love AI. Controversial, I don’t care,” she told the Las Culturistas podcast. “Here’s the thing, I love AI. There are very amazing things with AI that I’m obsessed with. But also, and I’m very into it artistically too, I have fun with it just like everybody else does. But when you see AI artists competing on a chart with humans, I have an issue. I think there should be a separate chart.”Grimes, one of my own favorite musicians, has begun promoting her first new album in six years, Psy Opera, which she described tothe Paris Reviewas capturing the “emotion of being thrust into the future”.Stereogumdescribed the album as “AI-inspired but not AI-generated”, citing Grimes’s own insistence that her team of 70 be credited rather than reduced to machines.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGrimes offered a free license of her own voice to AI enthusiasts to make what they would three years ago. That she declined to generate her own music indicates that, even to a futurist like her, AI-generated music is lacking, similar to Rocky’s stance.I have also found myself listening to an AI-generated song, Bomboclat Wallahi, brought to my attention viafrenetic, overstimulatingvideoson Instagram. Despite the song’s comical sonic maximalism, it lacks any staying power. Listening to it the day after I first heard it left no impression, similar to the way low-quality food leaves me hungry again just a few hours after eating. “Slop” is still the best word to describe AI-made content.In contrast with artists’ nuanced stances, fans are making their position on tech-made music clear: they don’t want it.Billboard’s chartsof the most popular albums and charts of the past week showcase a preference for music without obvious modification. Songs and albums that feature a simple voice-and-guitar arrangement are dominating. On the Top 200 album charts, most of the Top 10 albums foreground a singer over analogue instrumentation – Olivia Rodrigo’s You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, Ella Langley’s Dandelion, Olivia Dean’s The Art of Loving, Taylor Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl, Noah Kahan’s The Great Divide and Stick Season, and Morgan Wallen’s I’m the Problem. In the Hot 100 singles chart, the top four songs bear the same sonic signatures: Swift’s Patient Zero, Langley’s Choosin’ Texas, Stella Lefty’s Boston, Wallen’s Been by Now.Incredibly, the Beatles’ Rubber Soul, released in 1965, also made an appearance at No 4 on last week’s Billboard rankings. Some listeners want to return to a time when producing music with artificial intelligence wasn’t even an option.Explore more on these topicsMusicAI (artificial intelligence)SpotifyGrimesA$AP RockyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch by Thure Erik Lund review – is this the greatest living Norwegian writer? | Fiction in translation | The Guardian
description: Translated into English at last, this portrait of a man appalled by modernity and desperate to get back to nature is brimming with Nordic weltschmerz
Author: Sukhdev Sandhu
Headline: Translated into English at last, this portrait of a man appalled by modernity and desperate to get back to nature is brimming with Nordic weltschmerz
Content: Thure Erik Lund.Photograph: Niklas LelloView image in fullscreenThure Erik Lund.Photograph: Niklas LelloFiction in translationReviewThe Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch by Thure Erik Lund review – is this the greatest living Norwegian writer?Translated into English at last, this portrait of a man appalled by modernity and desperate to get back to nature is brimming with Nordic weltschmerzSukhdev SandhuWed 21 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleT-O-M. The initials of Tomas Olsen Myrbråten, the narrator in Thure Erik Lund’s The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch, spell out the Norwegian word for “empty”. Approaching 38, he’s already a relic. He spends his days slumped at the kitchen table or staring out of the window, convinced that the ceiling is about to fall and crush him. He sobs about the state he’s in and the state of society around him. Of one thing he’s sure: “It is no longer me who cries, but the world, the world crying, in me.” Nordic weltschmerz: you’d have to be a saint not to giggle.Lund has been described by Karl Ove Knausgård as the “greatest Norwegian contemporary writer”; this novel, originally published in 1999, is his first to be translated into English. In it, Tomas describes himself, over and over and over again, as a “life-of-the-mind individual”. Cursed as much as blessed, life-of-the mind individuals have a keen and unconsoling sense of how things are (“one is a wretched, contemptible, and unworthy being”) and how things will end for them (“in the sewers of society, at nature’s nadir, incessantly ground down into the mud and the mire so that one day, millions of years from now, they become oil, life-of-the-mind oil, at the very bottom of life itself”). Is he making fun of himself? In 2026, he seems closer to an eco-prophet.Perhaps it was always meant to be this way. His family line consisted of poor, mostly illiterate farmworkers in eastern Norway and, after he moved away to university, he learned to speak about his upbringing in casual, almost condescending fashion. Over time though, especially as he travels across the country, he begins to question his snobbery. He’s aghast at how history is being turned into heritage, ancient folk traditions repackaged for tourists, culture seen as being not so much about lived experiences and relations as a commodity. Wildness is disappearing. Even mountain roads no longer wind like they used to. There are echoes of Thoreau in his invocations of “children getting lost in the woods, in a world without human signifiers, without signage or trails, only celestial bodies and natural forms”. Echoes too of John Berger’s Pig Earth, as he charts the impact of machinery on how peasants speak and engage with each other.double quotation markThis is a universal story of modernity and its discontents, but Lund is at pains to give it a Norwegian dimensionThis is a universal story of modernity and its discontents, but Lund is at pains to give it a specifically Norwegian dimension. Like one of Thomas Bernhard’s grumpus narrators railing against Austrian idiocracy, Tomas lays into his country’s governing class (“a gang of boasting sanctimonious humanistoid individuals”) which has ushered in “a thoroughly criminal, narcotised shopping-mall world”, a “Norwegian global hell” full of “pale, withered souls who seek solace in cinemas and fitness studios”. Listing his present-day false prophets – “computer engineers, course facilitators, business commissioners” – he sounds like someone who’s read the Unabomber Manifesto.What’s funniest – or maybe funny-tragic – is that Tomas thinks he can express all this not only in a think piece commissioned by the Royal Norwegian Ministry of Culture, but to the face of the culture minister herself. She is not amused, especially when he blurts out a four-letter word. Dragged out of her office by security guards, his reputation and social standing are destroyed. He’s assumed to be a nationalist, a Nazi even, is unable to get work, and becomes homeless.Then things get even worse: in a nightmarish middle section, somewhere between Hieronymus Bosch and Lars von Trier, he returns to his parents’ farm. He’s hoping to turn his back on decadent city ways, but there’s nothing Arcadian here. In this perverted pastoral Tomas digs ditches, lives with his drunken wife Helena, whose gaze is a “pustulated mongrel-eyed leer”, cages his mentally defective brother and dumps him in a remote Swedish village. Is this the authentic Norway he’s been hankering for? It’s in a state of decomposition and liquefaction – all slime, moonshine, blood, vomit, grease.Language is a key actor throughout. Paragraphs are often long, larded with clauses that repeat, with sententious neologisms that David M Smith translates as “enfletted”, “enhammered”, “vocabulation”. At other times, when Tomas lets go his urban sensibilities, the sentences are slangy and pungent.The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch is prescient about the “language forms” that digital capitalism requires – the data and information, the “demonic and inhuman” scientism, the fear of allegory. Its astonishing final section sees Tomas, alone in a forest, all ears. He can hear himself, his surroundings, the past, the future. He’s attuned to what connects him to shit, steel wire, dead plant tissue, bacterial cultures. Eureka! “That’s what I was. A kind of pulverised form of language which, by chance, had been imbued with natural substances, here and there.” Nordic weltschmerz: what a wonder it is.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
