title: On Another Planet They Can Save Me by Lieke Marsman review – an astonishing memoir of terminal illness | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: Published four months after her death, the poet’s reflections on mortality are both agonising and profoundly life-affirming
Author: Edward Posnett
Headline: Published four months after her death, the poet’s reflections on mortality are both agonising and profoundly life-affirming
Content: Lieke Marsman.Photograph: Tom CornelissenView image in fullscreenLieke Marsman.Photograph: Tom CornelissenBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewOn Another Planet They Can Save Me by Lieke Marsman review – an astonishing memoir of terminal illnessPublished four months after her death, the poet’s reflections on mortality are both agonising and profoundly life-affirmingEdward PosnettWed 21 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are no atheists in foxholes, goes the saying, and indeed social scientists and evolutionary biologists have argued that the experience of war or conflict drives religious belief; in 2019, Joseph Henrich and others surveyed almost 2,000 people in three post-conflict societies – Uganda, Sierra Leone and Tajikistan – and concluded that their experience of conflict had prompted them to participate in Christian and Muslim rituals and groups. Atheism, it seems, may be as fragile as faith.“No matter how attached you are to your own rational worldview, your rationality won’t survive long under the threat of imminent death,” writes the former Dutch poet laureate Lieke Marsman in her book On Another Planet They Can Save Me. Part scream, part song, it charts the gradual dissolution of her own rational assumptions, which govern everything from her views on God to extra­terrestrial life. It is a brilliant, playful, layered and humane plea for openness and hope in the face of her own foxhole of intolerable suffering.Marsman was not a soldier, but she knew a thing or two about living with constant reminders of her own mortality. In 2018, at the age of 27, the poet was diagnosed with a rare and incurable form of cartilage cancer. “There are little balls of failed cartilage in my lungs, balls that will slowly, agonisingly, take over until, at last, I suffocate,” she writes. When a doctor informs her that her illness is terminal, she lets out a scream. “[H]ow else are you supposed to behave when handed a death sentence?” she asks. Desperate to live, Marsman undergoes a barrage of treatments, including an operation to remove her arm and shoulder.double quotation markShe cites Pasolini, Alanis Morissette, Spinoza, Euripides and WittgensteinHowever grim her situation, there is remarkably little about her body in this book, and the trials of her cancer treatment, from surgery to immunotherapy. “After all, isn’t a disease only really interesting to the one who has it?” she wonders. “The temperature of my anus doesn’t affect the temperature of the world.” Instead, she writes about her relationship with certainty, gradually unpicking her own materialism and positivism. She opens herself to God, reads about the supernatural, and wonders whether aliens may come down and take her away. “Sometimes I think I’m going crazy, at other moments I think how crazy I was not to have allowed myself to broaden my perspective until now.”This is well-trodden ground, but Marsman’s language is so beautiful (her translator, Sophie Collins, has done a fine job), and her textual references so original, that it feels as if we are walking on fresh turf. Her range is wild: she cites Leopardi, Pasolini, Alanis Morissette, Robert Musil, Spinoza, Euripides, Wittgenstein and William James. The most interesting sections, for me, related not to artists’ or writers’ reflections on mortality or rationalism, but those of scientists who expressed doubts about the solidity of the scientific framework that they themselves constructed. “To speak in terms of Plato’s well-known simile,” wrote cosmologist James Jeans, “we are still imprisoned in our cave, with our backs to the light, and can only watch the shadows on the wall.”Side by side with these reflections are Marsman’s poignant memories of the quotidian reality of a terminal cancer diagnosis, which form a strange blend of the mundane with the otherworldly. She writes that she and her girlfriend spent hundreds of euros on empanadas. “[E]ven when you’re dying, you have to eat, and those things only need a blast in the oven.” When she wakes up from an operation without her arm, she recalls that the first thing she craved was … a croissant. If the narrative vibrates with pain, there are also releases of humour; at one point she considers all the absurd things she could do to spice up her obituary, such as crashing in a paraglider or go-kart.Any reviewer knows that the author may read what you have written; a review is intended for potential readers of a book, yes, but I also think of it as a dialogue with its author. Here there is no right of reply: Marsman died in June of this year, aged 35, and this book, more than a memoir, is a testament; to review it almost feels like a sacrilegious act, and perhaps it is best to let the author speak. “[D]ying with hope, however far-fetched and unrealistic that might be, is always better than continuing to live without it. And in those moments when everything in the here and now turns out to be utterly hopeless, I allow myself to think: on another planet they can save me.” I hope that that other planet exists, and somewhere, somehow, Marsman is still writing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: ‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon | Games | The Guardian
description: As video games chase spectacle, Modern Warfare 4 makes a case for putting character and consequence at the heart of its biggest battles
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: As video games chase spectacle, Modern Warfare 4 makes a case for putting character and consequence at the heart of its biggest battles
Content: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 combines large-scale battles with a story centred on the people caught up in the conflict.Photograph: ActivisionView image in fullscreenCall of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 combines large-scale battles with a story centred on the people caught up in the conflict.Photograph: ActivisionPushing Buttons newsletterGames‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weaponAs video games chase spectacle, Modern Warfare 4 makes a case for putting character and consequence at the heart of its biggest battlesDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 21 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn these strange, subdued weeks before the much-anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI, there have still been some welcome surprises. Onimusha: Way of the Sword revived a half-forgotten samurai action series with much aplomb, while Silent Hill: Townfall transported all of the franchise’s bloody, dread-filled psychological horror to … the picturesque Scottish coast. Even moreshocking to games writers, though, is the fact thatthe forthcoming Modern Warfare 4has one of the best Call of Duty campaign modes for at least six years – and might even be up there with the original Modern Warfare trilogy.The setting is an invasion of South Korea by its northern neighbour – a setup that could have fuelled a hundred instantly forgettable Netflix films, but hasproved controversialin a video game. The authoritarian regime has a new (fictitious) ruler and a powerful experimental weapon, which it’s not afraid to use as the opening gambit in an explosive attack. You take on the role of Park Hyun Jun, a conscripted South Korean soldier who, along with his small unit of similarly inexperienced grunts, gets caught in the firestorm as cities burn and enemy paratroopers fill the skies.On the other side of the globe, meanwhile, series hero Capt John Price has gone rogue, teaming up with cartel boss Valeria Garza to track down his nemesis, Makarov. How these narrative strands intertwine is the propulsive engine of the story, and along the way this game throws an arsenal of gigantic set-piece battles at you, edging you closer to a layered finale.Most positive reviews of the campaign mode have mentioned how the story combines its own ideas with themes and plots from the previous titles. So how did the game’s lead developer, Infinity Ward, set about creating a story that could support a giant first-person juggernaut such as CoD? “The DNA of a Modern Warfare story is that it is something you believe could happen in the real world,” says narrative director Jeff Negus. “‘Does it feel grounded?’ is the first question. Additionally, we ask, ‘What is going to resonate with a modern audience?’ It was important to us not to tell the same story again, not to show the same characters being the same people, because what they’ve been through has deeply affected who they are.”View image in fullscreenInfinity Ward says the story of Modern Warfare 4 puts its characters and their relationships at the centre of the action.Photograph: Infinity WardInfinity Ward brought in a range of military and cultural consultants to ensure the story’s accuracy. “Some of our actors were conscripted in Korea, so they’re able to identify with some of what’s happening,” says Negus. “We use a wide array of military consultants across many different branches and types of service. Our dialect coach, June Yoon, was invaluable because he understands the dialectical differences between North and South Korea, and he could help us reword lines in a more colloquially appropriate way.”One key element of the game is the combination of quieter, character-led narrative moments and apocalyptic action set-pieces. “There is a very healthy symbiosis between both parts,” says Negus. “We start with strong narrative and gameplay, and the very first thing that we ask is, ‘How can we interweave these things in a way that feels intentional?’ One must be complementary of the other, in such a way that we’re able to say, ‘I can’t imagine telling the story without this mechanic.’” Negus compares it to an explosion in an action movie, saying: “It can be spectacular, but if you don’t know the people who are a part of it, it won’t be meaningful. Back when I was working at Naughty Dog, and now with the team here, we talk about player-protagonist parity, and how, when you feel what the character feels, you’re all a part of the same story – the audience gets to be in on it.”Surprisingly, iteration is an important part of the process – even though this is a game filled with cinematic sequences that may have to be filmed and animated early in the development process. “We certainly map out the story visually,” says Negus. “Justin [Harris], our lead writer, will put in these story beats, much like a season of television or a movie would do, but we do it with levels. And sometimes we’ll need to move things around, particularly in a story where we can shift the timeline in certain ways. When someone comes up with something, it gets moved around, it gets debated and analysed, and it’s road-tested pretty hard before it becomes inked.”To me, the Modern Warfare 4 campaign is a story of dysfunctional families – the actual North Korean ruling family, Park Hyun Jun’s ragtag squad and Price’s Task Force 141. The tensions between these groups gives the story its human underpinning. Disaster movies usually centre on one or two main characters so that we, the audience, get to experience the drama vicariously through them.Infinity Ward has successfully brought that structural and emotional toolkit to the finale of the Modern Warfare series, and that’s at least partly why it works. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 might not be a Pulitzer prize-winning story, but in these odd days before the arrival of GTA VI it certainly gives you something to think about – and people to root for – as you blast away with your rifle, grenade launcher or helicopter gunship.What to playView image in fullscreenOver the Hill swaps military action for off-road exploration, inviting players to discover its landscapes at their own pace.Photograph: Funselektor LabsIf you like the look of extreme off-road driving sims such as MudRunner, but are put off by their unyielding difficulty level,Over the Hillis definitely for you. It’s a cosy exploration game where you drive a 4x4 through a bright low-poly landscape of babbling brooks and lush woodlands, occasionally using a winch to get out of muddy puddles or up steep hills.Along the way, you unlock cabins to allow fast travel and visit a mechanic to customise your vehicle. Spot an interesting bird or critter and you can photograph it, adding it to your scrapbook. The pace is slow and gentle, but there is a fulfilling challenge in mastering the winch and getting yourself out of tight spots.I wish more games simply gave you a world to explore and the tools to do it and then left you alone – although, if the solitude gets to you, there’s a co-op multiplayer mode too, so you can disappear into the wilderness with pals. Bliss.Available on:PC (coming to Switch, PS5 and Xbox in 2027)Estimated playtime:10-plus hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenThe Game Boy Museum’s catalogue has been adapted to run on a cartridge for Nintendo’s original handheld console.Photograph: Marcel Pflug“Let me be honest from the start: nobody was waiting for this.” Thus begins alovely Eurogamer featureon theGameBoy Museum, or more accurately, the museum’s creator, Marcel Pflug, and his attempt to fit the whole of hiswebsiteon to a cart that actually plays on a Game Boy. I love projects like this, which use games and games hardware as repositories of information. See also:The Uncensored Library, which collects banned books inside a Minecraft server.A question that haunts me, as a 55-year-old, is: “Why do I still play video games?” People are often ecstatic to tell me there are more constructive things I could be doing. I enjoyedthis essayby Lene Clement aboutthe non-utilitarian nature of gamesand the annoying lifestyle influencers who instruct us that “uselessness” is a bad thing because everything has to be productive now.I am readingThere Is No Antimemetics Divisionby Sam Hughes, better known asqntm. Now out inpaperback, it’s a novel about a government agency tasked with finding and battling “antimemetic” entities that feed on humans but can’t be seen, remembered or recorded. It’s a very video game-like premise and the staccato, almost episodic nature of the chapters reminds me of game missions. This is very much a recommendation.What to clickFrom Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six TacticsThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K eraPenguin Colony – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenGetting started on game design can be as easy as signing up for a course and building a prototype with software such as GameMaker.Illustration: Roman Motsak/Getty ImagesThis week’s question fromKatevia email is something I think all gamers have wondered:“If I had an idea for a game butno idea of how to create it, who would you suggest I contact? It’s more a game to learn things rather than [one with] combator sci-fi, etc.”Remember that old saying, often attributed to Thomas Edison: “Genius is 10% inspiration, and 90% perspiration”? The same goes for video-game design, or indeed film-making, painting and writing novels. Nobody will pay you for an idea, because everyone is having them practically all the time. The most realistic way to realise your idea is to sign up foragame development course, where you may find like-minded people who enjoy your concept and want to work with you. You could invest in an application such asGameMakerand start building your own prototype, or you could study game design via books or YouTube videos.I also highly recommendA Theory of Funby Raphy Koster,The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lensesby Jesse Schell andChallenges for Game Designersby Brenda Romero and Ian Schreiber. All of these provide a really good way to structure your ideas and think about how they may work as a functioning game. This way you can work on a design document that lays out all the rules and systems of your game, and this will help you discover if a) there’s something practical in it, and b) you have the drive and time to work on a game project. A great idea is a great start, but it is really only ever that: a start.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Our Friends in the North: The Thatcher Years review – old pals back on the toon as TV series gets squished | Theatre | The Guardian
description: They have appeared in epic BBC dramas since their RSC debut but Peter Flannery’s immortal foursome now return in an 80s-focused play
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: They have appeared in epic BBC dramas since their RSC debut but Peter Flannery’s immortal foursome now return in an 80s-focused play
Content: Likely lads … Jack Robertson and Scott Turnbull in Our Friends in the North at Newcastle Theatre Royal.Photograph: Chris BishopView image in fullscreenLikely lads … Jack Robertson and Scott Turnbull in Our Friends in the North at Newcastle Theatre Royal.Photograph: Chris BishopTheatreReviewOur Friends in the North: The Thatcher Years review – old pals back on the toon as TV series gets squishedTheatre Royal, NewcastleThey have appeared in epic BBC dramas since their RSC debut but Peter Flannery’s immortal foursome now return in an 80s-focused playMark LawsonWed 21 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe four thwarted, postwar north-eastern dreamers created by dramatist Peter Flannery have now played more than a whole day of drama across different formats. The 1982 RSC world premiere of Our Friends in the North featured almost four hours in the lives of lawyer-councillor Mary, drifting philanderer Tosker, photo-journalist Nicky and petty criminal Geordie. The award-winning 1996 BBC Two version ran 10 hours, as did the 2022 Radio 4 adaptation. Now Flannery brings the quartet home to the stage and toNewcastle(where the first version toured) in another play.Starting in 1964, with Labour PM Harold Wilson promising a new Britain, the first stage version ended in 1979, as Margaret Thatcher’s victory heralded a rightwing transformation. Exploiting the way that saga dramas test characters against landmark events, the TV version took them to 1995 (brink of Blair) and the radio one to 2020 (Boris Johnson and Covid). It would be intriguing to know if the idealism of these now triple-locked pensioner characters burns again under Burnham, but Flannery has tracked back to 1979-85, adapting the sixth (Thatcher in) and seventh (miners out) TV episodes.View image in fullscreenEpic courtship … Ryan Nolan and Sam Neale in Our Friends in the North.Photograph: Chris BishopA piece begun when he was an RSC writer in residence always had Shakespearean ambitions and these continue with the tremendous Trevor Fox, like the Chorus in Henry V, galvanising our imaginations and dropping historical footnotes. Fox, who starred in the TV and radio series, doubles as Nicky’s dementia-affected dad, Felix, a subplot especially poignant in what will be a memory play for much of the audience.All forms of the story have used soap opera domestic tension to offset socialist history and here the epic courtship of Sam Neale’s Mary and Ryan Nolan’s Nicky affectingly shows campaigners for social change yearning for romantic conformity. The largely wasted lives – the piece’s bleak sub-theme – of Tosker and Geordie are caught by Jack Robertson, pointlessly optimistic, andScott Turnbull, accepting defeat. Jude Nelson makes a small part large as a Tory MP who achieves a prophetic early breach in Labour’s “red wall”. The politics are Kinnockian, accusing Labour’s Militant tendency and miners’ union leader Arthur Scargill of swelling a rightwing electorate that led to 18 years of Tory rule.View image in fullscreenKinnockian politics … Our Friends in the North.Photograph: Chris BishopThe different Our Friends in the North directors have tended to panic at its politically expository dialogue and in this case it sometimes feels as if director Jack McNamara is searching for action such as slow-motion strobing for clashes between colliery pickets and riot squads.For completists, this is a must-see but, paradoxically, it feels incomplete. In all media, the story has had length and breadth and, though these two episodes were a logical choice, Flannery perhaps acknowledges losses from selection and compression when Fox’s Chorus laments: “There’s always so much more to say.” The events depicted partly explain why a regional theatre would struggle to put on an all-day epic, but this dramatically immortal foursome needs it.AtTheatre Royal, Newcastle, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMargaret ThatcherNewcastleTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Why has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shaped | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Ibrahim Mahama put an entire factory in this exhibition exploring Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism. And it’s just one dazzling installation in a show full of hope
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: Ibrahim Mahama put an entire factory in this exhibition exploring Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism. And it’s just one dazzling installation in a show full of hope
Content: Not left to rot … parts of an old bottle factory appearing in Ibrahim Mahama: The Harvest Season, Fondation Cartier, Paris.Photograph: Benoit FougeirolView image in fullscreenNot left to rot … parts of an old bottle factory appearing in Ibrahim Mahama: The Harvest Season, Fondation Cartier, Paris.Photograph: Benoit FougeirolArt and designReviewWhy has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shapedFondation Cartier, ParisIbrahim Mahama put an entire factory in this exhibition exploring Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism. And it’s just one dazzling installation in a show full of hopeEddy FrankelWed 21 Oct 2026 08.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 08.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIbrahim Mahamahas dug through the ruins of post-colonial Ghana, sorted through the ashes of its ancient history, picked through the industrial detritus, the corporate waste, the piles of rubbish, and found something pretty unique: hope.View image in fullscreenIbrahim Mahama, pictured at the Barbican Centre, London, in 2025.Photograph: Christian Cassiel/Barbican CentreSit on one of the Asante stools in his circular Parliament of Ghosts and you can almost feel a new future being worked out right in front of you. It’s the first installation in this huge exhibition at the Fondation Cartier inParis, and it sums Mahama up pretty neatly. He’s looking at the collapse of the Ghanaian government in 1966, the way the hope of the post-colonial project was crushed in a military coup, and he’s looking at ancient Ghanaian history, at the empires that fell centuries ago and the way colonialism tore them to shreds. But he’s not lamenting any of them. He’s not mourning. Instead, he’s reclaiming them, asking how things can be rebuilt, how we can move forwards by learning from the past.And he does it over and over. In 2024 he bought an old bottle factory – a symbol of industry and its collapse. He’s rebuilt it here, in the centre of Paris. Its steel roof beams, rusted and crumbling, reach up to the ceiling, its walls are lined with thousands of green bottles in Coca-Cola, Schweppes, Kool and Club Minerals crates. It’s a whole history of manufacturing, of commerce in WestAfricapost-independence. Not left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new.View image in fullscreenNot left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new … Parliament of Ghosts by Ibrahim Mahama.Photograph: Benoit FougeirolNearby, he’s taken some of those bottles and piled them around a collection of local pottery. The industrial meets the artisanal, two lost arts creating a new one.But this huge show isn’t really about Mahama, it’s about the people around him. Most of the work here is by nine other artists and collectives. Mahama runs three art centres near Tamale inGhana, giving time, space and opportunities to local artists. Their work is given priority here, alongside art by his mentors and collaborators. He’s taken this massive exhibition opportunity and used it as a chance to celebrate his community. It’s almost as if he’s trying to make the rest of us feel bad.Way up on the top floor, a long scroll of jute and bark byDorothy Akpene Amenukeundulates across the floor. If it looks like Mahama’s work, it should: she was his art teacher back in 2013. Knowledge, and the past, gets reconfigured and reshaped once again.Nearby, the wall of a farmhouse has been built by artist and architectCourage Dzidula Kpodoout of red earth clay, a material lost as modernism brought in concrete. Now, historic methods become a kind of resistance, a symbol of tradition’s ability to endure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHistoric methods as a kind of resistance … an artwork from Ibrahim Mahama’s The Harvest Season, Fondation Cartier, Paris.Photograph: Benoit FougeirolThose core ideas get repeated through pretty much every presentation here. Influential 97-year-old photographerJames Barnorcaptures the communities around Mahama in large format, grainy Polaroids.Gideon Appah’s hazy, dream-like paintings imagine fictional Ghanaian youths staring out to sea, congregating on beaches in utopian, idealised visions of the country’s past. Some of the works are absolutely stunning, like Peter Doig and Noah Davis transported to Accra.The best work, appropriately enough, isn’t by one artist but a collective. On the top floor, a bunch of lumpy, surreal sculptures of birds, bodies and men wrestling bulls is by theCongolese Plantation Workers Art League (CATPC). Each one is made of chocolate, sculpted in the DRC but poured into moulds in Amsterdam. Everything they make from selling the art goes towards buying back land confiscated in the early 20th century by the Lever Brothers, who we now know as Unilever. The work is a whole conversation about global trade taking place in sculptural form, an act of resistance and reclamation through chocolate.This exhibition is essentially an ambitious, ultra-idealistic group show of West African art. It is art exhibition as political utopianism. Which is great, even if not everything in it is good. And the real draw is Mahama, with his archival approach to monumental installation art, and it’s a shame to not get a load more of it.Mahama has sacrificed himself for the greater good, basically. But this collaborative approach is the point: he’s saying collective action, community, togetherness, that’s how we’ll build a future. It might sound a bit cloying and earnest, but then you see the results, you see the art and the ideas, you see the community and the hope and the idealism and you eventually say: “Get me a one-way ticket to Accra. I’m in.”Ibrahim Mahama: The Harvest Season is atFondation Cartier, Paris, from 22 October to 28 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designInstallationExhibitionsGhanaColonialismAfricaArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: High School Musical review – Disney fave is sweet, slick and as squeaky clean as ever | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Harry Judd is the coach while KayCee Stroh from the original movies is back to play a teacher in the hoop-shooting, pompom-waving romance
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: Harry Judd is the coach while KayCee Stroh from the original movies is back to play a teacher in the hoop-shooting, pompom-waving romance
Content: Entertainingly grating … Luke Bayer and Caitlin Tipping in High School Musical.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEntertainingly grating … Luke Bayer and Caitlin Tipping in High School Musical.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewHigh School Musical review – Disney fave is sweet, slick and as squeaky clean as everTroubadour Wembley Park theatre, LondonHarryJudd is the coach while KayCee Stroh from the original movies is back to play a teacher in thehoop-shooting, pompom-waving romanceHolly O'MahonyWed 21 Oct 2026 06.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince soaring on screen 20 years ago, this Disney Channel favourite has cemented itself as a squeaky clean, painstakingly earnest but no less beloved descendant of Grease. Like Danny and Sandy, Troy Bolton and Gabriella Montez share a holiday romance and wind up at school together the following term, where the social pecking order initially keeps them apart. Driven by a shared love of singing, they defy conventions to end up together.This new stage production, first seen at Salford’s Lowry, is directed by Hope Mill theatre founders Joseph Houston and William Whelton. No, it can’t escape the limitations of the story’s spectacularly two-dimensional characters, who are siloed into the camps of jock, brainiac or drama kid, and whose stock traits are indulged in the book by David Simpatico, but it’s bright and buzzy nonetheless.View image in fullscreenBright and buzzy … Tobias Turley and Leonor Correia in High School Musical.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe thrust stage of Andrew Exeter’s basketball-themed set positions us courtside, while Rory Beaton’s bright lights, Matt Peploe’s thunderous sound design and George Reeve’s videography – beamed on to screens surrounding the gym – help animate the spectacle playing out on court, where the school’s Wildcats team are shooting hoops and pompom-waving cheerleaders are drumming up hype.It’s dizzying and dazzling – never more so than during the revival of Bop to the Top, led by Luke Bayer and Caitlin Tipping as siblings Ryan and Sharpay Evans, who are every bit as entertainingly grating as their screen counterparts. Aaron Renfree’s nimble choreography rotates montages from the all-important science competition, basketball game and musical callbacks, as Troy and Gabriella race against the clock to make it to auditions.View image in fullscreenNimble choreography … Harry Judd, centre, in High School Musical.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe headline names belong to the teachers: KayCee Stroh, who played hip-hop-loving Martha Cox in the films, is now over-the-top drama teacher Ms Darbus, while McFly’s Harry Judd plays austere Coach Bolton with brow-furrowed concentration.As Troy and Gabriella, Tobias Turley and relative newcomer Leonor Correia bring a sweetness, but their chemistry is yet to fully bloom. Gabriella’s When There Was Me and You is, here, a duet sung by the pair of them in an arrangement that cops out of the high notes, but throbs with teenage longing. Breaking Free really does see them soar, albeit on a stiff-looking swing.Still, if it skirts the ring more than it nets the ball, I suspect adoring fans won’t leave disappointed.AtTroubadour Wembley Park theatre, London, until 3 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Cyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’ | Cyndi Lauper | The Guardian
description: As she auctions off her treasures, the synth-pop savant opens up about her eccentric style and why she doesn’t believe in cancel culture
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: As she auctions off her treasures, the synth-pop savant opens up about her eccentric style and why she doesn’t believe in cancel culture
Content: Cyndi Lauper.Photograph: Greyshock. Courtesy of Bonhams.View image in fullscreenCyndi Lauper.Photograph: Greyshock. Courtesy of Bonhams.Cyndi LauperCyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’As she auctions off her treasures, the synth-pop savant opens up about her eccentric style and why she doesn’t believe in cancel cultureOwen MyersWed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeforeCyndi Lauperrose to fame as one of the most singular pop breakouts of the 1980s, she was queen of the cash register at the edgy Manhattan boutique Screaming Mimi’s. The vintage emporium is still a downtown staple, but a little of its spirit comes uptown this month withCyndi Lauper: A Suitcase of Memories, a two-part auction of her fashion and personal items at the New York auction house Bonhams.Cyndi Lauper review – 80s pop eccentric hasn’t changed a bitRead moreOn a recent Thursday morning inNew York, the singer is sporting seafoam green hair and is in good spirits as she leads a private tour of the collection. It is an Aladdin’s cave of outfits from her five-decade career, with clashing prints, jutting tutus and statement headwear in every color you can imagine. As she strides around in her platform creepers, she gives a few final notes to the Bonhams team. Is that rainbow fan at the right angle? And can we confirm that more mirror balls are on their way?“Over there is my grandmother’s pyjamas,” she says, walking over to a mannequin that displays the leopard print sleepwear Lauper wore in theGirls Just Want to Have Fun video. The ensemble was originally purchased from her family’s favorite mail order catalog. “Frederick’s of Hollywood gave people in Queens a glimpse of glamor and sexiness,” she says. “You know, they’re flannel pyjamas, but come on – they’re leopard!”View image in fullscreenLauper’s leopard print pyjamas from the Girls Just Want to Have Fun video, 1983.Photograph: Courtesy of BonhamsBorn in Queens, Lauper was raised as part of a large family who worked in New York’s Garment District as cutters and seamstresses. After leaving home at the age of 17 armed with not much more than a toothbrush and a copy of Yoko Ono’s book Grapefruit, she honed her eclectic style while working at Screaming Mimi’s in between singing at downtown local clubs.“I went to art school but I didn’t finish,” Lauper says. “So what happened is this, I guess.”Lauper captivated a generation with performances which combined music with art and fashion, selling more than 50m records. Her fantastic debut She’s So Unusual became the first debut album from a woman to produce four top-five singles upon its release in 1983. Hits like True Colors and I Drove All Night followed, as well as new ventures: she co-founded the True Colors United foundation in 2008 to benefit homeless LGBTQ+ youth and, in 2013, won a Tony award for her Kinky Boots score.View image in fullscreenCyndi Lauper.Photograph: Greyshock. Courtesy of BonhamsAfter retiring from live performance last year, Lauper says she is enjoying the chance to take stock. Leading us past the metal bra and headdress from her True Colorsvideoand a red plaid dress she wore to the inaugural VMAs in the early 80s, she seems nostalgic for the freedom of the decade. “It was a time where there was a little bit of a wildness,” she says. “We’ve been corporatized – we kind of have braces on our brains. You know, it would be nice if you could think for yourself sometime.”As well as ephemera such as handwritten lyric sheets, the exhibition features a Raggedy Ann doll from the Girls Just Want to Have Fun video and a multi-colored spotted couch that could have come from the set of Pee-wee’s Playhouse. “I did this to inspire people,” Lauper says of the show. “To inspire us who are older to remember the individuality of creativity, and to inspire the young to discover that creativity is individual.”Lauper is a great storyteller – I could listen to her anecdotes for hours – and as no-nonsense as you might expect from a born-and-bred New Yorker. As we admire the singer’s newspaper skirt from her True Colors album art, a guest asks Lauper if she worried that the fragile-seeming skirt would fall apart. “What do you mean? No,” she replies crisply. “It was aphotoshoot. I was good.”View image in fullscreenLauper’s newspaper skirt ensemble from the True Colors album cover shoot.Photograph: Courtesy of BonhamsLast year,Chappell Roanwore a replica of the newspaper skirt while inducting Lauper into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Lauper says that Roan is the one of the few current stars whose creativity she relates to.I can see that with Roan’s edginess and use of color. “It’s not just that,” Lauper tells me in a conference room later that morning, adding that she sees songs like Pink Pony Club as landmarks for LGBTQ+ representation. “It’s how she wrote about a lifestyle and made it normal. And then the clothes, sure.”In 2022, Lauper released a new version of her abortion rights song Sally’s Pigeons to protest against the US supreme courtoverturningRoe v Wade. “If we don’t have control over our own bodies then we have no real freedom,” she said at the time. “We need to mobilize. We need to let our voices be heard.”She sees the exhibition as coming at a “great time to have people inspired and come alive again” as the midterms approach. Despite gentrification squeezing out artists from the city, she says “the good news is that, because of Mamdani, the billionaires might be moving out, giving us our city back.”In 2023, Lauper gave her blessing forNicki Minajto sample Girls Just Want to Have Fun in a song from Minaj’s Pink Friday 2 album; Lauper joined her on stage for a performance a few months later. Given Minaj’s recent alliance with Donald Trump, does she feel differently about the collaboration now?“No,” Lauper says flatly. “First of all, I don’t believe in cancellation. And second of all, the fact that she did Girls Just Want to Have Fun musically – it’s a political thing anyway, babes.“Girls just want to have fun. They’re entitled to a joyful experience in this world. Like it or not, we’re here. We’re not going out in the rice fields any more. Yes, rise up and put your foot down, and she did. I don’t know what she’s doing now. But I still don’t think you cancel people, because otherwise there’s no room for discussion.”View image in fullscreenCyndi Lauper.Photograph: Ruven Afanador / Courtesy of BonhamsLauper says that she learned the importance of breaking bread with those across the political spectrum through her advocacy work. “If you want people to listen to you, you need to listen to people,” she says. “If you don’t let people evolve, what are you doing?”Vast Beatles museum, hailed as ‘extraordinary’ by Paul McCartney, to open in Liverpool in 2028Read moreThe exhibition shows how Lauper’s own tastes evolved too. In the 90s, she became increasingly drawn to sculptural pieces from Vivienne Westwood andAlexander McQueen, styling designer pieces with a DIY twist. For 1994’s Twelve Deadly Cyns album, she paired an electric blue Dolce & Gabbana shrug with a bowler hat that she spray-painted and decorated with feathers to match. “I wanted it to look like art,” she said, pausing by the ensemble as she wraps up the tour. “I remember that because it was another invention.“That’s what makes it exciting,” she says. “That a young person would look and go, ‘I could do that.’”Cyndi Lauper: Suitcase of Memories, Part Iis a live auction at Bonhams New York on 22 October.Part IIruns online until 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsCyndi LauperExhibitionsNew YorkPop and rockElectronic musicNicki MinajChappell RoanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: New prize launches for books co-written with AI | Books | The Guardian
description: After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs
Content: Once upon a time … the prize was founded by tech entrepreneurs.Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOnce upon a time … the prize was founded by tech entrepreneurs.Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty ImagesBooksNew prize launches for books co-written with AIAfter months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMsElla CreamerWed 21 Oct 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA prize for AI-written books has launched this week.The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA invites submissions of manuscripts co-written with AI tools, with the winner promised publication.Entrants are asked to submit an unpublished manuscript of between 10,000 and 50,000 words, along with information about which AI model and prompt were used to generate the text. All major language models are allowed, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA. Entrants can be based anywhere, but entries must be submitted in French.The Prix Pascal is named after Blaise Pascal, a French polymath who helped invent one of the first mechanical calculators and also wrote theological texts, including Pensées, which Pope Francispraised forits “philosophical depth and literary charm”.While the terms and conditions ask for a work of fiction, the prize also states that submitted texts should help solve an ethical, social or ecological problem threatening humanity. The prize was founded by Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré, all of whom are technology entrepreneurs.Rodriguez is a founding partner at the mergers and acquisitions advisory firm Avolta, and is described as a “leading figure in the European crypto and blockchain industry” on the company’s website. Serviant is a digital media entrepreneur and former chair of the LGBTQ+ magazine Têtu. Meanwhile, Mentré is a former civil servant with a PhD in philosophy who teaches at Harvard and the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Mentré also co-founded Electis, an online voting platform.The Prix Pascal is launching after months of controversy over the possible use of AI by finalists and winners for a number of literary prizes this year, including theCommonwealth short story prize, theCaine prizeand thePrix Goncourt, France’s most prestigious literary prize.Applications for the Prix Pascal opened on Tuesday, with entrants invited to submit via theprize’s website, and are set to close at the end of November. A shortlist of 10 will be drawn up before the winner is announced in early December. The jury will be made up of a panel of five or six writers, critics, journalists, philosophers and publishers, to be announced early November.Explore more on these topicsBooksAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingAwards and prizesFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: A grieving female elephant carrying a stillborn baby: Federico Veronesi’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘She carried the dead calf for hours even though it wasn’t hers. She had had a miscarriage two years before – and now picked up the stillborn babies of other mothers’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘She carried the dead calf for hours even though it wasn’t hers. She had had a miscarriage two years before – and now picked up the stillborn babies of other mothers’
Content: ‘People sometimes think it’s a young elephant hugging its mother’ … Federico Veronesi’s award-winning photograph.Photograph: Wildlife photographer of the Year 2026View image in fullscreen‘People sometimes think it’s a young elephant hugging its mother’ … Federico Veronesi’s award-winning photograph.Photograph: Wildlife photographer of the Year 2026My best shotArt and designA grieving female elephant carrying a stillborn baby: Federico Veronesi’s best photograph‘She carried the dead calf for hours even though it wasn’t hers. She had had a miscarriage two years before – and now picked up the stillborn babies of other mothers’Interview byChris BroughtonWed 21 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy love of African animals, in particular elephants, dates back to when I was three or four years old, growing up in Milan in a house full of old nature books. When I was six, my parents took me on my first safari in Kenya – I cried on the plane home, feeling I was being torn away from the savanna I’d dreamed of, somewhere I really loved. But for the past 20 years, that’s where I’ve lived, guiding photographers on the Maasai Mara National Reserve and elsewhere in Africa.I’ve spent time photographing other animals, especially big cats, but elephants are still my favourite subject. They have this extraordinary presence, dominating the landscape and making it come alive. I love to follow them in different habitats. They are extremely adaptable – in Kenya they’re associated with the savanna and acacia woodland, and they can also live in extremely arid areas, such as the deserts of Namibia, where this photograph was taken.I was there last September, guiding a group of photographers. We had been following a group of elephants walking along a dry riverbed as night fell. Even though there is no water in these rivers, they retain some vegetation and act as a lifeline for the elephants, who follow them from the hills in the west towards the Atlantic Ocean.Because it’s a sandy river, it was quite easy to follow their tracks until we found them again the next day. But among the tracks was something quite unusual, like a dragging mark. Sometimes bull elephants, when they’re full of testosterone, will do crazy things to demonstrate their power and intimidate their opponents – I’d seen one lift a log before, and thought perhaps that’s what was being dragged.double quotation markI’ve since read that 17 out of 19 calves born during the past four years have not made it. She has been picking them upWe drove on until we found them, and that’s when I realised one of the females was carrying a baby. When people see this picture, they sometimes think it’s of a young elephant hugging its mother, but in fact the calf is dead and the leg you can’t see is wedged between the adult’s tusk and trunk. As I took this photograph, another elephant was approaching and the female swung her head so the baby was lifted up and out of its way. I have other photographs that make the reading of the scene more straightforward, but this one leaves the interpretation open and adds a layer of mystery.We followed the herd for several hours, and the female carried the calf for the entire time, only putting it down so she could feed before picking it up and continuing on her way. She was still carrying it when we last saw her – eventually the elephants started climbing into some rocky hills where we couldn’t follow.I’ve since read that 17 out of the 19 calves born in that area during the past four years have not made it. There’s clearly a problem, but researchers aren’t yet clear why this is happening. What has come to light, however, is that the elephant carrying the calf was not its mother, as I had assumed. Her mammary glands were not swollen as they would have been if she’d recently given birth, and the researchers were able to identify her as a female who had a miscarriage a couple of years before, and had since been seen picking up the stillborn calves of other mothers. In a sense, that makes the image even more deep and profound, as it implies that she perhaps hasn’t moved past that trauma.Most of my elephant photographs are in black and white. Sometimes I use colour – in Tsavo, Kenya, elephants are often covered in red earth, which makes for a striking contrast against green vegetation, and in Etosha, Namibia, there’s a place where they visit a waterhole full of white clay and end up looking like ghosts. But black and white highlights the texture of elephants’ skin, and also, as here, removes distracting elements and exposes emotion in a more straightforward way.This is a painful image to look at, but at the same time it reveals so much of the psychology of elephants, their interior complexity, personality and feelings. Here we see a creature that feels just as much as we do, that experiences the same grief at losing a baby, the same sense of not wanting to let it go. My hope is that photographs like this help people realise how important it is to coexist peacefully and respectfully with animals that look different to us on the outside, but inside are very similar.This image is the adult grand title winner of Wildlife Photographer of the Year. The exhibition is at theNatural History Museum, London,until 11 July 2027.View image in fullscreenFederico Veronesi’s CVBorn:Milan, Italy, 1975. Moved to Kenya in 2002High point:Probably this award, and the three books I publishedTop tip:Explore ways to convey emotions to the viewer through your photographs, carefully choosing light, atmosphere, shooting angle, framing, backgrounds, and so onExplore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotConservationWildlifeWildlife photographer of the yearPhotographyNatural History MuseumfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Wonderhaul: has Liam Gallagher really got into metal detecting?  | Liam Gallagher | The Guardian
description: The Oasis frontman and famous fibber has claimed on social media that he is a budding detectorist. Some might say it’s a perfect fit, but either way, the gentle pastime is booming in the UK
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The Oasis frontman and famous fibber has claimed on social media that he is a budding detectorist. Some might say it’s a perfect fit, but either way, the gentle pastime is booming in the UK
Content: A jacket made more for rainy fields than stadiums? Oasis on The White Room in 1995.Photograph: Des Willie/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA jacket made more for rainy fields than stadiums? Oasis on The White Room in 1995.Photograph: Des Willie/Getty ImagesLiam GallagherWonderhaul: has Liam Gallagher really got into metal detecting?The Oasis frontman and famous fibber has claimed on social media that he is a budding detectorist. Some might say it’s a perfect fit, but either way, the gentle pastime is booming in the UKStuart HeritageWed 21 Oct 2026 06.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiam Gallagher is one of the country’s foremost trendsetters. When Oasis emerged in the 1990s, you couldn’t move for the sight of young men doing their darndest to look like him – wearing parkas and swaggering around as if they had just wolfed down a breakfast that didn’t agree with them.Which is to say, we should probably expect stocks of metal detectors to run low in the coming days, because Gallagher has apparently outed himself as a keen detectorist. “I’m a big fan of the metal detector phenomenon,” hetweeted on Sunday, adding in a separate message that: “I do it for the buzz n the bing.”View image in fullscreenGoing underground … a beach-based detectorist.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/ReutersAssuming that Gallagher is telling the truth here – and that’s a big assumption, given his tendency to tweet falsehoods about everything from the existence of a newOasisalbum to the possibility that Peppa Pig would soon join them on drums – doesn’t it make perfect sense?View image in fullscreenA British Museum photograph of Tudor coins found in the New Forest, Hampshire.Photograph: The Trustees of the British Museum/PAIf nothing else, it means that he has finally found an appropriate pastime for his uniform. It’s a little ridiculous for him to wear big coats when he’s singing songs to thousands of people in a stadium, but stick him in a field on a drizzly Thursday afternoon and it suddenly all falls into context. Plus, you know, what is Oasis if not an exercise in getting stuck in the quagmire of the past?And if it is real, it couldn’t be more timely. Metal detecting, by all accounts, is on the up and up. Not only do 1% of British adults say they have tried metal detecting in the last year, but they are finding things at an extraordinary rate. Last year the government released itsreported treasure findsfor 2023 and 2024, noting that a provisional 2,883 pieces of reported treasure were found across the UK (though not including Scotland) over those years – the highest figure since records began – with many of the finds being acquired by museums. And the overwhelming majority of these treasures were discovered by metal detecting.‘Something special’: Mackenzie Crook and Toby Jones on bucolic comedy beauty Detectorists, 10 years onRead moreNow, there is no point attributing this popularity solely to Gallagher, because he has only just jumped on to the bandwagon. More likely the rise is down toDetectorists, the bucolic comedy-drama written by Mackenzie Crook, and co-starring Toby Jones, which ran from 2014 until 2022. That show was so gentle, and painted such an idyllic picture of detecting, that membership of the National Council of Metal Detecting has reportedly quadrupled over the last decade.And, excitingly, there is still plenty out there to be discovered. More than 800 iron age objects wereunearthed in North Yorkshire’s Melsonby hoardin 2021. That same year, amedieval gold coinworth almost £650,000 was found in Devon. And two years before that came theChew valley hoard, where seven Somerset detectorists found 2,584 silver coins that were subsequently valued at £4.3m.With riches like this still lying beneath our feet, no wonder Gallagher has taken to the pursuit with such aplomb. Especially since, given the perennial palaver over his band’s ticket prices, he seems especially well versed at extracting every last penny from well hidden spots.Explore more on these topicsLiam GallagherOasisArchaeologyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best gifts for nine-year-olds, picked by nine-year-olds and parents | Toys | The Guardian
description: Popcorn makers, Lego Fortnite and the coolest water bottle around … surprise the mini tween in your life with our pick of the top gifts and toys
Author: Zoë Phillimore
Headline: Popcorn makers, Lego Fortnite and the coolest water bottle around … surprise the mini tween in your life with our pick of the top gifts and toys
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterToysThe best gifts for nine-year-olds, picked by nine-year-olds and parentsPopcorn makers, Lego Fortnite and the coolest water bottle around … surprise the mini tween in your life with our pick of the top gifts and toysThe best gifts for eight-year-oldsZoë PhillimoreWed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe start of the tween years, nine years old, is a sweet spot between curiosity and growing independence, making it a fun, though sometimes tricky, age to buy for.Kids at this age are up for a challenge, whether that means trying a trickier craft set, playing a more complex game or stepping up their sporting interests. Pitch a gift right and you’ll not only get the whoop of joy when they first receive it, but something that will hold their interest and help them develop their skills, interests and hobbies over time.How I selectedView image in fullscreenVarious gifts and toys were sent to nine-year-olds for testing and feedback.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianAs an experienced toy tester, I have dedicated a lot of my career to observing children play. I’ve worked in schools as a teaching assistant and in children’s publishing, where knowing what makes children tick is essential. I also have three children of my own, so I understand what works on home turf once the gift-opening frenzy is over. When researching for this article, I aimed to strike a balance between children’s outlandish wishlists (one Christmas my son asked for a ghost for his present) and what a parent wants in their home (not a ghost).I spoke to a lively gang of nine-year-olds with varied interests and hobbies who were only too happy to shout over each other about what they want for Christmas. I also checked in with their parents on the gifts that got their seal of approval – and offered long-term value – and spoke to childhood play experts about the best presents to suit this stage of development.Testing primarily took place at home with one nine-year-old tester, with additional help from their friends. I also spoke to other nine-year-old children and had gifts sent to them for testing and feedback, so it wasn’t just one kid’s opinion. I noted the child’s initial reaction, how they used a toy and whether they returned to it. After testing, we had a lot of surplus toys in our house, so anything that could be donated went to the Salvation Army, which sells preloved items to raise money for its work.The best gifts and toys for nine-year-oldsOn the right trackView image in fullscreenTrain of thought: our tester found Mexican Train dominoes easy to pick up, with plenty of room for strategy.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian“I want a game called Mexican Train dominoes. I played it with my older cousins on holiday, and it was fun,” says one of my nine-year-old testers. This game was pretty fast-paced and was easy to pick up, with some strategywhen we played it. Players build their “train line” by matching tiles up to a central hub – but you can sneakily block each other’s play. “Peer-based play is really valuable for nine-year-olds,” saysLaura Moore-Williams, an early years consultant. “Children value being part of a group at this age. More advanced games, team sports and long-term creative projects give them a sense of belonging and achievement.” This set comes in its own box, making it easy to take to their mates’ houses.View image in fullscreenJaques of London Mexican train dominoes£28.72 at Jaques of London£27.99 at AmazonMaterials:resin, plastic, wood, metal tinSuitable for:6+Colourful creations“I would like some really good colouring pencils. I’m really into comics – I started a comic club with my friends. And I’m trying to get my artwork better. I think colouring pencils might help my drawings look more grown up,” says one nine-year-old tester. Whether they’re into comics or other creative projects, a decent set of colouring pencils is a great open-ended gift for kids of this age. I spent a long time sitting with my tester, colouring side by side using these pencils. My nine-year-old loved how softly they glided across the page, and how they produced smooth, even shading. The non-slip surface is comfortable to hold for extended periods; there’s a great range of colours; and they’re made from a durable wood-based composite containing upcycled wood chips from PEFC-certified forests.View image in fullscreenStaedtler 24 Norix colouring pencils£13.99 at Tesco£9.40 at AmazonMaterials:wood, oil, pigment, binder, waxSuitable for:6+A stitch in time“I really enjoyed doing this hanger project,” says one of my nine-year-old testers. “I did sewing in school on a project last year, and wanted to do more.” This little kit is an ideal party bag gift or rainy-day project to have in your back pocket for kids of this age. It’s not too prescriptive as there’s no set design, so it requires the child to work out what they want to create first. I found this called for gentle assistance when my tester tried it – although my ideas for letters or nature scenes got vetoed in favour of a Minecraft Creeper. Whether you get roped in or not, it’s a nice way to develop fine-motor skills for nine-year-olds working towards their pen licences at school.View image in fullscreenCotton Twistmake your ownstitched banner decoration£4.95 at Not on the High Street£4.95 at Cotton TwistMaterials:cotton, metal, woodSuitable for:5+Pet soundsI was stuck in a battle between my nine-year-old wanting to listen to music independently and my desire to keep them screen-free. Then I found the Mighty 3, and it has kept us both happy. It may remind some of the iPod Shuffle – it’s a tiny box you can upload music to and then whack your headphones into. My young tester has loved developing the art of playlist curation, poring over Spotify for hours with parental supervision. You then upload these playlists on to the Mighty using its app (Spotify Premium account required), and you’re ready to go. It has transformed long car journeys and even an 11-hour flight, and my tester has enjoyed the independence and grownup feeling it’s given them. It is worth noting that Mighty will stop supporting Spotify from April 2027 and only be compatible with Amazon Music.View image in fullscreenMighty 3£89.99 at Mighty£99.99 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, electronic componentsSuitable for:8+Flight of fantasy“I loveLegoand Fortnite,” says one enthusiastic nine-year-old. “This Lego is absolutely perfect!” Kids at this age are able to focus on longer-term projects – especially if they catch their interest. This is a good option even if they don’t yet play Fortnite but know it’s “cool”. My tester and I spent many happy hours sitting side by side building this set. The recommended age is 10+, but my nine-year-old relished the challenge. You end up with a toy (there are a generous nine minifigures in the set) that can be played with or put on display.View image in fullscreenLego Fortnite Battle Bus£89.99 at Lego£90 at ArgosMaterials:plasticSuitable for:10+Sip happensWater bottles are a big deal to kids – they’re a way for them to show off their personal style at school, where they’re otherwise in uniform. Many nine-year-olds are desperate to feel more grown up, and Owala’s FreeSip for adults won mybest water bottletests earlier this year. On a practical level,it’s durable, easy to use and (less important for the nine-year-old, but key for the adult) easy to clean. This is a smaller version of my winner, which makes it lighter for kids to carry around all day. The different colourways available allow for self-expression, and they’re popular, so they’re a big tick in the “trending” box.View image in fullscreenOwala Kids FreeSip water bottle£25.99 at Owala£26 at NextMaterials:BPA‑free Tritan plastic, silicone, stainless steelSuitable for:3+Get your skates on“My friends all play with Tech Decks at school during playtime,” a nine-year-old tester told me. “They’re so cool. You can learn tricks. And they fit in my pocket for school. I really want some new ones for my collection.” This enthusiasm for a finger skateboard might mystify adults – myself included – but nine-year-olds seem crazy for them. This set is a good place to start – there are various “ramps” you can invest in later if you want. This set comes with six boards, 20 wheels and four trucks, plus stickers. My tester enjoyed customising their boards with the trucks and wheels included (they’re interchangeable) and spent a long time trying to master tricks; I live in hope that this transfers to a love of actual skateboarding.View image in fullscreenTech Deck Sk8shop bonus pack£17.95 at Maqio£13.99 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, metalSuitable for:6+Stay in the pictureView image in fullscreenSnap happy: our tester loved printing and decorating their photos with this instant camera.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianMy nine-year-old tester loved this instant camera. They snapped photos, printed them off and coloured them in or stuck them up around their bedroom. The camera feels grown up but still has a foot in the “toy” arena. The Photo Creator is similar to the Fujifilm camera our11-year-oldsrated, but it’s less pricey to run for impulse-driven nine-year-olds as it prints on rolls of paper rather than Instax film. As it’s technically a thermal printer, it only prints in black and white, but there are kid-friendly filters they can put on the photos and an all-important selfie lens.View image in fullscreenPhotoCreator instant camera£45 at Argos£45 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, electronic componentsSuitable for:8+Put your records on“I love this mini record player that really plays music,” one nine-year-old tester told me. “You can build up a mini record collection with the surprise balls.”(The balls in question are plastic spheres that have collectible items inside – in this case teeny records – and you don’t know which ones you’re going to get before you open them, which apparently adds to the fun.)Every child who came across this record player seemed totally transfixed. “It was the biggest hit for my daughter,” one friend told me. “I love that she’s listening to records – I hope it’ll get her into vinyl.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWho knows if it’ll stick, but the delight of playing a record was palpable with my nine-year-old tester. It comes with one record – APT by Rosé and Bruno Mars – and you canadd to your collection with the capsules, which are £15 for two capsules with four records each. Put a record on the turntable, and the record player will play an extract of the song using chips to trigger digital playback. I only wish I could play my vinyl on it – but alas it’s not compatible with standard records.View image in fullscreenMini Brands Really Works Vinylplay set£20 at Argos£19.99 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, electronic componentsSuitable for:3+Turf wars“We have family game nights at home, and I’d like a more grownup board game now I’m nine,” my tester told me. Kids at this age have a better understanding of cause and effect, helping them think critically and solve problems. “Valuable play for children aged nine includes social games for interaction,” says Sydney Piercey, former au pair and nanny, and author ofSustainable Play. Risk ticks all of those boxes, and should see them through game nights into adulthood. Wannabe despots can conquer territories and control the world by deploying armies, attacking opponents and forming temporary alliances. Fair warning though: nine-year-olds are probably going to need an adult or two to play with them to explain and supervise gameplay.View image in fullscreenRisk board game£35 at Argos£32.99 at AmazonMaterials:cardboard, plasticSuitable for:10+Lights up“My brother got a circuit set for his birthday, and now I want one too. I want to make the ultimate circuit that does loads of cool things,” says my nine-year-old tester. This set should cater to their every wish, with 175 different projects. You simply link the components together to make various circuits that do exciting things – the glow-in-the-dark fan was a favourite with my tester. Instructions guide you through simple circuits, but during testing I noticed how quickly kids of this age learn and experiment. It quickly felt like a miniature version of the Blackpool Illuminations had been created on my dining table, and when a circuit didn’t work, my tester did some problem-solving. I just sat back and became the battery supplier (unfortunately it rinses through them at an alarming rate – and they’re not included).View image in fullscreenSnap Circuits light set£94.95 at CyntechMaterials:plastic, metal, electronic componentsSuitable for:8+Snuggle up“I love getting new pyjamas,” says my nine-year-old tester. No matter your age, a new pair of PJs rarely misses if you’re looking for a good gift. These by Polarn O Pyret are the best pyjamas I’ve found – and my research has been extensive. They’re made from organic cotton and are just the right weight for all but very warm weather. Plus, they wash so well – I’ve put pairs through so many cycles, and they haven’t faded, but the cotton softens beautifully. The foldable cuffs are designed to let the PJs grow with your child, the stripes are a crowd-pleaser, and they’re available in several colours to keep everyone happy.View image in fullscreenPoP striped pyjama set£30 at Polarn O PyretMaterials:organic cottonSuitable for:1+Laugh out loudView image in fullscreenPage-turner: Diary of a Wimpy Kid had our nine-year-old tester laughing out loud.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian“Everyone in my class has been reading this book, and I want to get into it,” one nine-year-old told me. Diary of a Wimpy Kid is a great book for kids of this age as the format – drawings, onomatopoeia bubbles (eg “Boom!”) for making sound effects, and short chapters – makes it accessible. The story follows relatable but hapless Greg as various annoying (yet funny) things happen to him at school and in his family life. It made my nine-year-old roar with laughter. It’s quick to read, but this is the first in a lengthy Wimpy Kid series.View image in fullscreenDiary of a Wimpy Kid£7.99 at the Guardian Bookshop£5.99 at AmazonMaterials:paperSuitable for:8+The sky’s the limit“My child enjoyed GraviTrax marble runs well below the recommended age … he continues to play with it aged 11,” says Daisy Upton, play specialist and author of theFive Minute Mumbook series. These sets are brilliant for nine-year-olds who like to problem-solve and get creative in a hands-on way. The SkyTrax is a newer addition to the popular GraviTrax range, and allows builders to create complex marble runs that change levels, flip the marbles and spin them around. I found it almost dizzying how fast the marbles fly around the track. It’s definitely more complex than any other marble run I’ve tested, but a great “next step” for nine-year-olds who enjoy this kind of play.View image in fullscreenGraviTrax XXL SkyTrax action set£79.99 at John Lewis£88.63 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, metalSuitable for:8+Movie-night snacks“Movie night just got so much better,” whooped my nine-year-old tester when we fired up this popcorn maker. Many niche kitchen appliances feel like a bit of a novelty (we looked at chocolate fountains and slushie makers too), but this gadget felt exciting to use – my young tester loved watching the popped corn pouring out of the canister – and it gets plenty of use in our family, where popcorn is a movie-night must. This maker works without oil, which was a nice bonus for me.View image in fullscreenLakeland popcorn maker with bowl£37.99 at Lakeland£37.99 at AmazonMaterials:metal electrical components, plasticSuitable for:8+ with adult supervisionMaking memoriesIf you’re still stuck for an idea, an experience gift is great for a nine-year-old. They’re old enough to enjoy the anticipation and start to accept that “things” aren’t everything. It’s possible to buy vouchers for theme parks such as Legoland, and for other activity experiences. I took a nine-year-old to Legoland recently, and they completely embraced the day. They were able to tolerate queueing and were tall enough for all the rides. Otherwise, Virgin Experience Days offers a wider range of activities such as treetop adventures, theatre tickets and crafting days.View image in fullscreenLegolandgift vouchersFrom £39 at LegolandExperience gift voucherFrom £13 at Virgin Experience DaysWhat to buy for nine-year-olds“The key developmental needs of nine-year-olds are building confidence, identity, teamwork and deeper problem-solving skills,” says Moore-Williams. “They’ll be interested in group games, coding and tech, creative expression (art, music, writing) and competitive sports.ToysI really rate for this age group include advanced Lego sets, Stem kits like Snap Circuits and coding robots, strategy games, arts and crafts kits and sports equipment.”Kids of this age are able to dive into more complex play – and are desperate to do so and feel more grown up. They want to be challenged by trickier craft kits and board games, and many will enjoy more complex imaginative play too – character-based figures might scratch that itch well. All these types of play can give them a sense of achievement and boost their self-esteem and resilience. “So much holistic learning and development can be supported through opportunities to play games together in groups,” says Moore-Williams.The experts I spoke to all acknowledged children’s need for sociable play with their peers. Getting them active with team sports or games is important at this age. More than one expert recommended buying a ball for a nine-year-old – they’re versatile for so many different types of play and easy to take around with you. “A small football is portable, sociable and can be played independently and together,” says Piercey.What to get for nine-year-olds who don’t play with toys?Many of the nine-year-olds I spoke to mentioned an experience gift. There is a good variety to choose from, including theatre vouchers, an annual pass to an attraction and days out. Some parents I spoke to asked people to contribute towards sports-club membership as a gift too. While this may not have the immediate “play” factor, it should make the recipient feel seen and supported.A Noble Giftlets you bid on experiences such as being a football mascot or tickets for kid-friendly concerts (though be warned, some are very pricey), with the winning bids going to charity (an additional platform fee applies). If you have something specific in mind, you can always contact the organisation to see if they will allow you to do something with them, even if it’s not readily available as a voucher.For more, read our guides to thebest toys and gifts for eight-year-olds, thebest toys and gifts for seven-year-oldsand thebest sustainable toys for kidsZoë Phillimore is a journalist with 20 years of experience. She’s tested many things, from mattresses to makeup, and she’s slightly obsessed with finding small new businesses to spotlight. Aside from this, Zoë loves travel, being outside – especially on the beach – and finding screen-free things to keep her three very active children busy.
