title: Sali Hughes on beauty: cream blush sticks for every skin type | Beauty | The Guardian
description: With new shades and formulations, the latest cream blush sticks are eminently wearable
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: With new shades and formulations, the latest cream blush sticks are eminently wearable
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Sali Hughes on beautyBeautySali Hughes on beauty: cream blush sticks for every skin typeWith new shades and formulations, the latest cream blush sticks are eminently wearableSali HughesWed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s something so irresistible about cream blush sticks. The fact that one can scribble on and smoosh in the instant appearance of good health makes sticks a practical handbag essential that ticks off both lips and cheeks.Whereas previous incarnations were broadly samey and could mostly be differentiated by colour alone, the new crop includes a formulation for any skin type – even oily.Milk Makeup built an entire brand on easy, “back of a taxi” application sticks of cream colour. And so the new reformulation of their push-up bronzers, contours and blushers brings the excitement of a full relaunch. The opportunity wasn’t wasted. The newLip & Cheek Blur(£24) is not for me, but it’s absolutely for someone blessed with some natural oil in their cheeks who might previously have struggled to make cream blush stay on. Shade, a very pretty brownish mauve that (it must be said) looks very similar to Merit’s popular Bespoke, is gorgeous and blends out softly with either fingers or brush.double quotation markThe finish catches the light, but not in a year 9 school disco way – this looks healthy, carefree and chicSpeaking of Merit (its Flush Blush creams are among the most popular out there, after all), Jones Road’s recently droppedBlushing Sticks(£30), feel and look pretty identical, so if you love those, you’ll love these. The shades are very different and, as is typical of Jones Road, very easy and wearable. Bare is a suits-everyone rose that gives a flush of good health on any skin tone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSali Hughes on beauty: a buzzy new brand is aimed at women over 40 – and the industry is taking noticeRead moreKosas’s recently launchedImpressionistMultisticks(£32) are emphatically for skins, tastes and temperaments able to handle shiny, glassy colour that will probably need topping up in the afternoon. But one application of Nuance, a muted, pinky beige, and another of Intuition, a dusty shade of pink, had me fully on side. The shades here are exceptionally well chosen and hard to find elsewhere. The finish catches the light, but not in a year 9 school disco way – this looks healthy, carefree and chic.My most worn of the lot has been Bobbi Brown’sSkin Enhancer Multi-Stick(£29), specifically Beach, an irresistible warm, toasty brown with a hint of pink that resembles – in the best possible way – slightly sunburnt skin. The formula is one of the brand’s best in a while – less shiny than the Kosas, but with more slip than the Milk Makeup and with a wear time that sits somewhere between the two. It can be daubed on carelessly, and the moisturising formula won’t rip up any foundation or powder you’ve laid underneath.Explore more on these topicsBeautySali Hughes on beautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to turn brown bananas into the best vegan bread of the bunch – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Use over-ripe fruit to flesh out this loaf with chocolate, spelt and miso – truly top banana
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Use over-ripe fruit to flesh out this loaf with chocolate, spelt and miso – truly top banana
Content: Tom Hunt’s chocolate, spelt and miso banana bread.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s chocolate, spelt and miso banana bread.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodHow to turn brown bananas into the best vegan bread of the bunch – recipeUse over-ripe fruit to flesh out this loaf with chocolate, spelt and miso – truly top bananaTom HuntWed 21 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter nine years, I can’t believe I’ve never written a recipe for banana bread for this column, so it had better be a good one, especially after I picked up a huge bunch of brown bananas at the corner shop for next to nothing the other day. This is a vegan bread made with olive oil instead of butter and with the mashed bananas acting as a binder in place of eggs; I’ve also added some miso to boost the umami and overall satiety – the salt enhances the sugar, boosting the sweetness while rounding it off nicely. In the interest of biodiversity and flavour, I’ve used wholemeal spelt flour, but any will do.Chocolate, spelt and miso banana breadThis has become our go-to banana bread at home because it has crazy levels of deliciousness. The recipe is inspired by a plant-based banana bread recipe I found onLaura Wright’s wonderful The First Mess website, and my tweaked version of her loaf uses extra-virgin olive oil and wholegrain flour for nutrition, flavour and biodiversity; I’ve also used miso instead of salt, to bump up the umami factor.Makes1 loaf280g wholemeal spelt flour1 tsp ground cinnamon1 tsp baking powder1 tsp bicarbonate of soda150g dark chocolate chunks150g walnut pieces6 very ripe bananas120ml maple syrup, or brown sugar120ml extra-virgin olive oil1tsp vanilla extract1 tbsp miso, or ½ tsp saltHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and grease and line a 1kg bread tin. Mix the flour, cinnamon, baking powder and bicarb in a large bowl. Set aside about seven pieces each of the chocolate and walnuts to decorate the loaf later, then stir the rest into the flour mix until well distributed. Peel five of the brown bananas and, in a second bowl, mash them with the maple syrup, olive oil, vanilla extract and miso. Add the banana mix to the bowl of dry ingredients, stirring until properly combined, then pour into the bread tin and level out the top. Peel the last brown banana, cut it in half lengthways and arrange on top of the dough with the reserved chocolate and walnut pieces. Bake for an hour, until just cooked through, then leave to cool before slicing.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteBreadFruitBakingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Veggie Thursdays and vegan surprises! How Ghent became a plant-based paradise | Food | The Guardian
description: In 2014, 13% of the population of this Belgian city described themselves as flexitarian. This year, 83% did. Here is how everyone was convinced to eat their greens – and love them
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: In 2014, 13% of the population of this Belgian city described themselves as flexitarian. This year, 83% did. Here is how everyone was convinced to eat their greens – and love them
Content: Cheesy pumpkin quiche and salad is served at a social restaurant in Ghent called Parnassus. The restaurant is set in a former Franciscan church.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCheesy pumpkin quiche and salad is served at a social restaurant in Ghent called Parnassus. The restaurant is set in a former Franciscan church.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianEuro visionsFoodVeggie Thursdays and vegan surprises! How Ghent became a plant-based paradiseIn 2014, 13% of the population of this Belgian city described themselves as flexitarian. This year, 83% did. Here is how everyone was convinced to eat their greens – and love themRachel DixonWed 21 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSixty bowls of slime-green soup sit waiting for the children to arrive. Pupils rush in from their morning lessons, grab the bowls by the handles and start slurping. No complaints, no refusals. (OK, maybe a few “bleurgh” faces.) Chicory soup dispatched, they get stuck into the main course: falafel, Mediterranean vegetable tagine and couscous. Some ask for seconds; most grab a piece of fruit for dessert and run out to play.This is a typical Thursday lunchtime in BS De Stadspoort primary school in Ghent, Belgium. Similar meat-free menus are being eaten in other schools and nurseries across the city, plus community centres, care homes and assisted living facilities, not to mention many work canteens and restaurants. Thursday in Ghent is officially“Veggie Day”, with residents encouraged to eschew any meat or fish. So how did a city get its children – and everyone else – to eat their greens?View image in fullscreen‘Veggie Thursday’ for schoolchildren in Ghent.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianIt didn’t happen overnight. “The success story of Ghent is one where we had an amazing grassroots movement, with people asking for more climate action. But the magic happened when politicians actually listened and implemented policy to introduce the Thursday Veggie Day in 2009,” says Vanessa Debruyne, the head of communications for the nonprofit organisationProVeg Belgium, who is showing me around town. “It got the ball rolling, companies and restaurants joined, the population got used to it, and more entrepreneurs made the move to plant-based. We’ve been unstoppable ever since! Ghent is the best town in Belgium for plant-based food.”Veggie day was just the start, agrees Hafsa El-Bazioui, the Green deputy mayor of Ghent, who has cycled over to join us (the city centre has been largely car-free since 2017). “A few years ago, we changed to prioritise plant-based protein,” she says. In 2021, the Flemish government launched theGreen Deal Protein Shift– a commitment to switch the ratio of animal to plant proteins consumed from 60:40 to 40:60 by 2030. Ghent has already reached the target.View image in fullscreenHafsa El-Bazioui, right, the Green deputy mayor of Ghent, chats to schoolchildren.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianAs well as vegetarian Thursdays and vegetarian options every day, school caterers have turned traditional meat dishes such as burgers, sausages and meatballs into hybrids, cutting out at least half the beef or pork and replacing them with, say, lentils. Stews might combine meat with chickpeas or beans. An incredible amount of effort is put in to making each dish taste good: they are screened by a “taste panel” made up of dietitians, chefs, childcare professionals and people with sensitivities to flavour, bitterness, texture and mouthfeel. Recipes are constantly modified and improved after feedback from children, parents and school staff. As a result, children get to eat the food they know and like, but the dishes are healthier and better for the planet – Ghent has reduced the carbon footprint of its school meals by 38% since 2018.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to make desserts that everyone could enjoy’ … Laura Verhulst, founder of Madam Bakster.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianAlthough she is a vegan herself, El-Bazioui believes reducing meat consumption across the board is the most effective and achievable policy, rather than trying to convince people to cut it out altogether. “When you approach a lot of people, the impact is more than if you focus on a small group of vegans,” she says. “That’s my philosophy in food, in politics, in life.”This stealth approach is echoed all over the city. I pop in to theViernulvier art centre, AKA De Vooruit, for a chat with Tom De Vleesschauwer,its kitchen coordinator – De Vooruit is as popular for its large art deco cafe as for its programme of theatre, dance, film and music. “A few years ago, we made oat milk the default: if you don’t ask for cow’s milk, you get oat,” says De Vleesschauwer. “About 90% of customers now have oat milk. If we had a sign saying you can choose, it would only be 10-20%.”There have been other changes in De Vooruit’s cafe, too. The soup is now always vegan; the dish of the day is vegetarian; the staff and performers are served a daily “Ottolenghi-style vegetarian buffet” instead of cheese and charcuterie. And, as in the school canteens, the few meat dishes on the menu – today just spaghetti bolognese and meatballs in tomato sauce – have been hybridised. “We cut down the meat by 70% and increased the carrots, cutting them to the same size – 30% still gives the flavour and the idea of meat, and carrots give sweetness,” says De Vleesschauwer. “People say plant-based is niche, but we have a very wide audience.”There are plenty of fully vegan businesses in the city, too, such asMadam Bakster, where I drink coffee with homemade hazelnut milk and devour rich, chewy chocolate-chip cookies fresh from the oven. Laura Verhulst, the founder, sees her cafe as more, not less, inclusive. “I wanted to make desserts that everyone could enjoy: vegan, allergen-free, non-refined sugar,” she says. AtKnol & Kool, a vegan restaurant-cum-minimart, 85% of customers aren’t even vegetarian. The owner, Stijn Sprengers, says: “Our vibe is not, ‘Fuck you, meat-eaters’. We try to be as hospitable as possible and make everyone feel welcome.”View image in fullscreenCoffee with homemade hazelnut milk at Madam Bakster.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianOh!Mais a restaurant specialising in plant-based Belgian comfort food. “We serve meals that feel like home: stew, vol-au-vent, meatballs,” says Hannah, a student and waitress. “We introduce it to people’s lifestyles in a non-pushy, non-in-your-face way. A lot of people are shocked the food is vegan. Most walk-ins don’t realise.” The restaurant makes all its own plant-based meat alternatives and condiments, such as Belgium’s beloved sauce andalouse, essential with fries. It says each plant-based dish saves up to 5kg of CO₂ and 2,000 litres of water compared with its animal-based equivalent.Hannah isn’t a vegetarian herself, but Oh!Ma’s “chicken” and mushroom vol-au-vent and “cheezy bacon” loaded fries have won her over. “I prefer the betterballs [a vegan take on the bar snackbitterballen] to the originals,” she says. “I’m looking for plant-based more often. I thought it wasn’t going to taste good – working here has changed that.”As well as these sorts of independent businesses, Ghent also has a proud tradition of affordable “social restaurants”, where all are welcome – tourists included – and prices for residents vary according to their ability to pay. I have lunch atParnassus, a social restaurant in a beautiful former Franciscan church, where a two-course meal is €16 [£13.50] full price, or €7/€3.50 for those receiving certain social welfare benefits. Last year, 67% of customers paid a discounted rate. The cost includes a vegetable soup (today courgette) and a choice of two main courses. As it is Thursday, the two mains are vegetarian (a big wedge of cheesy pumpkin quiche) and vegan (seitan and mushroom stew with roast potatoes), both served with salad. There is a meat option twice a week and a fish dish on Fridays, meaning 70% of the menu is vegetarian or vegan.View image in fullscreenAt the vegan restaurant-cum-minimart Knol & Kool, 85% of customers are not even vegetarian.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianNicholas, the head chef, explains his cooking style. “We believe in pure enjoyment with a minimal impact on the planet,” he says. “We cook as natural as possible: fresh, healthy and without heavy cream or fats. We also actively fight food waste.” He and his team feed about 180 people a day, sometimes as many as 250, and produce almost zero waste. Lunch is winding down when I arrive, but the church is still half full of people of all ages: alone, in couples, with family or groups of friends.View image in fullscreen‘We try and make everyone feel welcome’ … Stijn Sprengers, owner of Knol & Kool.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianParnassus is one of four restaurants operated byAteljee, a company that runs employment projects in Ghent; other initiatives include secondhand shops, a bike shop, city gardening and digital skills hubs. Tom Wauters, Ateljee’s general manager, says: “The restaurants employ people who have been long-term unemployed, to help them get back into the labour market. We strongly believe that everyone has talents.” The chefs at Parnassus are certainly talented – my stew is delicious – and the daily changing menus are full of creative plant-based dishes.After lunch, I head to a biotech lab on a science park that is part of Ghent University. This is the home ofThose Vegan Cowboys, a new venture by the founders of The Vegetarian Butcher, an alternative-meat brand now owned by the Dutch company Vivera. Ghent has a history of fostering plant-based innovation: the dairy-free brand Alpro was founded here in 1980, and is still headquartered in the city.View image in fullscreen‘The cheese of the future’ … a test camembert developed by Those Vegan Cowboys.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianThose Vegan Cowboys are at the cutting edge of the protein transition. They are producing casein – the animal protein used in cheese production – from microorganisms instead of cows, sheep and goats. Steven Geysens, the head of molecular biology, explains why. “Cheese is one of the main things people crave when they go vegan. It is the holy grail of animal-free products.”Why is vegan cheese still, by and large, so bad? “No plant protein has the same effect as casein. It is important for gelation, stretchiness, meltability, nutritional value, taste …” Geysens says that alternative cheese makes up just 1% of total global cheese purchases, whereas dairy-free milks now constitute 14% of milk sales. He shows me around various rooms in the lab, where white-coated technicians are busily working away. I feel humbled that so many brilliant minds are devoted to giving vegans a tastier cheeseboard, but Geysens corrects me – Those Vegan Cowboys have a far bigger vision. They see this as the cheese of the future.View image in fullscreen‘About 90% of customers now have oat milk’ … Tom De Vleesschauwer, kitchen coordinator at De Vooruit.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The Guardian“This is something that can be durable, sustainable and help feed everyone on the planet. It will have less saturated fat and be lactose-, antibiotic- and hormone-free.” He shows me figures that demonstrate dairy cheese’s environmental impact: it is the worst food in terms of water use, and worse than pork for land use and greenhouse gas emissions. Farmers will still be needed to make animal-free cheese, he says, to grow lower-impact crops such as sugar beet to be used in the fermentation process. “It’s good for farmers to have an opportunity to diversify,” he says.View image in fullscreenSeitan and mushroom stew with roast potatoes at a Parnassus.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianTwo cheese scientists, Hannes Decadt and Mathilde Blin, proudly show me some of their creations: gouda, camembert, mozzarella and feta. They look exactly like the real thing and I’m desperate to try them, but sadly they are still going through the EU’s stringent food safety regulations. I’ll have to rely on the scientists’ verdicts: “We know we’re not completely there yet,” says Decadt. “It’s much closer to real cheese than all the vegan cheeses on the market because of the casein. It’s the same texture. Now we’re focusing on ripening.” Blin will know they’ve cracked it when she is happy to serve her camembert to her parents: “My family are French and they’re really harsh, so they’re the best critics,” she says.What else does the future hold for Ghent? ProVeg is now focusing on higher education. Next month, it isrunning a campaignin 15 universities and colleges, taking plant-based chefs into student restaurants to run cooking and tasting sessions. It is also looking at healthcare, having alreadyhelped one psychiatric hospitalto double the number of plant-based meals, andlinked up other hospitalswith local organic vegetable farmers.View image in fullscreenCheese scientists Steven Geysens, Mathilde Blin and Hannes Decadt of Those Vegan Cowboys.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer/The GuardianI wonder why Ghent’s protein transition has proved so successful. Debruyne thinks it is due to a “unique combination” of public pressure and policy. Verhulst, the baker, believes the change is linked to Ghent’s strongly socialist history and the energy from its large student population. “It is anchored in the identity of the Ghent spirit. In Antwerp, for example, everything is perfect and symmetrical. Ghent is more alternative.”Whatever the reason, it is working. “Twelve years ago, 13% of the population described themselves as flexitarians. This year, a whopping 83% did,” says Debruyne. “It’s a silent revolution.”Explore more on these topicsFoodEuro visionsVegetarian food and drinkVegan food and drinkVeganismVegetarianismBelgiumfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mushroom magic: Alissa Timoshkina’s eastern European soup and stew recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Two dishes that may feel like “home” to cooks connected to the region
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Two dishes that may feel like “home” to cooks connected to the region
Content: Alissa Timoshkina’s mushroommačankastew with potato pancakes.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenAlissa Timoshkina’s mushroommačankastew with potato pancakes.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.FoodMushroom magic: Alissa Timoshkina’s eastern European soup and stew recipesA tangy mushroom stew with potato pancakes for dipping, and a rustic but versatile cabbage and mushroom soupAlissa TimoshkinaWed 21 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 03.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAthick, creamy and tangy wild mushroom stew, inspired by Belarusianmačankaand traditionally served with thick buckwheat pancakes for dipping. My version, however, features another Slovak dish in the form oflokše, which are crepes or flatbreads made with mashed potato dough. The result issogood. Then, a simple, seasonal soup made with just a handful of ingredients that captures the heart and soul of eastern European soup making. While it doesn’t belong to any single location, I hope it will taste like “home” to readers connected to the region.Mushroommačankastew with potato pancakes (pictured top)I first came across this dish a few years ago when working on my previous cookbook,Kapusta. The recipe was brought up in a conversation with a wonderful food writer of Belarusian lineage, Anastasia Zolotarev, whom I’d asked to contribute to the book. Mačanka did not make it into Kapusta, but I was very glad to see it in Anastasia’s own debut book,Sour Cherries and Sunflowers. Looking into the origins of the dish, I have discovered that mačanka exists in Slovak cuisine, too, where it appears as a thick soup infused with sauerkraut brine – oh my! Both dishes are rooted in central and eastern European peasant culture of simple, hearty, nutrient-rich stews made with a handful of accessible ingredients. So here is my own play on both recipes.Prep20 minCook1 hr 30 minServes4–6For the stew100gsalted butter1 onion, peeled and thinly sliced2 garlic cloves, peeled and minced1tsp fresh or dried thyme600gchestnutmushrooms, slicedSalt and black pepper, to taste30gdried porcini, soaked in 250ml just-boiled water150mlsauerkraut brine, or to taste30gplainflour300mlsinglecream2tbsp chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley, to garnishFor the topping2tbsp vegetable oil1 onion, peeled and finely sliced1 small pinch sugar1 small pinch saltFor the pancakes350gpotatoes, quartered125gplainflour, plus extra for dusting1 small egg, beaten1 pinch saltButter, melted, for brushingMelt half the butter in a large saucepan on a medium heat, add the onion, garlic and thyme, and fry for 10 minutes, until the onion softens. Add the sliced fresh mushrooms and a generous pinch of salt, cover and cook for about eight minutes, until they release their liquid. Strain the porcini through muslin, reserving the liquid. Rinse the porcini to get rid of any residual grit, then chop finely and add them and the reserved soaking liquid, plus the sauerkraut brine to the pan. Season with black pepper and simmer on a low heat for 15-20 minutes, to develop the flavours.In a second pan, melt the remaining butter, stir in the flour and cook, stirring constantly to avoid any lumps, for two to three minutes, until lightly golden. Gradually whisk in the cream to make a smooth sauce. Stir this into the mushroom base and cook uncovered for about five minutes, to thicken.To make the topping, heat the oil, then fry the sliced onion with the sugar and salt until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen towel. Top the stew with the fried onions when ready to serve, and don’t forget a sprinkle of fresh parsley!To make the pancakes, put the quartered potatoes in a small pan of salted water, bring to a boil, then simmer for 20-25 minutes, until cooked through. Drain thoroughly, then mash well and leave to cool completely.In a large bowl, combine the cooled mash with the flour, egg and salt, and mix to form a dough. Transfer to a well-floured surface, roll into a 5cm-diameter log, then cut into 12 equal pieces. Roll each piece into a ball, then use the rolling pin to flatten each ball into a 3mm-thick disc.Put a dry, nonstick frying pan on a medium heat. Lay the pancakes in the hot pan (cook them in batches, if need be) in the hot pan one at a time, and cook for two to three minutes on each side, until golden brown spots appear. Remove, brush one side with butter, then stack and keep warm under a clean tea towel. Serve with the mushroom stew.Cabbage and mushroom soupView image in fullscreenAlissa Timoshkina’s simple cabbage and mushroom soup.This soup is wonderfully versatile, easily adapting to the seasons and whatever ingredients you have to hand. Swap fresh cabbage for sauerkraut or fresh mushrooms for dried in this hearty staple that comes together almost effortlessly.Prep15 minCook40 minServes4–62tbsp neutral vegetable oil1 onion, peeled and diced2 carrots, grated1 pinch caraway seeds1 pinch dried thyme1 pinchsalt250gchestnutmushrooms, chopped½ small cabbage(350g), shredded2–4 potatoes, diced1½ litresvegetable broth1 bay leafFresh dill, to garnishBlack pepper, to tastePut the oil in a lidded stockpot or saucepan on a medium-low heat, add the onion, carrots, caraway, thyme and salt, and fry for eight to 10 minutes.Add the mushrooms, cook for another five to eight minutes, or until their liquid is released, then add the cabbage, potatoes, vegetable broth and bay leaf. Simmer gently for 15-20 minutes, until the potatoes are cooked through but the cabbage still retains a little bite. Garnish with plenty of dill and black pepper.These recipes are edited extracts from Lozhka: Eastern European Soups, Stews & Other Things We Eat with a Spoon, by Alissa Timoshkina, published by Quadrille at £28. To order a copy for £25.20, visitguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFoodSoupStewVegetablesEastern European food and drinkPotatoesHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I can charge my car for £6’: could new rules cut costs for EV drivers? | Motoring | The Guardian
description: Owners in England with no driveway can now slash their costs by installing a cross-pavement gully – but it’s a postcode lottery
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Owners in England with no driveway can now slash their costs by installing a cross-pavement gully – but it’s a postcode lottery
Content: By charging in front of their house via an energy supply in their home, rather than using a public charger, drivers can cut the cost by up to 90%.Photograph: Kerbo ChargeView image in fullscreenBy charging in front of their house via an energy supply in their home, rather than using a public charger, drivers can cut the cost by up to 90%.Photograph: Kerbo ChargeMotoring‘I can charge my car for £6’: could new rules cut costs for EV drivers?Owners in England with no driveway can now slash their costs by installing a cross-pavement gully – but it’s a postcode lotteryShane HickeyWed 21 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Alison Williams bought her electric Volkswagen ID.3 two years ago, she thought she was making the right choice for the environment, having already upgraded her end-of-terrace London home with insulation and solar panels.However, charging the car has proved more costly than she hoped, as she is not able to install the cross-pavement gully – a narrow electric vehicle cable channel embedded in the pavement – that she would need to charge at home. That will remain the case despite a change in the law.From Wednesday, drivers inEnglandwho do not have off-street parking will no longer need to get planning permission to put in a pavement gully outside their home.The gullies sit flush within the pavement and allow an EV charging cable to reach a parked vehicle without creating a trip hazard.View image in fullscreenThe EV charging cables reach parked vehicles through a gully in the pavement, so there is no trip hazard.Photograph: Gul-eBy charging in front of their house via an energy supply in their home, rather than using a public charger, drivers can slash the cost byup to 90%.But some of the 9.3 million households without off-street parking will be left frustrated as more than 20 local authorities will still not allow the installation of gullies after the law changes.Williams’s council is Ealing, whichdoes not allow themfor cost and safety reasons. She charges her car at a public charger, at much greater cost than if she could do it at home.“It’s really frustrating,” Williams says. “When we decided to buy an electric car … the reason we wanted to buy one was for the environmental impact.“You either have to have enough money to have a house with a driveway, or you have to be able to afford the additional cost of charging at a public charger.”The rulesMotorists are not allowed to string EV charging cables across the pavement from their home to the road, but many councils allow cross-pavement charging if you use a gully. To use one, a charging cable is run from the home through the gully and then plugged into the car.This previously meant getting planning permission from the local authority.double quotation markSimpler rules will make it easier for people to switch to an electric carLib Dem peer Caroline PidgeonRemoving that step will save drivers between £300 and £500. However, anyone who lives in a conservation area will still have to apply.Caroline Pidgeon, a Liberal Democrat peer, campaigned for the change in the law. She says one in three households in England do not have a driveway. Approval for the gullies has taken up to 15 months in some areas, she says. “Simpler rules will make it easier for people to switch to an electric car,” she adds.The government has given £25m in funding to councils in England for pavement gullies for people with on-street parking, but the money is being distributed in different ways, depending on the local authority.The costsHow much you pay for installation varies widely around the country.If you want to apply for a gully to be installed, you should check with your council to see whether it allows them and, if it does, it should direct you on how to apply.Kerbo Charge, a company that installs gullies, operates a postcode checker you can use to see whether you can get one in your area and sign up for an alert if that changes.View image in fullscreenA Kerbo Charge employee demonstrates the company’s charging gully.Photograph: Kerbo ChargeBen Whitaker of Kerbo Charge says the average fee for the work is about £1,200 (including VAT) without a grant.“Some [councils] are using it [the funding] to provide half-price channels to early adopters, others are making it totally free while funds last – but, after that, residents will have to pay full price,” he says.“For example, Surrey is £499 for the channel and installation, South Gloucestershire is £250,” he adds. “Sadly, there is quite a variety of approaches and prices.”To illustrate the difference in prices between local authorities, Redbridge council in London says the grant will cover up to £1,200 of installation costs. But applicants must pay £815 in fees and for a bond, as well as any additional installation costs.On top of the cost of installing the gullies, some councils charge an additional annualfeefor maintenance. For example, Redbridge chargesan “ongoing annual licence fee”of £185. Enfield, also in London,charges £107 a year.Shayne Rees of Gul-e, a company that has installed 400 gullies, says it takes between one and two hours to put the unit in place. “It’s a really heavy-duty steel channel that can take a truck driving over it, and once we put it in the ground, that will be there for decades and decades without any maintenance,” he adds.View image in fullscreenA Gul-e cable channel installed in Surrey.Photograph: Gul-eCouncil refusalsIt emerged in May thatmore than 20 local authoritiesappear to be holding out against having the gullies installed, among them Kent, Leicester and Worcestershire. Most of the holdouts are in London, including Waltham Forest and Hackney.The reasons given often concern safety and maintenance, and because of issues over who will be liable if there is an injury. For example, Waltham Forest says gullies “raise significant concerns including safety and accessibility of footways, parking pressures, maintenance responsibilities and liability, electrical safety and earthing standards”.Leicestershire county council says: “This is a new and very challenging area for local highway authorities to address.”Ealing council says it decided not to proceed with a trial of the gullies.“We took into account the needs of the people using the borough’s pavements, including elderly people and less able-bodied individuals, especially those on wheels and people with visual impairments,” a spokesperson says. “Gullies can have a significant impact on the feel and safety of pavements for residents walking or wheeling.”Carl Cashman of the Local Government Association, which represents councils, says local authorities would like to support on-street charging as much as possible “but have limited resources and significant demands to meet”.The different views of councils, sometimes neighbouring ones, have frustrated some drivers. Nick Theobald lives in Fulham in London, where he is not allowed to put one in yet. A pilot scheme with a small number of houses has been launched by Hammersmith and Fulham council.“You’ve only got to go over the river to Richmond and it’s completely permitted there,” he says.‘A public charger would be considerably more’View image in fullscreenGregg and Lauren Francis and their sons outside their home in Wales.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianFor people without off-street parking, charging an EV at home is much cheaper than doing so at public charge points.Since the beginning of this month, the VAT charged on domestic electricity has been cut from 5% to 0%, while the tax on public charging remains at 20%.Gregg Francis, who lives in Carmarthenshire in Wales, had a gully fitted outside his house two and a half years ago for free, as part of a scheme run by the local council. This allows him to fully charge his Vauxhall Vivaro Life for £6. He usually recharges it fully twice a week.“If we went to the public charger, we could be looking at £30 to £63 for the same amount of electricity,” he says.“We had a diesel Ford Focus that would cost about £70 a week to use on normal routine. That would now be considerably more as I’m comparing with two years ago.”View image in fullscreenFrancis had a car charging gully fitted outside his house two and a half years ago.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianFigures from ChargeUK, the industry’s trade group, put the average cost per kWh for off-peak at-home charging at 8p, while the standard public charging cost averages 54p.Vicky Edmonds, the chief executive of EVA England, which represents drivers, says people with a driveway can save an average of £1,400 a year compared with driving a petrol or a diesel car. Some of her members who do not have off-street parking estimate that they are now paying more than when they had a car using fossil fuels, she says.Explore more on these topicsMotoringConsumer affairsElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsLocal governmentEnglandEthical and green livingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I closed my eyes and stuck my finger on a map of western Europe: ‘This is where we’re going on holiday!’ | France holidays | The Guardian
description: Sick of relying on internet recommendations, I left my next destination to chance. Luckily, it led to me discovering a magical hamlet in the Cévennes mountains of south-central France
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sick of relying on internet recommendations, I left my next destination to chance. Luckily, it led to me discovering a magical hamlet in the Cévennes mountains of south-central France
Content: The view from the cottage veranda.Photograph: Camilla YatesView image in fullscreenThe view from the cottage veranda.Photograph: Camilla YatesFrance holidaysI closed my eyes and stuck my finger on a map of western Europe: ‘This is where we’re going on holiday!’Sick of relying on internet recommendations, I left my next destination to chance. Luckily, it led to me discovering a magical hamlet in the Cévennes mountains of south-central FranceCamilla YatesWed 21 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn unruly rabble bursts on to the street: a noisy eruption, bubbling towards us. This isn’t closing time on the Croisette in Cannes. A flock of sheep bustles past our cottage towards the shade of a huge chestnut tree, driven by three generations of herders and their dogs. The waterlike cacophony of their bells slows until only the odd tink tink punctuates the cicadas’ hum. The sheep graze, the shepherds doze off, and the mountain hamlet is still again.My partner and I had set off by Eurostar less than 24 hours before, yet this place felt a world away from the ad agency where I work.We’d booked cheap tickets to Paris months ago, intending to plan a trip on from there by train. As our departure approached, Instagram seemed to be full of aspirational, yet similar, holiday photos, and almost every other TikTok post I flicked past offered the promise of a hidden destination … discovered.I find ratings, reviews and recommendations just as reassuring as the next person, especially when faced with a limited holiday allowance. The safety of the search bar helps to give me the confidence that I’m spending my hard earned money as wisely as possible. I work in a world that runs on data and optimisation and I love it, but I wondered whether I’d optimised the adventure out of my own holidays.double quotation markI wondered whether I’d optimised the adventure out of my own holidaysSo, we tried a simple experiment. We closed down the tabs and opened a map of western Europe. Embracing a bit of low-tech randomness, we chose to let chance decide our trip.I shut my eyes and we promised to go wherever my finger landed. I waved my hand like a magic wand and pointed, then took a deep breath, eyes still closed. What if we ended up in some industrial wasteland? But we were in luck. My finger landed upon the commune of Saint-Hilaire-de-Lavit in Cévennes, a place we’d never heard of and almost certainly would never have found by searching “places to go in France”.View image in fullscreenA shepherd and flock in Les Ayres.Photograph: Camilla YatesAfter overnighting in Paris, a three-hour fast train zipped us down to Montpellier, where we hired a car. We stopped for provisions in a Lidl on the edge of town, stocking up for the whole trip – we weren’t expecting to find any shops at our journey’s end. A short drive inland, and the roads began to get narrower and more sparsely populated. As they climbed and zigzagged into this south-east corner of the Massif Central, we entered a south of France far removed from the honeypots served up by algorithms.We pulled into a grassy layby on a high mountain pass where there was one other car parked. Had we arrived? We’d followed the cottage owner’s directions as there was no signal here for Google Maps, so it was hard to tell. Stretching our legs in the fresh, cool air, the first thing we noticed was the quiet. No traffic, no tourists. Just stillness. But the languid buzz of big insects flying by and the whirring chorus of cicadas told us this place was alive.double quotation markNo traffic, no tourists, just stillness. But the whirring chorus of cicadas told us this place was aliveSquinting into the low sun, we saw someone waving. Our host, Guilaine, had appeared as if by magic and was beckoning us to the cottage a little farther down the road. We had found the hamlet of Les Ayres: a cluster of maybe 10 stone buildings, 800 metres above sea level. The rough-walled dwellings huddled either side of the narrow road, making the most of the tiny strand of level ground before the mountain’s spine fell away into steep forest. A long wooden awning and some outdoor tables suggested a cafe opposite our cottage, but the building was shuttered, and Les Ayres’ only potential customers seemed to be ourselves and Guilaine. She took us to the back of our accommodation, to a veranda that looked out over chestnut and pine-clad mountains rolling into the horizon. It’s a landscape that appears wild but has actually been shaped by farming, forestry and the seasonal movement of livestock for thousands of years.The next morning, as I watched the sheep and their guardians settle down in the shade, I felt the ancientness of the place. Shepherds must have moved their flocks along the same path and most likely slept under the same chestnut trees for centuries. Traditional farming practices endure here in part because the area is veined with crystal-clear mountain streams, meaning animals traversing the paths are never too far from a drink. So rather than opening the internet, we let these ancient tracks, known asdrailles, guide our hikes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘We discovered that shady, secluded river pools were waiting for us on all the paths that led down from our cottage.’Photograph: Camilla YatesWe took sweaty, daylong expeditions without seeing another human or hearing the sound of cars. The forests protected us from the worst of the sun’s blaze but, on our first trek, the real treat came when we rounded a corner to find that what we thought was the sound of wind in the pines was actually water gushing through a narrow gorge below us. Another couple of switchbacks and we arrived at a deep, clear pool created as the stream carved a corner into the rock. Dappled sunlight filtered down through trees clinging to the steep-sided valley, creating spotlights for damselflies to dart through. We stopped for a picnic and a swim in the freezing mountain water, picking wild strawberries from the bank for dessert.We discovered that these shady, secluded river pools were waiting for us on all the paths that led down from our cottage. As well as being the ultimate pit stops for mid-hike refreshment, they were teeming with wildlife – tadpoles wriggled in the shallows, fish flickered in the depths and a huge variety of butterflies, dragonflies and other insects skimmed the surface. We even saw a snake swimming across water we’d been submerged in just minutes before.We spent our last afternoon reading on a rock, summoning the energy to walk back up the mountain (one drawback of staying high up on a pass). We watched the sun swing over the water and the light change as the day wore on. When the air began to cool, we worked our way back towards the cottage. As the path turned into an empty, single-track road, a car approached – a big event after so much seclusion. It was Guilaine – the only person apart from the shepherds we’d encountered.In the evening, as the light faded, the sound of brass band practice drifted towards our veranda. Later, owls called to each other and a distant wild boar screeched into the quiet night. None of this had appeared in my search results. There was no review promising unexpected trumpeting, no listicle recommending the best pool for swimming among tadpoles, and no algorithm that could have told me where the sheep would pass on that first morning. We hadn’t looked at our phones for days – maybe that was the real discovery.Explore more on these topicsFrance holidaysEurope holidaysRail travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: What a privilege it is to witness bird migration on such a scale | Birds | The Guardian
description: Poole, Dorset: At this time of year, migrants are constantly on the move here, whether leaving, arriving or just stopping to refuel
Author: Mya Bambrick
Headline: Poole, Dorset: At this time of year, migrants are constantly on the move here, whether leaving, arriving or just stopping to refuel
Content: Every so often, the dunlin ‘are spooked by something and lift into the air, their white undersides catching the sunlight’.Photograph: Steve Taylor ARPS/AlamyView image in fullscreenEvery so often, the dunlin ‘are spooked by something and lift into the air, their white undersides catching the sunlight’.Photograph: Steve Taylor ARPS/AlamyCountry diaryBirdsCountry diary: What a privilege it is to witness bird migration on such a scalePoole, Dorset:At this time of year, migrants are constantly on the move here, whether leaving, arriving or just stopping to refuelMya BambrickWed 21 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith the sadness of our summer migrants departing the UK for another year comes the joy of our wintering birds returning. Working in conservation at Poole harbour, I’m out most days, connected to the ebb and flow of this change.As it is one of the largest natural harbours in the world, and located on theEast Atlantic Flyway, birds are constantly on the move here, whether leaving, arriving or stopping to refuel.To name just a few, in recent weeks we’ve seen the departure ofswallowsfor southern Africa, andmeadow pipitsfor Europe and north Africa;tealsandavocetshave arrived in large numbers; and we’ve had sightings of passingcurlew sandpipers– scarce here.Today is a sunny, abnormally mild October afternoon on the Wareham channel, and the tide is very low, exposing broad expanses of mudflats bordered by heather, gorse and reedbeds on the shore. The mudflats teem with aquatic insects, crustaceans and worms – a vast buffet for waders. As we cruise near the shallows, taking care to remain in the deeper channels, I get a better view of the birds that have stopped to feed –curlews,oystercatchers,black-headed gulls,Icelandic black-tailed godwits.View image in fullscreenThe food-rich mudflats of Poole harbour.Photograph: Mya BambrickA bird that always catches my eye is thedunlin. They often congregate in huge flocks, and in the bright sunshine, I can just about make out their short, downcurved bills, brownish-grey upperparts and plain white underparts. They move erratically and constantly probe the mud. Every so often, they are spooked by something and lift into the air, their white undersides catching the sunlight.This group of dunlin may have travelled thousands of miles to reach the harbour. Despite weighing only around 50g, these little waders could have bred as far away as eastern Europe or Russia.They breed in the UK too, mainly on grasslands and moorlands in northern England and Scotland, moving south to spend the winter in continental Europe and north Africa. Here in Poole harbour, their numbers can exceed 2,000 by January.Bird migration is such an incredible spectacle; I feel privileged to see it happening on such a scale.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsBirdsCountry diaryDorsetWildlifeAnimalsRural affairsAutumnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A difficult line’: meet the editors tackling Wikipedia’s arms trade pages  | Wikipedia | The Guardian
description: Volunteers and new recruits come together for ‘wikithon’ to put more detail about industry into public domain
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Volunteers and new recruits come together for ‘wikithon’ to put more detail about industry into public domain
Content: Agnes Cameron: ‘This is not an anti-arms industry campaigning event.’Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAgnes Cameron: ‘This is not an anti-arms industry campaigning event.’Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianWikipedia‘A difficult line’: meet the editors tackling Wikipedia’s arms trade pagesVolunteers and new recruits come together for ‘wikithon’ to put more detail about industry into public domainGeorge Francis LeeWed 21 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Anyone can editWikipedia,” the adage goes. But, it turns out, a relatively small number actually do.What is worthy of a digital page in the world’s largest and most-read encyclopedia is decided by roughly 270,000 active volunteers, enthusiasts who populate the online resource with information on anything from 19th-century medicine to TikTok trends. Inevitably, some subjects are sidelined – the global south,notable women– but a new batch of Wikipedian recruits are waging war on one neglected topic: the arms industry.Last week, in a classroom in central London, two dozen volunteers huddled around laptops and free servings of vegan Ethiopian food for what is known as a “wikithon”, an event of collective and in-person Wikipedia editing. Some were veteran editors in their 70s, others young students who had never registered an account before. But their targets include subjects such as Palantir, Project Maven and Nitro-Chem.“Wikipedia pages about the arms industry, in general, are not always super-detailed,” said the group’s co-founder Agnes Cameron. The intention of the wikithon, started by fellows fromthe n-Space programmeat Somerset House Studios, was “to put better quality and more well organised information on the arms industry in the public domain”, the specialist technician said.View image in fullscreenA new batch of Wikipedian recruits were trained in how to edit a page.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianAttenders at the monthly event are trained in how to add to the internet’s most popular reference site. But while editing Wikipedia is surprisingly simple – just a few clicks to publish a change – ethical complications quickly bubble up.“The interesting thing about Wikipedia editing is that you’re encouraged to edit things you care about,” Cameron said. “What it looks like to have a conflict of interest is an interesting question.”Although Cameron enjoys editing pages about food in her spare time, her interests are also political. “We’re toeing quite a difficult line,” she said. “Difficult lines are important to toe.”Despite personal and political reasons for wanting to spread information on arms manufacturers and sellers, finding journalistic balance means using Wikipedia in good faith. Cameron said attenders’ chosen subject matter meant that it was “really important” that they followed Wikipedia’s standards to the letter. “This is not an anti-arms industry campaigning event. This is an event really about factual information on Wikipedia,” she said.View image in fullscreenThe main goal was to pull together publicly available information into one place.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianWhen it comes to information, Wikipedia’s rules demand that no original research is included on its pages and conclusions are not drawn. The main goal of the arms industry wikithon, then, was to pull together publicly available information from other sources into one place.Wikipedia has been repeatedly criticised for its lack of diversity in editors and its coverage. It has been accused of geographical bias towards the west, with most articles focused on the US and western Europe. Similarly, just 19% of the site’s biography entries are for women. In 2018, the female Nobel prize winner Donna Strickland, a physicist, was deemed“not important enough”for a Wikipedia entry.With a wider range of ages, genders and racial backgrounds at the wikithon, the trainee editors were helping to rebalance the scale, said Hannah Cobb, a co-founder of the event. “There’s a very specific idea of who edits Wikipedia … that doesn’t tend to be the demographic of who shows up,” she said. “There’s a really broad interest in Wikipedia in general. Everyone remembers that at school you were taught not to trust it because anyone could write it.”View image in fullscreenThe experience of editing a Wikipedia page can be ‘quite empowering’, said Hannah Cobb, a co-founder of the event.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianPrevious arms industry wikithons organised by Cameron and Cobb in Manchester andLondonhave drawn in more than 60 would-be Wikipedians at a time, including activists, journalists, Quaker members – and even Cameron’s own mother.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNewcomers to the group were interested in how Wikipedia could be used to broaden public knowledge of confusing geopolitics, said Cobb. “There is a sense of powerlessness when it comes to countering the narrative by big tech, by governments, by the military industrial complex at large,” she said.But for the arms industry page editors, those feelings can disappear over a few hours: “When you write something on Wikipedia, it appears immediately on the internet. I think that experience alone is quite empowering for people.”Cobb spoke of a sense of wonder “when people realise how easy it is to actually contribute”, but attenders have a respect for Wikipedia’s commitment to rigour and quality control. And though dedicated to accuracy, the group prefers to not advertise the details of its edits over concerns that the work could be undone by other editors in bad faith.Cameron said it was unclear if Wikipedia’s wider editorial culture would take offence over how the event was run. While wikithons are not new, the blurry line between activism and accurate dissemination of information stress-tests the platform’s rules.View image in fullscreenAnother wikithon session will be held later this winter.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianReal-world politics often spill on to Wikipedia, and editors often disagree publicly about changes. The site has also been covertly used as an informational battleground. The seasoned editor Ksenia Coffmanmade extensive editsto remove what she found to be flattering and sympathetic entries about Nazi party officials across Wikipedia, and in 2021, the Croatian-language version of Wikipedia was found to have been commandeered by nationalist, far-right organiserswho made ideologically motivated edits.Cameron hopes that the regular meetings can be formalised into a WikiProject, when organised groups of editors collaborate to improve certain topic pages. She hoped her group could be given advice by WikiProject Military history, which she called “far and away the most active project on Wikipedia by miles. It’s amazingly well run.”The London wikithon is to continue for another session in the winter, and Cameron and Cobb’s faith in encyclopedia editing as a political tool is steadfast. As Cameron said: “Wikipedia is fundamentally anti-fascist.”Explore more on these topicsWikipediaDigital mediaInternetLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: A moment that changed me: I was devastated by a breakup – and saved by a sweaty moshpit | Relationships | The Guardian
description: When my relationship broke down, my usual playlist of pop girl anthems and love songs left me in tears. Then I discovered hardcore punk
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When my relationship broke down, my usual playlist of pop girl anthems and love songs left me in tears. Then I discovered hardcore punk
Content: On the mend … Leoni Horton in HMV holding the Pop Culture EP by Knocked Loose.Photograph: Courtesy of Leoni HortonView image in fullscreenOn the mend … Leoni Horton in HMV holding the Pop Culture EP by Knocked Loose.Photograph: Courtesy of Leoni HortonA moment that changed meRelationshipsA moment that changed me: I was devastated by a breakup – and saved by a sweaty moshpitWhen my relationship broke down, my usual playlist of pop girl anthems and love songs left me in tears. Then I discovered hardcore punkLeoni HortonWed 21 Oct 2026 01.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNobody warned me that heartbreak would ruin my relationship withBeyoncé. I had always associated music with the happiest times in my life: going to Glastonbury, seeing Madonna play at Madison Square Garden, singing along to Kylie Minogue’s greatest hits on a road trip across Australia. Just over a year ago, after my first real relationship ended unexpectedly, things changed.When I listened to the artists I loved most, I was ambushed by memories and reminded of all the love and intimacy I had lost. My usual playlists, filled with indie bops and pop girl anthems, became unbearable. I’d never noticed before, but almost every song was about love, yearning, romance and sex. Every time I pressed play, I found myself sobbing in the shower or ugly-crying in public.Tired of burning through tissues, I decided to go no contact with music. In fact, I was determined to avoid the topic of love at all costs. You would be surprised how much that limits what you can do, because, to paraphrase Hugh Grant in Love Actually, love is – unfortunately – all around. I swapped my playlists for journalism podcasts, true-crime audiobooks and soothing ambient noise, but nothing seemed to fill the space that the lack of music had left in my life.“What’s the genre furthest away from my usual taste?” I wondered, scrolling through Spotify, a few months post-breakup. I clicked recklessly, ending up in a hardcore punk playlist. Not knowing where to begin, I pressed play on the first band on the list.It worked. Loud, heavy music came screaming out of my speakers, so frantic and raw that I could barely make out what the songs were about. I was delighted when I realised I could listen to bands such as Malevolence and Every Time I Die without crying so much that I had to press cold spoons over my swollen eyes afterwards.Knocked Loose, a hardcore punk band from Kentucky, became a fast favourite. A week after discovering them, I found out they had a special midnight show coming up in Manchester. It felt serendipitous that they were arriving in town when I needed them most, so I booked a ticket.“I’m going to die,” I thought a few weeks later, chewing my lip with worry as the Albert Hall in Manchester exploded with activity. It was 2am when Knocked Loose finally took the stage. I pressed myself against the wall while the crowd turned into a huge, pulsing crush of bodies. People were throwing their limbs about violently, slamming into one another at full force and clambering on top of each other to get on stage, only to immediately throw themselves back into the crowd.View image in fullscreen‘I was spellbound by the music’ …Knocked Loose performing in Manchester.Photograph: Courtesy of Leoni HortonI hadn’t seen anything like it before. I was spellbound by the music, but terrified of ending up in A&E. Yet, when the lead singer, Bryan Garris, called out for more movement, I felt unable to resist. I walked forward and let the crowd swallow me.Being inside the crowd was like that moment in Dirty Dancing when Baby sees Johnny and his friends dancing in the staff quarters. I was intimidated, but possessed by a deep longing to join in. But I had no clue how and no Johnny to lift me up by the hips. Then suddenly, someone barged into my shoulder, sending me stumbling into the person beside me. I looked around anxiously, but nobody was mad and nobody was hurt. I smiled. This wasn’t scary; it was fun.I quickly felt myself become a part of the hive mind of the crowd. It was such a relief to move my body however I wanted. I didn’t care where I ended up, whom I crashed into or what I looked like. And, gloriously, there wasn’t a single sad thought about my ex in my head. I had no desire to check my phone or doomscroll through his social media. I was safe in this sweaty bubble.By ghosting my playlists, I had been desperately trying to control my feelings. The music I loved had been urging me to accept my sadness and heartbreak, but I’d pushed it away and hidden behind loud, abrasive bands. However, as the night progressed and the band raged through their songs, I began to feel those familiar difficult feelings creep in. I’d been distracted by the noise, but suddenly I was hit by the blunt realisation that hardcore was emotional, too.Underneath Knocked Loose’s noisy exterior was the same vulnerability and grief from which I had been running. The difference was that, in their moshpit, I didn’t have to mope around. With every shove and collision, my feelings were spilling out of me. I realised that it hadn’t been music causing me pain: it was me and everything I was refusing to feel or accept. The whole night felt like a weird, radical form of therapy that I’d signed up for unconsciously.Afterwards, I gradually stopped avoiding my playlists. I began letting myself experience the difficult feelings music stirred up and my broken heart started to mend. Last week, I listened tothe latest Ariana Grande albumand I didn’t so much as sniffle. Of course, some Fleetwood Mac andPhoebe Bridgerssongs still sting; I’m only human. But the sad feelings those songs inspire no longer feel so consuming.I don’t have beef with Beyoncé these days. I owe it to the people of the hardcore community, who hauled me back to my feet. Now, when I don’t feel so crazy in love, I go to a hardcore show, throw myself into a moshpit and hope it knocks some of those sad feelings loose.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsRelationshipsA moment that changed meBeyoncéPunkShareReuse this content

title: Parents and teachers in England: share your views on two-week half terms | Childcare | The Guardian
description: We would like to hear from parents and teachers about their thoughts and experiences of two-week half terms

Headline: We would like to hear from parents and teachers about their thoughts and experiences of two-week half terms
