title: Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted | Guinea-Bissau | The Guardian
description: Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’
Author: Melody Schreiber
Headline: Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’
Content: A woman stands in a shared room at a residential care facility for pregnant mothers in Gabu, Guinea Bissau, on 22 May 2012.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APView image in fullscreenA woman stands in a shared room at a residential care facility for pregnant mothers in Gabu, Guinea Bissau, on 22 May 2012.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APGuinea-BissauControversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns haltedHepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’Melody SchreiberWed 21 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher,wroteon LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previouslydeniedthat the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when theysearchedthe offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.It was vital to supportGuinea-Bissauin rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.View image in fullscreenThe Minister of health, Quinhin Nantote, at the presidential palace in Guinea-Bissau on 29 November 2025.Photograph: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP/Getty ImagesSuch a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the WorldHealthOrganization (WHO).“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who hasco-publishedresearchraising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”Explore more on these topicsGuinea-BissauAfricaHepatitis BVaccines and immunisationHealthChildren's healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Severely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates say | Florida | The Guardian
description: Flights to third countries where the detainees have no ties are scheduled as early as Wednesday, relatives detail
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Flights to third countries where the detainees have no ties are scheduled as early as Wednesday, relatives detail
Content: The Krome detention center in west Miami, Florida, on the Fourth of July in 2025.Photograph: Pedro Portal/Miami Herald via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Krome detention center in west Miami, Florida, on the Fourth of July in 2025.Photograph: Pedro Portal/Miami Herald via Getty ImagesFloridaSeverely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates sayFlights to third countries where the detainees have no ties are scheduled as early as Wednesday, relatives detailSend us your questions about immigration and the midtermsRichard Luscombein MiamiWed 21 Oct 2026 09.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRelatives of gravely ill detainees at twoFloridaimmigrationjails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside twoImmigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)facilities in south Florida.The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions had been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent toAfrica,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference.“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by agovernment inspector’s reportlast month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband had been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa.’“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway.’ We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”Responding to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the homeland security department demanded to know the affected detainees’ personal information. The department did not respond further when provided with Sendra’s details.Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of the Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks and showers, andprevious complaintsincluded female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.Advocates sayDonald Trump’s sweeping second-term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that the DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.The controversial practice,approved by the US supreme courtlast month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.AHuman Rights Watch reportearlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.Explore more on these topicsFloridaUS immigrationICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda
Content: Children play outside a health centre in eastern Congo. Nigeria said Tuesday it had recorded its first Ebola case of Africa’s latest outbreak, as Kenya declared its ninth case, prompting a regional health official to warn of ‘an extremely serious threat’.Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/APView image in fullscreenChildren play outside a health centre in eastern Congo. Nigeria said Tuesday it had recorded its first Ebola case of Africa’s latest outbreak, as Kenya declared its ninth case, prompting a regional health official to warn of ‘an extremely serious threat’.Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/APEbolaNigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western AfricaCase in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from UgandaAssociated PressTue 20 Oct 2026 20.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.Ebola cases in Kenya highlight US failures amid Trump cuts to key servicesRead moreUganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed activeEbolacases”.Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region.Kenya confirmed its first caseearlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.View image in fullscreenHealth workers on the frontlines of the Ebola response receive vaccination in Beni, DRC.Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/ReutersDr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.“ThisBundibugyo Ebola outbreakhas already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola inKenyaand strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June afterthe outbreak in Congoin mid-May.The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.Explore more on these topicsEbolaNigeriaKenyaDemocratic Republic of the CongoGlobal healthAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes | Taiwan | The Guardian
description: Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say
Content: Huang Yi-hao was left with a bruised pelvis after the men rammed him with a car while he was riding his scooter.Photograph: Huang Yi-hao/FacebookView image in fullscreenHuang Yi-hao was left with a bruised pelvis after the men rammed him with a car while he was riding his scooter.Photograph: Huang Yi-hao/FacebookTaiwanTaiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokesPerson named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors sayGuardian staffWed 21 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party andXi Jinping.Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary.In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record.Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainlandChinawho was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation.The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.”China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said.The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.K refused to pay the full sum of NT$450,000 (US$13,900; £10,370) promised to the suspects because Huang’s injuries were only minor, the statement said.FBI arrests woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader’s family for ChinaRead moreOn Wednesday, Huang reposted a video from December 2025 in which he asked the audience to help him by shouting out the name of the person he was about to describe.In a fast-paced diatribe, the comedian, dressed in a traditional gown, evoked “swept-back hair” and a “plump figure”, and criticised policies on Hong Kong, Covid and the property market. After finishing with an expletive, the crowd chanted back Xi’s name before breaking into applause.In May, two people were prosecuted after spreading faeces and paint at a Taipei club hours before a Huang show.Lev Nachman, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University, said: “It is important to remember that what we are reading about is obviously a more extreme case, but there have been threats and acts of violence against critics of the Communist party here in Taiwan for many years.”Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council said in October that at least 126 individuals had been affected by Chinese transnational repression.The Guardian has contacted the Chinese foreign ministry for comment.In a post on Wednesday, Huang said: “If people can be subjected to this kind of treatment simply for criticising the Chinese Communist party when it does not even govern Taiwan, how can we expect to retain our current freedom of speech if the CCP were ever to rule Taiwan?”In another post on Facebook, Huang said he would not cancel future performances but that he was “no hero”.“I write it because it’s funny,” he said. “If I stop, it will only be because I’ve got bored of it.”Explore more on these topicsTaiwanChinaXi JinpingAsia PacificComedyFreedom of speechnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shark trapped for a month in South Korean canal is finally freed | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Bukang-i successfully guided out after month in which it drew 1.6m visitors and was watched over by YouTubers
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Bukang-i successfully guided out after month in which it drew 1.6m visitors and was watched over by YouTubers
Content: Shark in the canal during operation to guide it out in Busan, South Korea, on Wednesday.Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersView image in fullscreenShark in the canal during operation to guide it out in Busan, South Korea, on Wednesday.Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersSouth KoreaShark trapped for a month in South Korean canal is finally freedBukang-i successfully guided out after month in which it drew 1.6m visitors and was watched over by YouTubersRaphael Rashidin SeoulWed 21 Oct 2026 07.41 EDTFirst published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInSouth Korea, they call themjagyeongdan, a word whose meaning sits somewhere between vigilante group and neighbourhood watch. Each night they put on hi-vis vests, picked up their selfie sticks and gathered around the harbour in Busan to keep watch over an unlikely charge: astranded sharkaffectionately known as Bukang-i.On Wednesday, after more than a month in the canal and at the third attempt, the shark was successfully guided out, South Korea’s oceans ministry said. Officials expect her to move into open water in time.For the month that she was stranded, the group of self-appointed guardians took turns to protect her, patrolling the waterfront at night for visitors who might disturb the animal.Most are YouTubers who livestreamed the waterway, where the shark became a national celebrity. They stayedup through the night, calling out anyone shining torches or lasers into the water. Some of their videos have been watched hundreds of thousands of times.View image in fullscreen(Left to right) The YouTubers Kim Jong-hwan, Choi Won-jin and Na Tae-soo, who have been keeping watch over the trapped shark in BusanComposite: Supplied/ Yonhap News Agency“They bring fishing lamps, or the kind of lights people use at a campsite,” saidChoi Won-jin, one of the shark’s protectors. He would arriveas the lights went out along the canal and wait for the offenders Koreans online call “lantern villains”.The shark had been marooned in the canal since 18 September. Named after Bukhang, the Korean name for the city’s North Port, and about 3 metres long, the female dusky shark was one of a species classed as endangered worldwide. More than 1.6 million visitors came to see her, the city said, at a park that used to draw about 2,000 people on a busy Saturday.View image in fullscreenVisitors watching the shark trapped in a waterway in the south-eastern port city of Busan.Photograph: Jung Yeon-Je/AFP/Getty ImagesAuthorities had twice tried to guide her back out to sea and failed. Until she left, the shark remained in the canal, drawing crowds by day and leaving a handful of men to keep watch after dark. They patrolled the canal’s park to check everything was in order, ate snacks as the night wentby, and shared their grievances on air about the behaviour they witnessed.“We’re ordinary members of the public,” said Choi, who has had a YouTubechannel for 10 years and covers trending issues in South Korea.“So we have no choice but to put it nicely, and get them to understand as best we can.”“Don’t, please don’t switch the torch on,” said one of them, a YouTuber who lived nearby and went by the nameNa Tae-soo. Most people complied, he said. “The animal thrashes about at night because of the torches, and it’s dangerous.”View image in fullscreenCrowds flocked to the waterfront park in Busan to see the shark.Photograph: Yonhap/EPAHis footagecaptured the shark twisting sharply away from a beam of light at 2am and striking the side of the canal. The national institute of fisheries science later confirmed an abrasion on her snout and said a visitor’s torch was likely to have startled the shark into injury.Korean media reported that 105 officials from seven agencies watched over her, with a team on standby to reach the water within three minutes. Choi disputed this, saying that after dark it wasalmost up to him and the others.The waterfront was closed to the public from midnight until 5am, a restriction the YouTubers said was impossible to enforce across a park that size. One night, livestreaming from the walkway, Choi filmed a man tipping food waste into the water.Nobody saw the shark feed, though experts said feeding could happen in an instant and sharks her size did not need to eat often.Further attempts to free the shark had been paused on the grounds that more force would distress her.Cooler water had been expected to prompt her to move on. Dusky sharks prefer water between 18C and 26C, the fisheries institute said. Experts put 15C as the point below which her physiological functions would start to decline, and about 11C as the point at which survival would become precarious. Busan city officials had expected the canal to reach that temperature after the middle of November.View image in fullscreenThis aerial photo taken on 29 September shows South Korean coastguard boats spraying water in an attempt to guide the shark back to the sea.Photograph: Yonhap/AFP/Getty ImagesThe fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributed to warmer seas and more of the fish that sharks feed on.The affection for Bukang-i has meanwhile become an industry, with a commemorativesoju, a baseball mascot in a shark cape and an honorary city ambassadorship, and nearby shops reporting a surge in sales. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, visited the canal in mid-October.None of the shark’s guardians thoughtshe should be forced out. Choi said the city should protect her where she wasuntil she left of her own accord.Kim Jong-hwan, who runs a small business, keptwatch by day as well and livestreamed her almost every day. “I went to pass on information [to my followers], and after that I started observing her”, he said. “Watching her over time, with the water pumps being fired and then the nets, I came to find those things being done to her objectionable. So we ended up cheering her on.”“She’s just an animal, and she came in by her own choice,” Kim said. “If it gets cold, if there’s no food, if the water doesn’t suit her, she’ll leave by herself. I’d like her to just be left alone, to rest there comfortably until then, and go.”Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaSharksMarine lifeWildlifeAnimalsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labor, Coalition and crossbench MPs afraid at home and work after alleged attack on Helen Haines | Helen Haines | The Guardian

Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Home and office safety a common concern in Australian federal police and Asio safety briefings with politicians following alleged attack on MP Helen Haines
Content: Floral tributes outside the Helen Haines’s office in Wangaratta. Independent MP Monique Ryan says she supports more resources to secure offices. ‘If it makes my team feel better and safer to have bollards out the front, I’m happy.’Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFloral tributes outside the Helen Haines’s office in Wangaratta. Independent MP Monique Ryan says she supports more resources to secure offices. ‘If it makes my team feel better and safer to have bollards out the front, I’m happy.’Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesHelen HainesLabor, Coalition and crossbench MPs afraid at home and work after alleged attack on Helen HainesHome and office safety a common concern in Australian federal police and Asio safety briefings with politicians following alleged attack on MP Helen HainesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerandKrishani DhanjiWed 21 Oct 2026 19.04 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSecurity agencies will review safety precautions for MPs’ homes and offices after numerous federal politicians told police and Asio in safety briefings that they were worried about widening threats after the alleged attack onHelen Haines.The Labor government and politicians across the parliament are still considering how they will respond when they return to Canberra next week, with ideas being floated including a new committee on MPs’ safety, greater resources for police, and motions of condolence for Haines,who lost both her legs after Monday’s incident. Renewed calls from the crossbench for reforms to question time and the tone of debate in parliament are unlikely to be taken up by the major parties.In safety briefings with theAustralian federal policeand Asio granted to Labor, Coalition and crossbench MPs on Wednesday, security of homes and electorate offices was a common concern, according to Guardian Australia interviews with 10 MPs. While a broad review of safety and security is unlikely at this stage, multiple MPs across the political spectrum told Guardian Australia they had spent thousands of dollars of their own money to install safety features based on the advice of the federal police.Politicians say more security would ‘let bad people win’ after alleged attack on Helen Haines: ‘We don’t want to be locked off’Read moreFederal ministers receive stronger security assistance but numerous backbenchers said they felt under-resourced, saying many angry constituents may see all politicians as a homogenous group, and may not differentiate between cabinet members and ordinary local MPs.“People are getting activated now because they see us as part of the government. We represent the system to them, as much as anyone else,” independent Monique Ryan said.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereTwo years ago, the AFP recorded 951 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against office holders. Last year, that increased to 1,067.On Thursday, a Western Australian man was charged after he allegedly made verbal threats while in possession of nunchucks outside an electoral office in Perth.No one was injured as a result, Western Australia police said, and his bail was refused.‘Not well protected’A number of politicians asked to speak anonymously to discuss reflections from the briefings. While many praised the AFP’s response when their staff contacted them – for instance, to seek advice on holding public events – some said they had received less timely assistance from local police when they requested help, such as to respond to aggressive visitors.Numerous MPs said theydid not want security guards or armed escorts for themselves in publicbut that they felt alarmed for the safety of their homes and families.Some said they would feel more comfortable with cameras and floodlights at home, and had decided to pay for their own upgrades after not being offered such features in risk assessments conducted by security agencies. One independent MP said crossbenchers questioned whether extra home security features should be paid for by the public.Several MPs said they wanted more security and safety support but questioned how much impact that would have on their overall safety and how much more the AFP could do.Helen Haines has lost both legs but ‘heart and mind are in good shape’, husband says – videoGuardian Australia was told security officials had committed to assessing safety settings of MPs who raised specific concerns. While a broad-ranging government review is at this stage not expected, other responses could include giving MPs more information on the background work that policing agencies conduct year-round, such as threat assessments and periodic checks.The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, told News24 his government had overseen “an increase in funding for security for members of parliament in the last couple of years”.“We want to make sure that people can feel as much comfort as possible, that everything’s being done to maximise security,” he said. “But also, I think parliamentarians across the board are determined to make sure we can continue to engage as we need to in this great democracy of ours.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA spokesperson for the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said: “Reviews of the threats faced by high office holders are constantly conducted by our agencies.”Ryan, who is close with Haines, said she had rarely discussed safety arrangements with fellow MPs until recent times but claimed many colleagues were “now realising they’re having common experiences”. She was supportive of a broader review into safety and more resources to secure offices.“If it makes my team feel better and safer to have bollards out the front, I’m happy,” she said.Two Labor MPs said some government backbenchers had expressed frustrations towards the finance department for not adequately funding safety measures for their electorate offices or doing so in a timely way. One said money was “always an issue” with the department, and expected more MPs to be directly lobbying the prime minister to improve office security.Graph of threats to politicians increasingNationals MP Sam Birrell, whose electorate neighbours Haines’s in Indi, said regional politicians had particular concerns, with many being highly visible in their communities and locals often knowing where they lived.“Some of the MPs were frustrated there’s not clear advice on things like whether to advertise mobile offices or have signs on cars,” he said.“There were some complaints about whether people are able to get fairly modest security measures … that needs to be reviewed.”Multiple people across meetings raised concerns about how to protect electorate office staff.Liberal senator James Paterson told Radio National electorate offices were “very exposed” and were “not well protected”.Asio and AFP have been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsHelen HainesAustralian politicsIndependentsAustralian federal policeAustralian police and policingAustralian security and counter-terrorismAustralian intelligence agenciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: House prices falling in every Australian capital city for first time in 15 years | Housing | The Guardian
description: House prices in Sydney are at a two-year low after falling 4.7% in the September quarter to $1.66m, according to Domain report
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: House prices in Sydney are at a two-year low after falling 4.7% in the September quarter to $1.66m, according to Domain report
Content: House prices in Melbourne have fallen for the third consecutive quarter but remain in the million-dollar club, with a media price of $1.014m.Photograph: Diego Fedele/AAPView image in fullscreenHouse prices in Melbourne have fallen for the third consecutive quarter but remain in the million-dollar club, with a media price of $1.014m.Photograph: Diego Fedele/AAPHousingHouse prices falling in every Australian capital city for first time in 15 yearsHouse prices in Sydney are at a two-year low after falling 4.7% in the September quarter to $1.66m, according to Domain reportGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressWed 21 Oct 2026 17.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouse prices are falling across every capital city for the first time in 15 years and the second time on record, according to figures from Domain’s September Quarter 2026 House Price report.House prices in Sydney are at a two-year low after falling 4.7% in the September quarter, to $1.66m.House prices in Melbourne have fallen for the third consecutive quarter, slumping 3.3% in the September quarter, but remains in the million-dollar club, marginally, with a media price of $1.014m after experiencing its largest quarterly house price fall in four years.When pensioner Gail secured housing, it was the 'best day' of her life. Then she was ordered to vacateRead morePerth recorded the sharpest drop, with house prices falling a record 4.7%, while Brisbane and Adelaide also logged their steepest quarterly house price falls on record.“Geographically, the downturn has broadened, but also across property types with houses and units also falling,” Domain’s chief residential economist, Nicola Powell, said.“Homes are taking longer to sell, there is greater scope to negotiate and sellers are having to be more realistic about price expectations.”Higher interest rates, persistent cost-of-living pressures and changes to housing investment tax policy were driving the reductions, Powell said.“What this has really layered is weak sentiment across buyers in particular,” she said. “Ultimately we could see Melbourne close the year with the median house price below $1m.”Reduced borrowing capacity is also stifling sales, the data suggests.While the statistics show weakened confidence from buyers and vendors, the diminishing market has created the best start to spring for prospective purchasers, according to Powell.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSign up for the Breaking News Australia email“We are in a buyer’s market and many of our capital cities have got the highest levels of supply that they’ve seen in a number of years,” Powell said.“For buyers with secure finances and the capacity to transact, that creates opportunities that have been difficult to find in recent years.”Prices could continue to fall for many months to come, Powell said.“Something needs to shift to alter the confidence to transact and I cannot envisage the confidence changing until we see an interest rate cut or even the discussion that interest rate reductions are on the horizon,” she said. “And ultimately that prospect is in the latter part of next year.”Morgan Stanley economists agreed, predicting the market will bottom out in the second half of 2027. They expect the downturn to run as deep as 15% from peak to trough.Explore more on these topicsHousingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Huge moment’: long-awaited extension to Sydney’s metro line to open next week | Sydney | The Guardian
description: The south-west metro extension will open on Friday 30 October, more than two years after the former T3 heavy rail line closed
Author: Penry Buckley
Headline: The south-west metro extension will open on Friday 30 October, more than two years after the former T3 heavy rail line closed
Content: The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, announced that the south-west metro extension would open on Friday 30 October.Photograph: Bianca De Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenThe New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, announced that the south-west metro extension would open on Friday 30 October.Photograph: Bianca De Marchi/AAPSydney‘Huge moment’: long-awaited extension to Sydney’s metro line to open next weekThe south-west metro extension will open on Friday 30 October, more than two years after the former T3 heavy rail line closedGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPenry BuckleyWed 21 Oct 2026 16.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 16.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA long-awaited extension to Sydney’s metro line will open next week, bringing an end to more than two years of replacement buses for residents in the city’s south-west.In a video shared on Instagram on Thursday morning, theNew South Walespremier, Chris Minns, announced that the south-west metro extension would open on Friday 30 October. In a statement, the government said the first service would commence at 4.31am.Minns thanked “the thousands of commuters, families and local businesses for their patience while we’ve undertaken this major transformation.”“This is a huge moment for south-west Sydney,” he said.It comes more than two years after the former T3 heavy rail line, which serviced 10 stations in Sydney’s inner west and south west – Marrickville, Dulwich Hill, Hurlstone Park, Canterbury, Campsie, Belmore, Lakemba, Wiley Park, Punchbowl and Bankstown – closed in September 2024 to be converted to the driverless rapid transit system.‘I’ve had enough of pink buses’: the long wait for Sydney’s newest metro line is nearly overRead moreA continuous 66km metro line will span from Tallawong in the city’s north-west through the CBD to Bankstown in the south-west from next Friday.After regulator approval delayed the opening date of the city metro section in 2024, the Minns government had been at pains not to commit to a date for the south-west extension, despite media reports that it was aiming for launch on 18 October.Last week, the transport minister, John Graham, said that the opening was “very close” and “a matter of weeks, not months” after the operator, Sydney Metro, provided the final piece of safety data to the Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator (ONRSR).The project to connect the stations to the city metro, which opened in August 2024, was estimated to take 12 months at that time. In the interim, commuters have had to use pink replacement buses to connect to metro services at Sydenham, where the line currently terminates.The government says the pink rail replacement buses will continue to operate on 30 October and the first weekend of operation.When the line opens, a journey from Bankstown to Central is expected to take 28 minutes – a six-minute saving compared with the former heavy rail line. Longer journeys are expected to yield greater savings, such as Lakemba to Victoria Cross, which will take 37 minutes – a 24-minute saving on previous travel times.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe government says the extension will deliver capacity for an additional 17,000 people during peak hours. Metro services run every four minutes during peak hours, five minutes during the day, and 10 minutes in the evenings and on weekends.The project has been delayed amid challenges in converting the 130-year-old heavy rail line and historic stations, including the need to add mechanical “gap-fillers” to fill spaces between curved platforms and trains.When the south-west metro opens, six of the 360 doors on the line where gaps are widest – three doors at Dulwich Hill, and one each at Marrickville, Canterbury and Campsie – will not be in use while data is collected on the reliability of the gap-fillers.The project was first announced by the former Coalition government in 2014. Labor campaigned against it at the 2019 election but committed to completing it after Minns became premier in 2023. Amid blowouts, the city and south-west metro sections are expected to cost more than $20bn combined.Explore more on these topicsSydneyNew South WalesChris MinnsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Macron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrest | France | The Guardian
description: Leaders criticised for spreading misleading information as France prepares for further protests this weekend
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Leaders criticised for spreading misleading information as France prepares for further protests this weekend
Content: Macron made the comments during a visit to Qatar, where he was seeking energy deals to help offset rising fuel costs.Photograph: Tessier Benoit/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMacron made the comments during a visit to Qatar, where he was seeking energy deals to help offset rising fuel costs.Photograph: Tessier Benoit/ABACA/ShutterstockFranceMacron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrestLeaders criticised for spreading misleading information as France prepares for further protests this weekendJon Henleyin ParisWed 21 Oct 2026 19.06 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmmanuel Macron has accused Donald Trump and other foreign leaders of making “stupid comments” about France’s street unrest for political gain, as the country prepared for more protests this weekend.Speaking during a visit to Qatar, the French president did not name names but said “manipulation of information” afterSaturday’s riotshad led to “comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders”.Asked if he was referring to Donald Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.” The US presidenthas blamed France’s violenceon “migrants, jihadists and communists” as he campaigns for his Republican party before midterm elections.Macron told reporters in Doha that some leaders “in the middle of election campaigns, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic” were “naively spreading narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote”.They were “using our country for their own political campaigns”, the French president said. “And we don’t need that. We already have difficulties to deal with.”He said AI-generated images were circulating “depicting scenes that never actually happened inFrance. We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.”View image in fullscreenLargely peaceful demonstrations over the cost of living descended into violence and looting in cities including Paris and Marseille last weekend.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAThe Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections next weekend, has also said that France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam”. Analysts have dismissed claims that migrants were the main factor in France’s protests.Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has erupted six months before presidential elections to choose his successor. The government has admitted it “lost control” over widespread rioting on Saturday.Largely peaceful demonstrations over the cost of living rapidly descended into rampant violence andextensive looting, especially in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Limoges, where the town hall was set on fire and partly destroyed.Police said that protests would be banned in parts of Paris on Thursday as the city braced for more demonstrations.The ban, from 8am to 8pm, will apply to key landmarks, including the Elysee presidential palace, both houses of parliament, and tourist havens such as the Louvre museum and the Champs-Elysees.Other areas where rallies will be prohibited include the Bastille and République squares, and the Châtelet-Les Halles shopping area which was heavily targeted by looters over the weekend.The unrest has prompted several countries to issue travel warnings for France and rattled already nervous financial markets, with the yield on the French government’s benchmark 10-year bondspassing 5% on Wednesday, its highest since 2002.Macron pledged to prevent any repeat of last weekend’s convulsions, as thegilets jaunes(yellow vest) grassroots protest movement formally filed plans for a march through the centre of Paris ⁠on Saturday that is likely to be the ⁠government’s next big test.Student groups have also called for protests on the same day to push demands for greater investment in education. Thegilets jaunesactivists aim to revive their nationwide 2018campaign against rising living costsand declining public services.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe city hall in Limoges was destroyed by fire during the protests last weekend.Photograph: SDIS 87/AFP/Getty Images“Those who want to cause disorder in city centres next Saturday will be prevented from doing so,” Macron told reporters in the Gulf, where he was seeking energy deals to help offset rising fuel costs. “There must be no wavering at the top of the state.”Government ministers have promised a “massive” and vastly reinforced security operation after acknowledging shortcomings in their initial response last weekend, with some troops expected to be deployed alongside police reinforcements.Partial night-time curfews imposed on Monday and Tuesday in areas prone to violent protests and looting in cities around France, including Paris, Marseille and Lille, have helped ensure relative calm and were expected to be renewed on Wednesday.France’s main trade unions have separately called a nationwide mobilisation for 5 November. Sophie Binet, the head of the CGT union, said: “There is huge and legitimate anger, and the answer to that situation is not repression. It is a political response.”Macron insisted France “doesn’t need a state of emergency”, saying it “has the means” to control any further unrest. Union representatives met the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on Wednesday but no concrete announcements followed.Justice minister Gérald Darmanin said on Wednesday that, of the 2,500 people taken into custody during and after the protests, 174 had been jailed. Another 917 had been formally prosecuted, he added.Sometimes violent protests in European countries including Italy and Belgium have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading across the continent where with many nations, including France, face budget problems.Italy’s government has ordered 500 troopsto Milan to stem street violence there.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestGilets jaunes protestsEmmanuel MacronDonald TrumpEuropeCost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Steve Witkoff’s flattery of the Russian leader could be just the start of a mendacious stratagem from a US president who says Moscow ‘has been fine on Ukraine’
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Steve Witkoff’s flattery of the Russian leader could be just the start of a mendacious stratagem from a US president who says Moscow ‘has been fine on Ukraine’
Content: Students and teachers in the hallway at an underground school in Kharkiv, Ukraine.Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStudents and teachers in the hallway at an underground school in Kharkiv, Ukraine.Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The GuardianUkraineAnalysis‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and dieAndrew Rothin KharkivSteve Witkoff’s flattery of the Russian leader could be just the start of a mendacious stratagem from a US president who says Moscow ‘has been fine on Ukraine’Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.57 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.54 EDTShareThey say the first casualty of war is truth. For theTrump administration, the road to peace with Russia now encompasses some extraordinary lies.Steve Witkoff delivered one as he sat down withVladimir Putinin St Petersburg on Wednesday, aiming to close the deal on Russia’s land grab in Ukraine with the White House’s strategy of maximum pressure on Kyiv and saccharine flattery of the Kremlin.“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” said Witkoff, a real-estate mogul who, thanks to being Trump’s friend, is now the US’s senior envoy and diplomat to end the largest European conflict since the second world war. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”In Putin’s 26 years in power, it is a rare moment when he has been granted that specific honour. Skim through Russia’s past wartime exploits – from the bombing campaigns in Chechnya and Georgia and Syria, to the thousands of Russian citizens jailed for dissent, to the violent deaths of prominent opposition journalists and politicians in barely disguised assassinations and poisonings – and it will be difficult to identify Putin’s credentials as a humanitarian.View image in fullscreenVladimir Putin and Steve Witkoff meet in St Petersburg.Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/ReutersAnd that is before looking to Ukraine, where Russia chose to launch a full-scale invasion that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. The Guardianrecently obtained a Russian strategy documentshowing the Kremlin’s potential to black out Ukrainian cities this winter, cutting off up to 90% of electricity to cities such as Kyiv and Odesa and Kharkiv – where millions of people live – to intentionally create a humanitarian catastrophe. And judging by the nightly barrages levelled at power plants for cities across Ukraine, the Kremlin has decided to move forward with that strategy until Kyiv surrenders.As Witkoffmet Putin on Wednesday, schoolchildren in Kharkiv hastened down a reinforced stairway, sirens announcing the arrival of Shahed drones overhead. This is no ordinary bomb shelter; it is one of 10 underground schools Kharkiv has constructed because of Russia’s regular bombing of the city less than 20 miles from the border.Parents had welcomed the schools because they were safe, said teachers, and this was the one way that young people could have an uninterrupted school day during a war that could last years more – and reignite even if a shaky peace deal is reached.View image in fullscreenStudents and parents arrive and depart from the entrance to an underground school in Kharkiv.Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The Guardian“We all believed in Trump. We all really had hopes for America and for Trump to stop this monster Putin,” said Olena Svytlychna, the head of the education department of the Novobavarskyi region in Kharkiv, sitting in the school’s cafe on Wednesday.“And now we have doubts, we don’t believe them. And we are very scared.”As Witkoff spoke, the families of six people killed in a drone strike in a park near Kharkiv this week were holding funerals. The youngest victim of the strike was a one-year-old girl, Anhelina, who was killed as she was sitting strapped into her stroller in a playground. Her mother, Inna Mariukhna, a local schoolteacher, was also killed in the strike. The final death toll was four adults and two children, Anhelina and an 11-year-old girl.View image in fullscreenA destroyed building in Kharkiv after an air attack on Tuesday.Photograph: Sergey Bobok/AFP/Getty ImagesThose lives have barely earned a mention from the White House as it pushes forUkraineto capitulate as quickly as it can this week – and crucially before the 3 November midterm elections when voters will deliver a referendum on Trump’s leadership for the last two years.Shortly after the bombing, Trump told reporters on the White House lawn that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine”. After taking criticism for that remark, he mentioned the attacks in passing just to downplay the shelling of civilians: there were “some people in a town that got hit or whatever, but mostly young soldiers” died, he said from the Oval Office on Tuesday.For the White House, those words cost little. Witkoff’s goal was to bring home a US citizen, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, who had been detained in Russia. But if Witkoff wants to buy a peace deal by 3 November through flattering Putin, then this will only be the White House’s opening salvo in its war on truth.Explore more on these topicsUkraineUS foreign policyEuropeTrump administrationRussiaVladimir PutinDonald TrumpanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Thousands march in Greece over public education failures as Macron blasts ‘stupid’ commentary on French protests – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian
description: Students, teachers and civil servants demonstrate across Greece as Macron blasts ‘stupid’ commentary on French protests
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Students, teachers and civil servants demonstrate across Greece as Macron blasts ‘stupid’ commentary on French protests
Content: 08.42 EDTThousands march in Greece over public education failures and cost of livingCrowds are also marching in cities across Greece right now calling for better classroom conditions and higher pay for teachers.Thousands of students, teachers and civil servants have shown up in Athens, with demonstrations also in Thessaloniki and other cities. Some protesters say they’ve been inspired by the rallies inFranceand Spain.The primary school teachers union has launched a 24-hour strike while the high school teachers’ federation has also announced a three-hour stoppage, local media report.Students chant slogans during a protest over rising housing costs and underfunded education, in solidarity with students in France and Spain, in Athens, Greece, October 21, 2026.Photograph: Stelios Misinas/ReutersNationwide education protests are being held in many cities across Greece, with the participation of school pupils, university students, teachers, and public sector workers. title: Heidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attack | Israel | The Guardian
description: US photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incident
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: US photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incident
Content: Heidi Levine in her hospital bed on Wednesday before she was discharged.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHeidi Levine in her hospital bed on Wednesday before she was discharged.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianIsraelHeidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attackUS photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incidentJulian BorgerandQuique Kierszenbaumin Petah TikvaWed 21 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 20.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured byIsraeli settlers in the West Bank on Fridayhas described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians.Heidi Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds when she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by a crowd of masked settlers while she and other journalists were covering the olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.It is unclear whether the puncture wounds were caused by knives or other weapons. Levine said a witness to her attack had seen nails sticking out of some of the wooden clubs wielded by her attackers.Levine, 64, has covered multiple wars and had just returned from an assignment in Ukraine before Friday’s attack. She said she would most likely have been killed had she not been wearing protective body armour and a helmet.“I probably would have been dead, because for sure it doesn’t take much to kill a person with blows to the head,” she said shortly before being discharged from hospital on Wednesday in the Israeli city of Petah Tikva.Levine pointed out that Palestinians did not have such protection and more than 20 had been killed in settler attacks so far this year, in the course of an escalating campaign of aggression –described as terrorismby Israeli security leaders – across the West Bank, aimed at driving Palestinians from their land.“Every single journalist who looked at [the attack on me] are thinking they and I have gone to so many funerals of Palestinians killed by settlers,” Levine said.She said the olive harvesting at Abu Falah had begun peacefully but at some point a group of young masked settlers appeared on a nearby hilltop watching the group of Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying them. Levine said the attack began only after the Israeli army arrived on the scene.“Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said. “Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw teargas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me.“I managed to keep my face to the ground, and I don’t know if I took that position to protect myself with my face down or it was their initial blow. Otherwise my whole face would have been broken and I could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye.“They started kicking me and beating me with sticks. I can’t even count how many times, probably more than a hundred times. I actually tried playing dead so that they would stop. But it didn’t work.”1:57American photojournalist recounts Israeli settler attack in the occupied West Bank – videoWitnesses said the beating only ceased when young Palestinian men used slingshots to aim stones at settlers forcing them back, allowing another American journalist, Jasper Nathaniel, to reach Levine and, with other reporters, help her to safety.“Theshabab[Palestinian youth] put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing. It was like a biblical battle,” Levine said.After the attack,Nathaniel wrote: “Had theshababnot stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead. It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s.”He said the army pursued the young Palestinians after the incident, rather than the settlers. Palestinians risk being shot by settlers or soldiers if they try to resist attacks, and can face long periods in detention without charge.Levine, who has lived in Israel for four decades, said she would go back to reporting on theWest Bankas soon as she recovered. “My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.”Since the attack, she has received letters from Israelis expressing regret, and an apologetic phone call from the president, Isaac Herzog.“He was a teddy bear on the phone,” she said. “He kept saying I just want to give you a big hug and these are not representative of who this country is, they’re a dark stain, and he called them thugs.”The office of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, however, put outa statement on Xseeking to cast doubt on witness and video accounts of what he called an “alleged attack”.Levine was particularly angered by Netanyahu’s claim that some video footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”.“That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why,” Levine said. “They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me.”The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee,called the attacka “despicable act of terror” and demanded prosecutions. Israeli police arrested 10 suspects after the Abu Falah incident and another attack on Saturday aimed at European diplomats near the West Bank village of Taybeh.On Wednesday an Israeli court released four suspects in the attack on Levine and put them under house arrest, on the grounds there was insufficient evidence to keep them in custody.Asked if she expected her attackers to be brought to justice, Levine said her level of confidence was “two out of 10”.“I am not very hopeful,” she said. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it. But it’s not just arresting these teenage thugs. It’s going after their leaders, the rabbis, and how they’re organised.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelWest BankPalestineJournalist safetyWashington PostBenjamin NetanyahuUS press and publishingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Besieged Yemeni city on verge of ‘unmanageable’ crisis, aid workers warn | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Water and fresh food running out in Taiz as fighting intensifies and Houthi advance cuts off most supply routes
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Water and fresh food running out in Taiz as fighting intensifies and Houthi advance cuts off most supply routes
Content: People fill jerrycans with drinking water in Taiz on Wednesday.Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople fill jerrycans with drinking water in Taiz on Wednesday.Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/ReutersYemenBesieged Yemeni city on verge of ‘unmanageable’ crisis, aid workers warnWater and fresh food running out in Taiz as fighting intensifies and Houthi advance cuts off most supply routesPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorWed 21 Oct 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe humanitarian crisis in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is becoming unmanageable as the city runs out of water, fuel and fresh food, Oxfam aid workers in the country have warned.Iran-allied Houthi forces have largely encircled the city of more than 900,000 people, cutting it off from most supply routes. This week, heavy fighting has raged around the city’s old airport, causing extensive damage in a densely populated residential area.The conflict has intensified since forces loyal to the internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on the Houthi-held airport in Sana’a in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that had largely stopped the fighting.The UN has called for aid workers to be given access to Taiz. Oxfam in London called for the UK to send extra humanitarian aid to the country. The UK has allocated just £104m in aid to Yemen for each of the next three years, down from the £196m allocated in 2020. US aid to the stricken country has been virtually wiped out, and Germany, another leading funder, has halved its aid programme.Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthroughRead moreDonor countries have subscribed to only 23% of the cost of the UN humanitarian relief programme for Yemen this year, and pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia – itself cash-strapped by the cost of war – to make up the shortfall. The World Food Programme said wheat flour reserves in the city were nearly exhausted as of mid-October.View image in fullscreenPeople ride past a pile of burning rubbish in Taiz.Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/ReutersOn Tuesday the UK government allocated an unspecified sum in extra military help to Saudi Arabia to help protect its airports and infrastructure, but London has yet to decide on whether to back a much more robust military response, including supporting the possible deployment of foreign ground troops to Yemen.Fatma Jaffar, a Yemen-based advocacy manager for Oxfam, said local staff described an almost total siege of Taiz.“All the main entrances [to the city] have been blocked. The clashes are continuing and the casualties are very high,” she said. “Even people that have money are not able to buy food. Supplies are becoming very limited in the markets. No fuel has entered Taiz for two or three weeks. Drinking water is a massive issue. Even our staff are struggling to buy water.“Hospitals are struggling without medicines and a lot of people as a result are dying. Those that have been wounded by missiles – there have been attempts to get them out of the city, but because of the blockade they are not able to transfer anyone. Prices have rocketed.“Our staff told me that people are even searching for apples right now and they cannot find any fresh fruit, and basic commodities are not found inside the city. Garbage is piling up since they are not able to transfer the waste outside the city. They are trying to burn it, but we can only anticipate there will be diseases such as cholera in the near future. If this goes on much longer and access remains blocked, there will be casualties from missiles, hunger and disease from lack of water right across the city.“The situation was bad before the escalation – Yemen is one of the poorest countries on Earth – and now it is becoming unmanageable.”View image in fullscreenPeople wait to fill up cooking gas cylinders in Taiz.Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/ReutersPrices have rocketed: a 20-litre container of petrol that cost about $20 (£15) before the crisis is now worth $80 on the hidden market. Potato prices have doubled.The Houthi focus on Taiz reflects the city’s strategic importance, but the level of resistance inside the city may swallow the group’s resources, weakening its response elsewhere.Oxfam has been forced to transfer its limited resources from development to emergency humanitarian work, including offering cash transfers.The Halo Trust, the world’s largest humanitarian landmine-clearance organisation, said 30 of its staff were among hundreds of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city.In the Trump administration’s fiscal year 2027 budget request to Congress, the US state department has requested no economic support or development assistance specifically for Yemen. By comparison, the US committed roughly $760m in total aid to Yemen during the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.UN diplomats are still mediating between the two sides, but there is no sign that either theHouthisor the internationally recognised government are ready for a ceasefire, let alone a long-term settlement.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli military detain US and UK volunteers in West Bank including Democratic NY politician Brad Lander | West Bank | The Guardian
description: About 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers held near Nahalin in West Bank and taken to police station
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: About 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers held near Nahalin in West Bank and taken to police station
Content: Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander attends a vigil marking the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attacks on Israel, on 7 October 2026, in New York.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APView image in fullscreenDemocratic congressional candidate Brad Lander attends a vigil marking the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attacks on Israel, on 7 October 2026, in New York.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APWest BankIsraeli military detain US and UK volunteers in West Bank including Democratic NY politician Brad LanderAbout 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers held near Nahalin in West Bank and taken to police stationEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemWed 21 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Israeli military has detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including the New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander, several rabbis and Israel’s former deputy attorney general.“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis and volunteers,” Landerposted from a bustaking him to a police station. “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nahalin in the West Bank. The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”Lander, who is Jewish and an outspoken critic of the Israeli government,describeshimself as a liberal Zionist. He believes in the vision of Israel as a safe, Jewish home, but argues that it cannot be a true democracy while it denies Palestinians their human rights and freedom.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onplatform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueAn ally of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, Lander’s critical approach to Israel was a key factor in hisresounding primary victoryagainst Dan Goldman, a prominent supporter of Israel.He condemns Israel’s continued occupation of theWest Bankand Gaza, supported the restriction of US military aid to Israel and believes that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks amounts to genocide.Settler militants have unleashed extreme violence on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives from their trees across the occupied West Bank, and anyone accompanying them.Brad Lander speaks before being detained at olive harvest – videoAvicious assaulton a US photojournalist and attackson European diplomatsand a French mayor over the weekend drew international condemnation and calls for the Israeli government to crack down on militants.Wednesday’s olive-picking from trees outside the village of Nahalin was uneventful until a large contingent of Israeli security forces arrived, the organisers Protect the Harvest said in a statement.“All volunteers were peacefully harvesting on the private land of a Palestinian family who had invited them. For reasons that remain unclear, the Israeli army showed up and detained approximately 80 people who were present.”Soldiers said the area had been declared a closed military zone, separated the group by nationality and drove them to a nearby police station in minibuses for the Israelis and a larger bus for Americans.Joshua Schoffman, who served as Israel’s deputy attorney general for more than a decade, described the mass detention as a “complete hallucination” in apost on social media.“Just now, they told me that I’m being detained for the crime of olive harvesting,” he wrote. “We were asked to stop, and everyone complied. There was no friction whatsoever with settlers or with the security forces.”Lander was released with a warning but all the others were still being held, Protect the Harvest said. Detainees include Jill Jacobs, the chief executive of T’ruah: The Rabbinic Call for Human Rights, and 11 other American rabbis affiliated with the group.The detainees have been given water but no food. The Israeli military and police did not immediately respond to requests for comment.On Monday, Lander made afirst postabout his journey to Palestine. “Our goals for the trip are to help protect the olive harvest – and to shed a light on the reality of the occupation,” he wrote. “Thankfully, our corner of today’s harvest was peaceful and successful. But violence unfortunately is never far away.”Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Troubled waters: life during wartime for Iranians on the strait of Hormuz | Iran | The Guardian
description: Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there
Author: Stefanie Glinski
Headline: Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there
Content: One of the ships stranded in the Strait of Hormuz.Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work thereByStefanie Glinski; photographs by Mohammad Mohsenifar in Bandar Abbas/on Hormuz IslandWed 21 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCapt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.View image in fullscreenCapt Farouq pulls into the deeper watersView image in fullscreenHe’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second homeFarouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.View image in fullscreenOne of the ships stranded in the strait of HormuzEven with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait.
