In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers,sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel.With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.View image in fullscreenFishers returning from seaView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenFishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the streetFishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.View image in fullscreenLocal residents fishing for their own daily consumptionView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAnvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.View image in fullscreenAnvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas“This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.View image in fullscreenHassan, 28, cafe owner – has run a cafe on the island for eight yearsView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenHormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.View image in fullscreenYashar, a 35-year-old surferView image in fullscreenA group of local women swimming off the coast of Hormuz IslandLife here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.View image in fullscreenOmran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflictView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war“The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.View image in fullscreenThe Salt valley on Hormuz Island, one of the island’s tourist attractionsFrom the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.View image in fullscreenOne of the ships stranded in the strait of HormuzKhaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.View image in fullscreenKhaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter“Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.”Explore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayIranStrait of HormuzMiddle East and north AfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Indian court orders release of two leaders of Cockroach movement | India | The Guardian
description: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdown
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdown
Content: Saurav Das (centre) and Ashutosh Ranka (right) leave a police station after seeking approval for a protest earlier this month.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSaurav Das (centre) and Ashutosh Ranka (right) leave a police station after seeking approval for a protest earlier this month.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesIndiaIndian court orders release of two leaders of Cockroach movementSaurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdownHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiWed 21 Oct 2026 11.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka,had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jailafter being arrested by Delhi police last week.On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, which led to the barricading of central Delhi andthousands of young peoplebeing detained.11:32India’s Cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown - The LatestDas and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the rulingNarendra Modigovernment, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streetsRead moreThe CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have beencalling for the resignationof the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced theresignation of Modi’s education ministerafter sustained demonstrations.Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was alsodetained on Fridayafter he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”Explore more on these topicsIndiaProtestNarendra ModiSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Aneurin Bevan’s personal security file was ‘remarkably tame’ – National Archives | Labour | The Guardian
description: Some in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interest
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Some in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interest
Content: Aneurin Bevan came to the attention of MI5 in the 1930s.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenAneurin Bevan came to the attention of MI5 in the 1930s.Photograph: PALabourAneurin Bevan’s personal security file was ‘remarkably tame’ – National ArchivesSome in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interestCaroline DaviesWed 21 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAneurin “Nye” Bevan, the WelshLabourfirebrand who spearheaded the creation of the NHS, was monitored by security services for more than two decades, though his personal file was “remarkably tame”, according to official files released to the public.Bevan came to MI5’s attention in the 1930s over concerns about his links with known communists, papers released to theNational Archivesshow. Monitoring continued even after he became a minister in the postwar Labour government that created the NHS.At one point, his links to a known Russian spy led to the then director general ofMI5approaching prime minister Clement Attlee to warn him.However, the papers show, some in the security services questioned why Bevan was of interest. Although there is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, one officer wrote in 1943: “I do not think that Bevan’s activities are a matter in which we, the Security Service, should be involved.“In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently, as any copy of Hansard will show, and it would not therefore be possible to do anything positive.”Reviewing the file after his death in 1960, another MI5 officer noted: “Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame.”MI5 first opened a personal file on the backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in South Wales in 1933. He was described in one entry to have “inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the communist cause.”He was also noted to have been “in close touch” with Harry Pollitt, general secretary of the Communist party of Great Britain, and others in the party who backed his plan to organise “workers’ freedom groups” to defend against “capitalists”.Bevan fell out with his communist allies who had complained he was not interested in workers’ unity and was intent on building “a movement of his own”. But by 1936 they had reconciled, with Bevan supporting an application by the Communist party to affiliate with the Labour party.In 1949, MI5 became concerned about Bevan’s friendship with Wilfred Macartney, who had been convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.Recordings of Macartney’s conversations suggested he was passing on information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt. It led the director general Sir Percy Sillitoe to approach Attlee, who dismissed Macartney’s claims as a “tissue of lies” but agreed to “warn” Bevan about Macartney.The file was finally closed in 1975, 15 years after Bevan died.Other newly released papers show MI5 feared communists could attempt to disrupt the coronation of King George VI, with Communist party activists closely watched before the Westminster Abbey ceremony in 1937.While the party prepared a propaganda drive and printed a million anti-monarchist leaflets to be distributed during coronation week, members were warned to avoid antagonising a largely pro-royalist public.One MI5 report from April 1937 noted that a “comrade” in Manchester had been “severely censured” for proposing a series of demonstrations as it would be “playing into the hands of the fascists and police”. “It has been pointed out that members will be ‘going against the stream’ in doing this and they must be careful to speak in such a way that they do not make themselves unpopular with their neighbours.”Sir Michael Tippett, a leading British composer of the 20th century and a famed pacifist, was also monitored by MI5 as a suspected Trotskyist revolutionary, according to the files.MI5 believed he joined first the Communist party and then the Trotskyists in the 1930s, and remained an active supporter until the end of the second world war.The files suggest, however, he was unconvincing as a revolutionary. In one intercepted letter to a Communist party organiser in London, he complained of the difficulties of trying to combine his work as a communist with his life as a music teacher living in rural Surrey. His evening commitments meant that it was “quite impossible” for him to attend “cell” meetings in London, he complained.A report from 1955 noted that Tippett “has not come to notice in connection with communist or Trotskyist affairs”.However, his radical past meant that as late as 1959 he was blocked from taking up a Foreign Office-sponsored lectureship in Germany, and it was only in the 1960s that MI5 were prepared to give him a clean bill of health. In 1966, he was knighted for services to music. He died in 1998 aged 93.Explore more on these topicsLabourMI5National ArchivesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: Committee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decade
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Committee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decade
Content: It took the UK destroyer warship HMS Dragon more than three weeks to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt took the UK destroyer warship HMS Dragon more than three weeks to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesDefence policyRoyal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warnCommittee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decadeDan SabbaghDefence and security editorWed 21 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability ofRoyal Navysubmarines and warships, MPs on the defence select committee have said.The committee focused on the slow deployment of HMS Dragon to Cyprus this spring, declining numbers of frigates, and reports that all five Astute-class attack submarines were in dock this summer as evidence of a navy under-resourced for the threat.“The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the high north,” said Tan Dhesi, the committee chair. “Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments.”The high north, the seas beyond Scotland, have become increasingly strategically significant amid growing Russian interest in energy pipelines and undersea cables at a time when Arctic seaways are opening up because of global heating.The navy shadowed a Russian spy ship, the Yantar, operating inside the UK’s economic waters inNovemberandJanuarylast year, accusing sailors onboard of trying to map strategic cables and shining lasers at RAF pilots monitoring them.Map of high northRussia also wants to assert control over the emerging northern sea route, a 3,500-mile (5,600km) shipping lane running along the country’s Arctic coast. It is the quickest maritime route from China to Europe, navigable last year for four and half months.The MPs argued the UK needed to make “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade, and they called on theMinistry of Defenceto draw up a plan to ensure more warships and submarines are at sea by 2030.The problem would be particularly acute, the committee added, if the US did not support the UK in a crisis, a rare cross-party acknowledgment that under Donald Trump, US military help cannot be relied on, particularly if a small Nato member in the region was threatened or attacked.“There would be critical military gaps if the United States were not involved in countering such [Russian] aggression,” the MPs said, and they argued that the UK, as the next largest Nato military in the region, had to be prepared to increase its navy.It took more than three weeks for HMS Dragon, a destroyer, to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean in March after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone. No warships were available and Dragon had to be hauled out of dry dock to deploy.The navy has five frigates with sonar dedicated to detecting Russian submarines at distance, the committee noted, lower than a target of eight, as ageing warships have been scrapped without replacements coming into service. It could take until 2037 before it reaches its stated requirement, the committee added.None of Britain’s five Astute submarines, also used to track Russian maritime activity, were at sea from June and into the summer. They were in dock for a mixture of short-term and long-term refits, the committee noted, and they also lack the capability to operate under ice, unlike their Russian equivalents, although certification exercises are in progress.However, no significant extra money is expected to be available for defence until the next decade, with Andy Burnham’s government committed to medium-term spending plans agreed under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer.Though Starmer agreed to lift defence spending by about £30bn a year to 3.5% of GDP in 2035, he would only sign off spending to the lower level of 2.7% by 2030. That prompted the resignation of John Healey as defence secretary, only for him to return as chancellor under Burnham, with the old spending plans intact.In response to the report, an MoD spokesperson highlighted a recent £330m investment to protect undersea infrastructure, and noted that Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, had visited Iceland this month and watched how HMS St Albans, a frigate, tracked Russian submarines in the north Atlantic. “We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses,” they added.Explore more on these topicsDefence policyRoyal NavyMinistry of DefenceMilitarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Orangutans prefer food associated with sounds of laughter, study suggests | Animal behaviour | The Guardian
description: Apes in study more likely to choose treats linked to sound of peers having fun, suggesting emotions influence learning
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Apes in study more likely to choose treats linked to sound of peers having fun, suggesting emotions influence learning
Content: An orangutan tucks into a treat. The study suggests positive emotions could influence how the great apes learn and make decisions.Photograph: Elisabetta A Villa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn orangutan tucks into a treat. The study suggests positive emotions could influence how the great apes learn and make decisions.Photograph: Elisabetta A Villa/Getty ImagesAnimal behaviourOrangutans prefer food associated with sounds of laughter, study suggestsApes in study more likely to choose treats linked to sound of peers having fun, suggesting emotions influence learningNicola DavisScience correspondentWed 21 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOrangutans base their food choices on whether others appear to be having a good time, research suggests.Scientists studying captive orangutans have found that when the great apes heard the sound of their peers laughing before they searched a bowl for a tasty treat, they valued the reward more highly.Erica Cartmill, a professor of anthropology and cognitive science at Indiana University and senior author of the work, said the study is part of a larger project exploring whether animals feel joy and what the implications of those emotions are in areas such as cognition and learning.“One of our big motivations … is building on human research that shows that emotion has important effects on rational thought – and that they aren’t two separate things; they really influence one another,” she said. “We wanted to extend that to animals – in this case to orangutans.”Writing in the journal Biology Letters, Cartmill and her colleagues report how they worked with six orangutans based at two zoological institutions.The researchers first trained the orangutans to search through bowls to find food treats. They then presented each orangutan with two bowls. One contained a tasty morsel buried under a harmless substance such as moss or sawdust, while the other contained a different type of material but no treat.Crucially, just before the researchers presented the bowls to the orangutans, they played a recording. This was either the sound of orangutans playing and laughing or environmental sounds such as wind, with the choice of soundtrack depending on which of two substances was used to cover the food that day.On the fifth day the team presented the orangutans with two bowls, but this time each contained a treat buried beneath one of the two food-covering substances. They then asked the orangutans to pick a bowl.The results from multiple trials revealed that, overall, the apes preferred to pick the bowl containing the substance associated with the sound of laughter, with four of the six orangutans showing a clear preference.Cartmill said the preference could be rooted in the sound of laughter putting the orangutans in a more positive emotional state when they learned to associate the substance with food.Dr Adriano Lameira, a primatologist and evolutionary psychologist at the University of Warwick, who was not involved in the work, described the results as fascinating.“Effectively, hearing others clearly having a good time, orangutans placed their food order: ‘I will have what they are having, please!’” he said.Cartmill added the results suggest it is not only the quantity or frequency of a reward that can be important when learning associations.“What our work is showing is that it’s also about the state of the animal when they are learning that association,” she said.“Who you are in that moment – the context, the emotional states, what you’re feeling, what you’re thinking about – can also influence and can carry over in how you remember these things that you’ve learned.”The findings, she added, could have applications to humans, including in educational environments.“Students might learn at similar rates if they are in a good mood or not, but our research suggests that they would value information more if they learn it when they are in a good mood,” Cartmill said.She added that could be useful in helping to understand why some information is more trusted or why students choose to continue studying certain subjects.“If a student is anxious when they are learning maths for example, it might impact whether they prefer maths versus other subjects when choosing what to pursue in the future,” she said.Explore more on these topicsAnimal behaviourPrimatologyAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Tory election candidate suspended over contract killing claims | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Jack Ross was filmed allegedly discussing with an undercover reporter violent options to deal with enemies
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Jack Ross was filmed allegedly discussing with an undercover reporter violent options to deal with enemies
Content: Jack Ross at a London vigil after the murder of Charlie Kirk. He told Al Jazeera that his comments to its undercover reporter were not serious.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyView image in fullscreenJack Ross at a London vigil after the murder of Charlie Kirk. He told Al Jazeera that his comments to its undercover reporter were not serious.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyConservativesFormer Tory election candidate suspended over contract killing claimsJack Ross was filmed allegedly discussing with an undercover reporter violent options to deal with enemiesBen QuinnandHenry DyerWed 21 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 15.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former Conservative election candidate has been suspended from the party after he was seemingly filmed discussing the cost of hiring contract killers and offering to “broker” the services of a far-right activist with alleged paramilitary links.Jack Ross was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter “What do you want done?” before listing the type of violent options that could be bought.Ross appeared to tell the Al Jazeera journalist: “They can just kick the fuck out of someone. That’s a certain amount. They can start cutting people’s faces up, that’s another amount. And they can stab someone. They can shoot someone. They can kill someone.”Police inScotlandsay they will be reviewing and assessing the Al Jazeera documentary – Contract Killers and the Far Right – for any criminality.Ross is the chief executive of Turning Point UK, a spin-off from the campaign group founded by the murdered US Republican commentator Charlie Kirk.Footage released by TPUK last year showed Ross and others from the group meeting Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, after Kirk’s death.A profile page for Ross on the website of the Bow Group, a Conservative thinktank that lists him as a research fellow, states he has advised MPs and candidates on political and digital strategy. He has been pictured alongside Boris Johnson and other high-profile figures including James Cleverly, Jacob Rees-Mogg and Liam Fox.Ross wasreported by Al Jazeerato have introduced an undercover reporter to a violent criminal from Glasgow with links to the paramilitary Ulster Volunteer Force, who offers to have people killed for money.Al Jazeera approached Ross with a fictitious family problem where a deceased uncle’s business was at risk of being taken over by a gang, whose members were supposedly warned they would “get fucked” if anything happened.Ross replied to this: “Yeah, you have to deliver on that as well. You’ve got to explain to me what’s needed … I can then go and broker from there. But I’ve got to say, even to myself … if there’s lashback I’ve got to keep my name out of it.”The Scottish paramilitary contact was then filmed at a London hotel offering to arrange different types of killings, ranging from a hit-and-run that could be made to look like drink-driving to a stabbing.The meeting took place after Ross, apparently acting on behalf of the Zimbabwean government, had reportedly paid thousands of pounds to the Glasgow activist to organise a fake political rally in support of lifting UK sanctions imposed on the African country.Ross said: “I have had a few things and some of the Zims [Zimbabweans] have said to me they want stuff done. They wanted a fucking shooter.”He said he had asked them to talk to the paramilitary, adding: “I said I was not putting fucking prints on anything.”While TPUK was launched as a student movement, it has become increasingly involved in anti-migrant street protests. Its chief operating officer is Nick Tenconi, the leader of the far-right UK Independence party, who visited the Conservative conference in 2022 with Ross.Ross was filmed in 2022 telling an undercover reporter they should chat to him about what they wanted, adding “keep it simple” and then listing the various violent options that could be bought for cash, including murder.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Conservative party spokesperson said: “Mr Ross’s membership of the Conservative party has been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation. We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing.”At another point, Ross expressed concerns that journalists could be recording the sort of things he was saying and could pass them to police.“The journalist will put it out there and then the police will pick it up and fuck you,” he said. “You’ve got to think that what we were talking about and had someone film it we’d be fucking done for conspiracy.”Tenconi was filmed alongside Ross as they outlined a plan to use football hooligans to stir up trouble.Tenconi said: “So let Labour get in. So we build the new right and we have these armies … so, three-pronged. We keep winning MPs over. Then we build the second prong, we build an army, and that’s street demos, protest, just fuck things up, basically.”A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the documentary. It will be reviewed and assessed for any criminality.”Al Jazeera reported that Ross had “completely” denied its investigation’s findings, claiming that everything he said to the undercover reporter was not meant seriously.Ross, who was a local elections candidate for theConservatives, was approached by the Guardian for comment through TPUK. Tenconi was also approached for comment via his party.Explore more on these topicsConservativesUK Independence party (Ukip)ScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: No surprise and lasting anger: families of people who died in care homes react to Covid inquiry report | Covid inquiry | The Guardian
description: Relatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policy
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: Relatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policy
Content: The Covid memorial wall in London.Photograph: Matt Crossick/PAView image in fullscreenThe Covid memorial wall in London.Photograph: Matt Crossick/PACovid inquiryNo surprise and lasting anger: families of people who died in care homes react to Covid inquiry reportRelatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policyEsther AddleyWed 21 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“At the time it felt like a devil’s bargain – it was horrible, but it was what [we thought] we had to do to keep people safe,” says Amy of the “devastating” and “terrifying” restrictions that led to her maternal grandparents being locked down in separate care homes during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.Eva and Eric had been married for more than 60 years when her dementia and his increased frailty meant they needed separate residential support. When the first lockdown was announced in March 2020, however, it in effect cut them off from each other and their granddaughter, to whom they had been especially close after the early death of Amy’s mother.“I spoke to Grandad on the phone when it was possible – it often wasn’t possible due to staff not being able to take him a phone – and he was desperately lonely, isolated in his room, unable to talk to anyone because they were worried about [the spread of Covid],” says Amy, 39, who lives in Milton Keynes and works for a large software company. “I consoled myself that they were keeping him safe. That all the isolation was necessary.”Instead, she says, he was depressed and very afraid until he finally caught the virus in 2022. Amy saw him for the first time on a Covid ward, “when I had to beg and beg and beg the hospital staff to let me visit him”. Eric died shortly afterwards.View image in fullscreenEva and Eric.Photograph: SuppliedSix years after Covid struck, the latest report from the public inquiry into the pandemic, published this week, has convinced Amy that the policy of isolating residents was “cruel and pointless”, she says. “I want to smash something. I can never get that time with them back.“The impression I had at the time was that [the government] were doing their best in the face of an unstoppable tidal wave, but it sounds like they put out a hand and expected it to stop the ocean.”The inquiry concludedthat the entire care sector had been an “afterthought” to government planners, and that a claim by the then health secretary, Matt Hancock, to have put a “protective ring” around residents was entirely unfounded. Instead, the decision to discharge untested patients from hospitals into care homes led to the virus spreading “like wildfire”, while blanket restrictions on outside contact led to “immense emotional harm” and “profound isolation” for vulnerable residents.The findings are no surprise to the family members of care home residents, many of whom have told the Guardian of the immense distress their loved ones went through. Roger Dennison’s father, Lucius, was a sprightly 90-year-old care home resident when the first reports of the coronavirus emerged; they watched the news together in Lucius’s room and wondered how quickly it would peter out.Weeks later, Lucius’s care home had firmly locked down, and the only way Dennison could talk to his dad was through a window that had been opened a few inches at the top. “You’re standing on tiptoe, trying to shout in and then be heard on the other side,” he says. “It was very confusing. It wasn’t very happy as an experience.” They tried it just once but stopped because it was too distressing for Lucius.Lucius Dennison.Photograph: Roger DennisonAfter that, Dennison, who had previously visited every other day, was reliant on passing messages through staff, while Lucius was “in his room, largely on his own”. The disease “became a growing apprehension for me once it became clear people were coming into the home and bringing it with them”, says his son. “I think there was a sense of inevitability.” Lucius caught Covid in the first wave and died in hospital in April 2020.To care workers, too, the situation was terrifying and immensely distressing, says Nick (not his real name), who was a senior worker at a home in West Yorkshire. “The situation from the very start was frightening because we all thought that if you got Covid, you died or were going to be seriously unwell. I remember having to strip naked at the back door of my house because we had a resident return from hospital who had shared a ward with Covid patients. As a care home, we tried to refuse their return based on the risk of infection but were told [by the hospital] that we couldn’t.”From that point, he says, “all hell broke loose”. “Our first case of Covid was about a week later.” They had already run out of personal protective equipment, he says.‘Superficial damp squib’: Covid inquiry recommendations fail to impress bereaved familiesRead more“The mental health impact on all staff was huge. Watching people die at such a high rate in such a small space of time; having to say goodbye to so many people we came to know and love; putting our own health on the line every day and then quite possibly carrying that home to your family. Mentally, we were all spent.”Like many, Catherine Bennett, a retired teacher from Lewes in East Sussex, says she was not shocked by the inquiry’s findings: “We knew what was happening. I am, however, very angry.” Her father, who had been in a care home since 2018, “felt a terrible sense of abandonment” that no one was able to visit and became paralysingly afraid of catching the virus.“For a long time he didn’t go down for meals; he stopped doing all his activities so he wouldn’t meet anybody.” After some months, she says, the care home built a room where residents could talk to relatives through a glass panel and speakers. It was, she says, “very distressing for a man of his age to be separated from his loved ones in that way, to be able to see us through the glass but not be able to touch us or have any meaningful contact”. Her father died in the home in 2022.Diana, a retired social worker from Derby, feels a similar lasting anger about the experience of her sister, Helen, whose mental health needs meant she was living in a care home in Carlisle when the pandemic struck, and who experienced a similar bewilderment at her sudden isolation. The first time Diana was able to sit with her was after a year of lockdown when Helen was very unwell; she died the same day.“I just think they threw care homes under a bus while they partied in Downing Street, and I do feel rather cross about that,” says Diana. “I think it is a major trauma for this country and I think it should never be forgotten.”Explore more on these topicsCovid inquiryCoronavirusSocial careCare workersOlder peopleHealth policyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Officials confirm flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite found in US wildlife | Texas | The Guardian
description: USDA says screwworm found in elk in Texas, and warns hunters and ranchers to be vigilant to help stop spread
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: USDA says screwworm found in elk in Texas, and warns hunters and ranchers to be vigilant to help stop spread
Content: A New World screwworm and other botfly specimens under the microscope at a lab in Kerrville, Texas.Photograph: Kaylee Greenlee/ReutersView image in fullscreenA New World screwworm and other botfly specimens under the microscope at a lab in Kerrville, Texas.Photograph: Kaylee Greenlee/ReutersTexasOfficials confirm flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite found in US wildlifeUSDA says screwworm found in elk in Texas, and warns hunters and ranchers to be vigilant to help stop spreadGuardian staff and agencyWed 21 Oct 2026 19.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Department of Agriculture (USDA) said on Wednesday it had ⁠confirmed the ⁠first detection ​of flesh-eating parasite the New World screwworm in US wildlife in an ⁠elk in Pecos county,Texas.The elk was located on a game ⁠ranch and was reported after being harvested by ​a hunter, the ‌USDA said ‌in a statement.The Texas animal health ‌commission will modify a previously established infested zone, and the USDA and the Texas parks and wildlife department is conducting additional wildlife surveillance in the area, the USDA said.“We encourage all hunters and landowners to be vigilant for signs of New World screwworm while they are out in the field this season,” Texas wildlife division director Alan Cainsaidin a statement.Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central ​America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports.The US halted livestock imports ⁠from Mexico last year to keep out screwworm, ​but ​resumed trade in August ​at an Arizona port as part ​of a ‌phased reopening ​plan.The halt has tightened US cattle supplies and pushed beef prices to record highs for American consumers.Despite those efforts, the screwworm was detected in June on a calf in Texas’s Zavala county, located near the US-Mexico border. There have since been dozens of cases detected in the US this year, including on a horse and on a dog.Explore more on these topicsTexasUS politicsWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tesla beats earnings projections after Musk floats SpaceX merger plan | Tesla | The Guardian
description: Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but he declined to elaborate
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but he declined to elaborate
Content: A Tesla dealership in Santa Clarita, California. Wall Street has projected Tesla to report $27.9bn in revenues.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Tesla dealership in Santa Clarita, California. Wall Street has projected Tesla to report $27.9bn in revenues.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesTeslaTesla beats earnings projections after Musk floats SpaceX merger planMusk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but he declined to elaborateDara KerrWed 21 Oct 2026 19.03 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInvestors were paying close attention to Tesla’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executiveElon Muskfloated the idea of merging the car company with his rocket and AI company, SpaceX. But they didn’t glean further information after the company announced there would be no questions on the matter.“With regard to a potential merger withSpaceX, I think I said everything that should be said yesterday,” Musk, the CEO of both companies, said on Tesla’s earnings call. He repeated a phrase he said on Tuesday: “I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.”On acall with SpaceX investorson Tuesday, Musk said it would be a “good idea” to combine the two companies and that “there’s a lot of merit” that would come with it.Musk said on Tuesday that the board of directors for both of his businesses had put together special committees to explore the potential merger, but had not yet reached an agreement on the terms of the transaction. The move would require the approval of 50% of allTeslashareholders.Tesla and SpaceX explore merger as Elon Musk gives backingRead moreOn Wednesday, Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings, with a reported revenue of $28.05bn and $0.48 on earnings per share. That beat Wall Street’s projections of $27.9bn in revenue, with $0.43 on earnings per share. Still, the company came in at aslightly lower revenue than last quarter, which was $28.23bn. And its automotive revenue dropped 3% from the year prior.“We maintained strong momentum on many projects spanning Super Intelligence (SI), robotics and renewable energy that will be critical to building a future of Amazing Abundance,” the company wrote in itsreport.Despite the stronger-than-anticipated quarter, Tesla has experienced a rough year with falling stock and increased competition from cheaper Chinese automakers. The company’s share price has fallen by more than 11% this year, although it appears to have rebounded some since last week with the news of the possible SpaceX merger.Last week, Muskunveiled the company’s electric sports car, the Roadster 2, which he said uses technology from SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”. At a demonstration at a SpaceX facility in Texas, a remote-controlled version of the car drove up a steeply curved ramp and then used jet-like thrusters to flip over, hover and land. The vehicle is priced at upwards of $200,000.“Flying cars are real … It can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics,” Musk said at the event, adding: “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions.”During Tesla’s earnings call on Wednesday, he added that the event was “the coolest demo of any product ever”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTesla’s vehicle sales are not as crucial to its market performance as they once were, as the company has pivoted towards robotics, autonomous driving and AI. Tesla’s Optimus robot has faced production hurdles, however; and its driverless taxi service, Robotaxi, has hit road blocks in scaling its fleet and expanding to new cities.“Tesla’s leaders continue to make big claims about autonomous mobility and physical AI. The company has achieved remarkable things but continues to miss some of its leaders’ bolder bets,” said Paul Miller, a principal analyst for market research firm Forrester. “Tesla robotaxis are undeniably carrying passengers, but not yet at anywhere near the levels the company promised.”Musk has long declared the Robotaxi will have near-infinite demand and that “probably half the population of the US” would be using the autonomous ride-hailing service by the end of 2025. Similarly, the CEO has forecast the manufacture of as many as 1m Optimus robots each year. As Miller pointed out with Musk’s promises, he has failed to reach those lofty targets and rollout has been slow.Musk once again touted the robots on Wednesday, saying: “I remain convinced that Optimus will be the biggest product on earth and humanoid robots in general will be the biggest product on earth.” He added that no other company compares to Tesla in developing humanoid robots – this is despite Chinese competitorsmaking vast stridesin the technology.Explore more on these topicsTeslaQuarterly resultsElon MuskSpaceXnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nancy Pelosi’s office latest recipient of letter containing white powder | Nancy Pelosi | The Guardian
description: Former speaker is latest target of mailings sent to various Congress members in the lead-up to the midterm elections
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Former speaker is latest target of mailings sent to various Congress members in the lead-up to the midterm elections
Content: Nancy Pelosi at the US Capitol on 20 November 2025.Photograph: Tasos Katopodis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNancy Pelosi at the US Capitol on 20 November 2025.Photograph: Tasos Katopodis/Getty ImagesNancy PelosiNancy Pelosi’s office latest recipient of letter containing white powderFormer speaker is latest target of mailings sent to various Congress members in the lead-up to the midterm electionsDani AnguianoWed 21 Oct 2026 18.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCalifornia representative Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious letter” on Wednesday in what appears to be the latest incident of ill-intentioned mailings targeted at US Congress members before the midterm elections.The offices of more than three dozen members of Congress across the political spectrum havereceived envelopescontaining white powder in recent days. One lawmaker’s office said preliminary tests indicated the powder was not hazardous.More than three dozen Congress members’ offices sent envelopes containing white powderRead moreA spokesperson for Pelosi said the letter was “consistent with mailings reported by other congressional offices” and that everyone in the office was safe.“Speaker Pelosi remains focused on serving the people of San Francisco and is concerned for the members and staff whose offices have experienced similar incidents,” Nicholas Martin, a spokesperson for the speaker emerita, said in a statement.“She is grateful for the efforts of the US Capitol police, the San Francisco police department and other law enforcement agencies to thoroughly investigate this series of intimidation across America.”More than 100 letters thought to contain white powder were reportedly thought to be circulating in the US mail system. Election offices across the US have also reported receiving suspicious mail.The mailings are under investigation by the FBI, the Capitol police and the US Postal Inspection Service. The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement earlier this week: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.”Explore more on these topicsNancy PelosiHouse of RepresentativesUS CongressUS crimeUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Hunted like animals’: inside Trump’s war on the people who build America | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was a house framer before he was killed by ICE agents. Countless other Latino builders in Texas live in fear of a similar fate
Author: Ed Pilkington
Headline: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was a house framer before he was killed by ICE agents. Countless other Latino builders in Texas live in fear of a similar fate
Content: Workers build the wooden framing on the second floor of what will become a townhouse in Harlingen, Texas.Photograph: Michael Gonzalez/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWorkers build the wooden framing on the second floor of what will become a townhouse in Harlingen, Texas.Photograph: Michael Gonzalez/The GuardianICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)‘Hunted like animals’: inside Trump’s war on the people who build AmericaLorenzo Salgado Araujo was a house framer before he was killed by ICE agents. Countless other Latino builders in Texas live in fear of a similar fateEd PilkingtonWed 21 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTShareEvery morning long before dawn, while America sleeps, legions ofTexasconstruction workers grab their fluorescent vests and hard hats, sling ladders and tools into their trucks, and head down the highway for another day of grueling labour under the blistering sun.Elsewhere, before the first flush of daylight settles over Texas’s concrete sprawl, a separate army gets on the move in a fleet of shiny unmarked SUVs. They hover at gas stations, prowl around bodegas, pounce on the highways.They’re on their way to work too. But the federal agents who form this second army are on a different mission.Unlike the builders, they are not forging the US’s future one new starter home at a time. Their job is to pursue those who do the building: they follow the framers, track down the roofers, chase the cement masons and concrete finishers.They are hunters.Gone in 90 seconds: an ‘invisibilized’ ICE is arresting more people than everRead more“In Texas, you go deer hunting in the early morning,” said Jacob Monty, an immigration lawyer in Houston. “That’s what they are doing. They are hunting for construction workers, early in the morning, like you would an animal.”Texas and its construction workforce are the ground zero of Donald Trump’s latest mass deportation effort, dubbedICE 2.0. As the US president has pivoted from last year’s militarized “invasions” of Los Angeles and Minneapolis to this year’s less visible but no less devastating stop-and-search tactics, he has found rich pickings in Texas.Texas is seeing by far the greatest number of ICE arrests in the country. More than 12,000 inJuly alone, almost double the number in the next most affected states, Florida and California.Workers constructing townhouses at a subdivision in Harlingen, Texas in September.Many of the detainees are Hispanic builders. Of every 10 construction workers in Texas, fourare foreign born, most of whom are Hispanic and undocumented.“This is low-hanging fruit,” Monty said. “If you target Texas Hispanics in trucks, you have a good chance of nabbing an undocumented person, and feeding the mass deportation machine.”But there is a price to pay for ICE casting its dragnet through Texas barrios and building sites as it seeks to meet itsnew targetof 3,000 immigration arrests daily. The street-level apprehensions are roiling the state, distorting its economy, forcing up house prices and the cost of groceries.Hispanic families are also being torn apart. Hardworking people are being pushed into the shadows, others disappearing as they flee the country or are deported. The foundations of new homes are lying unfinished, building sites empty.With the midterm elections just days away, and hugely consequential congressional races as well as the gubernatorial contest hanging in the balance, there are also political costs. Trump appears to be digging a hole for himself with Texas’s Hispanic voters.double quotation markWe are here to protect our families, send our kids to college, to learn and growSergio BenavidesLatino Texans who were born in the US or have naturalised, and thus can vote, are increasingly angry and confused. Many of them voted for Trump two years ago, attracted by his promise of a stronger economy and a fortified border that would keep out “criminal” immigrants.They delivered Trump a historic victory, even in majority-Hispanic districts that had been Democratic strongholds for more than a century – voters like Sergio Benavides, 44, the owner of a home-building construction company in the Texas borderlands of the Rio Grande valley.A naturalised US citizen, he voted for Trump in 2024. He liked his campaign promises that he would lower prices and secure the border. When people warned him it would turn sour, he didn’t listen.He’s listening now. The prices of homes, food and gas have all gone up. Workers have to be paid more because so many have been deported. One of his subcontractors and his wife have disappeared, picked up by ICE, leaving behind three US-citizen children.“That makes me sad,” he said. “We are here to protect our families, send our kids to college, to learn and grow. This is not what I thought when I voted for Trump.”Benavides is part of a backlash that is showing up in the polls. Latino voters are turning against the president on the very issues that drew them to him – the cost of living, and immigration enforcement.A poll last month fromEquis Researchfound that disapproval of Trump had risen to 63% among Texas Latinos. In the critical US Senate race, which could determine which party holds the upper chamber during Trump’s final two years in office, 58% of likely Latino voters intend to back the Democratic candidate James Talarico, while only 33% support the scandal-ridden Republican, Ken Paxton. This, in a state that last returned a Democrat to the US Senate in 1988.Latinos make up a third of Texas’s registered voters, the second-highest number in the country. And they know it.Construction workers among them.Marco Antonio Osorio’s day begins at 5am. Same routine, six days a week.A member of his crew comes to pick him up at his house in Houston. They drive around in their shared white truck gathering other crew, then head off to the site of a new apartment complex where they spend the next 10 hours laying TV and wifi fiber optic cables.View image in fullscreenMarco Antonio Osorio, 50, and his wife Cecilia Rodríguez, 45, pose for a portrait at their home in Houston, Texas, on 14 September 2026.Photograph: Danielle Villasana/The GuardianIt’s their speciality. They are good at it, and in demand. If only they were left to get on with it.Around the beginning of the year Osorio, 50, noticed a surge in ICE street activity. “There were so many more sheriff’s vehicles, state troopers, ICE on the highways weaving between cars checking plates.”As an undocumented Mexican who came to the US in 1993, aged 17, he knew he was vulnerable. But he thought he had some cover. His US-born daughter Gabriela is serving as a marine at Camp Pendleton in California. She has helped him apply for residency, and the paperwork is being processed.Still, he wasn’t taking chances. He changed his habits. No going out of the house unless for essentials. No nights out at the movies. He couldn’t stop working, or else how would he pay the bills? But now he wears a button-down shirt on the drive to the site rather than his fluorescent yellow vest. No point advertising himself as a construction worker with ICE on the hunt.He told his company he didn’t want to work outside Houston any more. The freeways to Austin and San Antonio were crawling with cop cars. “The company told me there weren’t any jobs here – either go out of town, or you don’t work.”View image in fullscreenFramed pictures of Osorio’s daughter, who serves in the US military, photographed at their home in Houston.Photograph: Danielle Villasana/The GuardianSo he took a job in Austin. On 10 June, as he was returning home after another 10-hour shift, a sheriff’s car did a U-turn on the freeway and pulled him over. The officer said it was because his truck had a faulty rear light, but Osorio asked himself how they could have known that as they were traveling in opposite directions. More likely, he thought, was that his vehicle has a clear front screen. “They could see we were Hispanic.”Within two minutes of the traffic stop, ICE SUVs blocked him in, front and back. The speed with which they appeared, Osorio realised, meant it had to be coordinated.He told them his daughter was a US marine. He showed the officers the receipt for his residency application. An ICE officer replied: “Oh, that doesn’t count.” They took him to a freezing cell, the notoriouslas hieleras, and from there to an immigration detention facility near the border. He spent 40 days in the wilderness of ICE custody, until Monty got him released for lack of due process.As he awaits his appeal, Osorio continues to work. Those bills keep coming, his children need feeding. On drives to work sites in Houston, he thinks about his daughter serving the country whose government wants him gone. He worries about his youngest child, an autistic boy, and what will become of him. He imagines returning to Mexico, a place he hasn’t known for 33 years.As he drives, he spots apartment blocks all over the city that he helped put up. And he’s proud. “See those – I worked there 10 years ago. Or those – we built them 15 years ago.”He thinks to himself: “This is my home.”View image in fullscreenOsorio and his wife say goodnight to their son and give him a blessing.Photograph: Danielle VillasanaLorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, a Mexican national, had been in the US for 35 years, two longer than Osorio. A house framer, the skilled worker who puts up the wooden skeleton of new houses, he carried out his days with an identical drill. Out the door at 5am, pick up the crew, 10 hours of hard graft, then relax on the balcony of his self-built Houston home listening totierra calientemusic with Ñoño, his beloved dog whom he named after a podgy 1970s Mexican sitcom character.When ICE began to crank up its street arrests in February, Salgado spotted an opportunity. Many workers were too scared to leave the house, and new homes were standing half finished. A fearless entrepreneur, Salgado began accepting jobs that other undocumented framers like him would not contemplate.He took precautions. He swapped his construction vest for a suit jacket while driving to work. He removed the jumble of blueprints, invoices and receipts from the dashboard of his white van. It was like his mobile office on wheels, but it branded him as a building professional, so he cleaned it off.As time passed, and the ICE presence grew more oppressive, his three sons grew concerned. They are all American-born US citizens, and Salgado had high aspirations for them. They weren’t going to be builders like him – they were going to be educated, fulfill their own American dream. Ronaldo Salgado, the eldest, is a history teacher; Lorenzo Salgado Jr studied at the prestigious Tufts University and is now an engineer in Washington DC; and the youngest is at college, also studying engineering.View image in fullscreenFederal agents watch as people protest against ICE at the south Texas family residential center on 28 January 2026 in Dilley, Texas.Photograph: Joel Angel Juarez/Getty ImagesThe sons got together and prepared a plan for their dad. They gave him a phone number that he should call if ever he were stopped, and they made sure he carried a “know your rights” card in his wallet. They made him swear that he would never sign any ICE form, as they feared he would be hoodwinked into self-deporting.Some immigrants chose to leave the US. But is ‘self-deportation’ really becoming a thing?Read moreLorenzo Jr had an additional reason for being worried. On 29 October 2025, he was walking to work in DC. It was early morning, around the time his father would be getting on the road. That day he had a big presentation to make to a government agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).As he was walking down Georgia Avenue in the direction of the White House, he saw two unmarked cars coming towards him. They passed him and then both turned around, stopping on either side of him in a pincer movement. His first thought was that he was about to be mugged. But then he realised they were federal agents. They asked him his name and where he was going. As soon as they heard his perfect English, saw his neatly buttoned shirt, and took on board his FAA destination, they backed off. “OK, go ahead, you’re good to go.”Lorenzo Jr has no doubts he had been ethnically profiled. He was shaken by the experience. It freaked him out about his dad. If they could stop him, a Tufts-educated engineer on his way to advise the US government in the nation’s capital, what could they do to his father, an undocumented framer?On 7 July, Lorenzo Jr got a call: his father had been stopped by ICE. He rushed to the airport and got on the first flight to Houston. Onboard the flight he saw a news report of an undocumented person in the city who had been shot by an ICE officer.As the plane was still mid-air, Lorenzo Jr refreshed the article. The headline had been revised from “shot” to “shot, killed”.I met Lorenzo Jr and Ronaldo Salgado in a coffee shop about 10 minutes from where their father had been shot through the window of his van after ICE mistook him for a Guatemalan national they were searching for. There was a memorial shrine to their father in a corner of the cafe, with his photo in the center surrounded by lit candles and rosaries, a few of his construction tools, a sombrero and the Mexican flag.Both sons were still clearly stunned. But they were reflective.double quotation markEvery single day we are looking over our shoulders, thinking that maybe today is the day they catch usFortinoRonaldo talked about how his father had been hunted down by ICE “because he didn’t look a certain way. He didn’t match what an American is supposed to look like.”How cruel that was, he mused, considering that his dad had spent his entire life pursuing core American values. Ronaldo rattled them off: “Work hard. Pay your taxes. Have a family. Educate them. Good things will come to you.”Lorenzo Jr talked about how his father was killed by a government agent three days after the US celebrated its 250th birthday. On the Fourth of July, he himself had attended the fireworks in DC. He felt proud then to be an American. He recalled the history he had studied of Frederick Douglass, WEB Du Bois, Malcolm X, Martin Luther King and his biggest hero, Abraham Lincoln. He felt he was well on the way to achieving his own American dream.Three days later, he suffered what he describes as “extreme patriotic whiplash”. Now he has only one purpose: to get justice for his dad.Drive 350 miles south-west from Houston and you come to the border region of the Rio Grande valley. Life down here is a perfect fusion of Mexican and American. Tejano, they call it.The valley is dusty and hot. Midday temperatures frequently hit 105F (40.5C), rising to 110F. The day I visited a building site in Harlingen, about 10 miles from the border, it was already exceeding 100F, with the sun beating down mercilessly.A job site in Harlingen in September. With a limited workforce, sites are taking longer to complete.Four framers were working under a cloudless sky, erecting the second-floor wooden structure of a duplex house. They were swaddled in loosely fitting clothes to protect them from the sun, with heavy tools slung around their waists. They looked unperturbed by the heat, but then this was a normal working day – 10 hours a day, six days a week.The oldest of the four, the sombrero-wearing Joaquin, is the age that Salgado was when he was killed by ICE. Two months ago, Joaquin’s wife was taken away. She was hunted down on her way to work at a restaurant, and is now in detention awaiting deportation to Mexico.“Now I’m scared they will grab me,” Joaquin said in Spanish. “We have three kids, born here, who will take care of them?”His crewmate, Fortino, 38, his face hidden behind large ski glasses, is also undocumented. Two of his uncles have disappeared. “Right now, nothing is safe,” he said. “In Mexico we were taught to put our trust in God and go to work. But every single day we are looking over our shoulders, thinking that maybe today is the day they catch us.”View image in fullscreenJoaquin at a construction site building wooden framing.Photograph: Michael Gonzalez/The GuardianThe third crew member, Alexis, 33, has a green card. That doesn’t stop him feeling anxious. He drives to the site now only in ordinary civilian cars, never in white vans or trucks and never with tools visible, and he regularly changes the route.I asked him what he thinks of the argument that Trump made to the American people: that American jobs should be for Americans, not for those unlawfully residing here. Alexis laughed.“Sure, that’s fine,” he said, also in Spanish. “But most Americans don’t do the work. They won’t do it. This is hard work, under the blazing sun. No shade. Educated Americans, they demand an office job with air-conditioning. So it’s us Latinos who do this work.”The fourth crew member, 20-year-old Isaias, chimed in. He is a US-born citizen. Americans, he said, were used to having it easy. “Nacen en cuna de oro” – they’re born with a silver spoon in their mouths.The four framers filled the air with the noise of banging and hammering and sawing. To my untrained ear, it seemed a healthy cacophony: the sound of a new neighbourhood, a new community, being born.But for Ronnie Cavazos, 49, the manager of the site, the noise is symptomatic of sickness. There isn’t enough of it. It should be decibels louder. The four framers working on the house, there should be three times as many of them. Last week the site was entirely empty, he couldn’t find any crews. All his subcontractors had ceased operating.“We don’t have enough guys to do the work – they’ve been picked up, or are too scared to leave the house, or they’ve given up and gone back to Mexico.”Sites that were taking six months to complete are now taking 10 months. Overheads are going up. In the summer he had to pause construction for 60 days; there were no framers to call on.Cavazos is doing all he can to protect his workers, and encourage them back on site. He has erected a fence right around the 16 duplexes he is building to keep ICE out. He expects it’ll cost him $30,000 in fencing alone, but it will be worth it if it buys some peace of mind.View image in fullscreenRonnie Cavazos ties a rope around a fence at an active construction site in Harlingen, Texas, on 16 September 2026.Builders in the Rio Grande valley have turned to temporary fencing around their job sites in hopes of warding off ICE agents from crossing on to private property without a judicial warrant.Photograph: Michael Gonzalez/The GuardianHe led me inside an unfinished duplex and showed me a Murphy door under the stairs. It leads to a space where workers can hide should ICE turn up.One day his construction manager called Cavazos and alerted him to an ICE agent trying to enter the site. “I told him, ‘Get the fuck off my property!’ A lot of my workers ran away. Some went and hid behind the Murphy door.”A few months ago he had a crew sleep on site. They were so afraid of being pulled over as they drove to work, they decided to sleep right there on the concrete foundations until the job was done.“This is America,” Cavazos said, shaking his head. “What the fuck! This is America.”Cavazos is chair of theSouth Texas Builders Association(STBA), the largest such alliance in the Rio Grande valley. He and his fellow construction leaders have decided enough is enough.“It’s time to speak up,” Cavazos said. “A lot of people have been too afraid of what Trump will do to say anything. To stay quiet is not American. If we can’t tell the truth, what the fuck are we doing?”In July, STBA, with the American Business Immigration Coalition Action that advocates for comprehensiveimmigration reform, staged what they called a “rally in the valley”. The gathering, close to the border in Pharr, Texas, concluded with a warning for Trump and the Republicans: if you carry on hunting our people, you will feel our wrath.double quotation markThe dignity of our community is being walked all overBenny MelendezBenny Melendez, the owner of a small construction company in Weslaco, Texas, handles government relations for STBA. He voted for Trump in 2024, but since then 10 of his workers have been taken by ICE. As a result, his home-building projects are going up at half speed, and completed homes are costing $30,000 or more above the usual price.As part of his lobbying duties for STBA, Melendez began gathering smartphone footage of ICE raids and posting them on social media. They show masked police and ICE agents swarming over building sites, without a warrant, apprehending workers. In one video, a framer can be seen running off the site with agents in hot pursuit, like a fox and hounds.In another a police officer escorts several workers, hands cuffed behind their backs, from a site. “We’ll be back for the guys on the roof,” the officer threatens, adding: “It’s hot up there.”“We’re used to it, it’s what we do,” one of the workers replies. “We probably built your house.”Melendez made hisown videoto add to the collection, in which he vents his fury as a one-time Trump voter. At the start of the video we see Melendez fully masked, dressed in a black tactical utility uniform. He pulls off the mask and throws it to the ground. “Only cowards hide under a mask,” he exclaims. Next he discards his heavy armor flak jacket and replaces it with an orange construction vest and hard hat. “These are the tools we need to make America great again.”Melendez told the Guardian that for him, the Trump administration’s assault on the Rio Grande valley amounted to a humanitarian crisis. “The dignity of our community is being walked all over.”View image in fullscreenAn ICE agent makes an arrest after a traffic stop made by a Texas department of public safety officer in Mustang Ridge, outside Austin, on 16 April 2026.Photograph: Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesSTBA executives decided earlier this year to blast that same message directly at the Trump administration. A delegation of seven STBA leaders, including Melendez and Cavazos and the association’s CEO, Mario Guerrero, demanded a face-to-face meeting with the Department of Homeland Security in Washington.I wanted to hear about that meeting, so I visited Guerrero at the hub of his construction company in Edinburg, Texas. There was no mistaking his loyalties: the stars and stripes and flag of Texas dominated his office.Guerrero describes himself as a fourth-generation Mexican-American, and a proud patriot, who voted for Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. “I’m probably more American than JD Vance. More American than Marco Rubio. Definitely more American than that damn Stephen Miller,” he said.He voted for Trump because he was incensed by the record number of undocumented immigrants who crossed the border under Joe Biden, and because he thought Trump, as a businessman, would strengthen the valley’s economy.But he has been dismayed since Trump’s return by the soaring prices, and by the number of hardworking, law-abiding immigrants that the administration has detained.The ‘self-deportee’ hounded out of the US to Mexico: ‘There are days when I feel literally insane’Read moreGuerrero told me what happened when he joined the STBA delegation to DC. They were given just 15 minutes to address top DHS officials, who sat impassively along one side of a long mahogany table.ICE was spreading fear throughout the valley, the Texans, lined up on the other side, began. Agents were storming on to building sites without warrants, arresting people with work permits, using unmarked SUVs to hunt concrete trucks, then carting off all the workers as they poured foundations.Shortly before the allotted time was up, the Texans were invited to give closing words. Guerrero took this as his cue. He locked eyes with the top ICE official right across the table from him. He informed him that he had voted for Trump every time he was on the ballot.“We’re not getting what we voted for, man,” he said.“You know what you guys are doing is fucked up. If you carry on like this, your administration is going to lose.”Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)TexasUS politicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationShare

title: French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets | Bonds | The Guardian
description: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests
Content: Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities in France.Photograph: Michel Euler/APView image in fullscreenInitially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities in France.Photograph: Michel Euler/APBondsFrench borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook marketsYield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protestsPhillip InmanSenior economics writerWed 21 Oct 2026 09.17 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 09.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone.The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known asobligation assimilables du Trésor(Oat), issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%.The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasinglyviolent street protestsin recent weeks.Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living.Initially calm protests have often been met withaggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities. Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges.No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called asnap election in 2024. The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending.France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action.International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMatthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at the currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies.“The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said. “It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.”Explore more on these topicsBondsEurozoneFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tesla and SpaceX explore merger as Elon Musk gives backing | SpaceX | The Guardian
description: Billionaire, on SpaceX earnings call, says ‘I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies’
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Billionaire, on SpaceX earnings call, says ‘I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies’
Content: A SpaceX test flight at Starbase, Texas, last month.Photograph: Steve Nesius/ReutersView image in fullscreenA SpaceX test flight at Starbase, Texas, last month.Photograph: Steve Nesius/ReutersSpaceXTesla and SpaceX explore merger as Elon Musk gives backingBillionaire, on SpaceX earnings call, says ‘special committees’ exploring idea but no agreement reached yetNick Robins-EarlyTue 20 Oct 2026 21.10 EDTFirst published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs SpaceX released its second-ever public earnings report on Tuesday,Elon Muskdeclared his support for combining the aerospace and AI company with his electric vehicle company, Tesla. He said both companies had created special committees to explore a potential merger, but have not reached any agreement on terms of a transaction.“BothSpaceXand Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea at the request of shareholders and these special committees are, uh, consist of independent directors,” Musk said on the call. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees.”Musk also expressed his backing for the move, while cautioning about the hurdles involved achieve it. He stated that it would require the approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders.“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty and I think that would be overstating it,” Musk said, adding it would require shareholder approvals and special committees at both firms. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies.”The company revealed a far better financial quarter than Wall Street projected. SpaceX company, which encompasses rockets, artificial intelligence and satellite communications, reported a 161% growth in revenue year over year, driven by its Starlink and AI segments.The company declared $14.58bn in revenue against analysts’ projected $12.72bn. SpaceX reported earnings per share of 35 cents and a net income of $4.4bn.
