The company’s stock, which started the day down about 8% for the year, shot up 2% in after hours trading immediately after the results.Musk appeared alongside SpaceX’s president, Gwynne Shotwell, and CFO, Bret Johnsen, at his Starlink factory in Texas to deliver the earnings report, touting the company’s growth and plans for future rocket developments. Musk also highlighted its artificial intelligence segment, which the company refers to as Super Intelligence, that drew $7.6bn in revenue and now outperforms its Connectivity business, which provides internet services.Musk’s company once again found itself in the spotlight in recent weeks asinvestors have speculatedabout the potential merger with Tesla, the second-most valuable part of the tech mogul’s empire. Musk has also been at the center of geopolitical tensions after Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, last weekaccused SpaceX of restricting accessto its military-grade Starlink internet service.The disruption in service to Starshieldallegedly led to several failed Ukrainian combat missionsand left the country more vulnerable to Russian drone attacks, as well as highlighted how global internet infrastructure hascome to rely on Musk’s products. Musk denied responsibility for the disruption, stating that Starshield was controlled by the US government, not SpaceX. The White House has likewise denied hobbling Starshield.Moments before the SpaceX earnings call on Tuesday, the Wall Street Journalreportedthat Musk personally ordered the throttling of Starshield, citing unnamed US officials and people familiar with the matter. Musk faced no questions about the reports on the investor Q&A portion of SpaceX’s earnings call.While SpaceX’s role in international affairs faces scrutiny, Musk has taken on a resurgent role in US domestic politics. The world’s richest person hascontributed $366m in political spendingthis election cycle, backing Republican-aligned Super Pacs and pouring money into influencing key midterm races. Musk also agreed earlier this month toco-lead a Pentagon projecton the future of warfare, bringing him back into government work after his time as the de facto leader of the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMusk recently pledged to give every child in the US one of his SpaceX stocks next year, which Donald Trump stated would be facilitated through the president’s“Trump accounts” initiativethat creates savings plans for children. The prospective share giveaway is a rare display of philanthropy from Musk, who has criticized traditional aid organizations and has taken credit for dismantling the world’s largest single provider of humanitarian aid by gutting the government agency USAID.“Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way,” Musk posted on X, the social media company he owns.Tech leaders such as Musk have faced increasing public pushback over their extraordinary accumulation of wealth and power in the US, while this year AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic both announced big investments to their grant-making and non-profit arms. Musk’s announcement came after Anthropic announced earlier this week that it plans to donate 5% of its shares to anewly created public benefitfund within the company.Tesla will also reveal its latest earnings this week, with Musk set to deliver the quarterly report on Wednesday. The company’s stock received a slight boost this week after it unveiled itsnew Tesla Roadster 2 electric sports car, which Musk showcased in a dramatic demonstration that included the vehicle using pressurized air tanks to briefly lift off the ground and perform aerial stunts.Explore more on these topicsSpaceXElon MuskQuarterly resultsTechnology sectorSatellitesAerospace industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal’s Declan Rice strikes late to deny Bayern Munich after Harry Kane penalty | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Declan Rice’s late equaliser rescued a 2-2 draw for Arsenal in a blockbuster contest at Bayern Munich after Harry Kane had scored from the spot
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Declan Rice’s late equaliser rescued a 2-2 draw for Arsenal in a blockbuster contest at Bayern Munich after Harry Kane had scored from the spot
Content: Declan Rice knee-slides across the turf after scoring Arsenal’s equaliser late in the second half.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDeclan Rice knee-slides across the turf after scoring Arsenal’s equaliser late in the second half.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueArsenal’s Declan Rice strikes late to deny Bayern Munich after Harry Kane penaltyDavid Hytnerat the Allianz ArenaWed 21 Oct 2026 17.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is as if Harry Kane cannot get enough of tormenting Arsenal. TheBayern Munichstriker has plenty of form from his Tottenham days. He remains the top scorer in north London derby history with 14 goals. He made an impact yet again here and yet it was not a night when he had the final word. That honour fell to Declan Rice, the Arsenal midfielder storming into the Bayern area in the 82nd minute to guide home a low finish that Kane would have been proud to call his own.Arsenal were hunting their latest statement result. Only once had they ever won away against Bayern – the 2-0 in theChampions Leaguelast 16 second leg in 2013, although it did not prevent an away goals exit. Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player that night. When Eberechi Eze, who came on for the injured Bukayo Saka in the 10th minute, gave them the lead midway through the first half, their hopes surged.‘It doesn’t look good’: Mikel Arteta concerned as Bukayo Saka limps off against BayernRead moreEnter Kane. He wore his playmaker’s hat; some of his passing was sumptuous and it was his assist for Alphonso Davies that helped Bayern to draw level. He wore his finisher’s one, too, scoring from the penalty spot to put his team in charge. It meant he had scored in 10 consecutive Champions League games; one short of Cristiano Ronaldo’s record. There is a reason why Kane is the favourite to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday. He now has 16 goals against Arsenal; he has only scored more against one club – Leicester, against whom he has 20.Rice loosened Bayern’s grip. It was a lovely goal from him and Arsenal even hinted at a late winner, Jurriën Timber drawing a tip over from Manuel Neuer in stoppage time. That would have been too much because Bayern shaded an absorbing tie in terms of clear chances created. But Arsenal made their point. They were value for it.Arsenal knew they were inside a fortress. Bayern had not previously lost a Champions League group or league phase match at their own stadium since the 3-2 reverse against Manchester City in December 2013, 40 games ago. The following 39 featured 37 wins and two draws. Arteta’s players were not intimidated. They bristled with assurance at the outset and Rice rewarded their never-say-die spirit. Bayern had wanted revenge for their3-1 defeat at the Emirates Stadiumin the league stage last season. They did not get it.Arteta’s idea was to go pretty much as strong as possible with his lineup. He made just two changes, Timber for Ben White and Noni Madueke for Eze, albeit the latter was not on the bench for long. Saka had tussled with Davies and it looked innocuous. The alarm bells rang when Saka grabbed his thigh and went to ground, waving his hand in the air.View image in fullscreenBukayo Saka receives treatment after going down injured early on.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesWas it possible for the Arsenal support to think that Bayern had been stripped of their fear factor in the line behind Kane? Michael Olise was suspended, Jamal Musiala was injured and Luis Díaz was a substitute. He came on in the 68th minute only to be forced off before the end. Bayern were without the midfielder Joshua Kimmich for personal reasons.Arteta moved Madueke over to his more natural position on the right wing when he introduced Eze on the left and Bayern will still be wondering how the latter was afforded so much space up the inside channel on that flank to put Arsenal in front.It was a fabulous ball from Martin Ødegaard, who was in the mood, full of sharp turns and urgency, and Eze had the time to let it bounce before shooting first time into the far corner. An offside flag killed the Arsenal celebrations and there was one of those weird waits before the video assistant referee ruled that Eze was in fact onside.Kane was booed by the Arsenal fans. Of course he was. He dropped deep to link the play and there was a moment in the 17th minute when he started a move with a pass from inside his own penalty area. There was a glorious ping over Gabriel Magalhães, who was the last Arsenal defender, for Ismael Saibari on 23 minutes, although his teammate could not control, and Kane’s fingerprints were all over the equaliser. He was on halfway when he sculpted the low through ball for Davies which took Timber out of the equation. The Bayern winger’s finish was clinical.View image in fullscreenHarry Kane lashes in from the spot to put Bayern Munich 2-1 ahead.Photograph: Michael Zemanek/ShutterstockBayern had other chances in the first half, none better than the one for Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, in the 21st minute. It was Kane who began the attack, taking a quick goal kick – yes, really – and Gnabry was the man over on the right when the Bayern forwards worked it that way. Gnabry’s shot was too close to David Raya. Kane also saw Ezri Konsa produce a fine block to keep him out.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is never anything other than a pleasure to be at the Allianz for a showpiece match. All the staples were present and correct. The en masse scarf waving. The slightly slapstick oompah band notes. The fans at either end of the ground calling to each other. The non-stop drumbeat and songs from the Südkurve, who also bounced as one at times.The pre-game surprise had been the sight of Vincent Kompany in the Bayern dugout; the manager made a Lazarus-like rise from his sickbed and the action after the restart kept the blood pumping. Arsenal thought they had gone back ahead when Bruno Guimarães rose to meet Rice’s corner only for Neuer to produce an extraordinary save.The goalkeeper touched the ball up and on to the crossbar and away. Shades of Gordon Banks against Pelé. It was Raya’s turn next; his save to keep out Dayot Upamecano’s close-range header from Gnabry’s cross was of the highest order.View image in fullscreenMikel Arteta applauds the travelling fans after the final whistle.Photograph: Tiego Grenho/Every Second Media/ShutterstockIt was interesting to watch Kane after the penalty was awarded for handball against Timber. Bayern had worked the ball back to their No 9 and, when he shot, Timber’s arm was outstretched. Kane went through his mental processes. He could see that Raya did not retreat to his line for what felt like an age. Kane delayed even longer. He was in total control. He stuttered before banging the ball hard into the right-hand corner.Bayern were close to putting the game to bed. Konrad Laimer dragged narrowly past the far post when well-placed but it was Arsenal who produced the sucker punch. Eze was dangerous throughout. And when the opportunity knocked for Rice after a pass from the substitute Viktor Gyökeres, he made no mistake.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueBayern MunichArsenalmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Titans coach says Jordan Elliott pulling gun in team parking lot was not ‘criminal act’ | Tennessee Titans | The Guardian
description: The defensive lineman, released on Tuesday by the Tennessee Titans, ⁠went to his car to retrieve a gun after an altercation during practice
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The defensive lineman, released on Tuesday by the Tennessee Titans, ⁠went to his car to retrieve a gun after an altercation during practice
Content: Jordan Elliott has also played for the Browns and 49ers.Photograph: Stew Milne/APView image in fullscreenJordan Elliott has also played for the Browns and 49ers.Photograph: Stew Milne/APTennessee TitansTitans coach says Jordan Elliott pulling gun in team parking lot was not ‘criminal act’Player fetched firearm after altercation with JC LathamTennessee released defensive tackle on TuesdayRobert Saleh calls situation ‘lapse in judgement’Associated PressWed 21 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTennessee Titans coach Robert Saleh confirmed on Wednesday that defensive tackle Jordan Elliott was released after pulling a gun in the parking lot of the team facility but said it was a “terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a criminal act”.The Titans had announced Tuesday that Elliott was released, but said only that it came after his involvement in an unspecified incident at the team’s facility five days earlier.A person briefed on the incident told the Associated Press on Wednesday that Elliott had a gun in his car and went to the parking lot to retrieve it after a dispute with another player, believed to be right tackle JC Latham. Titans defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers is said to have helped deescalate the situation.Speaking to reporters, Saleh defended Elliott’s character. “Unfortunately, rules are rules with regard to guns on property, and sometimes it’s far greater than the kneejerk reaction of kicking somebody when they’re down,” the coach said.“He’s a good man. Made a terrible, had a terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a criminal act,” Saleh added. “He’s never committed a crime in his entire life and he pulled a gun, in the parking lot.”Latham called the episode an unfortunate situation.“I don’t really have too much to say about it,” Latham said Wednesday. “There ain’t never been no bad blood between us two. We were here on the summer getting treatment. Before that, we hung out whenever we were in the same city together. We actually had never had an argument leading up to it.”Elliott appeared in five games this season with one start and had 11 tackles. He followed Saleh to Nashville after a two-year stint with the San Francisco 49ers, where he played in 31 games with 29 starts.The 6ft 4in defensive tackle was selected by the Cleveland Browns in the third round of the 2020 draft. He spent his first four seasons in Cleveland before signing a two-year deal with San Francisco.Tennessee added him as a free agent in the offseason on a two-year, $8m deal.Explore more on these topicsTennessee TitansNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He was a great kid’: Chiefs mourn death of former player Allen Bailey at age of 37 | Kansas City Chiefs | The Guardian
description: Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid have spoken of their sadness after former Kansas City Chief Allen Bailey died at the age of 37
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid have spoken of their sadness after former Kansas City Chief Allen Bailey died at the age of 37
Content: Allen Bailey was a popular figure among teammates and coaches.Photograph: David Eulitt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAllen Bailey was a popular figure among teammates and coaches.Photograph: David Eulitt/Getty ImagesKansas City Chiefs‘He was a great kid’: Chiefs mourn death of former player Allen Bailey at age of 37Defensive end played for Chiefs for eight seasonsAndy Reid says player’s death ‘makes you sick’Guardian sportWed 21 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 16.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatrick Mahomes and Andy Reid have spoken of their sadness after former Kansas City Chief Allen Bailey died at the age of 37.The defensive end was found dead at his home in Florida on Tuesday by his wife. He is believed to have died from natural causes.“It’s terrible, especially with all the good he [did],” Chiefs head coach Reid said. “He’s got a family and that’s a sad deal. I know his father passed away young, too. It makes you sick when it happens to somebody that young … He was one of my favorite players, a great kid. I’m just sorry to see that happened to him.”Mahomes spent two seasons with Bailey after the quarterback was drafted by the Chiefs in 2017.“I tell this story every year: He was the first person I saw when I stepped into the locker room after the draft,” Mahomes said. “I see Allen Bailey and I’m like, ‘This isn’t [college] anymore.’ It was surreal to see him.“Obviously, it’s terrible to hear the news. A great teammate – he’s one of those glue guys on the team. He makes plays. He’s not necessarily a superstar, but the guy that kind of makes everything go. We’re praying for his family. [As] teammates, we’ve talked and we know that we’re going to do whatever we can to support those guys.”Bailey grew up on Sapelo Island, a barrier island off Georgia only accessible by boat and with a population of fewer than 70 people. “I’m from a place a little out of the normal,” Baileytold Distraction magazine in 2018. “It’s relatively quiet; no stop signs, no traffic lights. It’s mostly dirt roads.”From there he played college football for Miami before becoming a third-round draft pick for the Chiefs in 2011. He played for the team for eight seasons before spending the final two years of his career with theAtlanta Falcons.Explore more on these topicsKansas City ChiefsNFLAtlanta FalconsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Troy Aikman and Joe Buck: what next for the NFL’s $165m TV power couple as they head for a split? | US sports media | The Guardian
description: The duo have carved out lucrative and successful careers as TV audiences elsewhere are falling. It seems they won’t be together for much longer
Author: Tom Dart
Headline: The duo have carved out lucrative and successful careers as TV audiences elsewhere are falling. It seems they won’t be together for much longer
Content: Joe Buck and Troy Aikman have broadcast together for more than two decades.Photograph: Julio Aguilar/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoe Buck and Troy Aikman have broadcast together for more than two decades.Photograph: Julio Aguilar/Getty ImagesUS sports mediaTroy Aikman and Joe Buck: what next for the NFL’s $165m TV power couple as they head for a split?The duo have carved out lucrative and successful careers as TV audiences elsewhere are falling. It seems they won’t be together for much longerTom DartWed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTroy Aikman knew when it was time to go. Hisaching bodymade the decision for him when he ended his NFL career in 2001. A quarter of a century later, with one of the top quarterbacks of the 1990s established as half of the pre-eminent broadcasting duo in American sports, his potential exit from the booth is not so clearcut.Aikman clearly feels his voice remains in fine working order, but his bosses at ESPN may not agree. The color commentator’s Monday Night Football play-by-play partner, Joe Buck, is reported to haveagreed a new dealwith the network worth $108m over six seasons (his previous deal was for five years at $15m a season), yet Aikman has claimed ESPN does not want to renew his contract.The longest-running television broadcast partnership in NFL history looks set to end onceESPNbroadcasts the Super Bowl in February. It would be Buck and Aikman’s seventh Super Bowl together. After that, Aikman’s existing five-year, $90m deal expires.The prospective rupture is another tremor shaking the NFL’s media landscape only shortly after another ex-Cowboys quarterback turned high-profile TV personality,Tony Romo, was dropped by CBS. The network formallyparted wayswith the 46-year-old on 2 October, a month after he pleaded no contest to a civil charge of driving while intoxicated in Wisconsin in July.Jalen Hurts played through a blood clot. Are NFL players cattle?Read moreAdding to the intrigue, Buck and Aikman argued at SoFi Stadium before the Los Angeles Rams hosted the Buffalo Bills on 12 October after Buck broached the matter of the contract-related tension between them, according toFront Office Sports.The murky situation is an unwelcome distraction seemingly of its own making for ESPN, which will produce and show a live Super Bowl for the first time next year at SoFi. Itwanted hype; now it has hoopla. If Aikman’s version of events is accurate, it’s surprising the company would consider terminating the partnership having earlier this yearhaileda “surge” in viewership that “coincides with the Buck-Aikman era”. ESPN representatives did not respond to a request for comment, but the network haspreviously saidit “won’t be addressing talent contract specifics publicly before the Super Bowl”.Aikman has been less reticent about giving his side of the story. He essentially confirmed the Front Office Sports report in aninterviewwith a Dallas radio station, 96.7 The Ticket: “There’s probably a time and a place for all that to be discussed. I don’t know if now is the time. I don’t know that it’s hard to figure out kind of what’s happened. I’ll broadcast through this season and I’ll be a free agent at the end of the year and kind of see what happens. I’m looking forward to whatever the rest of this year does hold with the Super Bowl and all that and where my next landing spot might be.” He added toUnderscorethat he expects ESPN to “go in a different direction”. That is a logical assumption: why else enter negotiations with Buck during the season but not his partner?It could also make sense for Aikman to advertise his imminent availability to alert potential suitors and perhaps galvanize ESPN into making a late offer to keep him away from the competition. But publicly airing his disquiet also seems characteristically on-brand for a man who has built a reputation for candid analysis since swapping the field for the booth.A Hall of Famer, Aikman retired after guiding Dallas to three Super Bowl titles in 12 seasons. (True fact: the Cowboys used to win things.) He teamed up with Buck at Fox Sports in 2002 andcosplayed as Mr Twhen the network announced its new “A-Team”. Aikman and Buck loved it when a plan came together for them to jump ship to ESPN in quick succession in 2022, with Bucktradedfor the rights to a college football game. They have since broken the longevity record held by Pat Summerall and John Madden and brought stability to what was once a problem position for ESPN.Buck, a 57-year-old NFL and MLB media veteran who is the son of the beloved late St Louis broadcaster Jack Buck, is steady, authoritative but unobtrusive. Aikman, who turns 60 next month, has remained perceptive long after his playing career ended. He has also had many plays in his business portfolio over the years: car dealerships, co-ownership of a Nascar team, a light beer brewery in Dallas and a minority stake in MLB’s San Diego Padres. He’s also been aninformal consultantto the Miami Dolphins.Star broadcasters command similar salaries to elite players and attract similarly feverish examinations of their performances, contract status and potential free-agent destinations. Fox SportshandedTom Brady a 10-year, $375m contract in 2022 – inflating the market and presumably informing Aikman’s opinion of what his services are now worth – though the fast-evolving broadcasting landscape makes future negotiations hard to predict.The rise of streaming services has led to more games on more platforms. Unlike when Aikman retired from playing at 34 after concussions and back injuries, he may not be short of suitors. Calling Thursday matchups for Amazon Prime would not carry the same prestige as Mondays on ESPN, though theviewing figuresare similar. Amazon may be ready to freshen up its act, given that its lead commentator, Al Michaels, is nearly 82 and the analyst Kirk Herbstreit’s job security isreportedly tenuous. Netflix is streaming five games this season.View image in fullscreenThe NFL remains a ratings winner for broadcasters.Photograph: Tyler Kaufman/APAmong the legacy giants, CBS promoted former Houston Texans star JJ Watt from its No 2 crew to replace Romo. If it concludes that thesolidbut relatively inexperienced Watt isn’t ready for primetime, the network may be interested in Aikman as a permanent successor to Romo, who was its lead analyst since 2017.There’s a lot at stake. Viewing figures for live televised football remainextraordinarily resilientin the era of on-demand streaming and social media. Advertising inventory for the Super Bowl sold out inAugust, while last season Monday Night Football averaged15.8 million viewersover 21 games – ESPN’s second-best set of ratings for MNF in the 20-year history of the show at a time when TV audiences in general are plummeting. But anything that damages the product and turns off viewers – a new pairing who don’t have the chemistry and credibility of Buck and Aikman, for example – is a problem, considering the increasingly marginal economics of the media industry.ESPN completed itsacquisitionof the NFL Network inJanuary, with the league taking a 10% equity stake in the broadcaster. It pays the NFL $2.7bn a year in rights fees. But estimates suggest that ESPN’s reach via traditional bundled services hasroughly halvedover the past 15 years from a peak of100 millionhouseholds. Over that time, rights feesnearly doubled. And the league wants another huge increase for itsnext deals.Half the customers and twice the cost (or thereabouts): it’s not the makings of a viable long-term business in any sector. And other strategies in the cord-cutting era – job cuts, launching on-demandstreaming services,embracing betting, more intrusive and pervasive advertising – haven’t come close to replicating the lucrative success of the old-school cable and satellite subscriber model.The old certainties no longer apply, whether in the boardroom or on the air. One source of intrigue over the next couple of months is whether the teamwork of Buck and Aikman, as professional as they are, is perceptibly affected as the season’s climax and the likely end of their partnership looms. But nothing seemed out of the ordinary onthe broadcastMonday when the San Francisco 49ers beat the Washington Commanders.Buck stressed his friendship with Aikman, and the importance of getting along, in an interview with the Associated Press in 2023. “I think you need to put as much work on the personal relationship as you do the professional. I don’t know that everybody does that,” he said. “I know a lot of stories of broadcast partners that have been together for a nice chunk of time that didn’t really enjoy being with each other. I just can’t imagine being in that situation in this kind of a job when you’re relying on each other in front of millions of people live.”Explore more on these topicsUS sports mediaESPNUS television industryTelevision industryNFLUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gabby Thomas, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and the doping tensions dividing sprinting | Athletics | The Guardian
description: As women’s sprinting enters a golden era in the run-up to LA 2028, controversy surrounding a top coach threatens to overshadow the sport’s biggest stars
Author: Rob Draper
Headline: As women’s sprinting enters a golden era in the run-up to LA 2028, controversy surrounding a top coach threatens to overshadow the sport’s biggest stars
Content: Melissa Jefferson-Wooden of the US competes alongside Saint Lucia’s Julien Alfred in the women’s 100m final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest in September.Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMelissa Jefferson-Wooden of the US competes alongside Saint Lucia’s Julien Alfred in the women’s 100m final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest in September.Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty ImagesAthleticsGabby Thomas, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and the doping tensions dividing sprintingAs women’s sprinting enters a golden era in the run-up to LA 2028, controversy surrounding a top coach threatens to overshadow the sport’s biggest starsRob DraperWed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Olympic 200m champion Gabby Thomas came second at the recent track and fieldWorld Athletics Ultimate Championshipin Budapest, she tried her best to be diplomatic: “I am an equal-opportunity doping hater,” she said. “If you are actively doping in sport, I do take issue with that. I’m not saying any names, no names are mentioned. But if you look at yourself and you think that’s what you’re doing, then so be it.”Thomas then went out of her way to congratulate her compatriot Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, who finished ahead of her that day, aware of the territory into which she was straying.Last year, Thomas posted on Instagram that “doping coaches should be banned for life from coaching in the sport.” Dennis Mitchell, who is one of the world’s leading sprint coaches, oversees Jefferson-Wooden’s training but had a long history of doping while he was competing. Most notably, he tested positive for testosterone in 1998,claiming the elevated levelswere due to having sex four times with his wife the night before. He was cleared by USA Track & Field, but not by the IAAF and wasbanned for two years. Helater testified under oaththat his former coach Trevor Graham had injected him with banned human growth hormone. (Graham denied the allegations.)Thomas and Jefferson-Wooden will probably represent Team USA at next year’s world championships, and then potentially compete to be the homegrown star of the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028. In that scenario, let’s just say that relay practice could be awkward.Indeed, there is a brewing toxicity in the sprint world that may eventually rival the Ben Johnson-Carl Lewis clash at the 1988 Olympics, with the legally significant caveat that no one involved has failed any drugs tests nor is there any evidence they have taken drugs nor has anyone been officially accused of taking drugs. But the rumors, suspicions and bad blood are simmering just as they were in the two years running up to the Johnson-Lewis clash.Throw into the mix that Jefferson-Wooden could soon smash the most controversial world record on the track – Florence Griffith Joyner’s 38-year-old 10.49sec 100m mark – and women’s sprinting is likely to be more talked about than at any time since that extraordinary Flo-Jo era.View image in fullscreenSha’Carri Richardson talks with her coach, Dennis Mitchell, during a training session ahead of the Xiamen Diamond League meeting in China in May.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesJefferson-Wooden is already the fourth-fastest women of all time – she ran the 100m in 10.61sec at the 2025 world championships in Tokyo. Last month in Budapest, she won the 100m at 10.62sec. But the two other athletes in front of her, other than Griffith Joyner, were aided by substantial (yet legitimate) tailwinds. Jefferson-Wooden, meanwhile, ran into a 0.2m/sec headwind in Budapest, meaning she could have come close to breaking Griffith Joyner’s iconic world record with a favorable tailwind. That would be a landmark achievement: there is widespread skepticism that the 1988 Olympic champion was clean. Griffith Joyner, who also still holds the 200m world record, died of epileptic fit at the age of 38. She never failed a drug test but her training partner Darrell Robinson said in a paid interview with German magazine Stern in 1989 that he had sold Griffith Joyner banned human growth hormone. Griffith Joyner vehemently denied the accusation and never failed a drugs test.It wasn’t just Jefferson-Wooden who ran off with the prize money – she won $300,000 after claiming the 100m-200m double – in Budapest. Kenny Bednarek, another Mitchell-trained athlete, also took home $300,000 after winning the men’s 100m and 200m.The issue for both of these athletes is not only that their coach, Mitchell, took drugs in his career. He has also been unfortunate in the company he has at times kept as a coach. His greatest success was guiding Justin Gatlin to world championship 100m gold in 2017 but that achievement was tainted by the fact that the Olympic gold medalist had served two previous doping suspensions, one for four years for testing positive for testosterone. Elite sprinting is a tight world of interconnectivity: Gatlin was banned while training under Graham, Mitchell’s own drug cheat coach in his competitive days. When Graham was banned for life as coach, Gatlin switched to train under Mitchell. (Gatlinhas denied ever taking PEDs.)In 2017 Mitchell and athletics agent Robert Wagner were filmed offering to supply testosterone and human growth hormone to a fake actorin an undercover operationconducted by the Daily Telegraph. Mitchell insisted afterwards that none of his athletes had ever taken drugs while Wagner said that they were playing along with the actors, who were pitching a film project. But Gatlin cut ties with Wagner and sacked Mitchell as coach.More recently, the 2022 world 100m silver medalist Marvin Bracy-Williams tested positive for testosterone shortly after he joined Mitchell’s group and was eventually banned for 45 months. The United States Anti-Doping Agency confirmed at the time that it had been tipped off about Bracy-Williams’s drug taking and sources with knowledge of the case say the inside information came from within the Mitchell training group.Mitchell’s lawyer, Ryan J Stevens, has told the Guardian that “Coach Mitchell is a different man than he was nearly 30 years ago. He’s committed to clean sport and strict compliance with anti-doping rules. He had absolutely no involvement in Mr Bracy-Williams’ personal choices that resulted in his sanction. Coach Mitchell insists on transparency, accountability, and integrity in every aspect of his coaching.”The Guardian has contacted Jefferson-Wooden for comment.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsUSA Olympic teamUS sportsLA Olympic Games 2028Justin GatlinUsada (United States Anti-Doping Agency)Drugs in sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cristiano Ronaldo asked for punishment ‘without mitigation’, then fought to cut it | Cristiano Ronaldo | The Guardian
description: Cristiano Ronaldo put forward several arguments to an inquiry with a view to reducing his punishment for walking out of a Portugal training camp
Author: Miguel Dantas
Headline: Cristiano Ronaldo put forward several arguments to an inquiry with a view to reducing his punishment for walking out of a Portugal training camp
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo was handed a 30-day suspension for walking out of Portugal’s camp in Denmark.Photograph: Patrícia de Melo Moreira/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo was handed a 30-day suspension for walking out of Portugal’s camp in Denmark.Photograph: Patrícia de Melo Moreira/AFP/Getty ImagesCristiano RonaldoCristiano Ronaldo asked for punishment ‘without mitigation’, then fought to cut itHe presented several arguments after Portugal walkoutInquiry chose to halve, then halve again his punishmentMiguel DantasWed 21 Oct 2026 08.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCristiano Ronaldo successfully fought to reduce his punishment for walking out on a Portugal training camp, after saying publicly that his sanction should be imposed “without mitigating circumstances”.Afterleaving the training camp in Denmarklast month, Ronaldo said in a lengthy statement on social media that he should be punished as the Portuguese Football Federation saw fit and that his role as captain constituted “an aggravating factor”.However, during the disciplinary council’s inquiry the 41-year-old put forward several arguments for cutting his punishment, including his clean disciplinary record in recent seasons and his services to football.Ronaldo receiveda 30-day suspension and a €255 (£215) fine, and the document accompanying the ruling reveals he presented three arguments in mitigation: his disciplinary record this season and in the previous three seasons; his services to football including recognition for sporting merit; and his contribution to establishing the facts of the case.Cristiano Ronaldo: the extraordinary eight points he says Jorge Jesus agreed to makeRead moreTo support these arguments, Ronaldo listed the club titles he has won and his achievements with the national team: the 2016 European Championship and two Nations League titles. His individual awards were also highlighted, including the fact that the Al-Nassr forward has won the Ballon d’Or five times. Beyond his achievements on the pitch, he mentioned the honours he had received from senior state officials.The decision-makers accepted Ronaldo’s arguments concerning his achievements and services to the country, using them to halve his suspension and fine. The punishment was then halved again because Ronaldo had accepted responsibility for his actions.Ronaldo’s suspension will be served in a period during which there are no international matches. It is unclear whether he intends to return to the national team – or whether the head coach, Jorge Jesus, will select him again.The account of events provides a clearer picture of the circumstances surrounding Ronaldo’s departure from the training camp. After head coach Jesus held a press conference in which he reiterated that he was in charge of the team and that no player would influence his selection decisions, Ronaldo requested a vehicle from the FPF and set off for Copenhagen airport.During the journey, he called the Portuguese federation’s president, Pedro Proença, and told him he was “not in the right frame of mind” to remain with the team.“The defendant [Ronaldo] did not inform or provide prior justification to the federation or the men’s national team officials regarding his intention to leave the stadium and the training camp,” the ruling states. It says that between 30 September and 4 October, Ronaldo missed more than 30 team activities, including travel, training sessions and meals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe federation says that Ronaldo’s promise on social media, after leaving the training camp, to tell his fans “the whole truth” brought further negative attention to the incident: “Given his prominence as a public figure on a global scale, the defendant could not have been unaware that his conduct, in the circumstances in which it occurred, would be subject to intense media scrutiny, as indeed it was.”Ronaldo was therefore “expected to exercise particular caution in choosing the timing and manner in which he expressed his dissatisfaction with the manager’s decisions and conduct”. Instead, the player “further fuelled speculation and public curiosity by posting on Instagram on the very day he left Copenhagen, announcing that, ‘in due course’, he would tell ‘all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to his departure from the men’s senior national team’,” the inquiry concluded.Portugal are scheduled to play Denmark again in their next game on 14 November in Braga.Explore more on these topicsCristiano RonaldoPortugalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kvaratskhelia asks ‘why me?’ after ACL rupture in most serious of three PSG injuries | Paris Saint-Germain | The Guardian
description: Khvicha Kvaratskhelia ⁠will undergo surgery after rupturing a anterior cruciate ⁠ligament in PSG’s Champions League win over ⁠Barcelona
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Khvicha Kvaratskhelia ⁠will undergo surgery after rupturing a anterior cruciate ⁠ligament in PSG’s Champions League win over ⁠Barcelona
Content: Khvicha Kvaratskhelia receives assistance after sustaining his knee injury against Barcelona.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKhvicha Kvaratskhelia receives assistance after sustaining his knee injury against Barcelona.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty ImagesParis Saint-GermainKvaratskhelia asks ‘why me?’ after ACL rupture in most serious of three PSG injuriesKvaratskhelia to undergo surgery on right kneeDembélé and Marquinhos out for weeksAgenciesWed 21 Oct 2026 05.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 08.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParis Saint-Germain’s Khvicha Kvaratskhelia ⁠will undergo surgery after rupturing the anterior cruciate ⁠ligament in ⁠his ​right knee in theChampions League win over ⁠Barcelona.Kvaratskhelia twisted ⁠the knee during PSG’s 4-2 ​victory on ‌Tuesday and was ‌helped off the pitch just ‌before the hour, with the Georgian unable to put any weight on his right leg.The winger landed awkwardly after sprinting back to make a tackle on Xavi Espart and looked in severe pain as he clutched his right knee. He played a leading role in helping PSG to back-to-back Champions League titles and is one of the contenders for the Ballon d’Or, which will be awarded on Monday.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“Before ‌every game I asked God ‌to let me leave the pitch healthy,” Kvaratskhelia wrote ‌on Instagram. “But it was in vain. Not much time has passed, yet one thought keeps circling in my head: why me? I never held anything back. I think I prepared for this game better than I ever had before. I thought I was ready for everything – but not for this. I know I have to come back stronger for my people, who are ‌always by my side. I won’t let you down - I promise I won’t waste a single moment.”ACL injuries typically require a recovery period of ​at least six months.Ousmane Dembélé had earlier been forced off with a thigh injury and the defender Marquinhos was substituted with a similar injury. PSG ⁠said both players would have treatment ​for the next ​few weeks.The PSG head coach, Luis Enrique, used Dembélé sparingly in the French league last season and has rested him twice in Ligue 1 this campaign. The France forward, who scored six goals at the World Cup, struggled with injuries last season and had been beset by leg muscle injuries at his previous club, Barcelona.In the 2024-25 Dembélé played 50 games in a season for the first time in his career and his performances earned him the men’s Ballon d’Or.View image in fullscreenThe ‘Massacre, Parisien style’ banner that has sparked a complaint to Uefa from Barcelona.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPABarcelona have made a complaint to Uefa over a “chainsaw massacre” banner displayed on Tuesday. The banner carried the slogan “Massacre, Parisien style” and depicted a masked man in a PSG shirt cutting through a Barcelona crest with a chainsaw, with pyrotechnics giving the effect of sparks flying as the saw made contact.Sources close to the Catalan club said the content of the banner, and some offensive chants from the stands, were reported to Uefa’s match delegate.Explore more on these topicsParis Saint-GermainEuropean club footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Austin GP is about much more than potential for Antonelli’s first F1 world title | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The young Italian driver’s maiden championship is all but secured but Mercedes upgrades will inform next year’s run to the line
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The young Italian driver’s maiden championship is all but secured but Mercedes upgrades will inform next year’s run to the line
Content: Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli is primed to become F1’s youngest champion – but his team’s dominance is under threat for next season.Photograph: DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMercedes’ Kimi Antonelli is primed to become F1’s youngest champion – but his team’s dominance is under threat for next season.Photograph: DPPI/ShutterstockFormula One 2026AnalysisAustin GP is about much more than potential for Antonelli’s first F1 world titleGiles Richardsin AustinYoung driver’s maiden championship is all but secured but Mercedes upgrades will inform next year’s run to the lineWed 21 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 15.45 EDTShareThere is nothing quite like a potential title decider to bring the fiercest of spotlights to bear as doubtless Kimi Antonelli will discover when he attempts toseal his first championshipat the United States Grand Prix this weekend.For the young Italian the goal is straightforward and the culmination of a childhood dream. However, for his Mercedes team there will be scrutiny over performance in Austin that has significant implications going into next season.F1 returns to Africa for first time since 1993 with 10-year Rwanda deal from ‘early 2030s’Read moreThe 20-year-old Antonelli holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton is fifth or lower. It is not an entirely impossible scenario but even if he does not clinch the title in Texas, in all likelihood he will be crowned in Mexico a week later.Antonelli has been exceptional in only his second season in F1, but also enjoyed what was for the opening half of the season an all but untouchable car. Mercedes can no longer boast that advantage. Max Verstappen has won the past two races as Red Bull’s upgrades finally unlocked the performance they felt was there to be exploited.Ferrari, too, are now close to Mercedes, capable of beating them and have a raft of aerodynamic upgrades arriving in Austin. McLaren, having dropped back a tad in recent races, have repeatedly proved to have the measure of the championship leaders and have upgrades planned for the coming triple-header in the US, Mexico and Brazil.Mercedes had not had it all quite their own way then when they brought their second and final improvements to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. Yet an expected uplift of as much as three-10ths a lapwas met with disappointment. The upgrades did not deliver as expected and the car became a handful to drive, gains in lap time unsurprisingly elusive.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli finished third in Singapore, enough to maintain a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell.Photograph: Yichin Hou/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe Mercedes is less forgiving, switching between understeer and oversteer in a narrow window, working the tyres harder.Such was the discrepancy between what occurred on track and what was expected that after Malaysia they reverted to using the old spec on Russell’s car and the new one on Antonelli’s to better assess the issues atthe following Singapore GP, after which the Italian felt there had been an improvement.All of which is part of the development process, especially in a season of new regulations. But as the Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, noted these updates were not only intended to enhance and improve but were of paramount importance because they would inform next season’s car.“Was it an easy car like the previous one? I don’t think it was. Does it have the performance that we were hoping the upgrade would bring? I don’t think so yet. But it was a step in the right direction,” Wolff said after Singapore. “In Austin, we should see whether we can continue to consolidate that and whether it has more performance, because it’s crucial for the development direction for the next year.”View image in fullscreen‘In Austin, we should see whether the Mercedes has more performance, because it’s crucial for the development direction for the next year,’ says Toto Wolff.Photograph: DPPI/ShutterstockWhile Malaysia and Singapore might be considered outliers, Austin is a typical circuit, with medium- and fast-speed corners on a flowing track where good balance and a quick, well-behaving car is rewarded – the type of track where Mercedes were in control for the much of the season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat said, some at the team may be forgiven for experiencing a discomforting sense of deja vu. In each of the previous four years, with many upgrades not delivering as expected and in some cases setting the team back.Kimi Antonelli admits he can taste F1 glory after Verstappen wins Singapore GPRead moreTo be fair, Mercedes are far from such straits now and are still quick. Yet they have nowhere near the level of dominance they enjoyed in the 2014-2020 period when they remained all but untouchable and missteps along the way were almost unheard of.At the time the opposition closed on them but in most cases that was because Mercedes were already switching resources to the following year, confident they were ahead of the game and in where they needed to go with next year’s model.As this season draws to a close there is no such clearcut advantage. The frontrunners are all still feeling their way toward exploiting the maximum from the new regulations. The direction for 2027 is vital because the field is far more closely matched and developing at a fearsome rate, as Red Bull have demonstrated.Mercedes’ lead this season is nonetheless formidable and while they cannot seal the constructors’ championship this weekend, Antonelli’s drivers’ title is surely all but done and dusted. Austin, however, might yet suggest whether they can repeat the feat in 2027.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Kimi AntonelliMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Ex-tennis pro Megan Rose appointed to lead 2031 men’s Rugby World Cup in US | Rugby World Cup | The Guardian
description: World Rugby has appointed Megan Rose, a USTA executive, as managing director of the the men’s Rugby World Cup in 2031
Author: Martin Pengelly
Headline: World Rugby has appointed Megan Rose, a USTA executive, as managing director of the the men’s Rugby World Cup in 2031
Content: Megan Rose has held several high-ranking positions in tennis.Photograph: Javier AguilaView image in fullscreenMegan Rose has held several high-ranking positions in tennis.Photograph: Javier AguilaRugby World CupEx-tennis pro Megan Rose appointed to lead 2031 men’s Rugby World Cup in USTournament coming to the US for the first timeRose says tournament is a huge opportunityMartin Pengellyin Washington DCWed 21 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorld Rugby has appointed Megan Rose, an American tennis pro turned United States Tennis Association (USTA) executive, as managing director of the 2031 men’sRugby World Cup, a key appointment as the governing body prepares to host what is by some measures the third-biggest global sporting event on American soil for the first time.Rose said: “Rugby World Cup is one of the iconic events in global sport, defined by unforgettable moments on the pitch and the passion of fans around the world. To be entrusted with bringing Men’s Rugby World Cup to the United States for the first time is an extraordinary honour, and I’m thrilled to join this team.”As a tennis player, Rose was a five-time collegiate All American out of the University of Miami, and a national indoor champion. After competing on the WTA Tour, she coached Princeton to an Ivy League women’s tennis championship thenworked for the WTA and the USTA, becoming managing director of major events and team leader for USA Olympic Tennis.Measures vary but on a world scale, the Rugby World Cup is generally placed third in size and prestige behind the Fifa World Cup and the Olympic Games. Australia will host the next two Rugby World Cups, men in 2027 and women in 2029. The US will host the 2031 men’s tournament and the women’s World Cup in 2033.Rose’s appointment comes a little more than a month since more than 68,000 fans traveled to Baltimore, Maryland, to seeSouth Africa’s men beat New Zealandin the fourth Test of the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series, an attendance record for rugby union on US soil. Smaller-scale internationals will be played this weekend in Nashville, Tennessee, where theUS Eagles womenwill face Italy before the Eagles men take on an Australia XV. The following weekend in New Jersey, the Eagles women will play England, the world champions, while the men face the Australians again.Rose said the 2031 World Cup was “a once-in-a-generation opportunity to bring millions more Americans into the game and create a lasting impact for rugby in this country. I look forward to working closely with USA Rugby, and the clubs, players, supporters, and stakeholders who have built rugby across the United States, alongside the global rugby community, to deliver an incredible Rugby World Cup and build something that lasts well beyond 2031.”The World Rugby chief executive, Alan Gilpin, said: “Megan is an outstanding leader with a proven track record of delivering world-class sporting events and driving innovation. She joins us at a pivotal moment as our US project enters its next phase – an appointment that reflects the scale of our ambition. Her experience, vision and deep understanding of theUS sportslandscape make her ideally placed to deliver a defining chapter for rugby in the United States and around the world.”The US currently supports a men’s pro competition, Major League Rugby, and a women’s semi-pro league, Women’s Elite Rugby. MLR has survived since 2018 but is nowdown to just five teamsafter a series of failures, with a possible sixth entrant for 2027 mooted but not confirmed.WER has just five teams too. The US college game has deeper roots and greater strength than is generally known around the rugby world but ispolitically splitand subject to steep challenges in funding and facilities. The US Eagles men failed to qualify for the 2023 World Cup in France but will compete in Australia next year. In England last year, the Eagles women fielded breakout social media star Ilona Maher but failed to get out of their pool.Such hard realities have fueledskepticismaround the global game about whether a US World Cup can be successful, at least in terms of engaging the American public and boosting the American game. In Baltimore, around the Springboks-All Blacks fixture, executives from World Rugby and the competing unionsexpressed confidencethat it can.Announcing the appointment of Rose, World Rugby said: “With more premium match content being played in the US than ever before, 25 highly engaged cities involved in the applicant process and stakeholder engagement building and fan and media interest continuing to grow, the US is poised to provide an unprecedented stage for Rugby World Cups that will redefine the sport’s future and support the ambitions of its global growth strategy.”Explore more on these topicsRugby World CupRugby unionUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Angry’ Carrick on the brink as Fernandes hits out at Manchester United tactics | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: The manager apologised to Manchester United fans after the 4-1 defeat in Como, while his captain criticised the team’s tactical approach
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: The manager apologised to Manchester United fans after the 4-1 defeat in Como, while his captain criticised the team’s tactical approach
Content: Michael Carrick offered a mea culpa to those Manchester United fans who stayed past the final whistle in Como.Photograph: Alessandro Garofalo/ReutersView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick offered a mea culpa to those Manchester United fans who stayed past the final whistle in Como.Photograph: Alessandro Garofalo/ReutersManchester United‘Angry’ Carrick on the brink as Fernandes hits out at Manchester United tacticsManager apologises to fans after 4-1 defeat in ComoCaptain criticises ‘decision from the staff’ not to pressJamie Jacksonat the Giuseppe Sinigaglia StadiumWed 21 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick’s future asManchester Unitedmanager is in the balance after a humiliating 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como on Wednesday night.Before Bournemouth’s visit to Old Trafford on Sunday his future may be discussed by Jason Wilcox, the director of football, Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the co-owner who controls sporting policy.Como demolish dismal Manchester United to pile more pressure on CarrickRead moreOn a torrid night an “angry” ­Carrick insisted afterwards that he had not given his position any thought and was forced to defend himself against Bruno Fernandes after his captain questioned the manager’s tactics of not pressing against Cesc Fàbregas’s team. Carrick also criticised his side for not running. The defeat by Como in the third Champions League group game leaves United with only two wins all season from 11 games. ­Carrick’s side are in 13th place in the Premier League and wereeliminated from the Carabao Cuplast month.The 45-year-old was asked if he fears for his job. “Listen, I’ve not given my own position any thought,” he said. “[My thoughts are] for the supporters – I was one of them watching that and I wasn’t happy at all.”Carrick was then asked if he could walk away following the latest defeat in Europe. “No. It’s not about me right now and my feelings in that regard,” the manager said. “It’s more of as a team and as a football club, what we want to look like, what we should look like. And as I said, the results can come and go at times, but you got to do it in a certain way. And that wasn’t it.”700 United sup­porters travelled. At the end around 200 remained and Carrick went to ­apologise to them, noticeably ­ignoring his players. After United conceded Nico Paz’s second-minute goal, Carrick’s men were unable to mount any resistance. By 57 minutesComoled 3-0, due to Tasos Douvikas’s strike and Paz’s second, before Jacobo Ramón completed the scoring for the Italian side on 76 minutes. Joshua Zirkzee netted in added time for the visitors.Fernandes openly challenged ­Carrick’s strategy during the match. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” he said.The captain was asked if Carrick’s tactics were wrong. “That’s on the manager and staff to see, not me,” he said. “Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable. As you saw with them, the centre-back was coming to mark me in my own half. We need to do that as a team but we were unable to.”Fernandes’s criticism was put to his manager after the match. “We actually half-pressed man-to-man the second half and then conceded a goal from that,” Carrick said.“Whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCarrick was asked how he can raise the mood before Bournemouth’s visit.“I’m bitterly disappointed, I’m frustrated; more than frustrated, I’m really angry. But you’ve got to move on. You got to deal with what’s next and see what that looks like.“At this moment in time, there’s a lot to do before that next game to get the team ready because that was a difficult night for everyone. I have to apologise to the supporters.”View image in fullscreenBruno Fernandes and his United teammates were second-best throughout.Photograph: Alessandro Garofalo/ReutersExplore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickComoCesc FàbregasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barkley and Buendía on target as Aston Villa sink Viking to maintain perfect start | Champions League | The Guardian
description: An own goal from Henrik Heggheim completed Aston Villa’s 3-1 Champions League victory against Viking, their third consecutive win of the league phase
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: An own goal from Henrik Heggheim completed Aston Villa’s 3-1 Champions League victory against Viking, their third consecutive win of the league phase
Content: Ross Barkley soaks in the cheers after giving Aston Villa a first-half lead.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoss Barkley soaks in the cheers after giving Aston Villa a first-half lead.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersChampions LeagueBarkley and Buendía on target as Aston Villa sink Viking to maintain perfect startNick Amesat Villa ParkWed 21 Oct 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a little over 20 minutes, Aston Villa could look down on the rest of Europe. They had scaled theChampions Leaguesummit on goal difference when Henrik Heggheim put through his own net and the fact was not lost on the Holte End, who reflected their position in song and perhaps allowed themselves another glimpse back to the days when their supremacy was undisputed. “We’ve conquered before, we’re prepared for more,” the pre-match tifo display had read.Perhaps Villa really will rekindle the spirit of 1982 but the frustration here, albeit minor in the wider scheme, was that they could not maintain their bird’s-eye view over the continent. A superbly taken volley by Peter Christiansen, awarded by the video assistant referee after initially being disallowed for offside, gave Viking a consolation their second-half display deserved and meant Unai Emery’s side must make do with slumming it just behind Paris Saint-Germain.Declan Rice strikes late for Arsenal to deny Bayern Munich in blockbusterRead more“Collectively and individually we did a good job and some players also made a step forward in their confidence,” said Emery, who was pleased with Villa’s seriousness against opponents still finding their way in a first campaign at this level. “Each match has an objective to get better, to be consistent and be very demanding.”The hard work had been done in an opening period whose scoreline hardly did justice to Villa’s total dominance. Viking had drawn at home with Bayern Munich in their previous game, a fact that would look more explicable when they emerged from their shell later, but were barely afforded a kick and looked vulnerable every time the ball was delivered from wide.Nicolas Jackson, electric in the6-0 thrashing of Fenerbahce, fluffed two free headers in the opening seven minutes and a similarly resounding win came to appear possible. Emery had made four changes but Villa, working the play smoothly from side to side, were a consistent threat and unfazed by opponents whose attacking ambition was initially minimal.The breakthrough arrived after a spell of pressure sparked when a cross from João Gomes, the makeshift right-back, deflected on to the bar. Two corners later, an inswinger from the livewire 18-year-old Ibrahim Mbaye was met by Ross Barkley, who leapt highest to plant a firm header across Arild Østbø at the near post.Barkley had scored twice in the previous week’s big win but the rest of the first half resembled a quest for Emiliano Buendía to put his mark on the scoresheet. Straight after the opener Buendía looped a header wide of the vacant goal after Østbø had parried from Alysson, who was a rangy threat throughout, and then he charged on to a clever John McGinn corner only to aim straight at the keeper.View image in fullscreenRoss Barkley heads Aston Villa’s opener from Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAIt was third time lucky when the VAR reviewed a needless challenge by the Viking captain Zlatko Tripic on Alysson, who had run into traffic in the box, and led the referee Sebastian Gishamer to award a penalty. Buendía rolled it in, his fourth goal in consecutive European games; 37 minutes had passed and Viking had still not produced a meaningful attack.After the restart they showed some of the intensity and verve that had ruffled Bayern, the richly promising midfielder Tobias Moi warming Zion Suzuki’s midriff and seeing a goalbound effort blocked. Suzuki also beat away a Tripic drive. But Villa could now exploit space in behind and, after flashing an angled effort just wide, Alysson got away once again to create the third. This time his attempted centre snicked off Heggheim, who was desperately trying to recover, and gave Østbø no chance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNow Villa were, as the home choirs gleefully announced, top of the league and they received further opportunities to hammer home the point. Alejandro Garnacho saw one of them saved by Østbø after a strong run but Viking remained a threat and Christiansen’s finish, emphatically converting Kristoffer Askildsen’s deep cross, was by some distance the best of the night.“The second half was much more like the Viking we want to be,” said Morten Jensen, whoco-manages the Norwegian championsalongside Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim. “Maybe we had too much respect for them in the first half, they were all over us.”View image in fullscreenEmiliano Buendía calmly doubles Aston Villa’s lead from the penalty spot.Photograph: Alex Livesey/AVFC/Getty ImagesNine points from nine, not to mention 12 consecutive home wins in Europe, mean Villa are flying. Sweeping Fenerbahce and Viking aside can “give us confidence and comfort for the next challenges,” Emery said. They will need plenty of it given a trip to Barcelona follows the relatively soft run presented so far. Maybe the peak is yet to come.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueAston VillaViking FKmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Champions League: Silva sparks Real Madrid’s demolition of Leipzig as Lask stun Sporting | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Bernardo Silva opened the scoring as Real Madrid beat RB Leipzig 4-1, while Galatasaray swept past Lille and 10-man Inter edged out Shakhtar Donetsk
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Bernardo Silva opened the scoring as Real Madrid beat RB Leipzig 4-1, while Galatasaray swept past Lille and 10-man Inter edged out Shakhtar Donetsk
Content: Bernardo Silva jumps for joy after scoring Real Madrid’s opener against RB Leipzig.Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBernardo Silva jumps for joy after scoring Real Madrid’s opener against RB Leipzig.Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueChampions League: Silva sparks Real Madrid’s demolition of Leipzig as Lask stun SportingBernardo Silva opens scoring as Madrid win 4-1Galatasaray sweep past Lille; 10-man Inter edge ShakhtarGuardian sportand agenciesWed 21 Oct 2026 18.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReal Madridclaimed a thirdChampions Leaguevictory in as many games by thrashingRB Leipzig4-1 on Wednesday, with Kylian Mbappé and Yan Diomande among the goals for José Mourinho’s side.Bernardo Silva opened the scoring for Madrid from close range towards the end of a tight first half, with Arda Guler doubling the record 15-time European champions’ advantage soon after the interval.Declan Rice strikes late for Arsenal to deny Bayern Munich in blockbusterRead moreMbappé bent home a third before Tidiam Gomis pulled one back for the German side and Diomande rammed a volley into the top corner to cap Madrid’s triumph late on.“We know every point is important to get into the top eight, we know we have to win as many games as possible – we’ve won three and there are five to go,” Mbappé said. The France forward,who hopes to win the Ballon d’Or next week, has netted in each of Madrid’s Champions League matches this season and has 12 goals in 12 games.“I’m doing well [but] I think I can do more,” he said. “I’m one of the few players who always has to demand more from himself ... right now it’s a good moment, but we have to keep going and I have to do more.”Lasklaunched an impressive comeback atSportingto earn their first Champions League win of the season. The Austrian champions went behind when Luis Suárez scored from the spot after five minutes, but equalised 10 minutes later through Christoph Lang.The visitors then stunned the Estádio José Alvalade as Sasa Kalajdzic and Krystof Danek put them 3-1 up, the former rounding off a smart team move and the latter firing in at the near post. Suárez scored again for the hosts late on, but it was not enough.View image in fullscreenVictor Osimhen, with Yunus Akgun on his shoulders, after rounding off Galatasaray’s 4-2 win at Lille.Photograph: Matthieu Mirville/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockGalatasarayswept pastLilleat the Stade Pierre-Mauroy, setting the tone with a goal after two minutes from Yunus Akgun.Lille levelled the score via Soriba Diaoune, who then put them 2-1 up in the 39th minute. Aleksey Batrakov made it 2-2 just before half-time, however, before an own goal from Nabil Bentaleb and Victor Osimhen, in action against his former club, sealed a 4-2 victory.Interhad Alessandro Bastoni sent off midway through the second half before Carlos Augusto’s late goal secured a 1-0 win at home toShakhtar Donetsk, as the Italian champions got their first points of the league phase.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBastoni was sent off for two yellow cards in as many minutes, putting Inter on the back foot. Carlos Augusto saved the day in the 77th minute, capping a lightning-fast counterattack with a low finish.View image in fullscreenIsco wheels away after netting from 12 yards to put Real Betis 1-0 up against Feyenoord.Photograph: Antonio Pozo/PRESSINPHOTO/ShutterstockReal Betis, who beatFeyenoord1-0 via a penalty kick from Isco, made it three from three in the Champions League to extend their strong start to the season.Betis had the lion’s share of the chances, but only broke the deadlock when Jeremiah St Juste was adjudged to have handled in the box. Isco stepped up and fired low into the right-hand corner for what proved to be the winner.Club BruggedefeatedLens3-0 at the Jan Breydel Stadium in a ruthless home performance. The Belgians went 1-0 up through Hans Vanaken in first-half stoppage time before Joaquin Seys and Carlos Forbs secured the win in the second half.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueReal MadridRB LeipzigLaskSportingInternazionaleShakhtar DonetsknewsShareReuse this content

title: Paris Saint-Germain sparkle on the pitch while the city of light burns around them | Paris Saint-Germain | The Guardian
description: PSG, the pet project of the state of Qatar, expresses the dualism of the city, a place of deprivation where the centre is perfect
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: PSG, the pet project of the state of Qatar, expresses the dualism of the city, a place of deprivation where the centre is perfect
Content: PSG fans’ tifo sends a chilling message before their game against Barcelona.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAView image in fullscreenPSG fans’ tifo sends a chilling message before their game against Barcelona.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAParis Saint-GermainParis Saint-Germain sparkle on the pitch while the city of light burns around themBarney RonayPSG, pet project of the state of Qatar, expresses the dualism of the city, a place of deprivation where the centre is perfectWed 21 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.55 EDTSharePASSION!GOOOOAL!MVP!The security deployment will be massive.Those who sought to bring down the Republic will have to answer for it.Tell you who would have loved this? Who would have been utterly engrossed scrolling the hashtag #Paris on Tuesday night as two things happened simultaneously, theharrowing of the Barcelona defenceat the Parc des Princes, and the harrowing of Paris itself via tales of city-centre thuggery and end-of-days political doom‑mongering.The big man, Guy Debord himself. The Society of the Spectacle, you say? Actually, I think we’re past that now. Hold the society bit. We’ll just take the spectacle.The great Parisian Situationist philosopher wasn’t really one for managed fun. But it was impossible not to be bowled over by the extraordinary pre-match show for Paris Saint‑Germain versus Barcelona,Champions LeagueMatchday Three.Kvaratskhelia asks ‘why me?’ after ACL rupture in most serious of three PSG injuriesRead moreThe wild pyrotechnics, the plumes of smoke, the full-wrap light show, the lime-green robo‑text spelling out every player’s name on the pitch. Although not the Barcelona names, sadly, for anyone with an unrealised desire to see the words “ANTHONY GORDON” projected in vast letters for the delight of a shrieking crowd.Admittedly, the Halloween‑themed tifo banner showing a maskedParis Saint-Germainserial killer-type literally butchering the Barcelona badge to death with his bloodied chainsaw was perhaps a bit much. As were the Barça Puta signs, which are now reportedly the subject of a complaint to Uefa.But it was a wild and all‑consuming spectacle, annihilating every other impulse in your head to a green thought in a green shade. And in the process capturing the profound sense of cognitive dissonance in the city.View image in fullscreenPSG fans light flares after their team took the lead against Barcelona.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty ImagesJust walking around the streets of central Paris earlier in the day generated its own mild whiplash. On the face of it this was still the same city offlâneursand tourists and everyday bistro business, and not, repeat not, a civil war drama or some kind of emergent military caliphate.But the sense of dread was also tangible. You still got the occasional crunch of glass underfoot. Here and there charred bikes and scooters had been politely piled to one side. Even close to the Parc, away from the main hotspots, shopkeepers could be seen emerging warily into their doorways at the sound of a police siren.By Tuesday night, a total of 2,513 people had been taken into police custodyafter the events of the weekend. At least 420 rental bikes had been destroyed or maimed. Liberated high-value retail goods were already being sold on Vinted, a commendable show of entrepreneurial energy from the maligned younger generation.Not that you’d suspect these two worlds had any kind of overlap, lost in the booming triumphalism around PSG’s 4–2 win, one of the most beautifully luminous football matches you’re ever likely to see. Or indeed reading the coverage of an event that seems to have been treated in France like its own clear, clean space, floating above the flames, all the chat about the brilliance of Monsieur Dynamite, Désiré Doué, the wonderful television audiences on Canal+ TV, the whole of European football “kneeling before the machine” (are we sure this isn’t to do with anarchic rejection of social control?). “Paris est insubmersible!” was the headline in Le Parisien. But is it?Remember when football used to reflect the world? Or just provide clues, a commentary, some kind of metaphor? This is no longer the case. At a time when even the most thunderous of commentators is struggling to summarise all this in suitably trite and damning terms, it was hard to avoid the feeling Paris Saint-Germain, the pet power football project of the state of Qatar, expresses this dualism perfectly.Sometimes you just have to let football tell you things. “People who want to cause trouble in the city centres next Saturday will be prevented,” Emmanuel Macron announced on Tuesday evening, speaking, as it happens, from Doha, where he met Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, ultimate owner of PSG.View image in fullscreenDésiré Doué (left) with João Neves after scoring PSG’s first goal against Barcelona.Photograph: David Ramos/Uefa/Getty ImagesMacron is said to be considering deploying the French military to keep the peace on the streets before the next planned protests, although even here he may have to ask Qatar’s permission if he wants to deploy any of the French troops currently deployed working its missile systems, or embedded in the Doha security services.The key event Macron is tooling up for is this Saturday night, 24 October, the date thegiletsjaunessocial media feed has set for an even greater swell of disorder. And again this will be football adjacent, with PSG playing Lyon at home on Sunday, a top‑of‑the-table capital‑city clash played out against whatever wreckage is left, however many thousands of Dot bikes are savaged, whatever guerrilla skirmishes are still playing out in the Marais.What does this really have to do with football and theIci C’est Parisbrand appropriated by a state outreach project? Well, what are these demonstrations anyway? There have been many theories put forward as to what exactly is happening here, what is the spark, the kindling, the fire behind this disorder. School protests were the original line. Others have now roped in some kind of nebulous omni-cause, Instagram-activism, perhaps even a barbarian takeover, the decline of the west, savagery at the gates, of the type Donald Trump pretends to see.Do you need a single reason? Take a look around. Modern life is pretty alarming on a minute‑to‑minute basis. Disaffection, alienation, a sense of being transformed in real time into a passive economic consumer unit, a set of eyeballs, an avatar of consumption. French youth unemployment is close to 20%. Robots nobody wants are being lined up to take jobs that don’t exist. Why don’t these young people want to join a youth club? Why don’t they sign up for the Liberal Democrats? Why are they enjoying empowered disorder? Maybe because nothing is yours around here, not even the things thrust into your brain as digital distractions. So why not grab something when you can? Debord would have called this “a vicious circle of isolation”, lonely crowd, technologies based on isolation.On the other hand, what is PSG in Paris, other than the perfect expression of this? It often seems to surprise people that celebrations of PSG victories end up with riots and burnt-out cars. But Paris is both a beautiful and deeply dysfunctional city, a place of make‑believe and deprivation, where the centre is a perfect, performative relic, the suburbs shunted out to the ring roads, a life lived inside a box, noses pressed up against the glass, peering through your binoculars at the city of someone else’s love.Paris is the divide between overclass and churn expressed in a single city. It’s everything you might have had but never will.
