And PSG represent this like no other entity, a football club owned as an act of outreach by a staggeringly rich inherited monarchy, weaponised passion, borrowed culture, engineered spectacle, deeply cynical but also deeply seductive.View image in fullscreenDamage after the riots in Place de la République.Photograph: Telmo Pinto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockWhy are the Qataris splurging hundreds of millions into this project? Because they just really like high-pressing positional football? Qatar is the indentured labour state that employs Colin Kaepernick to promote its outreach projects. It will hymn its connections to the footballers of thebanlieue, which is true and real and valuable, but not because of anything this political project wants or needs other than public relations.It is in its own way a perfect human lab experiment, synthesised beauty, collectivism, with a cold, cold hand at its heart. And this is why there weren’t two versions of Paris in evidence on Tuesday night, just the same one, the dark side and the shiny side, an engine of the same divisions, the same kind of violence, right down to the sight of kids in PSG training gear dodging the police or taunting the barricades at the Place de la République.And now we have Sunday night to come, moreIci C’est Paris, more PASSION. What kind of background will it be played out against? Does it matter under the lights? Will anyone notice?Le Monde has described these events as a very basic test of the republic, its ability to bend, to remain essentially itself, the state’s willingness to pit itself against its own people. Football, as ever, holds these answers already. PSG’s Qatari owners have spent the past 15 years flaunting this city like a global luxury brand, extending its reach, creating its own ideal of conspicuous consumption, spectacle, triumph,son et lumière, bread and roses. As ever, if you want to know how and why, football has the answers.Explore more on these topicsParis Saint-GermainChampions LeagueFranceEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘A complete threat’: Rio Ngumoha’s electric display excites Van Dijk and Liverpool | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Teenager produced man-of-the-match performance against Villarreal and has learned from Salah, says Virgil Van Dijk
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Teenager produced man-of-the-match performance against Villarreal and has learned from Salah, says Virgil Van Dijk
Content: Rio Ngumoha performed confidently in his fifth start under Andoni Iraola against Villarreal on Tuesday.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenRio Ngumoha performed confidently in his fifth start under Andoni Iraola against Villarreal on Tuesday.Photograph: Nick Potts/PALiverpool‘A complete threat’: Rio Ngumoha’s electric display excites Van Dijk and LiverpoolTeenager produced man-of-the-match performance against Villarreal and has learned from Salah, says Reds captainAndy HunterWed 21 Oct 2026 09.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 16.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe shot sailed wide of Peter Gulacsi’s top corner and into the Kop, affording Villarreal much-needed respite at 4-2, but for Andoni Iraola it was a standout moment in a scintillatingChampions Leaguedisplay from Rio Ngumoha. To a coach who called for versatility from all of his wingers this summer, here was a significant step forward among many from the 18-year-old at Anfield.There were questions over how Ngumoha would adapt to playing on the right even before Liverpool increased the likelihood by signingBradley Barcola for £123mfrom Paris Saint-Germain. On his fifth start under Iraola on Tuesday, whichhis side won 4-3, Liverpool witnessed an answer: quickly, incisively and confidently. The teenager’s willingness to cut inside from the right and shoot from distance with his left foot captured Iraola’s imagination as much as the devastating run that created Alexis Mac Allister’s second goal of the game.Mac Allister double sparks Liverpool’s thrilling comeback win over VillarrealRead more“I’m happy with his attitude because he’s eager to improve the things that we think he needs to improve,” theLiverpoolhead coach said after the comeback win against their Spanish opponents. “He has played a lot on the right lately. He’s feeling so comfortable now that he’s even adding some shots with the left. He hasn’t scored but he’s getting there, and if he can add these small things to his game it will put him in an even better position.”Ngumoha’s 71st-minute attempt was reminiscent of Mohamed Salah in its intent, if not in execution. The Liverpool great’s final season at Anfield may have been the exception to the exceptional in terms of his own contribution but, as an education to a gifted and hungry young winger, it was not wasted.Virgil van Dijk noted that “a few senior players” have taken Ngumoha under their wing. “I would say Cody [Gakpo] is definitely part of that. Everyone is chipping in but for him to work with Mo last year was obviously massive. Mo was one of the best wingers at the club and experienced everything so why not soak in all the information and show it on the pitch and show your own qualities? I think he has shown it this season but there is still much more to come. He’s pretty electric at times and he showed it again. He was a complete threat constantly and their defender had a tough time.”View image in fullscreenRio Ngumoha proved a constant threat to Villarreal.Photograph: Richard Martin-Roberts/CameraSport/Getty ImagesThe Salah comparison was not the only throwback for Liverpool against Villarreal. It was a flawed performance with Van Dijk’s early mistake, Iraola’s initial formation and Liverpool’s lethargy on the ball all punished by Iñigo Pérez’s slick side. “It was a terrible start,” the Liverpool captain said. “I think the saying is you fight an uphill battle and as a defender it is pretty difficult to come back from it. I tried but it was a bad day at the office personally but we do it together with 11 players. We turned it around and that’s the main thing.”The rousing recovery, the relentless high press, Iraola’s bold changes and the character required to overturn a 2-0 deficit all carried echoes of the Jürgen Klopp era. Given that was where Liverpool wished to return when replacing Arne Slot with the Basque coach this summer, Iraola’s 11th game in charge showed development is not confined only to Ngumoha.Van Dijk said: “If you look at it from that perspective, it is like that. We train a lot, tactically as well, but because there are so many games you learn playing games and this was a test in that sense because Villarreal were good on the ball. They also rotated a lot so you have to find moments when you can press them and when you can win the ball high.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Is this squad used to that [pressing style] because I don’t think many players have been part of that? What the manager wants us to do is something which resonates with Liverpool and it is down to us to show it in each and every game. It’s not easy, it’s demanding, but if you want to win games and win games in the Liverpool way then we have to do it.“The first half was obviously not good at all and the second half was solid and we turned it around and that’s a good sign. Now we have to get ready for Brighton, a super team, which is coming.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolChampions LeagueAndoni IraolafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We can go all the way’: Jonas Eidevall on life at San Diego Wave and lessons learned from Arsenal | San Diego Wave | The Guardian
description: The Swede’s team are second in the NWSL and, he tells Tom Garry, he hopes to create some special memories at their 35,000-seater Snapdragon Stadium
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The Swede’s team are second in the NWSL and, he tells Tom Garry, he hopes to create some special memories at their 35,000-seater Snapdragon Stadium
Content: Jonas Eidevall’s San Diego Wave have secured a home playoff quarter-final in the NWSL.Photograph: Jay Biggerstaff/NWSL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJonas Eidevall’s San Diego Wave have secured a home playoff quarter-final in the NWSL.Photograph: Jay Biggerstaff/NWSL/Getty ImagesSan Diego WaveInterview‘We can go all the way’: Jonas Eidevall on life at San Diego Wave and lessons learned from ArsenalTom GarryThe Swede’s team are second in the NWSL and hope to create special memories at their Snapdragon StadiumWed 21 Oct 2026 07.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Ilove the ocean,” Jonas Eidevall says, and he references walks along the beach at Del Mar. “People are very relaxed, life is lived at a slower pace here. I’m a very simple person. I like to read a book, go to the gym and spend time with my wife and kids, that’s sort of all I need.”The former Arsenal head coach is revelling in a calmer world as the head coach ofSan Diego Wavebut it is not merely the beaches that are lowering his stress levels; his team are on a five-game winning streak in the NWSL and sit second in the table, one point off top spot, with two matches to go before the playoffs. Winning feels good and the club are targeting silverware, as he tells the Guardian: “It would mean everything. There are no guarantees in the playoffs, but the exciting part is saying: ‘We can also go all the way’ – that’s a possibility for us and we need to believe.”How Brazil’s election result could shape women’s football in the countryRead moreSuccess did not originally look destined, when the Swede took charge 21 months ago, at a time when San Diego Wave were enduring something of an exodus of senior players; the United States defender Abby Dahlkemper’s sale to Bay FC in August 2024 and Alex Morgan’s retirement a month later were followed by the USA forward Jaedyn Shaw’s departing for North Carolina Courage and her international teammate Naomi Girma joining Chelsea in January 2025. A reconstruction was needed.That is why, on a video call that winter, when Eidevall spoke to his players for the first time after taking charge, he began by quoting a proverb: if you want to go fast, go alone, but if you want to go far, go together. “My ideas are not worth anything if we don’t believe and buy into them altogether,” he says. “We focused everything on just building connections as human beings.” Detailed tactical discussions were initially kept to a minimum. They spent – as he recalls – around four weeks of their six-week pre-season focusing entirely on passing out from the back, to develop their style. Fast forward to the present day and it has paid off, with the Wave defenders Kristen McNabb and Kennedy Wesley being the division’s top two players for passes completed this season. More notable, though, has been the development of young players, such as the 18-year-olds Melanie Barcenas and Kimmi Ascanio.“From 2024, when the club was not performing well on the pitch and it led to a complete rebuild, we had to find an edge, finding players that could fit into the way we wanted to play,” Eidevall says. “Back then it was a bit different to many other teams in the league, because theNWSLwas seen as being dominated by athleticism and transitional play, which obviously then requires really fast players and maybe didn’t put a premium on technical supremacy.”He adds that the club therefore eyed players who are “really, really good technically. We had some young, talented players already – that has given us a really good advantage because we’ve been able to develop players in a salary cap league. That’s huge, because if you only buy readymade players, you will run out of salary cap space pretty quickly.”View image in fullscreenJonas Eidevall took over at San Diego Wave in January 2025.Photograph: SPP /AlamyIt is not just the salary cap that differs in the NWSL, compared to Eidevall’s previous jobs at Arsenal and Rosengård. The broad competitiveness of the American league means that, despite being second in the table, San Diego have lost almost as many games this season as Eidevall’s Arsenal across three English campaigns, and he says: “This was new for me. In European leagues the top teams very rarely go two games in a row without winning. Here, even the team that wins the league might go through spells where they don’t pick up points, so the way you handle those moments becomes very important.“Training [here] is also a challenge – sometimes it’s very hard to get 22 players because you have a limited roster size. The moment you start to have injuries … there’s no real second-team academy system like we have in Europe, where you can always have the numbers that you want. Here you might not, here you would like to do something XI v XI, but you have 18 players and you just have to be creative with how you coach.”Trying to play entertaining football has been a target in a campaign during which they have already set new club records for regular-season wins and goals scored. They have done it with the second-highest average possession share in the division, more shots on target than any other team and while facing by far the fewest shots on target.“That’s the most pleasing part, results through an identity rather than getting results the other way around,” Eidevall says. “The identity we have is to allow the players to be creative.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenEidevall has overseen a necessary overhaul of San Diego Wave’s squad.Photograph: San Diego WaveWe are speaking around two years after Eidevallresigned as Arsenal’s head coachon 15 October 2024, following a disappointing start to that season. In his three full campaigns at the helm in north London he had won two League Cups, reached a Champions League semi-final and secured a second-placed top-flight finish in 2022 – but was unable to win the WSL. Reflecting on what he learned from that spell, he says: “We had a lot of fluidity with how our wide players could play in Arsenal, which at times created too few central options. So, how do we get better central connections? How do we get more players central on the pitch? That was a long-term reflection on my time at Arsenal. And that’s also led to some tactical changes that we’ve done here with San Diego.”There is an aspect of his Arsenal tenure that he is determined to take inspiration from at San Diego, with his team having secured a home playoff quarter-final at their 35,000-seater Snapdragon Stadium.The 43-year-old fondly remembers the first sellout crowd for a women’s match at Arsenal’s 60,000-seater Emirates Stadium, for theirChampions League semi-final against Wolfsburg in 2023: “We want to sell out Snapdragon Stadium and in order to do so we need to do exactly what we were doing at Arsenal – we need to create special experiences at the stadium,” he says. “That is what’s going to draw people into there. Yes, play exciting football, but we also need to play games that mean a lot to be there. The ripple effect of that, that’s so big.”Explore more on these topicsSan Diego WaveNWSLWomen's footballArsenal WomeninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Coach banned until 2048 for training children in DR Congo while suspended for sexual abuse | Soccer | The Guardian
description: A coach in the DR Congo who was banned from football for 20 years by Fifa for for sexual abuse of a minor has had his ban extended by five years
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: A coach in the DR Congo who was banned from football for 20 years by Fifa for for sexual abuse of a minor has had his ban extended by five years
Content: Fifa’s ethics committee imposed its initial ban on the coach in October 2023.Photograph: Natee127/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenFifa’s ethics committee imposed its initial ban on the coach in October 2023.Photograph: Natee127/Getty Images/iStockphotoSoccerCoach banned until 2048 for training children in DR Congo while suspended for sexual abuseJonathan Bukabakwa gets extra five-year ban from FifaDR Congo’s FA must improve education and complianceEd AaronsandRomain MolinaWed 21 Oct 2026 05.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 08.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA coach in the Democratic Republic of the Congo who was banned from football for 20 years by Fifa for sexual abuse of a minor has had his ban extended by five years to 2048 by the world governing body.Jonathan Bukabakwa, known as Messi, has also been ordered to pay an additional fine of $15,000 (£11,200) afterthe Guardian revealedhe had continued to work with young players despite his suspension.The Congolese Association Football Federation (Fecofa) and Racing Club Baki, where Bukabakwa was coaching, have been fined $50,000 each by Fifa’s ethics committee for failing to comply with its decision to ban him for 20 years in 2023.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Fecofa has also been instructed to introduce a “comprehensive education, compliance and monitoring programme for its officials, affiliated clubs and registered members” to try to ensure there is no repeat.“The Congo DR Football Association, the club Racing Club Baki (formerly known as Esperanto FC), and the coach Jonathan Bukabakwa were found responsible for failing to comply with the decision rendered by the Fifa ethics committee on 18 October 2023,” said a Fifa statement.Bukabakwa, who previously coached youth teams in the Limpopo and Malabo regions, was convicted of sexually abusing minors by authorities in the DRC and was released from prison last year. A Guardian investigation in August revealed there was video footage of him coaching young players at Esperanto in the Limete district of the capital, Kinshasa. Local sources confirmed he had regularly been seen taking charge of players on a school field.Bukabakwa did not deny continuing to coach young players but claimed he had not been informed of his Fifa ban. He said he had not been questioned or received any communication from the governing body. He has denied the allegations against him.The case has raised further questions about safeguarding in Congolese football and the ability of authorities to ensure that suspended individuals do not continue participating in the sport. Bukabakwa was provisionally suspended by Fecofa in November 2022 after media reports of alleged widespread sexual abuse in the DRC. Several other coaches were provisionally suspended at the time, although investigations into some of those other cases did not establish sufficient evidence for further action by Fecofa or Fifa.VéronMosengo-Omba, elected as Fecofa’s president in May, has promised to look into the previous cases once he has re-established a disciplinary committee. Fecofa was under a Fifa-appointed normalisation committee from 2023 until his election. “We will make sure that no one who is behaving like this will be involved in football in this country,” he said.Explore more on these topicsFootballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Australia sprint champion Jake Doran charged with alleged child abuse | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Police charge 26-year-old with indecent treatment of a child under 16 while Australian Athletics ban sprinter from any involvement in the sport
Author: Jack Snape
Headline: Police charge 26-year-old with indecent treatment of a child under 16 while Australian Athletics ban sprinter from any involvement in the sport
Content: Former Australia sprint champion Jake Doran has been arrested in Townsville and charged by police with one count of indecent treatment of a child under 16.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreenFormer Australia sprint champion Jake Doran has been arrested in Townsville and charged by police with one count of indecent treatment of a child under 16.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPAthleticsFormer Australia sprint champion Jake Doran charged with alleged child abusePolice charge 26-year-old with indecent treatment of child under 16Australian Athletics ban sprinter from any involvement in the sportJack SnapeWed 21 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 21.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s 2022 men’s 100m sprint champion has been arrested in Townsville for alleged indecent treatment of children.Queensland police arrested Jake Doran on 13 October and he has been charged with one count of “indecent treatment of child under 16 (indecent film etc)”. Police investigations covered the period between January 2025 and September 2026.The 26-year-old was bailed to appear at Townsville magistrates court on 5 November.Doran, who works in business development at Tafe Queensland, has been training athletes in Townsville.AustralianAthleticsconfirmed he has no paid or unpaid role with the national governing body, but has banned him from any involvement in the sport while the matter is ongoing.“Based on information provided to Australian Athletics, the organisation has imposed a provisional action on the athlete, prohibiting him from attending club, member association or Australian Athletics events, as well as banning him from participating in athletics training,” a spokesperson said.“The safety and wellbeing of all participants in our sport is paramount, and we take all allegations of this nature very seriously.”Doran has deleted his Instagram account, and his profile no longer appears on the Australian Athletics website.Queensland Athletics declined to comment.A Tafe Queensland spokesperson said: “Based on the information available at this time, the allegations are understood to be unrelated to the individual’s employment with Tafe Queensland, and there is no indication they relate to Tafe Queensland students, staff, training delivery, campus activities or operations.“The employee has been suspended from duty while the matter is before the courts.”The sprinter was the winner of the 100m at the Australian national championships in 2022, when he crossed the line ahead of current Australian representative Eddie Nketia in a wind-assisted time of 10.05sec.Doran went on to compete for Australia at the world championships and Commonwealth Games, and also won the national 200m title in 2023.He has been unable to replicate his early promise, however, and has not run the 100m faster than 10.39sec since 2023.Queensland police said investigations continue.Doran has been contacted for comment.In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800; adult survivors can seek help atBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. In the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helpline InternationalExplore more on these topicsAthleticsAustralia sportQueenslandChild protectionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It doesn’t look good’: Arteta concerned as Saka limps off against Bayern Munich | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: ‘A player off with really sharp pain is never good news,’ the Arsenal manager said after his winger was forced off 10 minutes into the 2-2 draw in Munich
Author: David Hytner
Headline: ‘A player off with really sharp pain is never good news,’ the Arsenal manager said after his winger was forced off 10 minutes into the 2-2 draw in Munich
Content: Bukayo Saka was able to walk off the pitch unaided, but his injury has his manager and medical staff worried.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersView image in fullscreenBukayo Saka was able to walk off the pitch unaided, but his injury has his manager and medical staff worried.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersArsenal‘It doesn’t look good’: Arteta concerned as Saka limps off against Bayern Munich‘A player off with really sharp pain is never good news’Winger forced off 10 minutes into Arsenal’s 2-2 drawDavid Hytnerat the Allianz ArenaWed 21 Oct 2026 18.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta made no attempt to conceal his concern over the quad injury that forced Bukayo Saka out of Arsenal’s 2-2 Champions Leaguedraw at Bayern Munich, saying it did not “look good at all”.The manager was delighted with the fight that his players showed, Declan Rice earning a deserved point with an 82nd-minute equaliser.Arsenalhad led through Eberechi Eze, who came on in the 10th minute for the stricken Saka, before Harry Kane took centre stage. The Bayern striker set up Alphonso Davies for 1-1 before giving his team the lead from the penalty spot.Arsenal’s Declan Rice strikes late to deny Bayern Munich after Harry Kane penaltyRead moreIt was Saka’s setback that provided the sour note for Arsenal. He collapsed to the turf after a routine battle with Davies and walked off slowly after treatment. Saka was still moving in a very limited way as he left the stadium.“It doesn’t look good at all but we have to wait and see,” Arteta said. “They [the medics] are a bit concerned. A player who has to come off with a really sharp pain is never good news. Bukayo did not startthe game against Lillelast Tuesday, then he started at Nottingham Forest on Sunday and it happened very early in this game. The level of intensity that this game requires, as well, is something incredible.“You could see it on Tuesday night,the PSG-Barcelona game, what happened [with playersgetting injured]. This is man-to-man for 96 minutes in every action. There’s no breathing. The stress, the quality, the intensity, the level that you need … it’s unbelievable. It’s the highest level. And those things happen, unfortunately.”Arteta insisted that he wanted more than the draw. “We take it, although that doesn’t mean we are really happy about it as we prepared to win,” he said. “You could see that right from the beginning – the mindset, the purpose and the intention that the team has, to be very dominant, to come here and cause problems to Bayern. To press them and attack them. That’s certainly what we’ve done. We were the better team in the first 25 minutes, we got the goal … unfortunately we also got the injury of Bukayo, which was a big setback.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The team showed incredible composure, the spirit to keep going, to attack them. The finishers came in and made an impact, as well. After scoring the goal [for 2-2], you see the reaction of the team. We wanted to take the ball and go and attack them again to come and win the game.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetaBayern MunichnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jimmy Anderson set to retire from cricket as Lancashire opt against renewing contract | Jimmy Anderson | The Guardian
description: Jimmy Anderson is expected to call time on his remarkable career at the age of 44 after being told his contract at Lancashire will not be renewed
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Jimmy Anderson is expected to call time on his remarkable career at the age of 44 after being told his contract at Lancashire will not be renewed
Content: Jimmy Anderson claimed 50 wickets in just 11 county matches at an average of 17.68 as the Red Rose finished second bottom of Division Two.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJimmy Anderson claimed 50 wickets in just 11 county matches at an average of 17.68 as the Red Rose finished second bottom of Division Two.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesJimmy AndersonJimmy Anderson set to retire from cricket as Lancashire opt against renewing contractEngland bowler may have played last game at age 44Lancashire tell Anderson he does not fit their plansAli MartinWed 21 Oct 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJimmy Anderson is expected to call time on his remarkable career at the age of 44 after being told his contract at Lancashire will not be renewed for next season.A change of direction is under way at Old Trafford after the club finished second-bottom of Division Two in the County Championship this year and failed to get out of the group stages in both men’s white-ball competitions.The Spin | Writing a book with Chris Woakes showed the inner steel of the nicest man in cricketRead moreRichard Kenyon has since arrived from Nottinghamshire as Lancashire’s new chief executive and hired Paul Farbrace from Sussex as director of cricket. While Farbrace does not start officially until next month, the pair informed Anderson on Monday that he does not feature in their plans, as first reported by the Times.Anderson had been on season-by-season contracts with his boyhood club following his retirement from England duty in 2024, and he captained the first team in their most recent campaign. He combined this with 50 wickets at a princely average of 17, even if it could not prevent the club’s lowest finish in the two-division era.Unless an overseas deal follows this winter, or a hopeful county comes calling, it appears Anderson has played his final game of professional cricket. If so, then he will finish with 1,193 first-class wickets, and more than 400 in limited-over matches, to go with the knighthood he was awarded 12 months ago for services to the sport.View image in fullscreenJimmy Anderson poses for a portrait in the Old Trafford changing rooms in 2021.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianReports at the end of the season suggested Anderson was unlikely to remain as Lancashire captain but there were also indications that he wished to play on. This was only ever going to hinge on the new leadership’s view, however, after Daniel Gidney stood down as chief executive and Mark Chilton lost his job as director of cricket.The call has now been made by Chilton’s successor, Farbrace, who was head-hunted to revive the ailing county. Farbrace, a former England assistant coach, had been poised to remain at Sussex on a part-time basis – a new arrangement triggered by their financial difficulties – only to be swayed by the lure of a Test county.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor all that Anderson has raged against his advancing years, the decision is a bold one that has put sentiment to one side. A product of Burnley cricket club, and having made his first-team debut for Red Rose in 2001, there will doubtless be a large section of the membership who would have wanted one more season.The same went for a significant number of England supporters two years ago when Anderson was ushered into retirement by Rob Key, Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes. With 704 Test dismissals he finished as England’s record wicket-taker and the third highest in history overall – even if he personally remained unsated.Explore more on these topicsJimmy AndersonLancashireCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maro Itoje seals England future by agreeing new deal with Saracens  | Maro Itoje | The Guardian
description: Maro Itoje has reaffirmed his long-term commitment to England, rejecting interest from France by agreeing to a new deal with Saracens
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Maro Itoje has reaffirmed his long-term commitment to England, rejecting interest from France by agreeing to a new deal with Saracens
Content: England’s Maro Itoje was rested for England’s summer Tests against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina after showing signs of fatigue.Photograph: Ashley Western/Colorsport/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEngland’s Maro Itoje was rested for England’s summer Tests against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina after showing signs of fatigue.Photograph: Ashley Western/Colorsport/ShutterstockMaro ItojeMaro Itoje seals England future by agreeing new deal with SaracensCaptain will resist lure of big-money move to France‘Maro is everything we want at the club – a brilliant leader’Gerard MeagherWed 21 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaro Itoje has reaffirmed his long‑term commitment to England, rejecting interest from France by agreeing a new deal with Saracens.Itoje’s existing deal, signed in 2024, was due to expire after the World Cup next year but he has agreed terms with his club despite interest from Top 14 sides. A move to either Perpignan or Bordeaux had been mooted but the 31-year-old is to commit his future to the club he first represented in 2013 with a new deal, believed to be until 2029.No sour grapes: Venter on vintage form as he lays out Saracens visionRead moreThe extension is a significant boost forSaracens, who are in a period of transition with Brendan Venter at the helm for a second time and will enable Itoje, who has 102 caps, to continue his international career. It remains to be seen whether Steve Borthwick will still be in charge of the England side but either the national head coach or his successor is to benefit.“He is staying,” Venter said of Itoje. “He has agreed with the owner. It’s brilliant of Maro, Maro is everything we want at the club. He’s an unbelievable human being, he’s a brilliant leader, he’s such a good rugby player, I’m so glad the owner and him could agree terms.”Itoje was rested for England’s summer Tests against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina after showing signs of fatigue throughout the season on the back of several gruelling campaigns. He has made more Test appearances than any other player in the world game since his international debut in 2016 andrevealed last month that this summer he had enjoyed his first full pre‑seasonwith Saracens since 2014.“He’s always got energy so Maro’s been so good in the pre-season for us,” Venter said. “We’re lucky because Maro is always developing.”Itoje has been linked with a move to France before and was said to have explored the option of going to the Top 14 on loan when Saracens were relegated in 2020. Such a severe workload in recent seasons added to the speculation that he may seek a lucrative move across the Channel.He was also linked with the mooted R360 breakaway league but said at the time that “playing for England is the mecca”. Itoje was among the first tranche of players to receive an enhanced England contract worth £150,000 in 2024 and has since stayed in the selected group. It is understood, however, that none of the existing deals go beyond the World Cup in Australia next year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, the Lions lock Hyron Andrews’s death was caused by an aortic dissection, a tear in the body’s main artery, the South African rugby team have said. The former Sale player died at the team hotel last Friday, a day before the Lions played the French side La Rochelle in the European Champions Cup, a game that went ahead in honour of the 31-year-old. French media reported that Andrews was found unconscious in a shower cubicle at a hotel on the Île de Ré in France, where the team had been staying.Explore more on these topicsMaro ItojeSaracensEngland rugby union teamRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in? | Movies | The Guardian
description: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?
Content: Radical transparency? … Elizabeth Holmes with Nathan Fielder in the background in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24View image in fullscreenRadical transparency? … Elizabeth Holmes with Nathan Fielder in the background in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24Movies‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in?With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?Henry RobertsWed 21 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInYou Can See Everything, convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invites film-makers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into her home in a supposed act of “radical transparency”. Holmes is filmed, along with her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children, in the weeks before starting a prison sentence for defrauding Theranos investors. “The best way for people to see who she is,” Evans says, “is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”. It may also be the best way to market “Theranos 2.0”, which the couple are working on during filming. But the documentary questions whether Holmes is presenting her authentic self or a manufactured persona. Fielder speaks for the audience when he asks Holmes in a tense exchange whether she’s “being real” with him. “I’m always being real,” she says.That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew?You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreSome people, like Holmes, think a documentary will help rebuild their reputation after public disgrace. When Anthony Weiner, who resigned from Congress after tweeting a photo of his bulging groin, tried to stage a professional comeback with a New York mayoral bid, he allowed cameras to film the journey. Only, he had more to hide: when further sex scandals emerged, his campaign went from a story of public redemption to innuendo-laden humiliation. And all the while, the cameras kept rolling.Weineris a prime example of a subject losing control of the narrative.View image in fullscreenHumiliation … Launching a New York mayoral bid, Anthony Weiner, with wife Huma Abedin, 23 July 2013.Photograph: Kathy Willens/APWeiner may have wanted a sympathetic portrayal, but he should have known that film-makers always have their own agendas. In the book The Journalist and the Murderer,Janet Malcolmreflects on the relationship between journalists and their subjects: “The subject becomes a kind of child of the writer, regarding him as a permissive, all-accepting, all-forgiving mother, and expecting the book to be written by her. Of course, the book is written by the strict, all-noticing, unforgiving father.” The same is surely true of the documentarian.When Jackie and David Siegel allowed Lauren Greenfield to film their attempt to build a modern-day Versailles in Florida, the director wasn’t giving them free PR. Rather, withThe Queen of Versailles, Greenfield was interested in the corrosive effects of extreme wealth. The Siegels agreed to be filmed because they were proud of their success. When their dream collapsed following the 2008 financial crash, The Queen of Versailles turned from a story of Xanadu-like grandeur to one of hubristic overreach. David later sued Lauren – unsuccessfully – for defamation, but he should have known from the beginning: it may have been his story, but it was never his film.A few years after Versailles, Greenfield madeThe Kingmaker, about former first lady of the Philippines Imelda Marcos and her attempt to return the family to power. From the beginning of the film,Greenfield said, there was a power struggle over who was telling the story. Marcos, known for her lavish lifestyle during her husband’s brutal rule, understood the power of optics. In a children’s cancer ward, she hands out money to children in a public display of compassion. “Perception is real,” Marcos says in the film, “and the truth is not.”Some people agree to projects believing they will have editorial control. Idi Amin gave Barbet Schroeder unprecedented access after the director essentially promised that they would make the film together. But Amin was unhappy with General Idi Amin Dada: A Self Portrait and demanded some footage be cut, rounding up more than 100 French residents in Uganda and holding them hostage until his demands were met. Schroeder agreed. It helps to be as ruthless as Amin if you want final cut.Documentaries are often about the past, but some of cinema’s most memorable moments show people acting violently in the present, fully aware that they are being filmed.Frederick Wiseman’s austere filmsshow abuse in psychiatric institutions (Titicut Follies) and horrific police violence (Law and Order). Why did people do unspeakable things in front of a camera? “People basically go about their business,”Wiseman told an interviewer, “and the presence of the camera doesn’t have much, if any effect on their behaviour.”View image in fullscreenMorally complex … a scene from The Act Of Killing, 2012.Photograph: Real/Novaya Ze/Rex/ShutterstockBut cameras did have an effect on the subjects ofJoshua Oppenheimer’s The Act of Killing, probably the most morally complex example of the film-maker-subject relationship in cinema history. Perpetrators of Indonesia’s mass killings gleefully re-enact their crimes, restaging their violent memories in the style of Hollywood movies. They do not profess their innocence. Rather, they agree to be filmed because they are proud of what they did. They really do want us to see everything.UK cinemas report ‘bonkers’ demand for documentary You Can See EverythingRead morePerhaps the most interesting case of someone willingly putting themselves under scrutiny is Lance Armstrong.Alex Gibney’s documentary on Armstrongwas expected to be a puff piece. When the full extent of Armstrong’s doping was revealed, however, Gibney’s film changed direction, becoming a documentary not on a cyclist’s triumph but on a master manipulator who lied to everyone, including the film-maker. In The Armstrong Lie, Armstrong admits that he “was prepared to say anything” to keep his lie going.Some people are simply arrogant enough to think they can get away with their lies. But others become so invested in their skewed version of reality that to refuse a documentary crew would be like admitting their deception. So they welcome the cameras, often doing more damage than if they had simply retreated from public view. But unlike Armstrong, Holmes still insists she has done nothing wrong. As she says in You Can See Everything: “I have nothing to hide.”Explore more on these topicsFilmYou Can See EverythingElizabeth HolmesNathan FielderLance ArmstrongTheranosAnthony WeinerfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK watchdogs urged to tackle suicide social media content after death of girl, 14 | Internet safety | The Guardian
description: Adriana Retyte took her own life after viewing ‘high-risk’ material on the video-sharing platform TikTok
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Adriana Retyte took her own life after viewing ‘high-risk’ material on the video-sharing platform TikTok
Content: The head of online regulator Ofcom said there was no trust that the platforms could ‘clean up their own services’.Photograph: The Good Brigade/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe head of online regulator Ofcom said there was no trust that the platforms could ‘clean up their own services’.Photograph: The Good Brigade/Getty ImagesInternet safetyUK watchdogs urged to tackle suicide social media content after death of girl, 14Adriana Retyte took her own life after viewing ‘high-risk’ material on the video-sharing platform TikTokRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 21 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 04.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 14-year-old schoolgirl’s death after TikTok served her suicide content has prompted renewed calls for UK watchdogs to crack down on “toxic” social media feeds.Adriana Retyte, a pupil at Langley school in Norfolk, took her own life after she viewed videos and images related to suicide on the video-sharing platform, according to a coroner who last week found her access to the material on TikTok “may have played a significant part in her decision to take her life”.An inquest heard the teenager’s death had “a devastating effect on those close to her” and that her devices revealed she had “viewed a number of videos and images related to suicide on TikTok in the week preceding her death”.“It seems that Adriana’s access to this material may have played a significant part in her decision to take her life that evening,” the Norfolk area coroner, Johanna Thompson, said.Asked to respond, TikTok said its “deepest sympathies are with the family at this incredibly difficult time”. It said it enforces “strict rules against any content that promotes self-harm” and uses advanced technologies to proactively detect and remove content that violates its community guidelines. It is understood it had not yet investigated what happened with Adriana’s account.The case came as Melanie Dawes, the chief executive of the regulator Ofcom, told MPs: “We do not see a safety culture from these large social media companies … they are very slow to acknowledge that there are risks of criminal action, child grooming and also some of these issues of the way the algorithms feed suicide and self-harm material.” She added that “trust they can clean up their own services is simply not there”.The coroner added there was “no way of knowing” why Adriana acted as she did, but said it was clear that she may have been influenced by “the negative effects of her having viewed online content”. She is working on a prevention of future deaths report that will be circulated to bodies including Ofcom, which in June launched a separate investigation into whether TikTok was failing to comply with its legal obligations to protect children from harmful content.Adriana’s death came nine years after another 14-year-old, Molly Russell, took her own life after being served suicide and self-harm content on social media, including Instagram. A charity set up in her name, which campaigns for safer social media, called Adriana’s death “devastating”. The Molly Rose Foundation (MRF) is now calling on Ofcom to launch an investigation into TikTok’s algorithm, accusing the regulator of seeming to be “unwilling or unable to act on this deadly harm”.Andy Burrows, the chief executive of the MRF, said: “The three-quarters of teens who are still seeing high-risk suicide, self-harm and depression content saw it on TikTok. The case for action is clear, it just needs the will to take on big tech. Ofcom must now open an investigation into TikTok’s algorithm that is driving harmful content without delay. Anything less is a dereliction of the duty of a regulator.”Asummer 2026 surveyby the MRF of 1,825 children from 21 UK schools found that one in three were exposed to high-risk suicide, self-harm, depression or eating disorder content on major social media platforms in the week before they were surveyed. It also found that 7% had seen content that made suicidal thoughts “seem normal, appealing, or cool”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionConcerns about Adriana’s wellbeing were first raised on 31 December 2025, when a monitoring system on her school-issued tablet alerted staff to a search related to a method of death. This was followed up with the pupil and her mother, after which the use of the tablet returned to normal homework activity. Adriana denied making the searches, Caroline Pain, the school’s director of marketing, communications and admissions, told the inquest.Some minor issues with lateness and uniform breaches followed. Adriana was at school on 8 May when she was in classes and playing football. She was said to be behaving normally at home. But that evening she was found by her mother and stepfather having attempted to take her life. She died two days later after attempts to resuscitate her and an airlift to Addenbrooke’s hospital in Cambridge.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counsellor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsInternet safetySocial mediaTikTokOfcomChild protectionTechnology policyChildrennewsShareReuse this content

title: New prize launches for books co-written with AI | Books | The Guardian
description: After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs
Content: Once upon a time … the prize was founded by tech entrepreneurs.Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOnce upon a time … the prize was founded by tech entrepreneurs.Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty ImagesBooksNew prize launches for books co-written with AIAfter months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMsElla CreamerWed 21 Oct 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA prize for AI-written books has launched this week.The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA invites submissions of manuscripts co-written with AI tools, with the winner promised publication.Entrants are asked to submit an unpublished manuscript of between 10,000 and 50,000 words, along with information about which AI model and prompt were used to generate the text. All major language models are allowed, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA. Entrants can be based anywhere, but entries must be submitted in French.The Prix Pascal is named after Blaise Pascal, a French polymath who helped invent one of the first mechanical calculators and also wrote theological texts, including Pensées, which Pope Francispraised forits “philosophical depth and literary charm”.While the terms and conditions ask for a work of fiction, the prize also states that submitted texts should help solve an ethical, social or ecological problem threatening humanity. The prize was founded by Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré, all of whom are technology entrepreneurs.Rodriguez is a founding partner at the mergers and acquisitions advisory firm Avolta, and is described as a “leading figure in the European crypto and blockchain industry” on the company’s website. Serviant is a digital media entrepreneur and former chair of the LGBTQ+ magazine Têtu. Meanwhile, Mentré is a former civil servant with a PhD in philosophy who teaches at Harvard and the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Mentré also co-founded Electis, an online voting platform.The Prix Pascal is launching after months of controversy over the possible use of AI by finalists and winners for a number of literary prizes this year, including theCommonwealth short story prize, theCaine prizeand thePrix Goncourt, France’s most prestigious literary prize.Applications for the Prix Pascal opened on Tuesday, with entrants invited to submit via theprize’s website, and are set to close at the end of November. A shortlist of 10 will be drawn up before the winner is announced in early December. The jury will be made up of a panel of five or six writers, critics, journalists, philosophers and publishers, to be announced early November.Explore more on these topicsBooksAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingAwards and prizesFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A difficult line’: meet the editors tackling Wikipedia’s arms trade pages  | Wikipedia | The Guardian
description: Volunteers and new recruits come together for ‘wikithon’ to put more detail about industry into public domain
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Volunteers and new recruits come together for ‘wikithon’ to put more detail about industry into public domain
Content: Agnes Cameron: ‘This is not an anti-arms industry campaigning event.’Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAgnes Cameron: ‘This is not an anti-arms industry campaigning event.’Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianWikipedia‘A difficult line’: meet the editors tackling Wikipedia’s arms trade pagesVolunteers and new recruits come together for ‘wikithon’ to put more detail about industry into public domainGeorge Francis LeeWed 21 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Anyone can editWikipedia,” the adage goes. But, it turns out, a relatively small number actually do.What is worthy of a digital page in the world’s largest and most-read encyclopedia is decided by roughly 270,000 active volunteers, enthusiasts who populate the online resource with information on anything from 19th-century medicine to TikTok trends. Inevitably, some subjects are sidelined – the global south,notable women– but a new batch of Wikipedian recruits are waging war on one neglected topic: the arms industry.Last week, in a classroom in central London, two dozen volunteers huddled around laptops and free servings of vegan Ethiopian food for what is known as a “wikithon”, an event of collective and in-person Wikipedia editing. Some were veteran editors in their 70s, others young students who had never registered an account before. But their targets include subjects such as Palantir, Project Maven and Nitro-Chem.“Wikipedia pages about the arms industry, in general, are not always super-detailed,” said the group’s co-founder Agnes Cameron. The intention of the wikithon, started by fellows fromthe n-Space programmeat Somerset House Studios, was “to put better quality and more well organised information on the arms industry in the public domain”, the specialist technician said.View image in fullscreenA new batch of Wikipedian recruits were trained in how to edit a page.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianAttenders at the monthly event are trained in how to add to the internet’s most popular reference site. But while editing Wikipedia is surprisingly simple – just a few clicks to publish a change – ethical complications quickly bubble up.“The interesting thing about Wikipedia editing is that you’re encouraged to edit things you care about,” Cameron said. “What it looks like to have a conflict of interest is an interesting question.”Although Cameron enjoys editing pages about food in her spare time, her interests are also political. “We’re toeing quite a difficult line,” she said. “Difficult lines are important to toe.”Despite personal and political reasons for wanting to spread information on arms manufacturers and sellers, finding journalistic balance means using Wikipedia in good faith. Cameron said attenders’ chosen subject matter meant that it was “really important” that they followed Wikipedia’s standards to the letter. “This is not an anti-arms industry campaigning event. This is an event really about factual information on Wikipedia,” she said.View image in fullscreenThe main goal was to pull together publicly available information into one place.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianWhen it comes to information, Wikipedia’s rules demand that no original research is included on its pages and conclusions are not drawn. The main goal of the arms industry wikithon, then, was to pull together publicly available information from other sources into one place.Wikipedia has been repeatedly criticised for its lack of diversity in editors and its coverage. It has been accused of geographical bias towards the west, with most articles focused on the US and western Europe. Similarly, just 19% of the site’s biography entries are for women. In 2018, the female Nobel prize winner Donna Strickland, a physicist, was deemed“not important enough”for a Wikipedia entry.With a wider range of ages, genders and racial backgrounds at the wikithon, the trainee editors were helping to rebalance the scale, said Hannah Cobb, a co-founder of the event. “There’s a very specific idea of who edits Wikipedia … that doesn’t tend to be the demographic of who shows up,” she said. “There’s a really broad interest in Wikipedia in general. Everyone remembers that at school you were taught not to trust it because anyone could write it.”View image in fullscreenThe experience of editing a Wikipedia page can be ‘quite empowering’, said Hannah Cobb, a co-founder of the event.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianPrevious arms industry wikithons organised by Cameron and Cobb in Manchester andLondonhave drawn in more than 60 would-be Wikipedians at a time, including activists, journalists, Quaker members – and even Cameron’s own mother.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNewcomers to the group were interested in how Wikipedia could be used to broaden public knowledge of confusing geopolitics, said Cobb. “There is a sense of powerlessness when it comes to countering the narrative by big tech, by governments, by the military industrial complex at large,” she said.But for the arms industry page editors, those feelings can disappear over a few hours: “When you write something on Wikipedia, it appears immediately on the internet. I think that experience alone is quite empowering for people.”Cobb spoke of a sense of wonder “when people realise how easy it is to actually contribute”, but attenders have a respect for Wikipedia’s commitment to rigour and quality control. And though dedicated to accuracy, the group prefers to not advertise the details of its edits over concerns that the work could be undone by other editors in bad faith.Cameron said it was unclear if Wikipedia’s wider editorial culture would take offence over how the event was run. While wikithons are not new, the blurry line between activism and accurate dissemination of information stress-tests the platform’s rules.View image in fullscreenAnother wikithon session will be held later this winter.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianReal-world politics often spill on to Wikipedia, and editors often disagree publicly about changes. The site has also been covertly used as an informational battleground. The seasoned editor Ksenia Coffmanmade extensive editsto remove what she found to be flattering and sympathetic entries about Nazi party officials across Wikipedia, and in 2021, the Croatian-language version of Wikipedia was found to have been commandeered by nationalist, far-right organiserswho made ideologically motivated edits.Cameron hopes that the regular meetings can be formalised into a WikiProject, when organised groups of editors collaborate to improve certain topic pages. She hoped her group could be given advice by WikiProject Military history, which she called “far and away the most active project on Wikipedia by miles. It’s amazingly well run.”The London wikithon is to continue for another session in the winter, and Cameron and Cobb’s faith in encyclopedia editing as a political tool is steadfast. As Cameron said: “Wikipedia is fundamentally anti-fascist.”Explore more on these topicsWikipediaDigital mediaInternetLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content
