title: The best Kindles in the UK for every bookworm and budget – tested | Kindle | The Guardian
description: Whether you want a colour screen, somewhere to scribble notes or a child-friendly model, here’s what we recommend from Amazon’s e-reader range
Author: Andrew Williams
Headline: Whether you want a colour screen, somewhere to scribble notes or a child-friendly model, here’s what we recommend from Amazon’s e-reader range
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterKindleReviewThe best Kindles in the UK for every bookworm and budget – testedWhether you want a colour screen, somewhere to scribble notes or a child-friendly model, here’s what we recommend from Amazon’s e-reader rangeThe best e-readersAndrew WilliamsWed 21 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom that fresh paperback smell to the wrinkles in the spine, nothing beats a real book. But if you’re sick of the space they take up in your home, or the weight they steal from your holiday luggage allowance, it might be worth considering an AmazonKindle. It can fit thousands of weighty reads into as little as 158g, and as tech goes, it’s almost immune to the sort of pathological time-wasting features that come with modern phones and tablets.Amazon Kindles have been available in the UK for more than 15 years, so they’re an old-school gadget at this point. But in 2024, the biggest update yet arrived: colour, which added an important extra option to the existing Kindle lineup, alongside readers for children, for note-taking and for tighter budgets.With so many modern versions available now, I spent months testing them to analyse their pros and cons to help you find the best Kindle for your needs.A note on Kindle’s next generationAmazon clearly has a sense of humour, because no less than one day after I’d finished writing this guide the brand announced a whole new range of Kindles. I will keep this page updated with how the new line compares once I have fully tested them.Available to preorder ahead of their release on 11 November, theKindle PaperwhiteandColorsoftwill be a little lighter and thinner than their predecessors, with a fetching new array of colours.More significant changes have been made to the Signature Edition models, trading plastic backing for an aluminium one. But it’s the basic Kindle that’ll get the biggest upgrade, with the raised screen border replaced for a flat end-to-end design like the Paperwhite. There are Kids editions of thesee-readerscoming, too.The good news about fresh launches is that the models tested here are far more likely to be slashed in price, so you could save some money.At a glanceBest Kindle overallKindlePaperwhite (2024)£184.99 at AmazonBest budget KindleAmazonKindle (2024)£134.99 at ArgosBest Kindle for kidsKindleColorsoft Kids£274.99 at John LewisBest Kindle for note-takingKindleScribe Colorsoft£569 at AmazonBest budget Kindle for kidsKindleKids£159.99 at John LewisBest colour KindleKindleColorsoft (2024)£239.99 at AmazonWhy you should trust meI’m a long-term e-reader user; I first tried one in place of paperbacks in 2009, the Sony PRS-505, a year before the first Kindle arrived in the UK. Since then I have tested almost every member of the Kindle family going. From theKindle Fire HD(which some say never deserved the Kindle name at all because it’s more tablet than e-reader) to fondly remembered classics such as the Kindle Voyage and Oasis, I’ve lived with them all, for better and worse. I keep coming back to Kindles over other e-readers for their simplicity and reliability – and for Amazon’s ever-changing Kindle book sales.Most of my book reading is done on e-readers these days. Light, portable and ideal for bedtime reading, e-readers are among my favourite pieces of tech – even if nothing can quite replace the nostalgic charm of a real paperback.How I testedView image in fullscreenWell read: some of the Kindles were tested for about six months.Photograph: Andrew Williams/The GuardianTo test a Kindle, you need to live with one for a while. Many keep ebook readers for a decade or more – they can be remarkably long-lasting – so a cursory test wasn’t going to cut it.While I’ve tried each of these devices as my personal e-reader for several weeks (at the very least), I’ve used the key Colorsoft and Paperwhite readers for about six months, on and off. And for the Kindles designed to offer more than just reading, such as the Kindle Scribe, I wrapped them into my day-to-day routine, using the Scribe (for example) in place of a paper to-do list.Unlike a tablet, raw power is not important in e-readers. Page-turn speed does matter, but is now good across the whole Kindle lineup. What matters more is how comfortable the screen is to read from, how comfortable the e-reader is to hold, and of course how well it slots into your day-to-day life.Any remaining devices from this Kindle group test will be donated to Cancer Research UK.The best Kindles in 2026View image in fullscreen‘Still Amazon’s best e-reader’: the Kindle Paperwhite.Photograph: Andrew Williams/The GuardianBest Kindle overall:Kindle Paperwhite (2024)KindlePaperwhite (2024)from£184.99£184.99 at John Lewis£184.99 at AmazonWhat we loveThe reading experience and practicality are hard to beatWhat we don’t loveSo familiar that it’s a bit boring in 2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£184.99 at John Lewis£184.99 at AmazonTo my mind, Amazon’s best Kindle e-reader is still the Paperwhite. It has been around since 2012, and has been slowly, gradually and conservatively tweaked since. You can’t mess with perfection all that much, apparently.This best overall ranking is based on one key assumption: above all else, you want to use your Kindle to read novels.Why we love itAmazon’s 2024 Paperwhite has a 7in screen, which is fractionally bigger than the previous version. It’s exceptionally clear and clean-looking, with a whiter, less fuzzy-looking page background than the Colorsoft, which makes it easier to read outdoors in direct sunlight.This is one of the highest-contrast screens you’ll find in the e-reader kingdom, which is pretty important when one of the original selling points of e-readers was lower eye strain. A Paperwhite makes an hour with Agatha Christie feel like moisturising your eyeballs, relatively speaking.This is also as close as you get to a take-anywhere e-reader. It has excellent water resistance and weighs only 211g. For frequent getaway travellers, it could pay for itself purely in Ryanair’s oversized baggage fees.How waterproof is it? The official line is the IPX8 design can handle “2 metres of fresh water for up to 60 minutes and 0.25 metres for 3 minutes in seawater”. I haven’t dropped it in the sea, but may have dropped the Paperwhite in the bath a few times without incident.Its ergonomics are simple but excellent – one-handed reading is a joy – and while the interface hasn’t changed all that much in years, it’s easy to understand.It’s a shame that …there’s no pen stylus support for note-taking, or speaker for audiobooks. It’s all unnecessary fluff if you’re here for reading, and you can stream audiobooks to headphones or a speaker over Bluetooth,but it is worth noting.The real reader’s conundrum: how much of a turn-off is it that you can’t borrow books from UK libraries? It’s on offer in Kobo and PocketBook models, but not here, or on any of Amazon’s Kindle line.A Paperwhite could have also been the perfect vehicle for two features it lacks: page-turn buttons and a textured glass screen.Buttons let you move your hands even less when turning the page, and glass is much harder than the plastic screen on the Paperwhite and therefore less susceptible to scratching. And while glass could add to the weight, the older glass-screened Kindles – the Voyage and Oasis – were actually lighter than this Paperwhite, at 180-188g.Display:7in monochrome E InkStorage size:16/32GB (Signature Edition)Dimensions:127.5 x 7.8 x 176.7mm (WDH)Weight:211gKindlePaperwhite (2024)from£184.99£184.99 at John Lewis£184.99 at AmazonWhat we loveThe reading experience and practicality are hard to beatWhat we don’t loveSo familiar that it’s a bit boring in 2026Best budget Kindle:Kindle (2024)AmazonKindle (2024)from£134.99£134.99 at Argos£134.99 at AmazonWhat we lovePocketable, affordable and lightWhat we don’t loveNot slick-looking or – more importantly – water resistantView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£134.99 at Argos£134.99 at AmazonThis is Amazon’s smaller, humbler, more affordable Kindle, but it is still an excellent e-reader. In fact, for reading, the basic Kindle beats some more expensive models in some important display quality features.It has a 6in display rather than the Paperwhite’s 7in; the screen has a raised bezel rather than a flush front; and the light doesn’t have adjustable warmth, just intensity.Why we love itThe basic Kindle is near-unbeatable as an e-reader that’s large enough to act as your sole reading device, yet small enough to fit in a surprising array of pockets (especially now that skinny jeans have more or less been exiled to fashion’s Room 101).It also needs less careful treatment than some other Kindles. Its raised border means you can place it face down on a table without worrying as much about sand or grit scratching the screen. While e-reader screens are fairly resilient, they’re not immune to surface scratches.I found that contrast, text clarity and overall punchiness of the screen are on the same level as the Kindle Paperwhite, too. In testing, it was clear as anything, day or night, thanks to the front light.It’s a shame that …the Paperwhite is not a glamorous piece of tech, but it does offer some advantages over this more basic model. The Kindle’s raised bezel casts a shadow on the screen in some light conditions that may annoy some – although I can almost guarantee you’ll get used to it.There are two obvious practical concessions to consider, too. No water resistance means caution is required at bath time, and a smaller screen also means more page turns unless you can make do with smaller text. The larger you like (or need) your text, the more this stands out. For bedtime, a larger screen can be more comfortable in the weight-to-page-turn ratio.Display:6in monochrome E InkStorage size:16GBDimensions:108.6 x 8 x 157.8mm (WDH)Weight:158gAmazonKindle (2024)from£134.99£134.99 at Argos£134.99 at AmazonWhat we lovePocketable, affordable and lightWhat we don’t loveNot slick-looking or – more importantly – water resistantBest Kindle for kids:Kindle Colorsoft KidsKindleColorsoft Kidsfrom£274.99£274.99 at John Lewis£274.99 at CurrysWhat we loveIt’s an educational tool with just enough of a fun edgeWhat we don’t loveNot cheap, and colour is a little mutedView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£274.99 at John Lewis£274.99 at CurrysSome will say the ideal Kindle for kids is the cheapest one. But parents are in a war for reading v TikTok, YouTube and God knows what else. A Kindle Colorsoft Kids is arguably the most benign screen going.This is actually the same hardware as the standard Kindle Colorsoft, bundled with a loud and colourful case and a slightly different two-year warranty. That means it can grow with them – or you can co-opt the reader yourself if your child loses interest.Why we love itMany will have memories of rifling through books to find the illustrations as a child, or picking a book solely on the merits of its cover. A Kindle Colorsoft Kids retains more of that charm than the monochrome alternative thanks to its colour screen and vibrant case.A 12-month Amazon Kids+ subscription is included with the Kindle Colorsoft Kids, helping you make the most of that too. After the first year, it costs £7.99 a month (or £6.99 if you’re a Prime member) and grants access to loads of child-friendly content, including games and apps as well as books. Parents of comic book obsessives will probably have to pay for some of that content separately because the Kids+ library is mostly limited to primary-school-age-appropriate content, whileKindle Unlimited(£9.49 a month) includes lots of Batman and Spider-Man graphic novels for slightly older kids.The water resistance and all-round ruggedness of this e-reader pair well with Amazon’s“worry-free” warranty – “if it breaks, we’ll replace it,” to use Amazon’s own wording. While the warranty does come with caveats, it still offers some peace of mind.It’s a shame that …children aren’t always the best at managing their expectations, and some may be disappointed with the Colorsoft Kids as a result. Its colour is muted, which is all the more obvious if they also have access to a tablet or smartphone.A screen this size is also not ideal for comics and graphic novels, as it’s much smaller than they were designed to be read. It’s best described as a gadget for novels that can also handle other content.Display:7in colour E InkStorage size:16GBDimensions:132.2 x 12.7 x 178mm (WDH, including case)Weight:334g (including case)KindleColorsoft Kidsfrom£274.99£274.99 at John Lewis£274.99 at CurrysWhat we loveIt’s an educational tool with just enough of a fun edgeWhat we don’t loveNot cheap, and colour is a little mutedBest Kindle for note-taking:Kindle Scribe ColorsoftKindleScribe Colorsoftfrom£569£569.99 at John Lewis£569 at AmazonWhat we loveColour note-taking is great, and we finally get easy OCRWhat we don’t loveIt costs a small fortune considering its limitationsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£569.99 at John Lewis£569 at AmazonThink of the Scribe Colorsoft as the grownup version of my top pick for kids. It includes a stylus for highlighting text and writing notes, and you can email your notes as PDFs with or without OCR (optical character recognition), which turns your handwriting into standard text for copying and pasting into documents.Why we love itThe Scribe series is where Amazon lets more tablet influence enter the wider Kindle series design. It has a slim aluminium rear casing, which recently became an option in the Signature Editions of Amazon’s new-for-2026 models. It’s slick and super-slim at just 5.4mm thick.A Kindle display will never have the slight give of a paper notebook, but you become accustomed to scrawling on it fairly quickly. And unlike an iPad, the stylus is included rather than costing a small fortune.The screen is a stylus-friendly, smooth textured glass for a paper-like drawing and handwriting feel. But it has an end-to-end flat design, so it should be used with caution to avoid scratches.Drawing or writing with it has minimal lag, even though the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft is nowhere near as powerful as an iPad.Sticking to the style seen throughout the series, Amazon keeps things simple with the Scribe Colorsoft. You can annotate books and PDFs and create your own notebooks. Since its UK release in April 2026, it has evolved to turn handwritten text into digital text you can copy and paste without emailing it to yourself – which always felt desperately clunky to me in the Scribe’s early days.It’s a shame that …the Scribe Colorsoft is Amazon’s most expensive device in this class, and it doesn’t have any form of water resistance, unlike the more ordinary e-readers. Sure, you’re less likely to need a Scribe in the bath, but it’s a shame nevertheless.Some will also feel hemmed in by the software, which – despite Amazon’s deployment of the buzzword “AI” in the marketing – does not feel all that smart. Sketched objects beyond basic shapes can’t be cleaned up into digital object equivalents, and there’s no support for layers, which is standard stuff for graphics tablets and lets you edit elements of a piece of digital art separately.This is the other side of the Scribe series’ inviting simplicity. It could also be seen as basic or, in some areas, clunky. Given the very high cost, that may well sting.Display:11in colour E InkStorage size:32/64GBDimensions:189 x 5.4 x 245mm (WDH)Weight:400gKindleScribe Colorsoftfrom£569£569.99 at John Lewis£569 at AmazonWhat we loveColour note-taking is great, and we finally get easy OCRWhat we don’t loveIt costs a small fortune considering its limitationsBest budget Kindle for kids:Kindle KidsKindleKidsfrom£159.99£159.99 at John Lewis£159.99 at AmazonWhat we loveWorry-free guarantee provides peace of mindWhat we don’t loveThe design could and should be a bit more funView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£159.99 at John Lewis£159.99 at AmazonThe Kindle Kids deserves a nod for those shopping for a younger crowd, not least because the price of my top kids’ pick may have left a few open-mouthed.This is effectively the basic Kindle model set up as a child-friendly e-reader by default, with a better warranty and a bundled cover. For a bit extra, it’s a sound deal.Why we love itLike the Kindle Colorsoft Kids above, this model features Amazon’stwo-year“worry-free”guarantee, which assures customers “if it breaks, we’ll replace it”. Add the included sturdy flip-cover case plus six months of the up-to-£7.99-a-month Kids+ subscription, and the £25 bump from the basic Kindle seems like a steal.There’s nothing stopping you from using the Kindle Kids as an adult e-reader if your child grows out of it or gets bored either. You just switch to an adult profile.It’s a shame that …colour in the Kindle Kids design is limited to the bundled cover. The device body is black only, even though the adult Kindle comes in green too – granted, this would probably clash horribly with the cases.And while we’re at it, how about a few more case options? There are only three, and two are roughly sea themed – you can call it a “space whale”, but we’re still looking at a creature of the ocean.Display:6in monochrome E InkStorage size:16GBDimensions:114.4 x 13.6 x 158.8mm (WDH)Weight:256g (including cover)KindleKidsfrom£159.99£159.99 at John Lewis£159.99 at AmazonWhat we loveWorry-free guarantee provides peace of mindWhat we don’t loveThe design could and should be a bit more funBest colour Kindle:Kindle Colorsoft (2024)KindleColorsoft (2024)from£239.99£259.99 at Argos£239.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s what many of us have always wanted: a colour e-readerWhat we don’t loveRubber border deteriorated during testingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£259.99 at Argos£239.99 at AmazonMany long-term e-reader fans had been waiting for years for a colour Kindle when it finally arrived in the UK in 2024. At long last, we could judge books by their colour covers instead of monochrome ones. And the dream, for some, of reading comics on the go without tablet eye strain was realised – sort of.Why we love itAmazon technically gave us what many people were asking for before the Colorsoft arrived – a Paperwhite, but with a colour screen. Almost everything else remains the same.The design, weight, and in-hand feel while reading are all similar, letting Paperwhite owners transition as comfortably as possible. And even though its battery is rated a little lower – eight weeks compared with the Paperwhite’s 12 – I didn’t find the drop too obvious in testing.It’s a shame that …many people I’ve shown the Colorsoft to have been, to be blunt, disappointed. The technology here is a work in progress, and as with a lot of current-generation colour e-readers, its punch and depth are muted and gradients tend not to look all that refined.That’s because its colour is produced using a separate screen layer that ends up making the “white” of your e-reader page far more grey than a Paperwhite. That means you really need to use the display light all the time, which can impact battery life. I still found it to be a long-lasting device, however.A word of warning: I don’t recommend using a Kindle Colorsoft without a case. After six months of testing, the protective rubber border between the screen and the casing became extremely tatty.Display:7in colour E InkStorage size:16/32GBDimensions:127.6 x 7.8 x 176.7mm (WDH)Weight:16GB, 215g;32GB, 219gKindleColorsoft (2024)from£239.99£259.99 at Argos£239.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s what many of us have always wanted: a colour e-readerWhat we don’t loveRubber border deteriorated during testingThe best of the restKindle Scribe (2024)KindleScribe (2024)£279.99£279.99 at AmazonWhat we loveA savvy choice if you’re looking for a digital notebookWhat we don’t loveThe Scribe Colorsoft is a better option for most peopleView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Williams/The Guardian£279.99 at AmazonBest for:a digital notebookThis isn’t quite the Scribe Colorsoft minus the colour screen, as it has a slightly different design. Amazon’s monochrome model has a chunky thumb grip on one side in its 2024 iteration, which was binned in a2025 design refresh. At the time of writing, you can buy either model, but I tested the older variant.A premium stylus (worth £79) is included with this model, making it an all-in-one package that makes a lot of financial sense if you plan on using it as a digital notebook and aren’t too fussed about having a colourful display.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s a simple one. I felt colour may have an even bigger impact for Scribe users than Paperwhite ones. Colour only makes occasional meaningful appearances in novels. But for note-taking, PDFs and looking over presentation documents? It’s a big part of the equation. If you’re looking for a note-taking Kindle, I’d suggest the Scribe Colorsoft.That said, those not bothered about colour should obviously pick the standard Scribe as it is significantly cheaper. And it also has higher display contrast.Display:10.2in monochrome E InkStorage size:64GBDimensions:196 x 5.7 x 230mm (WDH)Weight:433gKindleScribe (2024)£279.99£279.99 at AmazonWhat we loveA savvy choice if you’re looking for a digital notebookWhat we don’t loveThe Scribe Colorsoft is a better option for most peopleWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenPaws for thought: from library books to refurbished models – what to consider when buying a Kindle.Photograph: Andrew Williams/The GuardianCan you borrow library books with a Kindle?Kindles cannot borrow ebooks from digital lending libraries in the UK.The two common digital book-borrowing services used across the UK are BorrowBox and OverDrive’s Libby. Unfortunately, Kindles don’t support either of these platforms in the UK. Kindle users in the US do, however, get to borrow books through OverDrive.To get library book loans, consider aKoboorPocketBook e-reader. Both support Libby. Head to your local library to see whether it supports such loans with a membership.What Kindle accessories are worth having?A case is highly recommended, particularly if you use a Kindle Colorsoft or Paperwhite. I learned the hard way. These e-readers have a border layer of rubbery material that sits between the rear casing and the screen. It acts as handy impact protection, but can become tatty through general wear in a few months if there’s no case to help out.Amazon’s own Kindle cases are good quality, if a little expensive, but alternatives are available. If you mostly read in bed, you may want to try one with a hand strap, which I’ve enjoyed using in the past.Does a Prime membership come with free Kindle books?An Amazon Prime membership doesn’t include Kindle Unlimited, but Prime Reading does provide access to a rotating but limited library of titles – the number of included novels tots up to a figure in the low thousands.That’s plenty to be getting on with for the casual fiction fan, but it’s going to be down to luck if a book you already want to read happens to be in there. It has never happened to me.Prime Reading is a borrowing service. You don’t have permanent access to these books once you pick them, but you can borrow up to 10 at a time for as long as you have an active Prime membership.Is Kindle Unlimited worth it?Kindle Unlimited costs £9.49 a month and includes “unlimited access” to a large number of books, audiobooks and magazines.There are a couple of limitations, though. You can borrow up to 20 titles at once, but unlike a library loan, there are no return dates. For most, this won’t be a major limitation, especially since you can just “return” one of the books if you hit the limit and want something new.The Kindle Unlimited collection doesn’t encompass the entire Kindle library either, giving access to about 4m titles. (Amazon doesn’t publish stats on how many books are in the full Kindle library, but some estimates have the figure at above 10m.) As such, if you are the kind of person who gets your heart set on reading something specific, you may find Unlimited frustrating.Happy to have a browse and pick something from a glance at its cover, summary or reader reviews? It could end up a real bargain for the voracious readers out there. You can try a month for free, and occasionally longer trials are available too. You can check over at theKindle Unlimitedlanding page.What to do with your old KindleKindles can fetch a good price secondhand on platforms such as eBay or Vinted. The main turn-off for buyers is usually scratches or damage to the screen. Alternatively, CeX accepts Kindles, although phone trade-in fave musicMagpie does not.If this sounds like too much effort, Amazon has a trade-in scheme for many sorts of Kindles – although you won’t get much for older-generation models – and you’ll get a 20% discount off a new Kindle. Digging a little deeper into the terms and conditions, your old Kindle needs to work, hold charge, be free of cracks and defects, and have no stickers or decals on the screen. Otherwise, your trade-in value will tank.How do you get a refurbished or cheap Kindle?Amazon sells refurbished Kindlesat a slight discount. And while you don’t quite get the level of promised quality that Apple’sCertified Refurbished iPadshave – including a guaranteed new casing and battery, for example – Amazon does claim a refurb should “look and work like new”.If you’d rather buy a brand-new device, it’s probably a good idea to wait for one of Amazon’s sales. Such sales periods are the best time to buy a Kindle.These are typically Black Friday in November and Prime Day in the summer, with additional sales in October and around Christmas. I’ve seen sub-£100 refurbishedKindle Paperwhitesduring these sales, representing £44 off the current refurbished price, £85 off the “new” cost.What are Kindle ads and can you remove them?When you buy most Kindles, you have the option to buy it “with ads” or without, and there’s a £10 to £15 saving if you pick the ads version. That means adverts will be displayed on the lockscreen when the e-reader is not in use.They are pretty inoffensive, as ads go, typically advertising a book – and are not shown while you are actively reading.However, you can also upgrade a Kindle with ads to ad-free software for a one-off fee whenever you like.Are Signature Editions worth it?ThePaperwhiteandColorsoftare available as Signature Edition models at a price bump.Upgrades include wireless charging, double the storage and an auto-adjusting front light. By tech standards, it’s not a pricey upgrade. However, none are all that noticeable unless you’re a real wireless-charging household.Kindle batteries last for several weeks, and getting close to running out of storage isn’t something most need to worry about. And the auto-screen-brightness feature is far less reactive than that of a phone, at times making you wonder if it’s doing anything at all.How much recycled material do Kindles use?Like several of the key tech manufacturers, Amazon likes to talk up the recycled materials used in its key products. All Kindle packaging uses 99% materials from “responsibly managed forests or recycled sources”. Here’s how the devices themselves stack up:Kindle Paperwhite (2024) – 29% recycled materials in total, internal frame is 90% recycled magnesiumKindle Colorsoft (2024) – 28% recycled materials in total, battery uses 100% recycled cobaltKindle (basic) – 75% recycled plastics, 90% recycled magnesiumScribe (2024) – 18% recycled materials in total, 100% recycled aluminiumScribe Colorsoft (2025) – 11% recycled materials in total, battery uses 100% recycled cobaltAmazon provides a sustainability data sheet for all key models on itssustainability website.For more, read thebest e-readersand the100 best novels of all timeAndrew Williams is a consumer journalist who has written about technology since before the first iPhone came out. As his flat is filled with the cardboard boxes of gadgets, he tries to get out for a run whenever possible to avoid them – often while testing a fitness tracker and a phone camera at the same timeExplore more on these topicsKindleThe FilterE-readersGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best gifts for nine-year-olds, picked by nine-year-olds and parents | Toys | The Guardian
description: Popcorn makers, Lego Fortnite and the coolest water bottle around … surprise the mini tween in your life with our pick of the top gifts and toys
Author: Zoë Phillimore
Headline: Popcorn makers, Lego Fortnite and the coolest water bottle around … surprise the mini tween in your life with our pick of the top gifts and toys
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterToysThe best gifts for nine-year-olds, picked by nine-year-olds and parentsPopcorn makers, Lego Fortnite and the coolest water bottle around … surprise the mini tween in your life with our pick of the top gifts and toysThe best gifts for eight-year-oldsZoë PhillimoreWed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe start of the tween years, nine years old, is a sweet spot between curiosity and growing independence, making it a fun, though sometimes tricky, age to buy for.Kids at this age are up for a challenge, whether that means trying a trickier craft set, playing a more complex game or stepping up their sporting interests. Pitch a gift right and you’ll not only get the whoop of joy when they first receive it, but something that will hold their interest and help them develop their skills, interests and hobbies over time.How I selectedView image in fullscreenVarious gifts and toys were sent to nine-year-olds for testing and feedback.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianAs an experienced toy tester, I have dedicated a lot of my career to observing children play. I’ve worked in schools as a teaching assistant and in children’s publishing, where knowing what makes children tick is essential. I also have three children of my own, so I understand what works on home turf once the gift-opening frenzy is over. When researching for this article, I aimed to strike a balance between children’s outlandish wishlists (one Christmas my son asked for a ghost for his present) and what a parent wants in their home (not a ghost).I spoke to a lively gang of nine-year-olds with varied interests and hobbies who were only too happy to shout over each other about what they want for Christmas. I also checked in with their parents on the gifts that got their seal of approval – and offered long-term value – and spoke to childhood play experts about the best presents to suit this stage of development.Testing primarily took place at home with one nine-year-old tester, with additional help from their friends. I also spoke to other nine-year-old children and had gifts sent to them for testing and feedback, so it wasn’t just one kid’s opinion. I noted the child’s initial reaction, how they used a toy and whether they returned to it. After testing, we had a lot of surplus toys in our house, so anything that could be donated went to the Salvation Army, which sells preloved items to raise money for its work.The best gifts and toys for nine-year-oldsOn the right trackView image in fullscreenTrain of thought: our tester found Mexican Train dominoes easy to pick up, with plenty of room for strategy.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian“I want a game called Mexican Train dominoes. I played it with my older cousins on holiday, and it was fun,” says one of my nine-year-old testers. This game was pretty fast-paced and was easy to pick up, with some strategywhen we played it. Players build their “train line” by matching tiles up to a central hub – but you can sneakily block each other’s play. “Peer-based play is really valuable for nine-year-olds,” saysLaura Moore-Williams, an early years consultant. “Children value being part of a group at this age. More advanced games, team sports and long-term creative projects give them a sense of belonging and achievement.” This set comes in its own box, making it easy to take to their mates’ houses.View image in fullscreenJaques of London Mexican train dominoes£28.72 at Jaques of London£27.99 at AmazonMaterials:resin, plastic, wood, metal tinSuitable for:6+Colourful creations“I would like some really good colouring pencils. I’m really into comics – I started a comic club with my friends. And I’m trying to get my artwork better. I think colouring pencils might help my drawings look more grown up,” says one nine-year-old tester. Whether they’re into comics or other creative projects, a decent set of colouring pencils is a great open-ended gift for kids of this age. I spent a long time sitting with my tester, colouring side by side using these pencils. My nine-year-old loved how softly they glided across the page, and how they produced smooth, even shading. The non-slip surface is comfortable to hold for extended periods; there’s a great range of colours; and they’re made from a durable wood-based composite containing upcycled wood chips from PEFC-certified forests.View image in fullscreenStaedtler 24 Norix colouring pencils£13.99 at Tesco£9.40 at AmazonMaterials:wood, oil, pigment, binder, waxSuitable for:6+A stitch in time“I really enjoyed doing this hanger project,” says one of my nine-year-old testers. “I did sewing in school on a project last year, and wanted to do more.” This little kit is an ideal party bag gift or rainy-day project to have in your back pocket for kids of this age. It’s not too prescriptive as there’s no set design, so it requires the child to work out what they want to create first. I found this called for gentle assistance when my tester tried it – although my ideas for letters or nature scenes got vetoed in favour of a Minecraft Creeper. Whether you get roped in or not, it’s a nice way to develop fine-motor skills for nine-year-olds working towards their pen licences at school.View image in fullscreenCotton Twistmake your ownstitched banner decoration£4.95 at Not on the High Street£4.95 at Cotton TwistMaterials:cotton, metal, woodSuitable for:5+Pet soundsI was stuck in a battle between my nine-year-old wanting to listen to music independently and my desire to keep them screen-free. Then I found the Mighty 3, and it has kept us both happy. It may remind some of the iPod Shuffle – it’s a tiny box you can upload music to and then whack your headphones into. My young tester has loved developing the art of playlist curation, poring over Spotify for hours with parental supervision. You then upload these playlists on to the Mighty using its app (Spotify Premium account required), and you’re ready to go. It has transformed long car journeys and even an 11-hour flight, and my tester has enjoyed the independence and grownup feeling it’s given them. It is worth noting that Mighty will stop supporting Spotify from April 2027 and only be compatible with Amazon Music.View image in fullscreenMighty 3£89.99 at Mighty£99.99 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, electronic componentsSuitable for:8+Flight of fantasy“I loveLegoand Fortnite,” says one enthusiastic nine-year-old. “This Lego is absolutely perfect!” Kids at this age are able to focus on longer-term projects – especially if they catch their interest. This is a good option even if they don’t yet play Fortnite but know it’s “cool”. My tester and I spent many happy hours sitting side by side building this set. The recommended age is 10+, but my nine-year-old relished the challenge. You end up with a toy (there are a generous nine minifigures in the set) that can be played with or put on display.View image in fullscreenLego Fortnite Battle Bus£89.99 at Lego£90 at ArgosMaterials:plasticSuitable for:10+Sip happensWater bottles are a big deal to kids – they’re a way for them to show off their personal style at school, where they’re otherwise in uniform. Many nine-year-olds are desperate to feel more grown up, and Owala’s FreeSip for adults won mybest water bottletests earlier this year. On a practical level,it’s durable, easy to use and (less important for the nine-year-old, but key for the adult) easy to clean. This is a smaller version of my winner, which makes it lighter for kids to carry around all day. The different colourways available allow for self-expression, and they’re popular, so they’re a big tick in the “trending” box.View image in fullscreenOwala Kids FreeSip water bottle£25.99 at Owala£26 at NextMaterials:BPA‑free Tritan plastic, silicone, stainless steelSuitable for:3+Get your skates on“My friends all play with Tech Decks at school during playtime,” a nine-year-old tester told me. “They’re so cool. You can learn tricks. And they fit in my pocket for school. I really want some new ones for my collection.” This enthusiasm for a finger skateboard might mystify adults – myself included – but nine-year-olds seem crazy for them. This set is a good place to start – there are various “ramps” you can invest in later if you want. This set comes with six boards, 20 wheels and four trucks, plus stickers. My tester enjoyed customising their boards with the trucks and wheels included (they’re interchangeable) and spent a long time trying to master tricks; I live in hope that this transfers to a love of actual skateboarding.View image in fullscreenTech Deck Sk8shop bonus pack£17.95 at Maqio£13.99 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, metalSuitable for:6+Stay in the pictureView image in fullscreenSnap happy: our tester loved printing and decorating their photos with this instant camera.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianMy nine-year-old tester loved this instant camera. They snapped photos, printed them off and coloured them in or stuck them up around their bedroom. The camera feels grown up but still has a foot in the “toy” arena. The Photo Creator is similar to the Fujifilm camera our11-year-oldsrated, but it’s less pricey to run for impulse-driven nine-year-olds as it prints on rolls of paper rather than Instax film. As it’s technically a thermal printer, it only prints in black and white, but there are kid-friendly filters they can put on the photos and an all-important selfie lens.View image in fullscreenPhotoCreator instant camera£45 at Argos£45 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, electronic componentsSuitable for:8+Put your records on“I love this mini record player that really plays music,” one nine-year-old tester told me. “You can build up a mini record collection with the surprise balls.”(The balls in question are plastic spheres that have collectible items inside – in this case teeny records – and you don’t know which ones you’re going to get before you open them, which apparently adds to the fun.)Every child who came across this record player seemed totally transfixed. “It was the biggest hit for my daughter,” one friend told me. “I love that she’s listening to records – I hope it’ll get her into vinyl.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWho knows if it’ll stick, but the delight of playing a record was palpable with my nine-year-old tester. It comes with one record – APT by Rosé and Bruno Mars – and you canadd to your collection with the capsules, which are £15 for two capsules with four records each. Put a record on the turntable, and the record player will play an extract of the song using chips to trigger digital playback. I only wish I could play my vinyl on it – but alas it’s not compatible with standard records.View image in fullscreenMini Brands Really Works Vinylplay set£20 at Argos£19.99 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, electronic componentsSuitable for:3+Turf wars“We have family game nights at home, and I’d like a more grownup board game now I’m nine,” my tester told me. Kids at this age have a better understanding of cause and effect, helping them think critically and solve problems. “Valuable play for children aged nine includes social games for interaction,” says Sydney Piercey, former au pair and nanny, and author ofSustainable Play. Risk ticks all of those boxes, and should see them through game nights into adulthood. Wannabe despots can conquer territories and control the world by deploying armies, attacking opponents and forming temporary alliances. Fair warning though: nine-year-olds are probably going to need an adult or two to play with them to explain and supervise gameplay.View image in fullscreenRisk board game£35 at Argos£32.99 at AmazonMaterials:cardboard, plasticSuitable for:10+Lights up“My brother got a circuit set for his birthday, and now I want one too. I want to make the ultimate circuit that does loads of cool things,” says my nine-year-old tester. This set should cater to their every wish, with 175 different projects. You simply link the components together to make various circuits that do exciting things – the glow-in-the-dark fan was a favourite with my tester. Instructions guide you through simple circuits, but during testing I noticed how quickly kids of this age learn and experiment. It quickly felt like a miniature version of the Blackpool Illuminations had been created on my dining table, and when a circuit didn’t work, my tester did some problem-solving. I just sat back and became the battery supplier (unfortunately it rinses through them at an alarming rate – and they’re not included).View image in fullscreenSnap Circuits light set£94.95 at CyntechMaterials:plastic, metal, electronic componentsSuitable for:8+Snuggle up“I love getting new pyjamas,” says my nine-year-old tester. No matter your age, a new pair of PJs rarely misses if you’re looking for a good gift. These by Polarn O Pyret are the best pyjamas I’ve found – and my research has been extensive. They’re made from organic cotton and are just the right weight for all but very warm weather. Plus, they wash so well – I’ve put pairs through so many cycles, and they haven’t faded, but the cotton softens beautifully. The foldable cuffs are designed to let the PJs grow with your child, the stripes are a crowd-pleaser, and they’re available in several colours to keep everyone happy.View image in fullscreenPoP striped pyjama set£30 at Polarn O PyretMaterials:organic cottonSuitable for:1+Laugh out loudView image in fullscreenPage-turner: Diary of a Wimpy Kid had our nine-year-old tester laughing out loud.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian“Everyone in my class has been reading this book, and I want to get into it,” one nine-year-old told me. Diary of a Wimpy Kid is a great book for kids of this age as the format – drawings, onomatopoeia bubbles (eg “Boom!”) for making sound effects, and short chapters – makes it accessible. The story follows relatable but hapless Greg as various annoying (yet funny) things happen to him at school and in his family life. It made my nine-year-old roar with laughter. It’s quick to read, but this is the first in a lengthy Wimpy Kid series.View image in fullscreenDiary of a Wimpy Kid£7.99 at the Guardian Bookshop£5.99 at AmazonMaterials:paperSuitable for:8+The sky’s the limit“My child enjoyed GraviTrax marble runs well below the recommended age … he continues to play with it aged 11,” says Daisy Upton, play specialist and author of theFive Minute Mumbook series. These sets are brilliant for nine-year-olds who like to problem-solve and get creative in a hands-on way. The SkyTrax is a newer addition to the popular GraviTrax range, and allows builders to create complex marble runs that change levels, flip the marbles and spin them around. I found it almost dizzying how fast the marbles fly around the track. It’s definitely more complex than any other marble run I’ve tested, but a great “next step” for nine-year-olds who enjoy this kind of play.View image in fullscreenGraviTrax XXL SkyTrax action set£79.99 at John Lewis£88.63 at AmazonMaterials:plastic, metalSuitable for:8+Movie-night snacks“Movie night just got so much better,” whooped my nine-year-old tester when we fired up this popcorn maker. Many niche kitchen appliances feel like a bit of a novelty (we looked at chocolate fountains and slushie makers too), but this gadget felt exciting to use – my young tester loved watching the popped corn pouring out of the canister – and it gets plenty of use in our family, where popcorn is a movie-night must. This maker works without oil, which was a nice bonus for me.View image in fullscreenLakeland popcorn maker with bowl£37.99 at Lakeland£37.99 at AmazonMaterials:metal electrical components, plasticSuitable for:8+ with adult supervisionMaking memoriesIf you’re still stuck for an idea, an experience gift is great for a nine-year-old. They’re old enough to enjoy the anticipation and start to accept that “things” aren’t everything. It’s possible to buy vouchers for theme parks such as Legoland, and for other activity experiences. I took a nine-year-old to Legoland recently, and they completely embraced the day. They were able to tolerate queueing and were tall enough for all the rides. Otherwise, Virgin Experience Days offers a wider range of activities such as treetop adventures, theatre tickets and crafting days.View image in fullscreenLegolandgift vouchersFrom £39 at LegolandExperience gift voucherFrom £13 at Virgin Experience DaysWhat to buy for nine-year-olds“The key developmental needs of nine-year-olds are building confidence, identity, teamwork and deeper problem-solving skills,” says Moore-Williams. “They’ll be interested in group games, coding and tech, creative expression (art, music, writing) and competitive sports.ToysI really rate for this age group include advanced Lego sets, Stem kits like Snap Circuits and coding robots, strategy games, arts and crafts kits and sports equipment.”Kids of this age are able to dive into more complex play – and are desperate to do so and feel more grown up. They want to be challenged by trickier craft kits and board games, and many will enjoy more complex imaginative play too – character-based figures might scratch that itch well. All these types of play can give them a sense of achievement and boost their self-esteem and resilience. “So much holistic learning and development can be supported through opportunities to play games together in groups,” says Moore-Williams.The experts I spoke to all acknowledged children’s need for sociable play with their peers. Getting them active with team sports or games is important at this age. More than one expert recommended buying a ball for a nine-year-old – they’re versatile for so many different types of play and easy to take around with you. “A small football is portable, sociable and can be played independently and together,” says Piercey.What to get for nine-year-olds who don’t play with toys?Many of the nine-year-olds I spoke to mentioned an experience gift. There is a good variety to choose from, including theatre vouchers, an annual pass to an attraction and days out. Some parents I spoke to asked people to contribute towards sports-club membership as a gift too. While this may not have the immediate “play” factor, it should make the recipient feel seen and supported.A Noble Giftlets you bid on experiences such as being a football mascot or tickets for kid-friendly concerts (though be warned, some are very pricey), with the winning bids going to charity (an additional platform fee applies). If you have something specific in mind, you can always contact the organisation to see if they will allow you to do something with them, even if it’s not readily available as a voucher.For more, read our guides to thebest toys and gifts for eight-year-olds, thebest toys and gifts for seven-year-oldsand thebest sustainable toys for kidsZoë Phillimore is a journalist with 20 years of experience. She’s tested many things, from mattresses to makeup, and she’s slightly obsessed with finding small new businesses to spotlight. Aside from this, Zoë loves travel, being outside – especially on the beach – and finding screen-free things to keep her three very active children busy. title: ‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon | Games | The Guardian
description: As video games chase spectacle, Modern Warfare 4 makes a case for putting character and consequence at the heart of its biggest battles
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: As video games chase spectacle, Modern Warfare 4 makes a case for putting character and consequence at the heart of its biggest battles
Content: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 combines large-scale battles with a story centred on the people caught up in the conflict.Photograph: ActivisionView image in fullscreenCall of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 combines large-scale battles with a story centred on the people caught up in the conflict.Photograph: ActivisionPushing Buttons newsletterGames‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weaponAs video games chase spectacle, Modern Warfare 4 makes a case for putting character and consequence at the heart of its biggest battlesDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 21 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn these strange, subdued weeks before the much-anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI, there have still been some welcome surprises. Onimusha: Way of the Sword revived a half-forgotten samurai action series with much aplomb, while Silent Hill: Townfall transported all of the franchise’s bloody, dread-filled psychological horror to … the picturesque Scottish coast. Even moreshocking to games writers, though, is the fact thatthe forthcoming Modern Warfare 4has one of the best Call of Duty campaign modes for at least six years – and might even be up there with the original Modern Warfare trilogy.The setting is an invasion of South Korea by its northern neighbour – a setup that could have fuelled a hundred instantly forgettable Netflix films, but hasproved controversialin a video game. The authoritarian regime has a new (fictitious) ruler and a powerful experimental weapon, which it’s not afraid to use as the opening gambit in an explosive attack. You take on the role of Park Hyun Jun, a conscripted South Korean soldier who, along with his small unit of similarly inexperienced grunts, gets caught in the firestorm as cities burn and enemy paratroopers fill the skies.On the other side of the globe, meanwhile, series hero Capt John Price has gone rogue, teaming up with cartel boss Valeria Garza to track down his nemesis, Makarov. How these narrative strands intertwine is the propulsive engine of the story, and along the way this game throws an arsenal of gigantic set-piece battles at you, edging you closer to a layered finale.Most positive reviews of the campaign mode have mentioned how the story combines its own ideas with themes and plots from the previous titles. So how did the game’s lead developer, Infinity Ward, set about creating a story that could support a giant first-person juggernaut such as CoD? “The DNA of a Modern Warfare story is that it is something you believe could happen in the real world,” says narrative director Jeff Negus. “‘Does it feel grounded?’ is the first question. Additionally, we ask, ‘What is going to resonate with a modern audience?’ It was important to us not to tell the same story again, not to show the same characters being the same people, because what they’ve been through has deeply affected who they are.”View image in fullscreenInfinity Ward says the story of Modern Warfare 4 puts its characters and their relationships at the centre of the action.Photograph: Infinity WardInfinity Ward brought in a range of military and cultural consultants to ensure the story’s accuracy. “Some of our actors were conscripted in Korea, so they’re able to identify with some of what’s happening,” says Negus. “We use a wide array of military consultants across many different branches and types of service. Our dialect coach, June Yoon, was invaluable because he understands the dialectical differences between North and South Korea, and he could help us reword lines in a more colloquially appropriate way.”One key element of the game is the combination of quieter, character-led narrative moments and apocalyptic action set-pieces. “There is a very healthy symbiosis between both parts,” says Negus. “We start with strong narrative and gameplay, and the very first thing that we ask is, ‘How can we interweave these things in a way that feels intentional?’ One must be complementary of the other, in such a way that we’re able to say, ‘I can’t imagine telling the story without this mechanic.’” Negus compares it to an explosion in an action movie, saying: “It can be spectacular, but if you don’t know the people who are a part of it, it won’t be meaningful. Back when I was working at Naughty Dog, and now with the team here, we talk about player-protagonist parity, and how, when you feel what the character feels, you’re all a part of the same story – the audience gets to be in on it.”Surprisingly, iteration is an important part of the process – even though this is a game filled with cinematic sequences that may have to be filmed and animated early in the development process. “We certainly map out the story visually,” says Negus. “Justin [Harris], our lead writer, will put in these story beats, much like a season of television or a movie would do, but we do it with levels. And sometimes we’ll need to move things around, particularly in a story where we can shift the timeline in certain ways. When someone comes up with something, it gets moved around, it gets debated and analysed, and it’s road-tested pretty hard before it becomes inked.”To me, the Modern Warfare 4 campaign is a story of dysfunctional families – the actual North Korean ruling family, Park Hyun Jun’s ragtag squad and Price’s Task Force 141. The tensions between these groups gives the story its human underpinning. Disaster movies usually centre on one or two main characters so that we, the audience, get to experience the drama vicariously through them.Infinity Ward has successfully brought that structural and emotional toolkit to the finale of the Modern Warfare series, and that’s at least partly why it works. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 might not be a Pulitzer prize-winning story, but in these odd days before the arrival of GTA VI it certainly gives you something to think about – and people to root for – as you blast away with your rifle, grenade launcher or helicopter gunship.What to playView image in fullscreenOver the Hill swaps military action for off-road exploration, inviting players to discover its landscapes at their own pace.Photograph: Funselektor LabsIf you like the look of extreme off-road driving sims such as MudRunner, but are put off by their unyielding difficulty level,Over the Hillis definitely for you. It’s a cosy exploration game where you drive a 4x4 through a bright low-poly landscape of babbling brooks and lush woodlands, occasionally using a winch to get out of muddy puddles or up steep hills.Along the way, you unlock cabins to allow fast travel and visit a mechanic to customise your vehicle. Spot an interesting bird or critter and you can photograph it, adding it to your scrapbook. The pace is slow and gentle, but there is a fulfilling challenge in mastering the winch and getting yourself out of tight spots.I wish more games simply gave you a world to explore and the tools to do it and then left you alone – although, if the solitude gets to you, there’s a co-op multiplayer mode too, so you can disappear into the wilderness with pals. Bliss.Available on:PC (coming to Switch, PS5 and Xbox in 2027)Estimated playtime:10-plus hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenThe Game Boy Museum’s catalogue has been adapted to run on a cartridge for Nintendo’s original handheld console.Photograph: Marcel Pflug“Let me be honest from the start: nobody was waiting for this.” Thus begins alovely Eurogamer featureon theGameBoy Museum, or more accurately, the museum’s creator, Marcel Pflug, and his attempt to fit the whole of hiswebsiteon to a cart that actually plays on a Game Boy. I love projects like this, which use games and games hardware as repositories of information. See also:The Uncensored Library, which collects banned books inside a Minecraft server.A question that haunts me, as a 55-year-old, is: “Why do I still play video games?” People are often ecstatic to tell me there are more constructive things I could be doing. I enjoyedthis essayby Lene Clement aboutthe non-utilitarian nature of gamesand the annoying lifestyle influencers who instruct us that “uselessness” is a bad thing because everything has to be productive now.I am readingThere Is No Antimemetics Divisionby Sam Hughes, better known asqntm. Now out inpaperback, it’s a novel about a government agency tasked with finding and battling “antimemetic” entities that feed on humans but can’t be seen, remembered or recorded. It’s a very video game-like premise and the staccato, almost episodic nature of the chapters reminds me of game missions. This is very much a recommendation.What to clickFrom Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six TacticsThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K eraPenguin Colony – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenGetting started on game design can be as easy as signing up for a course and building a prototype with software such as GameMaker.Illustration: Roman Motsak/Getty ImagesThis week’s question fromKatevia email is something I think all gamers have wondered:“If I had an idea for a game butno idea of how to create it, who would you suggest I contact? It’s more a game to learn things rather than [one with] combator sci-fi, etc.”Remember that old saying, often attributed to Thomas Edison: “Genius is 10% inspiration, and 90% perspiration”? The same goes for video-game design, or indeed film-making, painting and writing novels. Nobody will pay you for an idea, because everyone is having them practically all the time. The most realistic way to realise your idea is to sign up foragame development course, where you may find like-minded people who enjoy your concept and want to work with you. You could invest in an application such asGameMakerand start building your own prototype, or you could study game design via books or YouTube videos.I also highly recommendA Theory of Funby Raphy Koster,The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lensesby Jesse Schell andChallenges for Game Designersby Brenda Romero and Ian Schreiber. All of these provide a really good way to structure your ideas and think about how they may work as a functioning game. This way you can work on a design document that lays out all the rules and systems of your game, and this will help you discover if a) there’s something practical in it, and b) you have the drive and time to work on a game project. A great idea is a great start, but it is really only ever that: a start.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the Republicans’ midterms struggle: Trump has circuses, but voters also want bread | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Editorial: As prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promised
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Editorial: As prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promised
Content: Donald Trump at a midterm campaign rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at a midterm campaign rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesOpinionUS midterm elections 2026The Guardian view on the Republicans’ midterms struggle: Trump has circuses, but voters also want breadAs prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promisedWed 21 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.27 EDTShareIt is no great revelation that Donald Trump is enriching himself as president. Heraked in $2.2bnin 2025, with his position and his personal interests frequently overlapping. Yet this week’s poll finding that 34% of Republicans (and 66% of all American voters)thinkthat he is using his position to make himself rich merits attention.Separately, voters in a Fox News poll last week putgovernment corruptionat the top of their list of concerns – just ahead of inflation and high prices.Mr Trump pledged that people would be better off if they voted for him. Billionaires are; not the rest. He promised to lower grocery costs (they have risen) and to cut the price of gasoline to below $2 a gallon. It’s more than double that, thanks to his illegal war on Iran. Tariffs haven’t helped. Incumbents struggle when life feels unaffordable, andpolling for the Guardianhas shown the disenchantment of key voting groups. The gulf between his own prosperity and the lives of his base now looks less like an inspiration and more like an insult. Cash offers seem unlikely to help much.The president’s popularity rating sank toa record low of 36%in a poll on Wednesday. Mr Trump, of course, is not on the ballot. But he istouring red statesas he seeks to shore up the vote in places where the idea of a Democratic victory looked laughable two years ago. Democrats are rightly cautious about their midterms prospects, having been burned too many times. But less than a fortnight from 3 November, with many votes already cast, polls suggest that they will take the House and could well claim the Senate too.View image in fullscreenJames Talarico.Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesThe party is still unpopular, though impressive candidates are performing far better than anyone expected in surprising places – notably Texas and Kansas. But they are nowmore trusted on economic issues. Independents are turning away from Mr Trump and his party, and many Republicans seem unenthused, for multiple reasons. The “Maga-sympathetic” pollster Rich Barisarguesthat “Donald Trump did this to himself”. His base believed Mr Trump was their champion. Now they suspect that he is “just another politician”.There is merited concern about how the president has already used his powerto tilt the midterms, and more about what he may do if his party fares as badly as forecast. Republicans still hope to reclaim ground through traditional if unsavoury means, massively outspending Democrats.Yet whilesome polls are tightening, culture war attacks and salacious lies about opponents such as James Talarico in Texas do not seem, at least so far, to be as powerful as Republicans hoped. That’s not just because Democratic candidates are repositioning themselves. The toxic messaging of the presidential race – that Kamala Harris “is for they/them, President Trump is for you” – doesn’t land if voters believe that he’s actually for himself and his friends.Republicans nowpoint to France’s unrestand claim that a Democrat-dominated Congress would bring chaos and destruction to America. Their fearmongering has often motivated core voters. But while Democrats stick to the economic attack, Republicans are trying to change the subject instead of offering answers. Mr Trump’s bread-and-circuses politics is floundering,cage fights on the South Lawnof the White House notwithstanding, as voters ask what happened to the bread.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionTrump administrationDemocratsUS politicseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Usha Vance is a closed book – but her Goodreads account is surprisingly revealing | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: From Roman-era political potboilers to stories of Catholic priests struggling to impose their authority, Arwa Mahdawi wonders what the reading list of vice-president JD Vance’s wife could be trying to tell us
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: From Roman-era political potboilers to stories of Catholic priests struggling to impose their authority, Arwa Mahdawi wonders what the reading list of vice-president JD Vance’s wife could be trying to tell us
Content: A real page-turner … Usha Vance, at the Republican National Convention, 2024.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA real page-turner … Usha Vance, at the Republican National Convention, 2024.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesOpinionBooksUsha Vance is a closed book – but her Goodreads account is surprisingly revealingArwa MahdawiFrom Roman-era political potboilers to stories of Catholic priests struggling to impose their authority, what could the reading list of vice-president JD Vance’s wife be trying to tell us?Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTShareUsha Vance, a very clever woman with dubious taste in men, likes to keep herself busy. While lesser mortals (me) waste their one wild and precious life watching Love Is Blind, the second lady has various self-improvement projects on the go. She’sbrushing up on her German! She’s hosting aliteracy podcast!She’s rereading the classics! And, of course, she’s juggling four young children and the demands of being the vice-president’s spouse.How does she do it all? With the help of taxpayer dollars, I suspect. Easier to get some reading done when you’re beinghelicoptered everywhereand, as JD Vance has boasted: “People go to the grocery store for me.”But I’m not here to moan about how much the Vance family iscosting the taxpayer. I am here to share an important, and only slightly unhinged, theory. The second lady is notoriously private; people are constantly trying to understandwhat she’s thinking. Now, I think I’ve figured it out. While Usha herself is not an open book, I reckon her bookshelf – or, rather, herGoodreads account– is trying to tell us something. Either that or she’s trolling us.What have I done? I forced my kid to listen to Usha Vance’s podcast - now she’s a fan | Arwa MahdawiRead moreRemember, for example, when JD was trying to mansplain Catholicismto the popeback in April? (Pope Leo XIV, to be clear; pope Francis died the year before,one day after meeting Vance.) As all that was happening, Usha picked up Death Comes for the Archbishop by Willa Cather. Which, to be wildly simplistic, is a book about a French missionary priest tasked with imposing order and Catholic norms on a church in New Mexico, where some other naughty priests have gone a bit rogue. Make of that what you will.Then there’s all the recent chatter about whetherJD Vanceis going to be Trump’s heir. Per her Goodreads account, Usha has just finished reading I, Claudius by Robert Graves. That book is about a member of Rome’s imperial family who survives vicious palace politics because everyone underestimates him. All the infighting and murder means he’s the last man standing and becomes emperor almost by accident. Is that a reflection on her husband’s political future? Perhaps! Now that Usha is done with Graves, she’s reading the nonfiction book Medieval People by Eileen Power. Perhaps to prepare for the dark ages her husband is helping drag the country back to.“Arwa,” you might say, “you’re reading way too much into this!” Of course I am. I have a degree in English literature: that’s three years of explaining how doorknobs in Jane Austen novels represent the hollowness of colonialism. Nevertheless, I think I may be on to something. Let’s just hope that Usha’s next choice of reading material isn’t Annie Jacobsen’sNuclear War: A Scenario.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
