title: I spent a week watching Helen Haines in action in Canberra. It was the most inspiring week of my life | Tim Berenyi | The Guardian
description: Somehow, among all the meetings, media commitments and delivering rousing speeches – she managed to bake seven sponge cakes for the people around her
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Somehow, among all the meetings, media commitments and delivering rousing speeches – she managed to bake seven sponge cakes for the people around her
Content: Helen Haines’ ‘mission to bring more integrity and transparency into politics is founded in the belief that compassion will prevail’, Tim Berenyi writes.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHelen Haines’ ‘mission to bring more integrity and transparency into politics is founded in the belief that compassion will prevail’, Tim Berenyi writes.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianOpinionHelen HainesI spent a week watching Helen Haines in action in Canberra. It was the most inspiring week of my lifeTim BerenyiSomehow, among all the meetings, media commitments and delivering rousing speeches – she managed to bake seven sponge cakes for the people around herWed 21 Oct 2026 19.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 20.56 EDTShareLife has been feeling heavy for a while but since Monday it has felt overwhelming.Our communities have been through so much: bushfires, floods, fugitives, lockdowns and bushfires – and that’s only since 2019. Throughout all this there has been one familiar face lightening the load during uncertain times: the smiling face ofHelen Haines.During past disasters it always felt as though there were things we could do to help each other. Right now it’s really hard to know what to do. It’s pretty simple to understand how a fire starts or why a flood stops but in this moment things seem so much more complex.I had just returned from a run when I found out what had happened to Helen. The feeling is almost indescribable, a mixture of disbelief, anger and sadness.Helen Haines has lost both legs but ‘heart and mind are in good shape’, husband says – videoMy immediate thought was how could this have happened to her? Of all people? Surely this is not real. What do I say? What can you say to something so senseless?I felt sick. I still feel sick. I keep asking myself: what do I do? How do we respond to this? What do we do when the person we use for strength is the person needing ours?My late wife Jo Cox was murdered in her constituency in 2016. The alleged attack on Helen Haines is a punch to the gut | Brendan CoxRead moreThis grief and confusion is palpable throughout the hills and valleys of Indi, and it feels as though it has spread across the country. Everyone shares the same sense of bewilderment. We are all asking the question none of us can answer: how did we get here?Two years ago, at the age of 30, I decided to move home to my small country town. Mansfield sits at the base of the Victorian Alps and is in the Indi electorate.I’ve told people a multitude of reasons for moving home but, in truth, I moved back because I wanted to be more involved with what Helen and her team have been building up here. A genuine sense of community that is founded on the idea that democracy is for us and by us. Lasting outcomes are found in our commonalities, not our differences.Helen’s courage and humility as a leader inspired me to stand to be a councillor in the local elections. Like Helen, I ran as an independent. I wanted to emulate the kind of compassion and honesty she demonstrates.Representing your community is tough. Our communities are diverse, with an array of interests across a spectrum of issues. Some people agree with each other, some don’t. But that is the price we pay to live in a democracy. It’s between our differences that we find the best solutions.Helen is the embodiment of this. Her mission to bring more integrity and transparency into politics is founded in the belief that compassion will prevail.View image in fullscreenThe author with Haines in Canberra: ‘The access and respect that we volunteers would get because we were associated with Helen was astounding.’In May I spent a week in Canberra as part of Helen’s parliamentary volunteer program, attending meetings and observing how our representative serves our communities in the big house.That week was the most inspiring of my life.Somehow, during budget week – among all the meetings, media commitments and delivering rousing speeches – Helen managed to bake seven sponge cakes for the people around her. Seeing the way she interacted with people from across the political spectrum was inspirational. She gives everyone the same kindness, compassion and fair consideration.The access and respect that we volunteers would get because we were associated with Helen was astounding. Not just from politicians but from staff, from at the library to those in the canteen – Helen’s reputation afforded us all the same veneration.How many people can say that their reputation not only precedes them but rubs off on everyone around them too?I’m still not sure how she made all those cakes in a tiny kitchen but, at the end of the week, when we sat on the couch in her office, she told me why she did it. In typical Helen style, she simply said it was because people appreciate a bit of kindness, and everyone loves cake.The complex problems we face can feel insurmountable. But if we were all a bit more like Helen, we’d work our way through them together. Maybe it’s time for us to collectively do away with left-right polarisation and instead look forward together with a shared perspective.Because it’s only together that we will find the best solutions. As a collective we all pretty much want the same thing: clean air, fresh water and to spend time with the people we love. I for one hope that Helen gets a lot more time to do just that.Throughout all of this I come back to that same thought. What would Helen do?I think she’d be getting out into her community, wrapping her arms around everyone, and saying, “C’mon, have another slice of cake.”Tim Berenyi is a forest firefighter, Mansfield shire councillor and Voices 4 Indi committee memberExplore more on these topicsHelen HainesOpinionVictoriaAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: My husband Hiep Tran is in a Vietnamese prison. He has done nothing wrong | Chloe Dang | The Guardian
description: No Australian citizen, or anyone else, should have to endure the terrible nightmare our family is going through
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: No Australian citizen, or anyone else, should have to endure the terrible nightmare our family is going through
Content: Hiep Tran (left) and his wife, Chloe Dang.Photograph: Chloe DangView image in fullscreenHiep Tran (left) and his wife, Chloe Dang.Photograph: Chloe DangOpinionAustralian foreign policyMy husband Hiep Tran is in a Vietnamese prison. He has done nothing wrongChloe DangNo Australian citizen, or anyone else, should have to endure the terrible nightmare our family is going throughWed 21 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 20.54 EDTShareA bit more than a month ago my husband, Hiep Tran, went missing. It was the beginning of a terrible ordeal for Hiep, me and our entire family.We now understand thathe is being wrongfully detainedin a Vietnamese prison.‘We always do everything together’: Chloe has no way to contact her husband, a democracy campaigner detained in VietnamRead moreMy husband and I live a simple life, much like many other couples. We go to work each day, and every evening we come home and share a meal. I cook and he does the dishes. Afterwards, we watch movies and play with our cats. Some nights, he plays piano and I sing, although I’m never quite sure my singing is as pleasant as he makes it seem.We both love nature and outdoor activities. On weekends we often go hiking, camping or fishing, sometimes with family and friends. We love to travel, enjoying good food and exploring new things together. These ordinary moments are what make our life together so special.Hiep works in data analytics, but there are other things he has always been passionate about. He loves fixing things around the house and making wooden objects for our home. He also has a deep love of music. He used to play music at church. At family gatherings and get-togethers with friends, he often entertains everyone by playing the piano or guitar.It breaks my heart to realise that it has been a month since we were able to share these simple moments together.Just some days ago, I received a few fragmented details about his condition. I was told that he is in a fragile mental state, gripped by fear, and experiencing erratic blood pressure – symptoms which he had never experienced before. Knowing that my husband is suffering like this, unable to feel safe or at peace, is unbearable.View image in fullscreen‘My husband and I live a simple life, much like many other couples.’Photograph: Chloe DangThe only brief message I have received from him reads:“Hi, how are you all going? I want you to know that I never enteredVietnamon my own. I never crossed the border. I am struggling mentally – traumatised and terrified by the situation.”I read those words at 4am, in a report from a consular officer, and broke down in tears. It was truly heartbreaking. My husband had done nothing wrong to deserve being put through such a horrific experience.Next week, we will celebrate our 8th anniversary together. Hiep had booked tickets for a trip to South Korea for us to celebrate this special occasion. But instead, he is now living in fear and panic, trapped in a prison where he should never have ended up.His birthday was on 7 October. I thought being alone in prison would be the hardest part for him, but I was wrong. The “happy birthday” message and photos I tried to send him were not even allowed to reach him. Why are they so afraid of a simple message from his loved ones?He must be feeling incredibly desperate, not knowing that out here, my lawyer, his friends and so many others still care deeply about him and are doing everything in their power to bring him home as soon as possible.Living in a free country like Australia, we never imagined that helping others, speaking up for vulnerable people or simply travelling to another country could lead to a nightmare like the one my husband is now enduring.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Chloe DangOver the past month, the Australian government has provided tremendous support to me and my family, and I am deeply grateful. I sincerely hope the government will continue to do everything within its power to secure Hiep’s safe return. I also hope that people around the world with continue to speak up, raise awareness, and call for his release.No one, whether an Australian citizen or anyone else, should ever have to endure the nightmare my husband and our family are going through. All I want is for my husband to be safe, to be free and to come home to the life and family waiting for him.Please help bring my husband home safely to us.Chloe Dang is Hiep Tran’s wifeExplore more on these topicsAustralian foreign policyOpinionHuman rightsVietnamAsia PacificActivismcommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: This foolish decision undermines hopes that this government will take the necessary steps the climate crisis demands, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: This foolish decision undermines hopes that this government will take the necessary steps the climate crisis demands, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Illustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianOpinionClimate crisisBurnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a penZoe WilliamsThis foolish decision undermines hopes that this government will take the necessary steps the climate crisis demandsWed 21 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 21.29 EDTShareWhen the news broke that theUK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield, I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately, the theme suggested by readers was what can the public actually do in the face of what feels like paralysing climate doom?There is so much going on that is hopeful: biodiversity tracking, river protection, rewilding. Shruti Suresh, from the independent watchdog Global Witness, told those in attendance that if they wanted to effect change, they should protest against Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project. The message was so well understood that it didn’t need labouring.The mood in the room when the news came in was one of audible dismay. People had just watched the minister for climate transition declare that she could see the challenges ahead and was ready for them. The Jackdaw announcement will face immediate protest and legal challenge, but it sends a very clear signal from the government: we don’t mean what we say about ending emissions.It turns out you can take all imaginable personal responsibility to arrest the climate crisis, make lifestyle adjustments that even five years ago you wouldn’t have dreamed of, miraculously summon the energy to take collective action from what is often private despair, but it will be insufficient as long as corporations – assisted by the government – are working against you, in effect with impunity. At some point, you need to get the people you elected to do what we all know – and they acknowledge – is necessary.The Jackdaw decision had been quietly parked during the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when the threat of the Greens seemed greater to Labourthan it turned out to be. But while Labour successfully buried the issue during the campaign, the underlying issues surrounding Jackdaw – and Rosebank, which is yet to be decided upon – persist.Since the 2015 Paris agreement, we have been committed to try to limit temperature rises to 1.5C, and we’ve known for at least five years that means the vast majority of fossil fuels have to stay in the ground. As of 2024, there’s been scientific consensusthat the target of 1.5C is “deader than a doornail”, whilethis week’s emissions-gap reportcould not be clearer: the threshold will be breached and it will cause unimaginable damage, yet with urgent emissions reduction, there is a way back from the abyss. There is no workable argument that runs: “Everyone has to leave their fossil fuels in the ground, as a matter of the utmost urgency, except for us; everyone has to prioritise the long-term survival of a livable planet over energy bills, except for us; we all need to reach carbon neutrality and worry about high-skilled jobs later, except for us.” The Jackdaw field isn’t huge, will peak in a short timeand won’t on its own reduce energy bills, which are determined by global markets. So it’s tempting to shuffle it off as a side-order issue, but it matters: it destroys our moral authority as a nation and it extinguishes hope.The climate debate operates on two tracks that don’t meet. On the one hand, we talk about non-linear irreversible tipping points whose effects would be so seismic that the question of mitigation is too vast and, frankly, too painful to consider. The only bearable discussion of thecollapseof the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) – a system of currents within the Atlantic Ocean – is how to avoid it, and the contested matter of whetherthat is even possible. We talk aboutheat deaths across 854 European citiesover the past summer, and we talk about areas in the UK of environmental deprivation, flood risks and poorly insulated housing. We also talk about food security both in the short term, with potato crops destroyed by the weather, and in the long term, with supply chains subject to the incomprehensible devastation of every country going through its own particular climate crisis simultaneously.We look at the social unrest across Europe– which is thefastest-warming continent– and ask to what extent the deprivation created by an unstable climate is being weaponised by a far right hell-bent on choking off climate action.Then we gate off all that knowledge, all that anxiety, all that will to action, and turn our attention to the UK’s immediate energy compromises. The arguments here run that since we’re going to import gas from somewhere anyway, because any transition will take time, we may as well get it at home. Even though it’s well known that household energy priceswon’t be reduced, the government can use the tax take to reduce VAT. Some categories of emission are lower from UK gas than they would be from energy imported from the Gulf.We need to bring these conversations together, because what they describe is one shared reality. Alongside the carbon that Jackdaw and Rosebank would release, they’ve “sucked all the oxygen out of the debate around what to do about climate change”, Chris Stark, the former CEO of the Climate Change Committee, has said. A warm homes initiative would create vastly more jobs,research recently found, and by reducing bills would also bring far more prosperity, with the additional advantage of not undermining the climate goals we claim to hold.Thinking of agriculture alone, the headroom, investment and planning we’re ploughing into carbon extraction could make an immeasurable difference to building resilience for an already uncertain future. The most meaningful way to reduce household bills is to reduce reliance on increasingly turbulent world markets, by separating the renewable price from the fossil fuel price, which would immediately boost the already flourishing wind and solar sectors.Gas and oil proponents beg us to be pragmatic, while their own arguments are floridly impractical: conducted as though the outside world doesn’t exist; as though carbon emissions are tomorrow’s problem; as though there aren’t better solutions for high prices and insecurity everywhere you look; as though we have time to quickly exhaust all our bad answers before we move on to good ones.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne depressing aspect of the Jackdaw announcement – although by no means themost depressing – is that it’s all about the optics. Even its most trenchant supporters would admit that it’s not a long-term solution to energy security. Rather, it’s a flag to the fossil-fuel industry that the government isn’t an enemy. It’s a toxic smoke signal to the US that the UK might not be with it, but definitely isn’t against it. It’s a feeble attempt at domestic politicking byLabour, trying to deflate the Conservatives’ anti-net zero bubble. It’s a statement of intent to make no trouble, when the trouble is already upon us.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Can UK pop cut immigration and stop the boats? I suppose we’ll find out with GB News Music Radio | John Harris | The Guardian
description: An ‘all British, all day’ station is a nativist dream come true – but good luck with the playlist. And anyway: how many artists will want to be on Farage FM? asks Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: An ‘all British, all day’ station is a nativist dream come true – but good luck with the playlist. And anyway: how many artists will want to be on Farage FM? asks Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: ‘What will happen in the case of, say, the Gallagher brothers, who self-identify as Irish?’ Noel Gallagher on stage with Oasis at Maine Road, Manchester, April 1996.Photograph: Ilpo Musto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘What will happen in the case of, say, the Gallagher brothers, who self-identify as Irish?’ Noel Gallagher on stage with Oasis at Maine Road, Manchester, April 1996.Photograph: Ilpo Musto/ShutterstockOpinionGB NewsCan UK pop cut immigration and stop the boats? I suppose we’ll find out with GB News Music RadioJohn HarrisAn ‘all British, all day’ station is a nativist dream come true – but good luck with the playlist. And anyway: how many artists will want to be on Farage FM?Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTShareIf you want a quintessential “It wouldn’t happen now” story, try this. Two months before Margaret Thatcher became prime minister in May 1979, a national Militant Entertainment Tour wasorganised byRock Against Racism.On 20 March 1979, itcame to the West Runton Pavilionnear Cromer, the (very) small town on the coastal edge of East Anglia. The bill mixed the black and white musicians in three bands then at their artistic peak – the post-punk maestros Gang of Four, the punk-reggae hybridists The Ruts, and Misty in Roots, the renowned reggae collective from Southall in west London – and thereby made a stark symbolic point: that the multiracial nature of large swathes of the UK was not to be decried or attacked, but actively celebrated.The UK was then – and some of this may sound familiar – in a bitter, polarised state, seemingly locked into deep economic problems, amid rising fear about the neo-fascist National Front. The previous year,Thatcher had said– and this may feel familiar, too – that British people “were really rather afraid that this country might be rather swamped by people with a different culture.” Amid such a grim political atmosphere, RAR and the musicians who supported it felt duty-bound to try pulling their audiences away from such toxicity, and point out that what we now call diversity was something to be celebrated.Nearly half a century on, the lack of any comparable cultural response to this country’s equally unsettling current state seems quite remarkable. There is, then, a vacant cultural-political space – and look what has now come along to fill it. GB News, that bracingly rightwing TV channel whose regular faces include Nigel Farage, the Reform MP Lee Anderson and the party’s failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin, is about tolaunch a music radio station.According to its promotional blurb, it will be “dedicated exclusively to artists from Great Britain and Northern Ireland”, with tagline “all British, all day”. By way of further explanation, one of its presenters, the blackGB Newshost Nana Akua, says that “It’s easy to forget how this country has shaped the global music landscape” – a strange point instantly disproved by a mention of any number of artists (such as those four fairly successful fellas from Liverpool). But here, perhaps, is the strangest thing of all: according to GB Media, every track on the station’s playlist will be an “artist from Great Britain or Northern Ireland, or where the main proportion of the band is British.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yet | Polly ToynbeeRead moreThis sparks no end of questions. Does anyone in the ordinary world actually perceive music like this? Will someone frantically be employed to sift through Wikipedia, finding out whether this or that band fits the “main proportion” criterion? What will happen in the case of, say, the Gallagher brothers,who self-identify as Irish– and should, therefore, be excluded for the same reasons as U2, CMAT and Fontaines DC? Should the Jimi Hendrix Experience be ruled in or out, given that the two supporting members of the trio were respectively from Ealing and Folkestone? And to get into the real nitty-gritty, how exactly are the programmers defining “British”?We all know the jaw-dropping conversations taking place in GB News-adjacent circles about national identity. TheTory-to-Reform defectorsRobert Jenrick and Suella Braverman seeEnglishness as an ethnic identity. If this definition wins out, which is quite conceivable, what will happen then? A playlist cull that will leave little apart from the musical equivalent of sliced white bread?There are more fascinating questions to ask. There hasbeen an on-off debateabout whether Britpop was partly responsible for Brexit. As the writer of abook about that cultural wave, I have always clung on to the idea that because its nationalistic(ish) animus was focused on the US, and the demographics of Leave voters do not map on to the Britpop generation, no one had any case to answer. But this latest development brings on a slight pang of unease. In retrospect, the large-scale whiteness of Britpop was, as we say these days, rather problematic. On a musical level, it accounts for its chronically limited range of influences and inputs, which led to it burning out pretty quickly. But it also left it open to what might turn out to be a belated act of appropriation: whatever music the new station plays, I would imagine that Oasis, Blur, Pulp et al will be an integral part of its output. Put another way, the Farage-ist tanks are now surely heading for Britpop’s metaphorical lawn.That piping hot new TV show I just watched? I can’t recall a thing about it | Zoe WilliamsRead moreInquiries to a couple of music lawyers established that musicians cannot stop radio stations that possess the relevant licences and pay the required royalties from playing their material. Self-evidently, however, they could quite easily express their displeasure at the prospect of being part of a constant Farage-ist soundtrack. In the excellent new Oasis documentary, Don’t Look Back in Anger, Noel Gallagherrightly saysthat his band was never “a rightwing thing … All are welcome. It’s we and us.” In the context of GB Music Radio, he should translate that into something slightly more specific. So should the already embattled Ed Sheeran, Adele, what remains of the Rolling Stones, the former members of Dire Straits and everyone else who is – and isn’t – mentioned in the station’s launch statement. The music all of them make, after all, is founded on precisely the kind of cultural mixing that so many voices associated with GB News take against.Oh, and one last thing. This message needs to be out there in the fabric of people’s lives, not only pouring out of their phones, but arriving in their towns. The West Runton Pavilion was demolished in 1986. But imagine some modern equivalent of Militant Entertainment pitching up on the Essex coast, the old Nottinghamshire coalfield, the seaside towns of Kent, or any number of Reform’s supposed heartlands. Is that really now as inconceivable as it seems?John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGB NewsOpinionReform UKOasisPop and rockcommentShareReuse this content

title: Cost-of-living crisis? You wouldn’t know it by looking at these companies’ profits | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: We are so locked into believing the market must not be questioned that we just assume everything is happening as it should
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: We are so locked into believing the market must not be questioned that we just assume everything is happening as it should
Content: It sure is good to know Inpex’s profits are going to reach a record high due to the Ichthys LNG project, given how much it pays in tax: $0, writes Greg Jericho.Photograph: Darren England/AAPView image in fullscreenIt sure is good to know Inpex’s profits are going to reach a record high due to the Ichthys LNG project, given how much it pays in tax: $0, writes Greg Jericho.Photograph: Darren England/AAPGrogonomicsAustralian economyCost-of-living crisis? You wouldn’t know it by looking at these companies’ profitsGreg JerichoWe are so locked into believing the market must not be questioned that we just assume everything is happening as it shouldGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastWed 21 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.25 EDTShareIt is always quite striking just how greatly the overseers of the economy defend the status quo in order to ensure company profits keep rising.Right now, Australians are suffering from a cost-of-living crisis.It’s pretty obvious why this is happening.Exhibit 1:Click here if this graph does not displayAnd exhibit 2:Click here if this graph does not displayBut we too often default to the view that oil prices are rising, so petrol prices must also rise and nothing can be done about it. We are so locked into believing that the market must not be questioned that we just assume everything is happening as it should.Well this weekAmpol releasedits third-quarter report to the ASX. It noted that the growth in its operating profits “reflects the strength of the integrated supply chain to capture the benefits from prevailing market conditions”.Yep, the “benefits”.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereIt also reported that the “escalation of geopolitical tensions in the Middle East in recent weeks and ongoing constraints in supply of fuel products … continue to be net favourable for Ampol’s integrated supply chain”.Yep, “net favourable”.This isn’t about them selling more fuel. It’s about them increasing margins at Ampol’s Lytton refinery. Ampol noted that the margin in the third quarter of US$23.92 was more than double what it was a year earlier (US$10.62).This accords with earlier reports from Ampol showing just how good the US and Israel war on Iran has been for them:Click here if this graph does not displayIt’s whyAmpol’s net profit in the first halfof this year was up a rather stunning 376% from $180.2m to $857.2m.Then there isViva Energy, which owns the Geelong oil refinery and supplies, among others, Shell-branded fuel. It has announced “strong first half earnings”, with its operating profit up 154% from $304.9m to $774.4m.Again, this did not come from more sales – the volume of fuel it sold only rose 1.3%.It’s pretty astonishing when you are outperforming even the gas companies:Click here if this graph does not displaySo yes, oil prices are going up, but let’s not pretend the companies that are importing the oil are struggling. No, they are passing on the costs and then some, as we can tell from the increase in the prices charged by the petroleum and coal product manufacturing companies compared with the cost of their inputs:skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClick here if this graph does not displayThis is important because on Wednesday at hisfireside chatthe deputy governor of the Reserve Bank, Andrew Hauser, was asked about strong “corporate profitability” and whether companies needed to adjust “to a lower level of profitability over time in order to get the balance right … in order to have the social licence to operate”.It was a good question, and in reply Hauser suggested “companies are extremely conscious … about what is called in the trade their social licence” before talking about small business and then future problems with AI companies.But we don’t need to ponder what will happen in the future, because the problem of excessive profits leading to hardship for workers is happening right now and the RBA is saying nothing.And as for caring about their social licence, companies care about ensuring their marketing budgets are spentmaking them look like good corporate citizensrather thanactually being so.The IMF says we need to make ‘urgent choices’. But are they choices the Albanese government is willing to make? | GrogonomicsRead moreThey also spend an inordinate amountlobbying governmentsto ensure any concerns about social licence are overlooked.Consider thatJapanese gas companies, including Inpex, are currently complaining loudly about the proposed gas reservation policy and agitated against a 25% tax on gas exports because (as it wrote in aSenate committee submission) “Inpex’s contribution to Australia extends beyond taxation”.In AugustInpex reportedthat the times were very good, despite its Abu Dhabi operations being disrupted.It noted that “despite continued uncertainty surrounding the Middle East situation, full-year profit is expected to be a record high ¥510.0 billion, supported mainly by higher sales prices and stable operations at Ichthys LNG”.That Ichthys LNG operation is rather beloved by our current minister for resources, Madeleine King. Back in 2018, when she was the shadow minister,she attended the celebration of its first LNG shipmentand said “it plays a vital role in the economy of Northern Australia and will continue to contribute to the Australian economy for decades to come”.More recently shecrowed about how“this project provides resilience and security for Japan”.That’s nice. Especially given so much LNG is exported to Japan that it sells more of that gas to other countriesthan is used each year in all of eastern Australia.And it sure is good to know that Inpex’s profits are going to reach a record high due to the Ichthys LNG project, given how much it pays in tax and royalties that helps Australians:Click here if this chart does not displayGotta love that social licence.But don’t worry, I’m sure when AI firms make massive profits that increase inflation and pay little tax our governments and central banks will speak up and households won’t again be hit with higher interest rates or cuts to services.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyGrogonomicsCost-of-living crisisPetrol pricesBusinessTaxInterest ratesReserve Bank of AustraliacommentShareReuse this content

title: After three disastrous years, Israel needs to rethink itself. A new government would be a start | Dahlia Scheindlin | The Guardian
description: Only a clear opposition victory would let us begin to heal, strengthen democracy and establish Palestinian rights, says Dahlia Scheindlin, a Tel Aviv-based political analyst
Author: Dahlia Scheindlin
Headline: Only a clear opposition victory would let us begin to heal, strengthen democracy and establish Palestinian rights, says Dahlia Scheindlin, a Tel Aviv-based political analyst
Content: A print worker produces an election poster featuring Benjamin Netanyahu for the Likud party in Rosh Haayin  on Thursday.Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA print worker produces an election poster featuring Benjamin Netanyahu for the Likud party in Rosh Haayin  on Thursday.Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesOpinionIsraelAfter three disastrous years, Israel needs to rethink itself. A new government would be a startDahlia ScheindlinOnly a clear opposition victory would let us begin to heal, strengthen democracy and establish Palestinian rightsDahlia Scheindlin is a Tel Aviv-based political analystWed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 07.50 EDTShareIsrael’s 27 October election is fast approaching, with little clarity about who will win. But Benjamin Netanyahu ismore likely to lose. Hispolling is poor, and the fractious opposition parties may yet find a way to form the next government.What would such a government do? Most of the Zionist opposition parties, the frontrunners to lead such a coalition, have offered bromides about good governance and unifying the country. Others have focused on more specific plans to establish a state commission of inquiry into the government’s failures around the attacks of 7 October 2023, and end the exemption from military service enjoyed by most ultra-Orthodox Jewish men.But if a new government truly plans to build a better future,Israelneeds more profound changes. Simply ousting Netanyahu will not be enough.The two issues the opposition has highlighted are understandably important to Israelis. For so many citizens, the disaster of 7 October and subsequent two-year hostage crisis became a crisis of faith in the state itself. Without accountability through an independent inquiry, society cannot move on. And even staunch supporters of peace cannot tolerate the rank injustice of some citizens serving and dying in wars while others are systematically let off the hook.But what then? Israel’s war in response to 7 October has continued to devastate Palestinian society. But the past few years have damaged Israel internally as well.Social solidarity in Israelis abysmal. Hundreds of thousands of reservists have served for months, interrupting their studies, family life and income. Up to 30,000 people have been wounded, according to Israel’sministry of defence.Meanwhile, the current government hasslashed social-service budgetsin favour of defence spending. The psychological toll is immense, yet Israel had a shortage of psychiatristseven prior to the war. Dr Graciela Cors, a youth and child psychiatrist, told me: “The mental health situation is catastrophic, and so are the social systems that are supposed to support mental health, like outpatient clinics andKupot Holim[Israel’s state-mandated health funds].”These problems are urgent, but addressing them would amount to damage limitation. Without deeper change, better-funded services and greater conscription would do little more than help Israel cope with the next round of seemingly endless wars.View image in fullscreenAn election billboard featuring the centrist Yashar party leader, Gadi Eisenkot, in Tel Aviv.Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty ImagesIsrael desperately needs to confront the factors that brought the country to this point to begin with.Before Hamas’s attack, 2023 was already the year these long-festering problems burst into full view. Society was torn apart by two unreconciled, deeply interconnected questions: what kind of democracy Israel should be, and what is the future for the Palestinians?Historically, Israel has demonstrated aflawed, ambiguous commitment to democracy. It avoided writing a constitution, and has no law that explicitly guarantees equality to all citizens. But over roughly the past 15 years, that ambiguity has given way to a full-blown assault on democratic institutions. Attacks on the judiciarycame from top governing officials, culminating in Netanyahu’s government’s plans in 2023 to drasticallyweaken judicial independence.That top-down assault fell on fertile ground because of a deeper problem: the erosion of democratic values, shaped in part by education. Or Kashti, the former longtime education correspondent for Haaretz (where I also write), told me that the seeds of the judicial assault are found in the newcivics textbook adopted in 2016. He has traced a shift from vague treatment of democracy in earlier decades, to what he describes as “indoctrination”, with greater emphasis onJewish identityandstate power. This is a thin and misguided view of democracy, one that risks elevating the will of the majority above all other democratic values.The curriculum can also be alarmingly parochial. Kashti says that historymatriculation examsfocus on the second world war and the Holocaust, the wars of modern Israeli history and the establishment of the Zionist movement. “All other topics in history of the world are marginal,” he says. Religion, he adds, infiltrates unrelated subjects. “In geography or weather lessons, children are told to learn the prayer for rain. What’s the connection between prayer for rain and a lesson on geography and climate change?”This narrow conception of democracy helps explain how, in 2022,halfthe countryelected partiesthat sought to hobble judicial institutions as part of the coalition government’s programme. And when education gives barely any attention to human rights, civil liberties and the equality of all citizens – it becomes easy to see why Palestinian self-determination has dropped off the Israeli agenda entirely.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor decades, Israeli society has increasingly acted on the assumption that Palestinians could be contained through military force or control. In the years before 7 October, most Israelis saw no contradiction between democracy at home and their active military occupation regime effectively ruling over all Palestinians, without giving them rights or representation.Netanyahu’s current government has pursued the logical end of occupation –permanent annexation, ever-expanding settlements and ethnic cleansing. To do that, the government had to destroy the final guardrails on its power. The 2023 assault on the judiciary finally galvanised many Israelis, who feared that their own liberties were under threat. Massive protests followed, plunging the country into prolonged social turmoil.No Israeli government can offer a different future without fundamental and comprehensive change on these deepest issues. What is needed is a fundamental reassessment of the country’s entire social ethos.The good news is that such change is absolutely possible. Education curriculums can be rewritten to embrace the principles of a modern liberal democracy. Teachers, politicians andeven religious leaderscan embrace human and civil liberties, minority rights, checks and balances, good governance and the universal values that too many Israelis disdain today. Societies and people can change.In such a society, it would be the occupation, rather than democracy, that would become an unsustainable affront to the values of Israel. This is a long way off; the current opposition leaders demonstrate no vision leading to such an outcome, and change is needed much more urgently. Israel’s right wing and many ordinary citizens, shaped by years of fear, would fight any change favouring Palestinian independence. But without embarking on the path, the country will never get there; needless to say, Palestinians will never be free.None of this will transpire if Netanyahu wins or if Israel’s elections yield a stalemate. But an opposition victory should be the day when the hardest, yet most hopeful, work will begin.Dahlia Scheindlin is a Tel Aviv-based political analyst and author of The Crooked Timber of Democracy in IsraelDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsIsraelOpinionPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricaIsrael-Gaza warcommentShareReuse this content

title: A gen Z protest movement could be about to oust Serbia’s strongman. Here’s why that will shake Europe | Misha Glenny | The Guardian
description: Student activists seem set to defeat Aleksandar Vučić at the ballot box this Sunday. The EU should never have written off Serbian democracy , says journalist Misha Glenny
Author: Misha Glenny
Headline: Student activists seem set to defeat Aleksandar Vučić at the ballot box this Sunday. The EU should never have written off Serbian democracy , says journalist Misha Glenny
Content: A student-led protest in Belgrade, Serbia, 7 October 2026.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersView image in fullscreenA student-led protest in Belgrade, Serbia, 7 October 2026.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersOpinionSerbiaA gen Z protest movement could be about to oust Serbia’s strongman. Here’s why that will shake EuropeMisha GlennyStudent activists seem set to defeat Aleksandar Vučić at the ballot box this Sunday. The EU should never have written off Serbian democracyWed 21 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.06 EDTShareHistory may not be about to repeat itself inSerbia, but it is beginning to rhyme. Just over a quarter of a century ago, Serbian citizens turned out to vote in large numbers to inflict a historic defeat on the then strongman in Belgrade, Slobodan Milošević, who was seeking re-election as president. He lost despite his extensive control over the media, the judiciary and the security forces. When he was reluctant to leave office, Serbs poured on to the streets in their hundreds of thousands, finally forcing him to go.On Sunday, a new generation could have the decisive voice in an equally fateful election, this time for the national parliament. Today’s strongman, Aleksandar Vučić, recentlyresigned as president to fight the electionwith the aim of swapping the locus of power from the presidency to the prime minister’s office.But Vučić, who has been in almost total control of Serbia for 14 years, finds himself on the back foot for the first time since he assumed power, just as Milošević did in 2000. Like his close friend, Viktor Orbán, who wasdecisively beaten in electionsearlier this year, Vučić has felt compelled to pull out all the stops to halt the opposition electoral coalition, known as the Student List (SL).Unlike Orbán’s Fidesz party, Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) is unlikely to be humiliated in Sunday’s vote. Opinion polls vary widely – some giving the SL alead of almost 10 percentage points, others suggesting the race is neck and neck. Pollsters also suggest that the higher the turnout, the greater the chances for the opposition. Some fear that the aftermath could even be violent.Vučić is throwing the kitchen sink at the campaign to skew the result his way. He has tightened his grip on the media bysupporting a change in ownershipof what was until recently the most important independent news group, United Media. Last weekend,10 prominent journalistsfrom its most important outlet, the TV station N1, resigned in protest against senior editorial appointments believed to favour Vučić and the SNS.N1 had been key in reporting the rapid rise in support for the student protest movement since itemerged spontaneously in November 2024. Students first took to the streets when the canopy over the main rail station in Novi Sad in the north of Serbia collapsed, killing 16 people. The tragedy occurred just months after a Chinese consortium had finished renovating it in what critics claim was a corrupt deal.View image in fullscreenMass silent protest outside Novi Sad railway station to mark the first anniversary of the canopy collapse that killed 16 people, 1 November 2025.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersAt first, Vučić’s response was to wait until the demonstrations petered out. But despite various attempts to coerce the students to retreat from the streets, the protests grew throughout 2025 and 2026. In March 2025, during a 15-minute period of silence to honour the victims of the Novi Sad disaster, protesters alleged thatpolice deployed a sonic weapon, the US-made LRAD 450XL, causing the crowd to disperse in panic. The government denied the use of the weapon and later the interior ministryfiled a criminal complaintagainst one military analyst over his claim that a sonic weapon was probably used.The demonstrations have showed no sign of letting up in the past two years. The big challenge facing the students was how to channel the undoubted energy they generated through the movement into a coherent political force capable of challenging Vučić. The old opposition parties were riven by factionalism and lacking dynamic leadership. But this summer the students announced they had selected candidates to stand in a new formation, the Student List, including prominent academics, engineers, workers, cultural figures and students. Their straightforward slogan is “Serbia or the mafia”.Vučić has responded to the challenge by cranking up the nationalist rhetoric in recent months in order to mobilise the far right. He haswelcomed the supportof his neighbour, Milorad Dodik, the de facto leader of Republika Srpska, the Serbian entity in Bosnia. Dodik has long been regarded as Vladimir Putin’s main man in the Balkans and more recently hascosied up to Donald Trump, whose associates are investing in a gas pipeline with his help.Vučić, too, has been cultivating support from Moscow. Personal relations between Putin and the Serbian leader have been strained in the past. Vučić has been supplying Ukraine with a significant amount of munitions while playing his complex game of trying to balance friendly relationships with the west and Russia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRevealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump businessRead moreBut with the gloves off, the Serbian leader has become less coy. Another sign of how seriously he views the students’ challenge was his decision to allow the recent nationalist jamboree ofa state funeralfor the man known as the “Butcher of Bosnia”, convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić, with the aim of bolstering his support among nationalists.If despite all this the Student List emerges victorious at the election, the shock waves will be felt as powerfully acrossEuropeas they were when Orbán was defeated.Above all, it opens the possibility of a swifter integration with theEuropean Union, a move that would be welcomed not just in Brussels but in London as well. Successive British governments are concerned that the Balkans represents the soft underbelly of European defence where Russia can exert significant pressure. Since Brexit, Britain’s influence here is limited politically but it has been active in promoting security cooperation across the region, with Nato and the EU.Student activists and their supporters have been disappointed by an apparent indifference on the part of the EU to their political struggle and a general perception in the outside world that Serbia’s democracy is a lost cause. On Sunday, they aim to prove them wrong.Misha Glenny is a former central Europe correspondent for the Guardian and the BBCExplore more on these topicsSerbiaOpinionProtestEuropeEuropean UnioncommentShareReuse this content

title: From strife-torn France to the UK, rightwing populists win when they stir chaos while promising order  | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: Marine Le Pen and Donald Trump are arsonists who play at being firefighters. Nigel Farage is finding that act harder to pull off in Andy Burnham’s Britain, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: Marine Le Pen and Donald Trump are arsonists who play at being firefighters. Nigel Farage is finding that act harder to pull off in Andy Burnham’s Britain, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionMarine Le PenFrom strife-torn France to the UK, rightwing populists win when they stir chaos while promising orderRafael BehrMarine Le Pen and Donald Trump are arsonists who play at being firefighters. Nigel Farage is finding that act harder to pull off in Andy Burnham’s BritainWed 21 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 07.08 EDTShareAn election where one side represents chaos will nearly always be won by the party that promises order instead. Public fatigue after years of turbulent Tory rule accounted for Labour’s 2024 landslide victory more than any policy in Keir Starmer’s manifesto. Across the Channel, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally (RN), is currentlyon course to winnext year’s presidential poll with a pledge of “restored authority and security” for a country that has spent years cycling between enervating stasis and explosive crisis.Le Pen has been boosted in recent days byscenes of city centres ablazeand shops being looted as student demonstrations mutated into riots. Street confrontation is a more standard feature of the political repertoire in France than in most settled democracies, but the destruction was disturbing by any measure.President Emmanuel Macron’s government, debilitated by the lack of a parliamentary majority, looked unprepared for the scale of the unrest. There was ample indication that something big was brewing. What began with high school students despairing at the neglected state of secondary education evolved into a general mobilisation of anger at high living costs and a lack of economic opportunities. Aggressive police tactics radicalised the crowd. As night followed day, and just as predictably, political fury gave way to opportunistic pillaging.Prime minister Sébastien Lecornuaccused “ultra-left” provocateursof stirring disorder as part of a strategy to render the country ungovernable in the run-up to next year’s elections. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the populist left’s presidential candidate, countered thatviolence was the natural byproductof a degenerate repressive state that conspires to discredit resistance, and that the protests channelled the heroic spirit of May 1968.At 75, Mélenchon is old enough to remember that Paris spring of revolutionary fervour. He has a keen following in the current generation of activist students, but the insurrectionary rhetoric unsettles swathes of conservativeFrance. His pungency could put Le Pen in the Élysée Palace.In the past she has been locked out of the presidency bycoalitions of moderate and left voters rallying, often without enthusiasm, behind the candidate best placed to stop her. RN’s advances in parliament have been checked in the same way, although it is currently the biggest party.Macron has twice been the beneficiary of that dynamic, but he can’t run again, has no obvious successor and is so radioactively unpopular that the whole liberal centre ground is contaminated by his standing on it.Current polling indicates that the “republican front” would unravel if the only names in a second-round run-off were Mélenchon and Le Pen. The centre-right would break for the RN leader. It probably wouldn’t even be close.France’s crisis has not escaped notice across the Atlantic, where it is viewed through the warped lens of Maga ideology.Donald Trump explainedthat “France is burning” because the country has been overrun by immigrants “with hatred in their hearts”. JD Vanceagreed that“western liberals” were to blame for opening European borders to “the third world” and advised American voters to view French misfortune as a premonition of the future if Congress is captured by Democrats in midterm elections next month.Republican efforts to cast their rivals as catalysts of national ruin have limited traction when Trump is the obvious engine of chaos. Democrats didn’t start the war in Iran. Nor did they author a deranged trade policy that alienated the US’s friends, turning even Canada into a foe.This is a common problem for incumbent demagogues. In opposition, simple solutions are proposed for complex problems: tariffs as the remedy for industrial decline; expelling illegal immigrants as the answer to every social and economic grievance; trusting in the leader’s judgment as the answer to everything else.In office, those mechanisms fail to deliver the promised benefits. Someone needs to be blamed. The categories of undesirable element grow. Media, universities, courts and opposition parties are called crooked or treasonous. But purges disrupt the smooth running of a country. They are bad for the economy. This is how the insecure leader goes through the gears of tyranny. A craving for control generates dissent, which is attacked as a menace to society, requiring more draconian law enforcement. When that provokes more determined opposition, the dissenters are denounced as extremists who jeopardise public safety.Trump has travelled some way down that road already. He might accelerate a lot further after the midterms. One option is to make bogus claims of election fraud, denying the validity of results that, if allowed to stand, would empower Democrats to hold a rogue president to account. His despotic temperament and his record of refusal to admit any electoral weakness suggest he would rather trigger a constitutional crisis of existential dimensions for American democracy than acquiesce to cohabitation with an unfriendly Congress. He will plunge the country deeper into chaos and insist that the nation rally around him as the only one capable of restoring order.That is standard authoritarian operating procedure. The arsonists affect dismay at the conflagrations they ignite. They cavort in firefighter costumes and hose the flames with petrol.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is the role Le Pen is readying herself for now in France. If she wins next year’s election, the backlash from the left will be ferocious. That challenge will be eagerly confronted by an incoming president likely to be looking for pretexts to declare a national emergency and remake the republic as a vehicle for her personal authority.Britain’s radical right parties dream of an equivalent opportunity. They revel in lurid imagery of societal breakdown. Sometimes the fantasy is camouflaged as a warning about the dangers of unchecked immigration, but impatience for a violent reckoning is never far from the surface. ForRupert Lowe, leader of Restore Britain, there is seemingly no effort to conceal the relish. He told his followers on X last week that his agenda would certainly trigger “civil unrest and rioting,” and that “what needs to happen will be incredibly painful”.Lowe is still a relatively fringe figure but he exerts disproportionate influence in the conservative digital ecosystem thanks toamplification on X by Elon Musk, the platform’s oligarch proprietor. Lowe’s candidate beat the Tories and Liberal Democrats in Manchester’s mayoral byelection earlier this year. By competing for votes with Reform UK, Restore Britain has drawn Nigel Farageinto an arms racein fanatical anti-migrant rhetoric.Farage’s status as a more serious contender in the electoral arena allows him to launder ideas that were once self-evidently extreme – mass deportations, for example – as mainstream policy. That doesn’t automatically make them popular. There is an audience for ethnically selective nationalism but it has a ceiling. The voters who are motivated by determination to thwart Farage outnumber those who want him installed in Downing Street.That tactical coalition is easily galvanised because prominent figures on the British right wear their arsonist intent so brazenly. Also, a stable Labour government isn’t giving them opportunities to play at being firefighters.To advance on power, Reform UK has to win over the kinds of voters that Le Pen sees heading her way through the smouldering rubble of French politics: people exhausted and bewildered by the system unravelling, without hope that incumbent authorities can get the country back on track, and amenable to the argument that fanatical leftists are the more menacing agents of chaos. Thankfully, those are not the conditions of British politics. Andy Burnham’s every step should be guided by the need to keep it that way.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsMarine Le PenOpinionFranceEuropeNigel FarageRupert LoweThe far rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: Australian democracy is usually peaceful. But there’s a homegrown history of political violence  | Joshua Black and Frank Bongiorno for the Conversation | The Guardian
description: Like other features of our public landscape, both good and bad, political violence has a history in Australia – one from which we may learn
Author: Frank Bongiorno
Headline: Like other features of our public landscape, both good and bad, political violence has a history in Australia – one from which we may learn
Content: Tributes outside the electoral office of independent MP Helen Haines, who was struck by a car outside her office in Wangaratta, Victoria on Monday. She remains in a critical condition.Photograph: James Ross/ReutersView image in fullscreenTributes outside the electoral office of independent MP Helen Haines, who was struck by a car outside her office in Wangaratta, Victoria on Monday. She remains in a critical condition.Photograph: James Ross/ReutersOpinionHelen HainesAustralian democracy is usually peaceful. But there’s a homegrown history of political violenceJoshua Black andFrank Bongiornofor the ConversationLike other features of our public landscape, both good and bad, political violence has a history in Australia – one from which we may learnTue 20 Oct 2026 22.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 23.01 EDTShareThe alleged attack on independent MPHelen Hainesin Wangaratta has shocked a nation whose politics is normally peaceful even by the standards of mature democracies. A hard-working, decent parliamentarian with a strong moral compass and a gift for achieving consensus, Haines seems an especially unlikely figure to attract the kind of brutality allegedly visited on her on Monday.We do not yet know the motivation behind this alleged attack. But there is no questionAustralia’s politics have been fractiousover the past 12 months. Violence, literal and rhetorical, has been a growing feature of the landscape, shaping the relations between citizens and politicians – and among one another. The Bondi beach massacre of 14 December 2025 is widely regarded as a tragic turning point in this regard.But like other features of our public landscape, both good and bad, political violence has a history in Australia – one from which we may learn.My wife Jo Cox was murdered in her constituency in 2016. The alleged attack on Helen Haines is a punch to the gut | Brendan CoxRead moreAustralian assassinationsAustralian leaders have mostly avoided the assassinations more common in other places. Even Australia’s parent culture, Great Britain, lost a prime minister to an assassination in 1812 when John Bellingham shot Spencer Perceval through the heart in the lobby of the House of Commons.The 20th century alone saw two sitting American presidents murdered, along with leading activists and major aspirants to higher office. Two Indian prime ministers, Indira Gandhi and her son and successor Rajiv Gandhi, were slain in the century’s later decades, as well as an Israeli statesman in Yitzhak Rabin.No Australian prime ministers or premiers have been assassinated to date. The deaths of figures such as Joseph Lyons, John Curtin and Ben Chifley were the result of natural causes. The circumstances of Liberal prime ministerHarold Holt’s deathare well known but, notwithstanding conspiracy theories, did not involve foul play.Still, assassination attempts have occasionally blighted Australia’s political landscape. The first came in 1868 with the visit of Prince Alfred, second in line to Queen Victoria’s throne. Theprince was shotat a welcome event near Sydney by an Irish republican with evidence of mental illness.The assailant was executed, but the prince lived, saved by the bullet hitting a metal clip of his trouser braces. The attempt set off a new wave of sectarian animosity between Protestants and Catholics, ably stoked by Federation father Henry Parkes. (There was much less fuss after theapparent attempton the life of then-Prince Charles in Sydney in 1994, though in that case the bullets were blanks.)In the 1960s, it was war and peace that stirred political passions. Labor leader Arthur Calwell was an opponent of Australia’s involvement in the Vietnam war, and it was after a “rowdy meeting” about conscription in Sydney in 1966 that he was shot in the jaw by Peter Kocan, who had a leaning to far-right politics and was evidently ill.Calwell forgave Kocan, who became awriter of some renown.Crime and corruption were also potential motivators of assassination. In July 1977, anti-drug campaigner and Liberal candidate from Griffith in the Riverina,Donald Mackay, went missing. His vehicle was found stained with blood, but his body was never recovered. His presumed death precipitated a state royal commission into drug trafficking.In 1994,John Newman– Labor’s New South Wales state MP for Cabramatta and a committed opponent of criminal gangs – was murdered in his driveway. Fairfield councillor Phuong Ngo, a local notoriety with a party power base and criminal links, was later convicted, though with many questions left unanswered.Political violenceWhile assassinations have been rare, political violence has at times made its mark on Australia. The spearing of governor Arthur Phillip in the right shoulder in September 1790 was an early instance, though as Kate Fullagarexplains, this incident was likely a payback ritual orchestrated by Yiyura man Bennelong in the hope of enabling detente rather than committing murder.In the early 19th century, political violence centred onfrontier conflict and warfare between settlers and Indigenous communities. The University of Newcastle’smassacre mapremains a telling window into that world.Democracy itself was, at times, a violent thing. The goldminers’rebellion at Eurekain 1854 – triggered by unhappiness with licence fees and colonial administration generally – left more than two dozen dead, most of them miners or civilians. Miners also violently attacked Chinese diggers at Buckland River in Victoria (1857), with some fatalities, and Lambing Flat in NSW (1861).The prospect of similar violence hung in the air during the industrial strikes of the 1890s. Colonial troops in Melbourne were ordered to “fire low” on union agitators and “lay them out”. In western Queensland, soldiers intimidated striking shearers with Nordenfelt machine guns.Historian Sean Scalmerhas shownthat early colonial elections were marred by violence and even occasional killings on the hustings. Australia’s unique history of electoral innovation, including the secret ballot and broad suffrage, was partly an attempt to “contain contention”, as he puts it.There was growing violence in Australian politics – and society – from the 1960s. Anti-war protests occasionally erupted into conflict. On a few occasions, so did thedemonstrations against Sir John Kerr, who had dismissed the Whitlam government in November 1975. These involved various projectiles including, in one instance, a brick to smash open a window of the vice-regal car.Party struggles also contained an underbelly of factional violence. In 1980, leftwing Labor activist Peter Baldwin wasbashed in Sydney, the instigators presumed to be rightwing opponents. It was an extreme case, but factional battles in Liberal party branches in Sydney have occasionally descended intofisticuffsin the more recent past, too.The 1980s and 1990s saw several massacres in suburbs such as Sydney’s Milperra (1984) and Melbourne’s Clifton Hill (1987). Some, including Milperra, were precipitated by gang wars, but the ready availability of guns was of broader concern to many, including senior Liberal John Howard.I knew one of us could get hurt eventually. I never thought it would be my friend Helen Haines | Zoe DanielRead moreHe was prime minister by the time he went to the regional Victorian town of Sale, where he was explaining his controversial gun law reforms and firearm buyback program. The measures were a response to the devastating Port Arthur massacre in Tasmania. Howard famously wore abullet-proof vestto the lectern, an instruction from his security personnel but an apparent insult to his audience.Terror on southern shoresThe late 20th century was also an era of growing terrorism in Australia. Croatian extremists and Yugoslav agents wereseemingly at warwith one another in the streets of Melbourne and Sydney.In the latter city, adeadly attackon a gathering of world leaders at a regional Commonwealth heads of government meeting occurred in 1978. The likely suspects, an Indian religious sect-turned-cult, appear to have targeted the Indian prime minister, who was meeting with Malcolm Fraser and other leaders at the Hilton hotel. Multiple innocent bystanders, including two unlucky garbagemen who accidentally picked up a bomb left in a bin, were killed.There was also suspected terrorism at play when, in December 1980, an assassin’s bullets killed the Turkish consul-general Şarık Arıyak and his bodyguard outside the former’s Sydney residence. Armenian activists claimed responsibility for the murder, but evidence was lacking. Today, the NSW policereward for informationstands at $1m.Prime ministers and other senior politicians have sometimes been rumoured to be the targets of terrorists. Yet there was always risk of hoaxes. Asupposed planby a Sri Lankan PhD student to assassinate Malcolm Turnbull and Julie Bishop, and target major Sydney landmarks, was revealed to be fabricated. The conspirator, a colleague of the accused, waslater jailedover forged evidence.Threats to democracyPolitical officeholders are increasingly at risk of political violence around the world, and not only in autocratic settings where physical coercion is a regular political tool. In the past decade,British parliamentarians Jo Coxand Sir David Amess were killed in office, and more recently the former MPAnn Widdecombe was brutally killedin her own home.In 2022,the assassination of former Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abein Nara by a man with religious grievances shocked the world. So had the storming of the US Capitol a year earlier. In that case, a violent mob threatened to assassinate congressional leaders along with the sitting vice-president, Mike Pence.4:10The key Capitol attack footage shown on day two of Trump’s impeachment trial – videoSuch scenes at the heart of the United States, which historically thought itself a democratic beacon for the world, were astonishing. People forgot it was also the product of a revolutionary political culture.There are some common causes for concern. The internet and social media have made it easier for angry or unwell people to threaten politicians’ safety. On Monday night, Australia’s home affairs minister Tony Burke said there were1,067 reportsof “harassing and threatening behaviour against various high office holders” in the last financial year alone.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Created with Datawrapper/AFPTurning the temperature downWhile we still don’t know if the alleged attack on Helen Haines was politically motivated, condemnation of the incident has united politicians of different stripes. Haines is a much-admired figure across the parliament.Respondingto the alleged attack, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, called for the political “temperature to be turned down”.1:44AFP charging almost one person a week for targeting politicians, says commissioner - videoDemocracy is a practice as much as a system. It requires for its survival a steady nurturing by those – citizens as well as representatives – who perform it. Haines herself has been in the forefront of efforts to restore trust in a political system that has generated disaffection among many Australians in recent years. She has been repaid with a violence that is the polar opposite of all that she stands for.Politicians say more security would ‘let bad people win’ after alleged attack on Helen Haines: ‘We don’t want to be locked off’Read moreAustralia’s world-leading history of electoral innovation was partly an effort to mitigate against violence. But the innovations of an earlier generation may not be enough to defend democracy from today’s threats, not least those arising from a social media ecosystem that draws its oxygen from base emotions.Resting on the laurels of compulsory and preferential voting is not an option. Sober reflection from political participants – in practice, everybody – is what our present circumstances demand.Joshua Black is a lecturer in Australian political studies at the University of Canberra. Frank Bongiorno is director of the Vice-Chancellor’s Centre of Public Ideas and Donald Horne professor of history and public ideas at the University of Canberra.
