title: A grieving female elephant carrying a stillborn baby: Federico Veronesi’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘She carried the dead calf for hours even though it wasn’t hers. She had had a miscarriage two years before – and now picked up the stillborn babies of other mothers’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘She carried the dead calf for hours even though it wasn’t hers. She had had a miscarriage two years before – and now picked up the stillborn babies of other mothers’
Content: ‘People sometimes think it’s a young elephant hugging its mother’ … Federico Veronesi’s award-winning photograph.Photograph: Wildlife photographer of the Year 2026View image in fullscreen‘People sometimes think it’s a young elephant hugging its mother’ … Federico Veronesi’s award-winning photograph.Photograph: Wildlife photographer of the Year 2026My best shotArt and designA grieving female elephant carrying a stillborn baby: Federico Veronesi’s best photograph‘She carried the dead calf for hours even though it wasn’t hers. She had had a miscarriage two years before – and now picked up the stillborn babies of other mothers’Interview byChris BroughtonWed 21 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy love of African animals, in particular elephants, dates back to when I was three or four years old, growing up in Milan in a house full of old nature books. When I was six, my parents took me on my first safari in Kenya – I cried on the plane home, feeling I was being torn away from the savanna I’d dreamed of, somewhere I really loved. But for the past 20 years, that’s where I’ve lived, guiding photographers on the Maasai Mara National Reserve and elsewhere in Africa.I’ve spent time photographing other animals, especially big cats, but elephants are still my favourite subject. They have this extraordinary presence, dominating the landscape and making it come alive. I love to follow them in different habitats. They are extremely adaptable – in Kenya they’re associated with the savanna and acacia woodland, and they can also live in extremely arid areas, such as the deserts of Namibia, where this photograph was taken.I was there last September, guiding a group of photographers. We had been following a group of elephants walking along a dry riverbed as night fell. Even though there is no water in these rivers, they retain some vegetation and act as a lifeline for the elephants, who follow them from the hills in the west towards the Atlantic Ocean.Because it’s a sandy river, it was quite easy to follow their tracks until we found them again the next day. But among the tracks was something quite unusual, like a dragging mark. Sometimes bull elephants, when they’re full of testosterone, will do crazy things to demonstrate their power and intimidate their opponents – I’d seen one lift a log before, and thought perhaps that’s what was being dragged.double quotation markI’ve since read that 17 out of 19 calves born during the past four years have not made it. She has been picking them upWe drove on until we found them, and that’s when I realised one of the females was carrying a baby. When people see this picture, they sometimes think it’s of a young elephant hugging its mother, but in fact the calf is dead and the leg you can’t see is wedged between the adult’s tusk and trunk. As I took this photograph, another elephant was approaching and the female swung her head so the baby was lifted up and out of its way. I have other photographs that make the reading of the scene more straightforward, but this one leaves the interpretation open and adds a layer of mystery.We followed the herd for several hours, and the female carried the calf for the entire time, only putting it down so she could feed before picking it up and continuing on her way. She was still carrying it when we last saw her – eventually the elephants started climbing into some rocky hills where we couldn’t follow.I’ve since read that 17 out of the 19 calves born in that area during the past four years have not made it. There’s clearly a problem, but researchers aren’t yet clear why this is happening. What has come to light, however, is that the elephant carrying the calf was not its mother, as I had assumed. Her mammary glands were not swollen as they would have been if she’d recently given birth, and the researchers were able to identify her as a female who had a miscarriage a couple of years before, and had since been seen picking up the stillborn calves of other mothers. In a sense, that makes the image even more deep and profound, as it implies that she perhaps hasn’t moved past that trauma.Most of my elephant photographs are in black and white. Sometimes I use colour – in Tsavo, Kenya, elephants are often covered in red earth, which makes for a striking contrast against green vegetation, and in Etosha, Namibia, there’s a place where they visit a waterhole full of white clay and end up looking like ghosts. But black and white highlights the texture of elephants’ skin, and also, as here, removes distracting elements and exposes emotion in a more straightforward way.This is a painful image to look at, but at the same time it reveals so much of the psychology of elephants, their interior complexity, personality and feelings. Here we see a creature that feels just as much as we do, that experiences the same grief at losing a baby, the same sense of not wanting to let it go. My hope is that photographs like this help people realise how important it is to coexist peacefully and respectfully with animals that look different to us on the outside, but inside are very similar.This image is the adult grand title winner of Wildlife Photographer of the Year. The exhibition is at theNatural History Museum, London,until 11 July 2027.View image in fullscreenFederico Veronesi’s CVBorn:Milan, Italy, 1975. Moved to Kenya in 2002High point:Probably this award, and the three books I publishedTop tip:Explore ways to convey emotions to the viewer through your photographs, carefully choosing light, atmosphere, shooting angle, framing, backgrounds, and so onExplore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotConservationWildlifeWildlife photographer of the yearPhotographyNatural History MuseumfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Our Friends in the North: The Thatcher Years review – old pals back on the toon as TV series gets squished | Theatre | The Guardian
description: They have appeared in epic BBC dramas since their RSC debut but Peter Flannery’s immortal foursome now return in an 80s-focused play
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: They have appeared in epic BBC dramas since their RSC debut but Peter Flannery’s immortal foursome now return in an 80s-focused play
Content: Likely lads … Jack Robertson and Scott Turnbull in Our Friends in the North at Newcastle Theatre Royal.Photograph: Chris BishopView image in fullscreenLikely lads … Jack Robertson and Scott Turnbull in Our Friends in the North at Newcastle Theatre Royal.Photograph: Chris BishopTheatreReviewOur Friends in the North: The Thatcher Years review – old pals back on the toon as TV series gets squishedTheatre Royal, NewcastleThey have appeared in epic BBC dramas since their RSC debut but Peter Flannery’s immortal foursome now return in an 80s-focused playMark LawsonWed 21 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe four thwarted, postwar north-eastern dreamers created by dramatist Peter Flannery have now played more than a whole day of drama across different formats. The 1982 RSC world premiere of Our Friends in the North featured almost four hours in the lives of lawyer-councillor Mary, drifting philanderer Tosker, photo-journalist Nicky and petty criminal Geordie. The award-winning 1996 BBC Two version ran 10 hours, as did the 2022 Radio 4 adaptation. Now Flannery brings the quartet home to the stage and toNewcastle(where the first version toured) in another play.Starting in 1964, with Labour PM Harold Wilson promising a new Britain, the first stage version ended in 1979, as Margaret Thatcher’s victory heralded a rightwing transformation. Exploiting the way that saga dramas test characters against landmark events, the TV version took them to 1995 (brink of Blair) and the radio one to 2020 (Boris Johnson and Covid). It would be intriguing to know if the idealism of these now triple-locked pensioner characters burns again under Burnham, but Flannery has tracked back to 1979-85, adapting the sixth (Thatcher in) and seventh (miners out) TV episodes.View image in fullscreenEpic courtship … Ryan Nolan and Sam Neale in Our Friends in the North.Photograph: Chris BishopA piece begun when he was an RSC writer in residence always had Shakespearean ambitions and these continue with the tremendous Trevor Fox, like the Chorus in Henry V, galvanising our imaginations and dropping historical footnotes. Fox, who starred in the TV and radio series, doubles as Nicky’s dementia-affected dad, Felix, a subplot especially poignant in what will be a memory play for much of the audience.All forms of the story have used soap opera domestic tension to offset socialist history and here the epic courtship of Sam Neale’s Mary and Ryan Nolan’s Nicky affectingly shows campaigners for social change yearning for romantic conformity. The largely wasted lives – the piece’s bleak sub-theme – of Tosker and Geordie are caught by Jack Robertson, pointlessly optimistic, andScott Turnbull, accepting defeat. Jude Nelson makes a small part large as a Tory MP who achieves a prophetic early breach in Labour’s “red wall”. The politics are Kinnockian, accusing Labour’s Militant tendency and miners’ union leader Arthur Scargill of swelling a rightwing electorate that led to 18 years of Tory rule.View image in fullscreenKinnockian politics … Our Friends in the North.Photograph: Chris BishopThe different Our Friends in the North directors have tended to panic at its politically expository dialogue and in this case it sometimes feels as if director Jack McNamara is searching for action such as slow-motion strobing for clashes between colliery pickets and riot squads.For completists, this is a must-see but, paradoxically, it feels incomplete. In all media, the story has had length and breadth and, though these two episodes were a logical choice, Flannery perhaps acknowledges losses from selection and compression when Fox’s Chorus laments: “There’s always so much more to say.” The events depicted partly explain why a regional theatre would struggle to put on an all-day epic, but this dramatically immortal foursome needs it.AtTheatre Royal, Newcastle, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMargaret ThatcherNewcastleTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A vehicle to expose prejudice, bias, and stupidity’: Sacha Baron Cohen defends Ali G as satire | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor defended his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, saying his aim is to bring people ‘face-to-face with the danger of fanaticism and conspiracy theories’
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The actor defended his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, saying his aim is to bring people ‘face-to-face with the danger of fanaticism and conspiracy theories’
Content: ‘A delusional cultural appropriator’ … Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘A delusional cultural appropriator’ … Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianMovies‘A vehicle to expose prejudice, bias, and stupidity’: Sacha Baron Cohen defends Ali G as satireThe actor defended his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, saying his aim is to bring people ‘face-to-face with the danger of fanaticism and conspiracy theories’Andrew PulverWed 21 Oct 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSacha Baron Cohen has launched an impassioned defence of satire, the right to offend, and his Ali G character onin a lengthy article for Time magazine.On the eve of the release of his new film,Ali G: Who Iz I?, Baron Cohen described satire as “more important than ever”, adding that “along the way, some people, instead of laughing, wince or worse, take offence.”Comparing modern satirists to the traditional figure of the “bouffon”, Baron Cohen described satire as “the humour of the dispossessed … using biting and at times cruel humour to undermine systemic injustice”.Having previously released films containing controversial characters including Kazakh journalist Borat Sagdiyev, Austrian fashion show presenter Brüno Gehard, and a thinly disguised Colonel Gaddafi parody called Admiral General Aladeen, Baron Cohen directly took on critics of the Ali G character, who has been criticised in the past for laughing at black street culture anddescribed as a “black caricature”.Baron Cohen writes: “I made this latest film for the same reason I’ve always done this work. Not only to make people laugh, but also to bring them face-to-face with the danger of fanaticism and conspiracy theories.”Booyakasha! Ali G is back – but even he can’t match the absurdity of modern Britain | Jason OkundayeRead moreHe added: “I’ve always designed my characters and comedy as vehicles to expose prejudice, bias and stupidity, though I realise not everyone sees them that way. Ali G is a white imbecile – a delusional cultural appropriator – who steals the fashion and lyrics from his favourite gangsta rap and dancehall idols, from Compton to Kingston. The joke is on him, and on the predominantly white male establishment who take him seriously.”“The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him. The world he’s returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago. All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven’t just lingered – they’ve metastasised ... 20 years ago, Ali G would sit next to world experts spouting absurdities. Today – fed a steady diet of disinformation and conspiracy theories by social media influencers and TikTok news – we have created an entire world where ignorance reigns and truth is inverted.”Saying that “each of my characters has a specific mechanism to encourage people to drop their guards and show what they really believe, prejudices and all”, Baron Cohen suggests that “yes, satire can offend people other than the intended targets.” Aware that the release of his new film is likely to attract protests, he said that hisuniversity dissertation was a study of Jewish and black cooperationduring the 1960s struggle for civil rights in the US, and added: “As someone who has opposed bigotry and injustice throughout my life and partnered with civil rights groups, I don’t recognise myself in the warped portrayals of me that I sometimes see on social media, lumped in with the bigots I lampoon.”Pointing to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s path from TV comic to president of Ukraine, Baron Cohen suggested that “satire doesn’t just needle politicians or regimes – it occasionally helps bring them down”, and that the Trump administration’s actions against Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel showed that “ridicule is [far from] irrelevant”.Quoting George Orwell’s observation in his 1945 essay Funny But Not Vulgar that “every joke is a tiny revolution”, Baron Cohen concluded: “Maybe [satire] can even help shame more of our governments into finally making our Silicon Valley overlords – unelected billionaires who decide what billions of people see and believe – liable for the lies, conspiracies, and hate on their platforms that have already gotten people killed and will likely kill many more.”“We are once again entering an age of ‘virtuous’ violence, where any atrocity – by racists, Jew-haters, or Islamophobes, the right or the left – can be somehow justified. It is not a place any of us should want to live.”Explore more on these topicsFilmAli G: Who Iz ISacha Baron CohenComedy filmsComedyTime magazinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Popcorn with your Puccini: can opera on screen ever work?  | Music | The Guardian
description: Composers have harnessed TV and cinema since Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors pulled in five million viewers 75 years ago but for my money Kombat Opera’s satire showed us how to do it best
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Composers have harnessed TV and cinema since Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors pulled in five million viewers 75 years ago but for my money Kombat Opera’s satire showed us how to do it best
Content: ‘There are huge gains in seeing close up what the singers are doing as actors’ … people watch Madame Butterfly, projected live in Times Square, New York, in 2006.Photograph: Dima Gavrysh/APView image in fullscreen‘There are huge gains in seeing close up what the singers are doing as actors’ … people watch Madame Butterfly, projected live in Times Square, New York, in 2006.Photograph: Dima Gavrysh/APTom Service on musicMusicPopcorn with your Puccini: can opera on screen ever work?Tom ServiceComposers have harnessed TV and cinema since Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors pulled in five million viewers 75 years ago but for my money Kombat Opera’s satire showed us how to do it bestWed 21 Oct 2026 11.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.17 EDTShareIt’s not even Halloween, but here’s an operatic Christmas story for you. This is the 75th anniversary of the first opera made for television: Gian Carlo Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors, broadcast at Yuletide in 1951 and watched by five million people across the US in a production sponsored by Hallmark.You can watch the original broadcast on YouTube: it was introduced with wit, self-deprecation and early 50s elegance by Menotti himself (vastly less charmingly, the role of King Balthazar was played by a singer in blackface). Chet Allen’s performance as the boy, Amahl, is staggering, and even more moving is Rosemary Kuhlmann’s Mother, especially in her aria, All That gold!.Amahl is “an opera for children because it tries to recapture my own childhood”, Menotti said. It was played on US TV every Christmastime throughout the 50s, and was recorded and remade in new productions the next decade, while the BBC picked it up in 1953, and there was even an Australian TV version. Less than an hour long, Menotti’s festive fable works because of the intimacy of its story, and its refusal to patronise its intended audience.View image in fullscreenPatronising-free: the 1963 made-for-TV production of Carlo Menotti’s Amahl and the Night VisitorsPhotograph: No creditBut Amahl was a high-water mark. Another opera-made for-telly anniversary this year isBenjamin Britten’s Owen Wingrave, composed for the BBC and first broadcast 55 years ago. Britten’s piece definitely wasn’t made for children. Based on a gothic novella by Henry James, it’s the story of the pacifist Owen Wingrave’s struggles against his military forebears and his fiancee who is ashamed of him. Britten’s opera is uncompromisingly claustrophobic and intense, one of his most underrated scores – but it’s a piece that wasn’t designed to capture Amahl’s popularity on screen.The later story of operas made for TV in Britain is more about exploration of the possibilities of the medium rather than following in Menotti’s audience-first footsteps: in the 90s and 00s there are pieces composed for TV includingJudith Weir’s Armidaor Jonathan Dove’sWhen She Died …, written on the fifth anniversary of the death of Princess Diana, and there were filmed productions of existing operas especially remade for television, such as the director Margaret Williams’s scintillating versions of Thomas Adès’sPowder Her Faceor her version ofBritten’s Owen Wingrave, produced for Channel 4 in 2001 to mark the opera’s 30th anniversary.These days, opera is more often found on the big screen: cinemas all over the world can take you to a night at the opera, and here’s another anniversary for you – this autumn marks 20 years since theMetropolitan Opera started streaming its productions to cinemas, an innovation that the Royal Opera House in London quickly followed, finding new audiences, as well as a parallel stream of income and impact.View image in fullscreenThe mechanics of opera work through the other end of the telescope … Madame Butterfly in Times Square, New York, in 2006.Photograph: Dima Gavrysh/APThe Met: Live in HD has been controversial: Peter Gelb, the Met’s general manager suggested in 2013 that the cinema audiences were “cannibalising” the audience for live shows; but surely, from Japan to Brazil, and here in the UK, these broadcastsreach opera-loverswho are unable to go to the Met in person.On cinema screens there are huge gains in seeing close up what the singers are doing as actors, subtleties of facial expression and the relationships between the characters on stage that you can’t pick up when you are sitting at the back of the gallery. But the essential problem with broadcasting live opera on any screen remains the same as it was in 1951. We are watching performers who are projecting through the acoustic miracles of their voices into an auditorium that seats thousands.The intimacy of film, and especially TV, requires precisely the opposite mode of delivery. In drama on TV or film, the wonder and the illusion lies in sharing an intimacy of space and feeling with the actors, whereas the mechanics of opera work through the other end of the telescope, zooming out from their voices towards us in the audience, rather than zooming us in to be with them in each scene.Operaand film are essentially made for entirely different purposes.But if you do want to see what happens when opera is made for television from the ground up, there’s another anniversary to tell you about: it has been 19 years since Richard Thomas’s Kombat Opera Presents, half-hour shows broadcast in 2007 that sent up TV staples fromThe Apprenticeto theSouth Bank – Bragg! – Show. Thomas was hot on the heels of the success of his theatre show with Stewart Lee -Jerry Springer: The Opera, but the origins of Kombat Opera also go back to sketches in Simon Munnery’s Attention Scum series that aired on the BBC in 2001, with the soprano and contemporary music catalyst Loré Lixenberg, who made a new art-formdressed as a gothic uber-diva, filmed on the white cliffs of Kent.Lixenberg, and trained singers including Leigh Melrose, Janis Kelly and Sophia Ragavelas made every half-hour long episode of Kombat Opera their own, but it’s the way Thomas included parts for actors including Kevin Eldon, Hugh Dennis and Jon Culshaw, and mixed all the media together, that makes these shows so compelling.The format never feels as if it is selling either medium short: the heightened emotionalising and ridiculousness of opera serves the satire perfectly, joyously and concisely. Seems opera on screen works best when its turns its attention to the screen itself.***Talking of taking the artform into new places, Raymond Gubbay celebrates his 80th birthday with the Choir of King’s College, Cambridge atWigmore Hall, Londontonight. Gubbay’s Classical Spectaculars, his Christmas shows, his operas at the Royal Albert Hall – which included flooding the arena with 65,000 litres water every night for Puccini’s Madame Butterfly, a Turandot at Wembley Arena in collaboration with the Royal Opera House, and even hisSavoy Opera venture, a brave but doomed attempt to make repertory opera work in the West End without subsidy, are some of the most brilliant, energetic, and imaginative ways of popularising classical music over the last 60 years.View image in fullscreenSubsidy-free business model:  Raymond Gubbay, photographed for the Guardian in 2015.Photograph: David Sillitoe/The GuardianTo make large-scale classical music profitable is a vanishingly rare phenomenon. (Even if, while it’s true to say that as a business, Gubbay never took a penny from any Arts Council, most of the musicians and orchestras he worked with wouldn’t exist without it.) Gubbay’s 80th birthday concert will give its profits to another now Arts Council-free organisation, Wigmore Hall itself. Gubbay’s subsidy-free business model remains an impossible dream for most, but Wigmore Hall is an unlikely contemporary torchbearer for the same spirit of entrepreneurship.This week Tom has been listening to:Anna Meredith’s Dusky, the single from her new album.You know that feeling when you’re on the summit of the rollercoaster Stealth at Thorpe Park, and there’s that microsecond where your heart’s in your mouth before the drop? Dusky is like six and a half minutes spent in that place of delirious freefall, as rhythms grind against each other, melodic arcs rising and falling, to make time warp and your stomach pitch and yaw.Explore more on these topicsMusicTom Service on musicClassical musicOperacommentShareReuse this content

title: Why has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shaped | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Ibrahim Mahama put an entire factory in this exhibition exploring Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism. And it’s just one dazzling installation in a show full of hope
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: Ibrahim Mahama put an entire factory in this exhibition exploring Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism. And it’s just one dazzling installation in a show full of hope
Content: Not left to rot … parts of an old bottle factory appearing in Ibrahim Mahama: The Harvest Season, Fondation Cartier, Paris.Photograph: Benoit FougeirolView image in fullscreenNot left to rot … parts of an old bottle factory appearing in Ibrahim Mahama: The Harvest Season, Fondation Cartier, Paris.Photograph: Benoit FougeirolArt and designReviewWhy has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shapedFondation Cartier, ParisIbrahim Mahama put an entire factory in this exhibition exploring Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism. And it’s just one dazzling installation in a show full of hopeEddy FrankelWed 21 Oct 2026 08.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 08.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIbrahim Mahamahas dug through the ruins of post-colonial Ghana, sorted through the ashes of its ancient history, picked through the industrial detritus, the corporate waste, the piles of rubbish, and found something pretty unique: hope.View image in fullscreenIbrahim Mahama, pictured at the Barbican Centre, London, in 2025.Photograph: Christian Cassiel/Barbican CentreSit on one of the Asante stools in his circular Parliament of Ghosts and you can almost feel a new future being worked out right in front of you. It’s the first installation in this huge exhibition at the Fondation Cartier inParis, and it sums Mahama up pretty neatly. He’s looking at the collapse of the Ghanaian government in 1966, the way the hope of the post-colonial project was crushed in a military coup, and he’s looking at ancient Ghanaian history, at the empires that fell centuries ago and the way colonialism tore them to shreds. But he’s not lamenting any of them. He’s not mourning. Instead, he’s reclaiming them, asking how things can be rebuilt, how we can move forwards by learning from the past.And he does it over and over. In 2024 he bought an old bottle factory – a symbol of industry and its collapse. He’s rebuilt it here, in the centre of Paris. Its steel roof beams, rusted and crumbling, reach up to the ceiling, its walls are lined with thousands of green bottles in Coca-Cola, Schweppes, Kool and Club Minerals crates. It’s a whole history of manufacturing, of commerce in WestAfricapost-independence. Not left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new.View image in fullscreenNot left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new … Parliament of Ghosts by Ibrahim Mahama.Photograph: Benoit FougeirolNearby, he’s taken some of those bottles and piled them around a collection of local pottery. The industrial meets the artisanal, two lost arts creating a new one.But this huge show isn’t really about Mahama, it’s about the people around him. Most of the work here is by nine other artists and collectives. Mahama runs three art centres near Tamale inGhana, giving time, space and opportunities to local artists. Their work is given priority here, alongside art by his mentors and collaborators. He’s taken this massive exhibition opportunity and used it as a chance to celebrate his community. It’s almost as if he’s trying to make the rest of us feel bad.Way up on the top floor, a long scroll of jute and bark byDorothy Akpene Amenukeundulates across the floor. If it looks like Mahama’s work, it should: she was his art teacher back in 2013. Knowledge, and the past, gets reconfigured and reshaped once again.Nearby, the wall of a farmhouse has been built by artist and architectCourage Dzidula Kpodoout of red earth clay, a material lost as modernism brought in concrete. Now, historic methods become a kind of resistance, a symbol of tradition’s ability to endure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHistoric methods as a kind of resistance … an artwork from Ibrahim Mahama’s The Harvest Season, Fondation Cartier, Paris.Photograph: Benoit FougeirolThose core ideas get repeated through pretty much every presentation here. Influential 97-year-old photographerJames Barnorcaptures the communities around Mahama in large format, grainy Polaroids.Gideon Appah’s hazy, dream-like paintings imagine fictional Ghanaian youths staring out to sea, congregating on beaches in utopian, idealised visions of the country’s past. Some of the works are absolutely stunning, like Peter Doig and Noah Davis transported to Accra.The best work, appropriately enough, isn’t by one artist but a collective. On the top floor, a bunch of lumpy, surreal sculptures of birds, bodies and men wrestling bulls is by theCongolese Plantation Workers Art League (CATPC). Each one is made of chocolate, sculpted in the DRC but poured into moulds in Amsterdam. Everything they make from selling the art goes towards buying back land confiscated in the early 20th century by the Lever Brothers, who we now know as Unilever. The work is a whole conversation about global trade taking place in sculptural form, an act of resistance and reclamation through chocolate.This exhibition is essentially an ambitious, ultra-idealistic group show of West African art. It is art exhibition as political utopianism. Which is great, even if not everything in it is good. And the real draw is Mahama, with his archival approach to monumental installation art, and it’s a shame to not get a load more of it.Mahama has sacrificed himself for the greater good, basically. But this collaborative approach is the point: he’s saying collective action, community, togetherness, that’s how we’ll build a future. It might sound a bit cloying and earnest, but then you see the results, you see the art and the ideas, you see the community and the hope and the idealism and you eventually say: “Get me a one-way ticket to Accra. I’m in.”Ibrahim Mahama: The Harvest Season is atFondation Cartier, Paris, from 22 October to 28 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designInstallationExhibitionsGhanaColonialismAfricaArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He had this electrical charge’: the short life and long legacy of Jason Molina, master of Americana | Music | The Guardian
description: As a documentary celebrates the late US musician, friends and collaborators describe an incomparable storyteller who brought ‘myth and magic to everyday life’
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: As a documentary celebrates the late US musician, friends and collaborators describe an incomparable storyteller who brought ‘myth and magic to everyday life’
Content: ‘These are all time country songs’ … Jason Molina performing as The Magnolia Electric Co at All Tomorrows Parties in 2007.Photograph: Gary Wolstenholme/RedfernsView image in fullscreen‘These are all time country songs’ … Jason Molina performing as The Magnolia Electric Co at All Tomorrows Parties in 2007.Photograph: Gary Wolstenholme/RedfernsMusic‘He had this electrical charge’: the short life and long legacy of Jason Molina, master of AmericanaAs a documentary celebrates the late US musician, friends and collaborators describe an incomparable storyteller who brought ‘myth and magic to everyday life’Daniel Dylan WrayWed 21 Oct 2026 11.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJason Molina grew up in a trailer in the working-class city of Lorain, Ohio. The city’s skyline once flickered with blue flames and a warm orange glow emanated from clattering steel mills, but by Molina’s teenage years, Lorain was in a tailspin. “Things were really on the economic decline,” says Tommy Nickoloff, Molina’s childhood friend and director of a new documentary: You Fuckers Figure It Out: A Jason Molina Story. “Nobody had any money and we were encouraged to get out. It’s a place where the American dream was born and died. And we watched it die.”Molina did indeed get out: the singer-songwriter released almost 20 studio albums and numerous EPs, primarily under the monikers Songs: Ohia and Magnolia Electric Co, spanning lo-fi to slowcore via polishedAmericanaand alt-country. By 2009, he estimated he had written thousands of songs. But he died in 2013, aged 39, after years of alcoholism.View image in fullscreen‘It still shocks me how few people are aware of Jason and his legacy’ … Tommy Nickoloff.Photograph: Courtesy Tommy NickoloffThe documentary is a warm and intimate look back on Molina’s early life and how his rust belt upbringing, along with notions of home, place and landscape, became recurring themes in his bountiful songs. The audience for them has kept growing after his death: there’s been a biography, cover albums, a touring tribute band titled Magnolia & Johnson Electric Co made up of ex-bandmates, and he’s got a new generation of fans in Phoebe Bridgers, MJ Lenderman, Clairo, Kevin Morby, Waxahatchee and hyped young singer-songwriters such as Greg Freeman. “You have a moment with a handful of artists in your life where you hear their music and it clicks and you immediately fall in love,” says Freeman. “That happened with Jason’s music.”But this wasn’t always the case. “It still shocks me how few people are aware of Jason and his legacy, especially around home,” says Nickoloff, recalling a 2006 show in nearby Cleveland that drew just 70 people.When Songs: Ohia started in the mid-1990s, it was via lo-fi skeletal songs recorded to tape that were tender yet raw and delivered with a quivering high tenor reminiscent of Neil Young and soon-to-be collaborator Will Oldham. As grunge and alt-rock boomed, Molina went against the grain. “There was nothing less cool than a ukulele in 1994,” laughs his former bandmate Max Winter in the film. “Holy shit, he may as well have been playing bagpipes.”But Molina was unique from a young age. A voracious reader as a child, he consumed everything from instruction manuals to foreign language poetry. His teenage years were spent as a metalhead and by the time he was at college, his fervent, enthusiastic – sometimes annoying – energy earned him the nickname “sparky”. Now writing a song a day, he would sometimes play impromptu 5am shows on a roof or porch to show them off. “I’ve never met anyone like him,” says Nickoloff. “He’s like a 20-sided die in Dungeons and Dragons. Most people are lucky if they have six sides.”Chris Swanson, co-founder of record label Secretly Canadian, heard Molina’s first single, Nor Cease Thou Never Now, and was besotted. “We obsessively played it and drove 19 hours to New York to go see him,” he says. Songs: Ohia was the label’s second ever signing and a lifelong relationship began. “Without him there would be no us – plain and simple,” the label said after his death. A pattern of releasing at least an album a year followed, including 2000’s The Lioness, in which he decamped to Scotland to work with Alasdair Roberts and members of Arab Strap on a ghostly yet beautiful record of post-rock-folk-blues.Emma Niblett, who performs as Scout Niblett, was a friend, collaborator and touring partner of Molina’s. “He had this electrical charge around him, which matched his nickname,” she recalls. “And he had this ability to bring myth and magic to everyday life as a master of storytelling. You never quite knew if his stories were true or fantasy or a bit of both.”The late producer Steve Albini, who worked with Molina, also recalled this blurring of truths. “He was a big bullshitter,” Albini said in 2014. “A lot of the things that he said were fantastic and it seemed like he wanted things to be magical and awesome, and that he needed to create fables for himself to inhabit in order to do that.” Swanson describes this unusual quirk as “the elephant in every room with Jason”, adding: “He was just a consummate storyteller and if that meant him saying he was bitten by a tarantula which ended up quasi-paralysing him, then that’s the story.”This seeped into his songwriting too: Molina’s obsession with ghosts and hauntings added an otherworldly element to his work. “The songs belong in his own secret world,” says Freeman. “There’s an internal logic and language to his songwriting, the way motifs reappear and build this imaginary psychic place. Like he’s painting a dream.” Niblett describes him as “a magician”, “incomparable” and “a one-off, playing in a major league by himself”.In 2003, Molina released his magnum opus, Songs: Ohia’s The Magnolia Electric Co (confusingly, the name of the album then became the name of the band afterwards). Mike Brenner’s stunning, shimmering lap steel is all over the record. “When I was sent the demos, I was stunned by how much of a quantum leap it was,” he says of the progress from the previous record. “It sounded like a whole different game.” Swanson felt similarly. “You can hear it in the demos but when they made the album, it just became effervescent,” he says. “The songs had stepped up by a full magnitude of order and they just sounded timeless. It was like, holy shit! These are all-time country songs.”View image in fullscreen‘Supernatural powers’ … Jason Molina on stage at Primavera Sound in 2009.Photograph: Jordi Vidal/RedfernsProduced by Albini, with a full band, it was a lightning in a bottle moment for all involved. “The most otherworldly experience I’ve ever had in a studio,” says Niblett. “It felt like some supernatural powers were present. His writing felt like pure channelling. It was so clear, vulnerable, yet insightful, and undeniable. We all knew that something special was occurring.”However, changing your name halfway through your career is not an ideal scenario to help boost your profile. “It was very tricky,” says Swanson. “And this was also during the era when he’d go on tour and not play any songs from the album he’d just released, and only play ones that no one’s heard before.” Molina was driven, prolific, and at times stubborn and impatient: “He wasn’t super interested in doing things twice,” says Brenner.He was also capricious, says Brenner, which Swanson also recalls. “Very generous, sometimes to his own detriment,” he says. “He’d be like, ‘I just gave away our guarantee [fee] for the show to someone on the street who looked hungry.’ He would do very irrational things out of a generous impulse.”Molina continued to release albums and EPs at a remarkable pace but by the end of the 2000s things slowed down. “The later it got in the story, the more stressful and darker the touring became,” says Brenner. “It became less enjoyable and I don’t think the quality of the shows were at the forefront of his mind.” Niblett recalls seeing a change when watching him perform. “He seemed to slowly disappear,” she says. “Although he was present on stage, his presence diminished. He started leaning on the band to take the weight, so his powerful, unique, and nuanced way of carrying a song was fading. I could hear and see he had lost himself. He was literally hiding behind his band in the later years.”Unbeknown to many, Molina had begun to drink heavily. “He was a very light drinker in his 20s,” says Swanson. “But in his 30s, he went whole hog.” This eventually led to debilitating alcoholism that meant he retreated and stopped releasing music in 2009. The last four years of his life are described by his family as “pure chaos” in the documentary. For those who knew the young Molina, “it was unbelievable,” says Nickoloff. “It made zero sense. To the degree it was like: I don’t know anybody else named Jason Molina but they have to be talking about that person.”‘His ache is real’: Bob Dylan and more on the wild genius of honky-tonk hellraiser Gary StewartRead moreSwanson recalls visiting him a few months before his death in Indianapolis. “He had given away all his belongings, which was something he would do routinely,” he says. “So he was living in a shell. We made the decision to move him to Bloomington, where he had more of a community, as his community was with street people in Indianapolis around the projects he was living in.”But a week after that decision was made, Molina died of organ failure related to his alcoholism. “I honestly wouldn’t have believed it if you’d have told me years earlier that’s how his life would end,” says Niblett. “I don’t think the shock ever leaves.”Despite being a heartache of enormous magnitude, for Nickoloff it ended up changing his life in numerous ways. “Jason’s death saved my life,” he says. “I was in a terrible spot emotionally and psychologically. He’d always been this beacon for me, and then he’s gone. But as a kid he was the only voice that was encouraging and believed in me to do something. So, in that spirit, we made this film and what a tremendous pleasure it is to be a small vehicle in helping make people more familiar with him, his work and his life. He was my homeboy.”You Fuckers Figure It Out: A Jason Molina Story premieres 25 October (Rio Cinema) and 8 November (ICA) at London’s Doc’n Roll film festivalExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockIndieMusic documentaryAmericanafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Standup Jon Richardson on turning his dark teenage diaries into a tearjerking memoir: ‘I couldn’t sugarcoat those years’ | Jon Richardson | The Guardian
description: While facing grief, illness and a very public breakup, the comic reached for his diaries – and found a happy kid who spiralled into despair. Inspired by a Nobel laureate, he wrote a frank, funny book about that boy and what he grew into
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: While facing grief, illness and a very public breakup, the comic reached for his diaries – and found a happy kid who spiralled into despair. Inspired by a Nobel laureate, he wrote a frank, funny book about that boy and what he grew into
Content: ‘I have accumulated a horrific amount of paraphernalia from my own back story’ … Jon Richardson now and during his younger years.Composite: Ray Burmiston; SphereView image in fullscreen‘I have accumulated a horrific amount of paraphernalia from my own back story’ … Jon Richardson now and during his younger years.Composite: Ray Burmiston; SphereJon RichardsonInterviewStandup Jon Richardson on turning his dark teenage diaries into a tearjerking memoir: ‘I couldn’t sugarcoat those years’Brian LoganWhile facing grief, illness and a very public breakup, the comic reached for his diaries – and found a happy kid who spiralled into despair. Inspired by a Nobel laureate, he wrote a frank, funny book about that boy and what he grew intoWed 21 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt begins on Christmas Day, 1996: “It’s been a lovely day … I realised how much I love my family.” It ends three years later: “I’m lying on the floor in floods of tears and all I want to do is die.” Say what you like about adolescence but it is nothing if not an emotional tumult. “If I’d known as a teenager,” saysthe comedian Jon Richardsonruefully, “that I’d one day write a book about them, I couldn’t have bookended my teenage diaries with better quotes to show what a storm of shit those years can be.”The book is The Teenage Diaries of a Stand-Up Comedian, and it has been two years in the making. Two years that, if not quite the hormonal rollercoaster the book itself records, have been quite the ride. The project is borne of a crossroads moment in the Lancashire man’s midlife, after he experienced bereavement, serious illness among family and friends, and the breakdown of his marriage to fellow comic Lucy Beaumont. The last was an inevitably very public ending, splayed across the tabloids, to a relationship which itself played out in public, courtesy of the couple’s acclaimed mockumentary about their domestic arrangements,Meet the Richardsons.double quotation markIt’s a handbook – a way to make sure your kids don’t turn into me“There was a lot going on,” he recalls, “some of which called for self-reflection, and some that was completely beyond my control – to do with getting to a certain age, when the people around you get frailer, and you start looking differently at your relationships with your parents and your own childhood. So I was in quite a reflective period anyway.” But in Richardson’s case, there was a specific focus for that reflection. “I have genuinely accumulated a horrific amount of paraphernalia from my own back story,” he says. An inveterate hoarder, the 44-year-old had cupboards full of detritus (ticket stubs, photos, certificates, VHS videos, letters and emails – and of course, his teenage diaries) salvaged from the early years of his life.View image in fullscreenA relationship that played out in public … Richardson and his then wife, Lucy Beaumont, in 2019.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian“I felt like there must be a reason I’ve kept it,” says Richardson. “And perhaps the reason is that, one day, if you’re lucky enough to have the time, you can work out: what is of meaning, why did you keep certain things, what can you afford to get rid of? That’s the journey of the book really. It’s in the present tense because it documents me doing the reflecting and the clearing out. But it’s about those first 20 years and how much of them you carry over.”While writing, the comic deep-dived into teenage memoirs fromRae Earl’s My Fat, Mad Teenage Diary, via the works of Nobel prize winnerAnnie Ernaux(thanked by Richardson in the acknowledgements), to the recentComing of Age: How Adolescence Shapes Usby psychologist Lucy Foulkes. The resulting book may not be the one you’d expect from the neurotic standup once branded “the nation’s favourite worrier”, or from the team captain on Channel 4’s 8 Out of 10 Cats, or even from the presenter of popular documentaries about OCD. This is not a book to nestle snugly in the humour section of Waterstones, nor one that jauntily glosses the anxieties of adolescence.“I’m always very aware my job is to make people laugh,” says Richardson, “and I hope there is plenty of humour in the book.” There is. Its structure – diary extracts followed by grownup Jon reflecting ruthlessly thereupon – offers Richardson endless opportunities for entertaining self-abasement. And there is nostalgic delight to be had in the period detail: “Blockbuster video, Tupperware parties and Ann Summers.” And there is droll dramatic irony too, as per Richardson’s favourite entry, aged 14, apropos of nothing: “I’ve decided that although I’ll probably end up being a teacher, I’d love to be a comedian.”double quotation markA lot of kids just need to be told that it’s OK to be sad or strugglingHe says now: “But in terms of the emotions, I couldn’t sugarcoat what those years were. Very few people become comedians because they’re well-adjusted and just want to spread joy in the world. Going back to the 60s and 70s, and those people who now have BBC Four documentaries made about them, people tend to come to comedy through having unscratched itches, or to make amends for some shortcoming in themselves. And I’m no different.”In the book, we follow Richardson’s teenage self from 14 to 17. “I think I watched Zack Morris on [the sitcom]Saved By the Bell,” he recalls, “and thought, ‘Oh, teenagers are supposed to keep secret diaries.’ But those early entries don’t have anything to say. I’m in my room playing Mario Kart most of the time.” At first, teenage Jon comes across as kind, bright, tentatively happy. But as time passes, his diary increasingly records a sense of isolation, frustration and low self-worth. He goes to a single-sex school. He feels ugly. He is growing up in a town – Morecambe, Lancashire – that seems to him like the dead-end back of beyond. His parents are separated and, in a book that is eloquent on poverty and class, money is tight.View image in fullscreenIn a stir … Richardson on The Great Celebrity Bake Off in March.Photograph: Laura Palmer/Channel 4These are all factors in Richardson’s spiral into a dark place. “There were an awful lot of happy times that I never wrote about,” he insists. But “very quickly the diary becomes a place to put the emotions that you don’t want to burden other people with, a place where you only talk about the struggle. It can become quite unhealthy.” In the book’s final chapter – ring-fenced from the earlier material, says Richardson, because it’s hard to be funny about – diary entries show teenage Jon considering suicide.In 2023, alongside the former athlete Jessica Ennis-Hill and broadcaster Dan Walker, Richardson launchedBright Young Dreams, a fundraising campaign to support youth mental health – into which he will “put more of my energy over the next few years than anything else”. When I ask what might have made life more bearable for junior Jon, he would not, he replies, have changed any of the material circumstances of that boy’s life. What would have helped, he says, is “some understanding that it’s OK to be struggling and to be sad. A lot of kids just need to be told that, yes, itisreally hard, thesearedifficult years”.As the parent myself of a boy on the precipice of his teens, the book terrified me about what’s in store – while rallying my resolve to care for him through it. “If nothing else,” says the comic, “consider this a handbook for parents to make sure their kids don’t turn into Jon Richardson! That is a great gift I bestow on the nation.” But if his book offers a sobering reminder of the trials of teenagedom, it is also very affecting on family love. Its heroes, alongside the foundering teen centre-stage, are Richardson’s mum, dad and sister.“You can’t talk about those years without bringing other people’s lives into it,” he says. “My main concern was protecting the privacy of people who haven’t chosen to write a book.” But his loved ones, off the page as on it, have been unstintingly supportive. “I write about my dad’s depression in the book, and I had to say to him, ‘Do you mind if I tell that story?’ And he said: ‘You do what you want to do.’” That conversation, says Richardson, was easy. Far harder for this working-class northern male was having to address his family about – ugh – their love for one another. Towards the end of the book, he reprints an email from his sister, sent at a fragile time of Jon’s life, that is so trenchant and loving in its support of her wee brother, that I couldn’t read it without welling up.View image in fullscreen‘Now I take a difficult emotion and, instead of blurting it out on a page, I convert it into punchlines’ … Richardson performing in 2015.Photograph: Publicity image“It had the same impact on me,” says Richardson. “But my sister doesn’t know yet that it’s in the book. I haven’t been able to have that conversation. It’s easier to just put it in and not talk about it. ‘I love you. It’s in a book, so it’s a fact. Bye!’”Now living a life his teenaged self could scarcely have dreamed of, is Richardson still keeping a diary? He is not – give or take the purely factual records he keeps, in an array of journals behind his head on our Zoom call, of his every gig since taking up standup in 2003. Grownup friendships and counselling have all supplanted the role diaries once played in his life. “They ended,” he says, because “I started going to the pub and hanging out with people.” And then he discovered standup, which was “transformative”.“My approach to standup has always been: ‘How do I feel at this moment, and how do I package it in a way that’s interesting and amusing?’ It’s like a house conversion, like walking into a dilapidated wreck and turning it into something presentable. I take a difficult emotion and, instead of blurting it out on a page, I get to talk to people every night who’ve had similar experiences, and convert it into punchlines. And I can see people laughing and having a good night because I’ve confronted this emotion. And that,” says the tormented teenager, the teacher manqué turned comic and now memoirist, “has done wonders for my wellbeing.”The Teenage Diaries of a Stand-Up Comedian by Jon Richardson (Little, Brown Book Group, £25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.In the UK and IrelandSamaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineis at 988 or chat for support. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsJon RichardsonAutobiography and memoirComedyTV comedyTelevisioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: As fans reject AI-generated music, even boosters are drawing the line | Music | The Guardian
description: Enthusiasts like Grimes and A$AP Rocky may embrace AI-generated content, but they won’t produce it themselves
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Enthusiasts like Grimes and A$AP Rocky may embrace AI-generated content, but they won’t produce it themselves
Content: Grimes and A$AP Rocky.Composite: Getty imagesView image in fullscreenGrimes and A$AP Rocky.Composite: Getty imagesMusicAnalysisAs fans reject AI-generated music, even boosters are drawing the lineBlake MontgomeryEnthusiasts like Grimes and A$AP Rocky may embrace AI-generated content, but they won’t produce it themselvesWed 21 Oct 2026 09.22 EDTFirst published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTShareStreaming services, notable musicians and fans are confronting the growing presence of AI-generated music and drawing lines in the sand.On Tuesday,Spotifyannounced it had removed about 50m songs consideredAIslop from its recommendations to users over the past year.“Our editors hold the same standard and don’t program content identified as slop or spam,” a statement from the company read.Spotifyrequires “AI persona” badges on artist profiles that don’t represent a real human being, but it does not require individual songs generated by AI to be labeled. Other streaming services have taken more stringent stances.Though it is cracking down on slop tracks, Spotify is far from AI-shy. The company allows users to create playlists with generative AI and has promised a tool for making AI-generated remixes and cover songs.Cyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’Read moreUnable to ignore the tide, even early AI boosters like the singer and producerGrimes, former paramour of Elon Musk and mother to three of his 14 children, have declared their limits on allowable amounts of AI. She and other musicians say they are open to AI-generated music but wary.Fans, by contrast, have little tolerance for it. They are voting with millions of streams against artifice in music. Songs and albums harkening back to analogue instrumentation are dominating the Billboard charts, no futurism wanted.Both A$AP Rocky, rapper and partner to Rihanna, and Grimes have taken the same position: accepting AI-generated music but not making it.“I prefer to do things myself, practically,” A$AP Rocky toldBillboard: “If somebody does a totally AI-generated song where all they did was prompt something, then I think that’s their thing. But who am I to say what’s standard and what’s not? I’m just doing me out here, and I’m doing my music practically – the right way.”Kelly Clarkson similarly outlined her own boundary while expressing enthusiasm for AI.“I love AI. Controversial, I don’t care,” she told the Las Culturistas podcast. “Here’s the thing, I love AI. There are very amazing things with AI that I’m obsessed with. But also, and I’m very into it artistically too, I have fun with it just like everybody else does. But when you see AI artists competing on a chart with humans, I have an issue. I think there should be a separate chart.”Grimes, one of my own favorite musicians, has begun promoting her first new album in six years, Psy Opera, which she described tothe Paris Reviewas capturing the “emotion of being thrust into the future”.Stereogumdescribed the album as “AI-inspired but not AI-generated”, citing Grimes’s own insistence that her team of 70 be credited rather than reduced to machines.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGrimes offered a free license of her own voice to AI enthusiasts to make what they would three years ago. That she declined to generate her own music indicates that, even to a futurist like her, AI-generated music is lacking, similar to Rocky’s stance.I have also found myself listening to an AI-generated song, Bomboclat Wallahi, brought to my attention viafrenetic, overstimulatingvideoson Instagram. Despite the song’s comical sonic maximalism, it lacks any staying power. Listening to it the day after I first heard it left no impression, similar to the way low-quality food leaves me hungry again just a few hours after eating. “Slop” is still the best word to describe AI-made content.In contrast with artists’ nuanced stances, fans are making their position on tech-made music clear: they don’t want it.Billboard’s chartsof the most popular albums and charts of the past week showcase a preference for music without obvious modification. Songs and albums that feature a simple voice-and-guitar arrangement are dominating. On the Top 200 album charts, most of the Top 10 albums foreground a singer over analogue instrumentation – Olivia Rodrigo’s You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, Ella Langley’s Dandelion, Olivia Dean’s The Art of Loving, Taylor Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl, Noah Kahan’s The Great Divide and Stick Season, and Morgan Wallen’s I’m the Problem. In the Hot 100 singles chart, the top four songs bear the same sonic signatures: Swift’s Patient Zero, Langley’s Choosin’ Texas, Stella Lefty’s Boston, Wallen’s Been by Now.Incredibly, the Beatles’ Rubber Soul, released in 1965, also made an appearance at No 4 on last week’s Billboard rankings. Some listeners want to return to a time when producing music with artificial intelligence wasn’t even an option.Explore more on these topicsMusicAI (artificial intelligence)SpotifyGrimesA$AP RockyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: UK cinemas report ‘bonkers’ demand for documentary You Can See Everything | You Can See Everything | The Guardian
description: Tickets for film about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes said to be selling out after $15m opening weekend in the US
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Tickets for film about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes said to be selling out after $15m opening weekend in the US
Content: Film-maker Nathan Fielder, left, and Elizabeth Holmes, centre, in a scene from You Can See Everything.Photograph: A24/APView image in fullscreenFilm-maker Nathan Fielder, left, and Elizabeth Holmes, centre, in a scene from You Can See Everything.Photograph: A24/APYou Can See EverythingUK cinemas report ‘bonkers’ demand for documentary You Can See EverythingTickets for film about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes said to be selling out after $15m opening weekend in the USNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 21 Oct 2026 09.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the film everyone seems to be talking about, spawning memes and fuelling feverish online debate about its subject, thedisgraced Theranos founderElizabeth Holmes.Now, a month before Nathan Fielder’s documentaryYou Can See Everythingreaches UK cinemas, tickets for screenings are already selling out after its remarkable $15m (£11.3m) opening weekend in the US.Clare Binns, the creative director of Picturehouse Cinemas, said the excitement was reminiscent of the response to Greta Gerwig’s Barbie, which became a global box-office phenomenon in 2023.“People are hungry in a way that we haven’t really seen since then,” she said. “And for it to be a three-hour documentary, it’s bonkers.”View image in fullscreenElizabeth Holmes is questioned by Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24Tickets for the film, which opens in the UK on 20 November, went on sale at Picturehouse Central in London before its US opening, Binns said, and demand has prompted the chain to add extra screenings. At the Ritzy in Brixton, the first screen had almost sold out, leading the cinema to sell tickets for a showing at a second.“It’s fantastic, it proves again that there’s a different kind of audience coming to the cinema,” Binns said. “They came to see Backrooms, they came to see Obsession, they cameto see NAZA.“There’s a real appetite for smart films that talk to an audience differently than the studios have talked to them before. With this documentary, you’ve got a story that has been mined to some extent with the Dropout and podcasts. But I think the fact that Nathan Fielder spent a month withElizabeth Holmesis a huge draw. He’s a smart guy, and audiences want something they can relate to.”Cineworld has also reported strong demand. Stuart Crane, its international vice-president of content, said “the speed and scale of demand has been remarkable”.Initial screenings at Cineworld Leicester Square sold out after tickets went on sale at about 40 cinemas on Sunday. The chain has since added more screenings at Leicester Square and expanded bookings to a further 35 cinemas nationwide.Vue has reported similar excitement. Dean Cross, its senior screen content manager, said it was “seeing incredible buzz both within the industry and amongst cinemagoers”, and it was “particularly encouraging to see a documentary capturing the attention of younger audiences”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes at a federal prison camp in Bryan, Texas.Photograph: Adrees Latif/ReutersThe momentum forYou Can See Everythinghas been building since it was unveiled at a secret screening at the Telluride film festival in Colorado in September, where audiences were required to surrender their phones. A teaser trailer released the same day quickly went viral, with Holmes herself joining the online conversation, responding to tweets about the film and its trailer.Co-directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the film has won widespread critical acclaim. The Guardian described it as “a modern masterpiece of deceit”, praising its unsettling exploration of Holmes and the blurred boundaries between documentary and performance.Its US opening was the biggest for a documentary in more than 20 years, with more than 2,000 screenings selling out at 855 cinemas. More than 70% of its opening-weekend audience was under 35.“People want to enjoy films in a cinema with other people,” Binns said. “The younger demographic want shared experiences. They want to talk about it with their friends, and you can’t do that when you’re sitting on your own watching a TV.“Cinema has been ruled out so many times. Covid, the rise of streamers. Everybody is aware cinema has to change, it has to offer customers something different. But never rule us out.”Explore more on these topicsYou Can See EverythingElizabeth HolmesNathan FielderDocumentary filmsFilm industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: New prize launches for books co-written with AI | Books | The Guardian
description: After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs
Content: Once upon a time … the prize was founded by tech entrepreneurs.Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOnce upon a time … the prize was founded by tech entrepreneurs.Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty ImagesBooksNew prize launches for books co-written with AIAfter months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMsElla CreamerWed 21 Oct 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA prize for AI-written books has launched this week.The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA invites submissions of manuscripts co-written with AI tools, with the winner promised publication.Entrants are asked to submit an unpublished manuscript of between 10,000 and 50,000 words, along with information about which AI model and prompt were used to generate the text. All major language models are allowed, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA. Entrants can be based anywhere, but entries must be submitted in French.The Prix Pascal is named after Blaise Pascal, a French polymath who helped invent one of the first mechanical calculators and also wrote theological texts, including Pensées, which Pope Francispraised forits “philosophical depth and literary charm”.While the terms and conditions ask for a work of fiction, the prize also states that submitted texts should help solve an ethical, social or ecological problem threatening humanity. The prize was founded by Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré, all of whom are technology entrepreneurs.Rodriguez is a founding partner at the mergers and acquisitions advisory firm Avolta, and is described as a “leading figure in the European crypto and blockchain industry” on the company’s website. Serviant is a digital media entrepreneur and former chair of the LGBTQ+ magazine Têtu. Meanwhile, Mentré is a former civil servant with a PhD in philosophy who teaches at Harvard and the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Mentré also co-founded Electis, an online voting platform.The Prix Pascal is launching after months of controversy over the possible use of AI by finalists and winners for a number of literary prizes this year, including theCommonwealth short story prize, theCaine prizeand thePrix Goncourt, France’s most prestigious literary prize.Applications for the Prix Pascal opened on Tuesday, with entrants invited to submit via theprize’s website, and are set to close at the end of November. A shortlist of 10 will be drawn up before the winner is announced in early December. The jury will be made up of a panel of five or six writers, critics, journalists, philosophers and publishers, to be announced early November.Explore more on these topicsBooksAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingAwards and prizesFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: Residents of ‘1066 Country’ lose battle for Bayeux tapestry tickets | Bayeux tapestry | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: East Sussex MP Helena Dollimore says ‘shambolic’ museum phone line has made her constituents lose out to ‘queue jumpers’
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Exclusive: East Sussex MP Helena Dollimore says ‘shambolic’ museum phone line has made her constituents lose out to ‘queue jumpers’
Content: The British Museum says demand has been ‘exceptionally high’ for tickets to see the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe British Museum says demand has been ‘exceptionally high’ for tickets to see the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersBayeux tapestryResidents of ‘1066 Country’ lose battle for Bayeux tapestry ticketsExclusive: East Sussex MP Helena Dollimore says ‘shambolic’ museum phone line has made her constituents lose out to ‘queue jumpers’Helena HortonWed 21 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 08.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHastings residents have missed out on tickets for theBayeux tapestryafter being put on hold for hours by a “glitchy and shambolic” phone system, their MP has said.People from “1066 Country” were promised a chance to buy before a sales line opened to the public on Wednesday. But Helena Dollimore, the MP for Hastings and Rye, said it has been almost impossible for her constituents to get through to theBritish Museum.VIP guests including Maya Jama, Mick Jagger and senior staff at Samsung and Bloomberg have had no such issues gaining access to Bayeux viewings, having attended star-studded events held in the tapestry room since September.Hastings residents were told they could get early access to book the latest release of tickets from Monday this week by calling the British Museum box office and providing proof of their address. But Dollimore said her constituents were left on hold for hours.“Why do my constituents have to work on a glitchy phone line when online booking is clearly possible for others?” she asked.“One person booked after two hours and 38 minutes in the queue, another said he was on hold for two and a half hours.“If you can’t get access right for the people in the place this tapestry tells the story of, you need to sort that out before you start letting people jump the queue.”View image in fullscreenRosanna Konarzewski wears a Bayeux tapestry gown to host a ball at the British Museum on Saturday.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty ImagesCelebrities, businesspeople and politicians flocked to the museum on Saturday for a ball. The guest of honour, tech billionaire Igor Tulchinsky, posed next to Rosanna Konarzewski, a communications executive who was wearing a sweeping ballgown made of a replica Bayeux tapestry. Sources in attendance said that while the general public have been banned from taking pictures of the embroidery, some ball guests managed to photograph it.The Guardian revealed that another tech billionaire, Peter Thiel, wasgiven a VIP tour of the embroidery before it opened to the public. Guests of theOne Aldwych hotelare also allowed to view the tapestry if they book a £1,000-a-night room.Dollimore said: “I had a constituent who waited for hours with her elderly parent who was in her 80s, and they were sent away because of a corporate event. They promised the people of 1066 Country would be able to get access to the tapestry, but seem to be prioritising these corporates.”The MP has unsuccessfully tried to get tickets for herself and her family. “I have been trying since 10am to get through, and even I can’t,” she said.The MP managed to secure access to the tapestry for schoolchildren across Hastings after lobbying the museum. “To be fair to the museum, that has been a success,” she said.Members of the public faced online queues of up to nine hours when tickets went on sale for the first time this summer. There were reports of 40,000 people queueing by mid-morning, with that figure ballooning to almost 80,000 by mid-afternoon.The 70-metre (229ft) tapestry, which is made of linen with embroidered images of events surrounding the Battle of Hastings in 1066, arrived in the UK in July for the first time in nearly 1,000 years.Adult tickets cost £33 in peak hours and £27 at other times, compared with the €12 (£10) fee at the artwork’s home in Bayeux, Normandy.A British Museum spokesperson said: “Demand for the Bayeux tapestry exhibition has been exceptionally high. In recognition of the area’s historic connection to the Battle of Hastings we agreed to offer residents the chance to secure tickets before their wider release.“This offer is not guaranteed access – it is on a first-come, first-served basis in the same way tickets for the exhibition are on sale to our members and the public.“All residents are still able to book tickets as part of the general sale on 21 October and will have further opportunities in the new year when the third tranche of tickets are released.”This article was amended on 21 October 2026. An earlier version incorrectly described Rosanna Konarzewski as the “host” of a Bayeux tapestry ball held at the British Museum.Explore more on these topicsBayeux tapestryBritish MuseumWest SussexMuseumsLondonEnglandHistorynewsShareReuse this content
