title: The New Stanford Prison Experiment review – surely no one believes this insulting TV show is real? | Television | The Guardian
description: This rehash of the notorious study in which volunteers role-play as prisoners and guards pretends to be science. It isn’t – it’s patronising reality television
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: This rehash of the notorious study in which volunteers role-play as prisoners and guards pretends to be science. It isn’t – it’s patronising reality television
Content: ‘The have-nots are given scratchy bunk beds and eat tasteless slop’ … prisoners in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Photograph: Netflix 2026View image in fullscreen‘The have-nots are given scratchy bunk beds and eat tasteless slop’ … prisoners in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Photograph: Netflix 2026TV reviewTelevisionReviewThe New Stanford Prison Experiment review – surely no one believes this insulting TV show is real?This rehash of the notorious study in which volunteers role-play as prisoners and guards pretends to be science. It isn’t – it’s patronising reality televisionJack SealeWed 21 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTelevision has rerun theStanford prison experimentbefore, most notably in 2002 when the BBC aired The Experiment, which advertised itself as a more rigorous version of the stunt where volunteers role-play as prison guards and prisoners. The creator of the original 1971 experiment, Philip Zimbardo, would probably have criticised the new versions to preserve his own status, but the main point he made was valid. These people all know they’re on TV, he said. They’re playing to the cameras.Whether the participants in a behavioural study forget they’re part of a study is an eternal debate point. One of the strengths of the other notorious American people-are-awful research project, theMilgram experiment, was that it made the artifice part of the process, telling the volunteers that they’d spoil the science if they didn’t keep giving strangers electric shocks: “The experiment requires that you continue.” Without that, the stooges may never act naturally; if they know the experiment is also a TV show, they definitely won’t.Reality TV has a similar credibility problem: although a show might say it’s found a group of ordinary people and put them in such-and-such a situation, the obvious answer is always that they’re not ordinary people. They applied to be on reality TV, which ordinary people don’t do.The two issues combine in Netflix’s The New Stanford Prison Experiment, which has hired part of a real county correctional facility in Georgia and filled it with 30 people divided into two factions: eight guards, three of whom are women, and 22 prisoners, all male. The haves wear sleek grey uniforms, set the rules and retire to their hotel between shifts; the have-nots are given bright yellow jumpsuits and scratchy bunk beds, and eat tasteless slop under harsh strip-lighting.View image in fullscreen‘The haves set the rules and retire to their hotel between shifts’ … a group of prison guards in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Photograph: Courtesy of Netflix. © 2026It keeps pretending to be a study of whether power corrupts in an institutional environment, but it is undeniably reality TV to its core, starting with how it’s presented to us. As well as seeing what the prisoners and guards have done, we’re told about it by them in the obligatory to-camera interviews, filmed afterwards. Also informing us about events we have just witnessed for ourselves are a trio of experts – a behavioural psychologist, a former federal correctional officer and, er, a journalist – watching a bank of screens. The series runs to six episodes, which could have been four if the patronising recaps had been edited out.Inside the jail, any hope that the TV prisoners and guards might forget where they are and start behaving like actual prisoners and guards is soon lost. Everyone constantly references the “experiment”, and the show refuses to sit still for more than half an episode before drawing on textbook reality TV tricks to engineer discord: the guards are split into night and day teams, which undermine each other by approaching the task differently; they are asked to elect a head guard, which irks those not picked; at the halfway point in the series, some prisoners and guards switch roles.None of it is real, and nobody thinks it is. The show doesn’t create any moments where the contestants suspend their disbelief – as inThe Traitors, where the faithfuls sometimes start genuinely seeing the traitors as duplicitous villains. There is no game to win, no goal to work towards and, apart from the unspoken potential reward of a media career in every reality show, no prize. There’s nothing incentivising anyone to continue. More than one participant realises this and simply walks off the show.What is interesting – not enough to make The New Stanford Prison Experiment worth nearly six hours of your time, but it’s something – is how reality TV contestants, with their unusually high self-regard and their tendency to use a lot of loud, confident words to say very little, behave when they know what and where they are. The most fertile conflict here springs up between prisoners who want to disobey the guards to see what happens, and those who’d rather stick to the current dynamic. It’s not an illustration of how a carceral institution restricts free will and removes individuality. It’s people who know they’re co-authors of a piece of entertainment and disagree on how the story should develop. Who know they’re characters in a story and have ideas for their own narcissistic reality “journeys” that clash with those of the others.There is, however, one group that does fall for the conjuring trick. Up in the gallery, the three superfluous experts rather adorably persist in analysing hierarchies and interpersonal power struggles and the rest of it, as if any of those things are meaningfully occurring. They seem to have bought into The New Stanford Prison Experiment – watching at home, that’s impossible.The New Stanford Prison Experiment is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewNetflixreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou’s side-splitting comedy | Television | The Guardian
description: With guest stars including Steve Coogan, their sketch show will have you crying with laughter. Plus: a mindblowing science lesson. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: With guest stars including Steve Coogan, their sketch show will have you crying with laughter. Plus: a mindblowing science lesson. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Putting white bread to the test … Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White are back for a second series of Ellie & Natasia.Photograph: BBC/CPL ProductionsView image in fullscreenPutting white bread to the test … Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White are back for a second series of Ellie & Natasia.Photograph: BBC/CPL ProductionsTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou’s side-splitting comedyWith guest stars including Steve Coogan, their sketch show will have you crying with laughter. Plus: a mindblowing science lesson. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Ali CatterallandEllen E JonesWed 21 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEllie & Natasia10pm, BBC TwoThere is not one weak sketch in the opener of Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou’s comedy – they will have you weeping tears of laughter. Now in its second series, expect returning characters and new ones. There are lifestyle influencers shopping at Asda; hipsters spending all day in an overpriced trinkets boutique; and Mary Poppins at a gynaecological appointment. It also guest stars Steve Coogan, Sian Clifford and Jamie Demetriou.Hollie RichardsonThe Repair Shop: Beyond the Barn8pm, BBC OneThis minor variation on the Repair Shop formula continues: the barn is still open but the gang embark on a few road trips. Most notable this time is the Ukrainian tsymbaly (a hammered dulcimer) belonging to a woman from Cornwall. Once it’s been lovingly restored, it’s moving to see it being played.Phil HarrisonPortrait Artist of the Year 20268pm, Sky ArtsThe portrait competition where tears are expected by at least one of the celebrity sitters each week returns. This time, they are Olympian skeleton skater Matt Weston, poet Nikita Gill, and film director and actor Dexter Fletcher.HRAsteroids: Spark of Life8pm, BBC FourView image in fullscreenMindblowing stuff.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:GBH/GEDEON ProgrammesDenis Lawson delivers a mighty science lesson with this programme, which tests a theory about asteroids sparking life on Earth – rather than just extinguishing it. He rewinds 4bn years to tell the story of the newly formed planet, as scientists share their mindblowing research.HRGrand Designs9pm, Channel 4In 2017, energy conservationist Andrew bet it all on Britain’s first self-heating home, which would harness and store the summer’s warmth in vast insulated earth banks, to be deployed in winter. He’d soon come up against structural problems, spiralling costs and a teed-off wife. Years later, Kevin McCloud checks in to discover whether the project paid off.Ali CatterallThe Experiment10pm, Channel 4The makers of Channel 4’s next provocative social experiment have remained very hush hush about the details. title: Usha Vance is a closed book – but her Goodreads account is surprisingly revealing | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: From Roman-era political potboilers to stories of Catholic priests struggling to impose their authority, Arwa Mahdawi wonders what the reading list of vice-president JD Vance’s wife could be trying to tell us
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: From Roman-era political potboilers to stories of Catholic priests struggling to impose their authority, Arwa Mahdawi wonders what the reading list of vice-president JD Vance’s wife could be trying to tell us
Content: A real page-turner … Usha Vance, at the Republican National Convention, 2024.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA real page-turner … Usha Vance, at the Republican National Convention, 2024.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesOpinionBooksUsha Vance is a closed book – but her Goodreads account is surprisingly revealingArwa MahdawiFrom Roman-era political potboilers to stories of Catholic priests struggling to impose their authority, what could the reading list of vice-president JD Vance’s wife be trying to tell us?Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTShareUsha Vance, a very clever woman with dubious taste in men, likes to keep herself busy. While lesser mortals (me) waste their one wild and precious life watching Love Is Blind, the second lady has various self-improvement projects on the go. She’sbrushing up on her German! She’s hosting aliteracy podcast!She’s rereading the classics! And, of course, she’s juggling four young children and the demands of being the vice-president’s spouse.How does she do it all? With the help of taxpayer dollars, I suspect. Easier to get some reading done when you’re beinghelicoptered everywhereand, as JD Vance has boasted: “People go to the grocery store for me.”But I’m not here to moan about how much the Vance family iscosting the taxpayer. I am here to share an important, and only slightly unhinged, theory. The second lady is notoriously private; people are constantly trying to understandwhat she’s thinking. Now, I think I’ve figured it out. While Usha herself is not an open book, I reckon her bookshelf – or, rather, herGoodreads account– is trying to tell us something. Either that or she’s trolling us.What have I done? I forced my kid to listen to Usha Vance’s podcast - now she’s a fan | Arwa MahdawiRead moreRemember, for example, when JD was trying to mansplain Catholicismto the popeback in April? (Pope Leo XIV, to be clear; pope Francis died the year before,one day after meeting Vance.) As all that was happening, Usha picked up Death Comes for the Archbishop by Willa Cather. Which, to be wildly simplistic, is a book about a French missionary priest tasked with imposing order and Catholic norms on a church in New Mexico, where some other naughty priests have gone a bit rogue. Make of that what you will.Then there’s all the recent chatter about whetherJD Vanceis going to be Trump’s heir. Per her Goodreads account, Usha has just finished reading I, Claudius by Robert Graves. That book is about a member of Rome’s imperial family who survives vicious palace politics because everyone underestimates him. All the infighting and murder means he’s the last man standing and becomes emperor almost by accident. Is that a reflection on her husband’s political future? Perhaps! Now that Usha is done with Graves, she’s reading the nonfiction book Medieval People by Eileen Power. Perhaps to prepare for the dark ages her husband is helping drag the country back to.“Arwa,” you might say, “you’re reading way too much into this!” Of course I am. I have a degree in English literature: that’s three years of explaining how doorknobs in Jane Austen novels represent the hollowness of colonialism. Nevertheless, I think I may be on to something. Let’s just hope that Usha’s next choice of reading material isn’t Annie Jacobsen’sNuclear War: A Scenario.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: On Another Planet They Can Save Me by Lieke Marsman review – an astonishing memoir of terminal illness | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: Published four months after her death, the poet’s reflections on mortality are both agonising and profoundly life-affirming
Author: Edward Posnett
Headline: Published four months after her death, the poet’s reflections on mortality are both agonising and profoundly life-affirming
Content: Lieke Marsman.Photograph: Tom CornelissenView image in fullscreenLieke Marsman.Photograph: Tom CornelissenBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewOn Another Planet They Can Save Me by Lieke Marsman review – an astonishing memoir of terminal illnessPublished four months after her death, the poet’s reflections on mortality are both agonising and profoundly life-affirmingEdward PosnettWed 21 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are no atheists in foxholes, goes the saying, and indeed social scientists and evolutionary biologists have argued that the experience of war or conflict drives religious belief; in 2019, Joseph Henrich and others surveyed almost 2,000 people in three post-conflict societies – Uganda, Sierra Leone and Tajikistan – and concluded that their experience of conflict had prompted them to participate in Christian and Muslim rituals and groups. Atheism, it seems, may be as fragile as faith.“No matter how attached you are to your own rational worldview, your rationality won’t survive long under the threat of imminent death,” writes the former Dutch poet laureate Lieke Marsman in her book On Another Planet They Can Save Me. Part scream, part song, it charts the gradual dissolution of her own rational assumptions, which govern everything from her views on God to extra­terrestrial life. It is a brilliant, playful, layered and humane plea for openness and hope in the face of her own foxhole of intolerable suffering.Marsman was not a soldier, but she knew a thing or two about living with constant reminders of her own mortality. In 2018, at the age of 27, the poet was diagnosed with a rare and incurable form of cartilage cancer. “There are little balls of failed cartilage in my lungs, balls that will slowly, agonisingly, take over until, at last, I suffocate,” she writes. When a doctor informs her that her illness is terminal, she lets out a scream. “[H]ow else are you supposed to behave when handed a death sentence?” she asks. Desperate to live, Marsman undergoes a barrage of treatments, including an operation to remove her arm and shoulder.double quotation markShe cites Pasolini, Alanis Morissette, Spinoza, Euripides and WittgensteinHowever grim her situation, there is remarkably little about her body in this book, and the trials of her cancer treatment, from surgery to immunotherapy. “After all, isn’t a disease only really interesting to the one who has it?” she wonders. “The temperature of my anus doesn’t affect the temperature of the world.” Instead, she writes about her relationship with certainty, gradually unpicking her own materialism and positivism. She opens herself to God, reads about the supernatural, and wonders whether aliens may come down and take her away. “Sometimes I think I’m going crazy, at other moments I think how crazy I was not to have allowed myself to broaden my perspective until now.”This is well-trodden ground, but Marsman’s language is so beautiful (her translator, Sophie Collins, has done a fine job), and her textual references so original, that it feels as if we are walking on fresh turf. Her range is wild: she cites Leopardi, Pasolini, Alanis Morissette, Robert Musil, Spinoza, Euripides, Wittgenstein and William James. The most interesting sections, for me, related not to artists’ or writers’ reflections on mortality or rationalism, but those of scientists who expressed doubts about the solidity of the scientific framework that they themselves constructed. “To speak in terms of Plato’s well-known simile,” wrote cosmologist James Jeans, “we are still imprisoned in our cave, with our backs to the light, and can only watch the shadows on the wall.”Side by side with these reflections are Marsman’s poignant memories of the quotidian reality of a terminal cancer diagnosis, which form a strange blend of the mundane with the otherworldly. She writes that she and her girlfriend spent hundreds of euros on empanadas. “[E]ven when you’re dying, you have to eat, and those things only need a blast in the oven.” When she wakes up from an operation without her arm, she recalls that the first thing she craved was … a croissant. If the narrative vibrates with pain, there are also releases of humour; at one point she considers all the absurd things she could do to spice up her obituary, such as crashing in a paraglider or go-kart.Any reviewer knows that the author may read what you have written; a review is intended for potential readers of a book, yes, but I also think of it as a dialogue with its author. Here there is no right of reply: Marsman died in June of this year, aged 35, and this book, more than a memoir, is a testament; to review it almost feels like a sacrilegious act, and perhaps it is best to let the author speak. “[D]ying with hope, however far-fetched and unrealistic that might be, is always better than continuing to live without it. And in those moments when everything in the here and now turns out to be utterly hopeless, I allow myself to think: on another planet they can save me.” I hope that that other planet exists, and somewhere, somehow, Marsman is still writing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch by Thure Erik Lund review – is this the greatest living Norwegian writer? | Fiction in translation | The Guardian
description: Translated into English at last, this portrait of a man appalled by modernity and desperate to get back to nature is brimming with Nordic weltschmerz
Author: Sukhdev Sandhu
Headline: Translated into English at last, this portrait of a man appalled by modernity and desperate to get back to nature is brimming with Nordic weltschmerz
Content: Thure Erik Lund.Photograph: Niklas LelloView image in fullscreenThure Erik Lund.Photograph: Niklas LelloFiction in translationReviewThe Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch by Thure Erik Lund review – is this the greatest living Norwegian writer?Translated into English at last, this portrait of a man appalled by modernity and desperate to get back to nature is brimming with Nordic weltschmerzSukhdev SandhuWed 21 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleT-O-M. The initials of Tomas Olsen Myrbråten, the narrator in Thure Erik Lund’s The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch, spell out the Norwegian word for “empty”. Approaching 38, he’s already a relic. He spends his days slumped at the kitchen table or staring out of the window, convinced that the ceiling is about to fall and crush him. He sobs about the state he’s in and the state of society around him. Of one thing he’s sure: “It is no longer me who cries, but the world, the world crying, in me.” Nordic weltschmerz: you’d have to be a saint not to giggle.Lund has been described by Karl Ove Knausgård as the “greatest Norwegian contemporary writer”; this novel, originally published in 1999, is his first to be translated into English. In it, Tomas describes himself, over and over and over again, as a “life-of-the-mind individual”. Cursed as much as blessed, life-of-the mind individuals have a keen and unconsoling sense of how things are (“one is a wretched, contemptible, and unworthy being”) and how things will end for them (“in the sewers of society, at nature’s nadir, incessantly ground down into the mud and the mire so that one day, millions of years from now, they become oil, life-of-the-mind oil, at the very bottom of life itself”). Is he making fun of himself? In 2026, he seems closer to an eco-prophet.Perhaps it was always meant to be this way. His family line consisted of poor, mostly illiterate farmworkers in eastern Norway and, after he moved away to university, he learned to speak about his upbringing in casual, almost condescending fashion. Over time though, especially as he travels across the country, he begins to question his snobbery. He’s aghast at how history is being turned into heritage, ancient folk traditions repackaged for tourists, culture seen as being not so much about lived experiences and relations as a commodity. Wildness is disappearing. Even mountain roads no longer wind like they used to. There are echoes of Thoreau in his invocations of “children getting lost in the woods, in a world without human signifiers, without signage or trails, only celestial bodies and natural forms”. Echoes too of John Berger’s Pig Earth, as he charts the impact of machinery on how peasants speak and engage with each other.double quotation markThis is a universal story of modernity and its discontents, but Lund is at pains to give it a Norwegian dimensionThis is a universal story of modernity and its discontents, but Lund is at pains to give it a specifically Norwegian dimension. Like one of Thomas Bernhard’s grumpus narrators railing against Austrian idiocracy, Tomas lays into his country’s governing class (“a gang of boasting sanctimonious humanistoid individuals”) which has ushered in “a thoroughly criminal, narcotised shopping-mall world”, a “Norwegian global hell” full of “pale, withered souls who seek solace in cinemas and fitness studios”. Listing his present-day false prophets – “computer engineers, course facilitators, business commissioners” – he sounds like someone who’s read the Unabomber Manifesto.What’s funniest – or maybe funny-tragic – is that Tomas thinks he can express all this not only in a think piece commissioned by the Royal Norwegian Ministry of Culture, but to the face of the culture minister herself. She is not amused, especially when he blurts out a four-letter word. Dragged out of her office by security guards, his reputation and social standing are destroyed. He’s assumed to be a nationalist, a Nazi even, is unable to get work, and becomes homeless.Then things get even worse: in a nightmarish middle section, somewhere between Hieronymus Bosch and Lars von Trier, he returns to his parents’ farm. He’s hoping to turn his back on decadent city ways, but there’s nothing Arcadian here. In this perverted pastoral Tomas digs ditches, lives with his drunken wife Helena, whose gaze is a “pustulated mongrel-eyed leer”, cages his mentally defective brother and dumps him in a remote Swedish village. Is this the authentic Norway he’s been hankering for? It’s in a state of decomposition and liquefaction – all slime, moonshine, blood, vomit, grease.Language is a key actor throughout. Paragraphs are often long, larded with clauses that repeat, with sententious neologisms that David M Smith translates as “enfletted”, “enhammered”, “vocabulation”. At other times, when Tomas lets go his urban sensibilities, the sentences are slangy and pungent.The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch is prescient about the “language forms” that digital capitalism requires – the data and information, the “demonic and inhuman” scientism, the fear of allegory. Its astonishing final section sees Tomas, alone in a forest, all ears. He can hear himself, his surroundings, the past, the future. He’s attuned to what connects him to shit, steel wire, dead plant tissue, bacterial cultures. Eureka! “That’s what I was. A kind of pulverised form of language which, by chance, had been imbued with natural substances, here and there.” Nordic weltschmerz: what a wonder it is.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
