title: ‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in? | Movies | The Guardian
description: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?
Content: Radical transparency? … Elizabeth Holmes with Nathan Fielder in the background in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24View image in fullscreenRadical transparency? … Elizabeth Holmes with Nathan Fielder in the background in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24Movies‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in?With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?Henry RobertsWed 21 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInYou Can See Everything, convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invites film-makers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into her home in a supposed act of “radical transparency”. Holmes is filmed, along with her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children, in the weeks before starting a prison sentence for defrauding Theranos investors. “The best way for people to see who she is,” Evans says, “is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”. It may also be the best way to market “Theranos 2.0”, which the couple are working on during filming. But the documentary questions whether Holmes is presenting her authentic self or a manufactured persona. Fielder speaks for the audience when he asks Holmes in a tense exchange whether she’s “being real” with him. “I’m always being real,” she says.That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew?You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreSome people, like Holmes, think a documentary will help rebuild their reputation after public disgrace. When Anthony Weiner, who resigned from Congress after tweeting a photo of his bulging groin, tried to stage a professional comeback with a New York mayoral bid, he allowed cameras to film the journey. Only, he had more to hide: when further sex scandals emerged, his campaign went from a story of public redemption to innuendo-laden humiliation. And all the while, the cameras kept rolling.Weineris a prime example of a subject losing control of the narrative.View image in fullscreenHumiliation … Launching a New York mayoral bid, Anthony Weiner, with wife Huma Abedin, 23 July 2013.Photograph: Kathy Willens/APWeiner may have wanted a sympathetic portrayal, but he should have known that film-makers always have their own agendas. In the book The Journalist and the Murderer,Janet Malcolmreflects on the relationship between journalists and their subjects: “The subject becomes a kind of child of the writer, regarding him as a permissive, all-accepting, all-forgiving mother, and expecting the book to be written by her. Of course, the book is written by the strict, all-noticing, unforgiving father.” The same is surely true of the documentarian.When Jackie and David Siegel allowed Lauren Greenfield to film their attempt to build a modern-day Versailles in Florida, the director wasn’t giving them free PR. Rather, withThe Queen of Versailles, Greenfield was interested in the corrosive effects of extreme wealth. The Siegels agreed to be filmed because they were proud of their success. When their dream collapsed following the 2008 financial crash, The Queen of Versailles turned from a story of Xanadu-like grandeur to one of hubristic overreach. David later sued Lauren – unsuccessfully – for defamation, but he should have known from the beginning: it may have been his story, but it was never his film.A few years after Versailles, Greenfield madeThe Kingmaker, about former first lady of the Philippines Imelda Marcos and her attempt to return the family to power. From the beginning of the film,Greenfield said, there was a power struggle over who was telling the story. Marcos, known for her lavish lifestyle during her husband’s brutal rule, understood the power of optics. In a children’s cancer ward, she hands out money to children in a public display of compassion. “Perception is real,” Marcos says in the film, “and the truth is not.”Some people agree to projects believing they will have editorial control. Idi Amin gave Barbet Schroeder unprecedented access after the director essentially promised that they would make the film together. But Amin was unhappy with General Idi Amin Dada: A Self Portrait and demanded some footage be cut, rounding up more than 100 French residents in Uganda and holding them hostage until his demands were met. Schroeder agreed. It helps to be as ruthless as Amin if you want final cut.Documentaries are often about the past, but some of cinema’s most memorable moments show people acting violently in the present, fully aware that they are being filmed.Frederick Wiseman’s austere filmsshow abuse in psychiatric institutions (Titicut Follies) and horrific police violence (Law and Order). Why did people do unspeakable things in front of a camera? “People basically go about their business,”Wiseman told an interviewer, “and the presence of the camera doesn’t have much, if any effect on their behaviour.”View image in fullscreenMorally complex … a scene from The Act Of Killing, 2012.Photograph: Real/Novaya Ze/Rex/ShutterstockBut cameras did have an effect on the subjects ofJoshua Oppenheimer’s The Act of Killing, probably the most morally complex example of the film-maker-subject relationship in cinema history. Perpetrators of Indonesia’s mass killings gleefully re-enact their crimes, restaging their violent memories in the style of Hollywood movies. They do not profess their innocence. Rather, they agree to be filmed because they are proud of what they did. They really do want us to see everything.UK cinemas report ‘bonkers’ demand for documentary You Can See EverythingRead morePerhaps the most interesting case of someone willingly putting themselves under scrutiny is Lance Armstrong.Alex Gibney’s documentary on Armstrongwas expected to be a puff piece. When the full extent of Armstrong’s doping was revealed, however, Gibney’s film changed direction, becoming a documentary not on a cyclist’s triumph but on a master manipulator who lied to everyone, including the film-maker. In The Armstrong Lie, Armstrong admits that he “was prepared to say anything” to keep his lie going.Some people are simply arrogant enough to think they can get away with their lies. But others become so invested in their skewed version of reality that to refuse a documentary crew would be like admitting their deception. So they welcome the cameras, often doing more damage than if they had simply retreated from public view. But unlike Armstrong, Holmes still insists she has done nothing wrong. As she says in You Can See Everything: “I have nothing to hide.”Explore more on these topicsFilmYou Can See EverythingElizabeth HolmesNathan FielderLance ArmstrongTheranosAnthony WeinerfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Making Marie Antoinette review – sweet Coppola home movie reveals the family business | Movies | The Guardian
description: Shot by Sofia’s mother Eleanor this documentary shows something of the strain of shooting a period piece, but is a far cry from the tumultuous portrait of her husband in Hearts of Darkness
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Shot by Sofia’s mother Eleanor this documentary shows something of the strain of shooting a period piece, but is a far cry from the tumultuous portrait of her husband in Hearts of Darkness
Content: French fancies … Kirsten Dunst and Jason Schwartzman in Making Marie Antoinette.Photograph: Sofia CoppolaView image in fullscreenFrench fancies … Kirsten Dunst and Jason Schwartzman in Making Marie Antoinette.Photograph: Sofia CoppolaMoviesReviewMaking Marie Antoinette review – sweet Coppola home movie reveals the family businessShot by Sofia’s mother Eleanor this documentary shows something of the strain of shooting a period piece, but is a far cry from the tumultuous portrait of her husband in Hearts of DarknessPeter BradshawWed 21 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 04.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is 20 years since the release ofSofia Coppola’s Marie Antoinettestarring Kirsten Dunst; it is a supportively unjudging, unironised study of the queen’s early years before the 1789 revolution, lavishly and accurately costumed, shot on location at Versailles and based on the Antonia Fraser biography – but also subversively and amusingly using pop tracks from the 70s and 80s on the soundtrack. It got a storm of booing from French critics, reportedly annoyed at the way their history had been reduced to a music video and fashion shoot with no French actors involved. Or hardly any.In fact, for all the lack of political grit, the film was interesting and accomplished, and deservedly has a fanbase – and it is to that constituency that this making-of documentary from the director’s mother Eleanor Coppola is really addressed. It is basically a sweet family home movie on digital video which shows something of the strain and the longueurs of shooting a demanding period picture, but tactfully not seeing anything really explosive or bad-tempered. It is very far from Eleanor Coppola’ssensational behind-the-scenes film Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypseabout the tumultuous creation of Apocalypse Now, directed by her husband Francis Ford Coppola.Eleanor and Sofia edited the footage together during the Covid lockdown and diary entries by Eleanor Coppola, who died in 2024, are sensitively read by Diane Lane. There are innumerable shots of Sofia smiling at her mother’s camera, yet sometimes looking a little tired and ill. Jason Schwartzman, playing Louis XVI, grins cheerfully, while Marianne Faithfull, as Empress Maria Theresa, cheerfully banters with Sofia in a very naughty English way. Francis Ford Coppola arrives at one stage and says that his advice to Sofia had been to “throw a Marie Antoinette party and invite everyone to come to it…” A good description of the film, actually.Elsewhere, in Lane’s diary voiceover, Eleanor talks about the pain involved for her personally when Sofia all but broke off contact with her in her teen years, but Eleanor recognised that this was a process she had to go through before they became close again. Yet there is of course no hint of anything problematic here; this in effect is a very indulgent bonus feature, which in a DVD would come in at about 15 minutes, tops. But it does give what looks like a pretty faithful account of the patient slog needed to shoot a feature film.Making Marie Antoinette is out on 23 October in the UK and US, and on Mubi from 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsSofia CoppolaFranceEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Scream review – Wes Craven meta horror remains super smart and scary 30 years on | Movies | The Guardian
description: Self-aware romp through the genre is redolent of the 90s but its ghost-masked killer is as alarming as ever
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Self-aware romp through the genre is redolent of the 90s but its ghost-masked killer is as alarming as ever
Content: Shocking sights … (from left) Courteney Cox, Jamie Kennedy and Neve Campbell in Scream.Photograph: Dimension/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenShocking sights … (from left) Courteney Cox, Jamie Kennedy and Neve Campbell in Scream.Photograph: Dimension/Sportsphoto/AllstarMoviesReviewScream review – Wes Craven meta horror remains super smart and scary 30 years onSelf-aware romp through the genre is redolent of the 90s but its ghost-masked killer is as alarming as everPeter BradshawWed 21 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 30th anniversary re-release of the original Scream, from screenwriter Kevin Williamson and directorWes Craven, brings us to a locus classicus of the 90s: a self-aware romp through the horror genre. It features Skeet Ulrich’s high schooler Billy Loomis announcing that reality is “all one big movie – but you can’t pick your genre”, which is the meta-slasher equivalent of Jacques Derrida’s belief that there is nothing outside the text.A ghost-masked killer is murdering and terrorising the bland Californian town of Woodsboro, and we begin with his gruesome assault on Casey (Drew Barrymore); he makes chilling calls to people’s landline phones, in an era where that meant you more or less had them pinned them down to a certain location. (The existence of “cellular” phones was still an exotic novelty.) The mother of teen Sidney (Neve Campbell) had been brutally killed previously, a crime pinned on local man Cotton Weary (a cameo for Liev Schreiber) who is now in jail. But was he really guilty? Now Sidney is at risk like everyone else.Yet as one of the local horror fans points out: you’re safe as long as you stick to the three scary-movie rules: stay a virgin, avoid drink and drugs, and don’t utter the hubristic phrase “I’ll be right back”. (Perhaps someone could also have pointed out the difference in vulnerability-level between blondes and non-blondes.) So when Sidney has sex, she puts herself in mortal danger. Meanwhile, brash local TV reporter Gale Weathers (played by Courteney Cox, already a star from Friends) figures she can crack this case wide open, and she has a tendresse for the goofy young cop deputy Dewey Riley, played by Cox’s future husband, David Arquette.The self-aware references are many, and the action of Scream is often wittily juxtaposed with narrative sequences from a classic such as Halloween. What comes across from watching the original Scream 30 years on is that there is one horror classic that could be an influence but isn’t referenced, perhaps because it isn’t canonical in the purist slasher-film sense: Truman Capote’s reportage history In Cold Blood. (I think of this, when one character here dismisses the idea of “motive”.)What also emerges, perhaps not entirely intentionally, is how very obnoxious, and very possibly sadistic, male movie fandom can often seem in itself. It’s very apparent when the killer smugly challenges his victim with a trick question about who the killer is in the first Friday the 13th. This film is brash and smart in that distinctive 90s way – and the title sounds like an order.Scream is in UK cinemas from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsWes CravenDrew BarrymoreLiev SchreiberreviewsShareReuse this content

title: High School Musical review – Disney fave is sweet, slick and as squeaky clean as ever | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Harry Judd is the coach while KayCee Stroh from the original movies is back to play a teacher in the hoop-shooting, pompom-waving romance
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: Harry Judd is the coach while KayCee Stroh from the original movies is back to play a teacher in the hoop-shooting, pompom-waving romance
Content: Entertainingly grating … Luke Bayer and Caitlin Tipping in High School Musical.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEntertainingly grating … Luke Bayer and Caitlin Tipping in High School Musical.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewHigh School Musical review – Disney fave is sweet, slick and as squeaky clean as everTroubadour Wembley Park theatre, LondonHarryJudd is the coach while KayCee Stroh from the original movies is back to play a teacher in thehoop-shooting, pompom-waving romanceHolly O'MahonyWed 21 Oct 2026 06.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince soaring on screen 20 years ago, this Disney Channel favourite has cemented itself as a squeaky clean, painstakingly earnest but no less beloved descendant of Grease. Like Danny and Sandy, Troy Bolton and Gabriella Montez share a holiday romance and wind up at school together the following term, where the social pecking order initially keeps them apart. Driven by a shared love of singing, they defy conventions to end up together.This new stage production, first seen at Salford’s Lowry, is directed by Hope Mill theatre founders Joseph Houston and William Whelton. No, it can’t escape the limitations of the story’s spectacularly two-dimensional characters, who are siloed into the camps of jock, brainiac or drama kid, and whose stock traits are indulged in the book by David Simpatico, but it’s bright and buzzy nonetheless.View image in fullscreenBright and buzzy … Tobias Turley and Leonor Correia in High School Musical.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe thrust stage of Andrew Exeter’s basketball-themed set positions us courtside, while Rory Beaton’s bright lights, Matt Peploe’s thunderous sound design and George Reeve’s videography – beamed on to screens surrounding the gym – help animate the spectacle playing out on court, where the school’s Wildcats team are shooting hoops and pompom-waving cheerleaders are drumming up hype.It’s dizzying and dazzling – never more so than during the revival of Bop to the Top, led by Luke Bayer and Caitlin Tipping as siblings Ryan and Sharpay Evans, who are every bit as entertainingly grating as their screen counterparts. Aaron Renfree’s nimble choreography rotates montages from the all-important science competition, basketball game and musical callbacks, as Troy and Gabriella race against the clock to make it to auditions.View image in fullscreenNimble choreography … Harry Judd, centre, in High School Musical.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe headline names belong to the teachers: KayCee Stroh, who played hip-hop-loving Martha Cox in the films, is now over-the-top drama teacher Ms Darbus, while McFly’s Harry Judd plays austere Coach Bolton with brow-furrowed concentration.As Troy and Gabriella, Tobias Turley and relative newcomer Leonor Correia bring a sweetness, but their chemistry is yet to fully bloom. Gabriella’s When There Was Me and You is, here, a duet sung by the pair of them in an arrangement that cops out of the high notes, but throbs with teenage longing. Breaking Free really does see them soar, albeit on a stiff-looking swing.Still, if it skirts the ring more than it nets the ball, I suspect adoring fans won’t leave disappointed.AtTroubadour Wembley Park theatre, London, until 3 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ilford Boy review – Barbra Streisand teaches teen to smile about the way we are | Theatre | The Guardian
description: In Danny Lee Wynter’s drama, a quiet boy struggles amid the swirl of his family until a mercurial friend offers him another future
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: In Danny Lee Wynter’s drama, a quiet boy struggles amid the swirl of his family until a mercurial friend offers him another future
Content: Debut … Leo Whitfield Harris in Ilford Boy.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreenDebut … Leo Whitfield Harris in Ilford Boy.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewIlford Boy review – Barbra Streisand teaches teen to smile about the way we areDonmar Warehouse, LondonIn Danny Lee Wynter’s drama, a quiet boy struggles amid the swirl of his family until a mercurial friend offers him another futureKate WyverWed 21 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBroad Essex accents fill the stage in Danny Lee Wynter’s sprawling family drama. The busy script from theBlack Superheroplaywright is crammed with a fractious extended family treading heavily over old arguments, but the production sings when an old friend swans back into town. Set across the 80s and 90s in the shadow of the Aids crisis, this story’s beating heart travels around on tap shoes.Quiet teenager Ted (Leo Whitfield Harris in his stage debut) is surrounded by the loud swirl of his feuding family, with everyone’s rusty views on queerness, race and masculinity grating against each other as they clear out his showtune-loving nanna’s house in Ilford. His father (a bolshie Gershwyn Eustache Jr) is pushing him towards boxing and girls, so Ted grits his teeth and resists anything seen as weakness, but in doing so he resists kindness too.View image in fullscreenA chaotic neon home … Peter McKintosh’s set for Ilford BoyPhotograph: Helen MurrayThere is sharpness and humour within the core family’s spiky arguments, with an abundance of anguished love offered by Ted’s mum (Ria Zmitrowicz), though some of the wider family could have more substance. Flashbacks build up backstory, enabling the creative team to have fun with costumes and hair. In both timelines, Tim Sheader’s direction scatters the family across Peter McKintosh’s surprisingly sparse double-decked neon home that doesn’t quite reflect the chaos – or the occasional warmth – within.View image in fullscreenEffervescent … Craig Stein.Photograph: Helen MurrayBut then there’s Pat, Ted’s mum’s old friend, played by the mercurial Craig Stein. While everyone else is telling Ted how to be, here is a Black gay man showing him another way. As Ted is drawn in by Pat’s knowledge of Barbra Streisand, the play begins to move away from the more predictable father-son dynamics and towards something more effervescent.There’s a whole life in the way Pat looks with disgust at Ted’s father, in how he talks about his lost love, in the hand he stretches out to Ted when the teenager asks him to dance. Illuminated in a brilliant moment of boldness from the script, with glorious movement by Ebony Molina, this is the image we’re left with long after Pat’s left the stage and the rest of the family have turned away: a beautiful man, up above the audience, leg kicked high in the air, radiant with life.AtDonmar Warehouse, London, until 28 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreDonmar WarehouseEssexWest EndBlack British culturereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Cyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’ | Cyndi Lauper | The Guardian
description: As she auctions off her treasures, the synth-pop savant opens up about her eccentric style and why she doesn’t believe in cancel culture
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: As she auctions off her treasures, the synth-pop savant opens up about her eccentric style and why she doesn’t believe in cancel culture
Content: Cyndi Lauper.Photograph: Greyshock. Courtesy of Bonhams.View image in fullscreenCyndi Lauper.Photograph: Greyshock. Courtesy of Bonhams.Cyndi LauperCyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’As she auctions off her treasures, the synth-pop savant opens up about her eccentric style and why she doesn’t believe in cancel cultureOwen MyersWed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeforeCyndi Lauperrose to fame as one of the most singular pop breakouts of the 1980s, she was queen of the cash register at the edgy Manhattan boutique Screaming Mimi’s. The vintage emporium is still a downtown staple, but a little of its spirit comes uptown this month withCyndi Lauper: A Suitcase of Memories, a two-part auction of her fashion and personal items at the New York auction house Bonhams.Cyndi Lauper review – 80s pop eccentric hasn’t changed a bitRead moreOn a recent Thursday morning inNew York, the singer is sporting seafoam green hair and is in good spirits as she leads a private tour of the collection. It is an Aladdin’s cave of outfits from her five-decade career, with clashing prints, jutting tutus and statement headwear in every color you can imagine. As she strides around in her platform creepers, she gives a few final notes to the Bonhams team. Is that rainbow fan at the right angle? And can we confirm that more mirror balls are on their way?“Over there is my grandmother’s pyjamas,” she says, walking over to a mannequin that displays the leopard print sleepwear Lauper wore in theGirls Just Want to Have Fun video. The ensemble was originally purchased from her family’s favorite mail order catalog. “Frederick’s of Hollywood gave people in Queens a glimpse of glamor and sexiness,” she says. “You know, they’re flannel pyjamas, but come on – they’re leopard!”View image in fullscreenLauper’s leopard print pyjamas from the Girls Just Want to Have Fun video, 1983.Photograph: Courtesy of BonhamsBorn in Queens, Lauper was raised as part of a large family who worked in New York’s Garment District as cutters and seamstresses. After leaving home at the age of 17 armed with not much more than a toothbrush and a copy of Yoko Ono’s book Grapefruit, she honed her eclectic style while working at Screaming Mimi’s in between singing at downtown local clubs.“I went to art school but I didn’t finish,” Lauper says. “So what happened is this, I guess.”Lauper captivated a generation with performances which combined music with art and fashion, selling more than 50m records. Her fantastic debut She’s So Unusual became the first debut album from a woman to produce four top-five singles upon its release in 1983. Hits like True Colors and I Drove All Night followed, as well as new ventures: she co-founded the True Colors United foundation in 2008 to benefit homeless LGBTQ+ youth and, in 2013, won a Tony award for her Kinky Boots score.View image in fullscreenCyndi Lauper.Photograph: Greyshock. Courtesy of BonhamsAfter retiring from live performance last year, Lauper says she is enjoying the chance to take stock. Leading us past the metal bra and headdress from her True Colorsvideoand a red plaid dress she wore to the inaugural VMAs in the early 80s, she seems nostalgic for the freedom of the decade. “It was a time where there was a little bit of a wildness,” she says. “We’ve been corporatized – we kind of have braces on our brains. You know, it would be nice if you could think for yourself sometime.”As well as ephemera such as handwritten lyric sheets, the exhibition features a Raggedy Ann doll from the Girls Just Want to Have Fun video and a multi-colored spotted couch that could have come from the set of Pee-wee’s Playhouse. “I did this to inspire people,” Lauper says of the show. “To inspire us who are older to remember the individuality of creativity, and to inspire the young to discover that creativity is individual.”Lauper is a great storyteller – I could listen to her anecdotes for hours – and as no-nonsense as you might expect from a born-and-bred New Yorker. As we admire the singer’s newspaper skirt from her True Colors album art, a guest asks Lauper if she worried that the fragile-seeming skirt would fall apart. “What do you mean? No,” she replies crisply. “It was aphotoshoot. I was good.”View image in fullscreenLauper’s newspaper skirt ensemble from the True Colors album cover shoot.Photograph: Courtesy of BonhamsLast year,Chappell Roanwore a replica of the newspaper skirt while inducting Lauper into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Lauper says that Roan is the one of the few current stars whose creativity she relates to.I can see that with Roan’s edginess and use of color. “It’s not just that,” Lauper tells me in a conference room later that morning, adding that she sees songs like Pink Pony Club as landmarks for LGBTQ+ representation. “It’s how she wrote about a lifestyle and made it normal. And then the clothes, sure.”In 2022, Lauper released a new version of her abortion rights song Sally’s Pigeons to protest against the US supreme courtoverturningRoe v Wade. “If we don’t have control over our own bodies then we have no real freedom,” she said at the time. “We need to mobilize. We need to let our voices be heard.”She sees the exhibition as coming at a “great time to have people inspired and come alive again” as the midterms approach. Despite gentrification squeezing out artists from the city, she says “the good news is that, because of Mamdani, the billionaires might be moving out, giving us our city back.”In 2023, Lauper gave her blessing forNicki Minajto sample Girls Just Want to Have Fun in a song from Minaj’s Pink Friday 2 album; Lauper joined her on stage for a performance a few months later. Given Minaj’s recent alliance with Donald Trump, does she feel differently about the collaboration now?“No,” Lauper says flatly. “First of all, I don’t believe in cancellation. And second of all, the fact that she did Girls Just Want to Have Fun musically – it’s a political thing anyway, babes.“Girls just want to have fun. They’re entitled to a joyful experience in this world. Like it or not, we’re here. We’re not going out in the rice fields any more. Yes, rise up and put your foot down, and she did. I don’t know what she’s doing now. But I still don’t think you cancel people, because otherwise there’s no room for discussion.”View image in fullscreenCyndi Lauper.Photograph: Ruven Afanador / Courtesy of BonhamsLauper says that she learned the importance of breaking bread with those across the political spectrum through her advocacy work. “If you want people to listen to you, you need to listen to people,” she says. “If you don’t let people evolve, what are you doing?”Vast Beatles museum, hailed as ‘extraordinary’ by Paul McCartney, to open in Liverpool in 2028Read moreThe exhibition shows how Lauper’s own tastes evolved too. In the 90s, she became increasingly drawn to sculptural pieces from Vivienne Westwood andAlexander McQueen, styling designer pieces with a DIY twist. For 1994’s Twelve Deadly Cyns album, she paired an electric blue Dolce & Gabbana shrug with a bowler hat that she spray-painted and decorated with feathers to match. “I wanted it to look like art,” she said, pausing by the ensemble as she wraps up the tour. “I remember that because it was another invention.“That’s what makes it exciting,” she says. “That a young person would look and go, ‘I could do that.’”Cyndi Lauper: Suitcase of Memories, Part Iis a live auction at Bonhams New York on 22 October.Part IIruns online until 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsCyndi LauperExhibitionsNew YorkPop and rockElectronic musicNicki MinajChappell RoanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A moment that changed me: I was devastated by a breakup – and saved by a sweaty moshpit | Relationships | The Guardian
description: When my relationship broke down, my usual playlist of pop girl anthems and love songs left me in tears. Then I discovered hardcore punk
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When my relationship broke down, my usual playlist of pop girl anthems and love songs left me in tears. Then I discovered hardcore punk
Content: On the mend … Leoni Horton in HMV holding the Pop Culture EP by Knocked Loose.Photograph: Courtesy of Leoni HortonView image in fullscreenOn the mend … Leoni Horton in HMV holding the Pop Culture EP by Knocked Loose.Photograph: Courtesy of Leoni HortonA moment that changed meRelationshipsA moment that changed me: I was devastated by a breakup – and saved by a sweaty moshpitWhen my relationship broke down, my usual playlist of pop girl anthems and love songs left me in tears. Then I discovered hardcore punkLeoni HortonWed 21 Oct 2026 01.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNobody warned me that heartbreak would ruin my relationship withBeyoncé. I had always associated music with the happiest times in my life: going to Glastonbury, seeing Madonna play at Madison Square Garden, singing along to Kylie Minogue’s greatest hits on a road trip across Australia. Just over a year ago, after my first real relationship ended unexpectedly, things changed.When I listened to the artists I loved most, I was ambushed by memories and reminded of all the love and intimacy I had lost. My usual playlists, filled with indie bops and pop girl anthems, became unbearable. I’d never noticed before, but almost every song was about love, yearning, romance and sex. Every time I pressed play, I found myself sobbing in the shower or ugly-crying in public.Tired of burning through tissues, I decided to go no contact with music. In fact, I was determined to avoid the topic of love at all costs. You would be surprised how much that limits what you can do, because, to paraphrase Hugh Grant in Love Actually, love is – unfortunately – all around. I swapped my playlists for journalism podcasts, true-crime audiobooks and soothing ambient noise, but nothing seemed to fill the space that the lack of music had left in my life.“What’s the genre furthest away from my usual taste?” I wondered, scrolling through Spotify, a few months post-breakup. I clicked recklessly, ending up in a hardcore punk playlist. Not knowing where to begin, I pressed play on the first band on the list.It worked. Loud, heavy music came screaming out of my speakers, so frantic and raw that I could barely make out what the songs were about. I was delighted when I realised I could listen to bands such as Malevolence and Every Time I Die without crying so much that I had to press cold spoons over my swollen eyes afterwards.Knocked Loose, a hardcore punk band from Kentucky, became a fast favourite. A week after discovering them, I found out they had a special midnight show coming up in Manchester. It felt serendipitous that they were arriving in town when I needed them most, so I booked a ticket.“I’m going to die,” I thought a few weeks later, chewing my lip with worry as the Albert Hall in Manchester exploded with activity. It was 2am when Knocked Loose finally took the stage. I pressed myself against the wall while the crowd turned into a huge, pulsing crush of bodies. People were throwing their limbs about violently, slamming into one another at full force and clambering on top of each other to get on stage, only to immediately throw themselves back into the crowd.View image in fullscreen‘I was spellbound by the music’ …Knocked Loose performing in Manchester.Photograph: Courtesy of Leoni HortonI hadn’t seen anything like it before. I was spellbound by the music, but terrified of ending up in A&E. Yet, when the lead singer, Bryan Garris, called out for more movement, I felt unable to resist. I walked forward and let the crowd swallow me.Being inside the crowd was like that moment in Dirty Dancing when Baby sees Johnny and his friends dancing in the staff quarters. I was intimidated, but possessed by a deep longing to join in. But I had no clue how and no Johnny to lift me up by the hips. Then suddenly, someone barged into my shoulder, sending me stumbling into the person beside me. I looked around anxiously, but nobody was mad and nobody was hurt. I smiled. This wasn’t scary; it was fun.I quickly felt myself become a part of the hive mind of the crowd. It was such a relief to move my body however I wanted. I didn’t care where I ended up, whom I crashed into or what I looked like. And, gloriously, there wasn’t a single sad thought about my ex in my head. I had no desire to check my phone or doomscroll through his social media. I was safe in this sweaty bubble.By ghosting my playlists, I had been desperately trying to control my feelings. The music I loved had been urging me to accept my sadness and heartbreak, but I’d pushed it away and hidden behind loud, abrasive bands. However, as the night progressed and the band raged through their songs, I began to feel those familiar difficult feelings creep in. I’d been distracted by the noise, but suddenly I was hit by the blunt realisation that hardcore was emotional, too.Underneath Knocked Loose’s noisy exterior was the same vulnerability and grief from which I had been running. The difference was that, in their moshpit, I didn’t have to mope around. With every shove and collision, my feelings were spilling out of me. I realised that it hadn’t been music causing me pain: it was me and everything I was refusing to feel or accept. The whole night felt like a weird, radical form of therapy that I’d signed up for unconsciously.Afterwards, I gradually stopped avoiding my playlists. I began letting myself experience the difficult feelings music stirred up and my broken heart started to mend. Last week, I listened tothe latest Ariana Grande albumand I didn’t so much as sniffle. Of course, some Fleetwood Mac andPhoebe Bridgerssongs still sting; I’m only human. But the sad feelings those songs inspire no longer feel so consuming.I don’t have beef with Beyoncé these days. I owe it to the people of the hardcore community, who hauled me back to my feet. Now, when I don’t feel so crazy in love, I go to a hardcore show, throw myself into a moshpit and hope it knocks some of those sad feelings loose.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsRelationshipsA moment that changed meBeyoncéPunkShareReuse this content

title: Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine review – turgid tribute to pioneering star | Classical music | The Guardian
description:
Barbican Hall, London
Julia Bullock is magnetic in this discourse on Josephine Baker, but the 100-minute piece is slow-moving and lacking in intimacy
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Barbican Hall, LondonJulia Bullock is magnetic in this discourse on Josephine Baker, but the 100-minute piece is slow-moving and lacking in intimacy
Content: Transgressive … Julia Bullock in Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenTransgressive … Julia Bullock in Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewPerle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine review – turgid tribute to pioneering starBarbican Hall, LondonJulia Bullock is magnetic in this discourse on Josephine Baker, but the 100-minute piece is slow-moving and lacking in intimacyErica JealWed 21 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosephine Bakerwas many things: a civil rights activist; a spy for the French resistance; a woman who, born into poverty, became the best-paid stage star in Europe. But before she was any of these, she was an entertainer. So one wonders what on earth she would make of Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine, a turgid 100-minute piece developed by the soprano Julia Bullock, composer Tyshawn Sorey, poet Claudia Rankine and director Peter Sellars.This was its UK premiere, although Bullock and Sorey have been performing versions of it in the US and elsewhere over the past decade. It isn’t a tribute in the usual sense, but a discourse on racial discrimination, in Baker’s day and our own. Bullock, magnetic as ever, sings and speaks alongside six musicians, who include Sorey himself on piano, drum kit and percussion, plus electric guitar, violin, alto flute, saxophone and bassoon. On a platform, in front of a saturated square of brightly coloured light, Bullock declaims Rankine’s words and sings Sorey’s music, in which Baker’s songs are deconstructed, reformed, and mostly slowed right down. A riff on Bye Bye Blackbird has guitar and saxophone sounding suspiciously like the playout on a 1980s power ballad. Later, more rewardingly, the guitar gives a highlife flavour to a version of Je t’aime. But mostly the score is bloated and the instrumental episodes don’t unify the piece so much as draw it out. Ear-splitting bass drum and tam tam indicate emotional climaxes. Everyone is mic’d up, which works against any sense of intimacy.View image in fullscreen‘Baker’s songs are deconstructed, reformed, and mostly slowed right down’ … Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Mark AllanSurtitles translate the French, laying bare the sentiments that she slipped into unsuspecting ears. “Should I be white to please you more?” Bullock sings, holding a half bow and gazing out as if simultaneously accusing us and seeking our approval. One episode alludes to Baker’s famous “danse sauvage”, for which she wore a skirt made of rubber bananas, and almost nothing else. Braless under the sheer fabric at the top of her jumpsuit – and yes, the sight of a woman’s breasts is more transgressive on theBarbicanstage today than it was in the Folies Bergères a century ago – Bullock dances, making some of Baker’s grotesquely caricatured “savage” moves, and the effect is properly disturbing. Here, Perle Noire is hard-hitting. Otherwise, it’s hard going.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicJosephine BakerBarbicanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon | Games | The Guardian
description: As video games chase spectacle, Modern Warfare 4 makes a case for putting character and consequence at the heart of its biggest battles
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: As video games chase spectacle, Modern Warfare 4 makes a case for putting character and consequence at the heart of its biggest battles
Content: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 combines large-scale battles with a story centred on the people caught up in the conflict.Photograph: ActivisionView image in fullscreenCall of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 combines large-scale battles with a story centred on the people caught up in the conflict.Photograph: ActivisionPushing Buttons newsletterGames‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weaponAs video games chase spectacle, Modern Warfare 4 makes a case for putting character and consequence at the heart of its biggest battlesDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 21 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 18.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn these strange, subdued weeks before the much-anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI, there have still been some welcome surprises. Onimusha: Way of the Sword revived a half-forgotten samurai action series with much aplomb, while Silent Hill: Townfall transported all of the franchise’s bloody, dread-filled psychological horror to … the picturesque Scottish coast. Even moreshocking to games writers, though, is the fact thatthe forthcoming Modern Warfare 4has one of the best Call of Duty campaign modes for at least six years – and might even be up there with the original Modern Warfare trilogy.The setting is an invasion of South Korea by its northern neighbour – a setup that could have fuelled a hundred instantly forgettable Netflix films, but hasproved controversialin a video game. The authoritarian regime has a new (fictitious) ruler and a powerful experimental weapon, which it’s not afraid to use as the opening gambit in an explosive attack. You take on the role of Park Hyun Jun, a conscripted South Korean soldier who, along with his small unit of similarly inexperienced grunts, gets caught in the firestorm as cities burn and enemy paratroopers fill the skies.On the other side of the globe, meanwhile, series hero Capt John Price has gone rogue, teaming up with cartel boss Valeria Garza to track down his nemesis, Makarov. How these narrative strands intertwine is the propulsive engine of the story, and along the way this game throws an arsenal of gigantic set-piece battles at you, edging you closer to a layered finale.Most positive reviews of the campaign mode have mentioned how the story combines its own ideas with themes and plots from the previous titles. So how did the game’s lead developer, Infinity Ward, set about creating a story that could support a giant first-person juggernaut such as CoD? “The DNA of a Modern Warfare story is that it is something you believe could happen in the real world,” says narrative director Jeff Negus. “‘Does it feel grounded?’ is the first question. Additionally, we ask, ‘What is going to resonate with a modern audience?’ It was important to us not to tell the same story again, not to show the same characters being the same people, because what they’ve been through has deeply affected who they are.”View image in fullscreenInfinity Ward says the story of Modern Warfare 4 puts its characters and their relationships at the centre of the action.Photograph: Infinity WardInfinity Ward brought in a range of military and cultural consultants to ensure the story’s accuracy. “Some of our actors were conscripted in Korea, so they’re able to identify with some of what’s happening,” says Negus. “We use a wide array of military consultants across many different branches and types of service. Our dialect coach, June Yoon, was invaluable because he understands the dialectical differences between North and South Korea, and he could help us reword lines in a more colloquially appropriate way.”One key element of the game is the combination of quieter, character-led narrative moments and apocalyptic action set-pieces. “There is a very healthy symbiosis between both parts,” says Negus. “We start with strong narrative and gameplay, and the very first thing that we ask is, ‘How can we interweave these things in a way that feels intentional?’ One must be complementary of the other, in such a way that we’re able to say, ‘I can’t imagine telling the story without this mechanic.’” Negus compares it to an explosion in an action movie, saying: “It can be spectacular, but if you don’t know the people who are a part of it, it won’t be meaningful. Back when I was working at Naughty Dog, and now with the team here, we talk about player-protagonist parity, and how, when you feel what the character feels, you’re all a part of the same story – the audience gets to be in on it.”Surprisingly, iteration is an important part of the process – even though this is a game filled with cinematic sequences that may have to be filmed and animated early in the development process. “We certainly map out the story visually,” says Negus. “Justin [Harris], our lead writer, will put in these story beats, much like a season of television or a movie would do, but we do it with levels. And sometimes we’ll need to move things around, particularly in a story where we can shift the timeline in certain ways. When someone comes up with something, it gets moved around, it gets debated and analysed, and it’s road-tested pretty hard before it becomes inked.”To me, the Modern Warfare 4 campaign is a story of dysfunctional families – the actual North Korean ruling family, Park Hyun Jun’s ragtag squad and Price’s Task Force 141. The tensions between these groups gives the story its human underpinning. Disaster movies usually centre on one or two main characters so that we, the audience, get to experience the drama vicariously through them.Infinity Ward has successfully brought that structural and emotional toolkit to the finale of the Modern Warfare series, and that’s at least partly why it works. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 might not be a Pulitzer prize-winning story, but in these odd days before the arrival of GTA VI it certainly gives you something to think about – and people to root for – as you blast away with your rifle, grenade launcher or helicopter gunship.What to playView image in fullscreenOver the Hill swaps military action for off-road exploration, inviting players to discover its landscapes at their own pace.Photograph: Funselektor LabsIf you like the look of extreme off-road driving sims such as MudRunner, but are put off by their unyielding difficulty level,Over the Hillis definitely for you. It’s a cosy exploration game where you drive a 4x4 through a bright low-poly landscape of babbling brooks and lush woodlands, occasionally using a winch to get out of muddy puddles or up steep hills.Along the way, you unlock cabins to allow fast travel and visit a mechanic to customise your vehicle. Spot an interesting bird or critter and you can photograph it, adding it to your scrapbook. The pace is slow and gentle, but there is a fulfilling challenge in mastering the winch and getting yourself out of tight spots.I wish more games simply gave you a world to explore and the tools to do it and then left you alone – although, if the solitude gets to you, there’s a co-op multiplayer mode too, so you can disappear into the wilderness with pals. Bliss.Available on:PC (coming to Switch, PS5 and Xbox in 2027)Estimated playtime:10-plus hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenThe Game Boy Museum’s catalogue has been adapted to run on a cartridge for Nintendo’s original handheld console.Photograph: Marcel Pflug“Let me be honest from the start: nobody was waiting for this.” Thus begins alovely Eurogamer featureon theGameBoy Museum, or more accurately, the museum’s creator, Marcel Pflug, and his attempt to fit the whole of hiswebsiteon to a cart that actually plays on a Game Boy. I love projects like this, which use games and games hardware as repositories of information. See also:The Uncensored Library, which collects banned books inside a Minecraft server.A question that haunts me, as a 55-year-old, is: “Why do I still play video games?” People are often ecstatic to tell me there are more constructive things I could be doing. I enjoyedthis essayby Lene Clement aboutthe non-utilitarian nature of gamesand the annoying lifestyle influencers who instruct us that “uselessness” is a bad thing because everything has to be productive now.I am readingThere Is No Antimemetics Divisionby Sam Hughes, better known asqntm. Now out inpaperback, it’s a novel about a government agency tasked with finding and battling “antimemetic” entities that feed on humans but can’t be seen, remembered or recorded. It’s a very video game-like premise and the staccato, almost episodic nature of the chapters reminds me of game missions. This is very much a recommendation.What to clickFrom Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six TacticsThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K eraPenguin Colony – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenGetting started on game design can be as easy as signing up for a course and building a prototype with software such as GameMaker.Illustration: Roman Motsak/Getty ImagesThis week’s question fromKatevia email is something I think all gamers have wondered:“If I had an idea for a game butno idea of how to create it, who would you suggest I contact? It’s more a game to learn things rather than [one with] combator sci-fi, etc.”Remember that old saying, often attributed to Thomas Edison: “Genius is 10% inspiration, and 90% perspiration”? The same goes for video-game design, or indeed film-making, painting and writing novels. Nobody will pay you for an idea, because everyone is having them practically all the time. The most realistic way to realise your idea is to sign up foragame development course, where you may find like-minded people who enjoy your concept and want to work with you. You could invest in an application such asGameMakerand start building your own prototype, or you could study game design via books or YouTube videos.I also highly recommendA Theory of Funby Raphy Koster,The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lensesby Jesse Schell andChallenges for Game Designersby Brenda Romero and Ian Schreiber. All of these provide a really good way to structure your ideas and think about how they may work as a functioning game. This way you can work on a design document that lays out all the rules and systems of your game, and this will help you discover if a) there’s something practical in it, and b) you have the drive and time to work on a game project. A great idea is a great start, but it is really only ever that: a start.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I closed my eyes and stuck my finger on a map of western Europe: ‘This is where we’re going on holiday!’ | France holidays | The Guardian
description: Sick of relying on internet recommendations, I left my next destination to chance. Luckily, it led to me discovering a magical hamlet in the Cévennes mountains of south-central France
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sick of relying on internet recommendations, I left my next destination to chance. Luckily, it led to me discovering a magical hamlet in the Cévennes mountains of south-central France
Content: The view from the cottage veranda.Photograph: Camilla YatesView image in fullscreenThe view from the cottage veranda.Photograph: Camilla YatesFrance holidaysI closed my eyes and stuck my finger on a map of western Europe: ‘This is where we’re going on holiday!’Sick of relying on internet recommendations, I left my next destination to chance. Luckily, it led to me discovering a magical hamlet in the Cévennes mountains of south-central FranceCamilla YatesWed 21 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn unruly rabble bursts on to the street: a noisy eruption, bubbling towards us. This isn’t closing time on the Croisette in Cannes. A flock of sheep bustles past our cottage towards the shade of a huge chestnut tree, driven by three generations of herders and their dogs. The waterlike cacophony of their bells slows until only the odd tink tink punctuates the cicadas’ hum. The sheep graze, the shepherds doze off, and the mountain hamlet is still again.My partner and I had set off by Eurostar less than 24 hours before, yet this place felt a world away from the ad agency where I work.We’d booked cheap tickets to Paris months ago, intending to plan a trip on from there by train. As our departure approached, Instagram seemed to be full of aspirational, yet similar, holiday photos, and almost every other TikTok post I flicked past offered the promise of a hidden destination … discovered.I find ratings, reviews and recommendations just as reassuring as the next person, especially when faced with a limited holiday allowance. The safety of the search bar helps to give me the confidence that I’m spending my hard earned money as wisely as possible. I work in a world that runs on data and optimisation and I love it, but I wondered whether I’d optimised the adventure out of my own holidays.double quotation markI wondered whether I’d optimised the adventure out of my own holidaysSo, we tried a simple experiment. We closed down the tabs and opened a map of western Europe. Embracing a bit of low-tech randomness, we chose to let chance decide our trip.I shut my eyes and we promised to go wherever my finger landed. I waved my hand like a magic wand and pointed, then took a deep breath, eyes still closed. What if we ended up in some industrial wasteland? But we were in luck. My finger landed upon the commune of Saint-Hilaire-de-Lavit in Cévennes, a place we’d never heard of and almost certainly would never have found by searching “places to go in France”.View image in fullscreenA shepherd and flock in Les Ayres.Photograph: Camilla YatesAfter overnighting in Paris, a three-hour fast train zipped us down to Montpellier, where we hired a car. We stopped for provisions in a Lidl on the edge of town, stocking up for the whole trip – we weren’t expecting to find any shops at our journey’s end. A short drive inland, and the roads began to get narrower and more sparsely populated. As they climbed and zigzagged into this south-east corner of the Massif Central, we entered a south of France far removed from the honeypots served up by algorithms.We pulled into a grassy layby on a high mountain pass where there was one other car parked. Had we arrived? We’d followed the cottage owner’s directions as there was no signal here for Google Maps, so it was hard to tell. Stretching our legs in the fresh, cool air, the first thing we noticed was the quiet. No traffic, no tourists. Just stillness. But the languid buzz of big insects flying by and the whirring chorus of cicadas told us this place was alive.double quotation markNo traffic, no tourists, just stillness. But the whirring chorus of cicadas told us this place was aliveSquinting into the low sun, we saw someone waving. Our host, Guilaine, had appeared as if by magic and was beckoning us to the cottage a little farther down the road. We had found the hamlet of Les Ayres: a cluster of maybe 10 stone buildings, 800 metres above sea level. The rough-walled dwellings huddled either side of the narrow road, making the most of the tiny strand of level ground before the mountain’s spine fell away into steep forest. A long wooden awning and some outdoor tables suggested a cafe opposite our cottage, but the building was shuttered, and Les Ayres’ only potential customers seemed to be ourselves and Guilaine. She took us to the back of our accommodation, to a veranda that looked out over chestnut and pine-clad mountains rolling into the horizon. It’s a landscape that appears wild but has actually been shaped by farming, forestry and the seasonal movement of livestock for thousands of years.The next morning, as I watched the sheep and their guardians settle down in the shade, I felt the ancientness of the place. Shepherds must have moved their flocks along the same path and most likely slept under the same chestnut trees for centuries. Traditional farming practices endure here in part because the area is veined with crystal-clear mountain streams, meaning animals traversing the paths are never too far from a drink. So rather than opening the internet, we let these ancient tracks, known asdrailles, guide our hikes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘We discovered that shady, secluded river pools were waiting for us on all the paths that led down from our cottage.’Photograph: Camilla YatesWe took sweaty, daylong expeditions without seeing another human or hearing the sound of cars. The forests protected us from the worst of the sun’s blaze but, on our first trek, the real treat came when we rounded a corner to find that what we thought was the sound of wind in the pines was actually water gushing through a narrow gorge below us. Another couple of switchbacks and we arrived at a deep, clear pool created as the stream carved a corner into the rock. Dappled sunlight filtered down through trees clinging to the steep-sided valley, creating spotlights for damselflies to dart through. We stopped for a picnic and a swim in the freezing mountain water, picking wild strawberries from the bank for dessert.We discovered that these shady, secluded river pools were waiting for us on all the paths that led down from our cottage. As well as being the ultimate pit stops for mid-hike refreshment, they were teeming with wildlife – tadpoles wriggled in the shallows, fish flickered in the depths and a huge variety of butterflies, dragonflies and other insects skimmed the surface. We even saw a snake swimming across water we’d been submerged in just minutes before.We spent our last afternoon reading on a rock, summoning the energy to walk back up the mountain (one drawback of staying high up on a pass). We watched the sun swing over the water and the light change as the day wore on. When the air began to cool, we worked our way back towards the cottage. As the path turned into an empty, single-track road, a car approached – a big event after so much seclusion. It was Guilaine – the only person apart from the shepherds we’d encountered.In the evening, as the light faded, the sound of brass band practice drifted towards our veranda. Later, owls called to each other and a distant wild boar screeched into the quiet night. None of this had appeared in my search results. There was no review promising unexpected trumpeting, no listicle recommending the best pool for swimming among tadpoles, and no algorithm that could have told me where the sheep would pass on that first morning. We hadn’t looked at our phones for days – maybe that was the real discovery.Explore more on these topicsFrance holidaysEurope holidaysRail travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to turn brown bananas into the best vegan bread of the bunch – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Use over-ripe fruit to flesh out this loaf with chocolate, spelt and miso – truly top banana
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Use over-ripe fruit to flesh out this loaf with chocolate, spelt and miso – truly top banana
Content: Tom Hunt’s chocolate, spelt and miso banana bread.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s chocolate, spelt and miso banana bread.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodHow to turn brown bananas into the best vegan bread of the bunch – recipeUse over-ripe fruit to flesh out this loaf with chocolate, spelt and miso – truly top bananaTom HuntWed 21 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter nine years, I can’t believe I’ve never written a recipe for banana bread for this column, so it had better be a good one, especially after I picked up a huge bunch of brown bananas at the corner shop for next to nothing the other day. This is a vegan bread made with olive oil instead of butter and with the mashed bananas acting as a binder in place of eggs; I’ve also added some miso to boost the umami and overall satiety – the salt enhances the sugar, boosting the sweetness while rounding it off nicely. In the interest of biodiversity and flavour, I’ve used wholemeal spelt flour, but any will do.Chocolate, spelt and miso banana breadThis has become our go-to banana bread at home because it has crazy levels of deliciousness. The recipe is inspired by a plant-based banana bread recipe I found onLaura Wright’s wonderful The First Mess website, and my tweaked version of her loaf uses extra-virgin olive oil and wholegrain flour for nutrition, flavour and biodiversity; I’ve also used miso instead of salt, to bump up the umami factor.Makes1 loaf280g wholemeal spelt flour1 tsp ground cinnamon1 tsp baking powder1 tsp bicarbonate of soda150g dark chocolate chunks150g walnut pieces6 very ripe bananas120ml maple syrup, or brown sugar120ml extra-virgin olive oil1tsp vanilla extract1 tbsp miso, or ½ tsp saltHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and grease and line a 1kg bread tin. Mix the flour, cinnamon, baking powder and bicarb in a large bowl. Set aside about seven pieces each of the chocolate and walnuts to decorate the loaf later, then stir the rest into the flour mix until well distributed. Peel five of the brown bananas and, in a second bowl, mash them with the maple syrup, olive oil, vanilla extract and miso. Add the banana mix to the bowl of dry ingredients, stirring until properly combined, then pour into the bread tin and level out the top. Peel the last brown banana, cut it in half lengthways and arrange on top of the dough with the reserved chocolate and walnut pieces. Bake for an hour, until just cooked through, then leave to cool before slicing.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteBreadFruitBakingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mushroom magic: Alissa Timoshkina’s eastern European soup and stew recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Two dishes that may feel like “home” to cooks connected to the region
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Two dishes that may feel like “home” to cooks connected to the region
Content: Alissa Timoshkina’s mushroommačankastew with potato pancakes.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenAlissa Timoshkina’s mushroommačankastew with potato pancakes.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.FoodMushroom magic: Alissa Timoshkina’s eastern European soup and stew recipesA tangy mushroom stew with potato pancakes for dipping, and a rustic but versatile cabbage and mushroom soupAlissa TimoshkinaWed 21 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 03.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAthick, creamy and tangy wild mushroom stew, inspired by Belarusianmačankaand traditionally served with thick buckwheat pancakes for dipping. My version, however, features another Slovak dish in the form oflokše, which are crepes or flatbreads made with mashed potato dough. The result issogood. Then, a simple, seasonal soup made with just a handful of ingredients that captures the heart and soul of eastern European soup making. While it doesn’t belong to any single location, I hope it will taste like “home” to readers connected to the region.Mushroommačankastew with potato pancakes (pictured top)I first came across this dish a few years ago when working on my previous cookbook,Kapusta. The recipe was brought up in a conversation with a wonderful food writer of Belarusian lineage, Anastasia Zolotarev, whom I’d asked to contribute to the book. Mačanka did not make it into Kapusta, but I was very glad to see it in Anastasia’s own debut book,Sour Cherries and Sunflowers. Looking into the origins of the dish, I have discovered that mačanka exists in Slovak cuisine, too, where it appears as a thick soup infused with sauerkraut brine – oh my! Both dishes are rooted in central and eastern European peasant culture of simple, hearty, nutrient-rich stews made with a handful of accessible ingredients. So here is my own play on both recipes.Prep20 minCook1 hr 30 minServes4–6For the stew100gsalted butter1 onion, peeled and thinly sliced2 garlic cloves, peeled and minced1tsp fresh or dried thyme600gchestnutmushrooms, slicedSalt and black pepper, to taste30gdried porcini, soaked in 250ml just-boiled water150mlsauerkraut brine, or to taste30gplainflour300mlsinglecream2tbsp chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley, to garnishFor the topping2tbsp vegetable oil1 onion, peeled and finely sliced1 small pinch sugar1 small pinch saltFor the pancakes350gpotatoes, quartered125gplainflour, plus extra for dusting1 small egg, beaten1 pinch saltButter, melted, for brushingMelt half the butter in a large saucepan on a medium heat, add the onion, garlic and thyme, and fry for 10 minutes, until the onion softens. Add the sliced fresh mushrooms and a generous pinch of salt, cover and cook for about eight minutes, until they release their liquid. Strain the porcini through muslin, reserving the liquid. Rinse the porcini to get rid of any residual grit, then chop finely and add them and the reserved soaking liquid, plus the sauerkraut brine to the pan. Season with black pepper and simmer on a low heat for 15-20 minutes, to develop the flavours.In a second pan, melt the remaining butter, stir in the flour and cook, stirring constantly to avoid any lumps, for two to three minutes, until lightly golden. Gradually whisk in the cream to make a smooth sauce. Stir this into the mushroom base and cook uncovered for about five minutes, to thicken.To make the topping, heat the oil, then fry the sliced onion with the sugar and salt until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen towel. Top the stew with the fried onions when ready to serve, and don’t forget a sprinkle of fresh parsley!To make the pancakes, put the quartered potatoes in a small pan of salted water, bring to a boil, then simmer for 20-25 minutes, until cooked through. Drain thoroughly, then mash well and leave to cool completely.In a large bowl, combine the cooled mash with the flour, egg and salt, and mix to form a dough. Transfer to a well-floured surface, roll into a 5cm-diameter log, then cut into 12 equal pieces. Roll each piece into a ball, then use the rolling pin to flatten each ball into a 3mm-thick disc.Put a dry, nonstick frying pan on a medium heat. Lay the pancakes in the hot pan (cook them in batches, if need be) in the hot pan one at a time, and cook for two to three minutes on each side, until golden brown spots appear. Remove, brush one side with butter, then stack and keep warm under a clean tea towel. Serve with the mushroom stew.Cabbage and mushroom soupView image in fullscreenAlissa Timoshkina’s simple cabbage and mushroom soup.This soup is wonderfully versatile, easily adapting to the seasons and whatever ingredients you have to hand. Swap fresh cabbage for sauerkraut or fresh mushrooms for dried in this hearty staple that comes together almost effortlessly.Prep15 minCook40 minServes4–62tbsp neutral vegetable oil1 onion, peeled and diced2 carrots, grated1 pinch caraway seeds1 pinch dried thyme1 pinchsalt250gchestnutmushrooms, chopped½ small cabbage(350g), shredded2–4 potatoes, diced1½ litresvegetable broth1 bay leafFresh dill, to garnishBlack pepper, to tastePut the oil in a lidded stockpot or saucepan on a medium-low heat, add the onion, carrots, caraway, thyme and salt, and fry for eight to 10 minutes.Add the mushrooms, cook for another five to eight minutes, or until their liquid is released, then add the cabbage, potatoes, vegetable broth and bay leaf. Simmer gently for 15-20 minutes, until the potatoes are cooked through but the cabbage still retains a little bite. Garnish with plenty of dill and black pepper.These recipes are edited extracts from Lozhka: Eastern European Soups, Stews & Other Things We Eat with a Spoon, by Alissa Timoshkina, published by Quadrille at £28.
